Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
First Chapter.
That which, having been attained, is capable of destroying the fear of worldly existence and the suffering of the yogis, and which is highly honored by those of perfectly pure minds—
May that pair of lotus feet of Hari purify you—those feet by which he successively traversed the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. || 1 ||
May she protect you—she who is the sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance in the minds of all practitioners of yoga and the cause of liberation for the ascetic;
she who, as the deluding Māyā of the Lord, is the destroyer of pure and impure intellects in this multitude of living beings.
Having prostrated before the Lord, the primordial of the worlds, the Supreme Person who consists of eternal knowledge, I shall proclaim the Purāṇa named after Kālikā.
Having prostrated before Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, who was staying near the Himalayas, the sages Kamaṭha and others questioned him. (4)
O Blessed One, you have correctly explained the reality of all scriptures,
having extracted the essence from all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
O Brahmin, whatever doubt we had regarding all the Vedas and the Shastras has been severed by you, just as a mass of darkness is dispelled by the sun.
O best of the twice-born, foremost among those who grant longevity, by your grace we have become free from all doubt regarding the Vedas and the Shastras in every respect. (7)
"O Brahmin, we have accomplished our purpose by having studied from you in its entirety the Dharmaśāstra, along with its secret doctrines, as it was spoken by the Self-born One. (8)
We wish to hear further how, in the past, Kālī deluded Hara, the Lord and ascetic, by means of the form of Satī.
How did she disturb Hara— the supreme among ascetics, a self-controlled man whose abode is always meditation, and who is turned away from worldly existence?
Or how was the auspicious Satī born from the wives of Dakṣa? And how did Hara set his mind upon the act of taking a wife? (11)
Or how was it that in former times Satī, having abandoned her body due to Dakṣa’s wrath, was born again as the daughter of Himavat, and how did she come [to this state] once more? (12)
O best of the twice-born, explain all of this in detail: how did she again take away half the body of the enemy of Smara?
"There is no other who can dispel our doubt; there shall be none equal to you.
O best of Brahmins, knower of the self, act in such a way that we may understand this. (14)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, all you sages, to this which is more secret than the secret, my own teaching—meritorious, auspicious, perfectly bestowing knowledge, and supremely granting desires. (15)
Brahmā spoke this to the high-souled Nārada when questioned by him; he, in turn, told it to the Bālakhilyas.
Then the high-souled Bālakhilyas spoke again;
he [in turn] told it to the sage Yavakrīta, and he related it to Asita.
O twice-born ones, Asita related this to me in detail;
I shall now relate this ancient story to you,
having bowed down to the Supreme Self, the wielder of the discus, the Lord of the universe.

Salutations to the Creator who has the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest, whose form consists of existence and non-existence and manifestation, who is both gross and subtle in form, and whose form is the universe itself.
Salutations to the eternal one, whose knowledge is eternal, who is changeless, who is radiant energy, whose nature is both knowledge and ignorance, and who is the form of time. 20.

To the stainless one, who is devoid of the six waves and the like, to the dispassionate one, to the all-pervading one whose form is the universe, and to the agent of creation, preservation, and destruction. || 21 ||
I bow to that Supreme Light, whose nature is the innermost within, who is meditated upon by yogis who contemplate the final depths of the Vedānta.
Having propitiated him alone, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created all beings, including the gods, humans, and others. (23)
Having created the Prajāpatis, headed by Dakṣa, according to the prescribed rule—
namely Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, as well as Aṅgiras and Kratu— [he established them].
And when he created the ten mind-born sons— Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Pracetas, and Bhṛgu.
Then, from their minds, a beautiful woman of excellent form was born.
Known by the name Sandhyā, she is the Gāyatrī of the morning twilight;
such a one exists neither in the world of the gods, nor among mortals, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala),
for she shall remain endowed with perfect qualities throughout all three periods of time.
O best of the twice-born, she shines with her naturally beautiful, dark-blue mass of hair, like a peahen with its variegated plumage during the rainy season. 27.
Reddish-brown and soiled by locks of hair reaching to her ears, it shone like the beautiful bow of the Lord of the Gods or like the lovely crescent moon. 28.
Her pair of eyes, dark like a full-blown blue lotus, shone with a flickering movement resembling that of a startled doe. (29)
O best of the twice-born, her pair of beautiful eyebrows was naturally tremulous, extending as far as her ears, dark blue, and resembling a bow marked with a fish.
From the sunken region below the midpoint of her eyebrows, her long and prominent nose extends;
from her forehead, her loveliness seems to flow like the juice from a sesame flower.
That face, possessing the luster of a red lotus and the splendor of the full moon, shone with the crimson glow of its bimba-like lips, enchanting with its passion.
Furthermore, her face, filled with the qualities of beauty and charm,
seemed as if her two breasts were striving to reach all the way down to her chin.
O Brahmins, her breasts were shaped like lotus buds, full, lofty, and closely set; though her face was somewhat pale, they enchanted even the sages.

All beheld her waist, marked by folds of skin and diminished in the middle as if it could be grasped by a fist, appearing like a garment upon the body and equal in power to the god of love himself. (35)
Her pair of thighs shone—thick, elongated like the trunk of an elephant, resembling the trunk of a tusker, soft and slow-moving. (36)
Her pair of feet, as red as land-lotuses, was graced by beautiful heels;
with toes clustered like petals, they resembled the arrows of the flower-weaponed god of love.
She was beautiful to behold, slender, covered with a fine line of body hair, her face perspiring, with long eyes and a lovely smile. (38)
Seeing her, who possessed a pair of beautiful ears, was lovely, deep in three places, and elevated in six,
the Creator rose up and reflected within his heart.
Dakṣa and the others who were the creators, as well as Marīci and the rest who were born of his mind—
all of them, filled with longing, meditated upon her as soon as they beheld that woman of excellent complexion.
"What will her role be in this creation, or for whom will this most excellent woman belong?"—thus they all thought with great eagerness. (41)
O best of sages, as Brahmā was reflecting thus, a person emerged from his mind, powerful and manifest. || 42 ||
Having the yellow luster of gold dust, broad-chested, with a beautiful nose,
with well-rounded thighs, hips, and shanks, with dark hair encircling his head,
with joined eyebrows, restless, and with a face resembling the full moon. || 43 ||
His chest is as broad as a door-panel and is adorned with a line of body hair;
his thick, rounded arms are like the trunk of a white elephant;
and his palms, eyes, face, feet, and hands are slightly reddish. || 44 ||

With a slender waist and beautiful teeth, possessing the neck of an elephant in rut, with eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, and delighting the sense of smell with the scent of saffron; with a shell-like neck, bearing the fish-banner, tall in stature, and having the makara as his vehicle. || 45 ||
Armed with the five flowers as his weapons, impetuous, and adorned with a flowery bow,
the handsome youth whirled his two eyes with a sidelong glance.
Seeing that place, which was perfumed by fragrant breezes and frequented by those imbued with the erotic sentiment, Dakṣa and the other mental sons of Brahmā were moved.
Then Marīci and the other nine, their minds filled with wonder, experienced the utmost longing and attained a state of mental agitation.
Having beheld that Creator, the Ordainer, the Lord of the worlds, that person bowed down and spoke with his neck bent in humility. (49)
The man said:
"O Brahmin, what deed shall I perform? Enjoin me to that which is right; for a man, O Ordainer, shines when engaged in what is appropriate."
"Grant me that name which is appropriate, as well as a place and a wife, since you, O Lord of the worlds, are the creator of the universes. (51)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus heard the words of that high-souled being,
he remained silent for a moment, astonished even at his own creation.
Then, having thoroughly restrained his mind and properly cast aside all wonder,
Brahmā spoke to the Puruṣa, bringing to mind the purpose of that deed.
Brahmā said:
"With this beautiful form and with your five flower-arrows,
deluding both men and women, carry out the eternal creation."
Neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor kinnaras and mahoragas;
neither an asura, nor a daitya, nor vidyādharas and rākṣasas [could do so]. || 55 ||
Neither yakṣas nor piśācas, neither bhūtas nor vināyakas;
neither guhyakas nor siddhas, neither humans nor birds [dwell there]. (56)
Neither the domestic animals, nor the wild beasts, nor the insects, moths, and aquatic creatures—all these shall cease to exist, for none of them shall be targets for my arrow. (57)
Whether it be I, or Vāsudeva, or Sthāṇu, the Supreme Person—we shall all come under your control; what need is there for other living beings? (58)
Entering the hearts of living beings always in a concealed form,
and having yourself become the cause of their happiness, perform the eternal creation.
May that mind always be the primary target for your flower-arrows;
may you eternally produce intoxication and delight in all living beings.
Thus, I have again described to you the activity that sets creation in motion; furthermore, I shall also declare your name, which will be appropriate for you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the best of the gods then looked upon the faces of those born of his mind and,
in an instant, sat down comfortably upon his lotus throne.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Kāma," in the glorious Śrī-Kālikā Purāṇa. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all those sages, understanding his intention, [spoke].
Then Marīci, Atri, and the others gave him the appropriate name.
Having learned the news from elsewhere merely by observing his face,
Dakṣa and the other creators gave him a dwelling place and a wife.
Then, having deliberated upon names, the twice-born sages, headed by Marīci,
spoke together to that Supreme Person, O best of the twice-born.
The sages said:
"Since you were born from us after we had agitated our minds in such a manner,
therefore you shall become famous in the world by the name Manmatha."
In the worlds you can take any form at will; indeed, no one equal to you exists.
Therefore, O Mind-born One, become renowned by the name Kāma as well.
Because of your intoxication, you shall be named Madana; and because of Śambhu’s pride, you shall be Darpaka.
Furthermore, you will become renowned in the world by the name Kandarpa as well.
The power that belongs to your swift-moving arrows shall no longer exist;
such power shall belong to the weapons of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Brahmā.

In heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, and in the eternal world of Brahmā—all these are your abodes, since you are all-pervading. What need is there for further specific praise? In general, there is no one equal to you.
Wherever there may be a living being, or even grasses and trees,
let your abode be there, reaching as far as the realm of Brahmā.
"O Puruṣottama, this Dakṣa, who is indeed the primordial Prajāpati, will himself give his beautiful wife to you as you desire. (10)
And this maiden of beautiful form, born from the mind of Brahmā, shall become renowned in all the world by the name Sandhyā. || 11 ||
Since this excellent woman was born perfectly while Brahmā was meditating,
she shall therefore be known in this world by the name Sandhyā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, all those sages, the best of the twice-born, remained silent;
looking toward the face of Brahmā, they stood before him with bowed heads.
Then Kāma also took up his bow made of flowers,
renowned as "Unmādana," which was curved like the eyebrows of a beautiful woman.
Then those best of the twice-born took up five flowery missiles:
Harṣaṇa, Rocana, Mohana, and likewise Śoṣaṇa. (15)
Even those things that cause delusion to the Sage, such as the notions of "killing" and so forth, were contemplated by him there in his concealed form, as he reached a firm conclusion. (16)
Whatever eternal task has been assigned to me by Brahmā,
that I shall perform right here in the presence of the sages and the Creator.
The sages abide here, as does Prajāpati himself;
this very twilight was just now described by Brahmā in these words.
"I am Viṣṇu and Hara as well; we are all subject to your weapons. What need is there for other creatures? Therefore, I shall act on your behalf. (20)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus reflected and reached a firm conclusion in his mind,
the god of love discharged the flowery arrows of his flower-bow.
Then Kāma, the best of archers, assuming the ālīḍha stance and drawing his bow with great effort, formed it into the shape of a circle.
O best of sages, when that bow was strung, fragrant breezes blew there, perfectly causing great delight.
Then the Enchanter deluded all those mind-born sons, beginning with Dhātṛ, individually with his flower-arrows.
Then all those sages were deluded by the four-faced one;
being mentally deluded, they experienced a slight transformation from the very beginning.
All of them, their passion greatly increased, gazed repeatedly at the twilight with agitated hearts; for a woman is that which increases intoxication.
Then Madana, having deluded them all again and again,
acted in such a way that they experienced the various transformations of their senses.
When the Creator, his senses aroused, then gazed upon her,
at that very moment forty-nine states of being were produced from his body.
O twice-born ones, the gestures such as *vivvoka* and others, as well as the sixty-four arts, arose in Sandhyā when she was pierced by the arrows of Kandarpa.
Being gazed upon by them, she too repeatedly manifested expressions such as side-long glances and coy concealment, born from the falling of the arrows of Kandarpa.
Naturally beautiful, the twilight shone intensely as it produced those states born of passion, like the celestial river with its slender waves.
Then, observing the evening twilight while his body was filled with vital breaths, Prajāpati conceived a desire.
Then all those sages, headed by Marīci and Atri,
as well as Dakṣa and the other best of the twice-born, attained the Vaikārika-indriya state.
Seeing Brahmā along with Dakṣa, Marīci, and the others,
as well as Sandhyā, thus engaged in their respective duties, Madana then became confident.
When this task was assigned to me by Brahmā, his soul then became permeated with the conviction that "this too can be accomplished by me. (35)
Then Śambhu, stationed in the sky, having seen Brahmā in such a state,
laughed at Dakṣa and his mind-born sons, and they too laughed along with him.
Laughing at them all again and again amidst shouts of "Well done!",
the bull-bannered god, O best of the twice-born, spoke these words while putting them to shame.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, how has this state of desire arisen in you?
Having seen your own daughter, this is not fitting for those who follow the Vedas. (38)
"As a mother, so is a sister; as a sister, so is a daughter.
This is indeed the settled conclusion of the Vedic path that has issued from your own mouth.
O Creator, how then have you forgotten it for the sake of mere desire?"
O Brahmā, O four-faced one, how has this entire world been shattered by that wretched desire? O Creator, how was your fortitude destroyed? (40)
Why is it that those exclusively devoted to yoga always possess divine vision? And how was it that Dakṣa, Marīci, and others had minds so full of longing for women? 41.
How is it that even Kāma, dull-witted and ignorant of the proper time, having now attained his opportunity, has made you all his targets—he of such meager intellect? (42)
"Fie on that best of sages, whose beloved women forcibly draw away his fortitude and immerse even his mind in sensual desires! (43)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Giriśa,
the Lord of the World was instantly drenched with sweat that became doubly intense due to shame.
Then, having restrained his sensory agitation, the four-faced one abandoned that twilight, which had assumed a form according to his desire, even though he wished to seize it.
O best of the twice-born, from that body the water of dharma fell;
from it were born the classes of ancestors known as the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣadas. (46)
All of them resembled crushed collyrium; they possessed blossoming, living eyes, were supremely self-controlled, meritorious, and were entirely turned away from worldly existence. || 47 ||
Sixty-four thousand are proclaimed as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs,
and likewise eighty-six thousand are the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, O twice-born ones.
From the water of the Dharma that fell upon the ground from the body of Dakṣa, these excellent women were born, endowed with every virtue. (49)
She was slender-limbed, with a thin waist and a beautiful line of fine hair;
she had soft limbs, lovely teeth, and a radiance like refined gold.
At that time, the six sages headed by Marīci— namely Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, and Aṅgiras— restrained the activity of their senses except for their procreative functions.
And from those four, beginning with Ṛtu, who fell upon the earth, the hosts of Pitṛs were born, O best of the twice-born. (52)

The Soma-drinkers (Somapās) and the Ājya-drinkers (Ājyapās) by name, as well as others known as the Sukālins—all of them are proclaimed as the Havis-eaters (Havirbhujs), who carry the offerings to the ancestors (Kavyavāhas). || 53 ||
The sons of Ṛtu were the Soma-pās; those of Vasiṣṭha were the Sukālins;
the sons of Pulastya were known as the Ājyapas; and the sons of Aṅgiras were the Haviṣmants.
Then, O best of Brahmins, when those [groups] beginning with the Agniṣvāttas had been born among the classes of ancestors of the worlds, the Kavyavāhas appeared on all sides.
Brahmā is the grandfather of all beings;
Sandhyā is the mother of the ancestors (Pitṛs), since she was born for that purpose. || 56 ||
Then, humiliated by the words of Śaṅkara, that Grandfather suddenly became enraged at Kandarpa, his face contorted with a frown.
Having already understood his intention, that Manmatha too,
fearing the Lord of Creatures (Śiva) and Brahmā, quickly withdrew his arrows.
Then, O best of the twice-born, listen with composed minds to what Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, did when overcome by anger. (59)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Bewildering of Brahmā," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The Third Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thereupon, the lotus-born Lord of the World was overcome with anger.
He blazed forth with exceeding power, like a fire desiring to consume everything.
And Kāma said to the Lord: "O Bestower of Boons, since he has struck me with his flower-arrows in your presence, let him obtain the fruit thereof. (2)
O Mahādeva, having performed an exceedingly difficult deed, Kandarpa, deluded by pride, shall be consumed by the fire of your eye. (3)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the Creator himself cursed Kāma in the presence of Vyomakeśa and the self-restrained sages.
Then, having heard that most dreadful curse, the Lord of Rati became terrified; instantly abandoning his arrows, he appeared before him in person.
And he spoke these words to Brahmā, along with Dakṣa and Marīci; his speech was truthful yet faltering with fear, for fear indeed causes the loss of one's virtues.
Manmatha said:
"O Brahman, for what reason have I been cursed by you so terribly? O Lord of the World, I am innocent toward you, who follow the path of justice. (7)
"O Lord, as for that deed which you yourself said I should do, a curse is not appropriate for me in that matter, since nothing else was done by me. (8)
"I am Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu; all of us are within the range of your arrows"—this which was spoken by you has also been tested by me. (9)
"O Brahmin, there is no fault of mine in this matter, for I am innocent.
O Lord of the World, appease this terrible curse upon me."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his, the Creator, the Lord of the worlds,
replied repeatedly with compassion to Madana, whose self was restrained.
Brahmā said:
"Since this Sandhyā is my own daughter,
and because I was targeted by you from her presence, the curse was therefore pronounced by me."
Now, with both my anger and passion subsided, O Mind-born One, I speak to you so that the pacification of your curse may come to pass. (13)
O Madana, having been reduced to ashes by the fire from the eye of Bharga,
you shall later regain a body through his very grace.
When Hara, the Great God, takes a wife,
he himself will cause you to attain a body.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to Madana, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
vanished while the lords of sages and his mind-born sons looked on.
When he had vanished, Śambhu, the ordainer of all,
departed for his desired destination with the speed of the wind, while Brahmā likewise departed at that time.
When that Creator had vanished and Śambhu had departed for his own abode,
Dakṣa then spoke to Kandarpa, pointing toward him.
Dakṣa said:
"O Kandarpa, this daughter of mine was born from my own body; she is endowed with my form and qualities.
Accept her as your wife, for she is your equal in virtues. (19)
"O one of great splendor, she shall always be your companion; according to your desire, she will follow you in accordance with dharma throughout the ten directions."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, Dakṣa gave her, who was born from the water of the sweat of his body, to Kandarpa;
he placed her before him and gave her the name Rati.
Beholding that most enchanting woman named Rati, Madana was pierced by his own arrow; captivated by Rati, he fell into a swoon.
His wife was always like a deer-eyed woman, radiant with the luster of a momentary flash and exclusively devoted to Gaurī; she resembled a doe in her flickering side-glances. 33.
Beholding her pair of eyebrows, Madana fell into doubt:
"Has the Creator placed my maddening bow here? (24)
O best of the twice-born, having observed the swift movement of her side-long glances,
he no longer placed his faith in the swiftness of his own weapons, nor even in their beauty.
Having inhaled her steady breath, naturally fragrant,
Madana abandoned his longing for the Malaya breeze.
Beholding the face, which resembled the full moon and was marked by eyebrows like fine lashes,
Madana could not discern the difference between that face and the moon.
Her two breasts, resembling golden lotus buds, shone with their pair of nipples as if attended by a pair of bees. (28)
[He saw her] with firm, plump, high, and dense breasts hanging down to her waist,
and a slender, beautiful, and auspicious line of hair extending gracefully from her navel.
It was that bowstring of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma), laden with rows of bees, which he forgot once he had grasped it and gazed upon her. || 30 ||
Within the depth of her deep navel-cavity, she was surrounded by four sides,
like a pair of lotus-eyes within a face-lotus that is as red as a crimson lotus.
O best of the twice-born, with her body whose middle was slender and who possessed a natural radiance like that of a peacock, she appeared like a jeweled altar to Kāma.
Kāma gazed upon her pair of thighs, which were as soft and smooth as the stalks of a plantain tree, enchanting and equal to his own power.
Her two feet, with their reddish heels and the tips of the toes, were variegated and full of passion; there, the god of love resided.
Her pair of hands was enchanting, with nails red like *kiṃśuka* flowers and fingers that were rounded and possessed slender tips. (35)
Having seen this, O best of the twice-born, Smara thought: "Is she prepared to delude me with my own weapons, now doubled in power? (36)
That lovely pair of arms, long like a pair of lotus stalks,
soft and smooth, shone intensely like a flowing stream of the water of supreme beauty.
The captivating mass of hair, resembling a dark blue cloud, shone like the thick tuft of hair on a yak's tail, O beloved of Smara. (38)
Beholding that goddess, who was exceedingly enchanting like Rati, filled with a flood of the waters of luster, and possessing the lotus-buds of breasts and face, Madana [was struck]. (39)
Her face was a lotus adorned with lovely arms like lotus stalks, graced by the waves of the multitude of playful movements of her two eyebrows. (40)
She who possesses blue-lotus eyes that are like female bees hovering at the fall of her sidelong glances;
she whose fine body-hair is like the moss upon her, and who destroys the tree of the mind.
With wide-open eyes, he received her— whose deep navel was like a lake and who had arisen from the southern Himalayas— just as Mahādeva received the Gaṅgā.
And then Kāma, filled with an abundance of joy, spoke truthfully, having forgotten that most terrible curse bestowed by Brahmā. (43)
Madana said:
"O Moon, with this companion of such perfect beauty, you are capable of deluding Śambhu; what need is there for other beings?"
"O sinless one, wherever I aim with my bow,
there this illusion called Ramaṇī must also act."
"Whenever I go to a temple, or to the earth, or to the subterranean realm (rasātala), may this sweet-smiling woman always be my companion. (46)
O Lord of Creatures, just as Lakṣmī is the consort of Viṣṇu, as lightning is to the clouds,
so shall she be my companion.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Madana eagerly took hold of the goddess Rati,
just as Hṛṣīkeśa takes Lakṣmī, the most excellent one, as she rises up from the water.
Together with her, Smara, whose yellow radiance was broken,
shone like a cloud at twilight accompanied by a beautiful flash of lightning.
Thus the Lord of Rati, filled with intense joy, took that Rati into his heart, just as a seer of Yoga grasps a sacred knowledge;
and Rati, having obtained her supreme husband, attained satisfaction, like the lotus-born Lakṣmī upon reaching Viṣṇu, her face resembling the full moon.
Thus ends the third chapter on the Origin of Rati in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Four.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
From that time forward, Dhātṛ, who had previously vanished,
remained constantly tormented by the poison of Śambhu’s words and brooded over them.
Having seen my mere longing for a beloved, Śambhu censured me before the sages; how then could he take a wife for himself? (2)
Who will be his wife, and who dwells in his mind, that she, having obstructed his path of yoga, will cause him delusion? (3)
Even Manmatha will not be capable of deluding him;
for he is an absolute yogi who cannot endure even the mention of women's names.
If the wives had not been taken by Hara from the beginning, how could there be creation in the middle or at the end? Furthermore, their slaughter would not have been caused by anyone else.
Some very powerful beings will exist on earth who are to be subdued by me;
some are to be restrained by Viṣṇu, and some by means of Śambhu.
Since Śambhu is averse to saṃsāra and likewise entirely dispassionate, he will perform no other action except for our sake; of this there is no doubt.
While reflecting thus, Lokeśa Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
standing in the sky, beheld Dakṣa and the others once again established upon the earth.
And having beheld Madana, who was filled with joy and accompanied by Rati,
he went there once more and spoke, consoling the one whose arrows are flowers.
Brahmā said:
"O Mind-born One, you shine with this companion;
and she, united with you as her husband, truly shines forth."
Just as Hṛṣīkeśa is with Śrī, and as Haripriyā is with him; just as the night is joined with the Moon, and as the Moon is joined with her. || 11 ||
In that very way, the splendor and the marital union of you two have been honored;
therefore, you shall become the banner of the world, the banner of the universe. (12)
"O child, for the welfare of the world, you must delude the wielder of the Pināka bow,
so that Śambhu, with a happy mind, may take a wife."
In solitary and pleasant places, on mountains, and by rivers—
wherever the Lord went, he was accompanied by her.
Delude Hara, who has restrained his self and turned away from women;
for there exists no other deluder of him besides you. (15)
O Mind-born One, when Hari becomes filled with passion, the cessation of your curse will occur; therefore, act for your own benefit.
If the Mind-born god, filled with passion, desires that woman of noble form, then he will honor you for your enjoyment. (17)
Therefore, strive for the welfare of the world in the deluding of Hara;
having deluded Maheśvara, become the banner of Śiva’s success.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Supreme Soul,
Manmatha spoke the truth to Brahmā for the welfare of the world.
Manmatha said:
"O Lord, at your word I shall effect the delusion of Śambhu;
however, O Master, create for me there a beloved woman, for she is my great weapon."
"O Sustainer of the World, since Śambhu has been deluded by me, command that beautiful woman Manoramā so that she may bring about his further delusion."
I do not see such a woman by whom his delusion might now be produced;
O Creator, therefore devise a means for that end.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While Kandarpa was speaking thus, Dhātṛ, the Grandfather of the worlds, fell into this thought: "I shall create a woman who causes total infatuation."
Then, from the sigh that issued forth from him as he was overcome with anxiety,
Spring was born, adorned with a profusion of flowers.
Bearing mango buds and clusters of bees, and [carrying] *kiṃśuka* flowers like cranes, he shone like a tree in full bloom. (25)
Resembling a red lotus, with eyes like blossoming water-lilies,
his face was like the full moon risen at twilight, and he possessed a beautiful nose.
His ears were spiraled like conch shells, his hair was dark and curly,
and he was adorned with a pair of earrings resembling the garland of rays from the twilight sun.
With the gait of a rutting elephant, his chest was broad and expansive;
his arms were thick, stout, and long, and his pair of hands were firm. || 28 ||
With well-rounded thighs, hips, and shanks, a neck like a conch shell, and elevated shoulders;
with hidden collarbones and a broad chest, he was complete in all auspicious marks.
Then, when such a spring season had fully arrived,
a fragrant breeze blew and even the trees blossomed.
Cuckoos with sweet voices sang the fifth note by the hundreds, and the lakes became filled with blossoming lotuses and full-grown lilies. (31)
Then, beholding that supreme Madana who had arisen in such a manner, Hiraṇyagarbha spoke these sweet words.
Brahmā said:
"O Manmatha, this shall always be your companion and friend; for your sake, he will always act in accordance with your wishes. (33)
Just as the wind is the friend of fire and assists it everywhere, so shall this man be your friend and always follow you. || 34 ||
Since it is the internal cause for dwelling [there], let this place be called Vāsanta;
likewise, following after you shall be its function, as well as the delighting of the world.
May this springtime, the erotic sentiment, and the Malaya breeze in spring—may these states of being always remain under your control as your friends. (36)
May the playful gestures beginning with *bibboka*, as well as the sixty-four arts (*kalās*), foster intimacy for Rati, so that they may become your friends. (37)
O Kāma, together with these companions headed by Vasanta, and with this female companion who is your fitting retinue, you [should go]. (38)
"Delude Mahādeva and bring about the eternal creation.
Go wherever you desire, surrounded by all your attendants. I shall sustain her who will delude Hara. (39)
Thus addressed by the eldest of the gods, Madana was delighted;
he then departed for that place with his host, accompanied by his wife and followers.
Having bowed to Dakṣa and having saluted all those mind-born sons,
Manmatha then went to that place where Śambhu was.
O best of the twice-born, when Manmatha had departed with his followers, endowed with the sentiments of love and the like,
the Grandfather (Brahmā), together with the lords of sages headed by Marīci and Atri, spoke sweetly to Dakṣa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Origin of Spring," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 4 ||
Chapter Five. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Brahmā spoke to the great-souled Dakṣa.
And from Marīci and the others, this speech was uttered exactly as it is: || 1 ||
Brahmā said: "Who will become the wife of Śambhu? Who will enchant him?
Thinking thus, I am unable to settle upon a beloved.
Except for Viṣṇu’s Māyā, Dakṣa’s Mahāmāyā, and the Māyā consisting of the universe—
namely Sandhyā, Sāvitrī, and Umā— there could be no other creator of such delusion.
Therefore, I shall praise Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the Yoganidrā who gives birth to the universe; she, in her beautiful form, will delude Śaṅkara.
But you, O Dakṣa, should worship that very goddess who possesses all forms,
so that she may become your daughter and become the wife of Hara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Supreme Soul,
Dakṣa, being urged by Marīci and the others, spoke to the Creator.
Dakṣa said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, what you have spoken is true and for the welfare of the world;
we shall duly perform it so that she may become captivating to him."
I shall become such that my daughter herself,
becoming Viṣṇumāyā, will become the wife of the high-souled Śambhu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Marīci and the others had replied, "So be it," Dakṣa then began to perform a sacrifice to Mahāmāyā, who is composed of the entire universe.
Having established her, who was dwelling on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, within his heart,
he began to perform austerities in order to behold Ambikā directly before his eyes.
For three thousand divine years, Dakṣa,
self-restrained, with his mind controlled and firm in his vows, performed austerities with great discipline.
Subsisting on air, fasting entirely, subsisting on water, and eating only leaves,
he passed that time thus, meditating upon her who is identical with the universe.
When Dakṣa had departed to perform penance, Brahmā, the lord of the entire world,
went to the vicinity of Mount Mandara, a most excellent place more meritorious than the meritorious.
Having gone there, he praised for a hundred years with one-pointed devotion the Mother of the World, Viṣṇu’s Māyā, who is identical with the universe, using meaningful words.
Brahmā said:

I praise the Goddess, the sustainer of the world, whose nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance, who is pure, without support, and undisturbed; she whose form is both gross and subtler than the subtlest. (15)
I praise you, the eternal Nidrā, from whom arises that which is called the primordial matter (pradhāna) of the world and the supreme world itself, and of whom you are a constituent part. 16.
You are consciousness, you are supreme bliss, and you are the very nature of the Supreme Self;
you are the power of all beings, and you are the purifier of all. 17.
You are Sāvitrī, the sustainer of the world; you are the twilight, you are delight, and you are fortitude.
Indeed, in the form of light, you are the illuminator of transmigratory existence.
Likewise, always veiling the world with the nature of darkness,
you alone, in the form of creation, fulfill the cycle of worldly existence.
In her form as the Sustainer, she seeks the welfare of the worlds;
likewise, in her form as the Inner Essence, she brings about the end of the worlds.
You are Medhā, you are Mahāmāyā, you are Svadhā who delights the ancestors;
you are Svāhā, you are the utterances Namaskāra and Vaṣaṭkāra, and likewise you are Smṛti.
You are nourishment, you are fortitude, friendliness, compassion, and likewise sympathetic joy;
you alone are modesty, you are peace, you are splendor—the Sovereign Lady of the World. 22.
You are Mahāmāyā, Svāhā, and Svadhā, the deities of the ancestors;
you are our power of creation and the power of maintenance belonging to Hari.
Likewise, you are the power of the end and the sovereign power; you are that eternal Śakti.
Though you are one, you become twofold, bringing about both liberation and saṃsāra,
by way of the natures of knowledge and ignorance, through being self-luminous and non-self-luminous.
You are the fortune of all beings; you are the shade, you are Sarasvatī;
you consist of the triple Veda, you possess the three measures, and you are the essential nature of all beings.
You are the *udgīti* of the Sāmaveda, which delights the hosts of ancestors; you are the altar of all sacrifices, as well as the *sāmidhenī* verses and the oblation itself. (27)

That form of the Supreme Self which is unmanifest, indefinable, and partless, as well as that which consists of those subtle elements alone, and likewise that which is manifest and composed of the universe—[all these are one]. (28)
O Viśvambharā, you who delight in every form and sustain the earth,
may you always bestow power and prosperity upon the world.
You are Takṣmī, consciousness, and splendor; you are nourishment and you are the eternal one.
You are the Night of Time, you are liberation, peace, wisdom, and likewise memory.
O boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, O bestower of the bliss of liberation, be gracious! You are always the refuge and the intellect of all the worlds.
You are eternal and you are impermanent; you are the deluder of all that moves and is immobile.
You are the creative union, the illuminator of all yoga along with its limbs and sub-limbs.
You are the thought and the fame of ascetics; you are endowed with those eight limbs.
You are she who bears the sword, the trident, and the discus, and you are of terrible form.
You are the sovereign of all people; you are the bestower of grace upon everyone.
You are the beginning of the universe, yet you are without beginning; you are the source of the universe, yet you are not born from a womb.
You are infinite throughout the entire world, and you alone bring about its end.
For you are utterly pure, yet you are sung of as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasī);
you are indeed both violence and non-violence, and you are Kālī with four faces.
You are the Supreme, the Mother of all, the Subduer, and likewise the Lightning;
in you alone the universe dissolves, you shine as that reality, and you sustain it.
You are devoid of creation, yet you are creation; you are without ears, yet you possess hearing.
You are an ascetic, devoid of hands and feet, yet you are the supreme grasper. 37.
You are earth, you are water, you are light, you are wind, and you are space, mind, ego, and the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti) which is the source of the worlds. || 38 ||
Jagannābhi, who assumes the form of Mount Meru, is the supreme Nālikā; she is the pure essence of both the transcendent and the immanent, the Māyā that causes the cessation of delusion. || 39 ||
The cause and that which has become the effect, the truth, the peaceful, and both the auspicious and inauspicious;
these are your forms for the sake of the universe, as well as the fruits of the tree of passion. (40)
Exceedingly short and yet long, with a body that is both extremely minute and vast,
you are subtle yet pervasive throughout the entire world— you who are composed of the universe.

Devoid of pride, arising from the measure of celestial chariots and even superior ones, with a disposition free from attachment to enjoyments and the like—whatever that nature of yours is in Your majesty, and whatever delusion and so forth there may be; [all this is Yours]. (42)
Knowing the ripening of desirable and undesirable [results], as well as their desirable and undesirable causes;
likewise, [he knows] that form which consists of the beginning, middle, and end of creation, and that which is lowly. (43)
Having thus accomplished it repeatedly through the eightfold yoga of discernment, that reality which is made stable—that is Your eternal form. (44)
You are the external and the internal, pleasure and pain, knowledge and ignorance, dissolution and non-dissolution, affliction as well as peace, and the prosperity of the Lord of the world. 45.
Since even she cannot describe your power within the three worlds,
how can you— who cause such delusion even to her— be praised by me?
Yoga-sleep, the great sleep, the deluding sleep, the one who pervades the world, the illusory power of Viṣṇu, and primordial nature—who could possibly comprehend you through praise? (47)
Who is capable of describing the power or knowing the virtues of her, who consists of the embodiment of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and myself? || 48 ||

You alone are the light whose nature is the internal object of the illuminating sense-faculties; you alone are the single form existing both as the moving and the stationary, as well as the external object of perception.
Be gracious, O Mother of all the worlds, who has assumed the form of a woman;
O Sovereign of the universe, who possesses a universal form, be gracious to me, O Eternal One. (50)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus being praised by Viriñci, that Yoganidrā appeared visibly before Brahmā, the Supreme Soul.
Possessing the luster of smooth collyrium, beautiful in form, lofty, and four-armed;
seated upon a lion, holding a sword and a blue lotus in her hands, with her mass of hair loosened and flowing. 52.
Then, seeing her before him, the Creator, the teacher of the entire world,
with his lofty shoulders bowed in devotion, praised her and prostrated himself.
Brahmā said:
Salutations, salutations to you, who are the form of both worldly engagement and withdrawal, and the form of maintenance and creation;
you are the eternal power of all moving and non-moving beings, the enchantress of all. (54)

You who are Śrī, who always assumes the form of Keśava; you who are Viśvambharā, who sustains the entire universe; you who are the honored Yoginī Hrī, beautiful to the mind—you are she. Salutations to you, O essence of the Supreme Self! 55.

O Goddess, you are indeed that Vidyā who possesses various supports; she whom yogis, preceded by the Yāma and other stages, meditate upon in their hearts as perceived through valid cognition, endowed with light, purity, and the rest, and manifesting as Virāj.
Bearing the immutable, unmanifest, and inconceivable form that consists of time, you eternally produce the worlds— the seed of transformation— whether they be ancient, newly formed, or intermediate.

You are that state of equilibrium of these qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which is free from modification; you, the sole cause of the world, appear as if you enter into the space between the external and the internal.
Obeisance to you, Viṣṇumāyā, the seed of all worlds without exception, whose nature consists of both the object of knowledge and the means of knowing, and who exists for the welfare of the worlds.
Having heard his words, Kālī, the deluder of the world,
spoke to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, with a voice like the roar of a thundercloud.
The Goddess said: "O Brahmin, for what purpose have I been praised by you? Pay heed;
let that which is unassailable be told quickly before me. (61)
"Since I have appeared before you, the accomplishment of your purpose is certain.
Therefore, tell me what you desire; being gratified, I shall perform it for you. (62)
Brahmā said: "The Lord of Beings wanders alone; he does not seek a second.
Delude him so that he himself desires to take a wife."
"Except for you, no one else will be as captivating to him;
therefore, O Bhava, become his enchantress in a singular form. (64)
Just as you, assuming a physical form in the likeness of Lakṣmī, gladden Keśava for the welfare of the universe, so do you act now. (65)
The bull-bannered god censured my mere longing for a beloved;
how then could he ever take a wife according to his own will? (66)
But if the beloved is not grasped by Hara, how can creation proceed?
For that Śambhu is dispassionate, being without beginning, middle, or end as its cause.
Thus absorbed in thought, I have found no refuge here other than you;
therefore, for the welfare of the entire world, do this for me.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Lakṣmī, nor the god of love, nor even I am able to delude him, O Mother of the World; therefore, you must delude the Lord.
You are the fame of all beings, as you are the modesty of those who have restrained their souls;
just as you are the one beloved of Viṣṇu, so do you delude the Lord.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Now, O most excellent of the twice-born, listen to what the illustrious Kālī, who is composed of yoga, spoke again after addressing Brahmā.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Praise of Kālī within the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Six. The Goddess said:
O Brahmin, everything that you have said is indeed entirely true;
for there exists no one here who can delude Śaṅkara except me.
"If Hara has not yet taken a wife, this eternal creation will not come to pass;
that which was propounded by you is true. (2)
Great effort was already required by me for this Lord of the World;
today, upon hearing your words, my exertion has become doubly intense and most resolute.
I shall strive in such a way that Hara, being utterly deluded, will himself involuntarily take a wife.
O highly fortunate one, having assumed a beautiful form, I shall become subject to his will, just as the beloved of Hari is subject to Viṣṇu.
I shall act in such a way that he too shall always remain under my control here,
just as I do with other people.
O Creator, I shall follow that Śambhu— who is undisturbed and who constitutes the beginning, middle, and end of every cycle of dissolution—
in a female form, especially for this purpose.
"O Grandfather, born of Dakṣa’s daughter in a beautiful form, I shall honor Śaṃkara at every new creation. (12)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus addressed that Brahmā, O best of the twice-born,
she vanished right there while being gazed upon by the Creator of the World.
When she had vanished, the Lord Dhātṛ, the Grandfather of the worlds,
went to that place where the Mind-born one was stationed.
Remembering the words of Mahāmāyā, he became exceedingly joyful;
O best of sages, he then considered himself to have accomplished all that was to be done.
Then, seeing the high-souled Virañci proceeding by means of his swan-vehicle, Madana likewise rose up in haste to meet him.
Then, having approached him who was nearby, Manobhava, his eyes wide with joy and filled with delight, paid homage to the Lord of all the worlds.
Then the Blessed Lord Dhātṛ, gladdening Madana with affection, spoke these sweet and faltering words, which were well-uttered by the Goddess Viṣṇumāyā.
Brahmā said:
"O child, O Mind-born One, create that woman who, as you previously declared, shall be the one to bring about the further delusion of Śarva."
For that purpose, the Goddess Yoganidrā, who pervades the universe,
was propitiated by me with a one-pointed mind in a cave of Mount Mandara.
O child, by her very self appearing before me,
being pleased, it was indeed accepted that Śambhu was to be enchanted by me.
"O Mind-born One, it is true that Hara will soon be deluded by her once she has been born in the abode of Dakṣa. (22)
Madana said: "O Brahmin, what is this that is renowned as Yoganidrā, she who pervades the universe?
How can Hara, who is established in austerity, be brought under her control?"
O Grandfather of the World, I desire to hear from you what power that goddess possesses, who she is, and where she resides. (24)
Why should she not delude him, from whose field of vision we ourselves are unable to remain for even a single moment once he has abandoned his meditative absorption?
O Brahmin, seeing him with eyes as bright as blazing fire, his matted locks formidable with their rows of streaks, and bearing a trident—who would be able to stand before him? (26)
Since I have approached him who possesses such a nature with a desire for complete delusion, I wish to hear that [teaching] from you in its true essence. (27)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard the words of Manobhava, the four-faced one,
though desiring to speak, refrained upon hearing that speech which was a cause for discouragement.
While Śarva was being deluded, Brahmā became filled with anxiety, thinking, "I am not capable of deluding him," and he sighed again and again. (29)
From the wind of his breath were born various forms of great power; these hosts possessed flickering tongues, were restless, and were exceedingly terrifying.
Some had the faces of horses, some likewise had the faces of elephants;
others had the faces of lions and tigers, while still others had the faces of dogs, boars, and donkeys.
Some had faces like bears, cats, and wild dogs; others had the faces of śarabhas, parrots, monkeys, jackals, and even reptiles. 32.
Some had the form of cows and cow-like faces, while others had the faces of birds; some were very tall, some very short, some very stout, and others very thin.
Some had tawny eyes, some had eyes like those of a cat, some had three eyes, some had one eye, some had large bellies, some had one ear, some had three ears, and others had four ears.
They had thick ears, large ears, many ears, and deformed ears; they had long eyes, thick eyes, minute eyes, and squinting glances. || 35 ||
Some had four feet, some five, some three, and others but one;
likewise, there were those with short feet, long feet, thick feet, and large feet.
Some had one hand, some four hands, some two hands, or were bent in three places;
others were handless, or had misshapen eyes, while still others had the form of lizards.
Some had human forms, while others had the faces of porpoises; some were shaped like curlews, some like crows, and others had the appearance of swans and cranes.
Likewise, there were those with the faces of water-fowls, ospreys, herons, and crows.
Some were half-blue and half-red, others were tawny or reddish-brown;
some were blue, white, yellow, or green, possessing variegated forms.
They sounded conchs, kettledrums,
lutes, clay drums, ḍiṇḍimas, gomukhas, and paṇavas as well.
Indeed, while Brahmā was overcome with anxiety regarding the delusion of Śarva, he realized that he was not capable of deluding him, and thus he sighed again and again. (29)
From the breath of his wind, there arose hosts of various forms, possessed of great strength, with flickering tongues, restless, and exceedingly terrifying.
Some had the faces of horses, some likewise had the faces of elephants;
others had the faces of lions and tigers, and others had the faces of dogs, boars, and donkeys.
Some had faces like bears, cats, and wild dogs; others had the faces of śarabhas or parrots; some had the mouths of monkeys and jackals, while others had the faces of reptiles.
Some had the form of cows with cow-faces, while others had the faces of birds;
some were very tall, some very short, some very stout, and some very thin.
Some had tawny eyes, some had eyes like those of a cat, some had three eyes, some had a single eye, and others had enormous bellies; some had one ear, some had three ears, and others had four ears.
Those with thick ears, large ears, many ears, and deformed ears; those with long eyes, thick eyes, minute eyes, and squinting eyes. (35)
Some had four feet, five feet, three feet, or only one foot;
likewise, some had short feet, long feet, thick feet, or massive feet. (36)
Some had one hand, some four hands, some two hands, and others were bent in three ways; some were handless, some had deformed eyes, and others had the appearance of lizards.
Some had human forms, while others had the faces of porpoises;
some were shaped like curlews and herons, and others had the appearance of swans and cranes; likewise, there were those with the faces of water-fowl, ospreys, herons, crows, and ravens.
Some were half-blue and half-red, some were tawny and others reddish-brown;
likewise, some were blue, white, yellow, or green, possessing variegated forms.
They sounded conchs, kettledrums,
lutes, clay drums, small drums, horns, and cymbals.
O best of Brahmins, all the attendants were formidable with their high, tawny matted locks that stood close together, and they traveled upon chariots.
With tridents in their hands, nooses in their hands, swords in their hands, and bearing bows; with spears, hooks, maces, arrows, battle-axes, and lances in their grasp. || 42 ||
Wielding various weapons and letting out a great roar, those mighty ones went before Brahmā and cried out, "Kill! Cut him down! (43)
While they were saying, "Kill him!
Cut him apart!", he began to speak those instructions by the power of his yogic sleep (yoganidrā).
Then, having addressed Brahmā and beheld those hosts, Madana, the god of love, spoke while restraining the Gaṇas from speaking further in front of them.
Madana said:
"O Creator, what work will they perform for you, or where will they reside? What are their names? Assign them to those tasks accordingly. (46)
Having appointed these to their own duties and having assigned them names and stations,
you should afterwards describe to me the power of Mahāmāyā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then,
having heard those words, the Grandfather of all the worlds spoke to the Gaṇas who were filled with joy, assigning them their respective duties and other tasks.
Brahmā said:
"As soon as they were born, they repeatedly said, 'Kill! Therefore, let the name of these beings be 'Māra' (the Killer)."
Because they possess the nature of Māra, let them indeed be called Māras;
they will constantly create obstacles for living beings unless they are worshipped. (50)
O Mind-born One, following you is their primary duty;
wherever and whenever you go for the sake of your own work,
they shall go there at those very times to provide assistance.
They will cause the minds of those who are under the power of your weapons to become deranged,
and they will always obstruct the path of knowledge for the wise.
Just as all living beings perform worldly actions,
so too will these [beings] act everywhere, even in the face of obstacles.
"These shall abide everywhere, impetuous and able to assume any form at will.
You alone shall be their leader of the hosts; let them be the enjoyers of a portion of the five sacrifices and indeed the enjoyers of water for those who perform their daily rites. (54)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard this, they all then surrounded Madana along with Vidhi as they desired, having learned their own destiny.
O best of sages, how could their greatness and power be described on this earth, since they are so endowed with ascetic merit? (56)
They have neither wives nor sons, for they are always free from worldly desire;
those high-souled ones are all renunciants with vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas).
Then Brahmā, being pleased, proceeded to explain correctly the majesty of Yoganidrā to Madana.
Brahmā said: Having divided his purpose through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, by means of both unmanifest and manifest forms, he acts; therefore he is called Viṣṇu, Āya, and Iti.
That which, situated within the waters at the lowest point, having separated the Puruṣa from the shell of the cosmic egg, proceeds as it were— she is called Yoganidrā.
Devoted to the internal meditation on mantras, consisting of supreme bliss, she is said to be the essence of the knowledge of beings within yogis, pervading the entire universe.
She who continuously causes that which was endowed with knowledge within the womb to be born devoid of knowledge once impelled by the winds of childbirth. 62.

Having joined together each preceding [element] with the next through formative activity (saṃskāra), and having applied it to food and so forth, there then arises delusion, the sense of "mine," and doubt regarding knowledge. (63)
Having repeatedly cast [the mind] again and again into anger, obstruction, and greed, one should thereafter quickly engage it in sensual desire, joined with thought day and night. (64)
She who makes a living being filled with delight yet attached to worldly calamities is called Mahāmāyā; therefore, she is the Sovereign of the World.
That which arises from the manifestation of creation, attached to the ego and so forth,
is described by the world as "origination," though it possesses infinite forms.
Just as water originating from clouds causes a sprout that has arisen from a seed to grow,
so too would it cause beings who have already been born to grow.
That Śakti is the form of creation and the sovereign consciousness (khyāti) of all;
she is the eternal forbearance of the patient and the compassion of the merciful. (68)
Eternal, she shines within the womb of the universe in her eternal form;
as the supreme light, she is both manifest and unmanifest, illuminating all.
She is Vaiṣṇavī in the form of Vidyā, the cause of liberation for yogins; yet, through its opposite, she is the cause of the bondage of saṃsāra for those caught in worldly existence.
O Mind-born One, my second [wife] is most enchanting in the form of Lakṣmī;
she always resides upon my neck in the form of the Three Vedas. 71.

Abiding everywhere, all-pervading, divine in form, eternal, the Goddess who is all forms and known as the Supreme (Parā), she is at all times the deluder of Kṛṣṇa and others, and of every living being on all sides through her female forms. 72.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Yoganidrā," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The Seventh Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Brahmā, having established the true nature of Mahāmāyā, [spoke].
She spoke again to Madana: "He is indeed fit for the deluding of Hara."
Brahmā said:
Mahādeva previously gave his consent to act in such a way that he would take a wife through the power of Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
"O Smara, she herself declared that having become the daughter of Dakṣa, she would surely become the second wife of the high-souled Śambhu. (3)
O Śaṅkara, together with these of your own attendants, and with Rati and Madhu, act so that you may take a wife according to your desire.
O Smara, remember that once Śambhu has taken a wife, we shall have accomplished our purpose;
this creation will proceed without interruption, of this there is no doubt.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of the twice-born, the Mind-born (Kāma) spoke thus to the Lord of the World regarding that sweet act he had performed to delude Mahādeva.
Madana said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, to how we act to delude Hara, whether in his presence or in his absence; hear that as I speak it."
When Śambhu, having conquered his senses, remained established in meditative absorption,
then, O Lord of the World, I constantly fanned him with a fragrant, cool, and purifying breeze that induces enchantment.
Taking up my bow along with five arrows,
I wandered in his vicinity, bewildering his attendants.
There, I delight with pairs of Siddhas day and night;
indeed, all those gestures (bhāvas) and amorous expressions (hāvas) enter into them.
O Grandfather, once a living being has entered the presence of Śambhu, who indeed does not repeatedly engage in the state of duality there? (11)
By my mere entrance, may all living beings become such that neither Śambhu nor his bull undergo any mental agitation.
For when that lord of the Pramathas goes to your Prastha,
I shall go there at that very time, O Ordainer, along with the river Samadhu.
Whenever he goes to Meru, or whenever he goes to Nāṭakeśvara,
or whenever he goes to Kailāsa, I go there at that time.
When Hari remains for even a moment having abandoned his meditative absorption (samādhi),
I then yoke the pair of wheels before him.
O Brahmin, that pair of wheels, repeatedly joined with the gestures of the male and female,
performs through various moods the most excellent sequence of the conjugal union.
I repeatedly delude even the peacocks and their mates before him, as well as other deer and birds in his presence. (17)
When one beholds a pair of peacocks displaying various behaviors as they indulge in their pleasure, who would not then become filled with longing? 18.
And the deer standing before him, full of longing for their mates,
then displayed a charming demeanor at his side and in front of him.
My arrow never found an opening in his body;
therefore, he who supports all the worlds could not be struck down by me while his body remained intact.
It has been ascertained in many ways that Hara, being partless (niṣkala), cannot be deluded even with assistance, except through union with Rāmā. || 21 ||
Listen, O highly fortunate one, to that which Madhu performs for his own delusion—whatever action he undertakes—and furthermore, to what is eternally appropriate for him. (22)
Campakas, keśaras, mango trees, karuṇas, and likewise pāṭalas;
nāgakeśaras, punnāgas, kiṃśukas, ketakas, and dhavas.
Mādhavīs, mallikās, parṇadhārās, and likewise kuruvakas—
these all blossom wherever Hara indeed resides.
Fanning the lakes filled with blossoming lotuses with the Malaya breezes,
he diligently made Śaṅkara’s hermitage exceedingly fragrant.
There, indeed, all the flowering creepers, with their radiant beauty, entwined the clusters of trees whose foliage was in full bloom.
Seeing those trees with their abundance of beautiful flowers and those fragrant breezes, even a sage there would have fallen under the sway of desire.
O Lord of the World, his hosts as well—gods, Siddhas, and those who were exceedingly rich in asceticism—dwelt there with various most beautiful forms. (28)
Furthermore, we have not observed any cause for his delusion;
even when confronted with mere existence arising from desire, Śaṅkara does not act upon it. (29)
Thus, having seen and understood all this— the contemplation of Hara—
I have turned away from the delusion regarding Śambhu, certainly being free from Māyā.
Now, having heard your words, and having again awakened from the sleep of yoga, and having heard of her power and seen the hosts as my allies; (31)
"I am making repeated efforts to delude Śambhu;
may you, O Lord of the Three Worlds, likewise quickly bring about this Yoganidrā so that she becomes the wife of Śambhu. (32)

Of the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), of breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed constantly, of the posture (āsana), of Maheśa, and of the sphere of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra). || 33 ||
I believe that the occurrence of obstacles to meditation, to mental retention, and to concentration could not be brought about even by hundreds of Māras.
Nevertheless, let this host of Māras create obstacles to Hara’s mastery of the limbs of yoga;
for what is it that a king cannot do, or how could he be incapable of acting in the presence of another? (35)
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Words of Vadana," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The eighth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Brahmā also spoke these words again to Madana.
Having ascertained this and recalled the words of Yoganidrā, O you whose wealth is asceticism! (1)
Brahmā said:
"She will certainly become the wife of Śambhu as Yoganidrā;
you should provide her assistance there to the best of your ability."
"Go quickly with your own attendants, O Manobhava, to that place where Śaṅkara resides, together with Madhu."
Constantly deluding the world for one-fourth part of each day and night,
remain forever by the side of Śambhu with three parts, always together with the Gaṇas.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of all the worlds vanished right there;
then Madana, together with his attendants, went into the presence of Śambhu.
In the meantime, Dakṣa, who was devoted to penance for a long time and firm in his vows,
propitiated the Goddess with many observances.
Then, O best of sages, as Dakṣa, who was disciplined by his observances,
was worshipping Yoganidrā, Śivā appeared before his very eyes.
Then, having directly beheld Viṣṇu’s Māyā, which consists of the entire universe,
Dakṣa, the progenitor of creatures, considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Kālikā, seated upon a lion, black in complexion, with full and elevated breasts,
four arms, a beautiful face, and holding a blue lotus.
Bestowing boons and protection, holding a sword in her hand, endowed with all virtues, with reddish eyes, beautiful with loose hair, and captivating. || 10 ||
Having seen her, Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, filled with supreme joy and with his neck bowed in humility, then praised Mahāmāyā.
Dakṣa said:
I praise that auspicious Lakṣmī of Hari, who is the goddess whose form is bliss, who brings joy to the world, and who consists of the nature of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Maheśvarī, that supreme reality which is light through the manifestation of the predominance of *sattva*, the self-luminous abode of the universe—that is a portion of you. 13.

O Mother of the Universe, that manifestation of desire which arises from the predominance of the quality of rajas is the very nature of passion; it is situated in the middle, being a minute fraction of a fraction of You.
Whatever manifestation of delusion occurs through the predominance of the quality of darkness (tamas), which is the veiling of conscious beings— that pertains to the sphere of part and sub-part.
Supreme, consisting of the Supreme Self, pure, stainless, and the enchantress of the world—you are the threefold form, the triple Veda, fame, livelihood, and the refuge of this universe. (16)
Just as Mādhava sustains the Earth with his own manifested form, so too is that form of yours the benefactor of all the worlds. (17)
You are of great majesty, the universal power, subtle and unconquered;
you are that supreme [reality] which is manifested by the winds through the restraint of the upward and downward breaths.
That light of yours, intended for the sake of the Mother, is regarded as being of the nature of sattva;
it is the supportless, fruitless, stainless, and supreme [light] of the yogin. 19.
They take as their object that very reality which is within your range;
she who is well-known, immutable, highly celebrated, and exceedingly pure. (20)
That *jñapti* (consciousness) is devoid of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcā*), yet even while being proliferation itself, it is the illuminator.
You are knowledge (*vidyā*) and you are ignorance (*avidyā*); you are the support (*ālambā*) and you are without support (*nirāśrayā*).
You are the primordial power (*ādiśakti*) of the worlds, the Sovereign (*Īśvarī*), whose form is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). 21.
You are that pure speech, the goddess Vāṇī, who dwells in the throat of Brahmā and is sung forth; you are intent on revealing the Vedas and are the illuminator of the universe.
You are Agni, and likewise you are Svāhā; you are Svadhā together with the ancestors.
You are the sky, you are the form of Time, you are the measure of time (kāṣṭhā), and you abide as the exterior.
You are inconceivable, you are unmanifest, and likewise you possess an indescribable form;
you are the Night of Time, you are the peaceful one, and you alone are the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).
Since even the Creator and other gods know Your external form only for the sake of protecting the worlds of transmigration, who else could know You, the Supreme?
Be gracious, O Blessed Mother; be gracious, O You whose form is Yoga.
Be gracious, O You of terrible form, who pervade the universe; salutations be unto You!
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O twice-born ones, having been thus praised by Dakṣa, whose self was purified, Mahāmāyā spoke to Dakṣa, even though she already knew his desire herself.
The Blessed One said: "O Dakṣa, I am greatly pleased with this devotion of yours toward me.
Choose a desired boon, and I shall grant it to you myself."
O Prajāpati, by your observances, austerities, and hymns of praise, I am exceedingly pleased; I shall grant you a boon—choose what you desire.
Dakṣa said: O Great Illusion, who pervades the universe, if you are a granter of boons to me,
then become my daughter and now become the wife of Hara.
"O Goddess, this boon is not for me alone, but for the entire world;
likewise, O Sovereign of Creatures, it is for the Lord of the World, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as well. (31)
The Goddess said:
"O Prajāpati, having become your daughter born of your wife,
I shall before long become the wife of Hara."
When you become indifferent toward me once again,
then I shall immediately cast off my body, whether I am happy or otherwise.
O Prajāpati, this boon is granted to you at the time of re-creation:
having become your daughter, I shall become the beloved of Hara.
In this way, O Prajāpati, I shall delude Mahādeva so that,
during each period of re-creation, he will fall into confusion despite being naturally undisturbed.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to Dakṣa, the preeminent Prajāpati, the goddess Mahāmāyā then vanished while Dakṣa was looking on.
When the illusion had vanished, Dakṣa also returned to his own hermitage and attained great joy, thinking, "She will bear me a son."
Then he brought about the production of progeny without sexual union with a woman,
through the manifestation of his resolve and by means of mental contemplation alone.
O best of the twice-born, those sons who were born there wandered over this earth many times at the instruction of Nārada. (39)
Again and again, those sons who were born to him by the thousands—all of them followed the path of their elder brother at the word of Nārada. (40)
O best of the twice-born, you who are the creators upon this earth, behold the entire earth, extending to its very limits and boundaries. (41)
Thus urged by the words of Nārada, the sons of Dakṣa have not returned even today, as they continue to wander this earth. (42)
Then, in order to produce offspring born of sexual union,
Dakṣa married the desired daughter of Vīraṇa.
O best of beings, her name was Vīriṇī, also known as Asaknī; at that time, when the first intention arose in the Prajāpati toward her, (44)
O best of the twice-born, at that time Mahāmāyā was born from her;
as soon as she was born, Prajāpati became exceedingly pleased.
Seeing her blazing with splendor, he then thought, "She is indeed she. (45)
A rain of flowers fell and the clouds poured down water;
when she was born, the quarters of the sky became tranquil and [all portents] subsided. || 46 ||
The gods dwelling in the sky sounded auspicious musical instruments, and the fires blazed peacefully when that truth was uttered, O best of men. (47)
Dakṣa, marked by the lineage of Vīriṇī, beheld her, the sovereign of the universe, the great illusion who is Viṣṇu’s Māyā, and gratified her with devotion. || 48 ||
Dakṣa said:
I bow to that eternal one who is auspicious, peaceful, the great illusion (Mahāmāyā), the yogic sleep (Yoganidrā) consisting of the universe, and who is called the Illusion of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā). 49.
In the past, she whom the Creator employed for the creation of the world, he fashioned;
and by whose command Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, maintains the stability of the universe.
Then Śambhu said: "I bow to you, O Goddess, the most exalted one—changeless, pure, immeasurable, and radiant;
I prostrate before her whose nature is bliss, who is designated as both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. (51)

O Goddess, for one who meditates upon you as the supreme one, whose nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are forever held within the palm of his hand. 52.
Whoever beholds you, O Goddess, the purifier who illumines both knowledge and ignorance, even once before his very eyes, for him liberation shall surely come. (53)
O Yoganidrā, O Mahāmāyā, O Viṣṇumāyā, O you who consist of the universe!
That consciousness which is endowed with the fullness of all means of valid knowledge is your very self.
O Mother of the World, for those who praise you as Ambikā,
as the one consisting of the world, as Māyā, and as everything— all these shall be theirs.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised by the high-souled Dakṣa,
the Mother of the World then spoke to Dakṣa in such a way that his mother did not hear.
Then Ambikā, through her power of illusion (māyā), deluded everyone present there so that Dakṣa alone heard it, while no one else heard it. 57.
The Goddess said:
"O best of sages, that for which I was previously propitiated by you—
listen now, for that which you desired has been accomplished."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the goddess then assumed her own form and,
adopting a state of childhood, wept before her mother.
Then, having carefully prepared Vīriṇī according to the proper rites,
he gave her breast-milk and other nourishment for the child Śiśupāla in accordance with the prescribed method.
Protected by the skillful and high-souled Vīriṇī,
he grew day by day like the lord of the night during the bright fortnight.
O best of the twice-born, all excellent qualities entered into him,
just as all the enchanting digits enter the moon even during its infancy.
Whenever she was in the midst of her friends, she would play according to her own nature;
at those times, she would repeatedly draw the image of Bharga every day.
When she sang songs appropriate for childhood,
her mind fixed on Smara, she remembered Ugra, Sthāṇu, Hara, and Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, Dakṣa gave her the name Satī,
for she was praiseworthy on account of all her virtues, as well as her goodness and her conduct.
In those two, who were possessed of skill and heroism, an incomparable compassion increased day by day;
and toward that devotee, even in her childhood, it grew constantly and repeatedly.
O best of men, she who possessed all lovely qualities and was always endowed with prudence constantly delighted her parents. (67)
Then one day, Vidhi and Nārada beheld that virtuous Satī standing by her father’s side, a beautiful jewel upon the earth.
Seeing them both, that virtuous woman was delighted; then, bowing low with humility, she prostrated before the god Brahmā and Nārada.
At the conclusion of her salutation, seeing Satī bowed down with humility, Brahmā and Nārada likewise spoke this blessing: ||| 70 ||
"Obtain as your husband that very god who desires you alone and whom you desire as your husband—the omniscient Lord of the Universe. (71)
O auspicious lady, may he who has not taken another wife, does not take one now, and will not take one in the future— may that peerless husband be yours.
Having spoken thus and remained for a very long time in Dakṣa’s hermitage,
they were dismissed by him and returned to their own abodes, O best of the twice-born.
Thus ends the eighth chapter on the Origin of Satī in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Nine.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having passed her childhood, she then attained beautiful youth;
she was exceedingly captivating in all her limbs due to the excellence of her form.
Seeing her, whose internal youth had just begun to manifest, the Lord of the World, Dakṣa, reflected:
"How shall I give this daughter to Bharga?"
Then she herself also desired to attain Bharga; accordingly, with her mother’s permission, she worshipped him daily in her home.
In the month of Āśvina, on the day known as Nandaka, having worshipped Hara with salt and rice mixed with jaggery,
she paid her respects and took it away.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, having propitiated Hara with milk-rice mixed with cakes, he called to mind the Supreme Lord.
Having worshipped Hara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa with offerings of sesame seeds and barley-rice, he spent the rest of the day again in blue garments.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, having kept a vigil at night,
that virtuous woman worshipped Śiva in the morning with kṛsarā rice.
On the full moon day of the month of Māgha, having kept a vigil during the night on the bank of a river while still wearing wet clothes, she performed the worship of Dhara.
With various kinds of fruits and flowers that were properly available at that time, she,
her mind fixed on Hara, maintained a restricted diet for that month.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Tapasya, specifically,
he kept a vigil and worshipped the Lord with bilva leaves.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, she spent that entire day and night worshipping Śiva with palāśa flowers, keeping him in her constant remembrance.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,

having worshipped the god Hara with offerings of barley-rice, she subsisted on sacrificial oblations for an entire month; remembering the one whose vehicle is the bull, she passed her time without food.
Having worshipped the Bull-vehicled One (Śiva) on the night of the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha with garments and vṛhatī flowers, she passed that night without food.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
she indeed performed the worship of the god Kṛttivāsas with bṛhatī flowers.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
she worshipped Śiva with sacred threads, garments, and purifying offerings.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, having worshipped with various kinds of flowers and fruits, he then took only water as food on the fourteenth day.
As soon as Satī had undertaken that vow in the past,
Brahmā, accompanied by Sāvitrī, then went into the presence of Hara.
The Blessed Vāsudeva, together with Lakṣmī,
also went to that place on the plateau of the Himavat where Śambhu was stationed with his attendants.
Seeing Brahmā and Kṛṣṇa together with their wives, Hara addressed them appropriately and inquired about the reason for their arrival.
Seeing them thus united in the state of matrimony,
he conceived in his mind a certain desire for the acquisition of a wife.
Now, if you do not tell me the true reason for your coming, why have you arrived and what business do you have here? (21)
Thus questioned by Tryambaka, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
being urged by Viṣṇu, spoke to Mahādeva.
Brahmā said:
O Three-eyed One, hear the purpose for which we two have come;
especially for the sake of the gods and for the sake of the universe, O Bull-bannered Lord. (23)
Therefore, O Śambhu, I am the cause of creation, and likewise Hari is the cause of its preservation;
you, however, are the cause of its destruction and its re-creation within this world.
"In that task, by fate, I am indeed capable when accompanied by you both;
likewise, Hari is capable when with me, even though you two are present. You are able to bring about the end, but you will not succeed without us."
Therefore, O Bull-bannered Lord, it is always fitting for us all to provide assistance in one another's duties; otherwise, the world would cease to exist. (26)
O Maheśvara, some Asuras will be slain by me;
others will be slain by Hari, and likewise others by you.
