Some are born from that vigor, some indeed from my own portion, while others are born from Māyā; these enemies of the gods are to be slain.
Since you are always engaged in yoga and free from passion, hatred, and the like,
and since your sole delight is in compassion alone, these asuras should not be slain by you.

O Lord, O Bull-bannered One, if those [principles] are unimpeded, how can there be creation, maintenance, and likewise dissolution? This would be logical only if they were eternally so, eternally so. (30)
O Hara, when the acts of creation, maintenance, and destruction are no longer to be performed,
the dissolution of our bodies and of Māyā is not possible.
For we are indeed of a single nature, though appearing distinct due to the difference in our effects;
if the difference in effects is not established, then a difference in form is purposeless.
Having become threefold from being one alone, we have come to possess distinct forms;
know this to be the eternal truth, O Maheśvara. (33)
Māyā also, through her divided forms, became known as Kamalā,
Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and Sandhyā, due to the differentiation of her functions.
O Maheśvara, woman is the root of worldly activity and of passion; following the acquisition of a wife, there arises the emergence of desire, anger, and the like. (35)
But when passion has arisen due to causes such as desire and anger,
living beings here strive with effort to pacify it by means of the cause of detachment.
Attachment would be the very first [fruit] from the tree of passion;
from that, desire is born, and from desire, anger arises. (37)
Dispassion and cessation from even natural sorrow are the causes for turning away from saṃsāra, as is constant non-attachment. (38)
O Maheśvara, compassion should always be present there, as well as peace;
non-violence, austerity, tranquility, and the practice of the path of knowledge. (39)
As long as you remain devoted to austerity, free from attachment, and endowed with compassion, non-violence and peace shall always abide in you. (40)
Therefore, why would you exert effort toward the production of happiness?
Whatever criticism was raised regarding that which is uncreated has all been stated to you. (41)
Therefore, O Lord of the World, for the welfare of all and for the sake of the gods,
please accept this one beautiful and excellent maiden as your wife.
Just as Lakṣmī is to Viṣṇu and as Sāvitrī is to me, so too is she who shall be the companion of Śambhu; accept her now.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā in the presence of Hari,
Hara, his face suffused with a smile, then spoke to the Lord of the World.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahman, it is exactly as you have stated; my activity proceeds from the cause of the universe, not for my own sake, because I am perfectly absorbed in the contemplation of Brahman."
Nevertheless, I shall tell you what I will do for the welfare of the world;
listen to those words of mine, O illustrious one, for they are indeed appropriate. (46)
"Command that Yoginī, who is capable of assuming any form at will, to become my wife so that she may take a portion of my splendor here."
"When I am engaged in yoga, she will likewise become a yoginī;
but when I am attached to desire, she will become a deluder.
Therefore, O Brahmin, point out to me that woman of excellent complexion to be my wife. (48)
I shall meditate upon that eternal, supreme light, which the wise who know the Vedas describe as the Imperishable (akṣara). 49.
O Brahman, being always capable of such contemplation, I enter into meditation;
may that which causes obstacles there not exist for me here.
Either you or I am Viṣṇu; we are both of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
O illustrious one, we are but limbs [of that whole]; therefore, it is fitting to contemplate that [Supreme Reality]. (51)
"O Lotus-seated One, I shall not remain without thinking of her;
therefore, grant me a wife who will always follow my will. (52)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his, Brahmā, the Lord of the entire world,
with a smiling face and a joyful mind, spoke these words.
Brahmā said:
O Mahādeva, such a woman as you have sought does exist.
She who was the daughter of Dakṣa, named Satī and most beautiful,
she herself, being thus wise, shall become your wife.
Know her, O Lord of the gods, to be one who performs penance for your sake and desires to attain you; for you abide within all souls. (56)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, after the words of Brahmā had been concluded, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana said to him,
"Do everything that was spoken by Brahmā."
When he replied, "I shall do so," Hari and Brahmā, accompanied by Sāvitrī and Kamalā, departed for their own desired abodes, filled with joy. (58)
Kāma, too, having heard the words of Hara, was filled with joy; accompanied by his friend Rati, he approached Śambhu in a disguised form and remained there, constantly directing Vasantas.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Conciliation of Hara," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Ten.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, Satyā, having observed a fast,
worshipped the Lord of Gods with devotion in the month of Āśvina.
Thus, when the Nandā-vrata was completed on the ninth day, at the end of the day's portion,
Hara appeared visibly before her as she stood bowed with devotion.
Beholding Hara directly before her eyes, Satī, her heart filled with joy,
bowed down in shame and prostrated at his feet.
Then Mahādeva, the bestower of wonderful fruits, spoke to Satī who was observing that vow, even though he desired her as his wife.
Īśvara said:
"O daughter of Dakṣa, I am pleased with this vow of yours;
choose a boon, and I shall grant whatever is desired by you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Although Mahādeva, the Lord of the World, already knew her disposition in this matter,
he nevertheless said, "Choose a boon," desiring to hear her words.
She too, overcome with shame, was unable to speak what resided in her heart—
the desire of the young woman— since it was shrouded by modesty.
In the meantime, Kāma then observed Hara’s purposeful gestures through the movements of his eyes and face regarding the acceptance of Vāmā.
Having found an opening, he fixed an arrow with a flower as its shaft;
then, with that "Gladdening" (harṣaṇa) arrow, he pierced Hara in the heart.
Then Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, being filled with joy, gazed repeatedly at Satī,
having forgotten his meditation upon the Supreme Brahman.
Then, filled with joy, the Mind-born one pierced him again with the deluding arrow; Śambhu was then utterly bewildered.
Then, O best of the twice-born, when he, deluded even by his own illusion, manifested the state of both delusion and joy, || 12 ||
Then, having steadied her own modesty, when Satī spoke to Hara, she uttered words effecting her purpose: "O Giver of Boons, grant me the boon that is my desire. (13)
Then, without waiting for the conclusion of his speech, the bull-bannered god said repeatedly to the daughter of Dakṣa, "Become my wife."
Having heard these words of his, which brought about the realization of her desired fruit,
she stood silent and delighted, having obtained the boon she had cherished in her heart.
O best of the twice-born, there in the presence of the lustful Hara, that lady of lovely smiles displayed her inner feelings and various amorous gestures.
O best of Brahmins, having assumed their respective dispositions, the aesthetic sentiment known as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) then entered them both, or else a quarrel, as was appropriate.
Before Hara, she shone with the luster of smooth, moist collyrium,
like a streak of the moon's digit near the crystal-bright body of the Lord.
Then that daughter of Dakṣa spoke thus repeatedly to Hara:
"O Lord of the World, having brought my father within your range of vision, accept me."
When the virtuous goddess then spoke these smiling words, he, deluded by passion, said again: "Become my wife. (20)
Then, seeing this, Madana, the god of love, together with his friend Rati, became filled with joy;
he was constantly united [with her] and rejoiced in himself.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having consoled Śambhu, the daughter of Dakṣa,
filled with joy and delusion, went into the presence of her mother.
Hara, too, having entered his own hermitage on the plateau of the Himalayas,
became absorbed in meditation due to the sorrow of separation from Dākṣāyaṇī.
Although thus deceived, the Lord of Beings then remembered the words of Brahmā that had been spoken for the sake of accepting a wife.
Then, having previously gained confidence through the very words of Brahmā, the bull-bannered god meditated upon Brahmā with his mind. (25)
Then, while he was thus reflecting, that Parameṣṭhin, impelled by the attainment of his desired goal, quickly entered into the presence of the wielder of the trident.
Where Hara remained on this slope of the Himavat, deceived, there Brahmā together with Sāvitrī also arrived. || 27 ||
Then, beholding that Creator accompanied by Sāvitrī, Hara,
both eager and deceived regarding the truth of the matter, spoke to him.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahman, that which you have now spoken regarding the purpose of the universe and the undertaking of taking a wife appears to me as being full of meaning."
I was propitiated with devotion by Dākṣāyaṇī through her extreme piety;
when I arrived to grant her a boon, I was worshipped by her.
Then, in his presence, Kāma pierced me with his great arrows;
deluded by his illusion, O Lotus-seated One, I was utterly unable to immediately effect a remedy. (31)
And her desired wish, O Brahman, was this very one which I perceived: "O Lord, may I become her husband, endowed with joy, devotion, and the performance of vows. (32)
Therefore, O Prajāpati, act for the sake of the universe and for my sake,
so that Dakṣa, having invited me, may quickly give his daughter in marriage.
Go to the abode of Dakṣa and speak my words;
act in such a way that there may be an end to Satī’s separation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus in the presence of that Prajāpati, Mahādeva looked toward Sāvitrī, and Satī’s separation [from him] increased.
Having addressed him thus, Lokeśa, having accomplished his purpose and filled with joy,
spoke these words for the welfare and benefit of the worlds, as approved by Dhūrjaṭi.
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, O Śambhu, that which you have spoken for the sake of the universe is most certainly determined;
indeed, there is no self-interest for you, nor for me, O Bull-bannered Lord. (37)
Dakṣa himself will give his daughter to you;
and I too shall speak your words in his presence. (38)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus addressed Mahādeva, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
departed for the abode of Dakṣa by means of his exceedingly swift chariot.
Then Dakṣa, having heard the entire account from the mouth of Satī, reflected: "How could this goddess be my daughter for Śambhu?"
Even though Mahādeva had arrived, he departed while still appearing pleased; yet how was it that he came once more, desiring [the child] exceedingly for the sake of his son? (41)
Or rather, I should immediately dispatch a messenger to him;
for it would not be proper [for me] if the Lord were to refuse to accept her for himself.
Or rather, I shall worship that very one whose banner is the bull,
so that he himself may become the husband of my daughter.
In that very same way, he too was worshipped with great effort by her who desired,
"May Śambhu become my husband," and thus it was granted by him.
While Dakṣa was reflecting thus, Brahmā then appeared before him,
mounted upon his swan-vehicle and accompanied by Sāvitrī.
Seeing that Creator, Dakṣa bowed down in prostration and stood before him;
then, addressing him as was appropriate, he offered him a seat.
Then, O best of Brahmins, although Dakṣa was overcome with anxiety, he was also filled with joy; he questioned the Lord of all the worlds regarding the reason for his arrival there.
Dakṣa said:
O Teacher of the World, tell me the reason for your arrival here; have you come to this hermitage out of affection for your son, or perhaps due to some business? (48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus questioned by the high-souled Dakṣa, the best of the gods,
smiling, spoke these words, gladdening that Prajāpati.
Brahmā said:
Listen, Dakṣa, to the purpose for which I have come to you;
that which is for the welfare of the world is also what is desired by you.
"The boon that was requested by your daughter today from Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, after she had propitiated him, has come to our home of its own accord. (51)
"I have been sent back to you by Śambhu for the sake of your daughter; therefore, attend to that which is the most beneficial course of action. (52)
Ever since Śaṅkara arrived to grant the boon,
he has not easily obtained peace due to his separation from that daughter.
Even though he had found his opportunity, Madana then struck the Lord of the World violently with all his flower-arrows at one and the same time. (54)
Pierced by the arrow of desire, he abandoned all self-reflection and remained distracted, thinking only of Satī, like an ordinary man.
Having forgotten the speech he had begun before the assembly due to his separation [from her], Giriśa asks, "Where is Satī? even when another is speaking.
"O son, that which was previously desired by me, by you, and by Madana, as well as by the best of sages such as Marīci and others— that has now been accomplished."
Śambhu, propitiated by your daughter, also dwells on the Himavat mountain, desiring to grant his approval to her contemplation.
Just as Śambhu was propitiated by him through various means and through the vow of Satyanandā,
even so is Satī propitiated.
Therefore, O Dakṣa, give her without delay to Śambhu, for whom she was intended; by that, you will have fulfilled your duty.
"I shall bring him to your abode by means of Nārada;
you must bestow her upon him for whom she was intended. (61)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"So be it," Dakṣa replied to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
and Vidhi departed for that place where Giriśa was stationed.
When Brahmā had departed, Dakṣa, together with his wife and sons, became joyful;
his body felt as if it were completely filled with nectar.
Then Brahmā, the lotus-seated one, also being delighted and serene,
approached Mahādeva who was staying upon the Himavat mountain.
Beholding the Creator of the World approaching, he whose banner is the bull repeatedly entertained doubts in his mind regarding the recovery of Satī.
Then Mahādeva, whose mind was fixed on Smara and who was afflicted by the pangs of passion, spoke from afar to Lokeśa, who was accompanied by Sāma: || 66 ||
Īśvara said: O best of gods, tell me what your son himself has said regarding the matter of truth,
so that his heart may not be rent asunder by the god of love.
O best of gods, this separation, afflicting even me who am virtuous and devoid of death, strikes me down while abandoning all other living beings. (68)
"O Brahman, I know that she is always present even when I am occupied with other tasks;
therefore, act quickly so that she may be obtained by me. (69)
Brahmā said:
O Bull-bannered One, listen to that which my son has spoken regarding the true matter; understand that your own goal has been accomplished.
My daughter shall be given to him; she has been intended for that purpose.
Furthermore, this deed is pleasing to me even more than your word.
"O Hari, Śambhu was propitiated by my daughter for this very purpose; since he himself now seeks her out, she must be given by me."
"O Creator, come into my presence at an auspicious moment and a favorable hour;
then I shall give my daughter as alms to Śambhu. (73)
Thus spoke Dakṣa with joy; therefore, O Bull-bannered One, go to her house at an auspicious moment to request her hand in marriage.
Īśvara said:
"I shall go together with you and the high-souled Nārada;
therefore, O worshipful one of the world, remember you and Nārada immediately. (75)
Likewise, remember the ten mind-born sons beginning with Marīci;
together with them and my attendants, I shall go to the abode of Dakṣa.
Then, remembered by the Lotus-Seated One, those sons of Brahmā, swift as thought, arrived together with Nārada; having perceived the anxiety regarding Kāma, they came to where Hara and Vidhi were.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Recitation of Satī," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The eleventh chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all the mind-born sons [of Brahmā], together with Nārada, assembled there.
By the mere remembrance of the ritual, they were dispelled like a wind. || 1 ||
Then, at that time when the performance of the rite was imminent, Śambhu, accompanied by Brahmā and his attendants, went to Dakṣa’s abode filled with joy.
The attendants, filled with joy, followed Śaṅkara while playing conchs, kettledrums, ḍiṇḍimas, trumpets, and flutes.
Some, keeping time with their palms and making the sound of their feet,
follow the bull-bannered Lord in their own aerial chariots of exceeding speed.
Making a great clamor and various kinds of sounds,
the hosts of diverse forms went forth accompanied by noise.
Then the gods, filled with joy, along with hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
followed the bull-bannered Lord with musical instruments, merriment, and dances.
O best of brahmins, by the sound of those most eminent Gandharvas and their hosts,
all the quarters and the earth were filled.
Kāma also, accompanied by his attendants, followed him openly, delighting and enchanting Śambhu with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) and other such emotions.
When Hari went for the sake of his wife, all the gods,
beginning with Brahmā, themselves quickly played enchanting music.
O best of the twice-born, all the directions became perfectly serene;
the fires blazed peacefully, and a rain of flowers fell.
The winds blew fragrant, and even the trees were in full bloom;
all living beings became healthy, including those who had previously been unwell.
The swans, cranes, ducks, blue-necked pigeons,
and cātakas uttered sweet sounds, as if inciting the Lord.
The serpent, the tiger skin, the matted locks, and likewise the crescent moon, became his ornaments; by them he was made resplendent. (13)
Then, in an instant, Hara reached the abode of Dakṣa on a powerful, swift bull, accompanied by Brahmā, Nārada, and others.
Then the highly energetic Dakṣa, rising up himself,
offered Hara and Brahmā and the others seats as was appropriate for each.
Having performed for them the appropriate worship with water for the feet and other offerings,
Dakṣa then entered into a consultation with the mental sages.
Then, O best of the twice-born, at an auspicious moment and under a favorable lunar mansion,
Dakṣa joyfully gave his virtuous daughter to Śambhu.
Then, according to the marriage rite, the bull-bannered Lord, filled with joy, took the hand of that beautiful-bodied daughter of Dakṣa.
Brahmā, Nārada, and the other sages gratified the Lord with Sāman chants, Ṛks, and Yajus hymns that were most pleasant to hear.
All the hosts played musical instruments and the throngs of Apsaras danced;
and clouds gathered in the sky released a rain of flowers.
Then, having approached Śambhu together with the exceedingly swift Garuḍa and Kamalā, he whose banner is Garuḍa spoke as follows: || 21 ||
The Blessed One said: "O Hara, you shine with the splendor of Dākṣāyaṇī, who is dark like smooth blue collyrium,
just as I shine with Padmā, though in the reverse order."
Perform protection for the god or for men together with her.
"O Śaṃkara, together with her, always bring about the welfare of those wandering in saṃsāra; and you shall slay the bandits as is appropriate."
O Lord of Beings, you shall slay whoever, upon seeing or hearing of her, should become filled with desire; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (25)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"So be it," the omniscient one replied with affection to the Supreme Lord, who was joyful in mind, O twice-born ones, his face serene with delight. (26)
Then Brahmā, seeing the daughter of Dakṣa with her beautiful smile,
his mind possessed by love, gazed upon her face.
Then Brahmā beheld the face of Satī again and again; at that moment, he once more helplessly succumbed to the agitation of his senses.
Then, O best of the twice-born, his splendor, blazing with the brilliance of fire, suddenly fell upon the ground before the sages.
Then, from that [cloud], clouds accompanied by thunder arose—
namely Samvarta, Avarta, Puṣkara, and Droṇa—
roaring and releasing waters, O best of the twice-born. (30)
When the sky was thus covered by them and they were roaring, Śaṅkara,
beholding the goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, became utterly infatuated with desire.
Then, though deluded by desire, Saṃkara, remembering the words of Viṣṇu,
raised his trident and desired to slay Brahmā.
O best of the twice-born, when Śambhu raised his trident to slay Vidhi, Marīci, Nārada, and the others then raised a cry of "Hā! Hā! in lamentation.
Dakṣa, apprehensive, quickly approached and stood before the Lord of Beings, raising his hand and saying, "Not so! Not so! and thus restrained him.
Then, seeing Dakṣa with his eyes closed before him, Maheśvara spoke these unpleasant words, reminding him of the speech of Viṣṇu.
Īśvara said:
"O Lord of Creatures, O best of Brahmins, that which has just been uttered by Nārāyaṇa has also been accepted by me to be carried out right here."
"Kill him who looks upon her with longing; by killing this man, I shall make these words of yours come true. (37)
"How did Brahmā look upon Satī with longing?
He became one whose splendor was lost; therefore, I shall slay that offender. (38)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
To him who was speaking thus, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the entire world, quickly appearing as a precursor and restraining him from killing, spoke these words. (39)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lord of Beings, you shall not slay the creator, the foremost of the worlds;
by this very act, Satī has been ordained as your wife for your sake."
O Śambhu, this four-faced one has appeared to create progeny;
now that he is slain, there is no other creator of the world remaining in his natural state. (41)
"How indeed shall we perform the acts of creation, maintenance, and destruction—properly, by him, by me, and by you as well? (42)
"If one among these were slain, who would perform that task?
Therefore, O Bull-bannered Lord, the Creator must not be killed by you. (43)
Īśvara said:
"I shall fulfill my vow by slaying this four-faced one;
I alone shall create all beings, both the stationary and the moving."
"Or else, by my own splendor, I shall create another creator;
he alone shall be the maker of creation forever, with my permission. (45)
"O Lord of the Moon, fulfilling my vow, I shall indeed slay him according to the prescribed rule;
I shall create another sole Creator—do not stop me, O Four-armed One! (46)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Giriśa, the four-armed one,
his face brightened by a smile, spoke again, saying, "Do not say so."
"O best of the twice-born, he spoke these words of address to the Lord: 'It would not be fitting for me to fulfill my vow. (48)
Then again, how is it that my own self appears in the form of Śambhu?
This [form] is perceived as clearly distinct, standing right before me by direct perception. (49)
Then, smiling in the presence of the sages, the Blessed One whose banner is Garuḍa spoke these words, pleasing Mahādeva.
The Blessed Lord said: Brahmā is not distinct from you, nor is Śambhu distinct from Brahmā;
nor am I distinct from the two of you—this non-difference is eternal.
Of the Pradhāna and the Apradhāna, which consist of both the divisible and the indivisible and are composed of light, you two are one part and I am another portion.
Who are you, who am I, and who is Brahmā? This triad of parts is distinct from me alone, the Supreme Self, and serves as the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Contemplate the Self by means of the self; cultivate intimacy with the Self. Make the oneness of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva reside within your heart.
Just as the head and neck are distinct parts of a single substratum, so too,
O Hara, this triad of aspects belongs to my one self.
That light which is supreme, illuminating both self and others, immutable, unmanifest, and infinite in form;
eternal, and devoid of distinctions such as length and so forth—that is the Supreme, and we are not separate from it. 56.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of him, Mahādeva was bewildered;
though he knew their non-difference, he acted as if through forgetfulness due to thinking of something else.
He questioned Govinda again regarding the non-duality of the three—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Tryambaka— and the distinction between them as one.
Then, being questioned by Śambhu, Nārāyaṇa spoke and demonstrated the non-duality and the oneness of the three gods.
Then, having heard from the lotus-bud of Viṣṇu’s mouth that Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva are non-different in essence,
and having perceived his own true nature, Mṛḍa did not kill Brahmā, who shone like a bee amidst flowers.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, which establishes the oneness of the three deities, in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 11 ||
The Twelfth Chapter.
The Sages said:
Regarding that non-duality of the three gods which Janārdana proclaimed—
O best of the twice-born, we wish to hear that from you concerning Śambhu.
How did the one whose banner is Garuḍa demonstrate his oneness?
Explain that to us, O best of Brahmins, for our curiosity is indeed great. || 2 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O sages, to this supreme, secret, and most excellent teaching—
the non-duality of the three gods and likewise the vision of their unity.
O best of sages, being questioned by Hara, Govinda addressed him respectfully and spoke these words that convey the truth without deviation.
The Blessed Lord said:
This entire universe was then composed of darkness, devoid of worlds,
unknown and unperceivable, as if asleep on all sides.
Here there is no division of day and night, no sky, and no earth;
no light, no water, no wind, nor does anything else exist.
There was one supreme Brahman— subtle, eternal, beyond the senses,
unmanifest in the form of knowledge, devoid of duality, and without distinguishing attributes.
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are eternal and pervade all things;
O Lord of Beings, Time also exists as the single cause of the universe.
O Hara, that which is the one supreme Brahman is beyond its own essential nature;
these three forms are eternally His alone, the Lord of the universe.
Time is another form, beginningless and the cause of all;
it is joined with all beings through its own limitation.
Then that [Self], shining by its own self-luminosity, manifests its radiant form, itself agitating Prakṛti in an incomparable manner for the sake of prior creation. (11)
From the agitated primordial nature (prakṛti), the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) was born;
thereafter, from the principle of the Great One, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) became threefold.
Then, when ego had arisen from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra),
Viṣṇu created infinite space (ākāśa), which is devoid of form.
Then, having created water from the subtle element of taste, Maheśvara,
being himself without support, sustained it by means of his own māyā.
Then the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, once again agitated Prakṛti—which had remained in equilibrium through the balance of the three qualities—for the sake of creation. || 15 ||
Then that primordial nature (prakṛti), having become threefold as seed within those [waters],
cast the undisturbed seed of the universe into the waters.
Gradually increasing in that manner, it became a vast golden egg;
while still in the state of an embryo within that egg, he absorbed all those waters.
When the waters were established, Viṣṇu again held that egg within the womb of the golden egg by means of your very own incomparable illusory power (māyā). || 18 ||
It was likewise covered on all sides and in every direction by water, fires, winds, and space, outside that egg.
The water within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is measured by seven oceans as well as by the measurements of rivers and so forth; the rest, however, is situated outside.
Within that [egg], Viṣṇu himself, assuming the form of Brahmā,
having dwelt there for a divine year, split that egg asunder.
From that, O Maheśvara, Mount Meru arose;
from it the mountains were born as the placenta, and from its water the seven oceans were produced.
In the midst of that, from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), the earth was produced;
it was joined by the Lord and by primordial nature (prakṛti) and consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
Long before [the emergence of] mountains and the like, the Earth arose;
through the conjunction of fragments of the cosmic egg, she became exceedingly firm.
Brahmā himself, the teacher of all the worlds, remained within that very [egg]. When Brahmā, situated in the midst of the cosmic egg, had not yet become manifest,
at that very moment, light was perfectly produced from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra).
But from the subtle element of touch, when directed by primordial nature (prakṛti), wind arose as the vital breath for all beings on every side. (26)
The interior and exterior of that egg were pervaded by water, by incomparable fires, by winds, and likewise by space; yet another [element] was greedily seeking [to enter].
Then Maheśvara, by the power of his primary will, divided the body of Brahmā into three parts within Śambhu, making it tripled by the three qualities.
The upper portion of that became the Great Lord Brahmā, possessing four faces and four arms, with a body as fair as the filaments of a lotus. (29)
The middle portion of that [body] has a blue limb, one face, and four arms;
with a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in its hands, that body is indeed Vaiṣṇava.
The lower part became five-faced and four-armed,
white like a crystal cloud, with a body adorned by the moon upon his crest.
He directed his power of creation here and there throughout the realm of Brahmā;
he himself became the creator in the form of Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds.
The Great Lord applied his own power of maintenance, known as Māyā or Prakṛti,
to the body of Viṣṇu, and likewise applied his own power of knowledge.
Viṣṇu became the sustainer, and I alone am Maheśvara;
by the application of all powers, my nature is eternally that [of both].
He likewise applied the internal power to the body in the Śāmbhava [state]. He likewise applied the internal power to the body in the Śāmbhava [state]. || 35 ||
Śambhu, that very Supreme Lord, became the bringer of the end;
thereafter, he himself shines forth within the three bodies.
The Lord, the Master, is the supreme light whose nature is knowledge; he is without beginning, the one Great Lord who effects the creation, maintenance, and end [of the world]. (37)
He received the distinct designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
therefore, you, the Creator (Vidhātṛ), and I am not separate. Thus, our bodies, forms, and knowledge are internal [to one another]. (38)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
his face blossoming with joy, he spoke once more to Janārdana.
Īśvara said:
Maheśa alone is the stainless one whose form is light.
What indeed is māyā, what is time, or what is called prakṛti?
O Govinda, tell me how those individuals are non-different from Him; if they are different, how can there be oneness? Explain that power to me exactly as it is.
The Blessed Lord said: Abiding in meditation, you alone always behold the Supreme Lord within yourself as the very nature of the Self— of the form of light, eternal and imperishable.
O All-pervading Lord, you yourself are the knower of illusion, primordial nature, time, and the person (puruṣa); therefore, remain devoted to meditation through the yoga of contemplation.
Since I have now been deluded by the illusion belonging to you, I have consequently forgotten the supreme light due to my attachment to women. (44)
Now, filled with anger and forgetting yourself within yourself, O first Lord, you ask about the forms of Prakṛti and the rest. (45)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having heard those well-considered words there, Mahādeva,
while the sages were looking on, became absorbed in yoga and intent on meditation.
Having assumed the bound lotus posture with his eyes closed,
Maheśvara then meditated upon the Self within himself.
As he was thus reflecting, his auspicious body shone forth;
at that time, even the sages were unable to look upon it, for it was radiant with splendors.
At that very moment, Śambhu, though engaged in meditation, was abandoned by Viṣṇu’s Māyā and shone intensely, blazing with the splendor of his ascetic power.
Whichever groups then stood near Śaṅkara in service,
even they were unable to look upon Śaṅkara or the Sun.
Then Viṣṇu himself, with his mind deeply absorbed in meditative concentration,
entered the interior of Dhūrjaṭi’s body in the form of light.
Having entered his belly, the imperishable Nārāyaṇa himself displayed the very same order of creation as it had occurred in the past. 52.
Neither gross nor subtle, nor within the range of qualifiers;
eternal bliss yet devoid of [worldly] bliss, one, pure, and beyond the senses. (53)
The invisible one, the seer of all, devoid of qualities, the supreme state,
the Supreme Self, bliss itself, and the cause of the cause of the universe.
First, Śambhu beheld himself in that very form;
with his mind entered therein, he was devoid of external knowledge.

He beheld that very form, which was his own primordial nature (prakṛti), having assumed a state of differentiation for the sake of creation; though it was essentially one, he saw it as if it were separate in his immediate vicinity.
And he saw men dwelling there, O best of the twice-born, just as sparks continuously emerge from a large fire. (57)
That very [reality] shines forth repeatedly in the form of time, acting as the cause through its limitation by the conjunctions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (58)

Nature, the Person, and Time as well—though essentially non-different, yet appearing as distinct and having attained a state of differentiation for the sake of creation—[are thus described] again and again. (59)
The moon-crested Lord beheld them as both distinct and non-different;
there is only the one non-dual Brahman, for here there is nothing whatsoever that is manifold.
It shines forth in the form of primordial matter (pradhāna) and in the form of time;
likewise, it proceeds for the sake of transmigratory existence in the form of the individual soul (puruṣa). || 61 ||
For the sake of enjoyment, she constantly operates within the bodies of living beings;
that very Māyā, who is Prakṛti, deludes even Śaṅkara.
Likewise, you have become Hari, as well as Viriñci and others born from other wombs;
the primordial nature called Māyā deludes even a living being who is already pure.
She is always Lakṣmī in female form, the beloved of Hari;
she is Sāvitrī, Rati, Sandhyā, Satī, and she alone is Vīriṇī.
"The Goddess herself, in the form of intellect, is celebrated as Caṇḍikā"— thus Hara,
having entered the path of meditation, immediately beheld her himself.
Likewise, he himself [perceives] the sequence of creation through the divisions beginning with the Mahat.
O best of the twice-born, having shown Kāla, Prakṛti, and Puruṣa, Hari likewise showed them that other body.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa, which establishes the non-duality of the three deities.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then he showed the structure of the cosmic egg to Śambhu.
And the cosmic egg, situated within the mass of waters, increased as it had before.
In the midst of that, he beheld Brahmā, the lord of the world, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus,
appearing in the form of light for the sake of illumination and for the purpose of creation, yet existing as if separate.
And he repeatedly beheld within the cosmic egg a embodied being with four arms, whose splendor was unsurpassed, seated upon a lotus, and radiant with lights.
And right there he beheld the divine body divided into three parts;
its upper, middle, and lower portions consisted of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva respectively.
Just as the upper portion of his body then attained the state of Brahmā,
he likewise saw the middle portion become Viṣṇu and the lower part the nature of Śambhu.
Hara beheld his own single body repeatedly divided into three within his womb, and likewise this entire world.
Sometimes the Vaiṣṇava body may go to dissolution in the Brāhma body;
likewise, the Brāhma in the Vaiṣṇava, and the Vaiṣṇava in the Śāmbhava.
The Śāmbhava [state] dissolves into the Vaiṣṇava body, or the Brāhma into the Śāmbhava; Śambhu repeatedly attains absorption and oneness with them.
Vāmadeva also beheld his own body, though distinct, yet not separate, as it attained dissolution and entered into the Supreme Self.
In the midst of that, Śambhu saw the earth spread out upon the water,
covered here and there by clusters of great mountains.
He again beheld Brahmā creating heaven from the beginning,
as well as himself as a distinct entity and Viṣṇu seated upon Garuḍa.
There he likewise [honored] Dakṣa Prajāpati, his own Gaṇas,
the ten [sages] beginning with Marīci, as well as Vīriṇī and Satī.
Sandhyā, Rati, Kandarpa, Śṛṅgāra, and Vasanta;
likewise, the hāvas and bhāvas, as well as Māras, ṛṣis, gods, and the hosts of Maruts.
He saw clouds, the moon, and the sun; trees, creepers, and grasses;
as well as Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras.
Humans, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises;
meteors, thunderbolts, and comets; and worms, insects, and moths. (15)
He beheld a certain woman engaged in sexual union with someone who was already born,
someone currently being born, and someone about to perish.
The Supreme Lord Śambhu beheld some laughing and sporting, others likewise lamenting, and still others running about. || 17 ||
Some, covered in divine ornaments and anointed with garlands and sandalwood paste,
were seen being repeatedly sported with by Śambhu.
Some sages, whose wealth was their asceticism, beheld him as he praised, extolled, and likewise honored Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. (19)
Some were performing austerities on the banks of rivers in the forest of penance,
while others were devoted to the study and recitation of the Vedas.
In that very same manner, he saw the seven oceans, the rivers, and the celestial lakes;
likewise, he was seen by Śambhu himself standing upon the mountain.
Māyā, in the form of Lakṣmī, thoroughly deludes Hari;
likewise, Śaṅkara says that Satī, in the form of herself, deludes him.
He himself took delight with Satī on Mount Kailāsa, on Mount Meru,
on Mandara, and in the celestial grove frequented by the sentiment of love.
Having likewise abandoned her body as Satī, she was born as the daughter of Himavat;
and how Kārtikeya was born and how I slew the one named Tāraka— all that the bull-bannered Lord [Śiva] related in full and with complete accuracy.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by him in the form of Narasiṃha,
just as Kālanemi was slain and just as Hiraṇyākṣa was slain.
Hara beheld everything: the kind of battle that Viṣṇu had formerly waged against the hosts of Dānavas, as well as exactly how and which of them were slain.
Having seen again and again, one by one, the various manifestations of the world— beginning with Brahmā and others, including the stars, planets, humans, siddhas, vidyādharas, and so forth.
The Lord Śambhu saw himself withdrawing them;
at the conclusion of that withdrawal, he beheld Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, became empty.
When the entire world had become void, Brahmā, having entered the body of Viṣṇu, became absorbed;
and Śambhu likewise entered that very body.
He beheld only Viṣṇu, whose form is unmanifest;
at that time, Hara saw nothing else except Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu beheld that dissolution within the Supreme Self,
manifesting in the supreme reality, the eternal form of light.
Then he beheld nothing else but that which is eternal, consisting of knowledge, blissful, the supreme Brahman, and accessible solely through knowledge. (34)
Within his own body, he beheld both the unity and the diversity of the universe, as well as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world within the Supreme Self.
He beheld only the one, non-dual Brahman—the luminous Supreme Self, peaceful, eternal, beyond the senses, and nothing else whatsoever. (36)
"Who is Viṣṇu or Hara? Who is Brahmā? What is this world?"—such distinctions regarding Śambhu, the Supreme Self, were not grasped by him. (37)
As he was thus observing, Māyā emerged from the interior of his body to the outside and entered the one whose emblem is the bull.
Having demonstrated both non-difference and difference,
Janārdana then quickly emerged from that body of Śambhu.
Then, as Hara’s concentration was abandoned and his mind had wavered, being deluded by Māyā, his heart quickly went toward Satī. (40)
Then, O best of the twice-born, Hara gazed for a moment upon the beautiful face of Dākṣāyaṇī, which resembled a blossomed lotus.
Then, having beheld Dakṣa, Marīci, and the others among his own attendants, as well as the Lotus-Seated One and Viṣṇu there, Śaṅkara was struck with wonder.
Then Janārdana spoke to that Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, who was filled with wonder and whose face was blossoming with a smile.
The Blessed Lord said: O Śaṅkara, whatever you have asked regarding the unity and the diversity of the three gods, that has now been understood by you.
O Mahādeva, primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), time (kāla), and illusion (māyā) are known within your own interior; what are they like, and who indeed are they? (45)
Brahman is one, eternally peaceful, constant, and supremely great; how then has it come to possess differentiation? What kind of thing was that seen by you?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus questioned by the Blessed One, the Blessed Lord whose banner bears the bull spoke these truthful words to Hari, O best of the twice-born. (47)
Īśvara said:
There exists one Śiva, peaceful, infinite, and infallible Brahman; there is nothing else like Him.
Therefore, the entire universe is non-different from Hari, and forms such as Time and the rest are the cause of creation.
We are always of the nature of a true portion of that very one who is the source of all beings and is stainless;
the three forms—creation, maintenance, and dissolution—impelled by Him, shine forth as distinct from Him.
Neither I, nor you, nor Hiraṇyagarbha, nor the form of Time, nor primordial nature (prakṛti),
nor anything else is capable of impelling Him, even though His form exists here eternally.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Bull-bannered One, this reality has been proclaimed by you and understood;
we—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Wielder of the Pināka—are indeed portions of that. (51)
Therefore, O Śambhu, if you have realized the oneness of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of the Pināka bow, this Viriñci must not be slain by you. (52)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
and seeing their oneness, Mahādeva did not slay Vidhi.
Thus has been told to you how Viṣṇu declared his non-difference [from Śiva];
O twice-born ones, I shall tell you again that which was presented to Śambhu.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Appeasement of Hara’s Wrath," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 13 ||
The fourteenth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, while the clouds were thundering, Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, [appeared].
Having dismissed Viṣṇu and the others, he went to the Himavat mountain.
Having placed Satī, who was radiant with fragrance, upon a lofty bull,
he went to the delightful plateau of the Himalayas, which was filled with groves.
Then, near Śaṅkara, that woman of beautiful teeth and lovely smile shone,
seated upon her bull like Kālī at the edge of the moon.
Brahmā and all the others, as well as Marīci and the rest born of his mind,
and even Dakṣa— all of them, together with the gods and demons, became filled with joy.
Some playing conchs, some beating auspicious cymbals,
and some making merry laughter, they followed the bull-bannered god.
Although they were dismissed by Śambhu, Brahmā and the others followed him once more for some distance, filled with supreme joy.
Then, having addressed Śambhu, Brahmā and the others who were born of his mind departed for their respective abodes on swift-moving chariots.
All the gods, the Siddhas, as well as the hosts of Apsarases, the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and others who had gathered there. || 8 ||
Released by Hara, they returned to their own abode;
once the bull-bannered god had taken a wife, they became filled with joy.
Then Hara, together with his own attendants, having reached Mount Kailāsa, the place of delight, caused his beloved to descend from the bull there.
Then Virūpākṣa, having obtained this daughter of Dakṣa,
dismissed his own attendants, Nandin and the others, from the mountain cave.
Śambhu spoke these most excellent words to all of them, beginning with Nandin:
"O you whose minds are fickle, whenever I remember you here,
you shall then and there come to my side."
When Vāmadeva had spoken thus, Nandin, Bhairava,
and the others went to the great Kauśī-prapāta on the Himavat mountain.
Even Īśvara, being deluded when they had departed,
sported for a long time with Dākṣāyaṇī in secret every day to his heart's content.
Once, having gathered wild flowers and fashioned a beautiful garland, he placed it upon Satī in the position of a necklace.
Once, while the virtuous lady was looking at her own face in a mirror, Hara followed her and looked at his own face as well. (16)
Sometimes, his hair would rise up with joy as he playfully toyed with hers;
thus he would repeatedly bind it, loosen it, and even smooth it down.
The bull-bannered Lord, who is naturally red, makes his two feet— which are already reddened by the ochre robe and the bright [saffron]— possessing a deep red hue.
Even that which ought to be proclaimed loudly before others, she whispers repeatedly into his ear, desiring to touch the face of her lover.
Even after going a long distance and meeting her with great effort, he could not keep pace with her whose mind was fixed on another behind her back.
But the bull-bannered god, having vanished right there by means of his illusory power, embraced her;
she, terrified, became agitated.
Upon her two breasts, which resembled golden lotus buds,
he drew a musk tilaka in the shape of a bee.
Suddenly removing her necklace from her pair of breasts, Hara repeatedly joins it back in that very place with his hands.
Having repeatedly loosened his armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
he then placed them back again in their respective positions.
Saying to her, "Kālī is coming; she is your friend of the same complexion," he looked at her as she desired it and grasped her breasts.
Once, his mind intoxicated by passion, the Lord of the Pramathas joyfully performed playful acts with his beloved who was dear to his heart.
Having gathered lotus flowers and wild blossoms, Śaṅkara once adorned all her limbs with floral ornaments.
In all the delightful mountain bowers and forests, Hara, the husband of Satī, sported joyfully with her.
Neither in his vehicle, nor while seated, nor while standing, nor even while moving about,
did the bull-bannered god find any comfort for even a moment without her.
Having dwelt for a very long time in the caves of Mount Kailāsa,
he went to the Mahākauśī waterfall on the Himavat mountain.
When the bull-bannered god had entered that Himalaya mountain,
Kāma also departed together with his friend and Rati.
When Kāma had entered into Śaṅkara,
Vasanta spread his own splendors among the trees, the waters, and likewise upon the earth.
All the trees were in full bloom, as were the other creepers;
the waters were filled with blossoming lotuses, and likewise, bees hovered over the lotuses.
When Surata had entered there, the Malaya breezes began to blow,
and the city women were enchanted by the fragrance of the fragrant flowers.
Then the clever Smara, like one extracting clarified butter from a mass of buttermilk, churned the minds even of the sages and extracted their essence, O Surabhi.
Resembling the half-moon at twilight, they shone with leaf-like splendor;
possessing minds like those of Cupid’s arrows, they were always a source of delight.
The lotus flowers in the lakes shone forth, as did the goddesses of the clouds with their beautiful faces, both intent on deluding all people.
And the *nāgakeśara* trees, with their golden-colored blossoms, shone like the banner of the God of Love, appearing enchanting in the presence of Śaṅkara. (38)
The campaka trees repeatedly manifested the state of having golden flowers, shining brilliantly with their abundant blossoms that were clearly visible as well as those yet to open.
Just as the quarters of the sky become pale-red with the rays of dawn when filled with blossoming *pāṭala* flowers, so too do those flowering trees known by the name *pāṭala*. (40)
Having perfumed the breeze with the fragrance of the fragrant clove-creeper, it formerly used to utterly bewilder the hearts of those filled with desire. (41)
There, the *balvaja* grasses, perfumed by the spring breeze, truly shone;
they were enchanting, filled with the delight of bees greedy for their fragrance. 42.
The mango trees, beautiful and radiant with the luster of fire, shone forth with their crests covered by a multitude of Cupid’s arrows. 43.
The waters, free from impurity, shone with full-blown lotuses,
like the minds of sages from which the emergence of manifest light has occurred.
Then the frost-motes met their destruction upon contact with the sun's rays, just as the sense of "mine" vanishes from the hearts of those endowed with wisdom.
Then, every day, the cuckoos uttered their cries without fear,
as intensely as the sound of the flower-bowstring when striking the lives of living beings.
There, the bees dwelling within the flowers of the forest hummed like the roar of the tiger of passion (Smara) as he desired to enjoy the play of his beloved.

The moon bore its digits like frost, and the sun likewise; yet these were not all their full digits, which they assumed in succession for the delusion of people on earth—this is the auspicious [account]. (48)
Then the nights, together with the moon, became clear and free from frost;
they were as captivating as passionate women with their beloveds. || 49 ||
At that time, Mahādeva, together with Satī on that most excellent mountain,
sported for a very long time, concealed within the groves and the caves.
The auspicious daughter of Dakṣa also took her delight with him in such a way that Hara found no peace for even a moment without her.
In the matter of sensual enjoyment, the virtuous goddess, who was dear to his heart,
seemed to enter the body of Hara, as it were, while making him drink its essence.
Adorning her entire body with flower garlands fashioned by his own hand, he performed excellent jests for her.
Through conversations, glances, smiles, and likewise through dialogues,
Hara, the Lord of the Mountain, who is self-restrained, entered her consciousness.
Hara, his body sustained by drinking the nectar from that moon-like face,
never again experienced the slender state resulting from the consumption of Śeṣa’s poison.
By dwelling in her lotus-like mouth, by her playful charms,
and by her virtues, he was bound like a great elephant and could no longer move about.
Thus Maheśa took his delight every day with the daughter of Dakṣa in the mountain thickets, on the plateaus, and in the caves of the Himālayas;
as he sported for the duration of the seasons, nine, ten, and five other years passed for the lords of sages.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pastimes of Śiva and Satī," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Once, at the arrival of the rainy season, the daughter of Dakṣa...
[He saw] the bull-bannered Lord situated on a plateau of the mountain-like world-mountain. || 1 ||
Satyuvāca said:
This season of the arrival of clouds has arrived, a time most difficult to endure,
when the expanse of the sky and all directions are shrouded by masses of clouds of many colors.
The winds blow with extreme velocity, tearing at the heart,
raining down as it were droplets of water washed by the pollen of kadamba flowers.
Whose mind is not agitated by the clouds that thunder loudly while discharging torrents of rain, as if bearing the fierce lightning for their banners? (4)
Neither the sun is seen, nor is the moon obscured by clouds;
even by day it shines like night, creating a reversal of the conditions for those separated from their lovers.
O Śaṅkara, the clouds, driven by the wind, roaring and not remaining in one place, appear as if they are falling upon the heads of the worlds.
Great trees, struck by the wind, appear as if dancing in the sky;
O Hara, they terrify the fearful while being desired by lovers.
Behind the mass of clouds, dark as glossy blue collyrium,
the row of cranes shines aloft like the foam stirred up by the Yamunā.
Moment by moment this dark woman is seen to be flickering;
she has vanished like the blazing submarine fire within the ocean.
For even in the courtyards of palaces, grasses do indeed sprout;
O Virūpākṣa, what else could I say regarding the growth of grass elsewhere? (10)
With its dark and silver slopes, this bright Himālaya is like the Ocean of Milk with the leaves from the multitude of trees in Mandara’s hermitage.
And Kusumaśrī then resorted to the Kūṭaja tree, and thereafter to the Kiṃśukas,
just as Fortune in the Kali age abandons the virtuous for various lowly things.
The peacocks, constantly indicating rain, are repeatedly delighted by the sound of thunder and cry out "kekā" in every forest. 13.
The sweet cry of the cātaka birds, who look toward the clouds, is enchanting;
let it be heard as they are intensely excited by the indication of the imminent arrival of rain. 14.
Now Indra’s bow has made its appearance in the sky, having risen up as if to pierce the heat with its showers of rain-arrows. (15)
Behold, O Bharga, the noble conduct of the clouds here:
that they cause both the peacock who follows them and the cātaka bird to cross over [their distress]. 16.
O Lord of the Mountain, having witnessed the defeat even of their friend at the hands of the peacock and the cuckoo,
the swans go to Lake Mānasa, however far it may be.
In this difficult time, even crows and sparrows build their nests;
how will you find peace without a home? 18.
O wielder of the Pināka bow, a great fear arising from the clouds oppresses me;
therefore, at my word, strive to find a dwelling place without delay.
O Bull-bannered One, whether on Kailāsa, or on the Himālaya, or on the great Kauśī, or upon the earth— take up your residence wherever it is suitable for you.
Thus addressed then by that daughter of Dakṣa, Śambhu laughed once, his face white with the rays of the moon resting upon his head.
Then the high-souled one, who knew all principles, with his lips parted by a smile, spoke to the goddess Satī, pleasing the Supreme Goddess.
Īśvara said: "O charming one, dear to me, wherever I must dwell for your pleasure, there the clouds shall never go, O beloved."
Clouds move as far as the slopes of the mountain, even during the rains, O enchanting one, at that abode of perpetual frost. (24)
Likewise, O Goddess, as far as the base of Mount Kailāsa, the clouds move about;
they never go beyond that point.
The clouds, such as the Puṣkara and Āvartaka, do not rise above Mount Sumeru or the ocean; having reached the base of his knees, they turn back. 26.
And among these lords of mountains,
tell me quickly which one your heart desires for a dear dwelling place.

On that mountain born of snow, your curiosities regarding wandering at will should always be satisfied by flocks of birds with golden wings, moving in great swarms driven by the wind, and uttering sweet songs.

Desiring eternal friendship with you, those Siddha women will come to the mountain, where they sport at their own will upon jeweled pavements; out of curiosity, they will offer assistance and provide fruits and other gifts.

Those who are daughters of the gods, daughters of the mountains, and those who are daughters of the nāgas, as well as the foremost of horses—all of them shall constantly provide you with assistance through their playful expressions of joy. (30)

Beholding this incomparable form of yours and your most beautiful face, women—whose forms and collections of luster are surpassed by yours—will constantly treat their own bodies and the qualities of their beauty with disdain; thus, they shall possess the lovely forms of those with unblinking eyes. (31)

Menakā, the wife of the King of Mountains, who is renowned in the three worlds for her beauty and virtues, shall also constantly provide you with delight there through her suggestions and other means. (32)

May you always receive instruction from the groups of matrons who worship the King of Mountains and who spread noble joy; and may that instruction, though appropriate to your own lineage, be daily infused with affection and a multitude of virtues.
O beloved, why do you wish to go to that place which is always filled with the origin of spring, surrounded by groves of pleasure where the warbling of various cuckoos resounds? (34)
The Himālaya, the king of mountains, which was surrounded by hundreds of lakes filled with various kinds of clear water and joined by hundreds of lotus ponds. 34a.
It is covered with grassy meadows and trees known as *kalpa* that grant all desires; there indeed you shall enjoy its flowers.
O highly fortunate lady, that temple was filled with various herds of deer, surrounded by groups of sages and ascetics, and was free from any predatory beasts.
It shone with ramparts made of crystal, gold, and silver,
and was adorned on all sides by clusters of lakes such as Mānasa and others.
It was filled with golden lotuses having jeweled stalks, both in full bloom and as buds;
it was frequented by porpoises, conchs, tortoises, crocodiles, and large fish, and adorned with charming blue lotuses and other such flowers.
With all kinds of perfumes clinging from the bathing of hundreds of goddesses, and with saffron,
it was filled with waters scented by various garlands and possessed of clear luster.
Adorned by lush meadows and tall trees standing upon its banks,
it seemed to surpass its own source with its branches and treetops that appeared as if they were dancing.
It was adorned by flocks of *kādamba* geese, cranes, and intoxicated ruddy geese, and by bees and other insects that made sweet sounds and brought delight. || 41 ||
Of Vāsava, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa;
of Agni, the son of Kuṇapa, Māruta, and Hara. || 42 ||
The lofty Meru, the abode of the gods, resplendent with its peaks due to its cities,
and frequented by throngs of beautiful-limbed women such as Rambhā, Śacī, and Menakā.
But what do you desire—the great mountain that is the essence of all things? (43)
There, accompanied by hundreds of goddesses and served by throngs of apsarases, Śacī shall constantly provide you with worthy assistance. (44)
Or else, you desire my Kailāsa, the king of mountains, which is the eternal refuge and a place resplendent with the city of the Lord of Wealth.
It was purified by the flood of the Ganges' waters, possessed a luster equal to the full moon,
and was always frequented by yakṣa maidens in its caves and upon its peaks.
"O beautiful one, it is frequented by various herds of deer, surrounded by hundreds of lotus-pools, and equal to Mount Sumeru in all its virtues. (47)
"In whichever of these places your heart finds desire, tell me that quickly; I shall make my dwelling there for you. (48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Śaṅkara had spoken thus, the daughter of Dakṣa then slowly addressed these gentle words to Mahādeva, which revealed her own desire.
Satī said: "I desire to dwell with you on the Himālaya mountain itself;
do not delay, but make your residence on that very great mountain. (50)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then,
having heard those words, Hara was exceedingly delighted and went with the daughter of Dakṣa to the lofty peak of the Himālaya mountain.
Accompanied by a host of perfected women, he went to the lofty peak, inaccessible to clouds and birds, which was adorned with groves of Marīca trees.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, "The Forest-Dwelling of Himādri," in the glorious *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixteen.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Accompanied by Satī, he reached the lofty peak, variegated with gold and silver and speckled with jewels,
which was as bright as the rising sun.
In that place made of crystal stone, adorned with grassy meadows and rows of trees, endowed with various flowering creepers and lakes,
and decorated by humming bees upon the tips of the branches of blossoming trees; (2)
It was beautified by blooming lotuses, clusters of blue water-lilies,
and flocks of ruddy geese, kādamba ducks, swans, and cormorants.
It resounded with the cries of intoxicated cranes and peacocks,
and was filled with the sweet, melodious warbling of male cuckoos frequented by deer.
It was frequented by horse-faced Siddhas, Apsarases, and Guhyakas;
it was graced by Vidyādharīs, goddesses, and Kinnarīs,
and was filled with matrons, mountain-dwelling women, and maidens.
It was beautifully adorned by the sounds of the *vipañcī* lute, the *tantrikā*, and the deep resonance of the *mṛdaṅga* and *paṭaha* drums, and by dancing apsarases who had arisen out of curiosity.
It was completely covered by divine, fragrant celestial creepers and graced by bowers with flowers blooming upwards.
On a peak in the vicinity of the city of Śailarāja, the bull-bannered Lord sported for a long time with Satī on that most beautiful mountain.
In that place, which was equal to heaven, Śaṅkara sported joyfully with Satī for ten thousand divine years.
Sometimes Śaṅkara goes from that place to Kailāsa,
and sometimes to the peak of Meru, surrounded by the Goddess of the Gods, as in former times.
Having gone again and again to the gardens of the guardians of the quarters, to the forests, and to the surface of the earth, he took his pleasure there with Satī as his companion.
He perceived neither day nor night, neither sacred learning, nor austerity, nor tranquility;
with his mind fixed on truth, Śambhu indeed experienced only joy.
Satī beheld the single face of Mahādeva on all sides;
Mahādeva, too, always beheld the face of Satī everywhere.
Thus, through their mutual union, Śambhu and Satī caused the tree of passion to grow by watering it with the moisture of their affection.
In the meantime, Śakra, the benefactor of the worlds, began to perform a great sacrifice that sustains all living beings. || 15 ||
There, eighty-eight thousand officiating priests (ṛtvij) offer oblations;
sixty-four thousand celestial sages (surarṣi) serve as chanters (udgātṛ);
and an equal number, Nārada and others, act as Adhvaryu and Hotṛ priests. || 16 ||
Viṣṇu himself was the presiding deity along with all the hosts of Maruts;
Brahmā himself was present there as the one who demonstrates the ritual according to the three Vedas.
In that very manner, all the guardians of the quarters and the door-keepers arrived as protectors;
the sacrifice itself appeared in person, and the sacrificial altar became the earth itself.
In that great festival of sacrifice, Tanūnapāt also quickly assumed his own form in thousands for the purpose of receiving the oblations. 19.
Having quickly summoned Marīci and the others, each of whom bore a single sacred thread,
they kindled a flame everywhere with the Sāmidhenī verses.
The seven sages, chanting the Sāman hymns, performed them individually,
filling the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, and the sky with the sounds of the Vedic melodies.
No one was invited there to those sacrifices by the high-souled Dakṣa—not any ṛṣis, nor gods, nor humans, nor birds;
neither plants, nor grass, nor animals, nor wild beasts. || 22 ||

In his great sacrifices, Dakṣa invited the hosts of Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas, along with the Ādityas, Sādhyas, and throngs of Ṛṣis, together with the Yakṣas, all the excellent Nāgas, and even the stationary beings.
The kalpas, manvantaras, yugas, years, months, days, and nights— all the divisions of time,
beginning with kalās, kāṣṭhās, and nimeṣas— have arrived, gathered together.

The assemblies of great sages, royal sages, and celestial sages; kings together with their sons, ministers, and armies; and those host of deities headed by Vasu—all of them, surrounded by him, went to that sacrifice.
Insects, moths, and all aquatic creatures, along with monkeys and the terrible beasts of prey and obstacles;
clouds, mountains, rivers, oceans, lakes, and ponds—all these have gone and are encompassed by them.
Desiring to obtain their respective shares of the oblations, those performers of firm sacrifices approached the appointed time;
the Asuras dwelling in Pātāla assembled together, as did the Nāga women and all the divine assemblies.
Whatever exists in the world, whether sentient or insentient,
he encompassed it all and commenced a sacrifice in which his entire possessions were given as the sacrificial fee.
At that sacrifice, the high-souled Dakṣa did not invite Śambhu,
having determined that he was a wearer of a skull and thus unfit for the sacrifice.
Although Satī was his beloved wife and his own daughter,
she was not invited by Dakṣa to the sacrifice because he perceived faults in her.
Having heard that her father had thus commenced such a supreme sacrifice, Satī truly said, "I have not been chosen by the Kapalika. (31)
Then, with her eyes and face blood-red, she became violently incensed at Dakṣa; Satī then set her mind upon consuming Dakṣa with a curse.
Although she was overcome with anger, that virtuous woman remembered their previous agreement;
having thus resolved in her mind, she did not curse him then.
Enough with this curse; a very firm agreement was previously made by me:
"If there is contempt toward me, I shall certainly give up my life once again. (34)
When I was praised for a long time by Dakṣa, who was seeking a daughter, at that very moment this was my resolve: "I shall adorn him with a curse. (35)
Having reflected thus, that goddess then remembered her own eternal form— matchless, exceedingly fierce, partless, yet consisting of the entire universe.
Recalling that former form of Hari known as Yoganidrā,
the daughter of Dakṣa then reflected thus in her mind.
That purpose for which I was praised by Dakṣa, as directed by Brahmā, has not been understood even in the slightest; nor does Śaṅkara possess a son. (38)
Now there was only one concern for the host of gods:
that Śaṅkara had become full of passion for a woman on my account. (39)
"O Śambhu, no one other than me will ever again be able to increase your passion;
he shall not take another as his consort. (40)
Nevertheless, I shall cast off this body according to the previously established agreement;
for the welfare of the worlds, I shall manifest my appearance once again on the mountain.
Formerly, on a delightful plateau of the Himalayas resembling a celestial abode,
Śambhu, filled with affection, sported with me for a very long time.
Therein, that goddess Menakā, who possessed beautiful limbs and had observed her vows,
was well-behaved and the most excellent among the women of the city, even within the retinue of Pārvatī.
She addressed me with playful words regarding all my activities like a mother;
I felt an intense affection for her, thinking, "She shall be my mother. (44)
Having repeatedly engaged for a long time in childhood play with other girls and maidens of the mountains, I shall bring the greatest joy to Menakā. (45)
Furthermore, O Śambhu, I shall again become your most beloved wife;
through that means, I will undoubtedly accomplish the tasks of the gods.
Thinking thus, she, the daughter of Dakṣa, again enveloped in anger,
blazed up because of Dakṣa’s cruel deed.
Then that virtuous woman, her slender form with eyes red with anger,
blocked all the doors by means of yoga and caused them to burst open.
By that great explosion, her vital breaths,
having burst through the tenth door, issued forth from her own self.
Seeing her with her life-breaths departed, all the gods moving through the firmament then raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!", their eyes overwhelmed with grief.
Then Satyā, the daughter of her sister, came to see her;
seeing that Satī was dead, Vijayā cried out repeatedly in grief. (51)
"Alas, Satī! Where have you gone? Alas, Satī! What is this that has happened to you?
Alas, maternal aunt!"—such was the great cry that arose loudly at that time. (52)
O virtuous lady, since you have abandoned your life merely upon hearing unpleasant news,
how can I continue to live after witnessing such profound misfortune?
Then Satyā, repeatedly wiping her face with her hand while lamenting piteously, smelled his mouth.
She drenched Satyā’s heart and face with tears from her eyes;
lifting up her hair with both hands, she gazed repeatedly at her face.
With her head shaking up and down, her senses agitated by grief,
she struck her heart and likewise her head with her two hands.
And having heard of your death, her mother Vīriṇī, emaciated by grief, spoke these words with a throat choked with tears: (57)
How can she, who is currently sustaining her life-breaths, suddenly give up her life?
Such is your father—merciless and a doer of cruel deeds. (58)
Having heard that you had passed away, how indeed will Dakṣa sustain his life? Surely reflecting upon the cruel deeds he committed against you, he was then overwhelmed with grief. (59)
How can he who is devoid of knowledge be a performer of sacrifice? Or how could he, lacking faith and having abandoned his intellect, engage in a ritual?
"O Mother, give heed to me as I weep like a child! Cruel as you are, I am being torn by griefs that pierce my very vitals like arrows. (61)
"Do you not remember anything ever done by me for Śambhu?
O Mother, why do you not speak to me, who have fallen under the sway of indignation because of that?"
That very speech is your eye, that is your mouth, and that is your nose;
where have all these delusions gone, and where has your laughter vanished? (63)
Indeed, how could Hara endure seeing your pair of eyes free from tremors, your beautiful nose, and your face devoid of smiles? (64)
O Mother, who else besides you, having come to the hermitage of Hara, will repeatedly speak words that are as sweet as nectar and perfectly truthful? (65)
Faithful toward her kinsmen and following the disposition of her husband, endowed with all auspicious marks—who else could ever be equal to her? (66)
"O Goddess, without you, the Lord of Gods will have his consciousness stricken by grief;
he will become sorrowful in soul, devoid of energy, and motionless. (67)
Speaking thus, the virtuous Vijayā, seeing her dead and struck by excessive grief, fell to the ground, uttering cries of lamentation with her arms raised and trembling violently. (68)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Satī’s Body," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 16 ||
The seventeenth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the meantime, Śambhu [was present] at the beautiful Lake Mānasa.
Having completed his twilight devotions, he returned to his own hermitage.
Even as he was approaching, the bull-bannered god heard the fierce and intense outcry of Vijayā,
and he became alarmed.
Then Śarva, with great haste, reached his own hermitage by means of a powerful bull whose speed was like that of thought or the wind.
Then, having approached his beloved goddess, the daughter of Dakṣa,
Hara did not abandon her even upon seeing her dead, due to his exceedingly deep affection for the deceased.
Then, having gazed upon her face and wiped it again and again, he repeatedly asked Drākṣāyaṇī, "Why have you been sleeping? (5)
Then, having heard the words of Bhārgava, Vijayā, the daughter of his sister,
spoke of the death of the daughter of Dakṣa exactly as it had occurred.
Vijayā said: O Śambhu, Dakṣa invited all the gods, including Indra,
as well as the Daityas, Rākṣasas, Siddhas, and Guhyakas, to perform a sacrifice.
Then [he honored] the Brahmins, Govinda, Indra and the other guardians of the quarters,
as well as all those born of divine origin, such as the Sādhyas and Vidyādharas.
O Śaṅkara, those beings who were not invited by him to the sacrifice do not exist even throughout all the worlds because of Dakṣa.
Having heard these words of mine regarding this extensively arranged sacrifice,
she reflected upon the reason for Śambhu’s failure to invite her.
O Lord of Beings, perceiving that Satī was thus reflecting, I spoke to her as I had heard it, explaining the reason for the invitation to the sacrifice.
Śambhu is a wearer of skulls, and his wife is likewise; because of their association, she is held in contempt.
Therefore, neither Śambhu nor Satī shall appear at my sacrifice.
Thus, this reason for not being invited was previously heard by me from the mouth of Dakṣa himself,
as he was speaking gently to Vīriṇī in his palace.
Having heard these words of mine, she sat upon the ground with a pale face; overcome by anger, she said nothing to me.
O Hara, at that very moment her face became disfigured,
darkened, and furrowed with frowns, like the sky with a comet.
Having meditated for a moment as it were, she then released her life-breaths with a great explosion, bursting through the crown of her own head.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Vijayā,
the bull-bannered god (Śiva) rose up in extreme anger, like a fire desiring to consume everything.
As he was overcome with anger, from his ears, nose, eyes, and mouth there issued forth blazing,
terrible sparks emitting a great roar;
many fiery meteors emerged, possessing the brilliance of the sun at the end of an aeon.
Then Dakṣa went quickly to where the great ascetic was;
having gone there, Hara performed the sacrifice while remaining outside the sacrificial enclosure.
Bharga, overwhelmed by great anger, beheld that sacrifice,
which was provided with vast wealth and furnished with sacrificial vessels, posts, and other requisites.
It was nourished by offerings of clarified butter poured into the fire and resplendent with its blazing flames;
there, all the guardians of the quarters were stationed in their respective places, equipped with their weapons and banners.
The enraged Śambhu beheld Vidhātṛ as well as Viṣṇu stationed in the midst of the sacrifice; seeing them, he was overcome with extreme wrath.
Bhaga, Sūrya, and likewise Soma, surrounded by their wives, and the thousand-eyed Gautama, were stationed in the eastern quarter. (23)
Sanatkumāra, Mātreya, Bhārgava, the son of Vinatā, the hosts of Maruts, the Sādhyas, and Jātavedas, the son of Agni; || 24 ||
And Kāla, Citragupta, and Agastya (Kumbhayoni) along with Gālava;
likewise all the Viśvedevas and the ancestors beginning with Kavyavāha. || 25 ||
[He offered oblations] to all those beginning with the Agniṣvātta ancestors, to the fourfold collection of beings,
to the terrestrial spirits, to the hosts of pretas, and to the Siddhas stationed in the southern quarter.
And the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, beasts, and birds;
the carnivorous animals, small creatures, as well as the lord of the Puṇyajanas. || 27 ||
[He saw] the great seer Maudgalya, Rāhu, and likewise the Kinnaras;
the Mahoragas, as well as crocodiles, fish, sharks, and tortoises;
the oceans, the seven rivers, the streams, the sacred fords, and the Guhyakas. (28)
[He saw] all the lakes beginning with Mānasa, as well as the Gaṅgā and the Jambū river;
and Kāma, Madhu, Vasanta, and Varuṇa along with his followers.
[He saw] Śanaiścara, all the mountains situated in the western quarter,
the five vital winds beginning with prāṇa, the wind-god together with his hosts,
the wish-fulfilling trees, the Himālaya mountain, and the great sage Kaśyapa.
In the north-western direction, he offered a multitude of lotuses, fruits, the moon (the storehouse of digits),
various gems, golden objects, men, and likewise mountains.
The wise yakṣas headed by Himādri, Sthūṇakarṇa, and others,
along with Nalakūbara and Naravāhana, the king of the yakṣas, were present.
Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Viṣṇu, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are situated in the direction of Kubera.
Except for Vṛṣadhvaja, he [slew] all the Rudras, Jīva, and the Manus,
as well as various Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras on every side.
In the northeast, various kinds of foods, as well as rice and sesame seeds;
and between the northeast and the east, the Brahman-sages of firm vows.
The four great sages, the four Vedas, and likewise the six Vedāṅgas;
and Ananta, situated at the southwestern corner, and the White Mountain (Śveta-parvata). || 36 ||
There he saw seven hooded serpents accompanied by a thousand offspring of Kadrū, as well as Ketu and Kuṣmāṇḍa joined by a host of Ḍākinīs.
Likewise, Hara [beheld] other clouds of various colors accompanied by lightning, as well as the elephants of the quarters, headed by Airāvata, stationed there.
Having seen from afar that very sacrificial enclosure, which was situated in its proper place, joined by all the directional elephants, and filled with great wealth,
he quickly dispatched the one named Vīrabhadra toward it.
Vīrabhadra, too, surrounded by many various hosts of attendants,
then utterly destroyed the sacrifice of the great-souled Dakṣa.
Beholding Vīrabhadra performing the great sacrifice,
Vaikuṇṭha, surrounded by the hosts of all the gods, indeed restrained him.
Upon seeing him being restrained, the Lord, his eyes bloodshot with anger,
entered that sacrifice himself and destroyed it.
As he was indeed entering the sacrifice first, Bhaga,
stretching out his arms, approached the Lord of Beings with great haste.
Seeing him approach, Bharga also became violently enraged and struck his eyes with a blow from the tip of his finger.
Seeing his vulva with its inferior eye and its distorted form, Divākara,
vying with him, then proceeded toward everything with great haste.
Then Mahādeva, seizing the sun by the hand with his own hand and having cast him far away, being exceedingly enraged, rushed toward the sacrifice itself.
And Mārtaṇḍa, laughing, suddenly extended his two massive arms and,
saying "Come, I shall fight with you," confronted him.
As that Sūrya laughed, the bull-bannered god, in his wrath,
knocked out his teeth from his mouth with a blow of his hand.
Seeing Mihira thus deprived of his sight and Bhaga likewise, all the gods and the sages, as well as others who were there, fled away. || 49 ||
Having put all the gods and others to flight, Hara, filled with supreme rage,
pursued the sacrifice itself as it was fleeing in the form of a deer.
The sacrifice also entered the abode of Brahmā by way of the path of the sky;
the bull-bannered Lord Śiva, likewise enraged, went to the abode of Brahmā.
Frightened by Bharga, the sacrifice descended from the abode of Brahmā;
having descended, it entered the body of Satī through its own illusory power (māyā). 52.
Bharga also followed after the deceased daughter of Dakṣa; having gone near her, he then beheld the sacrifice and the corpse of Satī.
Then, seeing the goddess Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, deceased,
Hara forgot the sacrifice and stood at its conclusion, weeping for them.
