Reflecting upon her multitude of manifold virtues— her row of beautiful teeth, her face radiant as a lotus, and her pair of eyebrows with their reddish hue like fine cloth— the wielder of the trident, overwhelmed by intense and vast grief upon beholding them, wept. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The eighteenth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At that time, Gaurī’s husband (Śiva) was enumerating the multitude of virtues belonging to the daughter of Dakṣa.
Afflicted by extreme sorrow, he lamented like an ordinary man.
Then, perceiving Bharga to be lamenting, Makaradhvaja,
accompanied by Rati and Vasanta, approached Maheśvara.
As he was utterly overwhelmed by grief, weeping and deprived of his senses, the Lord of Love simultaneously struck him with five arrows.
Though his mind was struck by grief and agitated by the arrows of Smara,
he fell into a state of mental confusion and both lamented and fainted.
For a moment he falls to the ground, for a moment rising he runs;
for a moment he wanders right there, and then the Lord closes his eyes once more.
Sometimes, while meditating upon the goddess Dākṣāyaṇī and smiling,
he would embrace her as she stood upon the ground, as if she were present through the power of aesthetic emotion (rasa).
Having repeatedly uttered the name "Satī, Satī," Śaṅkara said,
"Abandon this vain pride," and touched her with his hand.
Having wiped her with his hand, he rearranged her ornaments exactly as they were before, having first untied them from their places.
While Bhūteśa was acting in this manner, Satī did not say anything at all when she died; then Bharga wept bitterly out of grief.
Then, seeing the tears falling from him as he wept, Brahmā and the other gods became deeply anxious and fell into profound reflection.
"If these falling tears were to burn this very earth, what remedy should be employed for that? they cried out, "Alas! Alas! (11).
Then the gods, beginning with Brahmā, reflected and slowly praised Śanaiścara for the reason that the foolish Bharga was shedding tears.
The gods said:
O Śanaiścara, highly fortunate one, you who bestow grace upon the worlds;
O you who have arisen from the primordial power (mūla-śakti), salutations to you, O son of the Sun! || 13 ||
Salutations to you who hold a trident in your hand, who hold a noose in your hand, and who wield a bow;
likewise, salutations to you who grant boons with your hand, and whose nature is the shadow of darkness.
Resembling a dark blue cloud and like a mass of crushed collyrium, homage to you, the cause of sustaining the life-breath of all worlds! 15.
O you whose banner is the vulture, salutations be to you; be gracious, O Blessed One, and protect us firmly. Guard our land from the tears born of sorrow, O Bharga.
Just as in the past you protected the rain-giver for a hundred years, so now, O Hara, draw the water from the clouds yourself.
Seeing the seizing of your bow, those clouds, Puṣkara and the others,
released a continuous rain at the command, it is said, of Mahendra.
All that rainwater was previously destroyed by you in the sky, just as vapor is; destroy it likewise for the sake of the Wielder of the Trident.
"No one other than you is capable of warding off the tears of Hara.
Should those tears fall upon the earth, they would consume the worlds of the gods, Gandharvas, and Brahmā, along with the mountains; therefore, sustain them through your power of illusion. (20)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While the gods were speaking in this manner, the son of Mihira replied to those gods as if his heart were not at all joyful.
Śanaiścara said:
"O best of gods, I shall perform your task according to my power;
however, act in such a way that Hara does not perceive me."
If I were to perish out of anger in the presence of this man, who is overwhelmed by suffering and grief and shedding tears, my body would surely perish; of this there is no doubt. (23)
Therefore, act in such a way that Bhūteśa, the husband of Satī, does not recognize me; remove from your eyes the collyrium of Hara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all those gods, headed by Brahmā, having gone into the presence of Śaṅkara,
were utterly bewildered by Hara’s yogic power (yogamāyā) along with his consort.
Then Śanaiścara also, having approached Bhūteśa, vanished;
by means of his illusory power (māyā), he then unleashed an irresistible shower of tears.
When that son of the Sun was unable to restrain his tears,
he then cast those tears upon the great mountain Jaladhāraka.
Near Lokāloka is the mountain named Jaladhārā,
situated on the back of Puṣkaradvīpa to the west of the Ocean of Water (Toyasāgara).
But he, equal in magnitude to Mount Meru according to all measures,
Śanaiścara then slowly deposited his tears upon it, being unable to restrain them.
Even that mountain was not able to sustain those tears of the Lord;
shattered by those floods of tears, it quickly split asunder at its center.
Those tears, having pierced the mountain, entered the ocean;
yet the ocean was unable to contain them due to its extreme depth.
Then, having split the ocean in the middle, the tears arrived;
by their mere touch, they breached that shore which had existed since the beginning of the sea.
Having burst through the shore, those tears, situated in the midst of Puṣkaradvīpa,
became the river Vaitaraṇī, which flows toward the eastern ocean.
Due to their separation from the stream of water and their contact with the ocean,
those vapors attained a certain coolness and did not split the earth.
At the gateway to the city of Vaivasvata, the river born from the ashes of Hara remains even today, extending for two yojanas.
Then, his soul bewildered by grief, the bull-bannered god, lamenting and placing the corpse of Satī upon his shoulder, went toward the eastern regions.
Seeing his state as he moved about like a madman, the gods,
headed by Brahmā, reflected upon the act of removing the corpse.
Due to contact with the body of Hara, this corpse will not undergo decay;
therefore, how could its destruction come to pass? (38)
Reflecting thus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śanaiścara entered the interior of Satī’s corpse, remaining invisible through their yogic power (yogamāyā).
Then, having entered the corpse, the gods cut the Satī-corpse into pieces and cast them down upon the earth, specifically at various locations.
First, the pair of feet fell upon the earth at Devīkūṭa;
then, for the welfare of the worlds, the pair of thighs descended at Uḍḍīyāna. (41)
In Kāmarūpa, on Mount Kāma, the circle of the womb fell;
right there, upon that mountain, the circle of the navel fell upon the ground.
In Jālandhara is the pair of breasts, adorned with a golden necklace;
in Pūrṇagiri is the neck; and from there, in Kāmarūpa, is the head.
As soon as Bharga went to the earth taking the corpse of Satī, that region alone was proclaimed among the easterners as the land of the sacrificers (Yājñika). || 44 ||
Other parts of his body, severed limb by limb by the gods,
went to the celestial Ganges, impelled by the wind.
Wherever Satī’s limbs fell, O twice-born ones,
there Mahādeva himself, overcome by delusion and driven by the power of his affection for Satī, remained in the form of a linga. || 46 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śani, and all the hosts of gods likewise worshipped the feet and other limbs of the Lord with affection and truthfulness.
On Devīkūṭa, the Great Goddess is celebrated as Mahābhāgā;
she is Yoganidrā, the mother of the world, merged within the pair of feet of Satī.
Kātyāyanī is at Oḍḍīyāna, Kāmākhyā is the one who takes forms at will;
Pūrṇeśvarī is at Pūrṇagiri, and Caṇḍī is on the mountain of Jālandhara.
In the eastern quarter of Kāmarūpa, the Goddess who dwells in the cardinal direction is likewise celebrated as Yoganidrā, known as Lalitakāntā. (50)
Wherever Satī’s head fell, there the bull-bannered Lord sat down,
gazing at the head while sighing and overcome with grief.
When Hara was seated there, Brahmā and the other celestial dwellers approached him from a distance, consoling Hara.
Seeing the gods approaching, Hara, filled with grief and shame, turned to stone right there and assumed the form of a linga. || 53 ||
When Hara had attained the state of a linga, Brahmā and the other celestial dwellers praised Tryambaka there, the teacher of the world, in his form as a linga.
The gods said:
[We praise] Mahādeva, Śiva, Sthāṇu, Ugra, Rudra, the bull-bannered one,
Bharga who dwells in the cremation ground, the supreme bringer of the end of all.
We bow with devotion to you, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita, the Lord of the Mountains, the boon-bestowing God, the creator of beings, and the imperishable one. (56)
Salutation to Śambhu, who is joined with beginningless and middleless saṃsāra and ignorance;
salutation to Śiva, the peaceful Brahman, whose form is the Liṅga.
Salutations to you, the matted-haired one, the lord of the mountains, the wielder of the power of knowledge;
salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman whose form is the Liṅga. || 58 ||
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman whose inner body is completely filled with the nectar of knowledge, who exists in the form of the Liṅga.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman whose form is the Liṅga, who constitutes the beginning, middle, and end, and who blazes with the fire of his own nature.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, to Brahman in the form of the Liṅga, who exists as the individual soul during dissolution and is the cause of the persistence of that dissolution.
Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman in the form of the Liṅga, who is beyond others, higher than the highest, and the Supreme Self. || 62 ||
Salutations to you whose limbs are encircled by garlands of flames, O you who possess the universal form!
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman, whose form is the Liṅga.
Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Reality, the lamp of knowledge, the Pervader;
salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman whose form is the Liṅga. || 64 ||
Homage to you, beloved of Dākṣāyaṇī, O Mṛḍa, Śarva, Maheśvara!
Homage to you, Lord of all beings; be gracious, O Blessed Śiva! (65)
O Maheśvara, while you, the Lord of the World, are acting thus in sorrow, all the gods are utterly distressed; therefore, abandon your grief.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Beings, the cause of all causes!
Be gracious, protect us all, abandon your sorrow; salutations be unto you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus being praised, Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe,
assuming his own form, appeared, struck by grief.
Seeing him thus overwhelmed by grief, bewildered, and fallen into a state of unconsciousness,
Brahmā, desiring to dispel his sorrow, praised the bull-bannered Lord with gentle words.
Brahmā said:
O Hiraṇyabāhu, you are Brahmā; you are Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe;
you alone, O Hara, are the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Pervading the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings with your eight forms,
you are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer— the maker of all.
O Mahādeva, having propitiated you, those seeking liberation have attained release;
being freed from passion, hatred, and the like, these wise ones have turned away from the cycle of worldly existence.
O Maheśvara, that third eye which is situated on the forehead, constantly blazing, should be meditated upon with wonder by those seeking liberation. (72ka)

O Maheśvara, that supreme reality consists of pure essence; it is devoid of the various elements of wind, fire, and floods of water; it is not situated at a distance, yet it is joined with the sun and moon; it stands in the midst of the three paths and shines forth as the unmanifest.

The thick flower of the eight-branched tree, which grows near the ocean of consciousness and has penance for its leaves and Lord Śiva as its fruit, is always under your control, being both subtle and proximate.

Having established the breath below and restrained its sound as it moves upward through the center of the *haṃsa* at night, let your radiance alone—the passion (*rajas*) made manifest within the lotus of the heart—be beheld by all. (75)

Through various breath-control practices—whether by inhalation, retention, or exhalation—that impelling force known as *parā* is perceived by yogis as both visible and invisible; these are the manifestations (*prapañca*). In truth, you have attained that which is pure and expanded.

O Maheśa, you possess that wealth which is subtle, pervasive throughout the world, swollen with a flood of qualities, sought after by the ocean of seekers, and whose form is both the means and the goal; it has never been carried off by thieves or guards, yet it is devoid of worldly riches.
Neither through anger, nor through grief, nor through pride, nor through deceit;
rather, by employing that wealth in a different manner, it increases. (78)
O Śambhu, deluded by māyā, you have forgotten that which resides within your heart;
having fully understood and pierced through māyā, sustain yourself by means of the Self.
O Maheśvara, Māyā was previously praised by us for the sake of the world;
by her, the mind absorbed in meditation was brought under control through great efforts. (80)
Grief, anger, greed, desire, delusion, the sense of otherness, envy, pride, doubt, compassion, malice, and loathing; || 81 ||
These twelve are the causes for the destruction of the intellect and the impurities of the mind; they are not practiced by those such as you. Therefore, abandon grief, O Hara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised with these words of conciliation, Śambhu recalled his own desire;
yet, being separated from Satī, he did not acknowledge himself at that time due to his grief.
Seeing Brahmā standing with his face turned downward, he slowly said this:
"O Brahmā, speak what is appropriate for the occasion; what shall I do? (84)
Thus addressed by Vāmadeva and all the deities,
the Ordainer (Brahmā) spoke these words, which were to destroy the grief of that region.
Brahmā said:
"Abandon your grief, O Mahādeva; by means of the self, remember the Self.
You are not the abode of sorrow, for beyond sorrow is your inner state. (86)
O Lord of Beings, while you are filled with grief, the gods and all creatures are seized with terror;
your wrath might bring down the world, and your sorrow would wither everything.
The earth would have been rent asunder, overwhelmed by your tears, had not Śani seized those tears;
he too was forcibly restrained by Kṛṣṇa.
Where the gods, together with the gandharvas, always sport with eager delight;
that which is like Mount Sumeru in measurement is the best of mountains. (89)
Entering that cool reservoir of lotus stalks, the clouds such as Puṣkarāvartaka and others used to drink up its waters.
O Hara, it was there that the great sage Kumbhayoni went again and again from Mandara and constantly performed austerities for the welfare of the world.
On that mountain, it is said, Agastya formerly stood and drank the ocean of water by the power of his asceticism, having brought it into the palm of his hand.
Because Śanaiścara was unable to carry you,
he tore apart that mountain called Jaladhārā by hurling clods of earth at it.
O Śambhu, having split the mountain, those vapors went to the ocean;
and having quickly pierced the ocean, which was crowded with terrified birds, they entered it.
They went to its eastern bank and broke through it;
having pierced the shore, they then quickly split the earth and the river.
They constructed a river named Vaitaraṇī flowing toward the eastern ocean,
which could not be crossed by boat, nor by celestial chariot, nor by raft, nor by carriage.
That river, consisting of scalding water and extremely terrifying, can indeed be crossed;
however, the Earth now supports it with great difficulty. (97)
Constantly scattering the sky-dwellers with her upward-streaming tears,
even the gods, overcome by fear, do not pass above her.
Turning back from the gate of Yama, it flows two yojanas wide, deep,
full, and terrifying the three worlds.
Scattered by the winds born from your sighs, the mountains and forests,
along with their agitated tigers and elephants, have not yet settled down even today.
The wind born from your sighing, which afflicts the happiness of the world, has not yet reached its cessation; it remains eternal and free from any diminution of its torment. (101)
Though they carry Satī’s corpse, which is falling apart at every step, the earth is not yet agitated; it does not relinquish its state of agitation. (102)
O Bull-bannered Lord, there is no being now to be found, neither in heaven nor in the netherworld,
who is not agitated by your anger and grief.
Therefore, casting off both grief and resentment, grant us peace;
for you know yourself by yourself, so sustain yourself by yourself. 104.
And when a hundred divine years have passed,
she shall become your wife at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by the Creator, Śambhu remained silent and absorbed in meditation;
then, with his face cast downwards, he spoke to Brahmā of immeasurable luster.
Īśvara said:
O Brahmin, until I rise above this sorrow caused by Satī,
you must act as my friend and dispel my grief.
At that time, O Creator, wherever I go, may you go there as well and effect the removal of my grief. (108)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having said "So be it" to the Lord of the World, he then set his mind on going to Kailāsa together with Hara and the bull-vehicled god.
Seeing Śambhu together with Brahmā and eager to go to Kailāsa, the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, approached him.
Then a bull, resembling a mountain and like a white cloud, appeared before Brahmā, looking as if it were made of red chalk.
And the serpents, headed by Vāsuki, quickly rose up and adorned Hara with their heads, arms, and other limbs, each according to its proper place.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, went to the Prāleya mountain together with all the hosts of gods. || 113 ||
Then, having emerged from the city of Auṣadhiprastha, the mountain,
accompanied by all his ministers, approached the supreme gods.
Then, having been honored by him along with the mountain,
his ministers, and the citizens, those foremost of gods rejoiced.
Then, right there in the city of the lord of mountains, on the medicinal plateau (Oṣadhiprastha), Hara beheld the daughter of Gautama together with her female companions.
She too, having bowed down to all the best of the gods, spoke to Hara;
she cried out, asking the Lord of the Mountain about Satī, her mother’s sister.
"O Mahādeva, where do you shine without her, Satī?
Even though she has been forgotten by you, O Father, she does not depart from my heart. (118)
Formerly, when she gave up her life before me out of anger, at that very moment I was pierced by the arrow of grief and truly found no happiness. (119)
Having spoken thus, she covered her face with the edge of her garment and,
weeping bitterly, fell to the ground and was then overcome by a swoon.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Śrī Kālikā Purāṇa*, in the section on Vijayāśoka.
The nineteenth chapter begins with Mārkaṇḍeya saying:
Then, seeing Dākṣāyaṇī fallen, he remembered her and was unable to endure the grief born of that agitation.
Then Śambhu, his fortitude shattered and his eyes clouded with tears,
became absorbed in anxious reflection while all the gods looked on.
Then, having consoled Vijayā, who was emaciated by grief,
the Creator spoke these words in a soothing manner while himself consoling Hara.
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, O ancient yogi, grief is not appropriate for you.
Why was your meditation directed toward another's abode, upon a woman here?
How has your own nature— which is powerful, supreme, peaceful, subtle, yet exceedingly vast, and eternal— been so diversely affected by grief?
That which is stainless, attainable through meditation by ascetics, higher than the highest, pure, and all-pervading;
that form of yours which is devoid of impurities such as passion and greed—that true nature of yours, grasp it with your intellect.

Grief, greed, anger, delusion, violence, pride, hypocrisy, intoxication, arrogance, excessive joy, envy, malice, impatience, and untruthfulness—these fourteen are indeed defects that destroy knowledge. (7)
Yogis contemplate you through meditation; you are Viṣṇu, the creator of the worlds.
That which is your Satī, the cause of great delusion, is likewise Māyā for the delusion of the world.
She who, at the time of birth and during the stay in the womb, deludes the consciousness of the previous body, and having destroyed childhood, now deludes this living being—you are she, O Śokā!
9. You are she who, at the time of birth and during the stay in the womb, deludes the consciousness of the previous body; having destroyed childhood, you now delude this living being, O Śokā!
In this manner, thousands of virtuous wives have been abandoned by you at the beginning of every kalpa and have thus perished;
yet for the welfare of the world of both mobile and immobile beings, this one has likewise been taken up by you once again.
In another existence, through the power of meditative yoga, behold the thousands of Satīs who have died;
just so, you have been abandoned, O you whose banner bears the king of bulls.

O Lord, behold by means of meditative yoga all that from which she will repeatedly arise and attain you—O Ruler difficult for even the three gods to reach—and how she shall again become your wife. 12.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus Brahmā spoke various kinds of Sāman hymns to Śaṅkara,
and from that city of the king of mountains, he caused Gayā to be cleared of people.
Then, on the plateau of the Himavat to the west of that city,
Brahmā and the others beheld a lake named Śiprā, filled with water.
Having reached that secret place, the gods, headed by Brahmā and Śakra,
sat down according to protocol, placing Maheśvara at their front.
That lake, known by the name Śipra, was pleasing to all embodied beings;
its waters were cool and pure, and it equaled Lake Mānasa in every quality.
Having seen it for a moment, he became eager to look further;
he then beheld the river named Śiprā, which flows out from that mountain toward the southern ocean, purifying the people of the world as she goes.
Having reached that lake filled [with water], Śambhu beheld many beautiful birds of various lands as they moved about. || 18 ||
He beheld pairs of ruddy geese dancing, as it were, upon the waves that were graced by the agitation of deep winds.
He observed the waves, which were joined with the beaks of water-birds, as being distinct from one another,
just as he repeatedly watched the birds flying up from the water.
With rows of *kādamba*, *sārasa*, and *haṃsa* birds formed along every bank,
that lake was like the ocean with its conch shells arranged in curved lines.
In various places there, the sound was enchanting, produced by birds who were struck with terror by the roar of the water agitated by the strike of great fish.
With blooming lotuses and, in some places, charming nets of water-lilies,
the lake shone like heaven with its large and small stars.
Amidst the great blue lotuses,
a solitary dark-blue lotus shone like a fragment of a dark cloud amidst the stars.
The swans situated in the midst of the lotus clusters were not noticed by some inhabitants of heaven, who stood motionless, mistaking them for blossoming lotuses. (25)
Having seen his own two blooming lotuses, one red and one white,
Brahmā censured the ruddiness and the blooming state of his own seat-lotus within his body.
Beholding that full-blown great blue lotus of the lake, Śaṅkara thought,
"The moonlight on my crest is now eclipsed by this blue lotus held in my hand."
Beholding it on all sides, he considered the lotus in his hand— blossomed by the rays of Hari’s own discus— to be identical to the lotus in the lake.
Having beheld that lake, full and teeming with various birds, covered by hundreds of lotus plants, and surrounded by clusters of blue water-lilies; || 29 ||
The water, scented by the pollen born of flowers from the deodar trees standing on its banks, brings joy to the heart. (30)
Seeing that place on every bank surrounded by great trees and lush grass, Śambhu stood there for a moment, filled with longing yet free from sorrow.
He beheld the Śiprā as it issued forth from that lake,
just as the Gaṅgā issues from the orb of the moon or as the Jāmbūnadī flows from Mount Meru; even so did the Śiprā emerge from the mouth of Maheśa upon being gazed upon by him.
The sages said:
"What is the lake named Śiprā? How did the Śiprā flow forth from it?
What is its power like? Describe that in detail. (33)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Listen, all you sages, to how the river Śiprā came to flow;
and, O highly blessed ones, hear me as I describe the power of Śipra."
O twice-born ones, when the lady Arundhatī was married by Vasiṣṭha, the Śiprā became the Sindhu through the nuptial waters.
Having arrived there by the command [of the Lord], she fell into the Śiprā lake,
just as the Mandākinī, possessing auspicious waters, falls from the foot of Viṣṇu into the ocean.
In the past, at their wedding, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva sprinkled water upon them as a rite of peace, reciting the Gāyatrī, the Drupadā, and other mantras.
That water, having become one, flowed from the cave of the Mānasa mountain;
it all fell into the Śiprā lake, which was like the ocean.
In ancient times, for the sake of the enjoyment of the gods,
the Creator fashioned a great lake named Śiprā upon the ridge of the snowy mountain.
Even today, Sunāsīra, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases and joined by Śacī, delights in those auspicious and tranquil waters.
Therefore, even today, it is guarded with constant effort by the gods as if it were a jewel;
no human being who is not a sage is able to go there.
By the power of their asceticism, the sages go with great effort to the auspicious lake named Śiprā to bathe and drink its water.
Having bathed and drunk there, by the power of destiny,
men with unimpaired senses necessarily go toward immortality.
"O best of the twice-born, this lake does not swell during the rains, nor does it go to dryness in the summer; it remains exactly as it always was. (44)
There, that water arising from the wedding of Vasiṣṭha fell,
having been poured forth by the lotus-hands of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva.
O best of the twice-born, it grew day by day while situated within the womb of the Śiprā;
and formerly, Hari cut that water apart with his discus.
Having split the peak of the mountain out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, he caused the most meritorious river Pṛthivī to flow forth. 47.
Turning back from Mahendra, purifying those who perform their ablutions,
the Jāhnavī flows toward the southern ocean, bestowing rewards equal to her own.
Since that great river issued forth from the lake named Śiprā,
its name was established as "Śiprā" by Brahmā long ago.
But that man who bathes on the full moon day of Kārttika goes to the abode of Viṣṇu by means of an exceedingly radiant celestial chariot.
Having bathed in the waters of the Śiprā throughout the entire month of Kārttika,
a person goes to the abode of Brahmā and thereafter attains liberation.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, tell us how the lady Arundhatī was wedded by Vasiṣṭha; whose daughter was she, or from whom was she born?"
Among devoted wives, she who is sought after as the most excellent in the three worlds shall not cast her eyes upon anything other than the feet of her husband. (53)
By merely remembering her story along with her greatness, women indeed attain the state of a chaste wife both in this world and in another birth after death.
Tell us of the birth of that woman who does not see the one whose time of death is near, whether he be a pure man or an evildoer. (55)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen how she was born, whose auspicious daughter she was,
how she obtained Vasiṣṭha as her husband, and how she became devoted to her husband.
She who was formerly Sandhyā, the daughter of Brahmā born from his mind,
having performed penance and cast off her body, became Arundhatī.
Having become the daughter of Medhātithi, that virtuous woman,
having observed her vow at the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa,
chose the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, who was firm in his vows, as her husband.
The sages said: How was penance performed by that Sandhyā, for what purpose, and where?
How did she, the daughter of Medhātithi, cast off her body and become a living being?
Or how was it spoken by the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— to her husband,
that she chose the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, who is firm in his vows?
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, relate all of that to us in detail;
for as we listen to this life-story of the truly great Arundhatī, O most excellent of the twice-born, our curiosity is exceedingly great. (61)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Even Brahmā, having previously beheld his own daughter Sandhyā, set his mind upon desire; yet she was indeed abandoned by him as a daughter.
And while those great-souled sages of pure mind were looking on, her heart wavered, agitated by the arrows of desire.
Having heard the words of Bharga regarding his mocking behavior,
[he reflected upon] his own lack of self-restraint and the instability of his mind toward the sages.
Seeing such a state of desire that repeatedly deludes even sages, Sandhyā herself felt shame there and became distressed.
Then, immediately after Madana had been cursed by Brahmā,
Vidhi disappeared and Śambhu also departed for his own abode.
Overcome by indignation, the high-minded Sandhyā became intent on meditation;
meditating for but a moment, she quickly recalled her former history.
At that time, Sandhyā reflected upon this as was appropriate:
"Seeing me, a young woman, as soon as I was born, he has been incited by passion. (68)
This grandfather, filled with affection, formed a longing for all the mind-born sages of purified souls. (69)
As soon as she saw me, her mind became unrestrained with desire;
my own heart, too, was churned by the evil-minded Madana. (70)
"Since my mind was violently agitated upon seeing all these sages, Madana himself has reaped the fruit of this sin. (71)
Enraged, the Grandfather himself uttered a curse in the presence of Śambhu:
"I now wish to obtain every fruit that is due to me. (72)
Since my father and brothers, seeing me before their very eyes while I was still full of desire, felt longing for me, therefore no one is a greater evildoer than I.
Upon seeing them all—even my own brothers—acting like husbands toward their own father, an immoderate state of passion arose within me as well. (74)
I myself shall perform the expiation for this sin;
I will offer myself as an oblation into the fire in accordance with the path of the Vedas.
However, I shall establish one boundary here on this earth, so that embodied beings do not become possessed of desire as soon as they are born. (76)
For this purpose, having performed most rigorous austerity and having established the boundary, I shall thereafter renounce my life.
"In this body for which my father himself formed a desire, there is no longer any purpose for my brothers. (78)
That the passion for one's own body and for one's own siblings was manifested by you, dear father, does not accomplish any virtuous deed. (79)
Having reflected thus in her mind, Sandhyā then went to that best of mountains called Candrabhāga, from which the river Candrabhāgā flows.
That mountain was forever presided over by her,
Suvarṇagaurī, who bears a perfectly even radiance,
like the moon risen at the time of twilight.
He shone perpetually like the mountain of sunrise.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Practice of Austerities during the Twilight Devotions," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The twentieth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, seeing Sandhyā having gone there toward that best of mountains, [he spoke].
To his own son, who was self-restrained for the sake of austerity, Brahmā spoke.
[He saw] Vasiṣṭha, whose self was disciplined, the omniscient one, a knower and yogi,
seated comfortably nearby, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Brahmā said:
"O Vasiṣṭha, go to where this high-minded Sandhyā has gone;
she has resolved upon asceticism, so initiate her according to the prescribed rite."
O best of sages, in the past, upon seeing you, me, and herself all full of desire here, she felt bashfulness.
Reflecting upon that improper deed committed in the past,
she now desires to give up the lives of both us and herself.
She will establish order among those who have transgressed all bounds through her ascetic power;
that virtuous woman has now gone to perform penance at Candrabhāgā.
O dear one, she does not know any true efficacy of asceticism;
therefore, you should act in such a way that she attains her goal according to the instructions.
Having cast off this form and assumed another supreme form,
you should perform penance in her presence according to her instructions.
Having seen this true nature of yours, she will not say anything before you, for she will feel as much shame upon reaching it as she did previously.
Having abandoned your own form, you have assumed another form;
therefore, please go to instruct Sanyā, who is highly fortunate.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having said "So be it," the sage Vasiṣṭha, assuming the appearance of a Vaiśya and wearing matted locks,
went to the vicinity of the Sandhyā river for the sake of Candrabhāgā.
There, that distinguished man then beheld the lake of the gods, full of virtues and equal to Lake Mānasa, as he approached its shore at twilight.
That lake, radiant with lotuses, shone with her standing on its bank,
like the sky at twilight when the rising moon and stars are present.
Having seen her there, the sage addressed her with curiosity and gazed upon that lake known as Vṛhallocana.
From that lake, the Candrabhāgā river was seen by him as it flowed toward the southern ocean, having pierced through the great mountain with its attendant peaks.
Having pierced through the western ridge of the Candrabhāga,
that river flows toward the ocean just as the Gaṅgā flows from the Himavat.
The sages said:
How did the Candrabhāgā river originate there on that great mountain?
And what was that lake named Bṛhallohita like, O best of Brahmins? (17)
How did that best of mountains come to be named Candrabhāga?
And why did the river named Candrabhāga arise with its bull-like waters?
As we listen to this, a great curiosity arises within us regarding the majesty of the Candrabhāgā river, as well as that of the lake and the mountain. (19)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of sages, hear now the origin of the Candrabhāgā river,
as well as the greatness of the Candrabhāga and the reason for its name.
Attached to the Himavat mountain, extending for a hundred yojanas,
and thirty yojanas in length, there is a mountain as white as a kunda flower or the moon.
Long ago, on that mountain, the Creator, the Grandfather, divided the pure moon— the storehouse of nectar— and fashioned it as food for the gods.
And likewise, for the sake of the ancestors, the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) established for him that which consists of the increase and decrease of lunar days, for the welfare of the worlds. (23)
O best of the twice-born, because the moon was divided within that cloud,
the gods in ancient times gave that mountain the name Candrabhāga.
The sages said:
While the sacrificial portions remained and the nectar born of the Ocean of Milk was likewise present, for what reason did the Lotus-seated One exclude the Moon from the gods' share? (25)
Since the moon remains constant, why did he ordain [the rites] for the ancestors?
And how did the moon become dependent on the waning and waxing of the lunar days (tithi), O Guru? (26)
O Brahmin, dispel this doubt of ours, as the sun dispels the darkness;
for there is no one other than you, O best of the twice-born, who can cut through this doubt.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In ancient times, the patriarch Dakṣa gave twenty-seven beautiful daughters, beginning with Aśvinī, to Soma.
Then Soma married all of them according to the prescribed rites,
and with the permission of Dakṣa, he led them to his own abode.
Then Candra, out of passion for all those maidens,
dwelt together with Rohiṇī, indulging in dalliances, festivals, and other delights.
He resorts only to Rohiṇī and rejoices together with Rohiṇī;
for without the Moon, Rohiṇī did not formerly obtain any peace whatsoever. (31)
Seeing the moon intent upon Rohiṇī, all those maidens approached the moon with various kinds of services.
When the Moon, despite being pursued day after day, did not direct his affection toward them at all,
they were all then overcome by indignation.
Now, those [nakṣatras] known by the names Uttarāphālgunī, as well as Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Maghā, Viśākhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā; 34.
Likewise, these nine, Jyeṣṭhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, being greatly enraged,
approached the Moon and surrounded him on all sides.
Then, surrounding the Lord of the Night (the Moon), they beheld Rohiṇī,
seated upon his left lap, sporting with him within his own orb.
Beholding Rohiṇī, who was so exceedingly beautiful in complexion, they all blazed up with intense anger, like a sacrificial fire fed with clarified butter.
Then Maghā, Ārdrā, and Pūrvā, as well as Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā, forcibly seized the highly fortunate Rohiṇī, who was situated with the moon as her mark. || 38 ||
Extremely enraged, they said to the man regarding Rohiṇī:
"O evil-minded one, while you live, the Moon shall have no affection for us. (39)
"At some time, when he arrives eager for sexual pleasure, we shall kill that evil-minded one for the sake of the welfare and prosperity of many. (40)

"Even by killing you, no sin whatsoever would accrue to us—you who are a destroyer of progeny, a woman with many husbands, and a sinner for failing to approach her husband during the proper season. (41)
Regarding that matter for which Brahmā formerly spoke to his son for the purpose of instructing him in the science of polity—that has indeed not been heard by us. (42)
When the destruction of a single evildoer proceeds, there is security for many; therefore, his killing is a bestower of merit. (43)
The thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed, and he who commits suicide—for him, death bestows merit. (44)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having understood their intention and observed their actions,
and having seen his beloved and most enchanting Rohiṇī terrified, [he spoke].
Reflecting repeatedly upon himself, his offense, and the suffering born of that lack of union,
he released the frightened Rohiṇī from their hands.
Having released Rohiṇī from his arms and embraced her,
he restrained all those passionate women, Kṛttikā and the others.
Then those wise women, Kṛttikā and the others ending with Maghā, seeking to restrain the Moon, looked toward Rohiṇī and spoke of their equality.
Neither shame nor fear arises in you as you cast off this sin, O Lord of the Night, for you behave like an ordinary person. (49)
How is it that, having rejected us who observe vows of conduct and are ever devoted, you serve this one alone like a fool? (50)
Have you not understood the Dharma rooted in the Vedas that was heard by you in the past, such that you perform an act devoid of Dharma which is censured by the virtuous? (51)
How is it that you do not look even at the faces of those who have been married and are performing their duties as prescribed by the Dharmaśāstras?
O Lord of Night, listen now to the meaning of Dakṣa’s treatise on dharma, which was previously heard by me from the mouth of my father as he spoke it to Nārada.
A man who has many wives but, out of passion, devotes himself to only one woman is a partaker of sin and is conquered by a woman; for him, impurity is eternal.
O Moon, there exists no other suffering whatsoever that is equal to the pain arising from the lack of union with a husband that women experience. (55)
That lowest of men who does not approach his virtuous wife when she is in her season—on those pure days of the fertile period—he becomes a killer of the embryo (bhrūṇahā). || 56 ||
She should remain his wife for as long as she is an Ātreyī; during that time, he should keep her awake. Furthermore, he should not perform any ritual act during sexual union with her.
For a man with many wives, there is no act whatsoever—be it the destruction of the seasonal union with his wives—that is not prescribed by the scriptures. (58)
One should constantly satisfy one's wives, who have been wed according to the prescribed rites, in accordance with the law;
for through their satisfaction comes prosperity, and otherwise, misfortune. (59)
In that family where the husband is always content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain.
She who, arrogant with the pride of her own good fortune, opposes her husband when he wishes to unite with a co-wife, shall become a prostitute in another birth. (51)
In this world as well, she incurs censure and demerit;
neither her father’s family nor the husband’s family finds joy in her.
When a husband is in conflict with his co-wife, whatever [action] she undertakes results in extreme suffering; thus, those two bring about misfortune.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While they were speaking in this manner with extreme harshness,
Candramas became enraged upon seeing the face of Rohiṇī soiled.
And Rohiṇī, observing their repeated ferocity, said nothing at all, being agitated by fear, grief, and shame. (65)
Then, being enraged, the Moon cursed those women:
"Since fierce and sharp words were uttered in my presence," (66)
And by you three, beginning with Kṛttikā,
fame as "the fierce ones" (Ugrās) and "the sharp ones" (Tīkṣṇās) shall be attained in this world and even among the gods.
Therefore, by this very method, these nine [constellations] beginning with Kṛttikā shall not be suitable for journeys day after day. (68)
Gods and others, as well as humans and others on earth, behold you;
because of that fault, their journey does not grant what is desired. (69)
Then, having heard that most terrible curse of his,
they all realized that Candra’s heart had become exceedingly hardened by the curse.
Then, filled with indignation, all of them— Aśvinī and the others— went to the abode of Dakṣa and spoke to their father Dakṣa with voices choked with emotion.
Soma dwells among us and always favors Rohiṇī;
he does not favor us, though we serve him, like a wife belonging to another.
Neither during a stay, nor at the conclusion, nor while eating, nor likewise while listening—without the moon being in conjunction with Rohiṇī—one does not obtain any peace whatsoever. (73)
While he was dwelling with Rohiṇī, his sons, seeing him, approached him;
however, fixing his gaze elsewhere, he did not look at them.
"Let there be no other true master who does not even look at our faces;
tell us what must be done by us regarding this matter. (75)
At that time, we both Anuruddha and Candramas were entreated by him;
for his sake, he then pronounced a severe curse upon us. (76)
"Having become cruel, excessively harsh, and subject to reproach in the world,
you shall become unable to sustain yourselves," thus spoke Vidhu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words of his daughters, the Lord of Creatures went together with them to where Soma was then staying in the company of Rohiṇī.
Seeing Dakṣa approaching from afar, Vidhu rose from his seat;
having reached his presence, he paid homage to the great sage.
Then Dakṣa, having accepted the seat offered to him, spoke with conciliatory words to the Moon, who had likewise performed his salutation.
Dakṣa said:
"Behave equally toward your wives; abandon partiality.
Many faults are proclaimed by Brahmā regarding partiality."
A wife has pleasure and offspring as her fruits, because of the persistence of desire toward her;
that persistence of desire arises from association, and association comes from meeting.
Union arises from longing and from gazing;
therefore, direct your longing toward your wives and perform acts such as gazing upon them.
If you do not act according to my word, which is constrained by dharma,
then you will become a sinner, defiled by the reproach of the world.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of the high-souled Dakṣa,
Candra also replied, "So be it," out of deference to Dakṣa.
Then, having offered prayers to his daughter, to Candra, and likewise to his son-in-law,
the sage Dakṣa, having accomplished his purpose, went to his own abode.
Then, when Dakṣa had departed, Candra approached Rohiṇī and,
out of passion, resumed his former attitude toward her as well as toward the other [wives].
Having reached Rohiṇī at that very place, he did not see anyone at all;
he dwelt in Rohiṇī alone, and because of that, they became angry once more.
Having gone, they said to their father with minds distressed by misfortune:
"Soma does not dwell among us; he always favors Rohiṇī alone. (89)
He did not heed your words either; therefore, be our refuge.
Filled with agitation and anger, the sage rose at that very moment;
reflecting in his mind upon what ought to be done, he went into the presence of the Moon.
Then, having approached Candra, Prajāpati spoke these words:
"Behave equally toward your wives; abandon this partiality."
If you do not understand these words of mine due to your folly,
O Lord of Night, I shall curse you for transgressing the scriptures of Dharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, out of fear of Dakṣa, the Moon, before him and for the sake of performing that task, accepted it with great trepidation, saying repeatedly, "So be it."
Then, having agreed to treat his wives equally,
Dakṣa, with the approval of Candra, departed for his own abode along with Vidhu.
When Dakṣa had departed, the Lord of the Night (the Moon), sporting intensely with Rohiṇī,
forgot the words of Dakṣa.
And although all those beautiful women, beginning with the Aśvins, were serving him, Candramas did not favor them; instead, he treated them with utter contempt. || 97 ||
But all of them, having been treated with contempt by Candra, went to their father’s presence and, distressed and crying out in piteous tones, spoke as follows. || 98 ||
O best of sages, Soma did not heed your words either;
he has shown us even greater contempt than before. (99)
Therefore, there is no purpose for us whatsoever with Soma;
we shall become practitioners of austerity—prescribe a course of penance.
"O best of the twice-born, having purified our souls through austerity, we shall renounce life; what is the use of life to us, who are so unfortunate? (101)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, all those daughters of Dakṣa, beginning with Kṛttikā,
then took hold of their cheeks with their hands and fell to the ground.
Seeing them in such a state, their senses agitated by grief,
Dakṣa, with an exceedingly dejected face, blazed up with anger like a fire.
Then, from the tip of the nose of the great-souled Dakṣa, who was overcome with anger, a terrifying consumption (yakṣman) issued forth.
His face was terrifying with its fangs, his complexion like the glow of black charcoal;
he was exceedingly tall with very short hair, emaciated, and covered with prominent veins.
With his face turned downward and a staff in hand, he coughs continuously;
with sunken eyes, he is ever-lustful for the enjoyment of women. (106)
And he then said to Dakṣa: "O Sage, in what place shall I abide? Or what shall I do? Tell me that, O high-minded one. (107)
Then Dakṣa said to him: "May you go quickly to Soma;
may you always eat the Soma, and may you abide in Soma according to your own will. (108)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the great sage Dakṣa,
Gada then gradually approached Soma.
Having reached Soma, that great disease then entered the heart of the moon, finding an opening like a serpent entering a termite mound.
When that terrible pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) had entered his heart, Candra fainted and fell into a violent lethargy. || 111 ||
O twice-born ones, because that disease first arose and then subsided among kings,
it became known in this world by the name "rājayakṣmā" (the king's consumption).
Then, overcome by that consumption (yakṣman), the lord of Rohiṇī went to his decline day by day, like a small river in the summer heat. || 113 ||
Then, as the moon waned, all the medicinal herbs perished;
and when the herbs had perished, the sacrifice could no longer proceed.
Due to the absence of sacrifice, all food for the gods went to ruin;
consequently, the rain-clouds perished, and thereafter no rain occurred.
O best of the twice-born, when there was an absence of rain, the food supplies of the people were exhausted, and the entire world was beset by the calamity of famine.
No practice such as the duty of giving (dānadharma) and so forth proceeded among the people;
all subjects were devoid of virtue, their faculties impaired by greed, and delighting in evil deeds, they committed only sin. (117)
Upon seeing these beings at that time, the guardians of the quarters along with Purandara,
as well as the gods, the oceans, and the planets, all fell into a state of extreme agitation.
Then, seeing the entire world agitated and oppressed by bandits,
all the gods, led by Śakra, went to Brahmā.
Having approached the Lord of Gods, the creator and lord of the worlds, the deities then bowed down as was appropriate and sat down. 120.
Seeing them all with dejected faces, as if overcome by an enemy or robbed of their own domain, the Grandfather of the World summoned Guru Indra and the Fire-god before him and questioned them.
Brahmā said:
Welcome, O hosts of gods! For what purpose have you come?
I perceive that your bodies are stricken with sorrow and that you are withered.
Having made you all free from affliction and fear, and having established you all within my own realm according to your desires, how can I see you now so distressed?
Whatever has become the seed of your suffering, or whoever is afflicting you—let that be told in its entirety, and let it be understood as already accomplished. (124)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Vṛddhaśravas, Jīva, and Kṛṣṇavartman, the sustainers of the world,
spoke to that self-born one regarding the cause of the gods' distress.
The gods said:
"Listen, O Creator of the universe, to the reason why we have come to you, and what the seed of our suffering is, by which our prosperity has withered. (126)
O Grandfather, sacrifices no longer take place anywhere in the world;
being without support and free from distress, all creatures have gone to their destruction.
Neither the practice of giving and other virtues nor ascetic austerities existed anywhere on earth;
the rain-cloud did not pour forth, and the earth became depleted of water. (128)
All medicinal herbs have perished, the crops are ruined, and the worlds are thrown into turmoil;
oppressed by bandits, the Brahmins no longer perform the recitation of the Vedas.
Having encountered a deficiency of food, many creatures die;
likewise, we are deprived of our enjoyments now that our shares in the sacrifices have been exhausted. (130)
But those who are weak and deprived of prosperity do not attain peace at all. || 131 ||
The moon remained for a long time in the mansion of Rohiṇī due to its retrograde motion;
now, situated in the sign of Taurus, it has waned and exists devoid of its luster.
Whenever the moon is sought by the gods, he never appears as their leader,
neither in the assembly of the gods nor in a gathering such as yours.
Sometimes Rohiṇī leaves him and does not go anywhere else;
only if there were no one else would the Moon remain outside. (134)
"He is seen deprived of his digits, with only a single digit remaining"—thus, O Lord of the World, such is the reversal of karma that occurs everywhere. (135)
Seeing him, we became terrified and have come to you for refuge;
for the asuras, such as Kālakañja and others, have risen up from Pātāla. (136)
"O Lord of the World, protect us from this terror before these [calamities] afflict us!
Why does this transgression against the worlds proceed?
We do not know any of it, nor even the cause behind this upheaval. (137)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of the gods, the Grandfather, who possesses divine vision, reflected for a moment and spoke to the best of the gods.
Brahmā said:
"Let all the deities listen to the purpose for which this upheaval of the world now proceeds, and by which its pacification shall come to pass. (139)
Soma married the twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, beginning with Aśvinī, as wives for the purpose of becoming his bride-consorts. (140)
Having married all of them, the Moon constantly dwelt with Rohiṇī alone; he proceeded out of passion and did not behave equally toward all of them.
All those twenty-six beautiful women, beginning with Aśvinī, being afflicted by misfortune and fever, set out for their own father.
He informed Dakṣa that he did not treat them with such affection as the Lord of the Night (the Moon) does toward Rohiṇī out of passion. || 143 ||
Then the highly intelligent Dakṣa, having praised the Lord of Creatures with conciliatory words and addressed him with many pleasant expressions, entreated him for the sake of his daughter.
The moon-like Anuruddha, together with the skillful and great-souled Dakṣa, made an agreement to proceed through those [arts] according to his desire. 145.
O noble one, when he had agreed to act equally toward them, Himāṃśu then departed for his own abode, and Dakṣa also, the best of sages, went from there.
When the best of sages had departed, the Moon abandoned his partiality toward them;
they, being perpetually angry, went to their father.
Then Dakṣa, again pursuing Candra regarding his other daughter, having promised him equal treatment, spoke these words: || 148 ||
"O Moon, if you do not behave equally toward all these women, then I shall curse you; therefore, act with impartiality. (149)
Then, when Dakṣa had departed and things were no longer proceeding evenly,
Candra went again to Dakṣa and spoke to him in anger.
"You do not honor our words, nor do you act upon them toward us; we shall practice asceticism and remain in your presence. (151)
Having heard those words of theirs, that great sage became enraged; he then resolved to utter a curse for the destruction of Candra. (152)
O great sage, from the tip of the nose of you who were angry and intent on pronouncing a curse,
a great disease named Kṣaya emerged.
Then, dispatched by the sage Dakṣa for the sake of Candra,
he entered the body of the Moon, and by him the Moon was diminished.
When the moon had waned, the moonlight of that great-souled one also went to its end;
when all the moonlight had perished, all the medicinal herbs likewise came to destruction. (155)
In this world, due to the absence of medicinal herbs, sacrifice does not proceed;
due to the absence of sacrifice, there is no rain, and from that follows the destruction of all living beings. (156)
Likewise, for you who have been deprived of your share of the sacrifice,
weakness has arisen as well as a distortion in your own sphere of activity.
Thus I have told you all about the upheaval of the world exactly as it occurred; now, O best of gods, listen to the means by which its pacification may be achieved. (158)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Candra from the Curse," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-one.
Brahmā said:
"O hosts of gods, go toward the abode of Dakṣa;
propitiate him so that the moon may become full once again."
When the moon is full, the entire world will return to its natural state;
there shall be peace for you all, and the herbs will come into being. (2)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā, the gods, led by Śakra,
then departed for the abode of Dakṣa with joyful minds.
Having approached the best of sages according to the prescribed custom, all the gods bowed to Prajāpati Dakṣa and spoke with gentle words.
The gods said:
"Be gracious, O Brahman, toward us who are sinking and beset by great suffering.
Lift us up, O one of great intelligence; save us from this ocean of grief. (5)
That form which is designated as Brahman, the supreme self that creates the universe—you are a portion of that, the supreme light; O you in the form of a brāhmaṇa, salutations to you.
Because he protects all the worlds and for the sake of guarding his subjects, he is Dakṣa and Prajāpati; we bow to him, the Lord of Yoga.
Salutations to you, the Great Soul, who are skillful for all the worlds, skillful for those of virtuous nature, and swiftly skillful for one's own welfare.
You are the very essence of the essence, for Dakṣa, the Supreme Self, who is constantly meditated upon by yogis of restrained senses.
The conduct of yogis is unassailable; he is the ultimate refuge for those who have reached the further shore.
Released from beginning and end through his daring, eternal salutations, salutations to him! (10)
Having heard these words of those enjoyers of the sacrifice, Dakṣa,
with a serene countenance, addressed Śakra as the foremost among them and spoke thus.
Dakṣa said:
"O Śakra, O mighty-armed one, from where has this suffering come upon you?
O Lord, tell me the cause of the suffering; I wish to hear it."
"What must I do for you to eliminate your suffering?
If I am able, I shall perform that beneficial task impartially. (13)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard those words of that high-souled son of Brahmā,
Śakra, the lord of speech and eater of oblations, then spoke to that sage.
They said:
"The lord of the night has become subject to waning; when he wanes, O best of the twice-born, all medicinal herbs go to ruin. His loss causes the failure of sacrifices. (15)
When the sacrifice was destroyed, all the subjects became distressed by the fear of hunger;
due to the absence of rain, they experienced great suffering, and some perished.
O Brahmin, this waning of the Lord of Night which proceeds from your anger has arrived for the sake of the non-existence of the entire world. (17)
O best of Brahmins, there is nothing now in the three worlds— neither among the stationary beings nor among the birds— that has not been agitated or thrown into disorder.
Sacrifices were no longer performed, and ascetics did not practice austerities;
deprived of prosperity due to the suffering of lack of food, the subjects were wasted away and afflicted by fear. (19)
O best of Brahmins, while this calamity thus prevails,
rescue [the earth] from the netherworld before the Daityas rise up and cause further affliction.
Be gracious, O Dakṣa; fulfill that [desire] of Candra by the power of your asceticism.
When the moon is full, the entire world will return to its natural state.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the son of Prajāpati then spoke to those hosts of gods, extracting the thorn from their hearts.
Dakṣa said:
"The words I have uttered regarding the cause for the curse directed at the Lord of the Night—I do not venture to make them false for any reason whatsoever. (23)
However, because my word must not be entirely false, he observed a means by which even the moon would increase. (24)
In this matter, there is this remedy: let the moon undergo waning for half a month and waxing for half a month, and let it behave equally toward all its wives.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard those words of his and having propitiated that Prajāpati,
all the hosts of gods went there to where the Moon was located.
O twice-born ones, when these words had been spoken by the skillful sage Dakṣa,
those best of gods then took Candra along with his wives and went joyfully to the abode of Brahmā.
Having gone there, those highly fortunate ones related everything exactly as it had been spoken by Dakṣa to Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
Having heard the words of Dakṣa and the speech of the gods, Brahmā then went to the great mountain Candrabhāga accompanied by the deities.
Having gone there out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures, the best of gods bathed the moon (Śubhrāṃśu) in the great red lotus lake.
Knowing the past, the future, and the present, the Grandfather,
the teacher of the world, had previously created this full lake here for this very purpose.
For a person who has bathed there in the one known as Vṛhallohitaka, freedom from disease and constant long life are produced.
Thereupon, as Candra bathed, at that very moment the disease Rajayakshma emerged from his body, manifesting its previously described premonitory symptoms.
Rājayakṣmā said:
Having emerged, Rājayakṣmā also bowed to Brahmā, the Lord of the World, and said to him, "What shall I do? Where shall I go? (34)
O Lord of the World, since you are the creator of the worlds, please ordain for me a place, a wife, and my eternal duty in accordance with my nature. (35)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Brahmā, beholding that moon— the lord of the night— who was emaciated by those exceedingly potent nectars circulating within his body, spoke to him.
Having personally seized him with your arms and squeezed him repeatedly on the mountain,
you indeed extracted the nectar from the body of Rājayakṣman.
And those nectars which had then quickly dissolved in the water,
he, the sustainer of the world, cast into the midst of the Ocean of Milk in secret.
Therefore, from that nectar, he took grain by grain from the Ocean of Milk those portions which had previously been diminished. (39)
Due to the association with consumption (rājayakṣman), which had only a single digit remaining, those fifteen digits that were previously of the nature of nectar became diminished. (40)
Those [digits] dwelling within the womb of the lunar consumption were crushed by the pain;
yet that which belonged to the Lord of the Kalās was held together by his splendor, moonlight, and nectar.
That body of the one afflicted by pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) becomes threefold while still in the womb.
The light became dust, and the moonlight dissolved into the consumption-disease (yakṣman) that afflicted the king;
all the nectars melted away and remained within the womb of the disease. (43)
When Brahmā extracted the nectar from within the consumption-disease (yakṣman),
then all the light of the moonlight-nectar emerged from it.
Then, having abandoned the gods on the mountain, he himself went quickly from there and cast all of that into the ocean of milk according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having washed the nectars and the powders of the lunar digits with waters,
he quickly returned to the mountain, taking those three with him.
Then, having reached Mount Candrabhāga from the Ocean of Milk,
Brahmā placed the powder of the lunar digits and the nectar-moonlight amidst the gods.
Having established those three, Brahmā stood in the midst of the gods and spoke to Rājayakṣman, pointing out his place and other details.
Brahmā said:
"O King, you who always indulge in sexual pleasure with women during the day, at night, and at the twilights— you shall dwell within that very act of lovemaking as consumption (rājayakṣman)."
One afflicted by catarrh, dyspnea, and cough should not engage in sexual intercourse;
for such a person, that act constantly causes the entry of phlegm into the [channels]. (50)
She who is known as Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Mṛtyu, who is equal to you in virtues—let her be your wife; she shall follow you constantly.
Your duty is to become diminished; therefore, make yourself an object [of my power].
Depart quickly as you wish, and turn your face away from the moon.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus dismissed by Brahmā, the great disease of consumption vanished from the sight of all the gods.
When the great disease had vanished, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
summoned Candra, who was augmented by fifteen digits.
With that [dust] washed by the ocean of milk and purified by nectar, the Self-born [Brahmā],
using fine powders together with moonlight, fashioned the moon as before.
When that moon, filled with its sixteen digits, shone forth as before, all the gods rejoiced at the sight of it. (56)
Then Candra, full [of light], having prostrated before the Grandfather, spoke these words while standing in the midst of the assembly of gods, not being excessively joyful: || 57 ||
Soma said:
"O Brahmin, happiness no longer dwells within my body as it did before; nor do I possess such vigor or enthusiasm, for the joints of my limbs are failing. (58)
I am utterly unable to perform my functions as before;
deprived of these functions, O Creator of the World, by what means shall I subsist day after day? (59)
Brahmā said:
O Soma, because of your being seized by consumption (yakṣman), your joints had previously become disjointed; though they were shattered, they did not indeed become whole again.
Now, the powder of your body has been extracted by me from your frame,
along with the nectar-moonlight that directly dispels consumption.
Since you are devoid of that which remained in the water when they were washed away bit by bit—namely, the moonlight and the nectar; (52)
Therefore, O King, your limbs and joints are now failing you;
I shall devise a remedy so that you do not suffer further. (63)
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Prajāpati is to be offered first in the Āhavanīya fire at the commencement of the sacrifice;
thereafter, the cake for Indra and then that for Agni are to be offered everywhere throughout the rite.

"Therefore, I have prepared a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as your portion. By constantly consuming that portion produced by sacrifice, your energy and dark prowess shall become as they were before. (65)
Those drops of nectar that remain in the waters of the Ocean of Milk, or those particles of your body’s powder, and even those fragments of your moonlight; || 66 ||
O Moon, through association with your moonlight, all that shall constantly increase day by day, like the interior of the ocean of milk.
When the second intermediate period, Svārociṣa, arrives, Durvāsas, born from a portion of Śaṅkara, will become a brahmin as fierce as the scorching sun.
Having pronounced a most terrible curse upon the Lord of the Gods for his lack of discipline,
he will render the three worlds, including the gods and asuras, bereft of splendor.
Therefore, when the world is bereft of Śrī, there will be a universal upheaval,
just as this total catastrophe has occurred through the waning of you, O Soma.
According to human measurement, when the third age (the Tretā-yuga) has begun,
it shall endure and remain for the duration of the four ages.
Then, when the fourth age, the Kṛtayuga, has arrived, Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and I, together with the gods, shall churn the Ocean of Milk.
"Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
and since the gods have hidden themselves within their sacrificial portions,
we shall then churn the Ocean of Milk together with the gods and the Dānavas for the sake of nectar."
"This nectar of your body which resides in the Ocean of Milk—we shall churn it and seize it; thus it will be gathered into a mass and [the ocean] likewise brought to exhaustion. (74)
O Moon, having placed your body within all the medicinal herbs,
we shall then cast it into the waters of the ocean for the sake of your physical restoration.
"After you have churned the ocean and subsequently extracted the nectar of immortality, your body shall then be restored to its former state. (76)
Your body shall become wonderful in its vital energy and prowess, lovely, imperishable, and composed of nectar; its joints shall be firm and it shall be beautiful. (77)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having thus addressed Sudhāṃśu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
exerted himself for half a month to cause the waning of the Moon and [the other half] for his waxing.
Just as Dakṣa had declared that the moon should undergo waning for half a month and waxing for half a month, the Creator (Vidhi) exerted effort toward that end.
Then the eldest of the gods divided the moon into sixteen parts;
having divided it, he spoke these excellent words to all the gods: (80)
Brahmā said:
"Of the sixteen digits of the moon, let one remain upon the head of Śambhu from this day forward; let the others go to destruction, yet not through actual decay."
If, according to the words of Dakṣa, the Moon is afflicted by the wasting disease (kṣaya) for half a month,
then there shall be no peace.
However, let that one digit of his which resides in Śambhu go toward the moonlight;
O best of gods, let those remaining fourteen digits be established in the moon month by month. (83)
"Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) until that fourteenth day, you all should indeed drink the fourteen non-material elements (abhūta-kalās). (84)
In this manner, during the dark fortnight, the portions of light of the moon gradually enter the solar disc on the fourteenth lunar day and thus undergo destruction.
Let the remaining digit of the moon, having fled to the green leaf on the new-moon day, remain during that first portion of the night belonging to the Lord of the Night. (86)
In the second part of the night, let him go to the temple of Rohiṇī;
then, having bathed in the Sarasvatī during the third part, the Moon arose.
In the fourth lunar day of the sun's portion, let this moon, complete with its orb, chariot, and horses, enter the solar mandala. (88)
Indeed, by the same amount of time that the first digit (kalā) reaches its end,
in this very manner, the first lunar day (pratipad) occurs in the dark fortnight.
In the dark fortnight, beginning from the second day, there is an increase and decrease of that same kind;
likewise, the cause for the increase of the lunar days occurs in both the bright and the dark fortnights.
Then again, during the bright fortnight, from the beginning until such time that the [lunar day] has not reached the increase as previously described, it shall be the first lunar day (pratipad).
Then, that portion of the second half which resides upon the head of Hara—
the digit that has indeed departed— shall return;
it shall become the nectar to be drunk by you day after day.
O best of gods, by means of the lunar days beginning with the second and ending with the full moon, the moon itself shall indeed arise through its conjunction with the moonlight.
O gods, just as the portions of the moon wane day by day, so do they increase daily in the bright fortnight. (94)
The portion of light will return once more from the solar disc;
it will proceed during the dark fortnight according to the same sequence of parts.
The moonlight will return daily from the moon on Shiva’s head;
a portion of its luster, raining nectar itself, will come from the solar disc.
In this way, the waxing of the moon will occur during the bright fortnight;
the whiteness and blackness of the two fortnights arise from the increase and decrease of the moon. (97)
For as long as it takes for a particular portion to undergo decrease or increase, for that duration of time that lunar day (tithi) shall remain. Furthermore—

Whether it be growth or decay, whether slowly or quickly—there is always decay from the rapid [movement] of the lunar days, while there is growth from the slow [movement] upon the entry into the lunar days. (99)
"Without Candra, the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya) will no longer be possible.
Therefore, let the deities protect Candra for the sake of increasing those two. (100)
The moon, whose digits are diminished month by month, becomes delicious to the taste;
on the afternoon of the new moon, he enters the abode of Rohiṇī along with the ancestors.
Because of his very tasting of it, the *kavya* will increase day by day;
through that *kavya*, the ancestors will indeed attain supreme satisfaction. (102)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then all the hosts of gods, for the welfare of the world, performed exactly as prescribed by the ritual for the waning and waxing of the moon.
Mahādeva, being intensely hungry, also assumed the form of the Supreme Self for the sake of the moon, according to the rite prescribed by the gods. 104.
That supreme light, which is eternal, unborn, undecaying, and imperishable—that very essence is the digit of the moon; yet, due to a curse, it has undergone decay.
When the light of supreme, undecaying bliss enters [them],
then the mental activity of those yogins will become dissolved.
"When the mind, which is a treasury of nectar, is dissolved and rests upon the head of Mahādeva,
liberation occurs through the moon"— such is the Vedic revelation.
Having understood this, Mahādeva, for the welfare of all the worlds, took up the Moon with his head—[the Moon] which is inseparable from waning and waxing. (108)
Through the conjunction with the moonlight, medicinal herbs attain growth;
when all the herbs have grown, the sacrificial rites then proceed.
When the sacrifices have commenced, the deities accept their respective portions, and likewise the ancestors accept the *kavya* offerings in abundance. (110)
The nectar created by Brahmā, which is more ancient than the gods—by that do those deities who are deprived of their sacrificial portions find satisfaction. (111)
Nourished by sacrifice, it indeed increases through the moonlight;
otherwise, deprived of the light of sacrifice, it would become diminished.
Therefore, the moon himself is the cause of this immortal sacrifice;
thus, for the sake of protection from Dakṣa’s curse, he desired to perform that [act].
Even today, during the dark fortnight, the nectar-rayed moon is drunk by the gods;
its splendor goes to the Sun, and likewise the moonlight of the crescent moon goes to Śambhu.
Furthermore, in the bright fortnight, the remaining digit then rises;
that second part of the moonlight is indeed the second lunar day (dvitīyā). || 115 ||
Others [arise] from the moon on the exceedingly fierce head and from the solar disc respectively;
there are sixteen digits of the moon, one of which is upon the crest of Śambhu. (116)
"The white and black fortnights are both the rise and the wane of the remaining [lunar days].
Thus has everything been explained to you, O best of mountains, how the moon is divided by Brahmā and how that [division] came about from the Moon. 117.

Because he made the moon the food of the gods when the sacrificial portion was established, and likewise the food of the ancestors when the *kavya* was established, according to the increase and decrease of the lunar days (*tithi*). (118)
Whatever man hears this most meritorious narrative even once, consumption shall never arise in his family. (119)
O best of men, he who is already overcome by consumption and hears these words of the rite shall soon become possessed by consumption. 120.
This auspicious rite is meritorious, the most secret of secrets, and auspicious;
whoever hears it with a single-minded focus shall become a partaker of great merit. 121.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation from the Moon's Curse," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Two.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the ridge of that great mountain, where the assembly hall of the gods was situated,
the river of the gods known as Sītā arose there by the command of Brahmā.
When they had bathed the Moon with charming, cool waters,
all those inhabitants of heaven drank from the Moon at the word of Brahmā.
Then, through the conjunction with the moon's bath, the water of the Sītā became imbued with nectar and fell into that lake known as Bṛhallohita.
Then that water, having increased, could no longer fit within that lake;
Brahmā himself beheld that water, which had grown and was filled with nectar.
From that water, upon seeing him, an excellent maiden arose;
then Brahmā himself gave her the name Candrabhāgā.
O one whose mind is fixed on Brahman, the ocean took her as his wife.
The Lord of the Night (the Moon), having pierced that mountain with the tip of his mace— which was itself presided over by her— caused the water to flow out from its western side.
Having pierced that lake of nectar-water named Vṛhadlohita,
that river Candrabhāgā flows toward the ocean.
Then Sāgara also carried his wife, the great river Candrabhāgā,
along with that flow of water to his own abode.
Thus, the river named Candrabhāgā arose there on the great mountain Candrabhāga; she was always equal to the Gaṅgā in her virtues.
All rivers and mountains are twofold by their very nature;
the water is the form of the rivers, while the other is their body.
Furthermore, there is another form of his body, as immobile as mountains;
it is like the subtle essence that exists within oyster shells and conch shells.
The external form, however, always continues to proceed;
thus, at that time, there was water in the rivers and mountains, as well as in stationary objects.
But the body that dwells within does not persist eternally. || 14 ||
The body of the mountain is nourished by its stationary [trees],
and likewise, the bodies of the rivers are always nourished by water.
In ancient times, for the sake of the stability of the world, Viṣṇu diligently fashioned the power of rivers to assume any form at will, and likewise that of mountains.
O gods, when the water fails, constant suffering arises for the river;
when the stationary [trees] wither, suffering born of the mountain-born [river] arises.
Then, on that mountain at the Candrabhāga, having seen Sandhyā dwelling on the banks of the Bṛhallohita, Vasiṣṭha questioned her with reverence.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O blessed lady, for what purpose have you come to this desolate mountain? Whose daughter are you, O Gaurī, and what is it that you intend to do?"
I desire to hear this from you, provided it is not a secret;
otherwise, why is your face, which resembles the full moon, bereft of its splendor? (20)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
and having beheld that great-souled one blazing like fire, [the king was filled with wonder].
Then, having respectfully prostrated before that ascetic who bore matted hair and whose bodily discipline was equal to that of Brahmacharya, Sandhyā spoke to him.
Sandhyā said:
"O best of the twice-born, that purpose for which I came to the mountain has been accomplished for me;
O Lord, it will be fulfilled by the mere sight of you."
"O Brahman, I have come to this uninhabited mountain to perform penance;
I am born from the mind of Brahmā and am renowned by the name Sandhyā. (24)
O best of sages, I do not know the instruction for asceticism;
if it is appropriate for you, please instruct me in that which is secret.
This secret is what he intends to do; nothing else exists.
Having resorted to this penance grove without understanding the true nature of asceticism, I am withered by anxiety and my mind is constantly trembling. (26)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard her words, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā—
who himself was a knower of all principles— did not ask anything further.
Then Vasiṣṭha addressed her, who was self-restrained and exceedingly resolute in her exertion for asceticism, as a teacher addresses a disciple.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Let Viṣṇu be placed in the mind—he who is the supreme great splendor, he who is the supreme great austerity, and he who is the supreme one to be propitiated. (29)
He alone is the primary cause for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
worship that one, the primordial of the worlds, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). 30.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, with eyes like lotuses,
resembling pure crystal, yet in some places possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud.
Upon Garuḍa, seated on a white lotus in the lotus posture, is Hari, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is peaceful, and who wears a supreme forest garland. 32.
