Wearing armlets and earrings, radiant with a diadem and crown; formless yet accessible through knowledge, possessing form as the bearer of a body.
O lady of auspicious countenance, worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, who is eternal bliss, without support, and situated in the center of the solar disc, by means of this mantra.
With "Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva" ending with "Oṃ," one should constantly begin the vow of silence; listen now to these rules regarding that practice. (35)
The bath should be performed in silence, and the worship likewise in silence.
For two of the six meal-times, one should subsist on leaves and water;
at the third sixth-meal-time, however, one should be devoted to fasting.
Thus, when the austerity is completed, the ritual should take place at the sixth meal-time;
wearing garments of tree-bark and likewise sleeping on the ground at that time, one should remain silent. This practice of the vow, known as austerity, bestows its fruit.
Thus, directing your austerity toward this end, think of Mādhava with longing;
he, being pleased, will before long grant you your desired object.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having instructed Sandhyā in the performance of ascetic rites, the sage Vasiṣṭha,
after addressing her according to custom, vanished right there.
Sandhyā too, having understood the state of his asceticism and having attained joy,
began to perform penance on the banks of the Bṛhallohita river.
As Vasiṣṭha had instructed regarding the mantra as the means for ascetic practice, Govinda worshipped with devotion by means of that vow. (41)
As she performed that very great austerity with a single-minded heart,
fixing her mind upon Viṣṇu, one cycle of four yugas passed away.
No one failed to be struck with wonder upon seeing her extraordinary asceticism;
indeed, no one else shall ever perform such a practice of penance.
Then, when one cycle of four yugas had passed according to human measurement,
he displayed his own form within, without, and likewise in the sky.
Pleased by that form which she had meditated upon,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, appeared visibly before her.
Then, seeing before her Hari, who was conceived of by her mind, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and possessing lotus-like eyes; (46)
Wearing armlets and earrings, radiant with a crown and diadem, seated upon Garuḍa, the lotus-eyed one, possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal. (47)
"Filled with trepidation, I shall speak; what shall I say, or how shall I praise Hari?"—becoming thus absorbed in thought, she closed her eyes. (48)
Entering the heart of her who had closed her eyes, Hari bestowed upon her divine knowledge, divine speech, and divine eyes. (49)
She attained divine knowledge, the divine eye, and divine speech;
beholding Govinda directly before her eyes, she praised the Lord of the worlds.
Sandhyā said:

Salutations be to You, Hari, whose form is formless, attainable through knowledge, who is neither gross nor subtle, nor yet lofty; whose nature is to be contemplated within by yogis—to You, I offer my salutation. (51)

I bow to You, the gracious Śiva—peaceful, stainless, changeless, beyond knowledge, supremely luminous and all-pervading, resembling the sun, standing beyond the realm of darkness, whose very form is You. 52.

Salutations to Him whose form is singular, pure, and radiant; who is the diversion, the joy of the mind, born of all beings, and the remover of sin; who is eternal bliss, truth, and exceedingly gracious; and who bestows prosperity. (53)
The nature of the self is to be meditated upon as manifested through the forms of knowledge, yet distinct and concealed by sentient beings;
it is the essence, the further shore of all purifiers, and the most sacred—salutations to that form of yours from which this [universe] proceeds. 54.
Salutations to You, the eternal and straightforward, devoid of decay, who are contemplated by those disciplined in yoga through the eight limbs of virtue;
salutations to You, the all-pervading Reality, having attained whom yogis reach the supreme state through the yoga of knowledge.

Salutations to You, who are endowed with yoga, whose form is with attributes, pure, beautiful, seated upon Garuḍa, shining like a blue cloud, and bearing the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace. 56.
The sky, the earth, the directions, as well as water and light, wind and time—these are his forms; homage be to you! (57)
Salutations be to you, Govinda, who are of unmanifest form, and in whom Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide as constituent parts of your activity. 58.
Salutations again and again to You, who are Yourself the five elements, who are Yourself their supreme quality, and who are Yourself the support of the universe.
Salutations again and again to You, the Supreme, the Ancient Person, the Supreme Self who pervades the universe, the imperishable and immutable God. 60.
Salutations again and again to You, who as Brahmā performs creation, who as Viṣṇu performs preservation, and who as Rudra will perform destruction.
Salutations again and again to the cause of all causes, the bestower of divine nectar, knowledge, and sovereign power;
to the one who brings delusion to all other worlds, whose nature is light, and who is higher than the highest.

Salutations be to you, Hari, whose vast manifestation is called the world—consisting of the earth, the quarters, the sun, the moon, and the speed of thought; from whose mouth came fire and from whose navel the atmosphere. || 63 ||
You are the Supreme and the Supreme Self; O Hari, you are various forms of knowledge, the Word-Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, and that which is higher than the highest object of inquiry.
How shall I praise that God who is beyond the reach of speech and mind, for whom there is neither beginning, nor middle, nor end, O Lord of the Universe? (65)
How can he be described by me, whose forms even the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is asceticism do not reveal?
O Lord, what can I, a woman, know of the qualities of You who are beyond all qualities?
Even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, do not know Your true form.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the World; salutations to you, who are composed of ascetic power.
Be gracious, O Blessed One; obeisance, obeisance to you again and again.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Now, her body was covered with bark garments and deerskins;
it was emaciated, yet graced upon the head by clusters of pure matted locks.
Seeing her face, which resembled a lotus flower withered by frost, Hari was overcome with compassion and spoke this to her: 70.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am truly pleased, O blessed lady, with your supreme austerity and with your hymn of praise, O lady of auspicious wisdom; choose now a boon."
Whatever purpose you have that is in your mind, which can be accomplished by a boon, I shall fulfill it; may prosperity be yours, for I am pleased with your vows.
Sandhyā said:
"O Lord, if you are pleased by my penance, then let this first boon be granted to me now. (73)
O Lord of Gods, let all living beings in this world, as soon as they are born, not be subject to desires in due course; rather, let them truly be free from desire.
"Just as I am renowned throughout the three worlds as a devoted wife, so shall I be none other; this alone is the boon I have chosen. (75)
O Lord of the World, my longing gaze shall not fall anywhere except upon my husband; for he, too, is my greatest merit. (76)
The man who looks upon me with lustful desire,
his virility shall then perish, and he shall become impotent.
The Blessed One said:
The first state is infancy; the second is called childhood;
the third is the state of youth; and likewise, the fourth is old age. (78)
But when the embodied being has reached the third stage of life, they may occasionally have their desires fulfilled at the end of the second stage. (79)
O highly fortunate one, your husband shall be endowed with ascetic power and beauty,
and he shall live for seven kalpas along with you.
Thus, those boons which were requested by you from me have been granted by me;
furthermore, I shall tell you something else that has long resided in my mind. (84)
The renunciation of your body in the fire was already promised by you previously;
that [was to take place] at the twelve-year sacrifice of the sage Medhātithi. (85)
Let an oblation be offered by you without delay into the blazing fire on this mountain slope, on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā. (86)
Medhātithi performs a great sacrifice in the hermitage of the ascetics.
Having gone there, you shall remain hidden and will not be perceived by the sages;
by my grace, you shall become his daughter, born from fire.
Whosoever is the husband you desire in your heart, keeping him within your own mind, cast your body into the fire. (89)
When you were performing austerities on the mountain during the terrible twilight,
four yugas passed away while that Kṛta Yuga was still in effect.
In the first part of the Tretā Yuga, the daughters of Dakṣa were born;
he gave twenty-seven of those daughters to the Moon.
When Candra was cursed by Dakṣa out of anger for that reason,
all the gods assembled in your presence.
In that twilight state, neither the gods nor Brahmā were seen by her as she fixed her mind upon me; nor, conversely, were you seen by them.
Just as the river Candrabhāgā was created by the Creator for the sake of liberating Candra from his curse,
at that very moment Medhātithi arrived there.
There has been none equal to him in asceticism, nor will there ever be;
by him this sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma of great ritual procedure, was commenced. (95)
There, in that blazing fire, cast off your own body.
"O ascetic lady, this has been established by me for your sake;
therefore, O illustrious one, perform it and go to the sacrifice of the great sage. (97)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Nārāyaṇa himself touched the twilight with the tip of his hand;
thereupon, that body instantly became composed of sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

In this great sacrifice of the Great Sage, which benefits the entire universe, let the fire not become a consumer of the offerings for the ancestors; it was for this very purpose that the rite was thus performed.
Having done this, the Lord of the World vanished right there;
Sandhyā also went to that sacrificial session where the sage Medhātithi was.
Then, by the grace of Viṣṇu, Sandhyā entered the sacrifice of the sage Medhātithi unobserved by anyone. (101)
In former times, having assumed the form of a female ascetic, that ascetic woman was instructed by Vasiṣṭha to perform penance at the command of Parameṣṭhin.
Then Sandhyā, having taken that Brahmin student as her husband, fixed in her mind him alone as the instructor of her ascetic practice.
While the great sacrifice was being performed with the fire kindled, the daughter of Brahmā entered [the fire] unobserved by the sages, through the grace of Viṣṇu. 104.
At that moment, her body, which was composed of sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), was consumed;
it spread an imperceptible fragrance of the sacrificial cake. || 105 ||
Then, having burned her body within the solar orb, the Fire-god,
by the command of Viṣṇu himself, caused her pure essence to enter once more.
Sūrya established [this] for the pleasure of the ancestors and the gods. || 107 ||
O best of the twice-born, that which was the upper portion of her body became the morning twilight (prātaḥsandhyā), situated at the beginning and middle of the day and night.
That portion which remained of her, situated between the end and the middle of the day and night,
became the evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā), which always bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
When the dawn of Aruṇa occurs first before the rising of the sun,
then the morning twilight arises, which brings delight to the gods.
Then, when the sun has set, the evening twilight, which is always like a red lotus and brings joy to the ancestors, rises.
Then, by means of his mind and through his divine body, the powerful Viṣṇu endowed her with vital breaths, making her a possessor of a body.
When the conclusion of the sage’s sacrifice had arrived, that daughter was obtained by the sage from the midst of the fire, resembling molten gold. (113)
Then the sage, filled with joy and moved by compassion, took that daughter; having bathed her with waters intended for the sacrifice, he placed her upon his own lap.
The great sage gave her the name Arundhatī;
surrounded there by his disciples, he experienced great joy.
Because she did not obstruct the Dharma for any reason whatsoever,
she obtained the name "Trilokaviditā" (Known Throughout the Three Worlds) along with her lineage.
Having completed the sacrifice and attained a sense of fulfillment, that great sage, overflowing with joy at having recovered his son,
dwells perpetually in that very hermitage together with his circle of disciples, cherishing him alone.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Account of Arundhatī’s Birth," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-three.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that goddess grew up in that excellent hermitage of the sage,
on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā, in the place known as Tāpasāraṇya.
Just as the crescent moon constantly waxes during the bright fortnight,
and just as the moonlight does, so too did Arundhatī attain increase.
When her fifth year had arrived, that virtuous Candrabhāgā then purified even the forest of ascetics by means of her virtues.
There is a sacred ford of great merit frequented by Medhātithi,
a pure place of play established by Arundhatī during her childhood.
Even today, a man who bathes in the waters of the river Candrabhāgā in the forest of ascetics, within the waters of the Arundhatī-tīrtha, goes to Hari.
Having bathed in the waters of the Candrabhāgā river throughout the entire month of Kārttika and having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu, one shall indeed attain liberation at the end.
Whoever should perform a bath even once in the waters of the Candrabhāgā on the full moon or likewise on the new moon day in the month of Māgha; || 7 ||
In his lineage, consumption shall never occur;
at the end of the body, having gone to the abode of the Moon, he goes to the home of Hari.
Having returned here due to the exhaustion of his merit, he shall become a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
by drinking the water of the Candrabhāgā, he shall attain the world of the Moon.
By bathing there even once according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.

Once, while traveling through the path of the sky, the lotus-seated Brahmā beheld Arundhatī on the bank near her father; she was playing with the frolics of childhood after bathing in the waters of the Candrabhāgā.
Then the Blessed One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, having descended,
beheld Arundhatī at that time as she was engaged in instruction.
Then Brahmā, honored by the sages led by Medhātithi, spoke to that great sage who was worthy of such praise.
Brahmā said:
O great sage, this is the time for instruction from Arundhatī;
therefore, you should place her in the presence of these virtuous women.
Women should be instructed by women; perhaps someone else exists elsewhere.
You are the daughter of the prolific Sāvitrī; establish her in my presence.
O great sage, having come into contact with those two, your daughter will before long become endowed with great virtues and sovereignty.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the Supreme Self, Medhātithi, the best of sages, then replied to him, "So be it. (17)
Then, after the best of gods had departed, the sage Medhātithi took his daughter and immediately set out toward the abode of the Sun.
There he beheld Sāvitrī, situated in the midst of the solar orb,
the white goddess seated upon a lotus throne, holding a rosary of beads.
She was seen by that sage as she emerged from the solar disc;
having become manifold, she quickly went to the Mānasa mountain.
Every day, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Bahulā, Sarasvatī, and Drupadā—these five [reside] on the Mānasa mountain. (21)
Having thus engaged in virtuous conversations with one another through discourses on the Dharma, she returns again to her own respective abode out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (22)
But Medhātithi, rich in asceticism, having seen all those mothers of the entire world gathered together in one place, bowed down to each of them individually. (23)
And that rishi, whose wealth was his asceticism, spoke gently to them all;
he was both filled with awe and struck with wonder at seeing them gathered together in one place.
Medhātithi said:
"O Mother Sāvitrī, this daughter of mine, Bahulā, possesses auspicious intentions;
this is the time for her instruction, and for that purpose I have come. (25)
"Commanded by the Creator of the World, she has entered into discipleship under you;
this daughter of mine has been brought to your side by him. (26)
"O two goddesses, mother, mother, salutations to you both! Train this girl of mine so that she may possess good conduct, O young men. (27)
Then the goddess Sāvitrī, accompanied by Bahulā, spoke with a smile to that best of sages and to the girl.
They both said:
"O Brahmin, by the grace of Viṣṇu, your daughter has already been well-conducted even before now, O Sage; what need is there then for that purpose? (29)
"But by the word of Brahmā, I, being many and a great satī, shall discipline your daughter so that she will soon become steadfast. (30)
By the power of your asceticism, Arundhatī became the elder daughter of Brahmā;
likewise, by the grace of Viṣṇu, she became your daughter.
She shall purify your lineage, she shall increase your truth, and she shall bring about the welfare of both the worlds and the gods. || 32 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, dismissed by them, that sage Medhātithi comforted his daughter,
bowed to Arundhatī, and departed for his own abode.
When that best of sages had departed with those two, Arundhatī,
protected like by her own mothers, rejoiced without fear.
Sometimes he goes to the abode of the Sun together with Sāvitrī at night;
likewise, he sometimes goes to the abode of Śakra accompanied by Bahulā.
Thus, sporting together with those two in the abode of the gods,
the goddess spent seven divine years.
Seated in that manner with those two, that virtuous woman soon came to know all the duties of women, having become like Sāvitrī herself, enriched by great wisdom.
Then, when that time had arrived,
there occurred for her a beautiful blossoming of youth, just like the luster of lotus ponds.
Having reached the bloom of youth, she beheld on Mount Mānasa the sage Vasiṣṭha, who was wandering about and possessed of beautiful splendor.
Having seen him, that virtuous woman desired him with a longing born of passion—
he who possessed the radiance of the rising sun, was of beautiful form, and was endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
Then that highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha, upon seeing the woman of excellent complexion,
had his passion aroused and gazed intently at Arundhatī.
O best of the twice-born, upon seeing one another, a great passion arose between them, becoming unrestrained like the god of love acting upon common folk.
Then, having summoned her fortitude, the daughter of Medhātithi steadied herself and restrained her mind from being agitated by passion.
Then Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great luster, summoning his own fortitude, steadied his mind which had been agitated by passion.
Then the goddess Arundhatī, leaving the presence of the sage, went to where Sāvitrī was, censuring her own desire. (45)
Afflicted by extreme mental anguish, the great virtuous woman,
reflecting upon me, indeed abandoned her state of chastity.
Due to the mental anguish born of that [separation], her face became discolored, her entire body grew withered, and her gait became faltering. (47)
She reflected on this, reproaching her own mind,
which was as delicate as a lotus fiber and severed in that very instant.
"Stability is destroyed by even a slight fickleness in virtuous women"; having thus instructed me in the duties of women, she, who had fulfilled her vows, spoke to me. (49)
This is the essence of the Sāvitrī, extracted from the very core of the duty of virtuous women;
today, however, that hope has been destroyed in a man belonging to another.
"What will become of me in this world and the next if I cause her to grow?"—thus did the daughter of Medhātithi reflect at that time. (51)
He approached Queen Sāvitrī, who was greatly afflicted by suffering;
and seeing her in such a state, with her face pale and dejected, he spoke to that virtuous lady. (52)
Devoted to meditation and reflection, Sāvitrī indeed endured;
having reflected with divine knowledge, she came to know everything.
Just as Vasiṣṭha had the vision of Arundhatī, so too did she have the vision of him;
and thus the love between them grew, becoming exceedingly difficult to endure.
And Sāvitrī, who possessed divine vision, was the cause of the change in his complexion;
then, placing her hand upon the head of Medhātithi’s daughter, she— 55.
The great goddess Sāvitrī, who had fulfilled her vows, said this:
Sāvitrī said, "O child, why has this face of yours become of a different color? (56)
Like a lotus with its stalk severed, scorched by the rays of the sun,
how did your body become withered, O you who are most endowed with virtue?
"Just as the orb of the lord of night is veiled by thin, dark clouds, so too,
O blessed lady, your inner mind appears to be filled with anxiety.
Therefore, tell me your secret, unless this cause of your sorrow is something you cannot reveal."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having cast her face downward out of shame, Arundhatī said nothing at all,
even though she had been questioned thus by her venerable mother Sāvitrī.
When she said something,
then Sāvitrī, the daughter of Idhmavāha and the wife of that ascetic, revealed herself and spoke to her.
Sāvitrī said:
"O child, that sage resembling the sun whom you have seen is Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā; he shall become your husband."
In former times, the Creator himself ordained the marital union between you and him.
Therefore, your status as a chaste woman is not diminished by seeing him;
or rather, your heart became filled with desire upon seeing him. (62)
"O daughter, that mental suffering does not cause any fault; therefore, abandon it.
O beautiful one, you performed supreme austerity in a previous birth. (63)
He alone is your beloved, and he possesses desire for you;
listen, my child, to how formerly this Vasiṣṭha was chosen by you as your husband,
and with what disposition you constantly performed penance therein.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, she became Sāvitrī, just as she had been in the past at twilight.
The penance was performed for that purpose on the mountain named Candrabhāga,
just as Vasiṣṭha had previously done in the form of a brahmacārī for the sake of Brahmā.
Following his instruction, she performed that penance so difficult to accomplish,
whereby the Lord Viṣṇu became pleased and appeared before her in person.
How he granted her a boon, how the boundary was established, and how that sage Vasiṣṭha was chosen by her as her husband; || 68 ||
Just as your body was offered into the fire at Medhātithi’s sacrifice, and how his daughters were subsequently born— this [shall be told] to you in detail then.
Sāvitrī related [the story] in due order along with Bahulā.
Then, having heard her words, that which had occurred in my previous birth was revealed; indeed, upon hearing it, everything within my mind became known to me.
Having become exceedingly ashamed at this, she stood with her face cast down;
by the word of Sāvitrī, she became one who remembered her previous birth.
Remaining likewise with her face turned downward, Arundhatī, possessed of divine knowledge, then remembered everything that had occurred in her previous birth.
Having previously become a seer of divine things through the grace of Viṣṇu,
she is now one whose divine vision is concealed by her state of childhood.
Having heard the account of her previous birth from the words of Sāvitrī,
she attained that entire knowledge of the past as if it were before her very eyes.
Having previously attained that knowledge which was bestowed by Viṣṇu in the past, this Vasiṣṭha said: "Indeed, in my former birth, I chose him as my own master. (76)
Thus, when the sight of Vasiṣṭha had previously arisen in her heart, that goddess Jñānavatī herself became Arundhatī, filled with joy.
Just as that affliction had arisen to obstruct her chastity, Medhātithi’s daughter herself then cast it away. (78)
Then, perceiving that the virtuous Arundhatī had abandoned all anxiety,
Sāvitrī went together with her to the abode of the Sun.
Then Arundhatī established Sāvitrī in the abode of the Sun, and that most excellent virtuous woman,
the all-knowing one, departed for the realm of Brahmā.
Then, having prostrated before Brahmā and being questioned by him at that very moment, Sāvitrī spoke these words to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor: || 81 ||
O Blessed One, Lord of the World, the virtuous Arundhatī beheld Vasiṣṭha, your son, upon the ridge of Mount Mānasa.
Merely by the sight of them, a great passion increased within their hearts; O Prajāpati, they both felt a longing for one another. (83)
Then, steadying their minds through fortitude despite being deeply distressed, those two dejected and ashamed departed to their respective abodes. (84)
Since things have proceeded in this manner, O best of gods, let that which is appropriate be performed now for the sake of the welfare of the worlds in the future. (85)
Having heard her words, Brahmā, the preceptor of the entire world,
perceived through his divine knowledge the future course of action.
Then the Grandfather of the World spoke these words of welcome:
"The time for the state of matrimony for these two has now arrived. (87)
"Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall go to promote that [practice].
Having thus resolved in his mind, Brahmā, accompanied by Sāvitrī,
went to Mānasaprastha, where the meeting of those two had occurred.
When the Grandfather had departed for that place, Śarva, whose banner bears the bull, arrived accompanied by the hosts of gods and by Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and others.
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva,

the Lord of the World who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, having been meditated upon by Brahmā with devotion, arrived there in person at the very place where Brahmā and Hara were stationed.
Then those lords of the world— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
dispatched Nārada as a messenger to Medhātithi.
Go quickly, O Nārada, to the mountain named Candrabhāga;
the supreme sage Medhātithi dwells in its valley.
Bring him at the proper time according to our word;
taking Medhātithi with you, may you come quickly yourself. 93.
Having heard the words of Brahmā and the others, Nārada also went quickly to bring Medhātithi for the accomplishment of this great task.
Then, having addressed Medhātithi with the words of the gods,
he took Medhātithi and went to Mount Mānasa.
All the hosts of gods led by Indra, the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
the Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas have assembled.
All the gods and goddesses, as well as those who are attendants of the gods,
and all other living beings, went to Mānasaprastha.
Then, when the assembly of the gods had gathered, the lotus-seated Brahmā spoke these words to the sage Medhātithi, granting him authority: || 98 ||
Brahmā said:
"O Medhātithi, give your daughter, who has observed her vows, to the Brahmin Vasiṣṭha according to the prescribed rite in the assembly of the gods."
Indeed, their status as bride and groom was created by me alone in the beginning;
and this act has also been authorized by Hari, for it is entirely proper. (100)
When this is done, there will be great glory for your lineage;
it will be for the benefit of all beings. Give yourself to me, and do not delay.
Then, having heard the words of Brahmā, the sage was exceedingly delighted;
bowing to those foremost of gods, he said, "So be it."
But at these words, the sage Arundhatī took his daughter and went together with the gods to Vasiṣṭha, who was absorbed in meditation.
Having gone into the presence of Vasiṣṭha, the sage was surrounded by the gods;
blazing with the splendor of Brahman, he was like a flaming fire.
With his intellect fixed separately upon dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
he beheld the sage seated in a cave of Mount Mānasa.
Then the sage Medhātithi, the father of Arundhatī, having placed his daughter at the forefront, addressed Vasiṣṭha— the best among the powerful, like the newly risen sun—
whose self was fully disciplined.
The sage said:
"O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, please accept this daughter of mine, who has observed her vows, as a gift given by me according to the Brāhma rite and in accordance with dharma."
O Brahmin, in whichever stage of life you choose to dwell,
she shall follow you out of devotion to you, like a shadow that never departs.
In each and every place, my daughter—of noble form, devoted to her husband, and a practitioner of vows identical to yours—will perform service for you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of the sage Medhātithi, Vasiṣṭha beheld the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, who had assembled there.
Having ascertained with his divine eye that this was bound to happen,
Vasiṣṭha, having said "So be it," then accepted the daughter of the sage Medhātithi with the approval of Brahmā.
Having taken his hand, that queen, being virtuous, cast her two eyes upon the pair of feet of her husband by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and other gods likewise delighted them both with festivals according to the marriage rites. || 113 ||
The goddesses headed by Sāvitrī, as well as the gods such as Indra, and the sages of immense ascetic wealth beginning with Dakṣa and Kaśyapa. (114)
Having untied the bark garments, the deerskin, and the matted locks at the word of Brahmā,
he quickly bathed the son of the Creator with the waters of the Mandākinī.
They adorned Vasiṣṭha with divine ornaments of Jāmbūnada gold that were captivating to the mind, and likewise they adorned the virtuous Arundhatī.
Then, having adorned them there and completed the rites according to the rules prescribed by the sages, Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, and Śiva performed the ceremonial bath for their marriage.
Having placed the water of all sacred fords into a vessel of Jāmbūnada gold,
[he should consecrate it] with mantras that bestow blessings, such as the Gāyatrī and the Drupadā verse.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara bathed them themselves,
as did the other great sages and the celestial rishis.
All of them repeatedly performed the rite of pacification for those two with the great sounds of portions from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with the waters of rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
Brahmā [gave him] a celestial chariot that traverses the three worlds, possesses the brilliance of the sun,
and moves without obstruction, as well as a water-filled ascetic’s pitcher.
To those two, Viṣṇu granted a boon: an unsurpassed and most excellent station, which is above all the gods and in the vicinity of Marīci and the other [sages]. || 122 ||
Rudra granted them the boon of a lifespan lasting until the end of seven kalpas;
then Aditi, having removed from her own ears a pair of earrings fashioned by Brahmā, gave them to her daughter of Medhātithi.
Devendra, together with the Lord of Wealth, bestowed upon Sāvitrī the state of being devoted to her husband, abundant progeny, and many jewels.
Thus the gods, the sages, the goddesses, and others who were present there,
each gave their respective gifts to the two of them individually.
Having thus married her according to the prescribed rites on the golden Mānasa mountain,
Vasiṣṭha rejoiced together with Arundhatī.

There, that divine [water] which had been brought by the gods for the sake of the purificatory bath at the conclusion of the wedding and for the sake of propitiation fell into the cave of Mount Mānasa. || 127 ||
That water, raised up by the hands of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva,
became sevenfold as it fell from the Mānasa mountain.
In the caves, on the peaks, and in the lakes of the Himalaya mountain,
that water fell separately into the Śiprā and into the lake enjoyed by the gods.
By him, Viṣṇu, the Śiprā river was brought forth upon the earth;
indeed, its water fell into the great Kauśī precipice.
She was born as the one named Kauśikī, brought down by Viśvāmitra;
because the water fell upon the field of Umā, she became a great river.
That [river] born from the Kāvera lake became known by the name Kāverī;
its waters fell from the mountain into the Mahākāla, the most excellent of lakes.
On the southern flank of the Himalaya mountain, in the presence of Śambhu,
a river named Gomatī was produced by them, which is celebrated as Gomad.
He who was the son of the king of mountains, named Maināka, equal to him— on that very peak he was born in former times, bestowed by Menakā.
The water that fell there became a great river called Devikā,
which, impelled by Mahādeva, flows toward the ocean.
Because this water gathered in the ravine in the vicinity of Haṃsāvatāra,
it became known by the name Sarayū, remembered as the most meritorious river.
Those waters which were in the vicinity of the great Khaṇḍava forest, in the southern cave of the Himavat, from the midst of the lake of Irā; || 137 ||
The river named Irāvatī was born from them, and she is the best of rivers;
all these [rivers] are equal to the Ganges through bathing, drinking, and service.
The rivers flowing toward the southern ocean always bestow fruits upon mortals;
they are eternal and serve as the seeds for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (139)
These seven great rivers always bestow divine enjoyments;
thus these seven rivers were born, their waters ever most meritorious.
At the marriage of Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha, in the presence of the gods.
Having thus married Arundhatī, Vasiṣṭha then departed by means of a celestial chariot to that abode bestowed upon him by the gods.
At the word of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, that best of sages [acted].
For the welfare of the entire world at all times throughout the three realms, [he assumes] whatever form women take in whichever particular age. 144.
Assuming various appearances, dispositions, and bodies, he wanders through the three worlds with a clear mind and vigilance, engaging beings in the practice of Dharma.
In this way, in former times, Arundhatī was wedded by Vasiṣṭha at the request of the gods for the sake of the welfare of the worlds. (146)
Whoever should constantly hear this narrative, which is a means for accomplishing dharma and is endowed with all that is auspicious, shall possess a long life and wealth. (147)
Any woman who constantly hears this story of Arundhatī shall become devoted to her husband in this world and attain heaven in the next. (148)
This supreme narrative is the highest blessing and the bestower of the highest dharma;
it always increases fame, renown, and merit. (149)

Whoever causes this to be heard during a marriage, a man’s journey, a funeral rite (śrāddha), or likewise at the Puṃsavana ceremony, there arises stability, the birth of a male child, success, and the gratification of the ancestors. || 150 ||
Thus has everything been told to you concerning the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and how Arundhatī was his devoted wife. 151.
Or he whose sons were born, how they were born, and where;
and how he was chosen as husband by the word of Brahmā, Hari, and Īśāna. || 152 ||
All this has been narrated to you—the supreme secret, more secret than the secret, which bestows merit, removes sin, and increases longevity and health. (153)

Whoever causes this history, which brings about the welfare of the vast multitude of the virtuous, to be heard even once here in the assembly of the twice-born, shall, at the end of his life, be freed from the weight of sins, assume a purified body, and become an immortal god, united with the companionship of the best of sages. 154.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Marriage of Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, on a plateau of the Himavat mountain, on the bank of the lake Śipra...
Seated there, Mahādeva beheld that lake nearby.
Being sent again and again by Brahmā and Hari, he,
being firm of soul, steadied his mind there in order to perform meditation.
By means of his vehicle, the Teacher of Mindfulness made a supreme effort specifically within himself to see the self by means of the self. (3)
Seeing him with his mind entered into meditation, and perceiving that the one called Māyā had entered Hari, Brahmā and the other gods praised him with concentrated minds.
Deluded by Māyā and deeply overwhelmed by grief for Satī, Bharga lamented as if to her, in order to delude the Mother of the World. || 5 ||
Having praised [her] and drawn her forth from the body of Śambhu,
we shall make this untroubled one the stainless mind of Śambhu, absorbed in meditation.
Until Satī takes up a body again as the consort of Hara,
for that long let him meditate on the partless [Brahman], free from sorrow.
Having thus reflected in their minds, Brahmā and the other inhabitants of the triple heaven began to offer this hymn of praise to Mahāmāyā, the Yoga-nidrā.
The gods said: With great devotion, we praise that Śrī-Śakti, the purifier, nourishment itself, the supreme and partless, who possesses a great and unmanifest form.
Auspicious, the bringer of auspiciousness, pure, gross, subtle, both supreme and inferior,
known as both knowledge and ignorance, she is the joy of single-minded yoga.
You are intelligence, you are fortitude, you are modesty; you alone are present in all spheres of experience.
You are the radiance residing in the sun, illuminating the manifold world.
You who are the structure of the cosmic egg, you who are the world within the seeds of the universe, and you who nourish all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— you are the river Apagā.
He who is the single life-breath of all worlds, the ever-moving wind, and the support of the gods—he, the Lord of the Wind, is a portion of you. (13)
Thus, that radiance which spreads forth is kindled everywhere;
it is that form, the seed of the universe, which is seen in manifold ways.
You are she who always pervades the space between the world of Brahmā and the netherworld (Pātāla), as well as the interior and exterior of the entire cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa). 15.
You are that Mādhavī, the Earth, the Mother of the World and Sustainer of the Universe, who, constrained by the wheel of the immovable and the movable, is the source of phenomenal manifestation. 16.
You are the intellect, you are its object; you are the Mother, the course of the Vedic meters.
You are Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas; you are Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.

You are the mother of all the worlds; you are the triple Veda, capable of assuming any form at will. Indeed, in the form of sleep, you delight and utterly delude all living beings, from the gods to mortals, including those who dwell in the celestial realms and elsewhere.
You are the fortune of those who perform meritorious deeds, and indeed you are the torment of sinners;
likewise, you are the prosperity of those who uphold justice, the bestower of happiness, and steadfastness.
You are the peace of all the worlds; you are the splendor residing in the moon;
you are the sustainer of all beings; you are Lakṣmī, the enchantress of Viṣṇu.
You are the essence of the five elements, the one who creates their core;
you are the three worlds, the Great Illusion, and the policy that causes delusion.
O Maheśvarī, you are that Māyā by which Maheśvara, having placed every living being upon the wheels of saṃsāra, continues to cause them to revolve.
You are Jayantī among those endowed with victory; you are Modesty, Knowledge, and the highest Policy;
you are the Song of the Sāmaveda, the Knot of the Yajus formulas, and the Oblation.

May she who is the power of the entire host of gods, who consists of darkness yet is perceivable solely through the quality of goodness (*sattva*), who brings about the experience of the manifold world of passion (*rajas*), and who bestows auspiciousness—may she be praised here. (24)
On the mountain, she indeed prostrated before her who is a boat that carries one across the suffering of the terrifying waves of the ocean of saṃsāra, who is free from weariness,
and who causes the diversion of playful songs in the form of the eightfold path that purifies others.
Holding fast to the nose, eyes, mouth, arms, chest, and mind, she always bestows happiness upon living beings;
may that blessed Sleep, who exists for all those born in the world and whose nature consists of fortitude, memory, and mental activity, be gracious to us. (26)

May that Māyā be gracious to us—she who consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; she who effects creation, maintenance, and dissolution; she who is the power of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (27)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then this Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), praised as the Yoga-sleep (Yoganidrā),
quickly and instantly issued forth from the heart of Hara.
When she had emerged, Madhusūdana himself,
assuming his universal form, entered the interior of Śambhu for the sake of pacifying him.
Having entered his heart, the Imperishable One displayed, in every kalpa as it occurred, the creation, the maintenance, and likewise the dissolution.
He showed him everything: how Satī became his wife, who was his daughter, and how she had cast off her body.
Having displayed the external world— which is manifest yet devoid of essence, a vast proliferation consisting largely of passion— he then caused the consciousness to enter the supreme light.
Then Hara, too, having repeatedly observed all those manifestations and considering them to be devoid of essence, fixed his mind upon the essential reality.
Then Māyā, being praised by those gods headed by Brahmā,
promised to perform what was to be done and quickly vanished on the spot.
The Blessed Lord Vaikuṇṭha, having restrained Śambhu’s mind at every step,
emerged from his body like a king emerging from the orb of the sun.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, having accomplished their purpose,
departed for their respective abodes, filled with joy after leaving Hara on the mountain.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, who was absorbed in meditation, Indra and the other gods addressed the silent Lord and departed for their respective abodes.
When those gods had departed, Kapardin, whose vehicle is the bull,
meditated upon the supreme light for a thousand divine years.
The sages said:
How did Madhuripu, having entered the heart of Śambhu, immediately manifest his maintenance, creation, and dissolution in every kalpa? (36)
Just as they had gone to the earth with passion for the sake of the world's manifold expansion, how was their worthlessness demonstrated by the Enemy of Kaiṭabha? (40)
"What indeed is that most essential secret, the supreme, eternal light, which was shown by him? Tell me that truth, O best of the twice-born. (41)
"We wish to hear this most excellent marvel from you, O Lord of Munis;
explain in detail this supreme Dharma that leads to the highest liberation. (42)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the primordial creation and the Vārāha [kalpa],
how the creation occurs in every kalpa, and what it is like in the Vārāha [kalpa].
Having shown the primary creation as well as the secondary creation, Hari displayed the manifestation of Śambhu; now learn of the dissolution and the other stages.
O Brahmins, I shall first describe the dissolution (pralaya), and after that the primary creation (sarga); thereafter, understand the secondary creation (pratisarga) and the Vārāha [Kalpa].
A unit of time called a *nimeṣa* is defined by the opening of an eye;
eighteen of those constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* make a *kalā*. (46)
A unit called a *kṣaṇa* is proclaimed to consist of that many *kalās*;
twelve *kṣaṇas* are said to constitute a *muhūrta*, and thirty of those [make a day].
Fifteen human days and nights constitute one of their fortnights;
two such fortnights make a human month, which is a single day and night for the ancestors.
Twelve months constitute a year for the gods, which is their day and night;
however, for the ancestors, the dark fortnight is considered their day for the purpose of ritual action.
The bright fortnight is proclaimed as the day for dreams, while the night is likewise declared;
for the gods, however, the six months of the northern course of the sun are said to be their day.
Night is for the sleep of the gods, and six months constitute their southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
A season (ṛtu) is said to consist of two months each of the solar year.
A human year is said to consist of three seasons (ayana);
a year consists of six seasons. Listen now to those [seasons] individually. (52)
O best of the twice-born, due to the distinction of their names, the months beginning with Caitra form pairs:
Caitra and Vaiśākha are Spring (vasanta), while Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha (Śuci) are likewise Summer (grīṣma).
The rainy season consists of Prauṣṭhapada and Nabhasya; autumn consists of Āśvina and Kārttika; Hemanta consists of Sahas and Pauṣa; and Śiśira consists of Māgha and Phālguna. (54)
These six seasons are declared to be separately ordained at the beginning of the sacrifice; by human reckoning, the duration of the Kṛta Yuga is one hundred and twenty-eight thousand years.
In this [era], the transitional period (sandhyā) consists of four hundred years;
the transitional sub-period (sandhyāṃśa) is said to be of equal duration, and it is desired that [the calculation] be included within that. || 56 ||
The Tretā age consists of twelve hundred thousand human years,
and its dawn and twilight together comprise three hundred and ninety-six thousand years.
The period of twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is proclaimed to be three hundred [years], and its end is likewise defined; as for their measure, there are eight lakṣas and sixty-four thousand [years].

Among them, the age known as Dvāpara would have two hundred [years] for its twilight (sandhyā), and two hundred [years] are desired for the portion of the twilight (sandhyāṃśa) contained within it. (59)
Indeed, there are four hundred and thirty-two thousand [years] of the Kali age.
The measure [of a day] is said to be one hundred years;
the *saṃdhyā* lasts for one hundred years, and the *saṃdhyāṃśa* within that interval is likewise one hundred years.
In this manner, according to human measurement, the four ages— Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and likewise Kali— come to be.
The measurement for the four ages consists of forty-three lakhs [of years], together with twenty thousand years for the dawn and the twilight periods. (63)
A single day of the gods, together with its night, is equal to a year of humans.
Calculating in this sequence by means of human cycles of four yugas,
twelve thousand divine years are proclaimed [to constitute a kalpa].
Twelve thousand divine years constitute a divine yuga;
that indeed is the four-yuga cycle of men, together with its junctions (saṃdhyās) and the portions of the junctions (saṃdhyāṃśas).
But for the sake of the gods, there is no application of the system of ages such as Tretā and Dvāpara, nor is there any distinction of dharma and so forth.
However, four human yugas shall always constitute one divine yuga;
seventy-one divine yugas make up a manvantara.
Two thousand divine yugas constitute a day and a night of Brahmā;
according to human reckoning, that would be two thousand sets of four yugas.
In one day of Brahmā, there would be fourteen Manus. Thus, by the measurement of a Brāhmaṇa, three hundred and sixty such days constitute a year of Brahmā, just as a year is for human beings.
Five hundred years of Brahmā are proclaimed to be a *parārdha*;
that constitutes one day for its Lord, and his night is celebrated as being of equal duration.
A hundred years of Brahmā constitutes the time of two *parārdhas*.
When two *parārdhas* have passed, the dissolution (*pralaya*) of Brahmā occurs.
When Brahman has dissolved into the Supreme, there occurs the primordial dissolution (prākṛta-laya) of the worlds;
that which is the support of the entire universe, imperishable, and higher than the highest.
Of that day-and-night belonging to him whose nature is Brahman, that which constitutes the latter half is called "Parā," and half of that is designated as "Parārdha."
The Lord, the Supreme Self, is the very nature of the universe—indestructible and immutable.
He is considered to be more gross than the grossest and subtler than the subtlest.
For Him, there is no distinction between day and night, nor is there a year. (74)
However, that day and night are postulated by the ancient seers, as well as by us who are like them, for the purpose of understanding creation and dissolution. (75)
He alone is night, he is day; he is the year and indeed the earth; he is the creator of the universe and Hara.
He is the ancient Puruṣa in the form of Viṣṇu; in him everything shines forth, and likewise, he shines within it all.
Then, when Brahmā has dissolved into the eternal Supreme Self,
the entire world gradually returns to that very same nature.
At the end of a hundred years of Brahmā, Janārdana, assuming the form of Rudra,
brings about the end of the world himself and indeed enters into the Supreme.
First, Savitṛ, having dried up all water with his fierce rays, will take away everything, both the stationary and the moving. (79)
Dry trees, heaps of grass, living beings, and likewise mountains,
would be ground to powder and shattered even in a hundred divine years.
Then the rays of the twelve suns became exceedingly powerful;
they became the twelve Ādityas, augmented by the objects of enjoyment for the world.
Through the gateway of their rays, all those suns, along with the worlds, scorched the earth and the sky; even the ground became heated.
Then, when all things, both stationary and moving, had perished, the god Janārdana, in the form of Rudra, [appeared] within the heat of the sun's rays.
Having emerged, he first went to the depths of Pātāla, rising up high.
The wielder of the excellent trident slew the Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas residing in the seven netherworlds, as well as the gods, the Ṛṣis, and Śeṣa.
Thus, that Janārdana slew all those living beings who were in heaven, in the netherworld, on earth, and in the oceans.
Then Rudra himself created a great wind from his mouth;
with its unimpeded course, it spread forcefully throughout the three worlds.
For as long as a hundred years, the wind, circulating within the interior of the world,
swept away everything whatsoever, just like a heap of cotton wool.
Having completely dispelled all that which exists throughout the world on every side,
that wind, possessing exceeding speed, entered the twelve suns.
Having entered their mandala along with their splendors, the Wind-god,
impelled by Rudra, began to raise great clouds.
Then those clouds, impelled by that swift wind and by the exceedingly fierce Rudra, completely enveloped the sky.
The great clouds known as Saṃvarta resemble heaps of crushed collyrium;
some are smoky, some are crimson-colored, some are white, and others are variegated and terrifying.
Some were shaped like mountains, some possessed a radiance equal to that of serpents (nāgas),
some resembled palaces, and others were terrifying with the color of cranes (krauñca).
Roaring, those great clouds, possessing a mighty sound, rained for more than a hundred years,
flooding the three worlds.
Then, by the falling of streams as thick as pillars,
the three worlds were indeed firmly filled with a great downpour of rain.
Then, having reached a state of instability while situated in the mass of waters,
Janārdana, assuming the form of Rudra, emitted wind from his mouth.
Then, cast by that gale-force wind, the clouds were swiftly shattered after a hundred years by its unimpeded motion.
When those clouds had perished,
the pitiless Rudra once again destroyed everything from Janaloka up to the realm of Brahmā.
When all the worlds had been utterly destroyed,
and especially when the realm of Brahmā had perished, Rudra went to the twelve Aruṇas.
Having gone there with great speed, Hari swallowed the twelve suns; with those suns remaining within his belly, he blazed intensely.
Then Rudra, who was like the Destroyer at the end of time, having reached the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
the exceedingly powerful one crushed it entirely with his fist.
"Let them pulverize the cosmic egg and even grind the earth to dust;
let all the waters be destroyed—Hari sustained them all through his yogic power. (102)
Whatever water was previously situated all around outside the cosmic egg, and whatever water was contained within it—all that has attained a state of oneness. (103)
When the waters had become one, pervading everywhere on all sides,
that mass filling the fragments of the cosmic egg floated like a ship.
Then, in due order, he took up the entire subtle element of smell, which is the essence of the earth;
thereupon, the earth perished.
Furthermore, that formidable Rudra again drew forth the splendors situated within his own body, which had once more become a mass.
They seized all those splendors situated everywhere—both within and without the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), as well as whatever light had gone elsewhere. || 107 ||
Having gathered all the splendor existing in the world into one place and blazing forth,
he then consumed the fragments of the fierce cosmic egg within the waters.
Having burnt the fragments of the cosmic egg and the blazing splendors,
he then extracted from the waters the essence, the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*).
Once their essence had been taken, those waters were then destroyed by that splendor.
When the waters had perished, that illustrious Wind entered their radiance;
becoming one with it, he assumed its subtle form.
Once the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) was seized, all fires were then destroyed; consequently, the wind became powerful and unobstructed.
Then, like a fire blazing upon encountering a wind of great roar,
Rudra himself agitated that very sky.
By that [wind], the agitated ether was then seized by the Maruts;
the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*) residing therein vanished, and consequently, the wind was destroyed.
When the wind had perished, Rudra then extracted the essence from space;
once that subtle element of sound was grasped, the ether vanished.
When the sky had vanished, that Rudra then entered the body of Brahmā;
he entered that agitated body of Brahmā— which was now supportless and tranquil—
into the body of Viṣṇu, which bore the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Then Śauri, of great splendor, quickly withdrew that body composed of the five elements by his own power, extracting from it everywhere its essential core— the infallible [Viṣṇu] bearing the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and excellent sword.
Supportless, formless, devoid of being, and unrestrained;
consisting of bliss, non-dual, and free from the distinctions of duality. || 117 ||
Neither gross nor subtle, that knowledge which is eternal and stainless—the one Supreme Brahman—existed as self-luminous on all sides. (118)
There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth; there was no darkness, nor light, nor anything else.
Only the one primordial Brahman existed then—the Puruṣa, who is perceivable through the intellect and the senses such as hearing. 119.
Thus, for as long as the creation remains, for that duration it is uncreated;
there was one supreme reality, and from that, creation proceeds. (120)

Since the entire collection of subtle elements (tanmātra) is established within primordial nature (prakṛti), that which has reached the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) is dissolution into primordial nature (prākṛta-laya). || 121 ||
When the manifest has subsided into primordial nature (prakṛti) and that dissolution has passed, this is therefore called the "primal" (prākṛta) re-absorption (pratisañcara). || 122 ||
O Brahmins, this great abode known as Prākṛta has been described to you;
now listen again to this account of the primordial creation as it is told by me.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dissolution," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 24 ||
Chapter Twenty-five.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Time (Kāla) is indeed the god himself, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
That dissolution is uninterrupted by any particular portion.
When the period of dissolution had passed, the desire to create arose within the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, whose nature is knowledge.
Then his primordial nature (prakṛti), thoroughly agitated by that intellect, became disturbed for the sake of all effects; she consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Just as a fragrance causes agitation by its mere presence, so too does this Supreme Lord [cause agitation] because the mind possesses the power of creating the world. || 4 ||
O Brahman, that very Supreme Lord is both the agitator and the object of agitation;
through contraction and expansion, He remains established even in the state of primordial nature (pradhāna).
By mere will, the Supreme Lord, the Master of the Universe, [prepared] for the purpose of creation; then he once again agitated [the source].
Then, from that state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
there arose at the time of creation the manifestation of the qualities.
Emerging from the principle of Pradhāna, impelled by the will of Īśvara, the Mahat-tattva first arose; it then enveloped that Pradhāna. (8)
From that [Prakṛti], being enveloped by Pradhāna, Ahaṃkāra was born;
it is threefold: Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi, which is Tāmasa.
This threefold ego, which arises prior to the Great Principle (mahat),
is indeed the eternal cause of both the elements and the sense organs.
That Great One (Mahat) enveloped that Ahaṃkāra as soon as it was born;
from him, thus enveloped, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) were subsequently produced.
First is the subtle element of sound, followed by the subtle element of touch;
the third is the subtle element of form, and likewise the subtle element of taste.
The fifth was the subtle element of smell; these [five] arose in succession.
Each of the subtle elements was individually enveloped by the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra). 13.
From the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he created space characterized by sound;
that Bhūtādi then enveloped space, which consists of sound alone.
From that subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra), accompanied by the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), wind was produced, possessing the quality of touch and endowed with sound. || 15 ||
Then, from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) conjoined with ether and air, radiant fire came into being; it increased on all sides. || 16 ||
It was born endowed with sound, touch, and form; then,
from that which was joined with ether, air, and fire, it indeed emitted water,
which was thoroughly pervaded on all sides by the subtle element of taste.
Then that power which is the support of the waters of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable, indeed held those waters which were themselves without support and shaken by the wind.
Into them the Supreme Lord first cast the seed;
from that there arose a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun.

The egg is composed of [the principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas; it is surrounded on all sides by water, fire, air, and ether; and externally, the egg is encased by the Tamasas, the Bhūtādi, and the Mahat, each ten times greater than the preceding.
Just as a seed is covered by external husks,
so too, O twice-born ones, is this incomparable cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) enveloped by water and the other elements.
Then, in the midst of that egg, Viṣṇu himself, having assumed a body in the form of Brahmā,
remained for one divine year and, by his own intelligence, took up the collection of seeds.
Having himself divided his own body into two through meditation, he remained thus for a mere moment;
at that very instant, the earth was created by him with all the groups of subtle elements, beginning with smell.
This entire earth has been made by all the groups of subtle elements (tanmātras) as the substratum for touch, sound, all qualities of form, smell, and taste. (24)
Born from that [seed], the mountain of gold (Meru) arose; from the fetal membranes (jarāyu), it became a mass of mountains.
From the stages beginning with the embryo (garbha), the seven oceans were formed; and by means of the two shoulders (skandha), it became the abode of the gods (Tridaśālaya).
With the two aggregates belonging to the other region, there are seven nāga-abodes;
they are known as Pātāla, the great blisses, wherein one is oneself, while beyond that is Maheśa.
From that mass of fire (tejas) there arose a world which became known as Maharloka;
from the womb of Marut, the world called Janaloka was born, and from meditation (dhyāna), the excellent Tapoloka came into being.
Above the upward movement of the cosmic egg, upon the fragment of the Brahmāṇḍa, resides Viṣṇu Acyuta—
that supreme state which the wise describe as accessible through knowledge and whose nature is perfectly established.
Having first assumed such a form for the sake of preservation, he himself became the very embodiment of Viṣṇu;
because his body manifested spontaneously, Viṣṇu obtained the renown of being "Svabhū" (Self-born).
Then Viṣṇu, becoming the stout Sacrificial Boar for the sake of uplifting the earth,
pierced through the middle of the sinking world and went with great speed below to support it.
Placing the earth upon the tip of his tusk, he rose up, transcending all the waters;
then, assuming an infinite form, he became endowed with seven hoods in order to support the earth.
Having extended his coils and placed the earth upon a single hood in their midst, Śeṣa, who was himself situated upon the waters, supported the world; thereafter, Yajñavarāha abandoned the earth.
All their hoods were spread out; one was in the east, another in the west, and the others in the south and north.
One [limb] went toward the northeast, another toward the southeast;
one remained in the middle of the earth, and his body indeed lay toward the southwest.
The northwest direction was empty there, and from that, the earth remained bowed down.
But when Ananta was unable to support that long body in the water,
Hari then assumed the form of a tortoise and bore Ananta’s vast body upon his back.
Having stepped upon the lower portion of the cosmic egg with his feet,
that Tortoise extended his neck toward the northwest and supported Ananta upon his back.
The great-bodied Ananta, having placed the earth upon the back of the tortoise with nine coils around his body, supported it with ease.
Then the earth, which rested upon the moving hoods of Ananta, was made firm and immovable by Varāha. || 38 ||
Having struck Mount Meru with a blow from his hoof upon the surface of the earth, he then dug into it; having pierced the earth, he subsequently entered its interior.
Due to the blow from the boar’s hoof, the great mountain entered sixteen thousand yojanas deep into the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
O best of the twice-born, by that blow, the summit of Meru became thirty-two thousand yojanas in extent.
Then the boar acted at the side of the Lord of Mountains, the boundary-mark,
so that this mountain, the upholder of the earth, would not move.
And he made each portion of the Himavat and other mountains, including the five [subsidiary peaks], separated from one another by a space of ground equal to their own height. || 43 ||
Then Brahmā, having paid homage to the Boar who had arisen from the earth,
caused the God of gods, Ardhanārīśvara, to emerge from his armpit.
As soon as he was born, he wept with a great sound;
Brahmā spoke to him as he was crying, "Why do you weep? (45)
Then Maheśvara replied to him, "Give me a name";
and because of his weeping, he said, "O noble-souled one, do not weep; my name is Rudra. (46)
Thus addressed, he then wept seven times;
thereafter, Brahmā again created seven other names.
Śarva, Bhava, Bhīma, and Mahādeva as the fourth;
Ugra-Īśāna as the fifth, and Paśupati as the supreme sixth.
Just as you have been divided by me, so let your own self be divided;
for you too, like me, are a Prajāpati for the sake of manifold creation.
Then Brahmā, having divided himself in two, became a male with one half;
with the other half he became a female, and into her the Lord created Virāj.
The Blessed Lord Brahmā said to him, "O Prajāpati, perform the act of creation.
Having performed austerities, he [Brahmā] then produced the Svāyambhuva Manu from the Virāṭ.
He too, having propitiated Brahmā through his ascetic penance,
was pleased by him in his mind and created Dakṣa for the purpose of creation.
Then, after Dakṣa had been created in ten ways and prostrated before him by Manu,
the Creator once again produced ten other mind-born sons.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada as well. (54)
Having said, "After producing these through your mind, you must create Manu Svāyambhuva once again," the Lord of the World vanished once more.
Then the Supreme Lord Varāha, having dug out the seven oceans with his snout, fashioned them into a circular rim around the earth.
Having created the seven oceans by revolving seven times,
and having demarcated the seven continents up to the edge of the earth, he then departed.
Having encircled the earth with the mountain called Lokāloka,
which rises two hundred thousand yojanas in height on all sides,
he established it as firmly as a wall at the edge of a house.
O Brahmins, this primary creation has been narrated by me to you;
I shall now speak of the secondary creation (pratisarga), which let the great sages listen to.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of Varāha," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-six.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
This creation is known as the Vārāha because it is presided over by Varāha;
the secondary creation (pratisarga) has been heard of by all, which was performed separately by Dakṣa and the others.
Rudra, Virāj, Manu, Dakṣa, and those beginning with Marīci were his mental sons;
whatever creation they performed individually is known as the secondary creation (pratisarga). || 2 ||
Virāṭ’s son created the lineage-bearing Manus by whom the world was expanded;
having created seven Manus, Manu produced progeny in great numbers. || 3 ||
Desirous of creating progeny, that Manu known as Svāyambhuva first created six other Manus, who were his sons. || 4 ||
Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and likewise the other, Vivasvat.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
vidyādharas, apsarases, siddhas, and many hosts of bhūtas.
Clouds along with lightning, trees, creepers, shrubs, grass, and so forth;
fish, animals, insects, as well as those born in water and those born on land.
All these [beings] were created by Manu Svāyambhuva together with his sons; that other [account] is proclaimed as the secondary creation (pratisarga).
The other six Manus, indeed, having themselves performed the work of creation at the beginning of each respective interval, attain mastery over all things mobile and immobile.
He created the sacrificial materials, the sacrifice itself, the sacrificial post, and the eastern hall,
as well as dharma and adharma and all the qualities, just as a boar creates [the earth].
Having procreated many sons— the most excellent of divine sages, many great seers who drink the soma juice, and likewise the hosts of ancestors— Dakṣa [departed].
He set the process of creation in motion; that is remembered as his secondary creation (pratisarga).
From his mouth the Brahmins were born, and from the pair of his arms the Kṣatriyas.
From his thighs [came] the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras; these four Vedas [issued] from the four-faced Brahmā.
This is the secondary creation (pratisarga) of Brahmā, and therefore it is known as the Brāhma-sarga.
Kaśyapa was born from Marīci, and from Kaśyapa the entire world arose;
the gods, the Daityas, and the Dānavas are proclaimed to be his creation. (14)
From the eye of Atri was born Candra, and from him the Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa) arose;
by him the entire world was pervaded, and that is proclaimed as his creation.
The sons and grandsons of Atharvan and Aṅgiras, as well as many others such as the Mantras and Yantras—all these indeed are remembered as belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras. (16)
The sons of Pulastya known as the Ājyapās, and other Rākṣasas endowed with strength and speed, constitute the secondary creation (pratisarga) of Pulastya.
The descendants of Kadrū were elephants and horses, as well as many other offspring;
this creation by Pulaha is thus proclaimed.
The sons of Kratu were the Bālakhilyas, all-knowing and of immense splendor;
eighty-eight thousand in number, they resembled blazing suns.
All those sons of Pracetas are indeed remembered as the Prācetasas;
they numbered eighty-six thousand and possessed a splendor equal to fire.
The sons of Vasiṣṭha, beginning with Sukāli, as well as other yogis, the fifty sons of Arundhatī—this is called the Vāsiṣṭha creation. (21)
And from Bhṛgu were born the Bhārgavas, who indeed served as the priests of the Daityas; those sages of great wisdom pervaded the entire world. || 22 ||
From Nārada, the stars were born, as well as celestial chariots;
likewise, there were other questions and answers, as well as dancing, singing, and wonders.
These [sages], Dakṣa, Marīci, and the others, having procreated many sons after procreating them,
filled both the earth and the heavens.
From their sons were born sons, and from those sons, further sons;
indeed, they have arisen and continue to exist in the worlds even today. (25)
The sun is known to have arisen from the eyes of Viṣṇu, and the moon from his mind; Vāyu was produced from his ears, and Agni was born from his mouth.
For this Viṣṇu is indeed the dissolution, as are the ten directions;
subsequently, for the sake of creation, the Moon descended from the eye of Atri.
And the Sun was born from Kaśyapa, accompanied by his wife. || 27 ||
And many Rudras were born, as well as the fourfold hosts of beings, having the forms of dogs, boars, and camels, and monkeys, jackals, and oxen-faced creatures. (28)
Some had the faces of bears and cats, others had the faces of lions and tigers;
all of them bore various weapons, possessed diverse forms, and were endowed with great strength. (29)
O best of the twice-born, this dissolution has also been told to you;
now hear of the daily dissolution occurring at the end of a kalpa.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of Creation," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The twenty-seventh chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
A Manvantara is the period of time during which a Manu protects his subjects.
One Manu is that period of time known as a Manvantara; so it is heard in the scriptures.
Seventy-one such yugas of the gods constitute one day of Brahmā;
fourteen of those [days] make up a single kalpa.
At the end of a day of Brahmā, a desire for sleep arises within him;
Mahāmāyā, the yogic sleep, approaches the Grandfather.
Then, having entered the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
the blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, rests there in comfort.
Then Janārdana himself, having assumed the form of Rudra,
destroyed all three worlds just as before.
Together with Vāyu and Vahni, he indeed caused it to burn,
just as at the times of the great dissolution, the entire threefold world is consumed.
Afflicted by the terrible fire at the time of the burning of the three worlds, the inhabitants of Maharloka depart, distressed by its heat.
Then, by means of clouds that were like the Destroyer at the end of time— multicolored and thundering with great sounds— they produced a massive rain, filling the three worlds.
Having placed these three worlds within his belly by means of masses of water with moving waves that reach even to the unstable regions, that Janārdana,
the Supreme Lord, reclines upon his serpent-couch.
Having established Brahmā within the navel-lotus of his reclining form, that Teacher of the World,
together with Śrī, burnt and consumed these three worlds.
That Brahmā, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, lies upon the couch of Śeṣa,
having come under the power of yogic sleep and being nourished by the swallowing of the three worlds.
When the entire three worlds had been consumed by the fire of time (kālāgni),
Ananta then left the earth and went into the presence of Viṣṇu.
Abandoned by him, the earth sank downward in a mere instant;
having fallen upon the back of the tortoise, it then became as if shattered. || 13 ||
Then the Tortoise, with great effort, supported the earth upon his back as it was moving in the water,
having pressed the cosmic egg with his feet.
"The earth would be pulverized by the collision of the fragments of the cosmic egg";
thus Janārdana, assuming the form of a tortoise, supported it. 15.
Then, due to contact with the surging mass of water, the earth shook,
and the back of the Tortoise was covered with exceedingly numerous ridges.
Ananta went there, to where the Ocean of Milk is located;
there he saw Janārdana, endowed with Śrī herself, lying down in sleep.
With his middle hood, he held that which was swollen by the swallowing of the three worlds;
having first spread his hoods upward and placed a lotus there, the one of great power named Śeṣa covered Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord. 18.
Ananta made his right hood a pillow for him;
the one of great strength made his left hood a pillow for the feet.
Then Śeṣa, assuming the form of a palm-leaf fan with his remaining hood,
fanned Janārdana as he slept.
The one of great strength likewise held the conch, the discus, the sword Nandaka, two quivers,
and Garuḍa with his hood extended toward the northeast.
The mace, the lotus, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise various other weapons— whatever else he possessed— he bore upon that southern hood.
Having thus made his own body a bed for Hari,
he then submerged the earth with the lower part of his body into the water.
[He saw] Janārdana, together with Brahmā and Lakṣmī,
the seed of the three worlds, the cause of the cause of the universe, accompanied by his quiver.
[He meditated upon] the Supreme Lord, who is eternal bliss, composed of the Veda, devoted to Brahman, the cause and agent of the world, and the cause of the cause of the world. || 25 ||
O Lord of the past, future, and present, you yourself bore upon your head that very form of yours, Hari, who is the supreme goal and the ultimate refuge.
In this manner, according to the very measure of a day of Brahmā, the immutable Nārāyaṇa, Hari, lies asleep, encompassing both the night and the two twilights.
Since this dissolution occurs day after day for Brahmā,
those who know the ancient lore call it the "daily" (dainandina) dissolution.
When the night had passed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
abandoned his sleep and arose once more, intent on the work of creation.
Beholding the three worlds filled with water, the Supreme Person lying there, and the Vaiṣṇavī Māyā— the Great Illusion consisting of the universe—
he praised Yoganidrā, who was established upon the body of Hari.
Brahmā said:
I bow to the power of consciousness, changeless, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman— the eternal Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the Yoga-sleep.
O Goddess, you are the knowledge of yogis; you are their goal, you are their intellect, and you are their praise.
You are creation, you are preservation, you are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, and here you are the sacred song.
You are the Sāma-veda chant, you are political ethics, you are modesty, you are prosperity, and you are Sarasvatī;
you are the yogic sleep, the great illusion, the sleep of delusion, and the Sovereign Goddess.
You are splendor, you are all-powerful; you are indeed the auspicious body of Viṣṇu.
You are the sustainer of all worlds, and you are the ignorance of embodied beings.
O Goddess, you are the foundational power; for you are indeed the sustainer of the cosmic egg.
You alone are the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all the worlds, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas). 35.
You are Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, both gentle and fierce, exceedingly beautiful;
you are the eternal creative impulse of Hari, and you are the state of dreaming and deep sleep.
You are nourishment, modesty, forgiveness, peace, fortitude, and the Supreme Goddess;
in the form of the earth, you alone sustain all that is moving and unmoving.
You are the waters, you are the mother of the waters, and you move within all things;
you alone are the praise, the object of praise, the praiser, and the power of praise itself. (38)
How indeed shall I praise you? Be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!
Salutations to you, O Mother of the World; awaken Janārdana. (39)
Thus praised by Brahmā, the creator of the world,
she who had emerged from the eyes, mouth, nose, arms, and heart of Hari,
assumed a passionate (rājasī) form and stood before the sight of Brahmā. (40)
Then Janārdana, having been abandoned by sleep for a moment from his serpent-couch,
arose and set his mind upon creation.
Then, in the form of a boar,
he quickly lifted up the earth that had sunk into the waters and placed it above the water.
Above that flood of water, she stands like a great ship;
and because her body is so vast, the earth does not undergo submersion.
Then Hari, having descended to the earth and withdrawn the ocean by his own power of illusion,
engaged himself spontaneously for the sake of the maintenance of living beings.
Ananta also, having gone to the surface of the earth as before, remained stationed upon the tortoise and supported the earth. (45)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, having brought forth all the Prajāpatis, caused the universe to be produced. || 46 ||
Whether Brahmā performs the creation or others do so,
it is by His will alone that Dakṣa and the other guardians of progeny act.
He, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman, constantly bestows grace;
and Prakṛti indeed bestows grace upon the five great elements.
And in the same way, the Great One (mahat) and the others are favored by the Person;
this occurs through the presiding influence of the Lord's will and from the eightfold collection [of qualities] within the Person.
Through the presiding influence of the Puruṣas, as well as that of the collection of great elements,
of Mahat and the others, and of the Great Time (Kāla), and through the presiding influence of Pradhāna, whatever is born comes into being. || 50 ||
Whether it be stationary or moving, stable or even extraordinary—O best of the twice-born, all this is born from that substratum. 51.
Thus everything has been told to you, exactly as the Blessed Lord Hari formerly showed those cycles of creation and dissolution to Hara.
Just as the utter worthlessness of the world's manifold expansion has been shown, so too listen from me, O twice-born ones, to that which has been shown to be the essence. (53)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Account of Creation," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 27 ||
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Indeed, the entire world is essence-less, impermanent, and a vessel of suffering."
