This arises from a moment, and from a moment this perishes. || 1 ||
In that very same way, the world swiftly arises from the essence as something devoid of essence;
then, at the onset of the great dissolution, they dissolve back into it.
Through the manifestation and dissolution [of the world], Hari,
the Lord of the worlds, revealed the worthlessness of the universe to Śambhu with his true intent.
There is but one Śiva—peaceful, infinite, infallible, higher than the highest, consisting of pure knowledge, and distinct;
non-dual, unmanifest, of inconceivable form, the sole essence. There is no other essence besides Him.
Since from this the entire universe arises as the foremost, and into this it is later dissolved and remains;
that essence of reality, like the sky, by which the universe is indeed sustained through its manifestation—like a mass of clouds—is the Truth.
The yogi who desires to attain that which is obtained through the eightfold limbs always purifies his own nature;
having reached that, he does not return to this world, for there is no other essence (sāra) like it.
The second essential dharma is that which leads to eternal attainment; therein, that which is called "cessation" is the essence, while that which is "active" is the non-essence.
One should gradually accumulate merit, just as an anthill builds up its mound from soil,
for the sake of companionship in the next world and for liberation from previous sins.
One dharma alone is the supreme good among all activities of worldly existence;
however, the other three—artha and the rest—arise from that dharma.
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head;
but the abandonment of dharma is censured in both the world and the Veda. (10)
By Dharma the world is sustained, by Dharma the universe is sustained;
it was through Dharma alone that all the gods attained the state of divinity in ancient times.
The Blessed One, Dharma consisting of four feet, protects the world incessantly;
he alone is the root, and that person is designated as Dharma. (12)
In this world, everything perishes, but Dharma never decays;
he who does not waver from Dharma is called the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 13 ||
This essence has been told to you: that the entire world is devoid of substance, just as Śambhu himself perceived it within his own inner self through his gnosis.
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, indeed revealed this;
Śaṅkara himself grasped it within his own self through meditation on the waters. 15.
The essence is the supreme reality, partless and devoid of form; this Dharma is that which possesses form.
Knowing that one is the essence and the other is devoid of essence, the person of great intelligence thus attains the eternal.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Essential and the Non-Essential," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 28 ||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
The sages said:
"Those four classes of living beings who were previously created by Śambhu..."
For what purpose have they arisen, or how do they possess manifold forms?
Some of the lords of the Gaṇas had bodies that were half-boar and half-toothed-tusked, while others had bodies like those of lions and tigers. || 2 ||
How were those cruel hosts, and what were the enjoyments of those of great power?
O best of the twice-born, we wish to hear all of this.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Let all you sages listen to how the attendants of Śambhu came to be,
for what purpose they were produced, and why they possess manifold forms."
This is the supreme secret for you, which bestows dharma, artha, and kāma;
for this is the highest splendor and the constant, supreme austerity.
Having heard this great narrative, one does not suffer in this world or the next;
it is conducive to fame, righteousness, and longevity, and it bestows supreme contentment and nourishment.
Then, O best of sages, when the primordial creation during the Varāha-manvantara was complete,
Śaṅkara spoke to the Lord of All, Varāha, the Master of the Worlds.
Īśvara said:
O Lord, that purpose for which you assumed the form of a boar has been fulfilled by you;
the earth has been established by you exactly as it should be.
Through your grace, the configuration of the oceans, as well as that of the rivers and the earth, and even the creation brought about by Brahmā, has come to pass.
For you indeed consist of all things, you are composed of sacrifice, and likewise composed of splendor;
you are the teacher of all teachers, and you are higher than the highest.
O Lord of the World, the earth is unable to bear you, as if it were shattered,
even though it was formerly restrained by the masses of mountains established by you.
Therefore, O Lord of the world, abandon this boar body—
you who are identical with the universe, whose form is the universe, and who are the cause of the cause of the universe.
O Lord, who else besides you would be capable of bearing this boar-form of yours?
Especially since the Earth was held by you within the waters with desire;
she, being subject to the laws of womanhood, conceived a terrible embryo through your vital energies.
O Lord of the World, since the earth, while in her menses, conceived this embryo, whatever son may be born from it will also incur ill repute. (14)
"Having attained this asuric state, he will become a harasser of gods and gandharvas," said the Lord of the World to me in the presence of Dakṣa.
O Lord of the World, abandon this lustful boar-like body, born of passion for a foul woman, which is wicked and brings about undesirable results. 16.
You alone are the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the world, the source of all beings; when the time arrives, you shall perform maintenance, creation, and withdrawal.
Therefore, O one of great strength, for the sake of the welfare of the world, having cast off this body when the time arrives,
you shall again take up another body as a boat.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Śaṅkara,
the Blessed Lord in his boar-form spoke to Mahādeva.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Maheśvara, I shall do as you have spoken;
I will undoubtedly cast off this body of Yajñavārāha."
"When the time arrives, I shall again assume another wonderful body as a boar, difficult to overcome, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds. (21)
Having spoken thus, that great-bodied one, the teacher of the world, the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the lord of the world, vanished right there.
When that god had vanished, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
departed for his own abode accompanied by the hosts of gods and his own attendants.
Vārāha himself also went to the mountain named Lokāloka and took his pleasure with Vārāhī and with Pṛthivī, who possessed a beautiful form.
Sporting with her for a very long time on that best of mountains,
the Lord of the World, who was intensely lustful like a boar, did not attain satisfaction.
O best of the twice-born, from that Earth, who was in the form of the Potṛ priest and was full of delight, three sons were born; hear their names from me. || 26 ||
Suvṛtta, Kanaka, and Ghora—all of them were indeed possessed of great strength. || 27 ||
Those children, on the golden slopes of Mount Meru,
took delight in the thickets and in the depths of the lakes, clinging closely to one another.
O twice-born ones, surrounded by those sons and sporting with his own wife, that boar did not at all consider the abandonment of his body at that time.
Once, embraced by those children in the midst of the mud,
the exceedingly powerful one engaged in playing in the mud together with his wife.
Smeared with mud, the boar, honey-tawny in hue, shone like an evening cloud dripping with water. || 31 ||
Delighted with his sons and with his wife Pṛthivī, he enjoyed himself upon the earth; then the earth became level in its center and free from depressions.
Even Ananta, having stepped upon the tortoise on the surface of the earth while bearing Hari,
became distressed with a broken head due to the intense pressure.
With its well-rounded golden rampart and its formidable golden [walls],
it was pierced by blows from the hooves [of horses], yet it remained level despite being broken by the gold.
O best of the twice-born, whatever golden structures were laboriously fashioned by the gods upon the summit of Mount Meru were all shattered by his sons.
Then those children made the lakes of the gods, such as Mānasa and others, turbid on all sides by the discharge of their urine. || 36 ||
The Earth, in the form of a woman, delighted the Boar;
yet, in her immobile form, she indeed experienced intense suffering.
And the oceans, though normally fathomable on all sides by Suvṛtta and the others,
were entirely thrown into turmoil as their herds of snouts scattered the strewn jewels.
And then, as children played here and there with elephants,
the worlds there— along with the rivers and the wish-fulfilling trees— were destroyed.
For even though he was the Lord of the universe, Varāha himself did not prevent them from causing suffering to the world, out of affection for his sons.
When Suvṛtta, Kanaka, and Ghora indeed approach heaven,
the hosts of gods become terrified and flee in the ten directions.
Thus, though he sported with his sons and wife as the sacrificer, he never attained any satisfaction;
his desire increased day by day, and being thus driven, he did not wish to abandon his body. (42)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Śrī Kālikā Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Vārāha and Śaṅkara. || 29 ||
The thirtieth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then all the hosts of gods, together with those born of divine origin, [assembled].
Together with Śakra, they deliberated thoroughly on what would be for the welfare of the world.
Then, having reached a decision, all of them— Śakra and the others, together with the sages—
sought refuge in the unborn, all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, the worthy protector.
Having approached Govinda Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World,
all the gods bowed down and praised him whose banner bears Garuḍa.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, the cause and creator of the universe;
O Blessed One, whose nature is Time, consisting of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa."
O Supreme Lord, O Puruṣottama, who pervades the gross and subtle worlds;
you are the creator of all beings, you are their protector, and you are their destroyer.
For you, indeed, by means of your illusory nature, delude the entire world—
whatever has been, whatever is yet to be, and whatever is currently unfolding.
O Supreme Lord, you are all that—both the stationary and the moving;
you are the wealth for those seeking wealth, and likewise the fulfillment of desire for those seeking desire.
For you are the Dharma for those seeking Dharma; you are liberation for those desiring Nirvana;
you are the seeker of desire, you are the seeker of wealth, you are the righteous one, and you are the eternal refuge.
From your mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born; from your arms the Kṣatriyas;
likewise the Vaiśyas from your thighs, and the Śūdras emerged from your two feet.
O Lord, the sun was born from your eye, and the moon, the mind-born one, from you;
the wind was born from your ear, as were the other ten vital breaths.
Above your head, the world of heaven and the other realms was born;
likewise, from your navel arose the ether, and the earth emerged from the soles of your feet.
From your two ears the directions were born, and from your belly the entire world;
for you, indeed, through your nature as Māyā, delude the universe.
For you are both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities; you are the pure, the one, higher than the highest.
You are without origin or sustenance, and you are superior to those whose qualities are imperishable.
O Lord of the World, you are meditated upon by the Ādityas, the Vasus, the gods, the Sādhyas, the Yakṣas, the hosts of Maruts, and by the sages seeking liberation.
The sages of specialized knowledge, possessing full experience, indeed know you to be composed of consciousness and bliss;
you alone are the seed, the water, the soil, and the fruit of the tree of worldly existence.
You shine like a lotus-pool with Padmā, bearing the excellent sword, discus, lotus, and bow;
you alone appear eternally upon Garuḍa, like a cloud accompanied by water upon the Golden Mountain.
You alone are the one clad in yellow robes (Viṣṇu), Śaṅkara, and the lotus-born (Brahmā); all this is you, and nothing else exists apart from you.
Your qualities cannot be fully comprehended by us, nor even by Brahmā, Hara, or the lords of the quarters.
Terrified, we have sought refuge in you with devotion; O Viṣṇu, protect us!
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus praised by the hosts of gods led by Indra, the God of gods, the source of the creator of all beings, spoke to them all with a voice like the rumbling of clouds.
The Blessed Lord said: "O gods, tell me quickly what purpose you have come for, or what danger has arisen, and whatever must be done by me in that regard."
The gods said:
"The earth is constantly being shattered by the sport of the one whose sacrificial priest is the bull;
all the worlds are agitated and find no peace. (20)
Just as a dry gourd fruit reaches a state of being shattered by blows,
so too has the earth been shattered by the strike of the boar’s snout.
His three sons—Suvṛtta, Kanaka, and Ghora—possessed a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction; by them, moreover, the entire world was devastated.
O Lord of the worlds, by their playful splashes in the mud, the lakes such as Mānasa and others were shattered; they no longer return to their natural state.
By those of great strength, the celestial trees such as the Mandāra and others were shattered;
O Lord, even today they do not sprout fruit, flowers, or leaves.
O mighty-armed one, when those three— Suvṛtta and the others— having ascended Trikūṭa and performed a leap, fall into the salt ocean,
then the entire earth is submerged by the surging masses of its agitated waters.
All people leap up and flee in the ten directions;
seeking to preserve their lives, they depart in the ten directions. || 26 ||
When the sons of Yajñavārāha went to the third heaven,
the gods, broken here and there, found no peace.
O Lord of the World, all those mountains were brought to a state of great subsidence at their peaks by those sons of Varāha as they sported there.
As they sport thus with their games, the entire universe is brought to destruction, O Vaikuṇṭha; therefore, protect the world, O Lord of the Universe! (29)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words as they were being spoken by them, Janārdana spoke to the god Śaṅkara and especially to Brahmā.
The Blessed Lord said: "On account of whom all the deities and all these creatures experience great suffering, and the entire world perishes. (31)
"O Śaṅkara, I wish to cast off this boar body;
yet it cannot be abandoned at will because it is bound by its own momentum.
Therefore, O Śaṅkara, cause me to relinquish that body now through your effort. (32)
"O Brahman, swell yourself repeatedly with splendors, remembering the Destroyer of Smara;
likewise, let the gods swell [with power], and may Śaṅkara slay the Boar. (33)
Because of his association with a menstruating woman and likewise because of his killing of Brahmins, he has become a perpetrator of physical sin; it is now proper to abandon him. (34)
Sin departs through expiatory rites; therefore, I shall perform penance.
For that purpose, let my body be stilled through effort. (35)
"The subjects are always to be protected by me, for they are constantly suffering on my account;
therefore, day after day, I shall abandon this task for the sake of the people. (36)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, Brahmā and Śaṅkara then said to Govinda, "That which has been spoken by you must be performed."
Vāsudeva, having likewise dismissed all those gods,
became himself intent on meditation in order to retrieve the Vārāha-splendor.
When Mādhava gradually withdrew that splendor,
the body of the Boar then became devoid of its vital essence.
When all the immortals perceived that his body was devoid of luster,
the Lord then assumed the wondrous form of Yajñavarāha.
Then all the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, followed Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, in order to bestow their splendor upon the chastiser of Smara.
Then all the hosts of gods deposited their respective splendors into the one who has the bull as his banner;
by that means, he became exceedingly powerful.
Then, at that very moment, Giriśa assumed the form of a Śarabha;
possessing eight legs extending both upwards and downwards, he was most terrifying.
The body of Vārāha is two hundred thousand yojanas in height and one hundred and fifty thousand yojanas in width;
its upper portion, however, is one hundred thousand yojanas in width.
Then, extending fifty thousand leagues on its side, it began to increase;
thereafter, [he beheld] that Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, in the form of a Śarabha.
The protector of the sacrifice saw him touching the moon with his head—he who had very long nostrils and claws, and whose body was as dark in luster as burning coals. (46)
He had a long face and a massive body, endowed with eight fangs; he bore a hairy tail and long ears, appearing truly terrifying.
He was placing four feet behind and likewise four below,
letting out a terrible cry as he leaped up again and again.
Then, seeing him approaching and rushing straight toward them with fury,
Suvṛtta, Kanaka, and Ghora, overcome by rage, confronted him.
Having approached that massive-bodied śarabha, the three brothers, endowed with great strength, simultaneously lifted it up with kicks intended to kill their grandson.
To whatever extent was the size of the Śarabha, to that same extent they became;
at the moment the Śarabha leaped up, three boars appeared through his illusory power.
Then, struck by their blow with the feet, Śarabha was flung up and fell upon the edge of the earth into the deep ocean of water.
When he had fallen there into that ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
those three leaped up and fell into that great sea in a fit of rage.
O best of the twice-born, when Suvṛtta had fallen into the terrible waters of the ocean,
Varāha, out of affection for his son and out of anger,
suddenly leaped up and plunged into that mass of water.
Then, leaping up, those boars and the Śarabhas indeed shattered the gods in heaven, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets.
Some gods were slain, and some fell to the ground;
yet other gods who possessed knowledge took refuge in Maharloka.
O best of the twice-born, the constellations fell from their celestial chariots onto the surface of the earth, appearing indeed as clusters wreathed in flames.
The extremely fierce momentum that arose from their leaping produced an exceedingly violent wind of extreme force. || 58 ||
Driven by that wind, the mountains on the surface of the earth were scattered;
some of those rocks fell once again upon other mountains. (59)
Having crushed trees and living beings, they fell down again and again; some, however, danced upon the surface of the earth after striking it with mountain peaks.
Even the mountains were shattered as they moved repeatedly across many regions; the mountains appeared upon the surface of the earth as if driven by the force of the wind.
Those other mountains, as if moving by colliding with one another,
were struck by those boars falling from the ocean and by the śarabha.
The masses of water were uplifted by the exceedingly lofty mountains;
when those masses of water were cast down with the force of their fall, [the earth shook]. (63)
In an instant, all the oceans became as if devoid of water; when all that water was cast down and reached the surface of the earth, [the world was flooded]. (64)
Then, all the subjects, having been overwhelmed, went to their destruction in an instant;
floating in the water, the subjects perished on every side.
"Alas, father! Alas, dear one! Alas, mother! Alas, son!
they lamented piteously, terrified, afflicted, and on the verge of death.
In whatever place the Śarabha fell together with the boars,
right there the earth sank down, torn apart by the force of his feet.
Another [wind], arising from the edge of the earth along with the mountains,
set the Janalokas in motion by means of its gusts.
Then Śarabha, filled with wonder, terrified, exhausted, and oppressed by pain, beheld the earth joined together in the Janalokas— appearing as if lifeless and bound by mountains like ships by ropes.
Then all those bulls fought with the striking of their dewlaps,
with blows from their hooves, with their tusks, and with violent tossings of their bodies.
Then Śarabha, with the tips of his tusks, sharp claws, and hooves,
as well as with blows from his tail and loud-sounding strikes from his snout— || 71 ||
By those four suckling calves, that single great śarabha was milked in solitude for a thousand years.
By their blows, by their impetuous rushes, by their circling movements and comings and goings,
by their slapping of arms, by their roars, and by their falling down one after another upon the ground,
all the serpents in Pātāla, together with the offspring of Kadru, were destroyed.
Then, having abandoned the ocean, they came to the middle of the earth;
as they fought with one another, the earth consequently became level.
The serpent Śeṣa also, having supported the earth with great effort by the strength of his eight hoods,
held it while his head was broken by the pain and scorched by its heat.
When Ananta had become dwarfed and the surface of the earth reached a state of levelness, as did all living beings, along with the moving waters and the mountains. (76)
When the three-fold descendants of Tri and Śara-bha had perished while fighting,
and the entire world was submerged by oceans consisting of water, [they sought refuge in] Hari.
Then the Grandfather, the eldest of the gods, overcome with anxiety, said:
"O Blessed One, the entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans—" (78)
The earth was shattered and destroyed; all things mobile and immobile perished.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, daityas, and even the reptiles were devastated, O Lord of the worlds, as were the sages whose wealth is their asceticism. (79)
You are the protector of all; you alone are the Lord of the universe.
Therefore, O Lord of the world, protect us all and the earth. (80)
You yourself must withdraw this boar-body;
O mighty-armed one, establish the earth once more with all things mobile and immobile.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Janārdana,
the infallible one, then made every effort to re-establish everything.

Then Hari, assuming the forms of a golden deer and a fish, protected the seven sages along with their wives—who were experts in all the Vedas—while he himself was intent on guarding the Vedas for the welfare of the world. (83)
Then [he approached] Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Kaśyapa, Viśvāmitra, and the sage Gautama;
the eminent Jamadagni, who was established in great austerity, as well as the sage Bharadvāja, a treasure-house of penance.
Having placed [the chariot] upon his back, he indeed stood in the midst of the waters within that most excellent great ship;
then, accompanied by Nārada, he went to comfort Śiva at the place where he had fought with the elephant-riders.
Seeing Hara approaching— exhausted by the excessive trampling of the boar's descendants, tormented, with mouth agape and gasping— the boar then recollected his former form as Narasiṃha.
Then, being remembered by him, his friend Nṛsiṃha arrived for the welfare of Varāha;
he took the splendor from his body for himself.
When the boar perceived that the splendor equal to the sun which had entered Viṣṇu was now gone from Nṛsiṃha,
he recognized him as being devoid of power and released a torrent of breaths.
Then many boars were born, of great size and with wondrously sharp tusks;
those illusory boars, free from fear, assailed Śarabha Giriśa.
Even then, they fought with Nṛsiṃha and severely crushed Giriśa;
for a moment they took on forms like great birds, and in another moment they became cows, horses, and men.
In an instant they were lions and in an instant boars; those jackals assumed various distorted forms.
In the battle, they displayed many terrifying shapes by means of their boar-forms.
Beholding Bharga thus oppressed by them, Mādhava then approached that Lord of the Mountain;
Viṣṇu touched Giriśa with his hand and deposited his own splendor there once again.
Then, as soon as he was touched by the Lord Viṣṇu,
he became exceedingly joyful, delighted, and powerful.
Then Śarabha let out a loud, powerful, and firm roar,
by which these fourteen worlds were filled.
From the mouth of him as he roared, droplets issued forth;
from them, the Gaṇas were born, possessing massive bodies and great prowess.
Just as the Gaṇas assume various forms from the breath of Varāha,
these boars are like that, yet they are even more powerful than those.
They had the forms of dogs, boars, and camels; they were monkeys, jackals, and those with the faces of oxen; they possessed the appearances of bears, cats, elephants, and porpoises.
Some had the faces of lions and tigers, some had the forms of snakes and mice; others had the necks of horses, the faces of horses, or the shapes of buffaloes.
Others, however, have the form of humans, yet with the faces of deer or sheep; some are headless trunks, others lack feet, while some are handless or possess many hands.
Some have the form of śarabhas, while others have the faces of lizards; some have the faces of fish and the faces of crocodiles; they are short, tall, weak, or emaciated.
Some had four feet, some eight, others three, or two; some had only one foot, while others had many hands, resembling yakṣas and kimpuruṣas. (101)
They have the forms of animals and possess wings; they have pendulous bellies and large bellies, long bellies, thick hair, many ears, and deformed ears. || 102 ||
O Brahmins, there are other living beings throughout the worlds who have thick lower lips, long teeth, and long beards.
Among those fourteen, they attained equality with them in form;
there is no creature here in this world, whether stationary or moving, that is not so. (104)
Since the host was not equal in form to Śaṅkara,
they [assailed him] with bhindipālas, swords, iron clubs, and likewise with tomara-spears.
And with mallets, swords, and clubs, as well as nooses and spikes, with skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅgas), tridents, skull-bowls, and likewise with spears (śaktis). || 106 ||
They were exceedingly terrifying, armed with sickles, goads, the tips of poles, staffs, three-pronged spears, darts, axes, arrows, and bows.
All of them were endowed with matted hair and crescent moons, and were all exceedingly powerful;
some possessed the form, vehicle, and ornaments of Bharga.
Equal [to him], with heads as white as the moonlight of half-mooned matted locks, and possessed of great strength,
some were Lords of Half-Women (Ardhanārīśvaras), just like Rudra himself.
But some, due to their beautiful forms which were as enchanting as those of the god of love, were born together with groups of women, eager for sexual pleasure.
All were wanderers of the sky, all moving according to their own will;
some were dark like the petals of a blue lotus, while others were white or red.
Some are red, some variegated, some green, and others tawny;
some are half-yellow and half-red, while others are half-blue and half-white.
Some are black and yellow, some are dyed half-black by white, some are single-colored, some two-colored, and others likewise three-colored. (113)
And some twice-born ones, numbering four, six, five, or ten times that amount, played ḍiṇḍimas, paṭahas, conchs, bherīs, ānakas, and kāhalas. (114)
Lutes called maṇḍūka, jharjhara, and jharjarī together with mṛdaṅgas;
vīṇās with five strings, as well as śakaṭas and dardaras. || 115 ||
All the Gaṇas played cow-faced drums, conchs, and cymbals, accompanied by hand-claps and rhythmic slapping, laughing again and again. || 116 ||
Facing the Boar, they stood there with joyful minds;
the Lord Śarabha, whose banner bears the bull, spoke to them all.
Slaying these hosts of Varāha with cruel deeds,
they became fierce and possessed of great strength through their cruel glances and cruel battles.
Then all those hosts, possessing various excellent forms and weapons, and being fierce in appearance, fought together with the hosts of Varāha.
All those who move through the sky, seeing the three worlds filled with water, abandoned them and both groups of hosts fought in the firmament itself.
Then, in an instant, the Pramathas of Hara struck all those mighty hosts of Varāhāsya, just as great winds strike the clouds.
Then, while those heroic Vārāha hosts were thus enraged, Varāha reflected: "Why has this situation occurred, first and then afterwards? (122)
Then, as he was reflecting, Janārdana entered his heart and informed him of everything that would be beneficial for the one in the form of a boar.
Then, intending to abandon his body,
the one of great strength struck Narasiṃha with the tip of his tusk at that time.
The Lord Śarabha divided Bharga into two parts in the middle;
and when Narasiṃha had become twofold, [he did so] by means of the human portion of that [being]. || 125 ||
He was born as a man, a great ṛṣi of divine form;
by virtue of his five-faced aspect, he is known as Nārāyaṇa.
The sage Uppin, possessing great splendor, became Janārdana;
both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were of great intellect, the causes of creation.
The power of these two is invincible in the scriptures, the Vedas, and in ascetic practices;
having then placed them upon a boat, he who has his self protected by the form of a fish [preserved] them.
The divine Boar, Śarabha, and Hari have approached me again;
for the welfare of the worlds, I must inevitably relinquish this body.
Thus, this endeavor is undertaken together with Hari, Śambhu, and Brahmā for the sake of that which was previously promised.
Having reflected thus, that Supreme Lord in the form of a boar then spoke to the god Śarabha, the Great God of great power.
"O Mahādeva, if you abandon me, I shall undoubtedly cast off my body for the benefit of the entire world, as well as for the gods and the officiating priests. (132)
O highly fortunate ones, having fashioned the sacrificial post from the various parts of my body, [arrange] the *śāmitra* fire and the *śruva* ladle and other implements separately. (133)
Therefore, for the welfare of the worlds, you three sons must sustain her,
who is composed of the universe, through Kanaka, Suvṛtta, and Ghora.
From sacrifice come the gods and indeed all creatures; from sacrifice come the foods for those who are bound by duty.
Everything is ever produced from sacrifice; the entire world consists of sacrifice.
That which Malini bore again as this "womb of the earth" (pṛthivīgarbha), the goddess herself shall long protect once it has been born. || 136 ||
When the time has come and the noble lady speaks thus, then that long-lived one will speak well; at that very moment, being afflicted by extreme passion, you shall slay him.
When the land of Bhārata is submerged one hundred yojanas below,
I shall then uplift it in the form of the boar Śṛṅgin.
Your son, who is destined to be the commander of the divine army and named after Rudra as the son of the six mothers, shall cause that body to cast off its duties once they have been accomplished.
While the mighty Yajñavarāha was thus speaking,
a vast radiance emerged, intensely illuminated by garlands of flames.
Then, a most wonderful thing occurred as it entered the body of the Blessed Lord Hari in his boar-form, which was as radiant as ten million suns. 141.
O twice-born ones, when Viṣṇu had entered that Vārāha-splendor,
Hari himself took up the formidable energy from the well-conducted Kanaka.
From their bodies as well, portions of light issued forth one after another, intensely blazing with garlands of flames.
He entered the body of Hari just as he had done for their father;
then Hari, Brahmā, and Mahādeva [acted] upon those words.
Having promised Varāha and repeatedly saying "Om," they made the supreme effort to sacrifice their bodies.
Then, by a blow from its snout, the śarabha tore through the middle of the boar's neck and cast its body into the water.
Having first struck down Suvṛtta, he likewise pierced the terrible Kanaka in the regions of his throat again and again, and slew him.
Having surrendered their lives, they all fell into the waters of the great ocean,
emitting cries in the water as they were overtaken by the fire of time.
When the boars had fallen, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, having come together once again, reflected upon the matter of creation. || 149 ||
Then all the hosts of Hara gathered around Bharga; those highly fortunate ones stood in attendance, divided into four groups.
O best of the twice-born, there are thirty-six thousand Pramathas;
among them, sixteen thousand are stationed in one particular division.
Those who indeed assume various forms, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon—all of them are endowed with complete sovereignty and devoted to meditation. || 152 ||
The yogis, free from intoxication, envy, hypocrisy, and egoism, with their sins destroyed and possessed of great fortune, are the supreme ones who bring delight to Śambhu. 153.
They never desired possessiveness or passion;
all those ascetics were turned away from cyclic existence and devoted to yoga. 154.
Surrounding Mahādeva as he remains in a state of meditative absorption, those who have observed their vows form an assembly with delight and remain there free from fatigue. || 155 ||
At the very moment the Lord of Ambikā contemplates the supreme light,
all his attendants immediately surround him.
Those sixteen crores who are firm in their vows have been fully described;
they possess forms resembling lions, tigers, and other such beings, and are endowed with the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 157 ||
Others are known as the amorous and very playful companions of Śambhu;
they possess diverse forms and ornaments, and are adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon. || 158 ||
Those bulls-bannered gods, possessing forms equal to Hara, were joined by women whose beauty resembled that of Umā. || 159 ||
Adorned with various garlands and ornaments, and decorated with divine wreaths and perfumes,
they, being themselves well-adorned, follow Umā’s companion as he sports.
Those eight crores of Gaṇas were adorned with amorous attire and ornaments;
others were Ardhanārīśvaras, [worshipping] Hara as Ardhanārīśvara. || 161 ||
Those who were equal in form to Hara entered into him as he remained in meditation;
for when Hara, accompanied by Umā, rejoices in blissful pleasure, [they enter him].
Those door-keepers, possessing bodies that are half-female and half-male,
constantly follow him as he travels along the path of the sky.
Those who serve the Lord while He is absorbed in meditation with water and other offerings,
bearing various weapons, are known as the Gaṇas of Śambhu, the Pramathas.
And in battles, they crush even those of great strength who are fighting;
indeed, those heroes of great might number nine crores. (165)
Others, being singers, danced and performed instrumental music with cymbals, mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and so forth, singing in sweet tones. || 166 ||
Indeed, assuming various forms, three crores of them constantly follow Maheśvara as he wanders about.
All were masters of illusion, all were heroes, all had reached the further shore of the meaning of the scriptures;
all were omniscient in every respect and always omnipresent. 168.
Within a moment, having gone to all the worlds, they return to rebirth;
endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), they are indeed possessed of great strength.
Others, named Rudras, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon,
always dwell in the third heaven by the command of the Lord of the Gods.
Their number is one crore, and all those hosts are exceedingly powerful; indeed, they constantly perform service to Hara at all times.
They strike down the most wicked and protect the most righteous;
they constantly bestow grace upon those who have undertaken the Pāśupata vow.
And these thirty-six crores of all the hosts of Hara constantly strike at obstacles for yogins of disciplined soul. (103)
For the purpose of destroying the host of Varāha, for the welfare of the worlds, and likewise for the service of Śaṅkara, these Gaṇas have arisen. (174)
Having seen the hosts of Varāha as well as Hari in the form of Narasiṃha,
he himself, assuming the form of a Śarabha, meditated and then let out a roar.
Since they were born from his *cītkāra* (roaring) and other such sounds, their forms are manifold.
Because it was said by Kapardin that "O Gaṇas, slay these [enemies] of Varāha with fierce glances, fierce battles, and cruel deeds," [they possess such power]. 176.
Therefore, those of great power, though born with cruel deeds and terrifying,
do not always perform cruel acts.
They are cruel to you merely by their sight, but not through their actions;
[they consume] fruit, water, as well as flowers, leaves, and likewise roots. (178)
They eat what has been offered on the slopes of forests and mountains, and they also gather and eat leaves, flowers, and other such things. (179)
Whatever may be the object of enjoyment for Bharga, those of great luster enjoy that;
and they do not eat meat, except on the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra.
There, Hara always eats the sacrificial food on the fourteenth day of the month of Madhu;
thereafter, all the Gaṇas there also eat pieces of meat.
When the host of Varāha was struck down by Bharga,
those Gaṇas themselves became fourfold and proclaimed themselves as "Bhūtakarma.
At that time, those who were divided into four parts attained the state of being *bhūtas*.

From the word of the Lotus-born [Brahmā], the aggregate of beings (bhūtagrāma) is therefore considered to be that world known previously as the fourfold aggregate of beings; because it is superior to those [four], it is called the "aggregate of beings. (183)
Thus has everything been told to you— how the beings are the attendants of Śambhu,
what their food is, what their forms are, and what their duties are, O ones of great luster.
Whoever should constantly hear this great and wonderful narrative becomes long-lived, always energetic, and endowed with yoga. (185)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Battle between Śarabha and Varāha," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The thirty-first chapter.
The sages said: How did the body of Yajñavarāha attain the state of being a sacrifice?
How did the three sons of Varāha attain the state of being Tretās? || 1 ||
Why was this untimely dissolution brought about by the Blessed One, the high-souled Varāha, resulting in such a terrible destruction of people? (2)
Or how were the Vedas rescued by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of a fish?
Furthermore, how did creation come to be, and by whom was the earth lifted up? (3)
O Guru, how did Īśvara abandon his body as a Śarabha?
O high-minded one, tell us what became of that body.
O tiger among the twice-born, you are an eyewitness to these matters;
therefore, O high-minded one, tell them now to us who are about to hear.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O tigers among the twice-born, to that wonder about which I have been questioned here;
let everyone listen with focused attention, for it bestows the fruit of all the Vedas. (6)
The gods are pleased by sacrifices; everything is established in sacrifice. By sacrifice the earth is sustained; sacrifice delivers all creatures. || 7 ||
Beings live by food; food originates from rain;
rain is born from sacrifice; therefore, everything is composed of sacrifice.
That sacrifice arose from the body of the Boar when it was torn asunder by Śambhu;
I shall relate that to you as it truly happened, so listen attentively, O twice-born ones.
At that very moment, when the body of the boar was torn asunder by Bharga,
the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, together with all the Pramathas, [emerged].
Having lifted that body out from the water, they cast it toward the sky;
Viṣṇu’s discus then shattered that body into pieces.
The joints of his limbs became the various sacrifices;
O great sages, listen now to which sacrifices were born from which specific limb. || 12 ||
The great sacrifice Jyotiṣṭoma was born from the junction of his eyebrows and nose;
and from the junction of his jaws and ears, Vahniṣṭoma was produced.
From the junction of the eyes and eyebrows was born Vrātyaṣṭoma;
from his lips and the junction [of the mouth] was born Paunarbhavaṣṭoma. || 14 ||
The Vṛddhaṣṭoma and Bṛhatṣṭoma were born from the root of his tongue;
the Atirātra and the Svarāja arose from the interior of his lower tongue.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the Pitṛs (pitṛyajña); the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali offering is the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña). || 16 ||
The daily sacrifices, beginning with the ritual bath and ending with the libations (tarpaṇa), all arose from the junction of the throat; likewise, the ritual injunctions arose from the tongue.
The Vājimedha, Mahāmedha, and likewise the Naramedha, as well as others who cause injury to living beings, were born from the joints of his feet. (18)
The Rājasūya and the Arthakārī, as well as the Vājapeya,
and likewise the Grahayajñas, arose at the junction of the Pṛṣṭhas.
The rites of consecration, the renunciation of vows, sacrifices, as well as gifts, ancestral offerings (śrāddha), and so forth,
and even the Sāvitrī sacrifice, have all arisen from the junction of the heart.
All ritual sacrifices and those which serve as expiations were born from the joint of his penis; such were the sacrifices of that Great-Souled One.
The Rakṣas-sacrifice, the Sarpasattra, all forms of malevolent magic (abhicārika),
the Gomedha, and the Vṛkṣayāga— these indeed arose from his hooves.
Māyeṣṭi, Parameṣṭi, Gīṣpati, Bhogasambhava, and likewise Agniṣṭoma were born at the joint of the tail. || 23 ||
And those occasional sacrifices (naimittika-yajñas) prescribed for the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) and other such occasions—
these have occurred at the joints of the finger-measures (lāṅgula), as well as during the twelve-year period.
Tīrthaprayoga, Sāmaujas, Yajña, Saṅkarṣaṇa, as well as Ārka and Ātharvaṇa—these have emerged from the junction of the channels (nāḍī). || 25 ||

The excellence of the *ṛc* verses, the field-sacrifices (*kṣetrayajña*), the five creations, the yoking, the sacrificial emblems, the structures, the *heḍamba*-sacrifices, the births, and the knees [are described]. (26)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, there arose one thousand and eight sacrifices,
by which the worlds are sustained even now.
The *sruc* was born from his *potrī*, and the *sruva* arose from his nose; other varieties of *sruc* and *sruva* were likewise born from the *potrī* and the nose. (28)
O best of sages, his fore-chamber (prāgvaṃśa) arose from the region of his neck;
and the merit of sacrificial offerings and public works (iṣṭāpūrta), as well as the Yajurvedic dharma, were born from the openings of his ears.
From his fangs the sacrificial posts arose, and from his body hairs the *kuśa* grass appeared;
likewise, the *udgātṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, the *hotṛ*, and the *śamitṛ* [emerged].
From the accumulation of his brain, sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) together with rice-offerings (caru) were produced, joined respectively to his front, right, left, upper body, and hind legs.
From his two eyes was born Kārśū, and likewise Yajñaketu from his hoof;
the central part became the sacrificial altar (vedi), and from his penis the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) was produced.
From the portion of the semen, likewise, the clarified butter (ājya) and the *svadhā* mantras emerged;

from the back part [of the body], the sacrificial hall (yajñālaya), and from the heart-lotus, the sacrifice itself (yajña). That whose self is the sacrifice is the Sacrifice-Person (Yajñapuruṣa); the *muñja* grasses emerged from the armpits (*kakṣa*).
In this way, as many vessels and sacrificial offerings as there are for sacrifices,
all those arose from the very body of the Sacrificial Boar.
Thus, the body of Yajñavarāha attained the state of a sacrifice, in order to nourish this entire world through the form of the sacrifice. || 35 ||
Having thus performed the sacrifice, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
intent on their exertion, approached the formidable, well-rounded golden [mountain].
Then, having gathered their bodies together individually,
the three gods destroyed those three bodies with the breath from their mouths.
The Creator himself then blew upon the body of Suvṛtta with the breath from his mouth and destroyed it; thereafter, he became the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
Keśava then caused Kanaka’s body to be cremated;
from it arose the Gārhapatya fire, which consumes the five sacrificial fires.
Śambhu himself indeed caused the body of Ghoras to blaze;
then, at that very moment, the Āhavanīya fire was produced.
By these three, the entire world with its triple root is pervaded;
O best of the twice-born, it is where this triad eternally resides.
All the deities dwell there together with their attendants;
this is the eternal Bhadrapada, which is indeed threefold in nature.
This is the locus of the threefold Vedic injunction; it is supremely meritorious, in that region where these three fires are offered oblations. (43)
In that country, the fourfold aims of life always flourish.
O best of the twice-born, I have told you all this that I was asked.
Just as the body of Yajñavarāha attained the state of sacrifice, and just as from the bodies of his sons the sacrificial fires arose; || 45 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Origin of the Sacrifice in the Boar Incarnation," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O highly fortunate ones, to this account of the destruction of the world by the Boar, which was brought about by the Blessed One in an instant. || 1 ||
Or how the Vedas were rescued by Śārṅgin in the form of a fish—
I shall relate that [account], which destroys all sins.
In ancient times, the great sage Kapila was a perfected one (siddha), the Lord Viṣṇu;
he who was Hari himself in person, that supreme sage among the perfected ones.
"For one who meditates, this entire world is accomplished by itself.
Because he was born from the body of Hari, he is therefore remembered as Kapila.
Once, having lived in former times during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara,
that best of sages spoke these words to Svāyambhuva Manu.
Kapila said: O Svāyambhuva, best of sages, embodiment of Brahman, O high-minded one! Grant now this desired object to me who entreats you.
This entire world is indeed you, and it is protected by you;
the whole world was created by you, and you alone are the Lord of the worlds.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, among gods, humans, and all living beings,
you alone are the Lord, the giver of boons, the protector, and the eternal one.
You are indeed the Ordainer and the Disposer; for you are the Lord of all lords.
The entire triad of worlds is eternally established in you.
As you perform penance, that [knowledge] will appear to you simultaneously:
the worlds together with the entire multitude of the principles of cause and effect.
"Grant me that secret place, difficult to find in the three worlds—a holy, beautiful, and supreme site that removes sin and is the source of knowledge. (11)
For I, having become the witness of all beings, shall uplift the world that has come into being by fashioning the lamp of knowledge. 12.
The entire world is now submerged in the ocean of ignorance;
by providing the raft of knowledge, I shall deliver the three worlds.
In this matter, you wish for me to be properly established here; for you, O Lord of the World, are our protector, our venerable one, and our guardian. (14)
Thus addressed by the high-souled Kapila, Manu replied to that great-souled Kapila of rigid vows.
Manu said:
"If you desire to compose the Lamp of Knowledge for the sake of the welfare of the entire world,
what need have you for the purpose of [claiming] a specific place?"
In ancient times, Hiraṇyagarbha performed a most great and wonderful penance;
O twice-born one, he requested from me a place for his asceticism, and not [anything else].
Śambhu performed penance for ten thousand years according to the measure of the gods, devoid of enjoyment; yet even he did not perceive a fixed place.
Devendra, Vītihotra, Śamana, the lord of the Rakṣasas, the lord of aquatic creatures, Mātariśvan, and likewise the lord of wealth; || 19 ||
Desiring the status of guardians of the quarters, these performed intense penance;
yet, O great sage, they did not seek any specific location whatsoever.
Temples, sacred fords, holy fields, and likewise rivers—many such merit-bestowing places exist here on the land of Kapila. (21)
O Brahmin, if you approach even one of those places and perform penance, what will not be accomplished there through the perfection of your austerities?
Your request for a place from me is merely empty boasting;
such boastful conduct is not appropriate for ascetics.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of Svāyambhuva Manu,
the perfected Kapila became enraged and then spoke to Manu.
Kapila said:
"Having placed my trust in you for the swift attainment of success in my asceticism, I requested this place from you; why then do you revile me with these arguments?"
Because of these exceedingly harsh words, I could not tolerate you, who possess such pride as to claim for yourself the title of "Lord of the Three Worlds. (26)
"Your boastful speech today regarding my request is intolerable;
you shall now reap the fruit of what you have said. (27)
This entire triple world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, shall before long be slain, struck down, and utterly destroyed. || 28 ||
By whom this earth was lifted up, or by whom it was established once again;
who was its creator, or who was its protector. (29)
Let all of them indeed destroy everything, including the moving and the unmoving;
before long, O Mind, you shall behold the three worlds filled with water,
shattered, struck down, and utterly devastated, which shall shatter your pride.
Having spoken thus, that lord of sages, Kapila, a treasury of asceticism, vanished;
at that time, the sage departed for the abode of Brahmā.
Having heard the words of Kapila, Manu, with a dejected countenance, accepted that it would indeed happen; he quickly said nothing further.
Thereupon, the wise Svāyambhuva, with his mind fixed on austerity,
desiring to see the one whose banner is Garuḍa for the welfare of all the worlds, [set out].
He went indeed to the vast Badarī near Gaṅgādvāra;
having gone there, Svāyambhuva Manu himself, the sustainer of the world, beheld that holy Badarī which destroys all sins. (34)
Always fruitful, ever possessing soft and fresh blossoms and clusters, providing excellent shade, smooth, and entirely free from withered or dried leaves. (35)
Her entire region, from the tips of her crest to the base of her roots, was sprinkled by the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā,
and she was constantly attended by various sages whose wealth was their asceticism.
That place is auspicious in every respect, filled with various flocks of bees,
possessing waters of blooming lotuses, delightful, and bestowing the merit of a bull-sacrifice.
Having entered [the hermitage], the creator of the worlds applied himself to austerity;
restricting his food, he remained in supreme meditative absorption.
He propitiated Hari, the cause of the causes of the universe, the Lord of all worlds, who possesses the luster of a dark cloud or collyrium. (39)
The god who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses, who wears yellow garments, and who is seated upon Garuḍa. || 40 ||
[He saw] the Lord of the World, who pervades the universe, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, the seed of the world, the thousand-eyed, thousand-headed Master. (41)
Reciting this supreme mantra, which consists of all the Vedas, the sage [meditated upon] Nārāyaṇa—the unborn, all-pervading, omnipresent, and universal support. 42.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge, and who takes the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and the Unmanifest.
As Manu, the son of Svayambhū, was thus reciting this prayer,
Keśava, the Lord of the World, then became gracious toward him without delay.
Then, having become a small fish with a luster like the blade of a dūrvā grass, he was radiant with a pair of eyes resembling a pair of camphor buds. || 45 ||
Then Janārdana, assuming the form of a small fish, approached the high-souled sage Manu, the son of Svayambhū, as he was performing austerities.
Then, filled with compassion, he spoke to that high-souled Svāyambhuva Manu, who was greatly terrified and speaking with a voice faltering from fear.
"O treasure of asceticism, O highly fortunate one, you ought to protect me who am terrified, constantly agitated by large fish intent on devouring me. (48)
"O illustrious one, every day fish run toward me from all sides to devour me; O Lord, you alone are capable of protecting me. (49)
Today, having been torn apart by many large, thick-furred creatures, I am exhausted; being so small, I am not even capable of fleeing.
Desiring life, I have come to you, the great-souled sage, for refuge;
if you have compassion for me, please protect me.
With my mind agitated, I am as terrified by the flickering shade of a tree and the trembling waves as a fish is by them. (52)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his, Svāyambhuva Manu, filled with supreme compassion, then spoke: "I am your protector. (53)
Then, taking water into the hollow of his hand and placing it there,
he observed its movement in the presence of a small fish.
Then that Manu, being compassionate, placed that fish of beautiful form into a large, water-filled jar.
As that fish grew day by day in that water-jar,
its body soon became like that of an ordinary rohita fish.
Every day, that great-souled one, emptying a water-jar filled with ten measures of water, caused the fish to grow;
and that young fish, with its very clear eyes, [grew] before long.
In the midst of the water in the jeweled vessel was Lomaśa, with a stout body.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fish Incarnation," in the glorious *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Thirty-three.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having himself seen that fish with a stout body...
Taking a full-blown lotus with his hand, he went to the lake.
In that holy Nārāyaṇa hermitage, there was a vast lake,
one yojana in width and one and a half yojanas in length.
Having reached that lake, which was filled with various schools of fish and possessed a mass of cool, pure water,
Manu then deposited the fish there.
Filled with supreme compassion, he nurtured him like a son;
in a very short time, that fish became plump and large.
O best of the twice-born, because of its great size, that large fish could no longer fit within that lake;
once, it [moved] between the eastern and western shores.
Quickly placing his head and tail together, he raised his body high and cried out to the great-souled Svāyambhuva, "Save me! (6).
Manu, having recognized that the fish with the thick tail was crying out in such a manner,
approached it and then seized it with his hand.
"I am not able to pull out this wonderful creature with its thick hair," he thought,
and even as he was thinking thus, he pulled it up with his hand.
The Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, Janārdana in the form of the Fish,
having reached the hand of Svāyambhuva, assumed a state of lightness.
Then, having lifted it up with his two hands and placed it upon his shoulder, Manu quickly carried it to the ocean and deposited it there in the water.
Grow here as you desire; no one shall slay you.
Before long, you shall attain a fully developed body.
Having spoken thus, that illustrious one, the best among all living beings,
fell into great amazement as he reflected upon his own lightness.
Then, before long, the fish became large with a full body and filled the ocean in every direction with the expanse of its form.
Beholding that full-bodied [being], who had risen up beyond the water, vast and piled with rocks like the mountain Mānasa; || 14 ||
At that time, the wise Svāyambhuva Manu did not perceive the fish as anything other than the entire ocean itself, which had been rendered immobile by the expanse of its body.
Then Manu Svāyambhuva, having reflected and beholding that wonderful form, questioned the fish with gentle words while observing its smallness.
Manu said:
"I do not consider you to be a fish; tell me, O best of beings, who are you? Reflecting upon your greatness and your minuteness, O most great one!"
Are you Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Śambhu in the form of a fish? O highly fortunate one, O great-minded one, if it is not a secret, tell that to me.
Matsya said:
"I, who am Hari, the eternal one, am to be constantly propitiated by you;
for the sake of accomplishing your desired wish, I have appeared here with a concentrated mind. (19)
O Lord of Beings, whatever you desire from me in this form of a fish, that I shall do today; know this to be my resolve.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
and having realized Viṣṇu to be present before his very eyes, Manu praised Keśava.
Manu said:
Salutations to you, O Hara, the unmanifest Lord of the universe, both supreme and inferior;
O imperishable one who bears the three eyes of fire, the sun, and the moon!

O cause of the universe, O omniscient one, O abode of the world, O Hari, O supreme one! O you whose nature is both the higher and the lower self, O protector of those who have crossed over, O cause of crossing beyond! 23.
O Hari, O Trivikrama, having sustained yourself by yourself and assuming the form of the earth, you, whose very self is the support, sustain all the worlds.
O you who consist of all the Vedas, O most excellent one, O cause of the maintenance of the abode, O Supreme Lord of the hosts of gods, O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of the gods! 25.
You are the unborn source of the world, yet you are the sourceless; you are the eternal movement, yet you are devoid of touch.
You are the light, yet you are without contact; you are the Lord of all, yet you are without a lord.
You are without beginning, the source of all, eternal, and both internal and external; you are that golden egg, the seed of the worlds, known as the Brahmāṇḍa.
That seed of yours is said by you to be light and also present in the waters;
it is the support of all, yet itself without support, causeless, and the cause of everything. (28)
I bow, I bow to you, O Lord of the Universe, O Sovereign, the source of all worlds!
You are the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution, assuming the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Salutations again and again to You, whose tenfold form is free from the six waves and the like; You are the Lord of Light, the ocean. 30.
O Supreme Lord, who is capable of describing Your nature— You who are grosser than the gross and whose form is consistent with the range of objects—
to You, who have become manifest today, let my salutation be eternal.
He is of the color of the sun, beyond darkness. || 31 ||
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand feet,
and a thousand eyes; he extends ten fingers' breadth beyond this entire earth.
May that fierce Viṣṇu be gracious to me here.
Salutations to you, O Lord in the form of a fish; salutations to you, O Blessed One, O Hari!
Salutations to you, the joy of the world; salutations to you, the lover of your devotees.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Praised by Svāyambhuva Manu, Vāsudeva, assuming the form of a fish,
then spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am pleased today by your austerity and by your repeated praise with devotion; and by your worship and your gift, O observer of noble vows, choose a boon."
"I shall grant you your desired object; there is no doubt about this. Choose whatever desires you wish for, or whatever is for the benefit of the worlds. (36)
Manu said:
"O Viṣṇu, if a boon is to be granted to me today that would be for the welfare of the worlds, then grant me that boon; I shall state it, so listen to me. (37)
Formerly, Kapila cursed the three worlds on my behalf, saying:
"May all of this become struck down, beaten, and utterly destroyed for you. (38)
By whom this earth was lifted up, by whom it was protected, and who will indeed withdraw it—let them now flood it. (39)
Therefore, with a distressed heart, I have come to you alone for refuge;
grant me this boon so that these three worlds shall not be submerged in water, nor utterly destroyed, struck down, and shattered. (40)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Kapila is not different from me, nor am I different from Kapila;
know that whatever was spoken by that sage was spoken by me. (41)
Therefore, whatever has been spoken by him shall be true and cannot be otherwise;
O Svāyambhuva, understand that I shall provide assistance in this matter.
When the three worlds have been struck down, crushed, and utterly destroyed, and have sunk into the waters, I shall indeed direct my mind there before long;
then you will recognize me by my dark-hued horn. (43)
"As long as you remain floating upon the waters, so long you must direct your mind according to my instructions;
now listen attentively as I speak these beneficial words. (44)
"Let a single boat be constructed from a multitude of all kinds of wood fit for sacrifice;
I shall make it so firm that it does not break apart in the waters. (45)
Ten yojanas wide and thirty yojanas long,
it is the sustainer of all seeds and the nourisher of the three worlds.
[He constructed] a [platform] made from the fibers of the bhūri and valvala creepers of all sacrificial trees,
nine yojanas in length and three vyāmas in width.
Quickly set your mind upon the great *īrikā-vaṭī* pill;
she is the sustainer of the world, the illusion of the world, the mother of the world, and identical with the world.
She will make that rope firm so that it does not break in any way whatsoever.
Taking all the seeds along with the seven sages and the Vedas,
you shall sit upon that boat while the flood of waters prevails.
"Having united with Dakṣa, you will remember me, O Manu;
when remembered, I shall quickly come into your presence.
Then indeed, by my dark-hued horn, you shall recognize me. (50)
"As long as the three worlds remain struck down, shattered, and destroyed, for that long I shall carry that boat on my back; of this there is no doubt. (51)
But when my horn has grown full and I have leaped up,
you shall then indeed fasten that boat firmly with a leather thong.
When my boat has grown large, I shall propel it for a thousand years by the measure of the gods, drying up the water from that vessel.
Then, when the waters had dried up, I moored that ship on a lofty peak of the Himālaya mountain.
If your mind is propitiated by this recitation which I have mastered, all success shall be his who satisfies me thereby. (55)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus granted him the boon, the fish—
the Lord of the World who acts for the benefit of all beings— was saluted by him and vanished.
When Lord Hari had vanished, Svāyambhuva also acted exactly as he had been instructed by Hari previously: he prepared a boat and a rope.
Then Svāyambhuva, having cut down a multitude of trees suitable for all sacrificial purposes,
had a boat constructed by means of axes and other tools.
Manu had that collection of threads produced from those fibers woven into cloth according to the measurements previously stated. 59.
Then, after a long time, a most wonderful battle took place between Viṣṇu in his form as the Sacrificial Boar, Śarabha, and Hara.
Then, when a flood of waters arose and the three worlds were destroyed, he likewise tied a boat with a rope and took all the seeds from every side. (61)
Then Manu, having indeed taken the seven seers of the Vedas and placed them upon that ship,
first set out upon the waters amidst the moving and the unmoving.
Then Svāyambhuva, situated upon the boat, remembered Hari in the form of a fish;
thereupon [the boat] rose above the waters like a mountain with its peaks.
And Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a fish, was sent by Ekaśṛṅga;
he arrived there before long at the place where Manu sat upon the boat.
Having boarded the boat upon the vast and terrifying expanse of water,
he placed the boat on his back as long as the water remained moving and unstable.
Having tied a small boat to a horn that had returned to its natural state in the water,
we propelled that boat for a thousand divine years.
Supporting his own boat, the Supreme Lord held it steady;
the Mother of the World, Yoganidrā, sat upon the lotus.
Then, as the water gradually dried up over a long period,
the western peak of the Himalayas indeed became deeply submerged within the waters.
It rises two thousand yojanas high, possessing a snowy luster;
its peak, moreover, rises fifty thousand [yojanas].
Then, having tied the boat to that horn, Hari, the Lord of the worlds who had assumed the form of a fish,
went quickly to dry up the waters.
Thus indeed were the Vedas protected by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of a fish.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
By the curse of Kapila, however, an untimely dissolution was brought about;
for this premature dissolution was caused by the Blessed One.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, everything has been told to you exactly as it is.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Account of the Untimely Dissolution," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, hear how the creation came to be after the dissolution at the end of the kalpa, and by whom the earth was uplifted. || 1 ||
When the dissolution had passed, the immensely powerful Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, assuming the form of a tortoise,
lifted up the earth along with its mountains by placing it upon his back,
and then made the entire world level as it was before.
Where the earth had become shattered by the footsteps of the Śarabha, the boar, and their sons, the Tortoise made each of those places level.
Then, having leveled the ground as before, the Supreme Lord supported Ananta, who was stationed upon the surface of the earth.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, the Supreme Lord, having assembled,
spoke to the seven sages residing within the belly of the boat, to Svāyambhuva Manu,
to both Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and to Dakṣa. || 5 ||
"Let all the sages, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, listen; we shall now speak of what Dakṣa and Svāyambhuva Manu have said."
The creation has been destroyed by the conflict between the Boar and the Śarabha;
therefore, listen to how our creation should now be carried out.
These two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have appeared for the purpose of creation,
performing supreme austerity for the sake of establishing the gods.
Having gratified both the gods residing in Janaloka through their ascetic power,
let them bring down others and eternally create many new hosts.
O Sage, let the constellations and the planets, along with their respective positions,
attain stability through the ascetic power of these two from their previous birth.
"Let this illustrious Janārdana himself create the structure of the sun’s chariot as well as the position of the moon’s chariot. (11)
"O Svāyambhuva Manu, let all seeds be sown by you upon the earth;
let the ground be filled everywhere with grain. (12)
O Svāyambhuva, he caused herbs, trees, creepers, and climbing plants to sprout everywhere, and he obtained the great seasonal fruits.
Let Dakṣa, together with the seven lords of sages, worship Hari through sacrifice,
performing this worship with the three fires produced from the body of the son of Varāha.
This sacrifice was born from the body of the Boar for the sake of creation;
by means of this very sacrifice, Dakṣa extends this creation.
By Nara and Nārāyaṇa, by the seven sages,
by Dakṣa, by you as well, by Yajña, and likewise by these fires.
"Let this creation be fulfilled in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld."
And we shall constantly strive so that this creation may be replenished as it was; you, however, must carry out the act of creation. (17)
"Therefore, let the creation proceed exactly as it was before;
first, however, you must now cause the seeds to sprout, O Mind. (18)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O highly fortunate one, having spoken thus, Āditya, Vidhi, Viṣṇu, and Vṛṣadhvaja then set out to establish the mountains in their proper places.
Then, on Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, and other such places,
they each separately constructed the cities of all the gods.
Then, having set down the earth, abandon the boat; Svāyambhuva sowed seeds upon the ground for the sake of all prosperity.
Then the trees, creepers, vines, shrubs, and forests,
as well as the young crops, the grains, and likewise the medicinal herbs, all became uniform.
Seeds, sprouts from stalks, spreading creepers, and water-born plants; those in full bloom and those opening their buds, as well as fruits, tubers, and leaves. (23)
All the grassy meadows (śādvala) became conducive to the increase of life for everyone; the earth was rich with crops, and those auspicious trees were like grassy meadows.
They appeared just as they had been seen before by Manu, who was filled with joy in his heart.
Then that man, a great yogi and high-minded one, performed most intense austerity for the sake of bringing about the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa among the gods.
Both Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the two supreme and most excellent of sages, having propitiated through austerity that which is supreme, consisting of light, and free from all affliction; || 26 ||

O Sage, by means of their great power of asceticism, they brought forth the hosts of people, the gods, and the best of divine sages— those who had previously died as immortals— and they created them separately, each in their own groups.
Janārdana himself established the two gods, the Sun and the Moon, as well as the ten guardians of the directions, and those who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
Just as before, we established the two wheels of the sun and the moon in their proper positions, O Acyuta, and likewise arranged the duration of day and night for them.
When the medicinal herbs had grown, O best of beings, as well as the sacrificial trees,
the seeds of grain, and the various gods, [he spoke].
Dakṣa began to perform the great sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma;
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Gautama [were present].
Jamadagni and Bharadvāja—these are the stainless Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). || 31 ||
With these seven lords of sages, Dakṣa himself, the son of Brahmā,
then performed the great sacrifice for twelve years.
O best of the twice-born, while those three fires were being kindled there again and again,
and while the Boar, in the form of a sacrifice, was being worshipped by the brahmins,
the fourfold classes of beings were born from that very sacrifice.
Then thirteen auspicious daughters were born to Dakṣa,
endowed with beauty and virtue, possessing boundless progeny for the sake of creation.
Dakṣa gave those daughters to the high-souled Kaśyapa;
from them were born many offspring, by whom the entire world was pervaded. (35)
Indeed, Kaśyapa was the progenitor of all creatures;
O tigers among the twice-born, it is certain that the entire world [originated] from Kaśyapa.
O all you sages, listen correctly as I relate their names and all the various offspring born from them, one by one.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Danāyū, Siṃhikā, Muni, Krodhā, Pradhā, Variṣṭhā, Vinatā, and likewise Kapilā.
These thirteen daughters of Kadrū are proclaimed as the offspring of Dakṣa. || 38 ||
He was born from the thumb of the right hand of Vidhi as he was meditating with his mind;
because of that, he is called Dakṣa among gods and men. (39)
The ten mind-born sons of Brahmā were proclaimed of old;
among them, six were creators of the world when this destruction of beings had passed.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu;
from Marīci was born Kaśyapa, the progenitor of the worlds. (41)
From his daughters, who were the wives of Dakṣa, offspring were born in great numbers;
now learn their names according to their mothers and their progeny. (42)
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Soma;
Bharga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu. || 43 ||
The twelve sons of Aditi are proclaimed as the Ādityas;
among them, the youngest is the virtuous one who always warms all creatures.
He indeed is proclaimed among you as the primary progenitor of the lineage, the Sun;
for Hiraṇyakaśipu was the sole powerful son of Diti. (45)
He had four sons who were joyful and endowed with the strength of pride:
Prahlāda, Saṃhlāda, Vāṣkala, and Śibi.
Prahlāda had three sons; of them, the first was Virocana.
Kumbha, Nikumbha, and the powerful [Bala]—these three are remembered as the progeny of Prahlāda. (47)
The son of Virocana was born as the great Bali, who was prodigal in giving;
and the son of Bali was known as the mighty Bāṇa.
That glorious follower of Śambhu was named Mahākāla;
and Bāṇa had a hundred sons, such as Kusumbha, Makara, and others.
Danu had forty sons, headed by Vipracitti;
likewise Śambara, Namuci, and Puloman. (50)
Asiloman, Keśin, Durjaya, Ayomukha, Aśvaśiras, Kṣaya, Śaṅku, and Viyanmūrdhan were all possessed of great strength. (51)
Vegavān and Ketumān, as well as Svarbhānu himself;
Aśva, Aśvapati, Kuṇḍa, Vṛṣaparvan, and likewise Ajaka. (52)
Aśvagrīva, Sūkṣma, Turuṇḍa, and likewise Māṇḍala; Ūrdhvabāhu, Ekacakra, Virūpākṣa, and Harāhara.
Niyantra, Nikumbha, Kūpaṭa, Paṭu, as well as Sarabha, Sulabha, and likewise Sūryācandramas. || 54 ||
Furthermore, these two sons of Danu are likewise Sūrya and Candramas;
those two preeminent among the gods are the Maker of Day and the Lord of Night.
By their sons, grandsons, and many great-grandsons, all endowed with strength and valor, this entire world has been pervaded. (56)
To Danāyuṣ were born four exceedingly powerful sons:
Vīrabhadra, Vikṣara, Vatsa, and likewise Vṛtta. || 57 ||
O best of the twice-born, many sons were born to these four; endowed with beauty, character, and strength, there were a hundred sons for each one.
The sons born of Kālā became renowned as the Kāleyas;
they were four famous lords of the Dānavas, possessed of great heroism. (59)
Vināśana, Krodha, Krodhahantṛ,
and likewise Krodhaśakra— these are proclaimed as the sons of Kālā.
From Siṃhikā was born a son, Rāhu, the crusher of the moon and sun;
also Sucandra, Candrahantṛ, and likewise Candravimardana.
Egavān, Ketumān, Ayaḥ, Surbhānu, Aśvodyapati, Kṛṣṭu, Aṣṭaparvan, and Ājusrus; || 62 ||
From Krodhā were born sons who performed cruel deeds;
and Siṃhikā and Krodhā likewise always had two cruel daughters.
And from those two, the lineage known as Prabhava originated; it is indeed remembered as being most cruel.
Only one son was born to the sage, the great Śukra, the seer,
who was always the preceptor of the Daityas, Dānavas, Kāleyas, and others.
Four sons were born to him, who were priests for the Asuras:
Tvaṣṭṛ, Avara, Atri, and Saukala; they were all eloquent speakers.
In splendor they were like the sun, illuminating the world of Brahmā,
as well as the worlds of the Asuras, the Daityas, and the Kāleyas.
Likewise, by the offspring of Krodha and the sons of Siṃhikā,
the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, was pervaded through successive generations of progeny.
O twice-born ones, as for their offspring who were raised in succession, because of their great number, it is impossible to calculate them even after a long time. (68)
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Anūru, Garuḍa, Āruṇi, and Vāruṇi are known as the sons of Vinatā. || 69 ||
Śeṣa, Vāsuki the king, Takṣaka, Kulika, Kūrma, and Sumanas—these are proclaimed as the sons of Kadrū. (70)
Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Suparṇa, Garuḍa, Gopati, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the heroic Sūryavarcas. || 71 ||
Arkadṛṣṭa, Prayukta, Viśruta, and likewise Suśruta; Bhīma, Citraratha, and the renowned Sarvavidbali. (72)
Śāliśīrṣa, Parjanya, Kali, and Nārada—these are proclaimed as the divine Gandharvas who are the sons of sages. || 73 ||
She gave birth to a daughter named Anavadyā, and [others] named Sānurāgā, Saṃvarā, Mārgaṇā, Priyā, Asūyā, Subhagā, and Bhīmā.
Prādhā was born from Kaśyapa, who is rich in asceticism, due to the emergence of all his virtues;
[her sons were] Viśvāvasu, Sucandra, Suparṇa, and Siddha.
Barhiṣ, Pūrṇa, Pūrṇāṅga, Brahmācārī, Ratipriya, Bhānu, and Daśama— these are proclaimed as the sons of Prādhā.
Thus these gods and gandharvas, constantly endowed with meritorious characteristics,
were born from the illustrious goddess Prādhā by the most excellent of divine sages.
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Gāminī, and Manoramā;
Vidyutprabhā, Anaghā, Rambhā, Aruṇā, Rakṣitā, and Atulā. (78)
Suvāhu, Suratā, Murajā, Supriyā, Vapu, and Tilottamā—these are remembered as the principal Apsarases. || 79 ||
Atibāhu, Tumburu, Hāhā, and likewise Hūhū—
these are proclaimed as the chief among the Gandharvas, who are equal to the gods.
The Brāhmaṇas are nectar, as are the cows, the sages, and the Apsarases;
the offspring of Kapilā are declared to be highly fortunate and bringers of great festivals.
Thus, those who are remembered as the sons of Kaśyapa from among the daughters of Dakṣa—by them this entire world, both stationary and moving, has been pervaded. (82)
Thus, from the three fires of Manu Svāyambhuva, that great-souled one, [the fire] was produced by the falling of Yajñavarāha, who is the embodiment of sacrifice. || 83 ||
And from the seven sages, beginning with Kaśyapa,
and from Nara and Nārāyaṇa, after the untimely dissolution had passed,
the subjects were again created in the past by Hari, who assumes manifold forms.
Thus occurred again the creation by the grace of that Hari, who brings about the creation, maintenance, and end [of the world], and whose nature is Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (85)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of Creation," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 34 ||
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
[Listen] how the Lord diligently cast off his body as a Śarabha.
Listen further as I relate it to you, O best of the twice-born. || 1 ||
When Yajñavarāha was slain, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
approached Śarabha and spoke words consistent with the agreement for the welfare of the universe.
The vast expanse of many yojanas has been filled by your bodily expansion;
therefore, withdraw this body that strikes terror into the world.
By your fighting, the entire three worlds have been destroyed.
Seeing you, Janārdana now fears even to go into the sky. Therefore, for the welfare of the higher worlds, do indeed cast off this body.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then,
having heard those words of the eldest of the gods, Śaṅkara instantly cast off his śarabha body right upon the water.
When that body was abandoned by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
the eight feet of him who possesses eight forms entered into those eight [regions].
First, his right foot quickly went toward the sky;
then his left reached the sun, and afterwards, the one born from the right [foot] reached the moon.
Vāmanu resorted to the fire, Pṛṣṭhāgra went to the earth,
Vāmapṛṣṭha to the water, and after him, likewise, Dakṣiṇa.
