In the wind, he placed his left foot upon the Hotṛ priest who faces all directions;
thus, at that very moment, his eight feet took their places within the eight forms of his eightfold manifestation, and each returned to its own respective abode of light.
The middle body of the high-souled Śaṅkara was that of a śarabha;
he was Kapālī, Bhairava, and Bhūta, possessing a fierce form and difficult to approach.
They offer meat mixed with the fat of the brain into the sacred fire,
and perform the worship of the gods with wine using a skull-cup as a vessel.
Bali always offered human flesh as food and blood as the drink; he performed the sacrificial feast with wine and wore a garland made of skulls.
Clad in a tiger skin, stained with dirt, and marked by three folds [of skin], those who observe the vow of the skull-fragment constantly act in this manner. (13)
Among them, the god Kapālī Bhairava is to be worshipped perpetually—
both he who is Śmaśāna-Bhairava and he who is named Mahābhairava.
He possesses the radiance of the rising sun and always has eighteen arms;
he is resplendent with red eyes and is forever surrounded by throngs of female consorts.
Constantly sporting with Kālī, Pracaṇḍā, and others,
he was a consumer of freshly burnt human flesh, his arms dangling and quivering as they moved.
Feeding on the remnants of blood, he was always among the spirits who eat such fare;
with a broad face, drooping lips, and dwelling in short, thick feet, he was a playful musician in the world, yet terrifying with his loud, boisterous laughter.
Thus that Great God, assuming the form of Mahābhairava, the mighty-armed one,
performed his task with a body having eight legs.
Then he went from there toward Hara’s attendants (the Pramathas);
likewise, that Bhairava sports in the sky together with his hosts.
That god Mahābhairava, being worshipped by the people of the world,
even today constantly accomplishes the desired wish of his devotee.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, whoever should worship Bhairava even once with honey, spirits, milk, fruits, meat, fish, and blood; || 21 ||
Having fully accomplished all his desires and enjoyed pleasures as he wished,
he ascends the supreme bull and proceeds to the abode of Śambhu.
All this that I was asked by you, O best of the twice-born, has been told to you;
whatever else may please you, ask me that.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Śarabha’s Body," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The thirty-sixth chapter begins with the sages saying:
How did this powerful being named Naraka, the son of Varāha,
come to be born as a preeminent asura, even though he was the son of a god and a goddess?
How did he become long-lived? For what purpose did he dwell for a long time in the womb? Where on earth was that one of great strength born? || 2 ||
How did he become the king of the asuras, and what was the name of his city? Furthermore, how was he born on earth from Malinī and the Boar (Potrin)? || 3 ||
O tiger among sages, it is heard [of you]; how did he become such as that?
Tell all of this in its entirety to us who ask you.
"You are our teacher and our scripture, the seer of all things directly before you;
how is it that you have obtained a boon from the powerful Brahmā? (5)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, all you sages, O best of the twice-born, to that which I have been asked:
how that great asura Naraka became the son of the Earth."
From the womb of a menstruating cow belonging to the Gotra clan, by means of the seed of Potrin, he was born;
though he was a son of a god, he became an asura wherever he went.
Knowing the Great Hero to be situated within the womb— the invincible son of Varāha, possessed of great strength and prowess— the gods, headed by Brahmā, [approached].
At that time, the gods firmly held him within the womb for a long duration by means of their power,
so that even when the time arrived, he was not born from the womb.
Then, once the Boar had abandoned his body along with his sons,
the Earth, the mother of the world, became intensely tormented by grief.
Agitated by grief, she lamented for a long time again and again;
then, having been consoled by Mādhava, she returned to her natural state.
Then, when the time had arrived, as the fetus was held back by the power of destiny and did not proceed toward birth, the earth became distressed.
When that queen, being heavily pregnant, was unable to bear the weight of the fetus,
she then went for refuge to the god Mādhava.
Having sought refuge with Mādhava, the protector of the worlds,
the goddess bowed her head and spoke these words.
The Earth said:
"Salutations to you, O unmanifest form of the universe, the cause of all causes;
O Pradhāna, who transcend the Puruṣa, and whose nature consists of maintenance, creation, and dissolution. (15)
O Supreme Sustainer of the enjoyment of *svāhā*, intent on the governance of the world; O Blessed One, Lord of the World, whose very self is the bliss that gladdens the universe! 16.
O imperishable Viṣṇu, who art the ordainer and the ordained, resplendent;
salutations to you, O sustainer of the world, abode of the three worlds, creator of the universe! 17.
O Lord of the Universe, I bow to you who, being ever intent upon it, protects and establishes the eternal norms in the form of restraints. 18.
You are Mādhava, the preeminent one, Kāma, the abode of desire, and dissolution; you are the Lord who is the cause of birth and death, the purpose, and the means of protection.
Salutations again and again to you, for whom water does not cause moisture, nor heat cause burning, and for whom cold does not cause chill. (20)
Salutations again and again to You, for whom the ocean does not cause a flood, nor fire for drying up, nor Yama for death. || 21 ||
That which is indeed upheld by yogis through their own efforts, which serves as the object of meditation for those on the wrong path,
and whose eternal form is ever-attached to the path—
Therefore, desiring protection, you must protect the earth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus praised by the Mother of the World, Hari Hṛṣīkeśa then manifested himself and spoke to the Earth, whose mind was dejected.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Goddess Earth, why do you lament with such a distressed mind?
What affliction has been inflicted upon you? I wish to know that. (24)
Your face is parched, your body is devoid of luster,
and your pair of eyes is agitated, lacking its usual play of the eyebrows.
Such a form as yours has never been seen before;
please explain the seed of suffering that lies in the transformation of this form. (26)
Having heard these words of Mādhava, the Lord of the World, the goddess Pṛthivī, bowed down in humility, spoke with a faltering voice: 27.
The Earth said:
"O Mādhava, I am no longer capable of bearing the burden of the fetus;
I am constantly and exceedingly distressed, therefore you ought to protect me. (28)
"In former times, you desired Malini while in the form of a boar;
by that very desire, this embryo which has been placed within my womb by you [has come to be]. (29)
O Mādhava, even though the time has arrived, this fetus does not fall away;
therefore, I am tormented day by day by this heavy pregnancy.
If you do not protect me from the suffering of pregnancy, O God, Lord of the World, I shall before long undoubtedly fall under the power of death. (31)
O Mādhava, never before has such a fetus been carried by any woman as this one,
which makes me, though immovable, tremble like a lake stirred by an elephant.
Having heard these words of the Earth, Hari, the lord of the earth, replied so as to gladden her, like one reviving a withered creeper.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Earth, this great suffering of yours shall not endure for long.
Listen to the manner in which this was experienced by you."
The fetus that you carried through association with Malinī turned out to be of asura nature; though he was the son of Ghṛṣṭi, he was indeed cruel.
Having learned of the circumstances regarding that embryo, Brahmā and the other gods,
bound by their divine powers, stood before you in your womb.
If, at the beginning of creation, such a son were born to you,
he would cause all these three worlds, including the gods and the asuras, to fall.
Therefore, having recognized his strength and heroism, the gods beginning with Brahmā placed that embryo within their own wombs at the time of the previous creation for the sake of the worlds. (38)
When the twenty-eighth cycle of four yugas has arrived from the beginning of creation,
you will give birth to a son in the middle of the Tretā Yuga.
"O lady of beautiful countenance, carry this great embryo for as long as it takes for the Kṛta age and half of the Tretā age to pass; such is the time allotted to you by me. (40)
"O nurse, as long as this most terrible fetus is not yet born, you shall not experience the suffering of being pregnant, O beautiful woman. (41)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu then touched the earth— who was pregnant and greatly distressed—
with the tip of his conch at her navel.
Touched by Viṣṇu, the earth felt her body become light;
even while in the womb, she attained an extraordinary lightness that bestowed great happiness.
Just as a woman is when she is not yet pregnant, so too did she become;
yet, though she had conceived, that mother of the world became joyful.
Then, having spoken these words once more, the Blessed One again sought to appease the Earth with many conciliatory words.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Mother of the World, O Great Being, you are Fortitude, whose nature is sustaining. Because you sustain all things, O Goddess, you are celebrated as Dhātrī.
Because she is capable of sustaining the world through her patience,
and because all wealth has been placed within you, she is therefore called Vasumatī.
"O Goddess, when that suffering arises for your son, you shall remember me; I myself will protect your son. (48)
O Earth, this secret must not be revealed by you anywhere;
O Goddess, that which has been told by me is the supreme, most excellent secret. (49)
O highly fortunate lady, your embryo shall manifest during the intermediate period of the Tretā age,
once the hero Rāvaṇa has been slain by the one known as Rāma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to the goddess Earth, who was oppressed by the burden of her pregnancy, the Blessed Viṣṇu gave his command and vanished right there.
The queen Dharā, though slender and physically light, was endowed with strength; filled with supreme joy, she moved as if she were without a womb. (52)
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Earth from Suffering," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O best of the twice-born, after a great deal of time had passed...
In the region of Videha, there was a powerful king named Janaka.
Endowed with all royal virtues and increased in statesmanship,
he was truthful in speech, virtuous, skillful, devoted to the Brahmins, self-restrained, and pure.
Always devoted to the worship of gods, the twice-born, and his gurus, he became the protector of all people, like a father. || 3 ||
When that king had no son even though the time had arrived,
he became despondent and devoted himself to anxious reflection.
Once, that king then heard from the mouth of Nārada:
"There was a great, aged king, childless by name, Daśaratha."
The high-minded [king] obtained sons of great prowess through a sacrifice in the city of Ayodhyā, with Ṛṣyaśṛṅga at their head.
Through sacrifices performed by sages, that king obtained sons:
Rāma, Bharata, Śatrughna, and likewise Lakṣmaṇa.

Having heard that [the child] would be a great being, a great hero, auspicious and like the offspring of a god, King Janaka entered his own inner apartments and consulted with his wives for the sake of performing a sacrifice to produce a son.
Having then consulted with his four wives, headed by his principal queen, the king himself was initiated for the sake of the sacrifice.
Then the king, having appointed the family priest Gautama, the best of sages,
and his son Śatānanda as his domestic chaplain, performed the horse sacrifice.
Two beautiful sons were born to him on the sacrificial ground,
and one virtuous daughter, auspicious, who had entered within the earth.
Then, following the instruction of Nārada, the king himself plowed the sacrificial ground with a plow, extending as far as the boundaries of the sacrificial arena.
The king, filled with joy, obtained from Sītā born of that soil an auspicious daughter who was endowed with all the marks of excellence.
As soon as she was born, the Earth herself, having emerged from the underworld, spoke these words to King Gautama Nārada: || 14 ||
The Earth said:
"O King, this daughter Manoharā has been given by me to you;
accept this fortunate lady, who brings auspiciousness to both families. (15)
"By means of this [teaching], which has become for me in truth the cause [of its removal], my great burden shall come to an end;
I shall release myself from this terrible suffering of the burden. (16)
Rāvaṇa and other great heroes, as well as Kumbhakarṇa and others—other Rākṣasas who are difficult to overcome—shall meet their destruction because of her. (17)
And you, O King, shall obtain an invincible joy born of having a daughter,
as well as the purification of your debt to the gods and the ancestors.
"But, O best of men, one condition must be made by you with me;
I shall declare it to you in the presence of Nārada and Gautama. (19)
Now that the heroic Rāvaṇa has been slain, I shall happily give birth to a noble son upon your sacrificial ground, freed from the burden of distress.
O best of kings, you shall protect him like a son until my own son reaches the end of his childhood.
"O King, once his childhood has passed, I myself shall protect him;
you shall act in such a way that he possesses human nature just like you. (22)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of the Earth, King Janaka, filled with joy,
bowed to the Earth and spoke to her with gentle words.
The king said:
"O Sustainer of the World, I shall do according to your word which you speak;
grant me also my desire; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess. (24)
O Goddess, I desire to behold your form directly with my own eyes;
you are Śakti, the mother of the worlds—salutations to you, be gracious unto me. (25)
Having heard these words of Janaka,
the Earth then revealed her form to the king in the presence of the sages.

Seeing that beautiful sustainer of the world, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, holding a rosary and a lotus with her two bright arms which shone like long lotus stalks, the king bowed down perpetually. (27)
Then the goddess Earth, having repeatedly touched Sītā, the daughter born of the king, with her hand, spoke these words: || 28 ||
This mother of the world shall attain a human state as your daughter, O best of kings; wait for the appointed time.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus to King Janaka by name, the goddess Earth,
after addressing Nārada and the others, vanished right there.
Janaka also, having obtained his daughter who was endowed with all auspicious marks,
and likewise having gained two sons, went to his own home filled with joy.
Then, when the time had arrived and Rāvaṇa, the Rākṣasa, was slain by the powerful Viṣṇu in his human form, [the world was restored].
Then, having gone to the sacrificial ground of the King of Videha,
the Earth gave birth to a heroic son at the very place where Sītā had formerly been.
When the son was born, the goddess, the sustainer of the world,
then remembered Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, recollecting the agreement made previously at the proper time.
As soon as he was remembered, the god then kept his promise;
he manifested himself at the very spot where a son was to be born from the Earth.
Then the Goddess, having prostrated before the Supreme Lord and having praised the Lord of the World with truthful hymns, spoke these words repeatedly: || 36 ||
The Earth said:
"This son of yours has been born, delicate and of great splendor;
remembering our former agreement, you must protect him. (37)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Goddess, this son of yours shall possess great strength and prowess;
remaining wise, he shall assume a human state for a very long time. (38)
As long as your son maintains his human state, he shall enjoy prosperity and rule the kingdom for a long time. || 39 ||
But when he, having abandoned his human state, begins to act in this way, then it is not possible for his life to endure much longer. || 40 ||

When his sixteenth year has arrived, he shall obtain the kingdom; endowed with wealth, jewels, elephants, sovereignty, and multitudes of chariots, this heroic one, having attained great and constant prosperity, shall enjoy it.
In whichever age whatever disposition arises among men, he will act according to that very disposition; therefore, act accordingly.
His secret kingdom is that which is known as Prāgjyotiṣa;
there, in that city, this son of yours shall long rule the realm.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to the Earth and addressed her, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world,
while being watched by her, quickly vanished right there, O Master.
Having given birth at midnight to a son of great splendor, the Earth informed her progenitor of the secret that had been previously declared.
The King of Videha, having learned that his son had been born from the earth,
performed his ritual duties and arrived at that very sacrificial enclosure during the night.
Seeing him going toward the sacrificial enclosure, the Earth then,
without saying anything to that king, immediately vanished from sight.
Then, having gone there, the lord of Videha beheld his son upon the ground, radiant with a splendor like that of the moon, the sun, and fire.
Weeping profusely and affectionately, with his two feet moving and trembling, he was embodied and radiant with splendor, like a second Kārttikeya. (49)
Rising up and weeping, that child of great splendor passed beyond the sacrificial ground and went a short distance away, lying prostrate on his back.
Then, having found the head of a dead man there,
the boy placed his own head upon it and stood weeping for a moment.
Then the King of Videha, searching for the son of the Earth,
passed beyond the sacrificial ground and quickly reached him outside.
Having approached the radiant boy, who was like a blazing fire,
equal to the moon in beauty and comparable to the sun in splendor.
Just as fire [seizes] the fire-stick placed within it, the king himself seized that arrow which had previously been in the hand of the son of Pāvaka, recollecting his agreement with the Earth.
Grasping it by the region of its head, he beheld a human head;
and he soon announced that it was a human head to Gautama.
Then, taking the child with him and entering his own inner apartments,
he told the queen that a son resembling Guha had arrived.
Seeing him— broad-eyed, with shoulders like a lion's,
long-armed, broad-chested, lovely, and with the luster of a blue lotus petal—
she rejoiced and said to the king, "He is to be protected by me. (57)
Then the king also said to her: "O beautiful one, this is my son, born upon the sacrificial ground; let him be raised by you according to your own will."
That which was spoken in private by the Earth, that best of kings, true to his promise, did not disclose even to his beloved queen, nor even what she herself had said. (59)
On that day, the excellent king rejoiced, thinking, "May this earth protect my sons and the lineage of my sons," and the queen,
having obtained a son equal to the Son of the Suras (Indra), [was filled with joy].
The exceedingly wise one, having conquered his enemies, tasted and rejoiced in the object of perception.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Account of Birth in Hell," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 37 ||
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O best of kings, by the great seer Gautama, for him—
He caused the funeral rites to be performed according to human custom.
Because he stood placing his own head upon the head of Nara,
the best of sages therefore gave him the name Naraka.
The sage performed for him other childhood rites according to the Kṣatriya custom,
up to the ceremony of tonsure, using the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
In his palace grew a son named Naraka, whose splendor increased day by day like the moon in autumn. || 4 ||
That king himself constantly engaged him with human affairs;
then, through the wise Śatānanda, the son of Gautama,
he caused him to grasp that eternal kṣatriya character and human conduct.
In that very manner, the goddess Earth, in the guise of a nurse, caused her son to adopt the auspicious conduct of a human being.
At the very moment the son was born, the Earth herself entered the king’s inner apartments in the form of an illusory human woman.
Having entered there with the king's permission,
O best of the twice-born, that goddess became his nurse by means of her manifestation as Kātyāyanī.
For as many as sixteen years were yet to come for that boy,
she herself protected him and caused him to master the *saṃnaya*.
Growing day by day, that Naraka, the son of the Earth,
surpassed all the sons of the high-souled Janaka.
Then, by means of his body, prowess, beauty, and strength—
with his bow and mace— the hero indeed surpassed the sons of kings.
Skilled in the doctrines of the treatises and proficient in the science of archery,
he had become unassailable by other heroes at the age of sixteen.
Having seen his great strength and prowess, the lord of Videha then became not at all joyful in mind, seeing that his own sons were inferior to him.
Having cast out my sons, he will seize my kingdom;
such was the thought that occurred long ago to that great hero when the time had arrived. (14)
When the king delights all his sons within the inner apartments,
he does not experience any greater joy than that which comes from beholding Naraka.
Then Queen Vasundharā, the king’s consort, perceived that [thought] of the monarch; she was filled with wonder at that state of mind of the ruler.
Then once, the Great Queen questioned her husband, the high-souled Janaka, the best of kings and lord of Videha.
The queen said:
"O Lord, I ask you something; if it is not a secret of yours, then tell it to me, if there is compassion for me."
Whenever all your sons are sporting before you,
at that very moment you appear as if dejected upon seeing Naraka.
Because of that, my astonishment increases greatly day and night;
and both doubt and fear never leave me. (20)
This son of yours is handsome, heroic, and likewise skilled in policy and discipline; he is wise and possesses great strength. (21)
Why do you not praise your son, who is difficult for others to overcome?
I wish to know that; tell me the truth if it be so. (22)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of his beloved, the lord of the earth remained silent for a moment and then spoke these words to the queen: ||| 23 ||
The king said:
"O beloved, I shall tell you the truth regarding what I have now been asked by you;
however, wait for a period of three months."
There is a certain secret matter here concerning the King's decree;
therefore, I shall not tell you anything of that secret at present. (25)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
This conversation took place in the presence of the king together with his wife;
at that time, Pṛthivī, the nurse of the world, overheard it.
Having heard that conversation between the queen and the king,
the Earth [goddess] waited for the three-month period granted by the monarch to the goddess.
At that time, the king was despondent with the thought of hell;
after three months had passed, he would have reached his sixteenth year.
Then the king will speak of that secret to the queen;
consequently, my secret will become known. || 29 ||
Having thus reflected upon her son, that goddess, the sustainer of the world,
determined this course of action appropriate for the occasion and then set about it.
Then, having approached that king together with Gautama in private,
the illustrious Mother of the World spoke these words for the sake of her son.
The Earth said:
"O sinless one, that agreement which was given by me has been observed by you;
and this son of mine, Naraka, endowed with humility, has also been protected. (32)
My son has attained youth and has been instructed by you in statesmanship;
through your grace, my son is happy and has grown old in your house. (33)
I shall lead that son of mine back according to our previous agreement; give me your permission—may prosperity be yours—regarding Naraka’s fate.
And you, along with your family priest, must guard this secret agreement;
O King, I shall lead [him] away in concealment, so do not give way to distress.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to the king, the lord of Videha,
the Sustainer of the Worlds vanished right there while they were looking on.
The king, having accepted her words, went toward the earth to that very spot in her presence, accompanied by his priest.
Then once, the goddess Earth, assuming an illusory human form as the nurse of that high-souled one, spoke privately to Naraka. (38)
"O mighty-armed one, my mind is set on going to the Gaṅgā together with you.
If you go, O son, I shall go this very day by means of the chariot. (39)
Naraka said:
"I will not go according to my father's word without you, O mother;
having obtained your permission, I shall go to the Gaṅgā with you by means of a chariot. (40)
Having obtained permission from the great king, I shall fulfill your desire, as well as that of his son, the preeminent twice-born Śatānanda. || 41 ||
The nurse said: "This is not your father Janaka, who is the lord of all the worlds.
He is your father; go with me and see him in the Ganges."
"This father of yours, O dear one, will not hand over the kingdom to you;
go, my son, to him who is your true increaser."
O son, whatever secret there is in this matter, I shall tell it all to you at Gaṅgā itself; otherwise, my secrecy would be violated.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having gained conviction through the words of the nurse,
Naraka then abandoned his vehicle at will and proceeded to the Gaṅgā on foot.
Then, having reached the Gaṅgā and having duly bathed her son,
the Earth revealed herself to her own offspring.
Leaving behind that illusory human form,
the Mother of the worlds [assumed] a body dark as the petal of a blue lotus, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Vasundharā showed her son Naraka her own form, beautiful in all its limbs, lovely, and adorned with various ornaments.
Then the Earth related this story, which had arisen in the past, to her son, so that conviction might be born [in him]. (49)
The Earth said: "O son, as you grow day by day within my womb,
Brahmā and the other gods shall behold you themselves."
A son of the high-souled Viṣṇu, born from the earth when it is defiled, will assume an asuric nature and slay all of us. (51)
Thus, intent on this thought, the gods then devised an evil counsel:
"Let him not be born from a womb; let him remain forever within the womb. (52)
Then, O son, due to the evil counsel of the gods, you dwelt within my womb for many ages, enduring great suffering. (53)
"O son, because I have held you, I have become as if dead;
therefore, I have sought refuge in the eternal Blessed One. (54)
"Because you were born from the word of Nārāyaṇa, O son, know for certain that my words are true. (55)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, just as wonder arose in the sonless man, at that very moment the Goddess herself spoke these words to her son: || 56 ||
Then, on the sacrificial ground of the King of Videha,
it was ascertained what kind of agreement had been made with the King of Videha.
She related everything to the high-souled Naraka regarding how she had come to possess that human form. || 58 ||
Then Naraka, having heard the words of the Earth and being possessed of only a slight doubt, spoke once again to that Earth. (59)
Naraka said:
"O auspicious one, today Viṣṇu is my father and you are my mother, the Earth;
let the Lord of the World come for my very deliverance."
"If that very Acyuta, the Lord of all the worlds, speaks to me, saying 'I am your father and this woman is your mother,' then believe it, O auspicious one. (61)
I was nurtured by you as my nurse while you were in human form;
I wish to see that form if your true form is such as this.
The Earth said:
"O dear one, I am your mother; you have been recognized by me, my son.
I am the Earth, the sustainer of the world; this clay is indeed my very form. (63)
O mighty-armed one, your father is the immutable Lord Nārāyaṇa, the infallible creator of the worlds, the Great Soul who assumed the form of a boar. (64)
Therefore, you were placed within my womb by him; you, O Purūravas, dwelt there for a very long time, and when the time arrived, you were born and protected here by the king.

Naraka said:
"Your mother was not known to me before, yet you speak as if she were Mahālakṣmī;
and as for the words 'Viṣṇu is my father,' no such father has been known to me. (67)
I know my father, the king who is the lord of Videha;
I also know his wife, named Sumati, as my mother. (68)
"The world knows very well that all those brothers were his sons, that Sītā was my auspicious sister, and that Sumati was my mother. (69)
"And Kātyāyanī, who was just now made my nurse by you—all this has been falsely asserted by you to me at present. Tell me the truth as it is; tell me that truthfully, for I am your son. (70)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of her son,
the Earth (Sarvasahā) then related that entire previous account to her offspring.
Just as in former times there was union with Malinī for the Boar,
and how the embryo was held by the God and for what reason that occurred.
And how she, afflicted by the suffering of pregnancy, sought refuge in Mādhava, and how he granted a promise to Janaka. (73)
The sages said: "For what reason was this agreement granted by the powerful Viṣṇu, now that the heroic Rāvaṇa has been slain by the great-souled Rāma? (74)
"A great son shall indeed be born to you; of this there is no doubt.
O Guru, sever these doubts, for you are always our teacher. (75)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of the twice-born, the earth, oppressed by the weight of Rāvaṇa and others who feed on flesh, sank down five yojanas.
This one was born again from the womb of the earth through the power of Varāha;
and this great king also became like the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.

"O best of the twice-born, Viṣṇu had previously granted a boon to the Earth that when Rāvaṇa was slain, she would descend, afflicted by her burden; thus, under the pretext of removing her weight, she shall sink down. (78)
"O illustrious lady, having seen your former form and having heard the words of the Teacher of the World, faith has arisen within me; I shall abide by your command. (79)
Having heard her son's words, the Earth then first assumed that illusory human form and received him before her.
Just as she had assumed the form of Kātyāyanī by which Naraka was protected, she took that very form and abandoned her earthly body.
Then, having seen the nurse Kātyāyanī, Naraka immediately questioned her regarding the previous events that had occurred in the royal palace.
She related everything exactly as it had occurred previously in the house of her father, King Pālita.
Having gained confidence therein, he entered hell;
and then the goddess Earth resumed her own form.
Then, at the time previously ordained, the Earth remembered Hari, the Lord and Master of the world, bowing her head repeatedly. 85.
Then, as soon as he was remembered by the Earth, Mādhava, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
the Lord of the worlds, became gracious and appeared before her eyes.
Having seen that god who has Garuḍa as his vehicle— dark as the petal of a blue lotus and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace— the goddess Earth [was filled with joy].
With great devotion, he prostrated before the Lord of the World, who wears yellow garments, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, and who is imperishable; he touched the earth with his head. (88)
Then the Mother of the World also spoke these words: "O Supreme Lord, O Lord of the Universe, O Cause of the Cause of the World, be gracious! (89)
But Naraka, upon seeing Hari, closed both his eyes;
overwhelmed by His splendor, he then sat down upon the ground.
When her son named Naraka was then seated,
the goddess of excellent complexion then propitiated him for the sake of her son.
Being propitiated by the Earth, the imperishable Hari Nārāyaṇa then touched the son named Naraka with the tip of his conch shell.
As soon as he was touched by Hari, Naraka became Sudarśana;
and being seen, he became full of energy and powerful.
Then, rising up, Naraka bowed down with devotion before the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, prostrating himself fully (sāṣṭāṅga) again and again.
Then the hero, having gained confidence, bowed down to the earth;
and, endowed with supreme devotion, he prostrated before the illustrious lady. (95)
With palms joined in reverence, he stood before him saying nothing at all out of fear;
then, for his sake, the Earth entreated Mādhava.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; observe your promise.
I was given to you as a son by you, O Lord of the entire world. Fulfill that which was promised for this purpose.
The Blessed One said:
"O lady, whatever you previously requested of me for the sake of a virtuous son, all that has indeed been granted; even my own kingdom has been given to you, my child."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, took up the one named Naraka along with the Earth and plunged into the Gaṅgā.
Having submerged himself, he reached the city of Prāgjyotiṣa in a mere moment,
where Kāmākhyā, the mistress of Kāmārūpa, resides in its center.
And that region, which had previously been occupied by Śambhu for the sake of his own kingdom, was now inhabited by powerful, cruel, and ignorant Kirātas. (101)
There he saw Kirātas resembling golden pillars, devoid of knowledge,
shorn of purpose, and solely intent on consuming liquor and meat.
Viṣṇu saw them enraged, and those best of the twice-born saw Viṣṇu.
There, their powerful leader named Ghaṭaka stood,
resembling a pillar of gold and blazing like a fire.
Filled with rage and accompanied by a great fourfold army,
he approached the Lord of the World and the mighty Naraka.
Having approached with a shower of arrows, King Ghaṭaka, the ruler of the Kirātas, together with his Kirāta followers, rained down upon the imperishable Lord.
Then Mādhava also dispatched his son Naraka, who was even more valiant,
to do battle with the king of the Kirātas.
Taking up his bow, Naraka fought there for a very long time with those even more powerful beings, discharging many weapons and missiles.
Then that powerful Naraka, taking up a crescent-headed arrow and fixing it to the bowstring, severed the head of the Kirāta king.
Enraged, the hero slew the foremost of the Kirātas and many generals, just as a lion slays elephants.
Then, when the king was enraged, some were intent on flight, while others among the Kirātas sought refuge in Naraka. || 110 ||
Having slain those who were fighting and having protected those who had sought refuge, Naraka went to his father, bowed down, and then reported [the matter]. || 111 ||
Naraka said:
"O father, Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Kirātas, has been slain by me, as have his other generals; what else shall I do? (112)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Slay the Kirātas as long as you do so;
having put to flight those who flee, protect those who have come for refuge. (113)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that hero Naraka, having mounted a white elephant—
four-tusked, massive in body, and the mount of the Kirāta king— [proceeded].
Equal to Airāvata in prowess and like Garuḍa in speed,
he put the Kirātas to flight as far as the regions inhabited by those dwelling in the quarters.
Returning once more to his father, he spoke these words.
Naraka said:
"Those Kirātas have been put to flight and have taken refuge as far as the edge of the ocean. (116)
Indeed, the great Kirāta lord named Ghaṭa has been slain,
having mounted a swift elephant equal to Airāvata in its qualities.
Now, command whatever else remains to be done by me.
The Blessed One said:
"As long as the Karatoyā remains ever united with the Gaṅgā up to the eastern region, and as long as Lalitakāntā exists, so long shall your city endure. (118)
Here, the illustrious goddess Yoganidrā, the mother of the world,
dwells eternally in her beautiful form as Kāmākhyā.
Here is this Lauhitya, the king of rivers, the son of Brahmā;
right here the guardians of the ten directions are established, each upon their own seat.
"O son, here Mahādeva himself, Brahmā, and I are established; and the moon and the sun dwell here constantly. (121)
All have come for the sake of sport to this excellent, secret place;
here dwells auspicious Śrī, and likewise there is much to be enjoyed.
Brahmā, stationed in its center, created the constellation Prajyotiṣa;
from that arose this city named Prāgjyotiṣa, equal to the city of Śakra.
Dwell here, may prosperity be yours; for you have been consecrated by me in person, and having taken a wife along with your ministers, you shall become a king of great power.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu himself, with the consent of Śambhu,
then settled all the Kirātas at the edge of the eastern ocean.
Having previously established a boundary for Lalitakāntā,
the Kirātas continued to dwell as far as the edge of the ocean.
Then, having again made the beautiful Lalitā his boundary marker,
he proceeded as far as the Karatoyā River, which is the abode of Kāmākhyā.
Therefore, having driven out the many Kirātas who transgressed the Vedas and Śāstras,
he settled there the twice-born and the eternal social orders.
Just as the study of the Vedas, giving of gifts, and other such practices continue constantly,
so did the omnipresent Lord act, causing the sages to dwell there.
At that time, the entire country known as Kāmarūpa became devoted to the recitation of the Vedas and dedicated to the duty of giving. 130.
Then Hari chose for the sake of a son the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, named Māyā, who was equal to Naraka in her virtues. (131)
Having married her himself in that best of cities, Hṛṣīkeśa consecrated his own son as king together with her.
And Mādhava made the city well-guarded by means of a mountain fortress—a water-fortress, auspicious on all sides, and difficult even for the gods to assail. (133)
Then, twenty-five thousand well-trained elephants with four tusks each, equipped with the trappings of great mahouts, [belonged] to the king of the Kirātas.
Whatever numerous jewels and various kinds of troops there were, as well as horses and ornaments—all that Naraka seized. (135)
Whatever fine ornaments, banners, and decorations belonged to the king,
Viṣṇu himself then gave them all to his son.
And he gave him a chariot difficult to obtain in the three worlds,
covered with eight wheels of iron and measuring half a yojana in width.
It was yoked with eight thousand horses swift as thought,
and it was richly adorned with various jewels and gold, with its width extending over the area of the altar-platform.
It was resplendent with a great golden vajra-banner,
enriched with banners on golden staffs, and possessed a pole made of lapis lazuli gems.
It was always covered with skins produced from lions and tigers,
draped with iron nets, garlanded with clusters of small bells,
equipped with all kinds of weapons, and endowed with many illusions. || 140 ||
And he gave him a spear that destroys all enemies, its body blazing with garlands of flames, appearing like a fire to the dry grass of his foes. 141.
And at this time, the Lord of the Earth spoke these words in the presence of the great-souled Nāraka for the benefit of Nāraka. (142)
The Blessed Lord said:
"You shall never employ this power against human beings, especially, except when there is a danger to your very life."
This wife of yours, the princess of Vidarbha, is equal to you in her virtues;
she shall remain beautiful for as long as you live. (144)
But you, indeed, will be diligent for the sake of progeny during the Tretā age;
however, when the end of the Dvāpara age has arrived, the progeny will come into being there.
O son, if you wish to live for a long time, you must never engage in conflict with sages or even with brahmins.
Neither with kings nor with gods is it fitting for you to have enmity,
O unconquered one, for you dwell in the midst of a great fortress.
Dwelling together with hosts of celestial women and possessing great enjoyments, may you remain for a long time on your own mountain, which takes any form at will, O Tūtuka. (148)
"O son, you shall not worship any other deity besides Mahādevī Mahāmāyā, the Mother of the World, Ambikā, who is known as Kāmākhyā. (149)
If you dwell otherwise than this, you will be deprived of life;
therefore, O Nāka, observe the agreement with all possible effort.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Having spoken thus to his own son Naraka, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu dismissed him and addressed these words to the Earth in secret: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca ityuktvā bhagavān viṣṇurnarakaṃ tanayaṃ svakam | tamapāsya rahasyenāṃ pṛthivīṃ vākyamabravīt || 151 || Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus to his own son Naraka, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu dismissed him and addressed these words to the Earth in secret:
"O beautiful one, whatever I have previously told you that ought to be done by you—teach all of that quickly for the sake of attaining prosperity and avoiding hell. (152)
O Sustainer of the World, when you yourself speak of slaying him,
then some human being will destroy Naraka.
The Earth said:
"This effort of mine for the sake of progeny would be censurable without offspring;
therefore, O Lord, grant me offspring and you shall protect them. (154)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Saying "So be it" to that Earth, the purifying Viṣṇu addressed Naraka and vanished on the spot in an instant.
When Hari had departed for his own abode, the Earth herself led that child to the place which she had previously been told by Hari. || 156 ||
At that time, the wise Naraka was one who had reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras;
he was skilled in the conduct of Brahmanical life, generous, and devoted to giving.
Devoted to the worship of Kāmākhyā on the great mountain Nīlakūṭa, he—
possessing great enjoyments and great fortune, and free from affliction by enemies—
ruled his kingdom for a very long time, like Indra in the abode of the gods. || 158 ||
Then the King of Videha, having heard of the splendor of Naraka, went to see Naraka accompanied by his son, his wife, and Guṇa. || 159 ||
Having gone to the city of Prāgjyotiṣa, situated within Kāmarūpa,
the king beheld Naraka, who was equal to the autumnal moon in splendor.
That king considered the city of Prāgjyotiṣa to be like Amarāvatī;
he regarded Naraka, adorned with excellent attendants and ornaments, as the Lord of the Gods himself.
Janaka said: Then Janaka spoke all those words to his queen:
"This is your illustrious son, protected by you, named Naraka. (162)
A beloved son has been born to the Earth in the form of Ghṛṣṭi;
behold him united with Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe. || 163 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, King Janaka related the account exactly as it had occurred in the past,
and how hell had come to pass.
Then, having stayed there for a long time in the city of Prāgjyotiṣa with joy, the king,
the lord of Videha, was honored by Naraka.
Therefore, surrounded by his own attendants, he went to his own abode.
Thus that Naraka was born as a son of the Earth;
possessing the nature of a lowly Asura, he dwelt upon the earth for a long time. || 167 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Consecration for Naraka," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The thirty-ninth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
That illustrious King Naraka was long-lived and possessed mighty arms.
Then he ruled the kingdom for a long time with a purely human disposition. || 1 ||
When the Tretā age had passed and the Dvāpara age remained,
there was a great asura named Bāṇa in Śoṇitapura.
His city was Agnidurga, and he was the powerful friend of Śambhu;
indeed, that invincible one with a thousand arms was the beloved son of Bali.
Great loving-kindness arose in him toward Naraka;
through constant mutual visits and acts of favor toward one another,
a great affection developed between them, like that between wind and fire.
And that Bāṇa, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe,
then moved about everywhere without fear, possessed by an asuric nature.
Due to that association, having witnessed his wondrous deed, that hell began to sport with him out of a sense of shared affinity.
O twice-born ones, he no longer honors the Brahmins as he did before,
nor is he as joyful as formerly in sacrifices and acts of charity.
Neither did he approach Viṣṇu in that manner, nor did he worship the Earth;
at that time, such devotion toward Kāmākhyā had not yet arisen within him.
In the meantime, the son of Dhātu, the most excellent sage named Vasiṣṭha, went to Prāgjyotiṣa to behold Kāmākhyā. || 9 ||
Naraka did not grant Vasiṣṭha access through the gate to go and see that goddess Nīlakūṭā, who was stationed within the fortress.
Then the sage Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, being enraged, spoke these harsh words to the heroic Naraka, censuring him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"How is it that you do not allow the son of the Earth, the direct offspring of Varāha,
to go in such a state to see the Goddess, as he is a Brāhmaṇa?"
"O son of the Earth, what action befitting your lineage are you performing?
Having gone to the goddess at Prāgjyotiṣa, I shall worship her who consists of the entire universe. (13)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that King Naraka, the son of Kṣiti, when his time had come,
insulted him with harsh words and cast him out.
Then that sage, filled with anger, cursed King Naraka.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"By that very being in human form through whom you were born, [you shall soon perish]."
Death shall come upon you, O wicked defiler of the boar race! 15.
"O sinner, when you are dead, I shall worship Kāmākhyā, the Great Goddess and mother of the worlds; stay here, for I am going to my own abode. (16)
O evil one, as long as you live, even though you are named Kāmā, the mother of the world,
may you vanish along with all your retinues.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, that sage, the son of Brahmā, departed for his own abode;
Vasiṣṭha, having been cast out by that son of the Earth, was exceedingly enraged.
When Vasiṣṭha had departed, Naraka, filled with wonder, quickly went to the abode of the Goddess on the great mountain Nīlakūṭa.
Having gone there, he did not see her who is named Kāmā and can assume any form at will; nor did he see her vulva-circle or any of her attendants.
Then, becoming despondent, Naraka called to mind his mother, the Earth, as well as his father, the Lord of the World, the immutable Sovereign.
O twice-born ones, even those two did not then come within the range of his perception,
for Śambhu was one who had transgressed his agreement and was devoid of moral conduct.
Having waited there for a long time, Bhauma Vajradhvaja, not having obtained Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu, then returned sorrowful to his own abode.
As he was going toward his own home, that son of Bhūmi beheld his city abandoned by its former splendor, like a woman who is soiled.
But when the Goddess had vanished, that city became devoid of the teachings of the Vedas, with its merit diminished and its people lacking in devotion.
Neither gods, nor Brahmins, nor great sages went there;
his city became a place where only the festivities of minor sacrifices took place.
Many calamities arose and many people died;
even the king of rivers, the Lauhitya, then became depleted of its waters.
Then, seeing many such portents, he considered his own death to be imminent due to the Brahmin’s curse.
Then the governor of Prāgjyotiṣa, his mind overwhelmed with grief,
went to his friend Bāṇa, the son of Bali, reflecting upon him in his mind.
That friend was equal to his very life-breath, constantly intent on protecting one another,
like Bāṇa and Naraka, or like the two Aśvins, the physicians of heaven.
In the meantime, the powerful Bāṇa, a friend and companion of Śambhu,
who was highly wise, sought to win him over by bestowing sacred mantras.
Such was the firm resolve of Vajraketu at that time,
and he dispatched a radiant messenger toward the city of Bāṇa.
Having gone to Śoṇitapura by means of his swift-moving chariot,
he then quickly reported the news concerning Bhauma to Vāṇa.
Just as [the city] was cursed by Vasiṣṭha, and just as Ambikā disappeared,
and just as an obstacle arose in the excellent city named Prāgjyotiṣa.
Just as there had been a transgression of the agreement between Bhūmi and Āditya,
so that messenger reported it to the son of Bali.
That lord himself went to hell to honor Samākāramitra’s complete defeat by fate.
It had a body variegated with gold, was yoked to three hundred horses,
possessed iron wheels, was covered in tiger-skin, and was adorned with a peacock banner.
He ascended the great chariot, which was covered by a white parasol with a golden handle and adorned with clusters of small bells, and was fashioned from a multitude of various jewels.
Possessing a thousand arms, glorious, and accompanied by the fourfold army,
he quickly arrived at Prāgjyotiṣa, the city of Bhauma.
Having reached that city, the mighty-armed Bāṇa beheld his friend, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, as well as that city, both bereft of their former splendor.
Urged by his son, the son of Kṛśānu (Agni) asked him appropriately:
"For what reason has your city become bereft of its splendor? (41)
Bāṇa said:
Your body does not shine as it did before, nor is your mind very joyful; tell me the reason for this. (42)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus questioned, Naraka, the son of the Earth,
related to him everything regarding how the curse of Vasiṣṭha had come to pass.
Having learned from the messenger what had previously been heard from the mouth of Bhauma,
Bāṇa spoke again to Vajradhvaja.
Bāṇa said:
"You should not harbor resentment toward the happiness or sorrow of embodied beings;
these two revolve like a wheel, and no one is permanently deprived by them. (45)
However, the wise must apply a remedy there for the sake of prosperity;
you, too, ought to provide a remedy at this very moment.
Whosoever among men on this earth, or even a Dānava, a Daitya, or an Asura, prospers through extraordinary splendors— || 47 ||
Neither a Rākṣasa nor a Kinnara, nor even Śakra himself, can endure them;
for by practicing deceit here and there against the hosts of gods in whatever manner possible, he surely causes him to fall from his prosperity.
For him, the eternal and ancient Lord Viṣṇu is ever most dear;
He does not allow even the slightest undesirable thing to affect the mind of one who is devoted to Him. 49.
"He who propitiates Viṣṇu while acting to the detriment of Śakra—grant him a boon with a hidden flaw, and then destroy him from this place. (50)
Viṣṇu, when propitiated for a long time, grants desired objects;
when worshipped with great physical hardship, he becomes fully pleased. (51)
What man has ever obtained such incomparable prosperity by worshipping his chosen deity—neither before nor even by those of the past? (52)
Previously, neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Īśvara was propitiated by you;
therefore, great obstacles have arisen for you today in your domain.
Or rather, Viṣṇu, though he is the protector, is not compassionate by nature;
however, he was repeatedly propitiated by her at the word of the Earth.
"Viṣṇu has granted you a loophole; you must not offend the twice-born.
Otherwise, we have heard that you shall become one whose prosperity is destroyed. (55)
"O King, you have offended the supreme sage Vasiṣṭha;
because of that, by his mere remembrance, Viṣṇu has not come to this earth. (56)
Therefore, O friend, understand the crookedness of Harimedhas;
O Bhauma, a posture of indifference is no longer appropriate for you. (57)
That conviction you held in your mind, thinking "this is my father," was indeed your father Varāha; he has gone to another world. (58)
As for what you have heard—that even Vārāha is a portion (aṃśa) of Hari—tell me, who among you utters such a reproachful statement that he is merely "a portion of a portion" (aṃśāṃśa)? (59)
Therefore, perform now the worship of either Śambhu or Brahmā;
he, being pleased with you, will grant your supreme desired wish.
Whether it be an obstacle, a sage’s curse, or a great affliction causing intense suffering,
it will soon come to an end once Śambhu or Vidhi is propitiated.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Bhauma, having gained confidence from Bāṇa’s words,
spoke these words with great pleasure, his voice steady and gurgling.
Bhauma said:
"O Bāṇa, you who are devoted to your friends, that which has been spoken by you for my benefit—that supreme practice of austerity—must be performed by me without delay. (63)
"You have stated the reason why Viṣṇu is not to be propitiated by me;
likewise, Śambhu is not to be propitiated because he is hidden within my city. (64)
Therefore, O Mitraka, Brahmā is to be propitiated at your word, O mighty-armed one, in the vicinity of the waters of Lauhitya, the son of that [sage]. 65.
And I have been taught by you, O wise one, as a disciple by a teacher, and as a friend by a friend, with exceedingly beautiful conciliation. (66)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, that mighty-armed Vajradhvaja,
who was devoted to his friends, then duly honored that friend as a friend would.
Having worshipped him as was fitting and having sent away the son of Bali,
the son of the Earth desired to perform an extremely rigorous propitiation of Brahmā.
On the bank of the great river Lauhitya,
he ascended Mount Brahmācala and settled there to perform austerities.
For a hundred years according to human reckoning, that prince honored his grandfather by observing a vow of subsisting solely on water.
At the end of a hundred years, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, being well-pleased,
appeared in person and stood before Naraka.
"I am pleased with you; I shall grant you a boon. Choose a boon, O observer of noble vows!
Thus did the Lotus-Seated One speak to Naraka at that time.
Having seen the Lord of all worlds, the manifest one seated upon a lotus, he bowed with palms joined in reverence and, with his neck bent low in humility, spoke. (73)
Hauma said:
"O best of gods, grant me this one boon: invincibility against all the gods, asuras, rākṣasas, and those born of the divine race. (74)
O Lord of the World, may my lineage remain uninterrupted as long as the moon and sun shall shine; let this be my second boon. (75)
May those goddesses, beginning with Tilottamā, who are endowed with excellent form and qualities—may they all be my beloveds, numbering sixteen thousand. (76)
"May invincibility and constant prosperity never forsake me at any time; thus, O Grandfather, these five boons have been chosen by me from you today. (77)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Deluded by illusion and forgetting the sage’s curse, Bhauma chose another boon; yet the sage’s curse remained as it was.
Having granted all those boons with the words "So be it," the Grandfather spoke thus to the celestial maidens at the twilight at the end of the Dvāpara age: || 79 ||
"O son of Tarkshya, Tilottama and the others shall become your wives on the surface of the earth;
however, O son of Vajradhvaja, they must not be united with you in sexual intercourse until Narada comes to your city."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of all the worlds vanished in an instant; and Naraka, having attained supreme joy, returned to his own abode.
Then that city, Muditaloka, was frequented by prosperity;
it was always filled with enthusiasm and entirely free from fear and obstacles.
Filled with herds of cattle, horses, and elephants,
it was like Amarāvatī, the beloved city of the king of the gods.
Having heard that Bāṇa had likewise obtained boons and had completed his ascetic penance,
Vajradhvaja then personally approached Bhauma.
Having gone to the city of Bhauma, called Prāgjyotiṣa, Bāṇa inquired after his friend Naraka, who was established in ascetic penance.
Where did you perform penance, or what vow did you observe?
What kind of boon was obtained by you? You ought to tell me. (86)
Your entire city has been seen, crowded with joyful people, filled with multitudes of horses, elephants, and jewels, and resounding with auspicious sounds. (87)
Today it is seen by you that [the earth] is to be protected, filled with grain and free from disease;
or rather, tell me how Brahmā granted this boon to you.
Bhauma said:
Brahmā himself, assuming the form of a mountain, has descended here to sustain Kāmeśvarī.
In that place, he himself now spends the day,
until Vasiṣṭha arrives from afar.
O son of Bali, this very one, who is served by hosts of gods and is a portion of the supreme immortals, shines here in my city;
there, I alone subsist on excellent water.
And indeed, for hundreds of years, I performed austerities.
On the bank of the Lauhitya, frequented by dense breezes,
enchanting, and bestowing happiness upon all living beings,
the face of one engaged in ascetic penance was beheld.
May there be for me but a single autumn among the hundreds of autumns. || 91 ||
Thereupon, the four-faced one became pleased and spoke to me directly for my benefit:
"I am gratified with you; choose a boon as you desire."
Then, appearing before him and saying, "I shall give it; take it," [he offered it]. || 92 ||
"May I be invulnerable to those born of the divine race; likewise, may my lineage never be severed by the gods,
and may my prosperity never forsake me."
And there were excellent women endowed with fresh youth. || 93 ||
"These five boons were chosen by me from him;
he too, having given his promise, departed for his own abode.
Then, with joy, I returned to my own city."
Accompanied by his most eminent ministers, he [addressed] them once again. || 94 ||
He gladdened the citizens, his kinsmen, and his attendants with gifts, honors, and food.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words spoken by Bali, the son of Bhauma did not rejoice at that moment.
He spoke these words to the son of the Earth, which were appropriate for that occasion and born of truth. (96)
Bāṇa said:
O friend, at that time before Brahmā, your mind was not inclined to disregard the curse of the sage.
But how, O prince, will your welfare here necessarily be constant in the future? (97)
There is no making of what has already been done; for an action presided over by destiny, that which is destined to be will necessarily come to pass, and even Brahmā cannot obstruct it.
Therefore, having made peace with those very great heroes, the asuras who resemble fire,
place them at the forefront and appoint them to the office of ministers.
Having stationed these heroes at the gate— beings difficult even for the gods to approach—
pass by the Lord of Gods, provided that you have obtained a boon.
Since a boon was granted by the Creator according to the prescribed rite, you ought to perform its fulfillment;
being childless, beget a son upon your wife.
Having spoken thus, Bāṇa departed after being duly honored by him;
Naraka then proceeded to carry out the words of his friend.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Earthly Austerities," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 39 ||
Chapter Forty.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In due course, when his wife had reached her season, that Naraka [approached her] at the proper time.
Bhagadatta, Mahāśīrṣa, Madavanta, and Sumālin. || 1 ||
The son of the Earth begot these four sons, who were possessed of great being and great heroism, and difficult for other heroes to overcome. || 2 ||
Then, at the word of Bāṇa, having bound Hayagrīva and likewise Muru,
he brought them together and appointed them to the office of commander-in-chief.
Having heard that Mura was nearby and that Hayagrīva had been struck down by Bhauma,
all those gods who were then present upon the earth assembled together.
Having heard that Hayagrīva had arrived with Muru,
the two asuras named Niśunda and Sunda, together with their soldiers, [advanced].
Then the Daitya Virūpākṣa arrived there with them all;
thereafter, Naraka came to the western gate accompanied by his army.
He made Mura the guardian of the eastern gate, and likewise Hayagrīva at the northern; Nisunda was at the eastern gate, while Virūpākṣa was at the southern.
In the midst [of his forces], he consecrated Pañcajana and Sunda for the command of the army;
he also yoked Muru and six thousand nooses with razor-sharp edges.
Thus, having disregarded his former and even more ancient ministers, he was honored by the son of the earth as the guardian of the city's gate.
That son of the Earth, having abandoned his former disposition, became constantly delighted by the very Asuras as if he were an Asura himself. (10)
Having assumed an asuric nature, he oppresses the dwellers of heaven;
he knows neither the gods nor all the sages, nor indeed anyone at all.
Accompanied by Hayagrīva, he quickly defeated Sureśvara;
thus, manifesting his asuric nature, he wandered upon the earth.
At Bāṇa’s word, he indeed harassed the sages and Śakra;
having thrice defeated the Lord of the Gods with Hayagrīva as his ally.
The pair of earrings of Aditi, renowned throughout the three worlds, which distill the nectar of all jewels and are supreme in removing suffering and obstacles. (14)
Naraka, the son of the Earth, being fearless of the sage’s curse, carried them away;
thus harassing the gods, the sages, and the Brahmins,
the son of the Earth ruled his kingdom in Prāgjyotiṣa for five thousand years.
In the meantime, the goddess Earth, oppressed by a great burden,
went for refuge to the gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu for the sake of protection;
and having bowed to the Creator together with Kṛṣṇa, the Earth spoke this.
The Earth said:
"Those Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Daityas who were slain by Hari have now been born in the palaces of kings, arrogant in their strength. (17)
I am unable to bear their exceedingly great burden;
they are all innumerable, and I do not venture to count them.
There were eight hundred thousand of them, the foremost among whom were possessed of great strength;
yet even now, I am not able to carry those who possess such exceeding power.
Bāṇa, the heroic son of Bali, Kaṃsa, Dhenuka,
Ariṣṭa, Pralamba, Sunāmā, Muru, and Śala.
The two wrestlers Cāruṇa and Muṣṭika [fought] the exceedingly powerful Jarāsaṃdha,
as well as Naraka, Hayagrīva, Nisunda, and Sunda.
Virūpākṣa, Pañcajana, Hiḍimba, Baka, Bala, Jaṭāsura, Kirmīra, Anāyudha, and Alambuṣa— || 22 ||
And Saubhākṣya, Jarāsaṃdha, and the monkey Dvivida;
the great Daitya Śrutāyudha and another, Śatāyudha.
And also Subāhu and Atibāhuka, the sons of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
as well as the Kālakañja Daityas who dwell in Hiraṇyapura.
But because of the agitation of these [mountains], I am shattered day by day;
I am unable to support the worlds, so let the best of gods destroy them. (25)
O best of gods, if you do not provide protection,
then I shall now go helplessly to the netherworld, utterly shattered.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having heard her words, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara spoke thus: "O Earth, we shall effect the removal of your burden."
Having entrusted the goddess Earth to the eternal one, all the gods gratified Mādhava for the sake of relieving her burden.
But he, the Lord himself, being pleased, said to all the gods, "Indeed, descend to the earth with your own portions in order to remove the burden," and then remained here. (29)
Then, for the purpose of relieving the burden of the earth, he descended into the womb of Devakī;
and the gods, knowing that the eternal Viṣṇu was about to incarnate, [prepared].
And Rambhā, Tilottamā, and other goddesses endowed with beauty and virtue produced sixteen thousand [daughters] upon the earth. (31)
While all those excellent women were sporting on the slopes of the Himalayas, Narakāsura, the son of the Earth, saw them and then carried them off by force.
Having thus violated those goddesses, he led them toward Prāgjyotiṣa;
they then made a request to Naraka regarding sexual union as a condition.
"O Bhauma, until Nārada returns toward the city, provide protection for us and do not release us from sexual union. (34)
O hero, he will come to you before long through our grace;
for we have been seen by him, and together with him we shall come to be united with you.
Thus entreated by them, Naraka, the son of the Earth, then recalled the words of Brahmā and repeatedly said, "So be it. (36)
In the meantime, the divine Lord, the creator of the world,
was born from the womb of Devakī and grew up in the house of Nanda.
Having slain Kaṃsa, Keśin, Pralamba, and many other Daityas,
he established his residence at Dvārakā within the waters of the ocean.
There, eight maidens were accepted by him according to his own dharma:
Kālindī, Mānuṣī, Rukmiṇī, and Ramaṇī; then— (39)
Satyā, the daughter of Nagnajit, and Lakṣmaṇā of the beautiful smile;
Suśīlā, endowed with virtuous character, and likewise the chaste Jāmbavatī.
Then, while he was indeed deeply attached to these women,
thirty-six years passed for him as he remained in the company of Baladeva.
O best of the twice-born, his sons, headed by Pradyumna and Sāmba, were born there endowed with great strength and proficient in both the sacred scriptures and the science of weapons.
Many Daityas who were a burden to the earth were then slain;
delighted and sporting, he dwelt in Dvārakā.
Then Śakra, having arrived there, was greatly tormented by Naraka;
accompanied by his hosts, he proceeded toward Dvārakā to behold Kṛṣṇa.
Having gone there and embraced Kṛṣṇa, who is worshipped by the world,
he was honored by him in many ways and sat upon a golden seat.
Śakra related to Hari the activities of Naraka, both as they had occurred in the past and how they were unfolding at that moment.
Śakra said:
Listen, O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, to the purpose for which I have come;
I shall tell you all of it, so do not entertain any doubt regarding that.
The son of Bhūmi was an asura named Naraka, the crusher of the gods;
in former times, he was long-lived and protected by Viṣṇu and the Earth.
Now, disregarding Viṣṇu, that invincible son of the Earth, at the word of Bāṇa, propitiated Brahmā. (49)
Having obtained boons from Brahmā, he indeed became exceedingly arrogant;
he never once remembered Mādhava or even the Earth.
Formerly, that righteous-souled one was a performer of vows who propitiated the gods;
now, having resorted to an asuric disposition, he oppresses everyone.
Out of delusion, he stole the two earrings of Aditi, which were born of nectar;
he harassed the gods and sages, being devoted to doing what was displeasing to the brahmins.
He, who moves at will and is difficult to overcome, constantly afflicts me as well;
he is a conqueror of gods and daityas and is invulnerable to all embodied beings. (53)
And since there is one who watches for your weakness, destroy that evil for the sake of your prosperity;
for your sake, all the gods have sent these daughters of the gods and Gandharvas. (54)
Formerly, on Himavat, the chief of mountains,
fourteen thousand two hundred and two [beings] were brought down.
All those maidens, that wicked and unassailable one, arrogant due to his boon, forcibly carried away with the assistance of Hayagrīva. (56)
Having gathered all those jewels that exist in the ocean, on the earth, and in the third heaven, and having overwhelmed both gods and men, (he shall rule).
On the bank of the Lauhitya-tīrtha, he constructed Mount Maṇi;
having caused a beautiful city named Alakā to be built upon that mountain, [he settled there]. || 58 ||
He caused all those women of the gods and gandharvas to dwell there;
they all wore their hair in a single braid and were deprived of all sensual enjoyment. || 59 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, make them have a protector; they await you alone, until the sage Nārada arrives at your city.
"O Bhauma, you shall not exert yourself in sexual union until then.
Thus did they establish a compact with the evil-minded Naraka. (61)
And at that time, Nārada arrived at the city of Prāgjyotiṣa,
when you were about to go to that excellent city to slay Naraka.
Therefore, slay that evildoer, who is like hell itself and difficult to approach—a thorn in the side of gods and men. (63)
Because of his slaughter, the goddess Earth shall not suffer grief for her son;
for he himself had requested from the gods that his own death should come to pass.
Therefore, slay that most wicked one, the sinful man Naraka;
having slain him, rescue even the jewels among women as well as the other treasures.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Śakra, the Lord of the worlds then and there indeed vowed to slay the son of the Earth.
Having promised his slaughter along with Śakra, Keśava then set out on an expedition toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Having mounted Garuḍa, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā alone, departed for Prāgjyotiṣa; Vāsava went to the third heaven.
As the two of great splendor, Kṛṣṇa and Śakra, ascended and proceeded toward heaven,
the Yādavas beheld them there like the sun and the moon.
Being praised by Gandharvas, gods, and hosts of Apsarases,
Kṛṣṇa and Śakra were seen in an instant as they had departed into the sky.
Then, in an instant, the Lord of the World reached the beautiful city of Prāgjyotiṣa, which had been brought under the control of Naraka by Garuḍa.
That fortress was surrounded on its sides by six thousand terrifying Maurava nooses with razor-sharp edges, standing high like the nooses of Death.
And he saw Nārada departing from that city;
for that illustrious celestial sage had come toward Naraka.
Then, having gone to Prāgjyotiṣa and being honored by him, Nārada announced the agreement regarding women to Naraka at their meeting. (74)
Today is the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
however, on the ninth day, O son of the Earth, we shall encounter great calamity. (75)
Then, on the fourteenth day, these women, having bathed well, should be enjoyed by you in sexual union there according to your pleasure. (76)
Having heard Nārada’s words, Naraka, bewildered by fear,
stationed both his reserves and his vanguard within the city.
The kingdom was protected by guards and guarded on all sides;
filled with both fear and joy, Bhauma observed the situation.
At that moment, Kṛṣṇa, whose banner bears the emblem of Garuḍa, reached the city of Prāgjyotiṣa and first arrived at its western gate.
Having cut the nooses into many pieces with six thousand razor-sharp blades,
he slew the Daitya Mura along with his followers and kinsmen.
Six thousand great heroic Dānavas were stationed at the gate;
they, along with Muru, were slain by Hari with his discus at that very moment.
Having slain Mura, he then killed thousands of his sons and six others,
and with his discus, he cut the remaining Dānavas into pieces.
Then, having crossed over a multitude of many rocks, Janārdana crushed Nisunda along with his hosts and his followers.
He who, possessing the prowess of a great hero, could formerly fight the gods alone for a thousand years, even surpassing Śakra himself. (84)
Having bypassed Hayagrīva, the Blessed Keśava,
the son of Devakī, slew him in the midst of the region known as Lauhitya.
Having slain Virūpākṣa and Sunda in Audakā,
the mighty and supreme lord then killed Pañcajana, O hero.
Having slain these massive-bodied, highly valiant, and unassailable foes,
the Lord of the World reached the city named Prāgjyotiṣa.
Being praised with shouts of "Victory! by all the deities stationed in the sky and by the high-souled Nārada, he entered like a sovereign lord.
Endowed with splendor, radiant, and adorned with ramparts and watchtowers,
Viṣṇu wondered whether that city could be Indra’s Amarāvatī.
There, a great battle took place, with various weapons raised,
causing terror to the timid and increasing the joy of the brave;
it was just like the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Then, standing upon Garuḍa, the mighty-armed Janārdana struck down those many Dānavas with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow.
Having slain eight hundred thousand and eight hundred Asuras, the mighty-armed one approached that Naraka.
Then, having heard that many asuras had fallen and seeing the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa of great strength mounted upon Garuḍa, that Naraka [was filled with rage].
He recalled Vasiṣṭha’s curse, the agreement with Mādhava,
the words of Nārada, and likewise the loophole in Brahmā’s boon.
When the time had come, he met with Keśava;
then, remembering the words of Bāṇa, he considered nothing but battle as the highest goal.
He ascended that excellent chariot made of gold, which had a banner of thunderbolts,
was equipped with eight iron wheels, and measured three *nalvas* in length.
Yoked with thousands of horses, adorned with a banner bearing the thunderbolt,
equipped with various weapons and provided with many quivers, Naraka, the son of the Earth, went forth quickly with his army. (97)
As he proceeded swiftly toward the battle, remembering the former words of Hari, he regarded the honored human state as contemptible and likewise the demonic state.
In an instant, he beheld Kṛṣṇa seated upon Garuḍa,
the infallible Lord bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the excellent sword.
Hari, the Supreme, adorned with a crown and earrings, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, his breast illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and wearing yellow garments.
That hero, Naraka, the son of the Earth and the valiant lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, fought with that powerful Viṣṇu. || 101 ||
Then, as he fought near Kṛṣṇa, Kālikā—who resembled Kāla—appeared;
she was tall, with red face and eyes, and bore a sword and a spear.
He beheld Kāmākhyā, the enchanting mother of the worlds.
Then, filled with wonder and fear upon seeing her, the mother of the worlds,
the asura Naraka fought, thinking only that he must wage war.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having engaged in a truly great and wondrous battle with him— such as had never occurred before among either gods or men— [105]
Then, after engaging in a long bout of martial play with that son of the Earth, Mādhava struck him, gladdening the Lord of the Gods.
Then, with his Sudarśana discus, Hari cut Naraka in two in the Middle Country; mangled, he fell to the earth.
Then, his body severed and fallen upon the earth, it shone like a mountain of red chalk split by a thunderbolt. || 108 ||
When her son had fallen, the goddess Earth beheld his body and, knowing that the time had come, then endured the surge of grief. || 109 ||
Taking the pair of earrings herself from Aditi, Kāśyapī approached Govinda and spoke these words: || 110 ||
The Earth said:
"In the past, when I was lifted up by you in the form of a boar,
my son Naraka remained there due to the contact with your body."
This very son of yours has now been both protected by you and caused to fall. || 111 ||
"Accept these two earrings, O Aditi, which grant all desires;
and always protect his progeny, O Govinda. (112)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Goddess, the slaying of Naraka was previously requested by you alone for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden; therefore, he has been slain by me."
"O Goddess, at your word I shall protect his lineage;
I will consecrate my grandson Bhagadatta as king in Prāgjyotiṣa."
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Blessed One Madhusūdana entered the inner apartments of Naraka, the treasury of wealth.
There the hero beheld various pure jewels heaped together like silver mountains. (116)
Mādhava beheld mountains of pearls, gems, and corals, as well as mountains of lapis lazuli,
peaks of silver, and peaks of diamond.
Heaps of gold, golden staffs, banners made of jewels,
various mounts, vehicles, and couches.
Inlaid with gold and jewels, they were both costly and immense;
whatever was seen, and however much wealth, gems, and precious stones there were—119.
And such a thing has not been seen by us anywhere else on earth except in the abode of hell—not even in the realm of Kubera, nor of the lord of men, nor of Yama, nor of the lord of the waters. (120)
There were as many treasures of wealth there in the abode of hell as there were;
then Keśava also arrived at that very place, accompanied by Nārada.
Then, having inspected the wealth within the inner apartments— both essential and most essential—
the slayer of enemy heroes took whatever was to be taken from them in great abundance.
That Vaiṣṇava power which had indeed been bestowed by the mighty Viṣṇu,
the son of Devakī seized after slaying Bhaumāsura.
Then Keśava, accompanied by Pṛthivī and Nārada,
[encountered] Bhagadatta, the son of Bhīma, at the excellent city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Having consecrated the king, he then established him in the middle of the city;
and upon seeing Bhagadatta thus consecrated, the earth [rejoiced]. || 125 ||
Then, for the sake of his grandson, he requested that spear from Keśava;
and Keśava, at the word of the Earth and with the approval of Nārada,
gave that spear to Bhagadatta with a very pleased mind.
That weapon known as Kāñcanasrāvin, which Bhauma had previously brought back after conquering Varuṇa, Hari took up.
Eight bhāras of gold flow from it every day;
it is one krośa in width and half a yojana in height.
All the most excellent jewels, as well as four-tusked elephants, and fourteen thousand honored women [were given]. (129)
Keśava caused the multitude of Daityas to be driven toward Dvārakā.
Those celestial maidens had previously been forcibly abducted by Naraka;
having released them from their bondage of braided hair, Hṛṣīkeśa [acted]. || 131 ||
Having honored them repeatedly with divine garments and ornaments, and having placed them upon a celestial chariot guarded by strong and powerful sentries, [he departed]. (132)
Under the supervision of Nārada, they all transported that mountain of jewels, which Bhauma had constructed for the sake of the celestial maidens, back toward Dvārakā.
Filled with a flood of precious gems and possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
that [mountain] was uprooted by the Lord of the World and placed upon the back of Garuḍa.
In the same manner, Mādhava, the gracious Hari, having placed the Varuṇa umbrella upon Garuḍa, sat together with Satyabhāmā.
Having addressed Bhagadatta and the Earth,
the heroic Lord of the World set out for Dvārakā swiftly by way of the sky.
Carrying Keśava along with Satyā effortlessly through the sky, he departed, holding a golden umbrella that dripped with gold and was adorned with jewel-mountains.
In an instant, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, reached Dvārakā and attained joy along with all his kinsmen and attendants.
Thus Kālī, Mahāmāyā, known as Kālikā, who is identical with the universe, [united] with Viṣṇu, the lord of the worlds, Hari, the master of both the transcendent and the immanent. (139)
Thus, one who possesses both attachment and aversion truly deludes himself regarding the Creator of the world, who is composed of knowledge and pervades the universe.
For he favors his friends and strikes down his enemies;
deluded by women, he takes pleasure in them and is even bewildered by the pairs of opposites. (141)
Thus, O brahmins, has been told to you how the asura Naraka came to be,
how he obtained his boons, and what his deeds were.
"O Brahmā, since you have been propitiated by the son of the Earth with the thought that he was a mere arrow, what else is appropriate? Let the best of the twice-born say. (143)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Naraka-upākhyāna of the glorious Kālikā-purāṇa. || 40 ||
