The forty-first chapter.
The sages said:
How did Kālī, the daughter of the mountain, become the mother of the worlds?
How did Dākṣāyaṇī, having abandoned her body, obtain Hara as her husband? || 1 ||
O high-minded one, tell us clearly as we ask: how did she take away half the body of the wielder of the Pināka bow?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O tigers among sages, how Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa,
formerly became the daughter of the Mountain and how she gave up half of her body.
When the goddess Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, formerly cast off her body,
at that very moment she went in spirit to Menakā on the Himavat mountain.
When the daughter of Dakṣa was sporting with Hara on the Himālaya, Menakā then became her well-wishing companion.
O twice-born ones, having formed the thought in her mind, "May I become her daughter," the goddess then gave up her life and became the daughter of Himavat.
When in ancient times Dākṣāyaṇī gave up her life-breaths due to Dakṣa’s anger, at that very moment the goddess Menakā, desiring to propitiate Śiva, [entered her body].
To Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, the eternal Yoganidrā, the deluder of all beings, and the refuge of all the gods. || 8 ||
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, she [should worship] on the ninth lunar day with sweetmeat offerings, flour preparations, milk-rice, perfumes, and flowers.
Beginning in the month of Caitra, she, being pure and desiring a son, worshipped him daily for twenty-seven days.
Having fashioned an earthen image at the Oṣadhiprastha on the Gaṅgā,
she sometimes remained without food and sometimes observed her vows.
Desiring the highest prosperity, the goddess Menakā spent twenty-seven years with her mind fixed on Śiva.
At the end of twenty-seven years, the Mother of the World, who is identical with the world, became exceedingly well-pleased; appearing before his very eyes, she spoke.
The Goddess said:
"O Goddess, whatever you have requested from me, ask for that now;
I shall grant you all that which may be desired in your heart. (14)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the goddess Menakā, having seen Kālikā standing visibly before her, bowed down and spoke these words: || 15 ||
O Goddess, your form has now been seen by me directly.
O Śivā, if you are pleased with me, I wish to offer praise to you.
Then Kālikā, the enchantress of all, saying "O Mother," embraced Menakā with her two beautiful, rounded arms.
Then the goddess Menakā praised Kālikā, the supreme sovereign Śivā, who stood visibly before her, with pleasing words.
Menakā said:
I bow down to Caṇḍikā, the sustainer of the world, who impels the abode of the universe;
I bow to the mother of the world, the accomplisher of all desires and goals. (19)
Thus, I bow to Ānandā, who consists of knowledge, the yogic sleep that gives birth to the universe,
the auspicious and pure one whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
I bow to you, O auspicious Citti, who are composed of illusion, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the destroyer of the grief of devotees, the consort of Kāma, and the source of well-being. 21.
You are that which, arising here from the predominance of *sattva*, is eternal and yet appears as the eternal intellect (*buddhi*) of living beings;
you are the cause for ascetics to sever their bonds.
In this world, such power belongs only to those like me. || 22 ||
You are the accomplishment of the Sāmans, the hymn of praise, as well as the recitation;
you are the long-lasting mode of conduct of the Yajus formulas, and you are the ritual violence of the Atharvaveda. You are she.
O beloved, fulfill my constant desire. || 23 ||
The multitude of elements is driven by those constituent parts—both eternal and non-eternal—which reside within it;
you are their power, eternally of an everlasting form.
What woman is capable of speaking what is appropriate regarding you?
You alone are the earth, the sustainer of the worlds;
you alone are the eternal, whose very nature is primordial matter (prakṛti),
by whom even the one whose form is Brahman is brought under control.
Therefore, O Mother, may you, who are eternal, be gracious to me. || 25 ||
O Jātavedas, you are the form of the power residing [within]; you are the burning power of the sun’s rays;
you are the delighting power of the abundant moonlight—I praise and bow to that very Ambikā. 26.
You are the woman for those who love women; you are the sacred knowledge for those of sublimated vitality;
you are the desire of all the worlds, and likewise, you are the illusory power (māyā) of Hari.
She who, assuming manifold forms, eternally effects creation, preservation, and destruction here,
and who is the cause of the bodies of Brahmā, Acyuta, and Sthāṇu.
Therefore, be gracious to me today once more; salutations to you!
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Kālikā, the mother of the worlds, spoke once more to the goddess Menakā, saying, "Choose a desired boon."
Then that illustrious woman first chose a hundred sons,
endowed with heroism and long life, and possessed of prosperity and supernatural powers.
Afterwards, likewise, he [gave] one daughter who was beautiful, endowed with virtues, a source of joy to both families, and rare to find in the three worlds. || 31 ||
Then the Blessed Lady, fulfilling her desire, spoke with a smile to Menakā, who resembled a sage.
The Goddess said: "Let a hundred sons, endowed with your virility, be born;
among them, one shall first be born as the foremost and most powerful. (33)
And I myself shall become your daughter, born of gods, humans, and rākṣasas, for the welfare of the entire world. (34)
"O Vaṃ, you shall always be easy in childbirth, likewise ever devoted to your husband, unfading in beauty, and fortunate. (35)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, the Sustainer of the World vanished on that very spot;
and Menakā, having attained joy, entered her own abode.
Then, when the time had arrived, [he struck] Maināka, the best of mountains,
which even today remains in the midst of the ocean together with its wing.
The goddess Menakā gave birth to the Lord of the Gods, who had arrived out of rivalry;
that virtuous woman then gave birth in due order to ninety-nine other sons.

Because of their great heroism and because they were great beings endowed with all virtues on every side, that goddess Kālikā, who is the yogic sleep (yoganidrā) and identical with the universe, [then appeared]. 39.
Having abandoned her former form as Satī, Śivā went to Menakā for the sake of birth; in accordance with the agreement, she entered the womb of Menakā.
Having arisen and come forth like the goddess Lakṣmī from the ocean,
she appeared in the spring season on the ninth lunar day through the conjunction with the asterism.
She was born at midnight like the Gaṅgā from the orb of the moon;
and when she had been born, the quarters of the sky became serene.
A favorable wind blew— deep, fragrant, and auspicious—
and there occurred a rain of flowers as well as another rain of water.
The fires blazed and then became calm; the thick clouds thundered and then ceased.
As soon as she was born, everything returned to a state of well-being.
Seeing her thus born, dark-complexioned and resembling the petals of a blue lotus,
the goddess Menakā attained a joy of exceeding delight.
And the gods repeatedly attained incomparable joy there;
and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, stationed in the sky, offered hymns of praise.
But after the funeral feast had been performed, Himavat called that daughter of the Himalayas, who was dark as the petal of a blue lotus, by the name Kālī.
By all the Andhras, that daughter of the mountain was celebrated by the name Pārvatī, and likewise by the name Kālī. (48)
Then that auspicious goddess grew up in the palace of the King of Mountains, like the Gaṅgā during the rainy season or like moonlight in autumn. 49.
Day after day, as she was being fanned, the lovely-limbed lady repeatedly attained greater beauty,
just as the dark fortnight approaches the lunar orb day by day until it reaches a single digit.
Having attained childhood, Kālikā experienced great joy while playing with her friends, just as the river Kālindī does with its multitude of streams.
O best of the twice-born, the six qualities, having been won over by her in a previous birth, went of their own accord to that goddess, just as dark clouds approach the rainy season.
That goddess surpassed the daughters of the gods with her virtues;
she excelled all the apsarases in beauty and the daughters of the gandharvas in song.
Even in her childhood, that auspicious girl, who was constantly dear to her circle of kinsmen,
delighted her relatives, as well as her father and mother, with her excellent qualities.
Constantly offering praise to her mother and devoted to the worship of her father, she was always accompanied by her brother; thus, at that time, she became the Mother of the World.
That Mother of the World is always present as a maiden;
she dwells near her father like the Yamunā beside the sun.
Then once, having placed her nearby, the Himavat mountain stood together with his sons, filled with great curiosity.
Then the sage Nārada, having arrived there from the world of the gods,
beheld Himavat seated comfortably together with his sons.
He beheld Kālī nearby, like a streak of light from the sun,
or like the full moonlight perfectly increased on an autumn night.
Honored by that mountain and having accepted a seat,
Nārada first inquired of the mountain regarding his circumstances.
Then, having learned the news, the sage Nārada, who was skilled in speech, spoke these words to Menakā, gladdening her.
Nārada said:
O King of Mountains, this daughter of yours has been raised by Ruci, like a pure ray of the moon; she is the primordial digit, endowed with all auspicious marks.
She will become the ever-favorable beloved of Śambhu and Hara;
this ascetic woman shall bring his mind under her control.
And he, too, will not marry any other wife besides her;
the kind of love that exists between these two is like unto nothing found among any others.
Whether she existed in the past, will exist in the future, or does not exist at present, by her many deeds for the sake of the gods must be accomplished. (65)
O best of mountains, by this very [moonlight], Hara shall become Ardhanārīśvara through friendship, just as the moon becomes so through its nectar-like radiance.
When Hara has been gratified by her ascetic penance, this Suvarṇagaurī, possessing a golden luster, will become half the body of Hara in her own abode.
This Kālī, who is as fair as lightning, shall become your daughter;
later, she will attain fame by the name Gaurī.
"You ought not to set your mind on giving this to anyone else here; and you shall keep this secret from the gods, not making it public. (69)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the celestial sage Nārada,
the learned Himavat spoke these words in reply to the muni.
Himavat said:
"It is heard that Mahādeva, having abandoned all attachments and possessing self-control, performs silent austerities, hidden even from the gods. (71)
O celestial sage, how could he, while established on the path of meditation, cause his mind—which is dedicated to the Supreme Brahman—to falter? In this matter, I have a great doubt.
The supreme imperishable Brahman is like the flame of a lamp;
he perceives it within everywhere, but does not look outward.
"O twice-born one, it is thus constantly heard from the mouths of the Kinnaras;
how then was Hara able to cause such a heart to falter? (74)
It is specifically heard that Hara previously established an agreement with the daughter of Dakṣa; listen as I relate it to you. (75)
"O Dākṣāyaṇī, O virtuous and beloved one, I shall not take any other woman as my wife except for you; I tell you this truth. (76)
Thus Satyā had previously made an agreement with him;
now that she has died, how could he take another woman? (77)
Nārada said:
"O King of Mountains, you should not entertain such anxiety regarding your daughter;
she has been born as Satī for the sake of Hara alone—of this there is no doubt. (78)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the divine sage Nārada related everything on the mountain regarding how Satī was born from Menakā.
Having heard that entire previous account from the mouth of Nārada, the Mountain,
together with his sons and wife, then became free from doubt.
Then, having heard that story from the mouth of Nārada, Kālī, her face downcast with shame and her countenance broadened by a smile, [remained there]. (81)
Taking her by the hand and lifting up her face, the Mountain smelled her head thoroughly and seated her upon his own seat.
Then Nārada spoke once more to that daughter of the mountain,
gladdening the King of Mountains as well as Menakā along with her children.
Nārada said:
O King of Mountains, what need have you for a throne of your own?
Śambhu’s thigh shall always be her seat.
O Mountain, having obtained the seat of Hara, your daughter will find constant satisfaction; indeed, such satisfaction as this cannot be found anywhere else on any other seat.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken these noble words to the king of mountains, Nārada departed for the third heaven at that very moment by means of celestial vehicles.
The Lord of Mountains as well, filled with anxiety, joy, and confusion,
entered the interior of the immovable one, which was like the heart of a lotus.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Arrival of Nārada," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 41 ||
The forty-second chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the meantime, Śambhu quickly abandoned that lake at that time.
He went to the supreme plateau of the Himalayas, where the Gaṅgā descends.
There, where the Gaṅgā formerly fell after flowing from the city of Brahmā,
there is that most excellent ridge not far from the city of Oṣadhīprastha.
Therein, Bharga is one's own self, the imperishable, higher than the highest,
consisting of consciousness and knowledge, eternal, of the nature of light, and undisturbed.
The Lord whose banner is the bull meditated with one-pointed focus upon that which pervades the universe, which resembles a lamp, and which is devoid of duality and free from distinctions.
While Hara was absorbed in meditation, the Pramathas became intent on meditation;
some others were the Gaṇas, such as Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and the rest. || 5 ||
The highly fortunate beings who were stationed as gatekeepers at the eastern gate—
those hosts there likewise did not utter even a single sound.
It was heard that they all then remained there in silence;
however, other groups who were stationed at a great distance continued to sport there.
With flowers, petals, and parched grains, and with water from mountain springs,
they gathered jewels while being adorned with minerals from the mountains.
Having thus seen Hara departing with his retinue, the King of Mountains emerged from Oṣadhiprastha to his own abode, accompanied by his attendants.

He approached for the sake of worship and honored him as was appropriate; and Śambhu, established in his primordial state, accepted that worship with supreme faith, just as he had done of old on the head of the Gaṅgā.
Suddenly honored by him, the Lord of the World, whose banner is the bull, established in the yoga of meditation, spoke as if smiling to the King of Mountains.
Īśvara said:
"I have come to this peak of yours to perform secret penance;
act in such a way that no one comes near me. (12)
You are the Great-Souled One, the abode of the world and the eternal refuge of the sages,
as well as of the gods, the rākṣasas, the yakṣas, and the kinnaras.
It shall be an eternal dwelling for the twice-born and forever purified by the Gaṅgā;
near this city of yours is the plateau known as Gaṅgāvatāraṇa.
O best of mountains, I have taken refuge in you; now do what is appropriate for this.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds, whose banner bears the bull, became silent;
then the King of Mountains spoke these words to Śambhu out of affection.
Himavat said:
"O Lord of the worlds, O Supreme Lord, I am purified by you having come today to this region; what further task remains for me? (17)
O Lord of the World, though you could not be attained by the gods even with great austerity and diligent effort, you have now appeared here of your own accord.
There is no one more fortunate than I, nor is there anyone more meritorious than I,
since you have arrived at the slopes of the Himalayas for the sake of ascetic penance.
O Supreme Lord, I consider myself superior even to the king of the gods,
since I have been obtained by you along with your retinue according to your own will.
Having spoken thus, the King of Mountains then returned to his own abode and addressed his attendants and hosts as well for the sake of their observance.
From this day forward, no one shall go to the descent of the Gaṅgā without my command;
indeed, I shall punish anyone who goes against it.
Having thus quickly restrained his own [senses], he took sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and fruit,
and went at once into the presence of Hara accompanied by his sons.
Then, having gone to Hara, the Lord of the World, who was then absorbed in meditation,
she bowed down his daughter Kālī, who was endowed with all virtues.
Having placed each item, such as sesame seeds and flowers, before him, and having brought his daughter forward, that king of mountains spoke thus to Śambhu: || 25 ||
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, this daughter of mine has been instructed by you to propitiate you;
she has been brought here, desiring to worship you. (26)
O Lord Śaṅkara, may I always serve you together with my two friends;
grant me permission for this service if you have favor toward me. (27)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Śaṅkara beheld her, who had first attained youth,
whose complexion was like the petals of a blooming blue lotus, and whose face resembled the full moon.
She displayed the grace of her attire through the mass of her hair, which was gathered in a single braid;
she possessed a neck like a conch shell, large eyes, and was radiant with a pair of beautiful ears. (29)
She was beautiful with a pair of arms whose extremities were as long as lotus stalks;
her breasts were thick, full, and elevated, resembling lotus-shaped earrings.
She possessed a slender waist from which her breasts rose, with the palms of both hands red, and was beautiful with a pair of feet resembling land-lotuses. || 31 ||
With a waist that was slender, yet possessed of large, firm, and radiant hips;
with shapely calves and thighs like those of an elephant; and adorned with a deep-set navel. (32)

With well-rounded and beautiful calves, possessing the three deep qualities and the six elevated features, she was complete in all auspicious marks and difficult to find even in the three worlds. (33)
She was the crest-jewel of the host of women, capable of causing even the mind of a sage—firmly ensconced within the cage of meditation—to falter at the mere sight of her. (34)

Having seen her— who was constantly devoted to asceticism, captivating to those engaged in meditation, the cause of obstacles, an increaser of passion, and capable of assuming any form at will— || 35 ||
At the word of the King of Mountains, Śaṅkara,
whose vehicle is the bull, accepted his daughter for the sake of seeking her out, out of respect as well.
Īśvara said:
That king of mountains spoke thus to your daughter:
"Let her serve me constantly with effort; indeed, let her remain here free from fear. (37)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to the goddess, Hara took her for service;
this indeed is great fortitude—that an obstacle does not cause an obstruction.
Whatever austerity is performed by the twice-born after they have reached a place free from obstacles; || 38 ||
He who proceeds despite overcoming the cause of obstacles is met with impediments;
yet such is your greatness and the fortitude of ascetics through their penances.
Then the Lord of Mountains returned to his own city with his attendants,
while Hara remained absorbed in the yoga of meditation, intent upon contemplating the Supreme.
Kālī, accompanied by her two friends, remained there daily serving Mahādeva, the moon-crested Lord, through her coming and going.
Once, Kālī, accompanied by her two friends, was performing auspicious singing before Śaṅkara and then produced the *pañcama* melody.
Once, while performing the ritual bath and honors for Hara with her two friends, she dwelt there, gathering sacrificial fuel such as kuśa grass and flowers.
Once, standing fixedly before him and gazing at the face of the Moon-bearer, she, filled with desire, thought of the Moon-crested Lord.
When she was occupied with her duties, she performed those tasks;
but when she was free from such work, she then meditated upon Hara.
"This Lord of Beings has given me his hand in marriage;
he shall sport with me through various manifestations of true affection. (46)
Thus absorbed in thought, Kālī, ever intent on meditation, worshipped the Supreme Lord even in her dreams. (47)
When Kālī had gone to the mountain and was meditating upon Maheśvara, then the Lord of the Vedas and the Bhūtas beheld her established in her natural state. (48)
But at that time, Giriśa did not accept Kālī as his wife because she had shaken off her body while still containing the seeds within her womb, for she was one whose vow remained unfulfilled.
Mahādeva, too, having seen her, then thought this:
"How might this daughter of the mountain perform the vow of ascetic practice?"
I shall take as my wife Kālī, who has observed her vows, who is devoid of the seed of pregnancy, my own beloved, born from a womb, and utterly defiled. (51)
Furthermore, the seed of the womb is liberated through vows and purificatory rites;
therefore, how could it be appropriate for Kālī to perform a vow at such a time? 52.
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Beings then remained with his mind absorbed in meditation;
as he was intent upon that meditation, no other thought arose within him. (53)
Kālī, however, served Śambhu with intense devotion every day, constantly meditating upon the form of that great-souled one. (54)
Hara, intent on meditation, forgot the previous events and, although Kālī was constantly present before his eyes, he did not see her even while looking at her.
In the meantime, a Daitya king named Tāraka,
arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, oppressed the gods and all the worlds.
Having brought the three worlds under his control, he himself indeed became Indra;
having put all the gods to flight, he established the Daityas in their respective positions and appointed them to the ranks of the divine beings themselves.
Yama does not subject the worlds to his own will while that king reigns;
likewise, the sun does not scorch the worlds according to its own will out of fear of him.
The Moon, acting as his companion in sport, joined with the Wind through its rays and performed service for him incessantly.
By the command of that king, a wind blew, fanning him, ever endowed with fragrance, depth, coolness, and softness.
Dhanada also, having diligently gathered wealth according to its essence,
performed service to him with great care, desiring his deliverance.
By the command of Tāraka, Agni became his cook;
then, according to his wish, he prepared various side dishes and foods.
Nirṛti, always accompanied by all the rākṣasas, out of fear caused them to drive away his horses, elephants, and vehicles. (63)
Amusing the gods, he who hated them sported with dancing apsarases, praising bards and genealogists, and singing gandharvas.
Thus, agitating all the worlds throughout the three times,
he extracted the essence from the essences even among the gods.
Oppressed by him, all the gods, led by Śakra,
being without a protector, went for refuge to Brahmā, the supreme lord.
Having prostrated themselves before that high-souled Grandfather of all the worlds, all those gods, led by Puruhūta, spoke as follows: || 67 ||
The gods said:
"O Lord of the World, the Daitya Tāraka, emboldened by your boon, has forcibly cast us out and seized our realms for himself. (68)
"Whether we remain here or flee elsewhere, he oppresses us day and night;
indeed, wherever we look in every direction, we see Tāraka. (69)
Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Vāyu, as well as Manuṣyadharma, accompanied by all their attendants. || 70 ||
O Brahmin, afflicted by him and acting at his very command, all these gods, subservient to him, are devoted to performing their duties without any desire of their own. (71)
The Daitya seized all those celestial women in heaven and all the hosts of Apsarases, as well as whatever essence existed in the worlds.
Sacrifices do not proceed, ascetics do not practice austerities, and not even the slightest bit of the duty of giving or other such virtues prevails in the worlds. (73)
His wicked general is a Dānava named Krauñca;
having gone to the depths of Pātāla, he oppresses the subjects day and night. (74)
Therefore, this entire triple world has been seized by Tāraka; O Grandfather, save the whole universe from that evil! 75.
And point out that place where we shall dwell;
for we have been displaced from our own abode by him, O Lord of the World, O Teacher of the Universe! (76)
You are our refuge and our teacher; you are our protector, father, and progenitor.
You alone are the creator, the sustainer, and the skillful ordainer of the worlds.
Therefore, O Lord of Creatures, as long as we have not been consumed in the fire known as Tāraka, it is not fitting for you to act in such a manner now. (78)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard the words of the gods, the Grandfather, the creator of the world of Brahmā,
replied to all the gods with words appropriate for that occasion.
Brahmā said:
"O dwellers of heaven, it was by my very boon that he named Tāraka was empowered; therefore, his death at my hands is not fitting."
And a recompense must be made by you for the service rendered;
however, being thus urged, I am unable to repay it adequately. (81)
Therefore, just as that which is called a star will itself go to its destruction, so should you act; I am merely the one who provides the instruction.
"Tāraka is not to be slain by me, nor likewise by Vanamālin;
he is not to be slain by Hara, nor even by other gods or men. (83)
"This very boon has been granted by me to that one performing penance;
a means has also been devised, so let the best of gods carry it out. (84)
In former times, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, having cast off her body for the sake of rebirth,
went to the goddess Menakā, the wife of the King of Mountains.
The Mountain begat her in the womb of Menakā, just as in ancient times my son Bhṛgu begat the renowned Lakṣmī. (86)
"O gods, Mahādeva will certainly take her hand in marriage,
so that he may soon become enamored with her."
Therefore, act in such a way that you may effectively counter his splendor—
that Śambhu of sublimated vital essence— by causing him to discharge his seed.
No other woman whatsoever is capable of performing this;
from whatever of his vital energy (tejas) has fallen away, the son who is born from it [shall be]. (89)
He alone is the slayer of the one named Tāraka; no other exists.
That daughter of the King of Mountains has now reached full youth. (90)

At the command of Himavat, Kālī, along with her two companions, constantly sought out Hara as he performed austerities on a mountain plateau; she attended upon the omniscient Supreme Lord while he remained absorbed in meditation.
Mahādeva, absorbed in meditation, did not desire even in his mind that woman of supreme beauty in the three worlds who stood before him.
O gods, act with diligence so that Candraśekhara may obtain Kālī as his wife without delay, just as he desires.
"Heaven is your own rightful place; therefore, even though I am a deliverer, I shall turn back.
Having come together, go forth, free from all anxiety."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of all the worlds approached the one named Tāraka;
having drawn near and addressed him with these words, he spoke as follows.
Brahmā said:
"O Tāraka, do not rule over the kingdom of heaven!
For that purpose, you did not perform penance in the past at the proper time."
"No boon has been granted by me, nor has sovereignty over heaven been given by me;
therefore, renouncing heaven, exercise your rule upon the earth. (97)
"O Asura, all things to be enjoyed by the gods shall arise for you right there.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of all the worlds vanished on that very spot.
Having abandoned heaven, that Tāraka descended to the earth;
remaining right there, he constantly harassed the gods.
He made the mighty Indra pay tribute and remain under his command.
Indra, constantly bestowing upon him objects of enjoyment for the gods and enjoying them himself in turn, was unable to satisfy the Lord. (100)
Thus afflicted by him and tormented by his wrath, the gods,
following the instruction of the Creator, exerted themselves against the lineage of Hara.
Then Indra, having consulted with his preceptor and reached a firm decision, summoned Kusumeṣu and spoke these words: || 102 ||
Indra said:
"By you this entire universe is protected; by you the entire universe is brought forth.
In ancient times, you were the cause of the pleasure of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. (103)
Just as Brahmā formerly accepted Sāvitrī, who had observed her vow with affection, so too did Mādhava accept Lakṣmī and Hara accept the virtuous Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
Just as they were created in the past for the pleasure of those lords of the gods, so too, O Kāma, always create delight for me, who am among living beings. 105.
O Kāma, you are not dear to anyone in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor on the surface of the earth; indeed, you are always regarded as such by all living beings in the worlds. 106.
You are the protector and the creator of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans; you abide within their hearts. (107)
Therefore, for the benefit of the entire world—including gods, dānavas, yakṣas, humans, and great-souled beings—perform your endeavor. (108)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Having heard these words of Śakra, Makaradhvaja, being well-pleased by those nectar-like words, spoke thus to the king of the gods: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca | etacchrutvā vacastasya śakrasya makaradhvajaḥ | devarājamuvācedaṃ suprītastadvaco'mṛtaiḥ || 109 || ||| Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of his, Śakra, Makaradhvaja, being well-pleased by those nectar-like words, spoke this to the king of the gods. || 109 ||
Madana said:
"O Śakra, you already know that deed for which I am the master;
therefore, command me to perform whatever is appropriate and possible for me."
My arrows are indeed five, and they are soft, made of flowers;
likewise, my bow is made of flowers, and its string consists of bees.
Rati is my beloved wife, Vasanta is my minister, the Malaya-breeze is my charioteer, and the ocean of nectar is my friend. (112)
Śṛṅgāra is my general, and the *hāvas* and *bhāvas* are my soldiers;
all of them are gentle and non-cruel, and I too am of such a nature. (113)
Whatever task is appropriate for someone, the wise person should employ him in that;
therefore, assign me to whatever work is suitable for me. (114)
Indra said:
"O Mind-born One, whatever I desire to have performed by you—that is a task worthy of you; may you be fully occupied with it. (115)
"O Mind-born One, although you have already accomplished your task and are successful therein, that which is difficult for others to achieve, I nevertheless appoint you to perform. (116)
For it is heard that the bull-bannered Lord was performing austerities,
established in meditation upon a plateau of the Himalaya mountain, free from desire for the sake of obtaining a bride.
Now, by her father’s command and with the consent of Hara, Kālī constantly attends upon him as he performs austerities, accompanied by her two friends.
Although she had reached the prime of youth and was a beautiful jewel among women,
Mahādeva, absorbed in meditation, did not desire her even in his mind.
O Bull-bannered One, act for the benefit of the gods and of the worlds as well, so that passion for her may arise within you. (119)
Just as the bull-bannered god, full of passion, had rejoiced with Satī, so too did he rejoice with this daughter of the mountain for her sake. (120)
Indeed, whatever splendor has fallen from Hara for her sake,
he who is born from that shall deliver us from Tāraka.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having heard the words of the king of the gods, the Mind-born One (Kāma) remembered the curse formerly pronounced by Brahmā, which had now reached its appointed time.
When Kāma struck with his flower-arrows the one who was performing the twilight rites after he had tested his weapon, then Brahmā cursed him.
"O best of the twice-born, you shall be consumed by the fire from Śambhu’s eye when Hara takes the hand of the Daughter of the Mountain in marriage. (124)
"Then you shall attain wholeness with your body";
remembering this curse of the Creator, the fish-bannered god (Kāma) remained fearful. || 125 ||
At the word of Śakra, Kālī consented to unite with Hara, and she further spoke these words appropriate for that occasion: || 126 ||
Madana said:
"O Śakra, I shall do as you say; I will bring about a union between Hara and Kālī, the daughter of Dakṣa, the Daughter of the Mountain, just as it was in former times."
"However, O deluder of Hara, you must grant me one favor:
when I, through the power of Sanmohana, enchant Hara, [you must assist me]."
Then, O Kuru, grant me your assistance; nourish me as I abide in heaven. Having entered Śaṅkara’s hermitage with the fragrant [wind], I shall soon [return].
"Having first produced a transformation of the mind through exhilaration, I shall then thoroughly delude the bull-bannered god with a spell of enchantment. (130)
"When the time arrives for my protection, you shall remember me;
O slayer of Bala, I shall go together with you to accomplish that."

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Madana then departed for the hermitage of Śaṅkara; and Śakra also then addressed these words to all the gods: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca ityuktvā sa jagāmātha madanaḥ śaṃkarāśramam | śakro'pi tridaśān sarvānidamāha vacastadā || 132 || Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Madana then departed for the hermitage of Śaṅkara; and Śakra also then addressed these words to all the gods: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca ityuktvā sa jagāmātha madanaḥ śaṃkarāśramam | śakro'pi tridaśān sarvānidamāha vacastadā || 132 || Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Madana then departed for the hermitage of Śaṅkara; and Śakra also then addressed these words to all the gods: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca ityuktvā sa jagāmātha madanaḥ śaṃkarāśramam | śakro'pi tridaśān sarvānidamāha vacastadā || 132 || Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Madana then departed for the hermitage of Śaṅkara; and Śakra also then addressed these words to all the gods: mārkaṇḍeya uvāca ityuktvā sa jagāmātha madanaḥ śaṃkarāśramam | śakro'pi tridaśān sarvānidamāha vacastadā || 132 || Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Madana then departed for the hermitage of Śaṅkara; "Provide assistance wherever the Mind-born [God of Love] goes;
follow him everywhere and inform me at the proper time. (133)
"When he deludes Śaṅkara with this delusion, then I too shall go there; O gods, recognize me. (134)

Having been addressed thus by Śakra, the gods went to the Lord of Love (Manobhava). He too, having gone to where Hara was on the peak of the mountain—laden with a burden of snow—at the descent of the Gaṅgā, directed Surabhi [to that spot]. || 135 ||
Then, as soon as that fragrant breeze had properly departed from there, its characteristic mark appeared without delay even among the trees, shrubs, and creepers.
There, the *kiṃśuka* trees were in bloom, as were the lovely *ketaka* flowers; there were lakes with lotuses and living creatures full of emotion. (137)
And a deep, fragrant wind, carrying the pollen of flowers,
blew very gently and pleasantly, as if drawing the forest along with it.
The birds and the beasts, as well as other living beings,
the Siddhas and the Kinnaras, all entered into pairs.
There, mango trees were in full bloom, adorned with fresh clusters of blossoms;
likewise, there were aśoka, pāṭala, and beautiful nāgakeśara trees. (140)
O twice-born ones, at that time the hosts of Śaṅkara also became subject to transformation;
they too visibly underwent change out of awe for Śambhu.
Then, bees were wandering there, repeatedly drinking the nectar fallen from the flowers, humming along with their mates.
When the Spring had thus set forth, Śṛṅgāra (the God of Love) also, accompanied by his hosts and endowed with gestures and expressions,
entered the presence of Hara.
Madana, dwelling there for a very long time with his retinue,
did not then find any opening by which he might enter Śambhu.
And when he found an opening, Madana, bewildered by fear and held back by Rati, did not go before him. || 145 ||
In this manner, O best of the twice-born,
a great deal of time passed for him as he continued to watch for a lapse on the part of that ascetic.
Who indeed is capable of approaching Śaṅkara, who resembles the blazing fire of cosmic destruction, possesses a radiance equal to a hundred thousand suns, and is absorbed in meditation? 147.
Then once, Kālī, the daughter of the Mountain, stood before him after performing her duties; having bowed down, she remained there with her two female companions.
Then Śaṅkara, too, having abandoned his meditation, remained for that moment intent upon his task,
directing his own attendants while free from anxiety regarding the light.
Having found that opening, Madana first gladdened the moon-crested Lord standing at his side with an arrow that causes exhilaration.
Then the Erotic sentiment (Śṛṅgāra), accompanied by the emotional states (bhāvas) and the gestures (hāvas), went toward Hara along with the fragrant scent, providing assistance to Kāma.
Greatly delighted by the act of exhilaration and attended by the sentiments of love and the rest,
Śaṃkara gazed meaningfully at the face of Kālī.
Having reached that opening, Kāma fixed upon his bow the "Mūrcchana" flower, which was surrounded by blossoms and augmented by garlands of flowers. || 153 ||
Then Rati appeared on his right side and Prīti on his left;
behind him was the beautiful Vasanta, holding a quiver made of flowers.
When the flower-arrowed god of love drew his bow back to his ear and remained composed,
the wind then approached him.
When the spring season had thus begun, Śṛṅgāra also, accompanied by his attendants and endowed with gestures and expressions,
entered into the presence of Hara.
Madana, dwelling there for a very long time with his retinue,
did not then find any opening by which he might enter Śambhu.
And when he found an opening, Madana, bewildered by fear and held back by Rati, did not go before him. || 145 ||
In this manner, O best of the twice-born,
a great deal of time passed for him as he continued to watch for a lapse on the part of that ascetic.
Who indeed is capable of approaching Śaṅkara, who resembles the blazing fire of universal destruction, possesses a splendor equal to a hundred thousand suns, and is absorbed in meditation? 147.
Then once, Kālī, the daughter of the Mountain, stood before him after performing her duties; having bowed down, she remained there with her two female companions.
Then Śaṅkara, too, having abandoned his meditation, remained for that moment intent on his task,
directing his own attendants while free from any thought of light.
Having found that opening, Madana first gladdened the moon-crested Lord standing at his side with an arrow called Harṣaṇa.
Then the Erotic sentiment (Śṛṅgāra), accompanied by the emotions (bhāvas) and the gestures (hāvas), went toward Hara along with the fragrant scent, providing assistance to Kāma.
Greatly delighted by the act of exhilaration and attended by the erotic sentiment and other aesthetic flavors,
Śaṅkara gazed meaningfully at the face of Kālī.
Having reached that opening, Kāma fixed upon his bow the "Enchanting" arrow,
which was surrounded by flowers and augmented by a garland of blossoms.
Then Rati was on his right side and Prīti on his left;
behind him was the beautiful Vasanta, holding a quiver of flowers.
When the flower-arrowed god of love drew his bow, filled to his ear, with self-restraint, then the wind arrived at him. 155.
When the flower-arrowed god had aimed his shafts, the moon-crested Lord,
experiencing a transformation of the senses, became desirous of seizing Girijā in union.
Then all the immortals, together with Śakra, having ascended into the sky,
considered the Mind-born (Kāma) to have been appointed to the task of the gods.
Then, having recollected, restrained, and suppressed the transformation of his sense organ, Mahādeva suddenly reflected upon this.
How can I, desiring union, wish to seize by force Kālī, who was born from a womb, born of the mountain, and devoid of asceticism and vows? (159)
I myself shall accept her whose limbs are purified by vows of austerity and who is honored for her practice of penance, just as [Śiva accepted] Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
How is it that I, whose desire has been transformed, now act as if unwilling, as though drawn by some unseen force to perform this union born of passion? (161)
Thus determining the cause of the transformation in his faculty,
he beheld before him the Mind-born God (Kāma) with arrow fixed.
In the meantime, Brahmā, having understood the situation and seeing the gods, came from his abode to that assembly out of grace.
Then, seeing the Mind-born [god] with his arrow fixed, he became enraged;
resembling a blazing fire, he flared up, desiring to forcibly consume him.
This Kāma, having recognized the opportunity, desires to delude me;
wishing to bring my mind under his own control, I shall send him to the abode of Yama. || 165 ||
As he was reflecting thus, fire arose from the radiance emitted by his eyes; as it grew, it became a blazing flame, and he cast forth that wrath from his eye.
Recognizing that those arrows of Kāma, fixed upon his flowery bow, were about to issue forth from him in the form of fire due to his wrath, [he acted].
Then that Grandfather (Brahmā), having drawn forth his power, his vital breaths, and likewise his very self, drove away the one who was dwelling there. 168.
Then, by his own power, Śambhu protected the Mind-born (Kāma) from his wrath;
meanwhile, the gods situated in the sky beheld Maheśvara enraged.
Be gracious, O Lord of the worlds; abandon your anger toward Kāma.
Just as you previously created him through the act of assuming the form of Śambhu.
And since the Mind-born [Kāma] performs that action which has been directed by you,
therefore, O Śambhu, withdraw the fire of your wrath toward Madana.
"Be gracious, O Lord of all beings; we have bowed down to you with devotion.
To those gods who were speaking thus, the Fire-god then [replied].
Born from the eye on his forehead, the fire, blazing intensely with garlands of flames, reduced the Mind-born (Kāma) to ashes after having burnt him. (173)
Then, paralyzed by the rite, he was unable to go toward Hara;
Mahādeva [took] that ash produced from the body of the Mind-born One.
Then Hara took the coating of ashes from all his limbs and, taking up the remaining ashes from that coating, he applied it [to himself]. (175)
Accompanied by his attendants, he vanished after leaving Kālī, as permitted by Brahmā;
meanwhile, Brahmā [beheld] the fire of Śambhu’s wrath burning all the gods.
Then, in the presence of the gods, she assumed the form of a mare;
at that time, the gods [beheld] that mare, gentle, auspicious, and with a mouth of flame.
Seeing her, those who had been previously tormented became free from anxiety;
then Brahmā, taking that mare Jvālāmukhī, [departed].
The Lord of the worlds went to the ocean for the welfare of the people;
having reached the ocean, Brahmā, being duly honored, spoke.
O best of Brahmins, announcing the agreement according to the truth:
"This is the wrath of Maheśa, which has assumed the form of a mare by you. (180)
The Jvālāmukha [mantra] should always be maintained until I have subdued you;
O Lord of Rivers, when I come to you and speak, [then it shall cease]. 181.
Then you must abandon this submarine fire of anger;
water shall be your food, and it shall belong to him. 182.
"This must be maintained with such effort that it does not slip away," having been told this by Brahmā, the Ocean then accepted his anger.
Then the fire, having entered the ocean as the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha), was unable to seize even the slightest [fuel] within the mouth of the mare. 184.
Completely consuming the reservoirs of water and brilliantly illuminated by garlands of flames,
he emerged from the eye of Śambhu and then incinerated Madana.
A very great sound arose, by which the sky was filled;
and by that great sound, in an instant, the burning of desire [was extinguished].
Then Kālī became frightened and filled with grief along with her two friends;
at that sound, Himavat was startled and amazed.
He quickly went to the hermitage of Hara where his daughter Kālī had gone;
there the Lord of the Mountain approached his auspicious daughter Kālī, who was overwhelmed by fear and grief and weeping due to her separation from Śambhu. (188)
Having approached her, he wiped her two eyes with his hand and, saying "Do not fear, Kālī! Do not weep! he then took hold of her.
Then Himavat, the lord of mountains, having taken his daughter into his embrace,
led her to his own abode and comforted her as she was afflicted.
When Hari had vanished, Kālī, due to her constant separation from him, while dwelling in her father’s house, grieved and fainted repeatedly. (191)
Then the king of mountains, Menakā, Maināka and the other chief [nāgas], and the two friends—
all of noble spirit— consoled her.
Thus she forgot Hara, yet she did not forget Noma.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 42 ||
Chapter Forty-three.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the divine sage went to the abode of Himavat.
Nārada, who could travel anywhere at will, was dispatched by the slayer of Bala.
Having been honored by that high-souled lord of the earth, he departed;
leaving him behind in private, he approached Kālī.
Having approached Kālī, that sage, having awakened her who was endowed with wisdom,
spoke these truthful words for the benefit of all the worlds.
Nārada said:
Listen to my words, O Kālī, and comprehend this truth:
that Mahādeva has been served by you here without [the need for] ascetic penance.
Although Mahādeva is devoted to you, he has sent you away;
Śaṅkara will not accept any other as a second wife besides you.
And you, too, shall not take another husband until you have attained the Lord; therefore, endowed with austerity, worship the Lord for a long time.
"O fortunate one, he will make you, who have been purified by asceticism, his second wife. Listen to this mantra of his, by which he [will act] before long."
When propitiated, Maheśvara will become manifest before you;
and by [reciting] "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," one is always beloved by Śaṅkara.
But meditating upon that form and remaining firm in your observances, O Girijā, you should mutter the six-syllabled mantra; by that, Hara shall be pleased.
Thus addressed then by the high-souled Nārada, Kālī accepted his words,
which were beneficial and true, as her duty.
Having taken leave of Kālī to perform penance, Nārada then departed for heaven,
and her mind became firmly resolved upon the vow.
Then, after the divine sage had departed, Kālī approached Menakā and informed her of her own resolve for ascetic practice and devotion toward union with Hara.
Kālī said:
"O Mother, I shall go to perform austerities in order to attain Maheśvara;
grant me permission to depart this very day for the penance grove."
"O Mother, quickly inform my father of my effort to perform austerities,
before I am consumed by the fire of separation from the Lord of Beings."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of hers, Menakā, emaciated by grief,
embraced her daughter and said, "Do not practice austerities, my dear."
"O daughter, you have a delicate body; do not undergo harsh asceticism. Your fragile frame is not capable of enduring the physical strain of a sage's penance. (16)
"Moreover, daughter, dwelling in the forest is not desired even by hosts of enemies.
Therefore, completely abandoning the asceticism arising from forest-dwelling, perform that beneficial austerity which is truly suited to yourself. (17)
Having heard her mother’s words, Girijā, with a distressed mind and intent upon the effort of her penance, then spoke these words to her mother.
Kālī said:
"Do not forbid me; today I shall go to the penance grove for asceticism.
Even if it be in secret, I shall go even without your permission. (19)
Menakā said:
"The gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, are always present in the home;
therefore, my daughter, worship the gods in your house according to your desire. (20)
It has never been heard that women go to the penance grove without their husband;
therefore, my daughter, it is not proper for you to set out on a journey of asceticism toward the forest.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Because she was sent away by Menā to go to the forest for asceticism, Satī then received the name Umā, as well as the name Soma.
Then, disregarding her mother’s words, the daughter of Himavat informed her father, through her two friends, of her resolve to undertake asceticism.
But the Lord of Mountains, having learned of his exertion in practicing asceticism,
permitted his daughter’s marriage, though with a mind that was not entirely joyful.
Having then taken leave of his father, he went toward the descent of the Gaṅgā, to the place where the Mind-born One had been consumed by Śambhu.
He did not even reach the descent of the Gaṅgā on the ridge of the Himavat;
then, being separated from Hara, he was beheld by Kālī, who was lost in thought concerning him.
Having stood for a moment at that place where, in former times, Śambhu had remained intensely absorbed in meditation, she became afflicted by the pain of separation.
"O Hara! crying out thus for a moment, the daughter of the mountain, afflicted by extreme suffering and filled with anxiety and grief, lamented there. (28)
Having lamented for a moment and then remembering her former birth,
that lotus-eyed Kālī fell into a state of delusion regarding Hara’s heart.
Then, after a long time, that passionate woman, the daughter of Himavat, steadying her delusion through fortitude, became initiated there for the sake of religious observance.
First, her rule was to subsist on fruits;
her practice was to endure the five fires, her meditation was on Śambhu, and her recitation was dedicated to Śambhu.
In the summer, the establishment of the fire is performed four times in the four directions using dry wood fit for sacrifice; there, the sun with its intense rays is the fifth.
Having established the four fires within her hands by means of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice,
she stood in their midst, clad in bark garments and gazing at the orb of the sun.
She spent the summer in the midst of fire and dwelt in water during the winter;
first she lived on the enjoyment of fruits, and secondly, she subsisted on water.
But for the third [fast], she ate the sprouts of the *svayaṃpāti* tree; then, in due order, the daughter of Himavat discarded even those leaves. (35)
Having undertaken the vow of fasting and becoming exhausted by the performance of austerities, the daughter of Himavat abandoned even leaves as her food. 36.
Because of that, she was called Aparṇā by the gods on the surface of the earth, due to her vow of five fires and her entry into the waters. (37)
Standing on one foot during the spring, that daughter of the Himavat chanted the six-syllabled mantra and performed great penance for a long time.
Clad in bark garments and wearing a mass of matted hair, she—though emaciated in body—was capable of deep reflection and surpassed even the sages through her asceticism. (39)
Śaṅkara himself protected her, who was capable of performing penance;
at that time, he nourished her and joyfully guarded her out of fear.
Thus, as Kālī was performing penance and meditating upon Maheśvara in the forest of asceticism, three thousand years passed by.
Having been consecrated by her own sight for six and three thousand years,
the Goddess thus became fit for Hari through divine ordinance.
Having stayed there for a moment— at that place where Hara performed penance for twelve thousand years— the beautiful woman then reflected.
Kālī said:
"Does Mahādeva not know me now, that I am established in my religious observances? For it is because of him that I have been permitted to remain engaged in penance for so long."
"O Lord of the Mountain, is there no one else in this world? Why is he praised by the sages?
The omniscient and omnipresent god Hara is proclaimed by the gods. (45)
He is all-pervading, omniscient, the self of all, and present within the hearts of all;
He is the God who bestows all prosperity and is the creator of all beings.
If Menakā is my mother and I am truly devoted to the bull-bannered Lord and to no other, may that Śaṅkara be pleased with me.
If this six-syllabled mantra has indeed issued from the mouth of Nārada, and if it has been recited by me with devotion, may Hara be pleased thereby. (48)
If truth has been practiced as austerity, if Hara has truly been propitiated, and if austerity has indeed become truth—may Hara be pleased by that! (49)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While she remained thus reflecting in the hermitage of Dhara— downcast,
dressed in humble attire, and adorned with matted hair and bark garments— (50)
At that very moment, a certain Brahmin, a celibate student firm in his vows, appeared,
wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment and holding a staff and a water-pot.
Radiant with Brahmanic splendor, golden-hued and most beautiful,
he was endowed with matted locks that hung down, possessing a slender body.
Then Śambhu, assuming the form of a brahmin, appeared before Kālī;
having first approached Kālī, the twice-born one then addressed her.
Desiring to know passion through direct perception and wishing to hear her words,
the eloquent one then questioned Girijā with various speech.
The brahmin said:

"Who are you, O auspicious one, and to whom do you belong? For what purpose do you perform this difficult austerity in the lonely forest, which is hard even for sages of self-restrained souls to practice? (55)
"You are neither a child nor an old woman, but a young woman of great beauty;
why do you now practice asceticism so persistently without a husband? (56)
Or perhaps this poor woman, O blessed lady, is the companion of some ascetic;
that ascetic has gone elsewhere to gather flowers and other offerings. (57)
Tell me this, if it is not a secret to you. Does any resentment still dwell in your heart at present?
Speak of it; I am capable of removing it as well. (58)
Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, Girijā then directed her own companion with a sidelong glance to provide him with an answer.
At her word, that friend Vijayā then spoke these words to the brahmin exactly as they were, while gazing at the face of the Daughter of the Mountain.
O best of the twice-born, this daughter of the king of mountains is renowned by the name Pārvatī and is also most beautifully called Kālī. (61)
She said, "Since no one has spoken to Śaṅkara, whose banner is the bull,
she is indeed performing intense penance, desiring him as her husband and lover."
The beautiful lady has been performing austerities for three thousand years;
yet even now, Śaṅkara does not accept the Daughter of the Mountain.
"Śaṅkara, Giriśa, Deva, Sarvaga, Parameśvara"—thus was he addressed by the gods, the sages, and those whose wealth is asceticism. (64)
"Does he not know her, or is she not on the mountain peak?"—depressed by such thoughts, she finds no happiness today. (65)
O you of noble vows, if you take pity on her even though she has not entreated you, or if you desire her happiness, then unite her with Śaṅkara this very day.
Having heard these words of hers, the twice-born student then spoke this speech to Pārvatī with a smile, as if in jest: 67.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"My vision is never in vain, and I am capable of bringing Hara here;
however, I shall now state one thing—listen to my firm resolve. (68)
I know that Mahādeva; listen as I speak of him to you:
Mahādeva has the bull as his emblem, he smears himself with ashes, and he wears matted locks. (69)
One was clothed in a tiger skin and a silken garment, wrapped in an elephant hide;
he carried a skull-bowl and was entwined by swarms of serpents upon all his limbs.
His throat was scorched by poison; he had three eyes, deformed eyes, and was terrifying.
His birth was unmanifest, and he was constantly deprived of the enjoyments of a household.
Deprived of kinsmen and relatives, devoid of food and drink,
he constantly dwelt in cremation grounds, entirely avoiding association with them.
Surrounded by a multitude of fierce, sharp, and roaring spirits,
he was devoid of the erotic sentiment and bereft of wife and sons.
For what reason do you desire him as your husband?
Previously I heard this very thing from him, and now he has done something further. (74)
Listen; I shall tell you today if it pleases you to accept it:
Satī, the virtuous daughter of Dakṣa, [chose] the one who has the bull as his vehicle.
In former times, Satī chose as her husband one who was excluded from ritual enjoyment due to fate; she was abandoned by Dakṣa because he was the son of Kapālī.
And Śambhu was also excluded from the distribution of sacrificial portions;
then, on account of that insult, she became intensely overwhelmed with grief.
She abandoned her own dear life-breaths, and by her abandonment, Śaṅkara was also forsaken;
you are a jewel among women, and your father is the king of all monarchs.
Why do you seek such a husband through severe austerity—is it the Lord of the Gods, or the Lord of Wealth, or the Wind-god, or even the Lord of the Waters? (79)
Whether it be Agni, or another god, or even the two celestial physicians, the Aśvins;
or a Vidyādhara, a Gandharva, a Nāga, or perhaps a human. (80)
Endowed with beauty and youth, possessed of all virtues, that illustrious man born of a noble lineage is a worthy husband for you. (81)
By which you [are seated] in this vast, priceless expanse filled with a flood of many jewels, adorned with the finest garlands and well-perfumed with incense powders. (82)
It was provided with soft carpets, spacious, and very beautiful; situated within a lovely palace, it was adorned with gold from the Jambū river.
"Having reached the surface of my bed, he shall become your worthy husband.
Knowing this, O fortunate one, if you desire Śaṅkara today, what further need have you for austerities? I shall unite him with you most certainly. (84)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard that reply of the brahmin, Kālī,
filled with anger, then spoke these measured and truthful words to that brahmin.
Kālī said: "You do not know the god Hara, yet you say, 'I know him.
O delighter of the twice-born, what is seen externally by you has been told to you. (86)
O son of a Brahmin, how can you, a mere child, know Bhava, whose true nature even the gods, including Indra and Brahmā, do not know?
That which you have heard spoken from the mouths of the lowly is trivial;
having merely heard it here and there, you speak of it without having seen it for yourself.
Therefore, I do not desire a boon from you, nor even a husband;
say something else, for I do not seek union with Hara from you. (89)
Having spoken thus, Kālī, the daughter of the mountain, looking at the face of her friend and with her mind overcome by doubt, then said this to the brahmin: (90)
Having propitiated Hara here through great contemplation and austerity, that son of a Brahmin spoke words intended for censure in my presence. (91)
Therefore, I shall now remove that [sin] by means of words of praise;
for whoever hears or even commits the disparagement of great-souled ones, [that sin must be expiated].
I previously heard from the mouth of my father that their passion was mutual;
therefore, I shall remove it—so restrain this brahmin! 93.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus to her friend, Kālī, her mind intent on union with Śambhu,
quickly began to praise Hara in order to wipe away her offense.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes; I offer myself to you, for you, O Supreme Lord, are my refuge. 95.
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, born from the lotus, who have entered into consciousness, fortune, and friendship, who are free from conceptual proliferation, and who possess golden arms.
To you, the primary seed for the welfare of the world. || 96 ||
As she was thus praising him, that twice-born one then,
observing Kālī, made an effort to speak some words to her once again.
Having understood this, the daughter of the mountain spoke to her friend.
This twice-born man wishes to say something,
yet he is unaware of the formidable Hara;
for by censuring Hara, he would indeed bring about his own destruction.
I am able to endure hearing censure here. || 98 ||
"O friend, as long as I do not hear her abundant words now, I shall go far away; O my beloved, arise! (99)
Having spoken thus, the daughter of Himavat rose up and departed together with her friend, having forcibly cast off that brahmin.
Then Śambhu, assuming his own form, followed Hara with a smiling face as he pursued the daughter of Himavat who was departing after having abandoned him.
"I am Hara, Mahādeva; you do not praise me now. Appear before me, O Kālī; console me, O Śāṅkarī! (102)
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva went before her as she was departing,
stretching out his hands to obstruct Kālī’s progress.
Upon seeing the face of Śambhu, the daughter of the Mountain instantly and forcibly became downcast,
like lightning startled by a wind.
Then, due to bashfulness, affection, and shame, that beautiful woman became as if paralyzed;
though she desired to speak, she was unable to say anything at all. (105)
O best of the twice-born, through the fulfillment of her desires, her body became filled with joy, as if saturated with nectar.
She had endured the hardship of asceticism for eighteen thousand years;
yet, having abandoned that effort in an instant, she became filled with joy and delight.
And beholding her in such a state, the bull-bannered god was deluded by love, which existed in the form of ashes residing within his own body.
Then, overcome by the pangs of separation, the bull-bannered Lord approached her and joyfully spoke these affectionate words to awaken her understanding: || 109 ||
But, O beautiful one, you do not seek to say anything at all to me;
why are you now angry with me, reminding me of the hardships of your asceticism? (110)
And I am consumed with grief without you, O fortunate one,
because the penance I had begun to perform together with you according to our agreement has been interrupted.
"Then, O beloved, being full of passion, I shall unite with you after performing the purificatory rites;
for the time that was previously agreed upon by me has now passed. (112)
And you too have been well-refined by austerity alone;
through intense reflection, recitation, and severe penance at that time, I have been purchased for a great price—make me, your slave, serve you. (113)
In the refining of your limbs and the dressing of your matted locks, and in casting off the bark from your body to clothe yourself in beautiful silken garments; 114.
"O auspicious one, if you have any affection for one such as me, quickly employ me in fastening the necklaces, anklets, armlets, girdles, and other ornaments. (115)
That passion which was consumed by me and exists in the form of ashes upon my body stands as if to retaliate against me, desiring to burn you in my presence.
Therefore, O enchanting one, deliver me from desire as one would from a fire;
be gracious to me, my beloved, by granting the nectar of your limbs. 117.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Kālikā Purāṇa. || 43 ||
Chapter Forty-four.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having heard the words of Śambhu, the daughter of the mountain was exceedingly delighted.
Then she considered Śambhu, her beautiful and beloved husband, to have arrived. || 1 ||
Then Kālī spoke to Śaṅkara through the mouth of her friend,
so that he might hear the words, for Śaṅkara desired to listen.
In this world, virtuous people do not proceed by transgressing boundaries;
may Śaṅkara, the Destroyer, accept my hand according to that rule.
A maiden may be given by her father, but she is never given by her ascetic penance;
if I am to be given through penance, then my father shall give me.
Therefore, having requested my father Himavat, the lord of mountains,
let Hara take my hand according to the marriage rite.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Kālī then ceased, filled with shame;
Hara also accepted her words as true, accurate, and appropriate.
Then Śambhu, together with his attendants,
took up residence there on the ridge where the Gaṅgā descends, just as he had done previously.
Kālī, surrounded by her friends, went to her father’s house; that virtuous woman, feeling dejected, did not look upon the faces of her elders.
In the meantime, the Moon-bearer (Śiva) then thought of the seven sages, headed by Marīci, in order to entreat Kālī.
At that very moment, the seven sages were summoned by the Enemy of Madana;
as if drawn by some unseen force, they arrived in his presence.
Śambhu beheld those sages, blazing like seven fires;
he also beheld the virtuous Arundhatī in the presence of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, seeing Arundhatī in the vicinity of Vasiṣṭha,
he considered the practice of taking a wife to be the duty abandoned even by sages.
Then all those sages, having worshipped the bull-bannered god,
spoke these pleasing words with great joy, drawn forth by their remembrance of him.
The sages said:
"That which is seen directly as a pure form, resembling the moon and adorned with a crescent moon— "
The internal consciousness cultivated by those sages was seen as their fortune, attained through the grace of destiny. || 14 ||
The Tantra of Wisdom and the Tantra of Meditation are eternally to be meditated upon by meditators as self-luminous;
they are perpetually present externally as a unified mass of reality.
The noble abode of Śambhu, attainable by the worthy. || 15 ||
Having seen even its foremost part, that vision which is like the sun would be for protection;
this splendor is the eternal abode of all.
Salutations to that body of Śambhu, which is to be praised with devotion.
May he who shines forth from the first and subsequent parts, who is established on the left and is the leader right here,
be our foremost guide for the sake of our own accomplishment.
He was held upon the forehead by the power of Hara. || 17 ||
May that Puruṣa, who consists of Pradhāna, who is joined with Sattva and Rajas and accompanied by Tamas, and who is the destroyer of all worlds, be gracious unto us. 18.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus praised the Lord of Gods, the sages, bowed down with humility, said:
"For what purpose have we been remembered by you? Let that be told to us. (19)
Having heard those words of theirs, Śaṅkara, as if smiling,
addressed all those sages individually and spoke to them.
Īśvara said:
"For the welfare of all the worlds,
as well as for my own enjoyment and for the increase of progeny, I desire to take a wife."
"Therefore, you all must now assist me in this matter;
for my sake, you should then entreat Kālī from the Snowy Mountain."
"Let Kālī obtain me as her husband quickly through great ascetic penance;
however, I shall accept her according to the prescribed rite, so let them entreat that mountain."
To whatever extent Śaila himself may strive to give Kālī, to that same extent you, endowed with the power of speech, must act. (24)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having addressed Hara, the sages went to the abode of the king of mountains.

Honored by him, those sages spoke to that mountain: 25. Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having addressed Hara, the sages indeed went to the home of the king of mountains; honored by him, those sages spoke to that mountain.
He who is the god Candraśekhara, who is considered the God of gods,
who is capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, and who alone is the Lord of the worlds.
He who withdraws all the worlds at the time of their dissolution; he who bestows prosperity upon his devotee; he who assumes manifold forms and is captivating to the mind. || 27 ||
He desires to take your daughter Kālī as his wife;
if you consider him a suitable husband who is equal to your daughter, [then grant her to him]. (28)
"Then bestow your daughter Kālī upon the Moon-bearing Mountain.
Thus addressed by them, the Lord of Mountains [reflected] for a long time upon that which had long resided in his own heart.
Knowing his daughter’s affection and having attained joy from her truthful words, he said this openly: "By your coming, I have been truly blessed. (30)
Purified by the tigers among sages and having my heart's desire fulfilled, I shall give my daughter to Śambhu, as I have been entreated by you all. (31)
Having previously performed austerities, she chose the Lord as her husband;
who else would venture to alter this decree of the Creator? (32)
Who else besides Hara is capable of requesting my daughter? Who else would dare to seek her, once she has been taken hold of by Hara? 33.
"Having taken Hara in her mind, she desires no other here";
having said this, [the king] together with Menā prepared to give his daughter to Śambhu.
Having accepted [the request] and been dismissed, they indeed reached Maheśvara;
all those twice-born sages, headed by Marīci, having gone there. (35)
When the king of mountains reported this, they said to the enemy of Madana:
"Hara is willing to give his daughter to you."
Whatever is now fitting for you to do, let that be done;
and grant us leave as well to depart for our own abode.
Knowing that the goal was accomplished, Hara was delighted and dismissed those sages, addressing each one individually in due order as was appropriate. (38)
"Come to me on the occasion of Kālī’s marriage," thus was it said by Hara; having given their promise, the sages departed. (39)
Then, out of mutual affection, Hara, having repeatedly gone back and forth, made a formal agreement with the Mountain for the sake of marriage.
In the month of Mādhava, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight,
on a Thursday, when the moon was in Uttaraphālgunī and the sun was situated in Bharaṇī and the following constellations.
The sages, headed by Marīci, arrived there repeatedly;
likewise, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were summoned by Hara.
And likewise, all the guardians of the quarters and the sages whose wealth is austerity, as well as Śakra together with Śacī, and the Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī; || 43 ||
And Nārada, the celestial sage and son of Brahmā,
went there together with these attendants and his own hosts, being refreshed by them.
Hara took the daughter of the mountain according to the marriage rite;
at that wedding of Śambhu and Girijā, there were eight serpents residing upon his body. (45)
Then those ornaments, fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold, appeared;
Mahādeva became two-armed, and his matted locks returned to the state of hair.
The crescent moon situated upon his head blazed with its rays. || 47 ||
O twice-born ones, his garment was then a tiger skin, and his body was smeared with fragrant unguents derived from Mount Malaya. (48)
There, Hara appeared in a fair form, a wondrous sight to behold;
then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas, [arrived].
Seeing Hara in such a state, they were filled with supreme wonder;
Himavat, along with his sons and Menā, was also delighted.
Seeing Hara in such a state, his kinsmen were bewildered;
then, beholding the captivating Hara, Brahmā spoke these words there.
O gods, because he who was well-attired became the cause of auspiciousness for all,
he is therefore celebrated in the worlds by the name Śiva, the most excellent Śiva.
Whoever constantly remembers such Maheśvara, joined with Umā, in their heart, for that person there shall always be well-being and the fulfillment of their desires. || 53 ||
Thus Kālī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the Yoga-sleep, and the Mother of the World,
having first been the daughter of Dakṣa, subsequently became the Daughter of the Mountain.
Although Kālī was herself capable of deluding Hara,
Śivā nevertheless performed severe penance for the welfare of the worlds;
thus did Kālikā delude the moon-crested Lord.
Thus all this has been told, how Satī, having cast off her body and become the daughter of Himavat, again obtained Maheśvara.
O twice-born ones, he who recites this meritorious account of Kālikā’s deeds shall have neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases, and he shall become long-lived. (57)
This is the supreme purifier; this increases auspiciousness.
Even by hearing this but once, one goes to the world of Śiva. (58)
He who causes the Brahmins to hear this great account of Kālikā’s deeds during a Śrāddha ceremony, his ancestors attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. (59)
Whoever should recite this in the presence of Brahmins or with a composed mind,
Hara himself goes there and listens along with Māyā.
Thus has this meritorious account, which destroys all sins, been told to you.
O best of beings, if anything else pleases you, please ask about it.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Kālī and Hara," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The forty-fifth chapter.
The sages said:
"O Brahmin, this wonderful account of the arrival of Kālī and Hara has been narrated."
It is meritorious, eternally removing sin, and the most excellent bestower of happiness upon hearing.
Speak further of the supreme half of Śarva’s body that is Kālī;
how did Gaurī seize it, or what was Kālikā like?
Or for what reason did Kṛṣṇā so quickly attain the state of being fair-complexioned (Gaurī)?
O best of sages, O most excellent of the twice-born, tell us that in accordance with the truth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now I shall relate this great narrative to you;
let the great sages listen to it as it truly is, for it is supremely auspicious. (4)
O Aurva, in former times King Sagara questioned the sage;
I shall now relate to you exactly how he explained it to him.
In former times, there was a king named Sagara in the Lunar dynasty;
he was illustrious, powerful, capable, and had reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.
Having conquered all the rulers of the earth with but a single chariot, he became a sovereign emperor,
a lord of men endowed with all the qualities of royalty.
The sages arrived to offer their highest congratulations to King Sagara, that best of monarchs, now that he had attained the kingdom.
Great-souled sages and brahmins from the east, the north, the south, and likewise the north, all assembled to see the king.
Then, when they had all arrived, the illustrious and high-souled sage named Aurva, who resembled a blazing fire, came to greet the king with joy.
Seeing that sage who had arrived, blazing like a fire,
Sagara honored him with great reverence.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, preceded by the arghya offering,
he seated that best of sages upon an excellent seat.
And King Sagara, having bowed down as was appropriate to that high-souled Aurva, the twice-born one, asked after his welfare.
And that best of sages said: "O King of Men, you are always well; I am eager for your welfare to see you."
Who else on earth among all the kings is as fortunate as you, who alone have swiftly conquered all the rulers of the earth? (15)
May your virtue increase constantly, O best of excellent kings; rule the earth, O lord of the earth, always through statesmanship and righteous conduct. (16)
In your prosperity lies the prosperity of the world; therefore, act so that it may increase, just as the ocean constantly swells with the waxing of the moon. 17.
O King, first let yourself be made a fit vessel through virtuous qualities;
thereafter, let your queen be made one endowed with those same qualities. (18)
For if a woman were herself eternally joined [to virtue], she would enter into her own virtues, remaining firm in her vows even in great adversity. (19)
It is heard that the daughter of Himavat had her mind fixed on union with Śambhu;
she was pursued by Śambhu through many ritual means.
Then, with exceedingly great love, the virtuous Pārvatī took half of Śaṅkara’s body with his very own consent.
From that time forward, O tiger among kings, Śaṅkara became Ardhanārīśvara and did not take another wife.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should quickly unite your own wife with excellent qualities; thereafter, unite her with a son.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words spoken by Aurva, King Sagara was filled with joy;
with a continuous smile, that monarch questioned the sage as follows.
Sagara said:
"O best of the twice-born, how did that goddess Girijā, being Satī, take half of Śaṅkara’s body? I am eager to hear that."
I am eager to hear that policy, consistent with righteous conduct, by which one should engage one's own self, wife, or son. (26)
O twice-born one, desiring to hear separately about the policy of kings, the conduct of the virtuous, and that of others who have perfected their souls, I entreat you.
O Brahman, if this is a secret, then I do not venture to hear it;
likewise, I shall not command you to speak, even though I am desirous of hearing that which is equal to it.
O Sage, if it may be told out of compassion, then please tell it.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Sagara had spoken thus, O best of the twice-born,
the compassionate Aurva replied to that high-souled king.
Aurva said:
Listen, O King, I shall explain everything that you have asked here— how,
in ancient times, the daughter of the mountain took away the body of Hara.
O best of kings, listen as I describe in due order the conduct of all people and the policy you must implement in every situation. (31)
When the daughter of Himavat was wedded by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
how long did he spend that time there together with Umā?
Delighting Pārvatī, Hara sported there for a long time with her upon the mountain peaks, in the groves, and in the caves.
Then, when the time had arrived, Śambhu went with his attendants and his wife to Mount Kailāsa, which resembled the celestial realm.
While playing with you, he abandoned his meditation and self-contemplation; he made your moon-like face the object of his eyes, as if they were cakora birds. (35)
Having gathered flowers from here and there, Śaṅkara fashioned an exceedingly beautiful garland that clung to every limb of Girijā.
Once, on the surface of a mirror,
the bull-bannered god beheld his own face simultaneously with the face of Aparṇā.
Once, Smarāntaka (the Destroyer of Love) traced a fragrant leaf-design with musk-pastes upon her pair of firm breasts.
With an ointment of sandalwood essence, she fashioned beautiful tilaka marks upon Ambikā’s body,
like the full moon at the junctions of thick clouds on her forehead.
Upon their masses of hair, which were entwined with the resin of the *umā* plant,
there was decorative painting made with ointments of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
By doing so, her mass of hair shone,
bearing a resemblance to the tail of a peacock that has descended for the purpose of dancing.
