The bull-bannered god (Śiva) then adorned his body with pure ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold, such as earrings and others that were captivating to the mind. 42.
Adorned with those ornaments made of Jāmbūnada gold, the body of the Mountain-born Goddess shines like lightning amidst a mass of clouds in the dark fortnight.
Adorned with all divine ornaments, various jewels, and fine garments, Kālī, being fully embellished, bore a resemblance to Prakṛti.
Thus Śambhu, the Lord of the World, ever full of passion for her,
sported with his beloved Kālī for the welfare of the world.
And Kālī, the Mother of the worlds, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who is composed of the universe—
Yoganidrā is the consciousness of the universe, consisting of the entirety of both knowledge and ignorance.
Prakṛti, the supreme form who brings about the creation and the maintenance until the end of the world,
having deluded Śaṅkara, sported with him for the welfare of the worlds,
like moonlight with the moon.
Then once, while the Destroyer of Smara was sporting joyfully with Umā on the peak of Kailāsa, he beheld beautiful Apsarases.
Endowed with beauty and youth, and possessed of all auspicious marks, among them was the captivating courtesan Urvaśī. (49)
All of them had limbs as red as gold and were adorned with every ornament;
they were capable of forcibly deluding the minds of even sages. (50)
Having bowed to Hara and beheld the enchanting Girijā,
they stood before them with palms joined in reverence, their heads bowed low out of fear.
Then Bharga spoke these wonderful words to Pārvatī in the presence of them all: "It would be improper to speak what is unpleasant to her. (52)
"O Kālī, dark as crushed collyrium, let a conversation be held here with you by Urvaśī and the other hosts of apsarases, through the nature of womanhood. (53)
Having heard those words of his, Urvaśī,
the daughter of the mountain, addressed the Apsarases appropriately and was dismissed by her.
Then Pārvatī, having fallen under the sway of anger,
was addressed by Bharga as "Kālī, dark as crushed collyrium," and in an instant she became so.

And she, filled with indignation, could not endure the boastful description of his qualities in the presence of the Apsarases— [the description] of the one who bears the digit of the moon upon the head of the Mountain-Daughter.
Then, filled with rage, she abandoned her bull-vehicle and hid herself upon the mountain slope,
having resorted to a concealment born of anger.
Then, searching for her and distressed by separation, the bull-vehicled Lord did not find Pārvatī on that best of mountains for some time. (58)
Perceiving that Hara was distressed by separation, Pārvatī herself revealed her own form on the hidden mountain peak.
Having approached her, Śambhu then spoke as if shattered: "O beloved, O Goddess, for what reason have you displayed this pride that drives away the mind? (60)
A husband's affection is the cause for housewives to accept his pride; O timid one, by accepting it in his absence, she incurs public reproach.
Therefore, O lotus-faced one, tell me quickly why you became angry; my mind finds no peace, O beloved. (62)
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara prepared to embrace the goddess;
Kālī restrained him and spoke these words.
O Lord of Beings, why do you, before the very eyes of the apsarases, treat me—who have never been seen by you before—as if I were a mere lump of collyrium? 64.
One should not, on account of that fault, reject one who is deficient in birth, deficient in livelihood, deficient in form, lacking in dexterity, missing a limb, or having an extra limb. || 65 ||
Thus Brahmā spoke in the past, having reached a definitive conclusion regarding the meaning of the multitude of Vedas;
yet, disregarding that, you speak with derision.
"I tell you the truth: as long as my body has not attained a golden hue, I shall not reunite with you. (67)
"O Śambhu, I shall not regain the whiteness of my body without you;
hear my solemn vow regarding this, and I swear it by my own head. (68)
Having spoken thus, the goddess then went before him to the excellent peak of the Himavat known as Mahākoṣī-prapāta.
Mahādeva, the omniscient one, having understood through his knowledge that he was destined for this and had reached a firm resolve regarding the matter, did not then dissuade Aparṇā either.
Having gone there as before, her mind intent on union with Śambhu,
she propitiated the bull-bannered Lord for a hundred years.
Lifting one foot and treading upon the earth with her left,
she remained without food for a continuous period, facing the north.
Clad in a tiger skin with her hair standing erect,
she beheld Śiva— the supreme, luminous, peaceful, auspicious, and excellent bestower of welfare.
Knowing the reality of the true nature of the Self, she worshipped Hara according to the truth;
meditating upon Him with supreme steadiness, her mind was fixed on that ultimate reality.
The assembly of sages thought, "He who does not know [the truth] in its true nature is like a pillar.
In this manner, as she was performing penance, a hundred years indeed passed away.
And for others as well, O best of kings, it is eternally one;
then, at the end of a hundred years, Śaṅkara, intent on yoga, [departed].
He revealed himself in succession, one by one;
first he revealed Brahmā, and after that, Hari.
Then [he taught] the body of Śambhu, and then their oneness, as well as their luminous nature, their purity, and likewise their status as the cause of all. (78)
Then Śaṅkara revealed his form as Śambhu, [and] Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, the Yoginī Kālikāmbikā. (79)
Having first shown her her natural form,
he then gradually revealed to her that she was indeed Pārvatī.
Having quickly attained knowledge through austerity accumulated by her, Pārvatī, through both inner and outer vision, understood reality exactly as it is. (81)
Brahmā regarded Śambhu as consisting of the universe, and likewise himself as consisting of the universe; so too did Viṣṇu and Hara, and thereafter this entire world [was seen as such]. 82.
"I am Yoganidrā, the primordial nature of all things"—
with this meditation, the Goddess attained that state and then abandoned her concentration;
opening her pair of eyes, she beheld Śambhu outside.
Having seen the god Śaṅkara, the god of gods and lord of Umā,
who is self-restrained and devoted to yoga, she praised him with pleasing words.
Pārvatī said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the worlds; salutations to you, O immutable Keśava!
You who transcend both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cause of the three causes.
This body of yours, O Śambhu, consists of yoga, delusion, and passion; it is composed of dharma and adharma, and its very nature is both knowledge and ignorance.
You, being joined with both the ultimate and the worldly good,
are visible and invisible, the embodiment of yoga, and wise;
you are the true nature of reality, characterized by perfect faith in human effort.
You indeed are the light, the very form of peace, from the beginning.
You are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara; you are Mahendra, Sūrya, Soma, Vāyu, Agni, and Dhaneśa;
you are the Lord of Waters, Śamana, and the Rākṣasa.
But there is no remainder whatsoever here that is distinct from you.
You are the earth, the sky, and also the path of those who dwell in heaven; you are the stationary and the moving, abiding in the world as the foundation.
You are knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that reality which is to be reached through meditation.
He is higher than the highest, manifest in form to others. || 89 ||

You are the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, and indeed the Pradhāna; you are the most eminent, the source of scripture, and attainable through knowledge. You are existence, action, and the fivefold form, comprising all things.
The spheres beginning with Rāśi lead to rebirth. || 90 ||
He is fame and poetry, the form of praise and praise itself;
He is the seer and the seen, the upholder of stability and the stable;
He is the eternal and the non-eternal, the union with liberation and the state beyond union.
The employment of sowing dissension and conciliation regarding giving and not giving. || 91 ||
Policy is to be understood; the initiated one and the sacrificial fees are the essence of essences; the ordainer is to be followed;
the noble and the ignoble are those who possess form and those devoid of form.
The divine, the human, and the non-human. || 92 ||

He is the object of creation and the creator, the protector and the form of that which is protected; he is the knower and the object of knowledge, as well as the wave devoid of waves; he is the singular form of both knowledge and ignorance, and of the Vedic doctrine.
He has both form and formlessness; he is sharp and gentle, appearing as a single form.
Existence and non-existence are auspicious; he is of pure form, eternally self-controlled, and the fierce peace of sages.
He is both dual and non-dual, all-pervading and yet not all-pervading.
He is both deluded and undeluded, and he bestows both accomplishment and non-accomplishment. || 94 ||
You are situated in one place yet the protector of all; you possess a beautiful body yet are bodiless; you are the singular body of the gods.
You are the gross, the subtle, the changeless, and the embodied one.
The Universal Soul is not distinct from you. || 95 ||
He whose two forms, the manifest and the unmanifest, pervade all that is to be done and not to be done, who is partless yet utterly full,
and whose nature is eternally established in the knowledge of yoga.
O Giver of Prosperity, salutations to you whose form is such. || 96 ||

To that fierce Lord, the bestower of boons, the most excellent one, who is the creator even of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), and who is the Supreme Ruler in the form of Time; to Him [I bow].
I bow to her who possesses the canopy of the science of consciousness. || 97 ||
Obeisance to You, the inexhaustible, the immutable witness, the knower of the field, the sustainer of the field, and the supreme; O Soul of the Universe, O Bull-bannered One, O Great Lord! 98.
Salutations to You, whose consciousness-moon constantly distills the nectar of knowledge; You are that single form which is to be known as consisting of pure devotion alone. 99.
Aurva said:
Thus praised, Mahādeva, who is compassionate toward all beings,
spoke with a gracious countenance, gladdening Pārvatī.
The Lord said: "I am pleased, O Goddess; may it be well with you. Choose the boon you desire.
By your ascetic penance, I, as well as Brahmā and Hari, have been nourished."
"In asceticism, in character, and in virtue, there is none equal to you; indeed, I find no satisfaction without you. O beloved, do as you desire. (102)
Then the daughter of Himavat, deluded by that illusion, said:
Aurva said,
"May my body now become fair as the luster of Jāmbūnada gold."
And may you, O Hara, likewise have no other beloved besides me. 103.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, Mahādeva then immersed that beautiful lady in the torrent of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Having emerged after plunging into the water, she became as white as lightning;
the goddess appeared like a flash of lightning amidst autumnal clouds in the midst of white waters.
Īśvara said:
O beloved, Śambhu has quickly consented; I shall not accept any other woman even in my mind without you—I tell you this as the truth.
Aurva said:
Then Pārvatī, having emerged from the water, was filled with joy;
freed from the exhaustion of her ascetic penance, she was like the moonlight of the moon.
Then, taking the goddess Pārvatī with him, the bull-bannered Lord went swiftly to Mount Kailāsa, his own cherished abode.
Then Hara went there, and having perfumed and adorned the Goddess,
he delighted her as before with jests, laughter, stories, and the like.
She too, her limbs golden-hued, beholding that captivating form and having obtained Śambhu who had accepted the agreement, rejoiced exceedingly.
Thus, as those two Śivas took delight in one another,
a very long time passed on Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
Then once, while seated near Mahādeva, the daughter of Himavat beheld her own reflection situated upon his chest.
In the beautiful heart of Śambhu, which is as clear as crystal or a cloud, she of lovely limbs was reflected upon the surface of the mirror of the yogi’s knowledge. (113)
On her charming left side, the daughter of the mountain beheld her own reflection in the form of a woman, with a smiling face and captivating beauty.
Then, through a deluded vision, Pārvatī gained this understanding:
"Even though Giriśa has made his vow true, why does he hold another woman? (115)
"Beholding me with a crooked glance, as if I were established upon her body by means of illusion"—
at that moment, her face became darkened and marked by a frown;
and Vṛṣaketu turned ashen, like an ill-omened comet.
Then, seeing that shadow and deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu, she was overcome with pride and anger, thinking the mountain peak had been removed. || 117 ||
Then Śaṅkara, agitated by separation, searching for her, finally reached the Goddess who had been hidden from him for a long time. Thus did Hara find her. 118.
Having approached his beloved, whose face was pale, the Great Goddess, desiring to know the cause of her resentment exactly as it was, spoke to her. (119)
Īśvara said:
"O beautiful woman, O angry one, for what reason are you angry with me?
O beloved, I wish to hear the cause of your wrath here."
I have not offended you in word, nor in thought, nor in deed; O passionate lady, how can you be angry with me? (121)
The Goddess said: "Previously, you were requested by me on a specific condition;
how is it that you now wish to abandon that and seek another wife?"
O Hara, I have seen with my own eyes within the interior of your heart a certain woman of beautiful limbs amidst the ashes emerging from the water.
You are the Supreme Lord, all-pervading and composed of omniscience;
though gratified by my multitude of austerities, O Maheśvara, you have not yet been fully satisfied by me.
Therefore, I am eager to go forth forever to practice asceticism;
grant me your permission, O Śambhu, and do not cause me further delay in vain. (125)
Aurva said:
Having heard her words, Śaṅkara, his face broadened with a smile, spoke to Pārvatī as if she were in doubt, O beautiful lady. (126)
Īśvara said:
"I shall not marry another woman, nor am I a breaker of my vow.
O deluded girl, this false notion has arisen in you now through your own foolishness. (127)
O Pārvatī, if you wish to hear the reason for that, then I shall tell you the truth; O proud lady, do not be angry. (128)
Upon my broad chest, shining as clear as a mirror,
the reflection of your very form was seen by you.
Awaken right now! Without you, she does not exist within me;
you should not harbor pride toward her who dwells within the depths of my heart. 130.
The Goddess said:
"While I am present, the shadow exists; without me, it does not exist again.
How is this to be understood by me? Tell that to me, O Bull-bannered One. (131)
The Lord said:
"Standing within the window, look through that charming lattice at my chest, which is smeared with the dust carried forth by the flood of water."
Likewise, having again beheld your adorned body in the surface of a mirror, approach my heart and behold such a reflection there. || 133 ||
Do for me exactly as you see yourself in your own body;
look at your own reflection, for that [body] does not exist apart from you. (134)
"You alone shall recognize my shadow upon your beautiful breast;
having recognized it, you too shall attend to me as I am being released. (135)
Aurva said:
Having been addressed thus by Hara, Pārvatī, who bears a digit of the moon,
then pierced her own heart with that arrow and beheld her own reflection once more.
Having seen her own face and body in the surface of a mirror, Pārvatī then gazed constantly at the chest of Śaṅkara.
Just as that goddess performs deceitful glances with her eyes,
so too does the shadow perform trembling of the hands and other such gestures.
Then, standing again at the lattice of the window, the daughter of the Himālaya gazed likewise upon the heart of Śambhu, which was now devoid of its splendor.
But there, upon the chest of the bull-bannered Lord, Pārvatī saw no woman at all; she saw only a circle of a net.
Thus, through these and other various means, the goddess, having her doubts dispelled, felt shame, O beautiful woman. (141)
Embracing with both hands that daughter of the mountain, who was ashamed, slightly afraid, and looking downward, Śambhu kissed her face.
Mahādeva spoke to her, repeatedly consoling the goddess:
"Do not be ashamed, O illustrious one; in whom does delusion not arise? (143)
"O Goddess, pride should be maintained by excellent women toward you, for it generates love;
yet even by you, O Goddess, pride should not be displayed constantly. (144)
Thus addressed by the God of gods, Mainākasaṃbhavā Ambikā spoke these truthful and sweet words to Śaṅkara out of affection: (145)
The Goddess said:
"O Hara, you ought to act in such a way that I may always follow you like a shadow, through constant companionship. (146)
I desire the touch of all your limbs and the playful embrace of you constantly, if you are worthy of performing this according to the truth.
The Blessed One said:
"O beautiful lady, that which you desire is pleasing to me as well.
I shall tell you the means for that; if you are able, do it. (148)
"O beautiful one, take half of my body;
let one half be a woman for me, and likewise, let the other half be a man. (149)
"If you too are able to make half of yourself like this, then, O fair-faced one, I shall take half of your body. (150)
"Let half of you indeed be a woman, and likewise let half be a man; I possess the power for this, so you ought to grant me permission. (151)
The Goddess said:
"O Bull-bannered One, I shall take half of your very body;
however, this is what I desire, if you wish to do it. (152)
When I remain having become half of you, then I shall relinquish that half of yours; when both are thus complete, then [the whole] will be restored.
O Śambhu, if the taking of half my portion should happen according to your desire, then I shall take half of your own body.
Īśvara said:
"So be it; let it be eternally as you deserve. Furthermore, the taking of half of your body shall be according to your desire. (155)
Aurva said: Then Gaurī, while established in her ascetic practice, reflected with her intellect upon that very nature of yogic sleep which she had previously experienced.
Having first bowed to Hara, and after that to Brahmā,
and then to Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Master of the three worlds.
Having reflected that their oneness is identical with the universe,
the ascetic woman then meditated upon herself as the yogic sleep (yoganidrā).
Then, out of great affection, Hari gave half of his own body to the right side of the body of the Moon-bearer, and likewise the left side of his own body to [the other]. (159)
Then Hara himself, desiring to do her an extraordinary favor, out of love placed half of his own body within that Gaurika.
Then Bharga, having remained with Kālī for a long time,
appeared thereafter as if distinct, shining with his own luster while casting off half of his body.
Having become Kālī while her other half of the body was golden-fair, she then attained Śaṅkara; filled with joy and satisfied, she who consists of the universe realized her own self.
Thus, when the Supreme Goddess, having taken half of the body, remains in the secret place, she then shines with exceeding splendor. || 163 ||
Half [of her hair] was bound in a braided chignon (dhammilla), while the other half was joined with a mass of matted locks (jaṭājūṭa);
on one ear she wore a serpent, and on the other part she was adorned with gold.
An earring shone upon one of her ears, while on her head it appeared as half-moon-eyed and half-bull-eyed. (165)
One half [of the faces] has a thick nose and is beautiful with a nose like a sesame flower;
likewise, one half has a long beard, while the other half is entirely devoid of a beard.
One [side] has beautiful teeth that are slightly reddish and lips that are likewise red; the other [side] has large white [teeth], while another tooth is long in shape. (167)
One half has a neck that is dark blue, while the other half is adorned with a necklace;
likewise, one half has arms equipped with bracelets and armlets, while the other is likewise [adorned]. (168)
One [arm] was adorned with a serpent-bracelet and possessed a thick arm without a ring;
the other half had a gracefully swaying beautiful arm, while the supreme [other] arm was like the trunk of an elephant.
In one [hand] there is a branch of the *soma* plant, while in the other it is held without that [branch];
the heart, however, has but one breast joined with half of a line of hair. (170)
With thighs like the trunk of a plantain tree, with beautiful heels and soft feet;
one [foot] was thus, while the other was thick, with joined shanks and lotus-like feet. (171)
One [leg] has a beautiful, soft, and thick thigh, which is most enchanting; likewise, the other is characterized by a firm hip and a well-knit, upward-turned foot.
One was covered with a multitude of tiger-skin strips and smeared with ashes;
the other was clad in soft silk garments and anointed with sandalwood paste.
Thus, one half was born likewise endowed with the characteristics of a woman,
while the other was powerful, massive, well-concealed, and possessed the form of a man.
Thus the virtuous Girijā, who is like Kālī and is the protector of all the worlds, took away half of the enemy of Smara for the welfare of the entire universe. 175.
O Indra among kings, her body was endowed with ever-increasing splendor;
even after searching throughout the three worlds, nothing exists by which it could be compared.

Neither the celestial Pārijāta tree nor the tree that was entirely pure in its lineage could equal them, just as neither could be matched by the unfailing creeper; indeed, even those two did not surpass them.
O lord of men, he and they took delight with him in many ways and separately;
yet at times, having become Ardhanārīśvara, he himself took delight.
Thus, although the Lord of Beings himself, the cause of the causes of all beings, was able at that time to make Kālikā fair-complexioned (Gaurī), [he did not do so]. 179.
Nevertheless, in the past, the Lord joined that daughter of the mountain with him through various means and numerous ritual methods.
Afterwards, Maheśvara made Gaurī from that body whose every limb had been purified by ascetic penance; he then gave half of his own body to her.
Not even Śakra and all the other gods know his true nature regarding the gift of half his body and his application to asceticism.
The great-souled ones of immense power know its true nature:
Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Vetāla, and likewise Bhairava. (183)
Those whose wealth is austerity, who are free from fear and have become limbs of Maheśa, have attained [this state] through the power of their penance by means of human bodies. (184)
They recognize you as the supreme Hara, the sovereign lord of the hosts;
therefore, O best of kings, you should always employ them along with their followers in this manner.
Therefore, by means of honoring women, you shall obtain prosperity.
Whoever should constantly hear this wonderful account that bestows merit, [shall likewise attain it]. (186)
It brings joy to Śiva and Śivā, involves the taking of half the body, and is the means for Gaurī’s attainment, bringing auspiciousness to Kālikā. (187)
No obstacles arise for him, and he is considered most meritorious;
may he be long-lived, happy, and endowed with sons and grandsons. || 188 ||
Constantly listening to the great deeds of Śiva and Śivā, one becomes a beloved of Śiva and attains the world of Śiva for a very long time. || 189 ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Śrī-Kālikā-Purāṇa*, in the account of Arddhanārīśvara. || 45 ||
The forty-sixth chapter.
Sagara said:
Who was this one named Bhairava, and who was the one known as Vetāla?
Or how did those two leaders of the Gaṇas come to possess human bodies?
O tiger among the twice-born, O great sage, tell me how those two came to be;
for I know, O Brahmin, that Nandin was the attendant of the Moon-crested Lord.
Just as you, O leader of the assembly, have heard that from the mouth of Nārada,
so too are Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla renowned as the two sons of Hara.
Or how did those two arise from you? I am eager to hear this, concerning him who was formerly [born] from Mahādeva in the form of a Śarabha. || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, was that one previously heard of as Kāyabhāga, who was named Mahābhairava, the very same person called Bhairava, or was it someone else?
O best of the twice-born, I desire to know all that in its true essence:
having been the sons of whom did they attain the status of leaders of the Gaṇas? And tell me today how it was that those two came to have the faces of monkeys.
Aurva said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the life-story of Mahākāla Bhṛṅgin,
and also that of Bhairava and the high-souled Vetāla.
That Bhṛṅgī, the son of Hara, and Mahākāla, born of Bharga—
those two alone, through the curse of Gaurī, were born together into human wombs.
Listen now to how Vetāla and Bhairava were born in a royal palace on earth, just as Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla were previously manifested.
He who is known as Mahābhairava, possessing a body like a śarabha, is Hara;
yet this Bhairava is distinct from him, being the leader of the Gaṇas and the son of Hara.
When the daughter of Himavat had been wedded by the high-souled Bharga,
Śambhu was formerly entreated for progeny by the gods, led by Śakra, with hymns of praise and prostrations for the sake of slaying Tāraka. (11)
Requested by the hosts of gods, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull began the great act of union with Umā for the sake of progeny.
O King, while that best of men was engaged in sexual union,
thirty-two years passed for him who bore the moon as if they were a single moment.
While engaged in great sexual union, Maheśvara did not attain satisfaction;
nor did Pārvatī reach satiety, for his emitted vital energy was inexhaustible.
At that moment of the great embrace, the earth clearly trembled;
all the gods and others who dwell in heaven became agitated. (15)
Then the entire world became agitated by those two Śivas through that act of great sexual union born of their withdrawal from worldly existence.
Then all the gods, together with Indra, being terrified by the playful deeds of Śaṅkara, went for refuge to Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds and the protector who grants sanctuary.
Then those best of gods, having assembled and bowed down to Dhātṛ,
related everything that was agitated by Hara’s act of sexual union.
Then, having placed all the hosts of gods behind him, the slayer of Vṛtra himself spoke to the Creator, his words uttered out of fear at that moment.
Indra said:
"All the worlds are agitated by the act of Hara’s union;
having encountered great fear, I have come here to you for refuge. (20)
O Brahmin, whatever son is born from such a union of Śaṅkara with Umā, he shall surpass me.
O Brahmin, even from that son of mine who was born merely by witnessing his deeds, fear has arisen in me today, and it is even greater than that of Tāraka.
Therefore, O Creator, you must act in such a way that his son does not oppress the gods;
thus, with effort, rescue us from this great danger.
Brahmā said:
"If a son is born to Umā through the splendor of Śaṅkara, he will be invincible even by all the lords of the worlds, including Indra, the gods, and the asuras. (24)
"I shall go to the presence of Hara with the gods and so arrange it that he will not beget Uma. (25)
I shall also ensure that the destruction of Tāraka occurs through the splendor of Śiva; let the fever of your mind depart.
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Creatures departed from Mount Kailāsa along with the hosts of gods;
and Giriśa took great delight together with the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having gone there, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, together with all the hosts of gods, praised Mahādeva, whose banner bears the bull.
The gods said:
"Salutations again and again to You, for whom there is no pleasure nor desire for the sake of gratification, whose mind is not born of passion, and who has no cause for rebirth. (29)
Salutations to that Three-eyed One, for whose sake alone the taking of a wife was undertaken for the benefit of the world; may that Śiva be gracious toward us. (39)
O God, we bow down to you, Hara, that deity whom the sentiments of love and the rest enter by their own power alone, even without Manmatha.
May you, the god who possesses golden seed, who has the luster of gold, and who is named Hiraṇyabhuja—
the destroyer of creation— be forever gracious toward us.
Yoganidrā, who pervades the universe, the powerful Māyā of Viṣṇu, became his own wife; salutations again and again to you!
We bow with devotion to you, the five-faced God, whose five heads, composed of the five elements, shine forth. (34)
Today we bow down to Sadyojāta, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Umāpati, and Īśāna, whom they indeed call Tatpuruṣa. (35)
Salutations to you, that Śiva, who is eternally inauspicious to the wicked and auspicious to those possessed of devotion, and whose very nature is both Śiva and Aśiva.
Salutations to Him who is celebrated as Śambhu, who perpetually effects the maintenance, creation, and destruction of the worlds through the three forms known as Īśa, Atna, and Śambhu.
This auspicious Virūpākṣa, the Lord of Śivā. || 37 ||

O Jātavedas, to you who possess the splendor of the fivefold forms— the trident, the khaṭvāṅga staff, and the crescent moon; who have the bull as your emblem and are endowed with power— to you, I bow.
Again and again, salutations to Śaṅkara! || 38 ||
O Brahmārciṣman, sustainer of enjoyments, slayer of Daityas, ender, warrior, and one whose womb is transcended by the world—
you who are infinite, may you, being thus praised by us, be gracious.
The primary [cause] is that which is eternally increasing, as previously described. || 39 ||
Ara is one who has the form of Brahmā, eternally liberated;
Niyata is the supreme light, infinite;
and Parajyotis is one who possesses the nature of the self beyond the spokes (ara).
May Giriśa, in the form of the sun, be for our prosperity. || 40 ||
Bowing down to Umāpati, Mahāmāya, Mahādeva, the Lord of the world, Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, and the peaceful one—may he be gracious. (41)
Aurva said:
Thus praised by Śakra and the other gods, Mahādeva himself,
Bharga, abandoned his union with Umā and went to the celestial realm.
By that very disposition through which he had at that time been so intent upon great sexual union, he fell into a swoon before Brahmā and the other gods.
Īśvara said:
Then Mahādeva, as if in haste, spoke to those gods:
"O immortals, tell me for what purpose you have come."
The gods said:
All the thirty deities, led by Brahmā and Śakra, spoke to him:
"O Bharga, because of your great act of sexual union, the entire world is thrown into turmoil."
O Śaṅkara, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles excessively; all the oceans, rivers, and streams are agitated.
All the gods and the guardians of the quarters indeed find no peace;
therefore, O Lord of all worlds, have compassion upon everyone. 47.
"Abandoning great sexual intercourse, apply yourself instead to mere pleasure.
Aurva said: "Having heard these words of that Brahmā, the Supreme Self..."
Lord Śaṅkara spoke, as if his mind were not very joyful.
Īśvara said:
"O best of immortals, this activity of yours is for the sake of Śiva;
once the great sexual union has been abandoned, it is employed merely for the purpose of pleasure."
A son shall be born to Nomā; for that purpose, this effort is undertaken. || 49 ||
The son who shall be born from my splendor upon the body of Umā will indeed slay the enemies and cause the gods to prosper. (50)
Therefore, the best of gods are exceedingly afraid of my great sexual passion;
let them each go to their own respective abodes, while I reflect upon that.
The gods said:
"O Hara, O Lord of the World, act in such a way that a son born from the body of Umā shall not come to be; therefore, abandon that great sexual union."
Īśvara said: "My son shall not be born from mere sexual pleasure;
however, Pārvatī will remain childless due to her complete renunciation of sexual union."
Therefore, at the word of the gods and likewise of Brahmā, I shall indeed abandon this great sexual union; however, O immortals, do one thing for me.
"May the immortals bring that radiant god who has emitted this splendor from me due to the cause of great passion; let them honor him. (55)
"O gods of the three realms, tell me who, having become unshakable and free from transformation, shall take up this splendor; I shall relinquish this bodily radiance."
Aurva said:
Having heard the words of the bull-bannered god, the deities, led by Brahmā,
then approached Vītihotra with the intention of seizing the energy of Hara.
Then, having addressed Brahmā and likewise having obtained the permission of the Fire-god, all the hosts of gods, including Indra, spoke these words to Hara: || 58 ||
The gods said:
"This glorious Vaiśvānara, powerful and consisting of abundant splendor,
shall indeed absorb your seed from this great act of union."
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus, all the thirty gods commanded Vītihotra, who stood before them,
to serve Śambhu, the cause of all.
Therefore, the mighty-armed one discharged his own sixfold semen into the wide-open mouth of the Fire-god, for the purpose of great procreation.
As the splendor of the moon-bearer was being cast into the fire,
two extremely minute atoms fell upon a mountain plateau.
From those two drops, two sons of Śaṅkara were immediately born;
one was black like a bumblebee, and the other resembled a split collyrium-stick.
Then Brahmā gave the name Bhṛṅgī to him who resembled a bumblebee;
and because his form was entirely and intensely black, the Sustainer of the World named him Mahākāla.
Then Śaṅkara protected those two with hosts of Pramathas, and they were likewise gradually nurtured by Aparṇā as well. 65.
When those two great-souled ones had grown up and were protected by Hara and Umā, Hara, having appointed them as the lords of the Gaṇas, stationed them at the gate.
Sagara said:
"O best of the twice-born, what became of that splendor which was cast into the fire?
I wish to hear about that as well; tell it to me in brief. (67)
Aurva said:
Having cast his splendors into the fire for that duration of time,
the bull-bannered god addressed the deities regarding the celestial Gaṅgā as follows.
Īśvara said:
O best of gods, this splendor is difficult to withstand for women or others,
except for the Goddess who is Yoganidrā, or else the Daughter of the Mountain.
Therefore, I shall declare how this [child] will be born by means of his splendor,
where the god will be, and who will receive him.
But this Gaṅgā, who courses through the sky, is another daughter of the King of Mountains;
she is the elder sister of Umā, and from her, Agni begot offspring.
He, of incomparable splendor through his own prowess and majesty, shall be born;
that illustrious subduer of enemies will become your general.
That Śikhidhvaja, empowered by me with the infallible great spear (mahāśakti), shall conquer Tāraka before you.
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus and dismissed all the gods, Mahādeva then took leave of Pārvatī and departed for the purpose of purification.
Having heard the words of the gods, which were unpleasant to her, Satī became enraged at the host of deities, though she was free from any desire for her son.
Then, as if burning with indignation, her lower lip quivering, she spoke thus upon seeing the gods and Hara who had ceased from sexual union: || 76 ||
The Goddess said:
"O gods, since Śambhu has been separated from me by you during our union, I have been made childless and tormented like a courtesan. (77)
Therefore, from this day forward, may all the hosts of gods remain perpetually deprived of sexual union with their own wives. (78)
Just as they have no sons born to them, so too may my divine and beautiful wives be without offspring. (79)
May all those goddesses who have fallen away from the hope of sons suffer exactly as I do, being deprived of the hope for a son. (80)
Aurva said:
Thus the daughter of the mountain, being exceedingly enraged, cursed the gods;
from that time forward, sons of the gods were no longer born in heaven.

Even now, sons have not yet been born to those wives of the drinkers of nectar (the gods). Likewise, when the time had arrived, Dahanah himself deposited within the womb of Gaṅgā his seed, which resembled gold and belonged to Śambhu.
By that semen, the goddess gave birth at the completion of the full term to a pair of daughters endowed with all auspicious marks and captivating to the mind.
One Skanda was named Viśākha, and the second bore a beautiful form;
both of them held two spears and were increased by splendor and luster.
Viśākha and Skanda quickly became one;
he became like a child who has gone forth as the son of another. || 85 ||
Then, seeing her newborn son in that state, Gaṅgā was greatly amazed and quickly released him from the jar into the midst of the Śara thicket.
Then Gaṅgā herself, having released that embryo to Bahulā, related the account of the pregnancy and how it had been born, and then departed. (87)
Having heard that and learned that he was born from the body of Mahādeva, Bahulā took up the son and Kṛttikā protected him.
Having informed Umā and Śaṅkara and having obtained their permission,
he then took that son, the crusher of enemies, and gave him to the Goddess.
Thus, having grown exceedingly great, Śaktidhara, possessed of immense strength and prowess,
was swiftly raised by Śaṅkara to become the commander-in-chief of the divine army.
Then the son of Hara, with the spear in hand, utterly crushed the mighty Tāraka, the enemy of the gods and leader of his hosts, who was himself the savior of the worlds.
O best of kings, I have thus related to you today exactly what occurred when the splendor cast into the fire was united with Bharga.
Now, O Indra among kings, listen to the present and edifying account of Bhṛṅgin Mahākāla, concerning how those two became human beings. (93)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter of the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 46 ||
Chapter Forty-Seven.
Aurvya said:
While Hara was being propitiated by the hosts of gods for the sake of the world, [the following occurred].
For so long he remained deprived of great sexual union with Umā.
He remains engaged with her through mere pleasure, always fulfilling her own desire;
Mṛḍa constantly fulfills the heart's wish of the Goddess.
Then one day, in a secret pleasure-chamber together with me,
Mahādeva, who delights in love, being filled with joy, engaged in playful dalliance.
When Gaurī went to the presence of the Destroyer of Smara for sport,
at that time Bhṛṅgi and Mahākāla were stationed as doorkeepers at the gate.
At the conclusion of the jest, that goddess, having loosened the binding of her braided hair,
grasped with her hand the garment falling from her limbs as it was no longer held fast.
With her pearl necklace disarrayed and her face disheveled by scattered perfumes and flowers, she no longer shone brightly;
the saffron paste was smudged, and the beauty of her lips was marred by their being bitten.
The lotus-faced one emerged from the abode of the coils of Rati,
her eyes slightly rolling and covered with beads of perspiration.
As that blameless woman, who was unfit to be seen by others except her husband, the bull-bannered god Śiva, was thus emerging from the house; || 8 ||
The two high-souled ones, Bhṛṅgī and Mahākāla, did not feel particularly joyful in their hearts; as the time had come, they both became enraged.
Seeing their mother in such a wretched state, those two excellent sons hung their heads and fell into deep anxiety; sighing heavily, they were overcome with grief.
While those two were looking on, the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, saw them;
then Aparṇā became enraged and spoke these words.
And why do you two look upon me, who am such as this, with such irrelevant glances—you two sons, pure and yet devoid of shame and moral restraint? (12)
Since you two, being shameless, have committed this act beyond all bounds, therefore let there be the birth of offspring for you both in human form. (13)
Having entered a human womb due to the fault of looking at me with passion, you two shall become those with the faces of monkeys on this earth. 14.
Thus, having been cursed by Umā, the two high-minded sons of Hara, Bhṛṅgī and Mahākāla, then [went] into the presence of their mother. 15.
Then those two sons of Hara, having encountered that suffering and being dejected in mind, could not endure her curse and spoke thus to the twice-born woman: || 16 ||
"O daughter of Himavat, we two are always sinless toward you;
how is it that you, our mother, have thus cursed us so impetuously out of anger? (17)
Just as we were appointed at the gate by Maheśa along with you,
so do we remain at the gate, restrained, carrying out that very command.
It is certainly not fitting for you to depart from this house by force;
for as soon as you arrived, we were seen to be perfectly self-restrained. (19)
Therefore, anger is useless; what fault of ours is there in that? Hence, O irreproachable mother, hear the remedy for that. (20)
"May you become a human woman on earth, and may Hara become a human; then, in the wife of the human Hara, by the power of Hara’s splendor," ||| 21 ||
"O human woman, we two shall likewise come to exist within your womb, if it be true that we are the sons of Hara and if we are indeed innocent. (22)
"O daughter of the mountain, let these words of ours both be true!"—having thus spoken this most dreadful curse to one another, they then departed. (23)
Thus they entered, O tiger among kings, along with Gaurī and those two sons of Hara;
then, after some time had passed, the omniscient one whose banner is the bull [Śiva] appeared.
Knowing that such a destiny awaited him, he himself became a human being;
from the right thumb of Brahmā, Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, was born.
Aditi was born as his daughter, and from her was born the one named Pūṣan.
Pauṣya was the son of Ūṣṇa, and he had mastered the meaning of all the scriptures.
That Pauṣya, the best of kings, who had no equal on earth—none who had been before nor any who would be—became a king without a son. || 27 ||
When his remaining years had arrived, Pauṣya, together with his three wives,
fully gratified Brahmā with supreme devotion.
Brahmā said:
The Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was pleased with him and said to that king: "Tell me, what do you desire? (29)
"I am pleased, O best of kings; I shall grant you whatever you desire. Tell me now what is wished for by your wives. (30)
Pauṣya said:
"I am the son of Irāṇyagarbha, and seeking a son, I worship you. If you are pleased with me, may a son endowed with auspicious marks be born to me. (31)
"For this purpose, I have approached you with devotion along with my wife;
O Lord of the World, act in such a way that a son may be born to me. (32)
"O son, you save your father and mother from the hell named Put;
therefore, O Great One, you ought to destroy the fear arising from that. (33)
Brahmā said: Listen, O Pauṣya, how your son shall be the upholder of your lineage;
I shall tell you that, so act accordingly with your wives.
"O best of kings, accept this fruit given by me;
it is always delicious and never becomes indigestible, even when a great deal of time has passed. (35)
"Taking this fruit, propitiate Mahādeva for three years; he will become pleased. (36)
O King, just as Bharga speaks, so shall you reap this fruit;
you shall experience its result together with your three wives.
Then, endowed with the auspicious marks, that son shall increase the lineage;
he himself will become a Teacher, a universal monarch (cakravartin) over the earth. (38)
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed; the king also, accompanied by his timid followers, began to worship Hara, endowed with supreme devotion. (39)
Free from desire and restrained in his diet, he sometimes subsisted on fruits;
having placed some fruit before him on the bank of the river Dṛṣadvatī, [he remained there].
He propitiated the bull-bannered Lord with flowers, water-offerings, lamps, and incense;
and when three years had passed, Mahādeva, the Lord of the universe, [appeared].
For the sake of King Pauṣya’s complete success in his aims, Mahādeva became gracious;
being pleased, he spoke to the king as if smiling: "For what purpose do you worship me? Tell me that, and I shall grant it to you. (42)
Pauṣya said:
"I am childless and desirous of a son; hear that, O Bull-bannered One!
O Bull-bannered One, act in such a way that I may indeed possess a son. (43)
Aurva said:
Thus the king spoke, filled with joy along with his wives; having bowed down preceded by hymns of praise, his mind was humbled by devotion.
Then, being pleased with the king who was seeking a son, the bull-bannered Lord took the fruit of Brahma-datta in his hand and spoke thus to him: || 45 ||
The Lord said: "O King, having divided this fruit given by Brahmā into three parts,
you should joyfully feed your wives with a steady mind."
Then, O King, when sexual union occurs with these women during their fertile seasons, your wives shall conceive simultaneously.
O best of kings, when the time has come, the delivery of your women shall occur simultaneously; you shall act in this manner therein.
The upper portion of the head shall be formed within the womb of one woman, while the middle portion of the belly shall belong to the other. || 49 ||
The portion below the navel shall belong to the other;
and that triad of segments, O King, shall each be situated in their respective places.
Later, you will have one son;
on his head, a crescent moon mark will be present from birth.
"And he shall attain fame on the earth by that very name.
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva himself then [placed] their embryos [within his own].
He brought this water from the Āhnavī to purify it for his own abode;
then the bull-bannered God himself entered into the fruit.
At that very moment, three parts of that fruit indeed became manifest by themselves;
Pauṣya, taking those fruits, was delighted along with his wife.
Having taken leave of the bull-bannered god, he went to his palace joyfully;
then, when the proper time arrived, it was eaten by them.
O tiger among kings, that was the fruit; the auspicious embryos were nourished, and when the period of gestation was complete, they were born from the wombs. (56)
O King, those three sections were likewise spoken by Bharga;
and having arranged those three sections in the Pauṣya according to their proper places, [he recited them].
He quickly formed it into a single mass, and there a son was born;
O King, at that time, an auspicious crescent moon was naturally present upon his head.
He shone like the digit of the moon in its proper place during the autumn season—endowed with all auspicious marks, broad-chested, and possessing a beautiful nose. (59)
Then, seeing him with the neck of a lion, large eyes, and long, extended arms, Pauṣya, together with his three wives, was filled with joy.
Having obtained that vast and excellent treasury, the poor man became wealthy;
then the king, together with his own brahmins and domestic priests, bestowed a name upon him.
Named Candraśekhara, equal to the moon in splendor, that illustrious son grew day by day like the moon itself. (62)
Like a radiant one with his digits, or like the moon in autumn, so was Hara born from the wombs of the three mothers. (63)
Therefore, he became renowned in both the world and the Vedas by the name Tryambaka.
At that time, the prince reached the stage of youth. (64)
He became equal to Viṣṇu, knowing the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures; he was his peer in strength, heroism, weaponry, sacred learning, and character.
"O tiger among kings, there has been no other such [ruler], nor will there ever be another on this earth;
therefore, having consecrated that prince, who is exceedingly powerful, in the kingdom—" (66)
At fifteen years of age, King Pauṣya, endowed with all royal virtues,
entered the forest together with his three wives;
for that most righteous king desired to perform the rites appropriate for an elder.
When his father had departed for forest life, that king of great power [reigned].
The minister Candraśekhara brought the entire earth under his control;
having become a sovereign emperor, he was served by other kings.
Endowed with splendor, he sported like the Lord of the Gods among the immortals;
thus, having become the son of Pauṣya, Tryambaka was fulfilled by his merit.
Having become king in the delightful city called Karavīra, situated on the banks of the river Dṛṣadvatī in the region known as Brahmāvarta, he indeed rejoiced.
Then once, O best of kings, that monarch himself became desirous of seeing his father, who had gone to dwell in the forest, as well as his mothers.
Then that moon-crested one, alone in a single chariot,
took up his massive bow along with a multitude of arrows.
Desirous of seeing his aged father together with his mother, he reached the holy penance grove situated at the edge of the kingdom.
As he was approaching his father, King Candraśekhara saw a great sage named Namuci performing austerities.
He was clothed in an upper garment of black antelope skin, radiant as the sun,
possessed of matted locks rising upwards, meditative, and emaciated.
Seeing him from afar—his body radiant with asceticism, motionless upon a seat of kusha grass—the hero descended from the seat of his chariot. (77)
And with his neck bowed in humility, he approached the best of Brahmins;
he prostrated before that sage, uttering these words: || 78 ||
O Brahmin, I am the son of Pauṣya, named Candraśekhara;
with great devotion, I bow down to you, the best of sages. (79)
Having spoken thus, the king stood before that sage with palms joined in reverence,
his mind and pride bowed down by devotion as he gazed upon the face of Namuci.
Even before the king had entered the forest for asceticism,
he honored that sage together with his wives at that very moment.
Having propitiated Namuci for a long time, Pauṣya, the supreme scholar whose words were truthful, sought to please the sage for the sake of obtaining a son.
"O best of sages, you dwell here performing austerities at the edge of the realm;
O sage, if you have compassion for me, I would ask one thing of you. (83)
My son is a young child, a king named Candraśekhara; endowed with the crescent digit of the innate moon, he is fickle due to his childhood nature. || 84 ||
If she should happen to offend you upon approaching you, O Sage, then please forgive her; this is what I have requested of you. (85)
Having heard Pauṣya’s words, the sage indeed accepted them;
then, seeing that son, the brahmin remembered Pauṣya’s speech.
Having remembered Candraśekhara, who stood before him for a long time with bowed head,
that compassionate sage named Namuci spoke as follows.
O Moon-crested Lord, I am pleased today with your disciplined conduct;
choose a boon, and I shall grant you your most cherished desire.
Having heard those words of his, King Candraśekhara bowed again and spoke these very truthful words to Namuci: || 89 ||

O best of the twice-born, whatever [merit] has been performed by me excessively through body, mind, or speech— all that belongs to my domain, since those such as you are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for it.
There is nothing in my mind that is difficult to attain or desirable;
that alone is to be chosen by me which you yourself bestow. (91)
Namuci said:
"O best of kings, when another seventeen years have passed, you shall become the husband of the excellent Rāmā; we [shall be yours]. (92)
Just as the daughter of the mountain belongs to Śambhu, as Lakṣmī belongs to the wielder of the mace,
and as Śacī belongs to the lord of the gods, so too shall she be yours.
Having spoken thus to the king, that sage, a treasury of ascetic powers, dismissed him;
and he too, filled with joy, departed.
Having gone there and reached his father and mother, Candraśekhara honored them as was fitting; he, the son, was then comforted by them in return.
Then the king returned to his own city of Karavīrapurī;
joyful and resembling the lord of the gods, he took delight together with his ministers.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 47 ||
The forty-eighth chapter.
Aurva said:
When Mahādeva had descended out of a desire for the happiness of Pauṣyajāyā, [the following occurred].
When three years had passed by human reckoning. || 1 ||
The Supreme Goddess Girijā also, by her own will, was born as the wife of King Kakutstha through Menakā, just as before.
Now, in the region of Āryāvarta, there was a righteous king named Kakutstha, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, who was devoted to Brahman and the best among heroes. || 3 ||
In the city named Bhogavatī, there was a destroyer of enemies,
endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of the virtues of a king.
His wife was the highly fortunate daughter of Bhargadeva;
she was named Manonmathinī, honored, and beloved by her husband.
From that best of kings, Kakutstha, she bore a hundred sons in a sacrifice who were like the offspring of gods, steadfast, and endowed with strength and heroism.
Since she had no daughter, for that purpose she prepared a secret sacrificial altar within her house and worshipped Caṇḍikā.
Being thus honored by the king's wife, the great goddess Caṇḍikā became pleased; after three years, she spoke these words to her in a dream.
Endowed with the auspicious marks of a woman, that beautiful lady will become your daughter, destined for a universal monarch, and adorned with a garland of stars.
That queen of the king also became joyful, having obtained a boon in her dream; that queen of the king also became joyful, having obtained a boon in her dream. (10)
Pārvatī herself also entered her womb at the proper time;
when the union of the seasons had occurred, that goddess, who agitates the mind,
conceived a great being, just as the moonlight holds a mass of nectar.
Then, when the full period had arrived, that goddess Manonmathinī gave birth to an auspicious daughter adorned with a garland of stars.
Seeing her adorned with a necklace, auspicious and resembling the autumnal moonlight, Kakutstha, together with his wife, became exceedingly joyful. (13)
Adorned with a natural necklace, the daughter of Kakutstha grew in his palace like the celestial river during the rainy season.
O best of kings, at the time prescribed, her father gave her the name Tārāvatī because of that very mark of the necklace.
In the course of time, that woman of excellent complexion passed her childhood and attained the charming blossoming of youth, like the Goddess Śrī in the month of Mādhava.
In splendor she followed Splendor, and in purity that virtuous and auspicious woman followed Pārvatī, who was excellent in character through her conduct and endowed with beauty. (17)
Then, seeing the emergence of her youth, King Kakutstha, together with his sons, caused a svayaṃvara to be held at the appropriate time.
When the month of Mādhava had arrived, on an auspicious day during the waxing moon,
Tārāvatī’s father, together with his sons, prepared a hall for her svayaṃvara.
The king quickly dispatched many messengers by means of mares and camels toward the kings of various lands.
Having heard that news from the messenger at that time, those kings quickly assembled for the svayaṃvara of Tārāvatī.
Having heard that, the son of Pauṣya, accompanied by his fourfold army and adorned with divine ornaments, went quickly to the svayaṃvara.
Having gone there, those best of kings took their seats appropriately in the midst of the assembly hall for the *svayaṃvara*, which had been constructed by Kakutstha. (23)
Then, while the kings were seated, Kakutstha set his mind upon leading his own daughter into the assembly hall when an auspicious moment arrived.
In the meantime, the king’s daughter, a woman of excellent complexion,
[approached] her own aged nurse, who was perfectly endowed with complete knowledge.
She sent her toward the assembly to behold the hall of the self-choice ceremony,
and then spoke to the nurse of the princess Sumaṅgalā.
"Having gone to the assembly hall of the svayaṃvara, O Earth, identify the king who possesses beautiful form and auspicious marks, and announce him to me in person. (27)
O mother, you desire my welfare and even my good fortune;
therefore, act in such a way that I may have a husband who bestows good fortune upon me. (28)
Having thus dispatched that nurse,
the princess went to where she, who was agitating his mind, was worshipping Caṇḍikā.
Then the highly fortunate and auspicious Tārāvatī went there;
having arrived, she bowed down to the Great Goddess named Kālikā.
Then, recognizing her as such through his own human nature,
he bowed down to her with great devotion and spoke these words.
I bow to Mahāmāyā, the yogic sleep, who is identical with the universe;
may that Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, be gracious to me. 32.
"If it is true that you were worshipped by my mother for my sake, by that truth may my husband be fortunate, O best of kings. (33)
"O beloved of Hara, be gracious and let the svayaṃvara take place today!
Having heard these words of hers, Caṇḍikā, who deludes Hara, [acted accordingly].
Just as she enchanted the princess so that she did not even know herself,
so too did she, whose form was invisible, speak these truthful words.
The Goddess said: "That son of Pauṣya who was named Candraśekhara,
possessing a captivating form, shall become your beloved husband."
O lady of beautiful hips, choose that best of kings, who is marked on his head by a digit of the moon, just as Pārvatī chose the bull-bannered Śiva. (37)
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī quickly opened the cave for the princess;
she too, bowing down with eyes blossoming with joy, vanished from sight.
She went to the auspicious chamber where her mother was staying;
then that nurse returned, having found a suitable husband for her. (39)
Then, O best of kings, Tārāvatī related the secret;
having seen that nurse standing before her, the princess was filled with joy, O King. (40)
She asked in secret, "What kind of king was seen by you? Seeing her standing before her, the nurse was delighted, O King, and [the daughter] spoke. (40)
He asked her privately, "What kind of king was it, or who was seen by you?
She replied at the nurse's word, "The kings have been observed by me. (41)
Handsome, of noble birth, and masters of both the sciences and the weapons—I am unable to enumerate their many virtues. (42)
"O lady of auspicious luster, I shall tell you of those in whom I take delight;
O auspicious one, among them, four men of beautiful form were chosen by me. (43)
There too, two other men were seen who were not gods; nor was there any purpose whatsoever in speaking of them as gods. (44)
Furthermore, of those two rulers of the earth, one was named Sarvāṅgakalyāṇa together with his son, and the other was Candraśekhara.
Between these two Nāsatyas, however, there is no distinction whatsoever;
in their form and the beauty of their bodies, they are all exceedingly captivating. (46)
Furthermore, those two kings were beings of great essence, with shoulders like lions and mighty arms;
their hands, eyes, faces, feet, and palms were all slightly reddish.
Both had broad chests and large eyes, with their two eyebrows joined together;
they were endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with divine ornaments.
Between those two as well, Candraśekhara was the more praiseworthy, for he was in the prime of his youth,
possessed of excellent character, truthful in speech, and esteemed in both sacred scripture and weaponry.
His beautiful and stainless face, with its slightly sprouting dark-blue hair,
shines like the moon marked by the *lakṣmaṇa* constellation.
He shines with even a radiant digit of the Lord of Night;
indeed, he is the Moon-crested One himself, bearing that innate mark upon his head.
"O beautiful one, he alone is a suitable husband for you by this very sign;
choose that king as your husband, who is worthy of you and brings about auspicious results. (52)
Having heard these words of the nurse, the princess said to her:
"Become my attendant and point out the best of kings to me. (53)
At that time, as they were conversing with one another, the king arrived at the hall of the svayaṃvara just as I was entering it. (54)
Then, at an auspicious time when fortune had dawned, Kakutstha himself went to lead his daughter to the assembly hall for her svayaṃvara, that abode of blessings.
Having approached his beloved daughter, who had been blessed with auspicious rites by the women,
he took a garland of fragrant flowers in his hand and placed it upon her hand.
Having given this, he quickly spoke while leading her from the abode of auspiciousness:
"O Mother, having entered the assembly, honor the most excellent one with another garland. (57)
"Whomever you desire—whether a king or a brahmin—you shall choose.
Having spoken thus, [he was placed] upon a palanquin by his own trusted and aged attendants. (58)
Then, seeing her arrive at the assembly hall, Śakra and the other gods of the thirty-three [heavens] were present.
The other guardians of the directions also arrived at the assembly hall at that very moment;
then Tārāvatī, having descended from her vehicle, joyfully reached it.
Accompanied by her nurse Anugā, she moved about within the assembly hall;
having sported for a long time in the midst of the court, that woman of excellent complexion [departed].
Due to her cultivated state, her fixed destiny, and the grace of Caṇḍikā,
she was awakened by that nurse because of their equality and oneness.
With her face covered by droplets of perspiration born from her exertion,
the virtuous princess Tārāvatī was the first to greet her husband, the king.
And that goddess Pārvatī herself chose the moon-crested Lord;
then, seeing him chosen, the brahmins [honored her] with Sāman chants.
O King, with diligent minds, the bards, singers, and musicians performed the auspicious wedding rites for the two of them, accompanied by the triple symphony of instrumental music, song, and dance.
Out of curiosity, they all praised, sang, and played instruments;
and all the gods found joy in the one who bears the moon as his crest-jewel.
Then, when Tārāvatī had been chosen, Kakutstha was also exceedingly delighted;
as for those other kings, headed by Subāhu, who witnessed this event— || 67 ||
The moon-crested Lord, though enraged, restrained them in the assembly;
then the gods departed for heaven according to their own will.
And when the kings had departed after being honored by Kakutstha,
that king Candraśekhara [performed] according to the marriage rites.
Then, with the consent of Kakutstha, he consecrated his wife Tārāvatī and informed the gods through Vedic sacrifices.
Having performed the sacramental rite of taking her hand, Candraśekhara quickly departed for Karavīrapura with his companion.
Furthermore, at that marriage ceremony, the one named Kakutstha gave twenty-two thousand female slaves to the husband of Viṭabhūti.
He likewise gave sixty thousand cows of the Saurabhi breed as a dowry to his daughter, along with male and female servants in great numbers.
Another was his own daughter, known by the name Citrāṅgadā, belonging to the king named Kakutstha; she was equal to Tārāvatī in her beauty. (74)
Having become the mistress of the female servants,
she then followed her own auspicious elder sister, Tārāvatī, the daughter of the king.
Having properly taken those servants with him, the great eldest son of Kakutstha,
named Viśvāvasu, [followed] Candraśekhara as he was departing.
Accompanied by Tārāvatī, the wise one followed behind in a swift-moving chariot toward Karavīrapura.
Together with Tārāvatī, King Candraśekhara, the son of Pauṣya and the crest-jewel of monarchs,
took his pleasure in the beautiful city of Karavīra.
Thus Mahādeva himself, having taken recourse to a human womb, and Pārvatī herself, the blameless one, was born from a human womb. (79)
Likewise, Bhṛṅgī and Mahākāla became their sons;
listen to that, O Indra among kings, as I describe their origin. (80)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 48 ||
Chapter Forty-nine.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, after some time had passed, the virtuous daughter of Kakutstha—
Surrounded by women, she was preparing for her ritual bath at the onset of menses.
[He saw] that river with cool, pure water, delightful and skilled in destroying impurity;
resembling crushed collyrium and expert in the destruction of turbidity. || 2 ||
The best of sages beheld the great lady, golden-complexioned, who had performed her ablutions but had not yet emerged, standing half-submerged like a female dove.
Having assumed the form of a dove out of fear of killing living beings, he wandered about;
because of that, he is remembered as Kapota.
Seeing her, who shone like the interior of gold and resembled the autumnal moonlight,
the pigeon, deeply pierced by the arrows of love, was filled with desire.
Tormented by the fire of desire, that sage approached the auspicious daughter of Kakutstha and spoke these words.
The pigeon said:
"Who are you? Whose wife are you, O beautiful lady? Or whose daughter are you?
For what reason have you come here to the waters of the Upāṃśu river? (7)
Your form is gentle and delightful; your face resembles the full moon, and the pair of your nostrils is like the sesame flower.
Your eyes are like blue lotuses trembling in the wind;
your arms are beautiful, rounded, and long as soft lotus stalks;
your thighs resemble the trunks of elephants; and your waist is slender as the middle of a sacrificial altar.
But with such a form as this, you are no human woman;
you are either a goddess or a daughter of the Dānavas, endowed with the qualities of an Apsaras.
Or else, O beautiful one, you have assumed the form of a woman for the sake of being enjoyed; tell me, are you Aparṇā or Śacī? (11)
Aurva said:
Having heard these words of the sage, the beautiful woman emerged from the water, bowed down to that sage with humility, and spoke these words. (12)
"O sage, know me as Tārāvatī by name, the daughter of Kakutstha; being a virtuous woman, I am the wife of King Candraśekhara. (13)
"I am neither a goddess, nor a gandharvī, nor a yakṣī, nor a rākṣasī;
I am a human, the daughter of a king, who observes the vows of virtuous conduct. (14)
The pigeon said:
"Upon seeing you, desire itself arose within me for union with you; moreover, I have been tormented by that very desire, which is manifest through your power. (15)
O soft-spoken one, quickly rescue me, who have fallen into the surging waves of the ocean of passion, by means of the boat of your thighs, so that I may be free from distress.
"O highly fortunate lady, from me two sons shall be born, beautiful and endowed with auspicious marks, great and possessed of strength and heroism. (17)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words of the pigeon, the eloquent daughter of Kakutstha, overwhelmed by fear and grief, then spoke these words in a faltering voice.
Tārāvatī spoke these words: "I must not perform another task that is highly censurable;
therefore, do not speak thus to me, for having bowed to you, I seek your favor. (19)
O ascetic, even for you this would not be fitting here;
it is censurable, destructive of my penance, and a cause for the ruin of my virtue.
The pigeon said:
"Whether it be the exhaustion of my ascetic merit or some other defect, let that be mine here;
nevertheless, O auspicious one, I do not wish to abandon you during our union."
"You must certainly grant me protection from these sensual desires here; otherwise, O enchanting one, abandoned by you, I shall be consumed by passion. (22)
"And I shall reduce you, along with your kinsmen, to ashes by my curse.
Then, having heard those words, the virtuous goddess Tārāvatī gave no reply at all out of fear of the sage's curse.
"I shall converse with my friends; stay here, O great sage."
Having spoken thus, the queen then went into the midst of her handmaidens, summoned Citrāṅgadā, and spoke these words: || 25 ||
"This man of beautiful armlets desires me intensely;
what shall I do so that I do not fall away from my state of chastity? (26)
The dove would instantly consume her husband and kinsmen with the fire of a curse; yet if I do not desire the sage, I shall fall into danger. (27)
Then Citrāṅgadā said: "Do not fear, O speaker of truth!
I shall tell you a means there, by performing which you will be liberated. (28)
If the sage does not abandon you, then, having adorned this single beautiful maidservant with fine ornaments, you should offer her to the sage.
Afflicted by lust and deluded by infatuation, the wretched sage will certainly not recognize her—covered as she is by your ornaments—as he would a doe hidden by the moonlight. (30)
"Act thus, O highly fortunate one; do not fall into anxiety, O auspicious lady. If you remain steadfast, then the sage will certainly come to know that you are virtuous. (31)
Then Tārāvatī spoke to that Citrāṅgadā, the princess endowed with beauty and virtue, who was ever characterized by modesty and truthfulness.
"Go yourself, O blameless sister, O wise one, after adorning your own body with my ornaments, to the place called Apota."
"O Brahmin, having become aware that another woman has been sent [to me], he will surely burn me along with my family with the fire of his wrath; therefore, go away, O beautiful one. (34)
"You are equal to me in all virtues and adorned with every ornament;
O auspicious one, unite me with the sage today and protect me along with my family."
Then, having heard her words and her humble yet distressed demeanor,
he remained silent for a moment, as if his heart were not at all joyful.
And she said to the illustrious Citrāṅgadā, the daughter of Kakutstha: "I shall do your bidding today; you shall remember me at the appointed time. (37)
For whose sake she will thus console this father, King Candraśekhara, as well as her entire circle of female friends.
Having spoken thus, Citrāṅgadā covered Tārāvatī’s ornaments and quickly departed for the sage’s festival of love. || 39 ||
Then Tārāvatī, wearing wretched clothes and devoid of ornaments, having joined the midst of the female slaves, followed after that very beloved woman. (40)
Then, seeing her approaching, Apoda, deluded by passion,
remembered his union with the wives of the sages.
Formerly, Pramlocā was indeed desired by the son of Vataṇḍa,
just as Padmā was desired by the wise Bharadvāja.
"In this way, I shall now desire that woman of excellent complexion; afterwards, by the power of my asceticism, I will likewise liberate her from the sin of [having committed] adultery. (43)
While he was thinking thus, the auspicious Citrāṅgadā approached that sage and, filled with shame, said something to him.
Having reached her, that illustrious pigeon, the best of sages,
mentally recalled Madana for the sake of the sentiments and attire of love.
Then, as soon as he was remembered, Madana himself approached the great sage and,
filled with great joy, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and fine garments.
Having consented, that brahmin, possessing a beautiful form, descended;
he blazed with splendor like a second sun. || 47 ||
Having thus seen that enchanting boat, which was like the god of love himself, all the women became filled with desire, with the exception of Tārāvatī. (48)
Seeing the sage, who was as beautiful as the god of love, Tārāvatī was struck with supreme wonder and considered the sage to be Kāma himself. || 49 ||
Then Citrāṅgadā, being well-pleased, immediately engaged the brahmin lover in sexual union, and he became satisfied in an instant. (50)
Then, two sons were born to her immediately; they resembled the offspring of gods, possessing a radiance like that of a blazing fire or the sun. 51.
When the two sons were born, the sage, having touched her with his hand, restored her to her former state and spoke these words: (52)
O beloved of auspicious countenance, remain with me for some time;
at my will you shall depart, and you need have no fear of the king.
"So be it," she replied to the sage out of fear of his curse;
then the muni dismissed her and the other women as well.
Then Queen Tārāvatī, surrounded by her maidservants and grieving for her sister, went to her own palace.
Having gone there, the descendant of Kakutstha then quickly reported that entire wonderful account of what Apotaka had done to the lord of Brahmāvarta.
Having heard this, that tiger among kings reflected for a moment and, with the permission of Apoda, undertook to assist Citrāṅgadā. (57)
Then, at that time, the father also performed the sacramental rites for those two sons born of her according to the prescribed procedure.
Sagara said:
"How did Citrāṅgadā then become the daughter of Kakutstha?
I wish to hear that; tell it to me, O best of the twice-born. (59)
Aurva said: Once, that Kakutstha went to the great mountain Himavat for the sake of hunting, and many deer were struck down.
Then, as Urvaśī was descending from the world of the gods toward the earth,
he saw her seated upon a mountain ridge like a courtesan for the sake of rest.
Having approached her, the great king, tormented by the arrows of love,
repeatedly requested union with her body as she remained on the mountain.
Having recognized that Kakutstha was a tiger among kings, resembling Indra himself,
Urvaśī delighted him as she desired within a mountain grove.
Then, from King Kakutstha, that tiger among kings, a daughter named Manoharā was born instantly to his celestial courtesan. (64)
Then, when Kakutstha was satisfied by her desire,
that blameless Urvaśī, having informed him of her wish for her desired destination, desired to depart.
The king said to that daughter of his: "O auspicious one, O lady of beautiful limbs, how can you wish to depart after abandoning me? Protect this daughter of yours instead. (66)
She said: "I am a celestial courtesan; who has not had a son or a daughter by me? Yet now, O princess, you have given birth to one this very day. (67)
By my own splendor, no transformation of the body occurs in me;
nor are my sons protected, due to my inherent nature as a courtesan. (68)
If you have compassion for your daughter, take her and raise her yourself;
grant me permission to depart, for I tell you this in truth. (69)
Having spoken thus, O King, Urvaśī departed quickly as she pleased;
and he, taking his daughter with him, entered his own city.
The king himself gave her the name Citrāṅgadā,
and he bestowed that auspicious daughter upon his wife Manonmathinī.
And then that best of kings spoke these words to the queen:
"O Queen, this is my daughter; you must protect her, who is endowed with excellent virtues. (72)
"You should not treat with contempt this stone-born [image] brought by me";
thus addressed by Pāla, the princess made up her mind accordingly. (73)
Placing her husband’s command foremost, she said nothing else at all;
yet once, out of childishness, she [spoke] to the great sage Aṣṭāvakra.
As she was walking away with a sidelong glance, she laughed and mocked him;
the sage became enraged and pronounced a most dreadful curse upon her.
She gave herself as a maidservant to the son of Kakutstha, saying, "May I belong to your lineage.
Thus, having become a servant while remaining unmarried, she bore two sons to her own lineage.
"O most sinful woman, you shall give birth [to him], and from that you will obtain prosperity.
Thus, O King, Citrāṅgadā became the daughter of Kakutstha.
Having become a maidservant, she was taken in by Tārāvatī;
though she remained unmarried, she obtained a pair of sons from that most auspicious and excellent sage.
"And those two illustrious sons shall perform a great task.
Thus, O King, I have told you how Citrāṅgadā became the virtuous daughter of Kakutstha; now hear what is relevant for the present.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the Śīkālikā Purāṇa. || 49 ||
Fifty-first Chapter.
Aurva said:
Then, after some time had passed, the auspicious Tārāvatī once again—
Having performed the prescribed bath for her menses, she reached the river Dṛṣadvatī. || 1 ||
Accompanied by thousands of female servants and adorned with various ornaments, she appeared just like Indrāṇī with Rambhā and the other celestial nymphs. || 2 ||
Having descended into the water, the fair-limbed goddess, radiant as lightning,
illuminated the river whose waters were like crushed collyrium.
Just as a golden image illuminates a clear glass surface with its own luster,
so too did she illuminate it by means of her reflection.
Then, O best of sages, the pigeon saw her once again, most beautiful, submerged up to her navel by the flood of waters.
Then, having seen her, the sage questioned Citrāṅgadā:
"Who is this woman who has descended into the waters of the Dṛṣadvatī with hundreds of female companions?"
Blazing with splendor and equal to Śrī herself, why is the daughter of the mountain not Aparṇā?
She shines exceedingly with her forms; why do you not praise her?
Then, having heard those words of the sage, the virtuous Citrāṅgadā,
out of fear of the rishi’s curse, said at that time, "I praise you."
This virtuous woman named Tārāvatī is the daughter of Kakutstha;
she is the auspicious and most beloved wife of King Candraśekhara.
O Sage, she was previously desired by you for the sake of pleasure;
having adorned me with her own ornaments, she gave me to you and returned to her home.
Furthermore, this sister of mine has come to bathe in the river; O Sage, it is not at all appropriate for you to say anything to that eldest sister of mine. (11)
"O best of brahmins, you remain here; having addressed my beloved elder sister, I shall return to you, provided you grant me leave to go. (12)
Having heard these words of hers, the sage became enraged at her for the deception previously committed by Tārāvatī out of affection.
This most wicked woman has practiced deception upon me;
today I shall certainly carry out her destruction.
Having spoken thus, the sage went together with her, named Citāṅgadā,
to where the auspicious goddess Tārāvatī was staying.
Having gone there and approached her, that best of sages, the pigeon,
spoke these words to Tārāvatī, appearing angry yet as if laughing.
"O unassailable one, you previously solicited me for the sake of desire through a ruse; I have been deceived by you—reap the fruit of that! (17)
O sinful woman, even before me you boast that you are chaste;
yet you did not desire me, who am the very cause of the destruction of your chastity. (18)
Therefore, a loathsome man—shaven-headed, grey-haired, deformed, and destitute of wealth—will surely desire you by force in secret. (19)
O sinful woman, within this very year, you shall now give birth to a pair of sons who are handsome, monkey-faced, and endowed with splendor.
Having heard these words of the sage, the goddess Tārāvatī then spoke to the sage,
her lips quivering with both anger and fear.
If my mother, having worshipped Caṇḍikā, obtained me, and if I have always been observant of vows toward the moon-crested King; 22.
