O best of the twice-born, if I am truly the daughter of Kakutstha, by that truth no one other than the gods shall desire me. (23)
If it is true that Mahādeva is constantly propitiated by me,
then by that truth, may [this be granted] to me from the God who bears the moon upon his crest.
"O tiger among sages, even in a dream no other shall desire me," she said,
and having bowed to the sage, she fixed her mind upon her husband.
The beautiful goddess Tārāvatī departed for her own abode;
once that goddess had gone, the sage reflected upon her.
And right before my very eyes, she roams about utterly fearless;
yet within this, a pure seed will remain hidden. (27)
Having reflected thus, that sage, with a mind absorbed in meditation and intent upon divine knowledge, took up the entire account of events.
Just as both sons, Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla, were cursed by the Goddess, so too did they both pronounce a counter-curse upon Pārvatī and Hara. (29)
For what purpose those two descended into human birth,
how Citrāṅgadā was born, and for what purpose she, a celestial maiden, came to be— [all this shall be told].
Having understood that through his divine knowledge, the sage did nothing at all;
instead, he then respectfully took Citrāṅgadā with him.
The brahmin sage returned to his own abode and honored her;
and Tārāvatī related all of that to King Candraśekhara.
The beautiful woman related the entire account of the sage’s curse;
King Pauṣya, filled with anxiety, reflected upon it all within himself.
Having quickly comforted his beloved wife, saying, "Do not fear,
O Queen," she [attained her goal] through constant service to her husband and the diligent pursuit of dharma and artha.
By avoiding what is unwholesome, the curse of the sage is removed;
therefore, O auspicious goddess, you who uphold the vows of virtuous conduct— 35.
"Endowed with auspicious fortune, you shall never encounter calamity.
Having spoken thus, that king, the lord of Karavīrapura, [departed]. (36)
He caused a vast palace to be built, lofty and scraping the clouds,
four hundred fathoms high and thirty yojanas in extent.
Its floor was inlaid within with jewels and crystal, variegated with multicolored gems,
covered with bright layers of lapis lazuli, and exceedingly beautiful.
For the protection of Tārāvatī, he had a golden pillar weighing a *tulā* of jewels, fashioned by Viśvakarman, constructed as a source of joy.
Endowed with jeweled stairways and featuring balconies of lapis lazuli,
the Sudharmā assembly hall was bound together with golden nīpa trees and was preeminent in its qualities.
In that place, Candraśekhara had all manner of enjoyable things— both delicious and soft— brought to him by trusted men.
Then, taking the goddess Tārāvatī with him, King Candraśekhara would constantly ascend that palace roof and take his pleasure.
Thus, for as long as a year, they guarded that goddess in a residence inaccessible to others, with trusted men stationed at the door.
Once, however, when that lord of Karavīra was absent,
Tārāvatī would always ascend to the high palace and remain there.
Thinking of that beloved king who bears the crescent moon on his crest,
she fixed her mind upon his feet like the devoted wife Sāvitrī.
And having then propitiated Mahādeva together with Pārvatī,
that goddess remained there, meditating upon her beloved deity.
There, as she was meditating upon the three-eyed one who bears the moon upon his crest,
she perceived no difference between those two who both bear the moon upon their crests.
Thus, standing upon the roof of the palace, the virtuous Tārāvatī was like the goddess Śacī, adorned with splendor, situated in the midst of the Sudharmā assembly hall.
Then, O King, the moon-crested Lord, traveling toward that palace together with Umā, arrived there through the sky. (49)
She was seen crossing over, resembling Umā in her virtues;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks, like Mādhavī to Mādhava.
Seeing her, the bull-bannered god spoke to the goddess Gaurī,
his face bright with a smile as if laughing at the beautiful woman.
Īśvara said:
"O beloved, this human form of yours, known as Tārāvatī,
was personally ordained for the birth of Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla."
"For I have no other beloved but you; I do not venture to go elsewhere.
O beautiful lady, you yourself must now enter this form.
From that, I shall bring forth Mahākāla and Bhṛṅgin. (53)
The Goddess said:
"O you whose banner is the bull, I myself am present here in human form; at your word, I shall enter this body, so procreate two sons. (53)
O Bharga, by means of the curse of myself, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, and Kapota, liberation shall thus come to pass; therefore, do what is pleasing to me.
Aurva said:
Then the Goddess herself entered the body of Tārāvatī;
Mahādeva also approached her for the sake of fulfilling his desire.
Then the virtuous Queen Tārāvatī, possessed by Sāparṇī,
herself joyfully approached Mahādeva as he was desiring her.
At that time, Garga appeared as a skull-bearer (Kapālin), wearing a garland of bones;
he was loathsome in appearance, foul-smelling, grey-haired, and possessed of an exceedingly hideous form.
O tiger among kings, at the end of her desire, two sons were born to her immediately, both having the faces of monkeys.
When those two sons were born, Aparṇā emerged from his body;
having thus deluded herself, she did not recognize her own offspring as Kakutstha’s.
I am Aurī, as well as Bhargabhāva and Mānuṣa.
Then Queen Tārāvatī, seeing her two sons standing upon the ground,
beheld herself fallen from her state of extreme asceticism, O beautiful lady.
Likewise, seeing Hara standing before him in his loathsome guise,
he then considered the sage’s curse to have arrived like the Destroyer at the end of time.
Thus, bewildered by grief, she censured her vow of chastity and,
beholding the trident-bearing Mahādeva, spoke these words to him.
"The vow of fidelity of virtuous women is even superior to the ascetic discipline of sages"—thus have those who know the past always declared, O steadfast ones. (64)
"I do not consider that to be true which has happened to me in this way," having said this, the goddess then grieved and fainted.
Then Mahādeva said to her: "O fair-faced one, do not grieve; O virtuous-minded one, do not revile even the vow of Satī."
O long-eyed one, as soon as you were cursed by him, you spoke right there in his presence; that which you said has now come to pass for you.
If it is true that the Great Goddess is constantly propitiated by me,
then by that truth, O God, may [this be granted] through the grace of the moon-crested Lord whom I worship.
"O tiger among sages, even in a dream no other shall desire me;
I am that very Mahādeva, the moon-crested one, who is to be propitiated. (69)
"O lady, though you have been desired by me, do not grieve," having spoken thus, that Mahādeva vanished right there.
Deluded by illusion, the virtuous Queen Tārāvatī sat down there upon the ground in a soiled garment, overcome with grief.
When both sons fell to the ground, that queen did not look at them,
constantly longing for her husband's arrival and remembering the words spoken by Bharga.
Nor did she shine in the house while remaining thus with her hair disheveled;
then, O illustrious one, that king Candraśekhara [appeared] in an instant.
Then he went to the roof of the palace to see Tārāvatī;
having ascended that palace, he [saw] his wife Tārāvatī at that time.
He saw her fallen upon the ground, with disheveled hair and devoid of joy;
her face was darkened, she was gasping for breath, and she was utterly intent on self-reproach. (75)
Then he saw the sun and the moon fallen upon the earth with the faces of monkeys, as well as the agitation of the bull's feet.
Having thus reflected on everything, King Candraśekhara,
both terrified and amazed, questioned his wife in great agitation.
"Tārāvatī, what has happened to you in that secluded house?
Or who indeed has dared to seize you, like a lioness? (78)
"Whose two broad-faced monkeys are these, so brilliantly radiant?
Tell me that quickly; who else has desired you? (79)
Aurva said:
Thus addressed by the king, the virtuous Tārāvatī then related the entire account to the one who has the moon as his crest-ornament.
With her throat choked with tears and her voice faltering, she related everything—how Bharga had arrived and what he had said in reply. (81)
Having heard those words of hers, Candraśekhara reflected and sat down upon the earth in order to ascertain what had occurred.
Reflecting within himself, the king made this deliberation:
"Lord Śiva has no other beloved; he has no one other than Pārvatī. (83)
Therefore, he will desire her; thus, he is not the glorious Supreme Lord.
For the curse of a sage is powerful, and it was precisely because of that curse that he became a Rākṣasa.
Someone endowed with the power of illusion has arrived in the guise of Śaṅkara;
this Satī, my beloved wife, has been defiled even by a Rākṣasa. (85)
"And how am I to receive this [mantra], as before in all rites?
And these two sons of his are Rākṣasas, born this very day. (86)
"Or otherwise, what kind of sons are these with the faces of monkeys?
While he was thinking thus, [a voice] dispatched by the host of gods [spoke]: 87.
Sarasvatī, stationed in the sky, spoke thus to the king:
"O best of kings, you must not entertain any doubt regarding Tārāvatī. (88)
It is true that Mahādeva united with his wife;
O King, you must protect these two sons of his.
"O Nārada, whatever other doubt you have regarding this matter, he will dispel it.
Having spoken thus, the sweet-speaking Goddess of Speech quickly became silent. (90)
Then the king, having gained confidence, consoled his wife;
he then performed the funeral rites for the two sons of the God of gods according to the prescribed ritual. 91.
The king protected [the earth] while awaiting the arrival of Nārada;
then the celestial sage Nārada came to his palace.
The king received him with many offerings;
having honored him according to custom along with Tārāvatī, the monarch [honored him]. (93)
Then Candraśekhara caused that sage to ascend a lofty, incomparable palace resembling the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
Then, in that place, King Candraśekhara, together with his wife,
asked in private about the events that had previously occurred.
"I am purified and graced by you, O son of Brahmā, O best of Brahmins, who traverse both the interior and exterior of lofty palaces. (96)
O Brahman, you ought to sever this one doubt residing in my heart;
other than you, there is no one anywhere who can dispel this doubt.
"By the curse of a rishi, this virtuous Tārāvatī, my wife, was violated by the one clad in animal skins, who assumed a loathsome form and appearance. (98)
Furthermore, these two sons of his were born as soon as they were conceived;
regarding this, a constant doubt perpetually arises in my mind. (99)
How did Giriśa, whose beloved is none other than Girijā Pārvatī, cause her to unite with a human woman born of an inferior lineage? 100.
How did he procreate his two human sons?
Tell me all of this, provided that it is not a secret to you. (101)
Aurva said:
Thus questioned by the moon-crested Lord of the Earth, that sage Nārada, the best of sages, recounted all of that. (102)
Just as Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla were produced in ancient times, and how they were both cursed by Pārvatī, he related those events just as they occurred. (103)
Just as Bharga, the son of Pauṣya, was born with the moon as his crest-ornament,
so too did Gaurī become Tārāvatī in the house of Kakutstha.
Nārada related all of that to the moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
and Nārada also recounted this supreme narrative.
Nārada said:
When the bull-bannered Lord addressed Aparṇā as "Kālī," then Umā departed for ascetic penance, desiring the whiteness of her body.
Filled with indignation at the words of Śaṅkara, the daughter of the mountain,
though being consoled by Bharga, went to the peak of the Himavat mountain.
When Pārvatī had departed, Śaṅkara, afflicted by the pain of separation,
abandoned Mount Kailāsa and then went to the summit of Meru.
Even there, being deprived of Pārvatī and deluded by Kāmadeva as well as by Yoganidrā, he found no peace.
Then one day, on the summit of Mount Meru, Śambhu beheld Sāvitrī as she was wandering, most enchanting and equal to Pārvatī in her virtues.
Upon seeing her, he was overcome by passion; tormented by separation from Pārvatī and possessed by ignorance, he became like an ordinary man.
Then, mistaking her for Pārvatī as she was wandering about, he pursued her, saying:
"Come to me, O auspicious Pārvatī! I am tormented by separation from you. (112)
"O beloved, this Kāma strikes me as he recalls our former enmity; therefore, I shall now take great vengeance upon him. (113)
Having spoken thus, as Sāvitrī was turning away and departing, the Bull-bannered God touched her shoulder with his hand; she then became exceedingly enraged.
Then Sāvitrī, who was exceedingly devoted to her husband, having come face to face with him, spoke thus to Mahādeva, censuring the bull-bannered god: || 115 ||
"O fool, Paśupati! Why do you, like an ordinary human being, seek to appease your wife here after having driven her away with quarrels? (116)
"With a deluded mind through lusts, you praise another's wife;
even without having praised her, it is fitting for you to inquire after one such as I. (117)
"O fool, do you think I am Pārvatī, that you place your hand upon my shoulder without recognizing me? Know me to be Satī, the daughter of Savitṛ. (118)
"O barbarian, since you treat me like a human being, therefore you shall experience sexual pleasure within a human womb. (119)
"O Bharga, since you have no other beloved except me, yet you desire another woman, this is the fruit of that [desire]. Go; abandon me! (120)
Having spoken thus, the virtuous goddess departed for her own hermitage;
and Hara, filled with both shame and wonder, also returned to his own abode.
Therefore, Śaṅkara performed this act of union in a human womb;
for that reason, O King, have no doubt: show compassion toward this virtuous Tārāvatī and protect these two children of Bharga.
Aurva said:
Then, having heard from the mouth of Nārada that he himself was Śambhu and that Tārāvatī was Gaurī, the king [was struck with wonder].
Both of them, whose banner bears the bull, were born in human wombs.
Having heard this, the king was exceedingly delighted and filled with wonder; O tiger among sages, he questioned Nārada again in order to understand this concerning himself.
And how you attained the state of Śaṅkara and Gaurī in the presence of Tārāvatī—just as I witnessed that, inform me of it with certainty. (125)
Nārada said:
"Placing Tārāvatī on your lap, you must close your eyes;
for a moment, let Tārāvatī also close her eyes. (126)
O Indra among kings, first close your eyes and then open them quickly;
thereafter, the knowledge of Śambhu and his very form shall manifest for you.
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, King Candraśekhara then took hold of the virtuous Queen Tārāvatī with his left hand.
Closing and opening his eyes together with her at that very moment,
at the time of their closing, he attained the nature of Śambhu.
Then the virtuous goddess Tārāvatī became the form of Gaurī;
the realization arose in them both: "I am Śambhu, I am Gaurī. (130)
Then Nārada, as if laughing, spoke to that Śambhu:
"You yourself are Śambhu manifest, and the goddess Gaurī is Tārāvatī herself. (131)
"O illustrious one, behold yourself by means of your own self through direct perception.
Then the king, having said, "So be it," [revealed] his own body.
Clad in a tiger skin, endowed with ten arms,
she holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with her hands grasping a spear and other weapons.
Seated upon a bull, adorned with a mass of matted hair, Tārā has limbs as white as lightning, holds a lotus in her hand, and possesses a beautiful face. 134.
Having observed this, he attained conviction even through knowledge regarding that Self;
then Nārada said: "Listen, O King, to my words. (135)
In human form, the Māyā of Viṣṇu deluded you both previously;
because of that, you did not perceive the nature of Śambhu within each respective body.
Now, O Śambhu, the nature of Śambhu has been revealed to you today;
close both your eyes and return once more to the state of a mortal.
"Having attained human birth, remain steadfast until the end of this body;
likewise, let the goddess Tārāvatī quickly become a human."
Aurva said:
Having perceived with his eyes the divine form of his own self and having gained full conviction, the king closed his eyes. (149)
Then Queen Tārāvatī closed her eyes;
once again, those two became a human couple—the queen and the king. (140)
But having opened their eyes and perceived their own human state, the knowledge arose in them both: "We are likewise mortals. (141)
Then, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, that couple developed the notion: "I am the king, and I am the queen. || 142 ||
Regarding that wife, she was of the opinion that they were portions of the gods; thus we two remained as the portions at the top [of her being], and we became marked with the signs of birth. (143)
Then that king joyfully spoke to the sage Nārada:
"What you have said is true; I shall carry out your word."
"I shall indeed always protect these two sons of Śambhu, who are attainable through truth; however, O tiger among sages, you must consecrate them according to the prescribed rites. (145)
Aurva said: Then, O King, at their request, Nārada gave them names;
the elder son of Aurva was named Bhairava, the terrifying one. (146)
"Kṛṣṇa is like a Vetāla; let the other likewise become a Vetāla. Thus the son of the celestial sage Brahmā gave them those names. 148.
And Nārada, the best of sages, performed all the other purificatory rites in due order according to the word of the moon-crested Lord.
Thus, having severed all doubts, that best of sages,
after performing the funeral rites for the two sons of Bharga, was dismissed by that king.
By that path through the sky, Nārada went to the surface of the celestial realm;
and when Nārada had departed, King Candraśekhara was filled with joy.
He took delight with Tārāvatī in the city named Karavīra;
for he was a portion of Śambhu, while Tārāvatī was a portion of Gaurī. (151)
Then, having conceived faith, the king ruled the earth for a very long time;
and thereafter, he [gave] his two sons to Hara—namely Vetāla and Bhairava.
Those two great-souled ones grew like the risen autumnal moon—the best of kings [being born] to Tārāvatī from King Candraśekhara. (153)
He had three sons of great heroism, endowed with perfect beauty:
the eldest among them was Uparicara, then Damana, and Alarka.
From Vetāla and Bhairava, those three became his elder sons;
thus were these the three sons of King Candraśekhara. (155)
Vetāla and Bhairava, the two sons of Hara born at the same time,
grew up with equal enjoyments under the protection of the moon-crested Lord;
they shared the same seats and vehicles along with his wife.
Thus, these five sons of great strength,
created by the Ordainer to be like the five elements,
first grew to encompass the entire world.
Having surpassed them with joy, they were arrogant in their strength. || 157 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 50 ||
Fifty-first Chapter.
Aurva said:
Then, in the course of time, those mighty ones grew up.
Skilled in the knowledge of weapons and missiles, they were thoroughly proficient in the meaning of the treatises. || 1 ||
Having attained youth, they were radiant and invincible to their adversaries;
they were skilled in the knowledge of dharma and artha, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth.
There, Vetāla and Bhairava always accompany him with affection;
likewise Alarka, Damana, and Uparicara—
these three brothers, who wear the moon as their crest, are his constant companions for eternity.
Among the three sons of the king, beginning with Uparicara,
his sense of possession was always greater, and likewise his affection and love were ever more intense.
Neither toward the Vetālas nor even toward Bhairava does the Lord who bears the moon upon his crest possess such affection as that which arises toward them.
Upon seeing those two, King Candraśekhara was never once satiated; he constantly felt an intense joy, as if they were his own sons.
Those two heroes were skilled in dharma, possessed of great strength and prowess,
expert in conquering the three worlds, and masters of the entire range of handheld weapons and missiles.
The king fears those two; when and what will they do?
These two, Vetāla and Bhairava, [might take] me, my sons, or even the kingdom itself.
Thus lost in thought, the king constantly observed his two sons, Vetāla and Bhairava, even though they remained bowed before him.
Then the king consecrated his eldest legitimate son, Upāricara, who was endowed with all the qualities of a sovereign, as the heir apparent.
There will be one named Rājoparicara, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures and who shall later unite all the kings through statesmanship. (11)
The lord of the earth likewise bestowed a dowry upon Damanaka and Alarka,
consisting of abundant wealth and jewels, as well as many thrones and chariots.
He bestowed upon those two, Vetāla and Bhairava, as much wealth and property as they desired, portion by portion; yet thereafter, wrath took possession of them both.
Overcome with indignation, those two heroes wandered here and there; desiring no worldly enjoyment and exerting themselves in asceticism,
they remained constantly in solitary places, never having taken wives.
At that time, Queen Tārāvatī, overcome with anxiety, perceived her two sons to have become the gods Vetāla and Bhairava.
Fearing King Uparicara and her husband, the moon-crested Lord Śiva, the fair-toothed woman said nothing at all; she merely signaled to them both that they should remain hidden.
In the meantime, the wise Kapota, the best of sages,
was enjoying the company of Citrāṅgadā and was satisfied by the festivities of their amorous union.
Having abandoned Citrāṅgadā, who was accompanied by her son and had been his constant companion,
he then spoke these words to Citrāṅgadā regarding their departure.
The sage said:
"O Citrāṅgadā, I shall go to the forest of asceticism to perform penance.
Tell me, O charming one, what pleasing service may I do for you here? (19)
Citrāṅgadā said:
"O you of excellent vows, Tumburu and Suvarcas are your two sons;
O best of sages, do what is appropriate to please them. (20)
"And having established me in the house of my sister, O best of the twice-born, then go to the forest of asceticism if it pleases you, O sinless one. (21)
Having heard her words, that best of sages, the pigeon,
without further reflection, went to the abode of Kubera for the sake of gold.
Having made a request to Kubera for six hundred pieces of gold and thousands of gold coins, that best of sages obtained them.
Having brought a hundred loads of jewels together with their transport animals,
the brahmin gave them to his two sons and especially to his wife.
Then, with the consent of Citrāṅgadā and also that of her two sons, he [gave] her along with her two sons and those abundant riches according to his intention.
Having taken leave of Suvarcas, Tumburu, and Citrāṅgadā as well,
that tiger among sages departed for the city of Karavīra.
Having gone there, that boatman spoke these words to King Candraśekhara and likewise to King Uparicara.
O King, this [lineage] born of Kakutstha was already known to you;
likewise, these two pure sons of mine were born from her at that very moment.
"With these riches, you must protect my two sons;
and let King Uparicara also protect my two children here. (29)
The king is the son of the childless; the king is the wealth of the poor;
the king is indeed the mother of the motherless, and the king is the father of the fatherless. (30)
The king is indeed the protector of the helpless; the monarch is the husband of the husbandless.
The king is the servant of the servantless, and the king alone is the friend of men.
Since the king embodies all the gods, therefore, O King, I entreat you.
Aurva said:
Then that king, Uparicara, spoke thus to that sage, the best of the twice-born: "I shall do as you say."
Then Citrāṅgadā took the king with the approval of the sage;
she gave her two sons, together with their wealth, to his eldest son.
And that Uparicara gave half of his glorious kingdom;
likewise, he then appointed Tumburu as the chief minister.
And the pigeon, being well-pleased, looked upon his son with half his own body;
having taken leave of the king, he departed for the forest of asceticism to practice penance.
As he was traveling on the road, that pigeon [beheld] the two charming sons of Śambhu, wandering alone like the sun and the moon. (36)
Then, seeing their faces in the form of monkeys, the ascetic remembered their previous story; having seen them, he questioned the two of them.
"Who are you two, resembling the offspring of gods, traveling alone on this desolate path? O best of men, tell me what has been said to you. (38)
Then, having prostrated before him and conversed with him appropriately,
the two sons of Śaṅkara spoke to that best of sages named Kapota.
"Know us, O tiger among sages, to be the two sons of Candraśekhara, born of Tārāvatī; we bow at your feet. (40)
O Sage, having observed the king’s constant contempt for us two, we have always been alone in secluded places, our hearts filled with resentment. (41)
O illustrious one, for what reason does the king, disregarding his two sons who are his own offspring and who constantly bow before him, refuse to grant them even their inheritance? (42)
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, we both desire to perform penance, provided that you would favor us by granting your instruction. (43)
Then, having heard their words and smiling, that best of sages, who possesses knowledge of the past, future, and present, spoke this to them: || 44 ||
The sage said:
"You two are not the sons of that King Candraśekhara;
you are the sons of Śaṅkara, born of Tārāvatī. (45)
Born at once with great prowess and esteemed for their status as Vetālas,
those known by the names Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla came to the earth due to a curse.
Therefore, he does not wish to grant you your beloved inheritance here;
go for refuge to your father, Śaṅkara, whose banner is the bull.
That very Maheśvara will accomplish everything for you both;
what indeed is the use of this most fierce penance that yields fruit only after a long time? 48.
Having spoken thus, that tiger among sages, the boatman who upholds the Supreme Self,
then explained everything to Bhūta and Bhavya, who were born of knowledge and are infinite.
Just as Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla, having been cursed, came to the earth, and just as Hara and Gaurī came to the earth, O King. (50)
Just as Tārāvatī was cursed by that very sage in the past,
and how those two were previously born from the womb of Tārāvatī.
Or rather, he related to his two sons everything concerning how Nārada himself had resolved the king's doubts regarding Giriśa.
Having heard that, those two high-souled ones, Vetāla and Bhairava,
became filled with supreme joy, O blameless one.
Then, becoming filled with joy as if sprinkled with the essence of nectar,
both Vetāla and Bhairava questioned the pigeon once again.
"O best of sages, it has been truly stated by you that Mahādeva is our father; he must be worshipped by us both according to the rules for the sake of spiritual perfection. (55)
O high-minded one, tell us where Hara is to be propitiated by us two, so that once he has been worshipped there, he will grant his grace to us before long.
O best of sages, we two have been blessed that you have made all this known to us and extracted the thorn from our hearts. (57)
O Lord of Sages, you who are filled with compassion, have mercy on us once more;
tell us how we may both attain Bharga before long.
The sage said:
"Listen, I shall tell you today where Hara was propitiated;
before long, he will come into your very presence."
I shall now declare that secret place which has been revealed, where Mahādeva dwells eternally for the sake of your satisfaction. (60)
There is a city named Vārāṇasī on the charming bank of the Gaṅgā;
it is always shaped like a bow, situated between the Araṇā and the Āsī rivers.
The bull-bannered Lord himself always dwells there among the yogins;
he is the yogi who eternally bestows joy, and he himself is the contemplator of the Self.
That city, situated in the sky, is eternally sustained by the power of its union with Bharga;
it bestows divine knowledge upon the man who dies there.
To him, Mahādeva himself, for the sake of liberation from the knot of saṃsāra,
became a supreme yogin and died there in that other existence.
Endowed with yoga and always accompanied by Pārvatī, Mahādeva, who is esteemed by Hara, attains Nirvāṇa through that which is indeed easily obtained. 65.
Hara is to be known as the eternal light of the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and humans; and that field has been revealed.
The god who grants desires does not become propitiated there for long;
but when propitiated with long-standing affection, he becomes propitious for the sake of nirvāṇa. || 67 ||
But that city, devoid of Gaurī, never goes there to the great field of Yoga-sthāna, which belongs to Śaṅkara. 68.
"O best of men, this field of yours, Vārāṇasī, which has been mentioned, is situated not far from here. (69)
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another secret sacred seat (pīṭha) that is eternally worshipped, joined with Hara and Gaurī, and which bestows the supreme [attainment] of dharma, artha, and kāma. (70)
Through exceedingly intense austerity, liberation is attained after a long time; however, that meritorious field (kṣetra) which grants desires without delay is called a sacred seat (pīṭha). || 71 ||

"That place where the god who grants desires does so after a long time, but where the one who grants knowledge does so without delay—that field is celebrated among the worlds by the ancient bards. (72)
Kāmarūpa is the great sacred seat (pīṭha), the supreme secret of all secrets;
there Śaṅkara is ever present together with Pārvatī. (73)
Before long, the God worshipped on that seat becomes gracious;
indeed, Pārvatī also bestows her favor there upon the devotee of Bharga.
The Supreme Lord grants the desired object to his devotee without delay;
I shall now describe that sacred seat (pīṭha), so listen, you two, at this moment. (75)
Extending from the Karatoyā river in the east as far as the goddess Dikkaravāsinī,
it is thirty yojanas in width and one hundred yojanas in length.
The triangular region, black in color and filled with many mountains,
joined by hundreds of rivers, is proclaimed as Kāmarūpa.
Kāma, having been consumed by the fire from Śambhu’s eye, attained a form there through the grace of Śambhu; because he obtained that form, he therefore became known as Kāmarūpa.
In the northwest of that pedestal, in the southwest, from the middle portion, in the northeast, in the southeast, in the center, and on the side, Śaṅkara [is located]. (79)
Having made his own hermitage beautiful in six locations,
he dwells there eternally with Pārvatī, engaged in playful jests.
In the center is the temple of the Goddess; Śaṅkara is subject to her there.
On that best of mountains called Nīla, Pārvatī resides.
In the northeast, on Mount Nāṭaka, is the great hermitage of Śaṅkara;
there the Lord dwells eternally, and Pārvatī is dependent upon him.
There are other eternal hermitages belonging to Hara and Gaurī;
yet no hermitage of Śaṅkara exists that is equal to these two. (83)
"O best of men, Mahādeva is to be propitiated by you both here;
keeping that place in mind, seek the grace of the bull-bannered god."
Etālabhairava said:
"O Sage, we shall go to Kāmarūpa, the secret mountain of Nāṭaka, where Gaurī and Hara are eternally present and ever-attentive. (85)
"O best of the twice-born, tell us how we may certainly propitiate Bhūteśa here in this world, so that we two may indeed worship him. (86)
O illustrious one, if you have favor toward us, please tell us that mantra by which the god may soon be propitiated. (87)
The sage said:
"O best of men, go to the excellent mountain Nāṭaka;
there the Great Goddess dwells eternally together with Aparṇā. (88)
There, on the Sandhyā mountain, the sage Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, worships Śaṅkara; you two should follow him. 89.
And when questioned, O Vetāla and Bhairava, he will indeed inform you both regarding the mantra and its ritual manual for the rite of propitiating Hara.
I wish to go for ascetic practice; the wasting of time is no longer appropriate for me.
Therefore, O best of heroes, release me.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages departed for the forest by boat;
having paid homage to that sage, the two of them went to their own abode.
Then, having made a covenant and been initiated for asceticism,
those two high-minded ones took leave of their parents, as well as their other brothers and kinsmen, and set out for Kāmarūpa.
Having recognized those two as they were departing, Śaṅkara, together with Umā, spoke thus to all the gods, including Indra, as if consoling them: || 94 ||
Īśvara said:
"O best of gods, my two sons have now gone forth for asceticism; O lords of the gods, since their minds are intent upon worshipping me, show them compassion."
"Having consecrated these two sons, Vetāla and Bhairava, by means of austerity, I shall appoint them to the rank of Gaṇapatya; let the gods perform the consecration. (96)
By this very body, those two shall attain the state of Gaṇeśa;
however, through their ascetic penance, their bodies shall cast off their human nature.
"I shall indeed act in such a way that they attain the state of being the Sun," having said this,
Vāmadeva, along with Pārvatī and his two sons,
departed through the sky; and out of affection, Śiva followed after them.
All the thirty-three gods, beginning with Śakra, as well as the other guardians of the directions and others likewise. || 99 ||
All followed Hara as he proceeded with his two sons;
then, having reached the river, those two, wearing black antelope skins, [stood there].
Having assumed the state of ascetics, they [crossed] the Dṛṣadvatī, which was like the Gaṅgā;
then the two ascetics were protected by the three-eyed God.
Then, together with the gods, they arrived at the hermitage named Kāmarūpa; having reached Kāmarūpa, they went to the waters of the river Karatoyā.
Then, O best of kings, having sipped water at Nandikuṇḍa and bathed there, they both sipped water again and went to the river Jaṭodbhavā.
Having touched those two there, and having bowed to the god Nandin who was steadfast in asceticism, they went to Mount Nāṭaka after speaking with the Lord.
Having reached Mount Nāṭaka and bowed to the bull-bannered Lord Śiva,
they recalled the words of Kapotaka for the sake of receiving instructions on his propitiation.
They went toward the southern quarter where the Sunset Mountain stands;
there is a river named Kāntā which was brought down there by Vasiṣṭha.
On its bank stands a great mountain with lush-shaded creepers and trees,
where Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, performed his evening prayers.
Therefore, the deities sing of it by the name Sandhyācala;
having approached Vasiṣṭha there, who was like the sacrificial fire itself in person— || 108 ||
He was propitiating Giriśa with a mind absorbed in meditation,
blazing with the splendor of his asceticism like a second sun.
Then, O King, having prostrated before him, Vetāla and Bhairava stood with palms joined in reverence, their necks bowed low in humility.
And bowing down to the son of Brahmā, those two who were born of Tārāvatī from King Candraśekhara spoke as follows.
"Know us to be two human beings born in the field of Bharga;
we wish to propitiate Hara for the accomplishment of our purpose. (112)
"O observer of noble vows, if you do not favor our desire,"—
having heard those words of theirs, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, [replied].
He said: "I have truly recognized you both as the sons of Hara;
O best of men, the worship of Hara is noble for you both."

"In this matter, I have a certain task; tell me what it is, O blameless ones. You have a purpose for propitiating the bull-bannered god (Śiva); consider that whatever is required for that purpose has already been accomplished. (115)
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
"O great sage, tell us that mantra by which Hara, when properly propitiated, will quickly bestow his grace upon the earth."
O tiger among sages, you should further explain all that regarding how we shall propitiate this tantra and what the sequence [of practice] is like. (117)
"By your instruction, we two shall attain Hara before long;
therefore, O best of sages, please grant us your guidance as we bow before you. (118)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Vṛṣaketu, together with Umā, is indeed pleased with you both;
before long, he himself will manifest his grace here.
Together with all the hosts of gods and accompanied by his wife, the bull-bannered Lord arrived through the path of the sky, bringing his two sons from their home.
However, having taken up human bodies and through ascetic vows,
he will himself go to Kailāsa after appointing you both to the rank of a Gaṇapati.
And I too shall instruct you both so that you may quickly attain Bharga; listen with one-pointed attention to that which concerns the son of Pārvatī. || 122 ||
One becomes serene through meditation after a long time, but not so through the mere worship of meditation;
therefore, today I shall explain meditation and worship according to their true nature.
Consisting of splendor, eternally pure, nourished by the nectar of knowledge, identical with the universe, consisting of consciousness and bliss, Śauri assumes the very nature of Brahman. 124.
Mahādeva is the great form, eternally endowed with great yoga;
the worlds are his forms—who is capable of describing them? (125)
However, those forms by which this Śaṅkara is worshipped here in this world—
I shall declare to you that which is beloved of me and accessible through knowledge.
First, O bulls among men, hear the mantra; then the sphere of meditation; then the sequence of worship; and finally, the conduct according to the sequence.
Of all the vowels, however, the remaining long ones are provided with the bindu;
they are devoid of *ṛ* and *ḷ*, possess the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and are conjoined with the letter *upāntya*.
The mantra of the Five-Faced One is proclaimed by means of these five syllables; they are known respectively as Sammada, Sandoha, Nāda, Gaurava, and Saṃjñaka. (129)
The remaining [portion] shall be the temple; thus five mantras are proclaimed.
With each one, one should worship each face of the deity. (130)
Having formed one [deity] as a collective, one should worship with five [offerings];
or else, with devotion, one should worship the five-faced God.
Among the *sammada* mantras, however, *prāsāda* is praised,
because this mantra exists through the grace of Śambhu.
Therefore, this is called "Prāsāda" by the best of sages;
consequently, among all mantras, Prāsāda is the supreme giver of joy. (133)
The mantra of Śambhu that produces fragrance is called *sammada*;
and because it completely fulfills the mind, it is also proclaimed as *sandoha*. (134)
The resonance (nāda) is the attractor; due to its weightiness, it is called "gravity" (gaurava).
This mantra of Śambhu is proclaimed as both separate and combined.
The five-syllable mantra that is proclaimed for the Five-faced One—
by that very mantra, you two should worship the Lord.
I shall describe meditation; listen correctly, O Vetāla and Bhairava! [One should meditate on the deity] who has five faces, a massive body, and is adorned with a mass of matted hair. (137)
Adorned on his head with a beautiful crescent moon and decorated by a mass of matted hair,
he is endowed with ten arms and wears a tiger skin as his divine garment.
He bore the *kālakūṭa* poison upon his neck, was adorned with a necklace of serpents, and had snakes as ornaments for his crown and arms. (139)
He bore upon all his limbs a divine luster bestowed by moonlight,
with every part of his body smeared with holy ashes in groups of three.
He is resplendent with fifteen eyes that shine like luminous bodies,
seated upon a bull, and clothed in an elephant hide.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and thereafter Tatpuruṣa, as well as Īśāna—these are proclaimed as the five faces. (142)
Sadyojāta is white, resembling pure crystal;
likewise, Vāmadeva is yellow-hued, gentle, and captivating to the mind. (143)
He beheld the non-terrible (Aghora) face, blue in color, which increases fear;
and the divine Lord Tatpuruṣa, red in color, possessing a celestial form that is captivating to the mind.
One should likewise meditate upon the dark-hued Īśāna, who is eternally of the nature of Śiva,
as the first in the west, and the second in the north.
One should meditate with devotion, intent on the deity Aghora in the south, Tatpuruṣa in the east, and likewise know Īśāna to be in the center. 146.
Then, in the right hands, [he holds] the trident, the khaṭvāṅga, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; likewise, in the left hands, the auspicious Śiva [is depicted]. 147.
One should meditate upon Śiva residing in the heart, endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭaiśvarya), holding a rosary, a citron, a serpent, a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and a lotus. 148.
Thus one should meditate upon Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, during meditation;
having so meditated, one should worship the gatekeepers, Gaṇeśa, and the others. || 149 ||
Having contemplated the purification of the five elements for a moment,
one should thereafter worship the eight forms with their eight names.
Then one should worship all his seats;
one should apply the eight flowers, beginning with Bhāva, using the Heart-mantra alone.
Striking it with the Nārāca-mudrā is prescribed;
then, one should perform the dismissal by displaying the Dhenu-mudrā according to the ritual injunctions. (152)
One should always wear the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) while mentally identifying them with Caṇḍeśvara;
one should wipe the limbs and other parts [of the deity] with each of the five mantras individually.
O best of men, by means of these previously mentioned [mantras] beginning with *samyak*,
one should worship Bālā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and immediately after that, Kālī.
The goddess Kālavikaraṇī, as well as Balapramathinī, Damanī of all beings, and likewise Manonmathinī. || 155 ||
One should worship those eight goddesses in sequence for the pleasure of Śambhu;
having thus worshipped Śiva, with a mind intent on meditation. (156)
Having taken up the rosary, one should recite the mantra while meditating upon it as well as the Guru;
[one should recite] either the single five-syllabled mantra or the single Prāsāda mantra.
"Having recited this with minds fixed upon it, you two shall quickly attain perfection. Thus have I told you both the mantra as well as the sequence for meditation and worship.
Go to Mount Nāṭaka; there, propitiate Hara. (158)
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
"O Sage, this five-syllable mantra has been accepted by you with approval;
by means of this very mantra, we shall joyfully worship the god Hara. (159)
Having spoken thus and having paid homage to them, O King, Vaitāla and Bhairava then went to Mount Nāṭaka with the permission of Vasiṣṭha.
There is a beautiful lake there, perfectly full and serene, always possessing clear water and blooming with lotuses and water-lilies. (161)
On its bank, however, is the vast and most beautiful hermitage of Hara,
which is always frequented by Dānavas, gods, Kinnaras, and Pramathas.
O tiger among kings, it is guarded by those devoted to dance and instrumental music,
because the Lord, ever intent on curiosity, dances there perpetually.
Therefore, this king of mountains is celebrated by the name Nāṭaka;
that mountain is umbrella-shaped, beautiful, and dear to Śaṅkara. (164)
Having reached the lake and gone there at that time,
the two of them did not see the unsurpassed hermitage of Hara.
O King, they were unable to go to their hermitage;
therefore, having quickly bowed to Hara on the very bank of that lake, [they remained there]. (166)
Having fashioned a beautiful sacrificial altar according to the procedure taught by Vasiṣṭha,
both Vetāla and Bhairava began to propitiate Hara.
While those two sons of Śaṅkara were thus propitiating the Lord of Beings,
Hara, together with the hosts of gods, beheld them on that mountain and dwelt upon its plateau in his own hermitage along with Aparṇā.
Seeing the two sons of Hara performing penance on the shore of the lake in the lower region, Śaṅkara stood there accompanied by the hosts of gods.
The sound of the drum for the dance that constantly arose from Hara—when they heard that sound, they were unable to go or even to look. || 170 ||
O King, presided over by Hara along with all the hosts of gods,
that mountain then shone like Sudharmā, the assembly hall of Vāsava.
As the two of them were meditating there at that time, the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull,
before long became immovable within the paths of their meditation.
O King, whether they were walking, standing, or worshipping the Moon-crested Lord,
they never for a moment abandoned him from their minds.
Worshipping the bull-bannered god with the five-syllabled mantra,
the two of them passed a thousand years.
Without food or with restricted food, their minds fixed on Hara,
they spent a thousand years through asceticism as if it were a single year.
When a thousand years had passed, the bull-bannered Lord himself,
having entered into their conversation, appeared before them in person.
Having then seen him directly before them, the Vetāla and Bhairava praised the bull-bannered Lord, who is attainable through meditation and now stood manifest.
Having seen the form of Hara, blazing with splendor, as it had been meditated upon and situated within the heart, they then inferred [the presence of] Aśiṣṭha through that [vision]. || 178 ||
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
We bow to the five-faced Great Poem, which consists of all knowledge, the supreme protector from the ocean of worldly existence, the one whose banner is the bull. (179)
You are the Supreme, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the beyond, and the Highest Person;
you are the immutable, the pervader of the universe, the primordial principle, and the Supreme Lord. || 180 ||
You are the self of form, the Great Reality, the Lord who is the abode of the knowledge of reality;
you are the pure abode of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the knower of the division of the three qualities.
You are eternal and you are impermanent; You are remembered as the creator of the world and its dissolution. You are both one and manifold in form, tranquil in activity, and pervaded by the universe.
Changeless, without support, eternal bliss, and everlasting—you are Viṣṇu, you are Mahendra, you are Brahmā, and you are the Lord of the worlds. 183.

He who is the sovereign jewel-garland of form within form, who has come into being through manifestation, who is unrestrained, and who, having descended through his desire, has realized the power of destruction.
The Lord of Yoga, whose course is knowledge, is indeed unapproachable.
Resembling the earth that supports the self whose nature is the object of knowledge,
possessing a body of nectar bound by the lord of serpents,
subtle in syllable, he is the undisturbable knower of reality.
You are the God of gods, the refuge of the deities.
The Supreme Self is the Person who is free from the body of conceptual construction, whose singular knowledge follows the abode of the inner purity, and who is fierce as he grows ever more powerful.
You are the discerning intellect of the flood of the sense-faculties.
O Lord of lords, you are the source of others, the refuge of sages, and accessible only to supreme yogis;
you are the sustainer of the earth, the upholder of fortune, and indeed infinite.
O Soul of the Universe, your manifestations are manifold. || 187 ||
You are the full moon that pours forth the nectar of wisdom, the supreme lamp for the darkness of delusion,
and the most excellent father to those who are your devoted children.
And in the realm of desire, he assumes the form of a lion. || 188 ||
Vivasvān is the first of all teachers; you, O Tanūnapāt, manifest the multitude of virtues;
in the form of Brahmā, you bring about creation.
And [he maintains] perpetual stability through forms identical to Viṣṇu. || 189 ||
In the form of Rudra, you bring about the end;
there is no other entity in this world besides you.
You are the lord of the night and the lord of the day.
You are Agni, the waters, the wind, and the earth. || 190 ||
Likewise, you are the sky, you are the priest who performs the ritual system, and you are the one of eight forms; there is nothing other than you.
Here, as the one of infinite forms, you exist in your primary state.
And the Trimūrti consisting of eight [aspects] is thus described. || 191 ||
O you of infinite form, how else could there be a number for your appearance, since you possess eight forms? You are Tryambaka, and you are the destroyer of Tripura.
You are Śambhu, the Lord, the Pacifier, and the Ordainer. || 192 ||
He has a thousand arms and golden arms; he possesses a thousand forms and five faces here;
he has abundant eyes and six half-eyes.
The Lord with many arms, the ten-armed one. || 193 ||
One who possesses abundant enjoyments, one endowed with moderate enjoyments, one who follows after objects of enjoyment, and one who is unrestrained. || 194 ||
Salutations to you, whose nature is both eternal and non-eternal, whose nature is the abode of eternity, whose nature is the supreme reality, and who are the very self of Śiva. 195.
O Bull-bannered Lord, since even Viṣṇu and Brahmā have not reached the end of your signs (liṅga), what can we two possibly do but offer words of praise? 196.
O Supreme Lord, since neither the gods nor the demons know your true nature, how indeed shall we two praise you? (197)
O Lord of Gods, O Bull-bannered One, O Lord of Gaurī, we two offer our salutation to you by mere devotion; again and again, salutations unto you! (198)
Aurva said:
O king of kings, having been thus praised by the high-souled Vetāla and also by Bhairava, Mahādeva was pleased and then spoke to them both.
The Blessed Lord said: "I am pleased with you both, my sons; choose the boon you desire.
I shall grant you what is wished for, for I am gratified by your austerities and vows. (200)
"O my two sons, through these praises, through self-restraint, and likewise through constant meditation, I have become repeatedly and most graciously pleased; I shall grant you your desire."
Vetāla and Bhairava said: "If you are truly pleased with us, O Bull-bannered Lord, and if we are truly your sons,
then grant us the desired boon right here."
Since we always perceive you, our father and the Lord of the worlds, as being of the nature of the Veda (Sūta), grant us this boon accordingly.
O Bull-bannered One, we do not desire sovereignty, nor wealth, nor anything else; by virtue of our devotion to you, we only wish to serve you. (204)
May my two eyes always attain the state of bees at your pair of lotus feet whenever you are pleased. (205)
Otherwise, may our two lives pass for thousands of millions of kalpas through thoughts of you, gifts to you, and worship of you, exactly as we have intended.
Aurva said: Then, having heard those words, Mahādeva, as if smiling,
together with all the hosts of gods, granted divinity to the two of them.
Śaṅkara, with the approval of the Lord of the Gods, brought nectar from heaven and caused Vetāla and Bhairava to drink it.
Then, upon drinking the nectar, those two best of men, having abandoned their mortal state,
attained immortality through the power of Śiva and Śakti.
At that time, while sleeping, those two subduers of enemies, endowed with the power of divine knowledge and possessed of divine forms, remained so. (210)
When those two had attained divinity with their very same bodies,
Śambhu then spoke to them, who were their sons and were filled with supreme joy.
The Blessed One said: "I am pleased with you both; therefore, desiring the wish granted by me, worship Pārvatī, my beloved consort, the Sovereign Goddess."
"Without her, however, I am unable to grant you the eternal desired [fruit], nor can I constantly serve you, my two sons; therefore, go for refuge to Śivā. (213)
"Let her go to this place or that, and by whatever means she will soon attain joy, let her be brought back by that very means. (214)
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Account of the Origin of Vetāla and Bhairava," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 51 ||
The fifty-second chapter.
Aurva said:
While the Lord of Beings was speaking thus, Vetāla and Bhairava [then...].
With eyes wide open in joy, the two of them spoke to Vyomakeśa.
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
"O Blessed One, we do not know Pārvatī’s meditation, her mantra, nor her ritual procedure;
please tell us correctly how we shall propitiate her. (2)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O my two sons, I shall instruct you truly in the procedure for Mahāmāyā, the mantra, and the ritual manual (kalpa), by which everything will be accomplished."
Aurva said:
O best of kings, having spoken thus, Giriśa explained to them both the great Māyā, the meditation, the mantra, and the ritual procedure in their entirety.
Then, with eighteen subsequent chapters, that Bhairava composed the *Nirṇayavidhikalpa* within the *Śivāmṛta*.
Sagara said:
What kind of mantra did Śambhu speak in the past to those two, by means of which,
having propitiated Mahāmāyā, they attained the status of Gaṇeśas?
I am eager to hear that [tantra] along with its ritual procedures (kalpa), its secret teachings (rahasya), and its auxiliary limbs (aṅga)—
that which Bhairava composed in eighteen chapters.
Aurva said:
Because of its vastness, it is only possible to speak of it over a long period;
therefore, having extracted immediately that which was spoken by Mahādeva—
I shall tell you the truth in brief; listen to that, O best of kings.
Then, as Vetāla and Bhairava were questioning Pārvatī regarding the mantra, that Mahādeva spoke: "Listen, O you two experts in the ritual application of mantras."

The Blessed Lord said: Listen, I shall proclaim the supreme mantra, more secret than the secret, consisting of eight syllables, belonging to the Vaiṣṇavī, which is the great festival of Mahāmāyā. (10)
Of this Śrī-Vaiṣṇavī mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), Śambhu is the deity (devatā), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and its application (viniyoga) is for the accomplishment of all aims. || 11 ||

The letters ending in *ha*, *na*, *ta*, *ya*, *va*, and *ra*; those ending in *na* and likewise in *ṇa*; the eleventh, eighth, and sixth vowels; and the letter *kha* preceded by *viṣṇu* (the letter *u*). || 12 ||
Having placed the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning, this mantra of eight syllables, which possesses a luster like a red leaf, should be recited by all practitioners. (13)
This great secret mantra is known as the Vaiṣṇava mantra; because it resides within the body, it is proclaimed to be a limb (aṅga). || 14 ||
This upward-facing seed-syllable of Mahādeva is thus proclaimed;
the syllable *oṃ* is the seed, and the letter *ya* is said to be the power (*śakti*).
The mantra with seed-syllables has been explained; now listen to the ritual procedure, O Bhairava, at a sacred ford, a river, a natural pool, a pit, a spring, or similar locations.
One should first perform the bath in water belonging to another; having sipped water (ācamana) and attained purity, one should take possession of a seat.
Then, facing north, he himself should sweep the sacrificial ground with his hand while reciting this mantra: "yūṃ sahaḥ kṣityai. (18)
With the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Sa" and with the "Fulfiller of Wishes" mantra,
one should sprinkle the site with water for the purpose of expelling the spirits.
Then, having taken hold of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with his left hand while remaining pure,
he should write the mantra with gold or with a sacrificial kusha blade.
Or else, one may use the king of mantras, "Oṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ";
then, with that very mantra, one should draw the triple mandala with straight lines.
In the case of daily (nitya) worship, one should not draw a maṇḍala with colored powders;
however, in the rites of preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) and in those performed for specific desires (kāmya), one should employ it.
First, one should draw a line in the north; immediately after that, in the west;
then, in the south; and finally, in the eastern part.
In the same manner, this sequence should apply to the castes along with their wives;
then one should worship the mandala with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Saḥ."

Having formed a mandala with the hand, one should then perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) according to the sequence, using the previously mentioned mantra for binding the quarters (āśābandhana).
One should also bind it here with one's own hand ending in *phaṭ*;
a single finger-breadth shall consist of eight barley-grains.
With hands joined that are not too long, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
one should prepare his mandala as a single cubit (hasta) according to that measurement.
The lotus should be one span in measure, and its pericarp half of that;
one should arrange the petals so that they are elongated and joined to one another. (28)
The sections should neither be deficient nor excessive, and they must be surrounded by an outer border. One should place the door in the middle section, neither too small nor too large;
one should contemplate that well-constructed mandala as being red in color.
If anyone constructs her fierce mandala otherwise than this, lacking the proper characteristics,
he shall not obtain the desired fruit.
Therefore, this mandala should be drawn here. || 30 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the eighteenth section of the Mahāmāyā-kalpa within the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 52 ||
Chapter Fifty-three.
The Blessed Lord said: Then, with the mantra "Lam," [one should prepare] the mandala for the arghya vessel.
Having quickly fashioned a square, devoid of gates and lotuses. || 1 ||
With the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ śrīmit*, one should first place the vessel for the offering (*arghapātra*) there upon the maṇḍala; having worshipped it, one kindles the fire.
With the mantra *oṃ hrīḥ hrauṃ*, one should place perfume, flowers, and likewise water into the arghya vessel; thereafter, one should arrange the maṇḍala therein.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should then fill the argha vessel with water in three parts and cast a flower into it.
Then, with the mantra *hrīṃ*, one should worship one's own seat;
thereafter, with the mantra *kṣauṃ*, the wise one should worship oneself.
Then one should perform worship at the head with perfumes and flowers;
with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ," [one offers] the flower held in the palm of the hand.
Having wiped it with the left hand and smelled it with the left hand,
the wise one should cast it toward the northeast using the aforementioned mantra.
Having taken a red flower and formed a "tortoise" position with both hands,
one should then perform the acts of burning, plunging, and so forth.
One should join the right little finger with the left index finger,
and likewise join the left thumb with the right index finger.
One should raise the right thumb and place the middle and other fingers of the left hand upon the back of the right hand.
One should place the left thumb and the middle and ring fingers of the right hand downward, using the *pitṛtīrtha*.
One should make the back of the right hand level like the shell of a tortoise;
thus bound, the "tortoise-hand" (pāṇikacchapa) bestows all accomplishments.
The wise one, closing both eyes and keeping the body, head, and neck straight, should perform this with a steady mind, drawing [the breath] close to the heart.
One should commence the meditation upon the Goddess, preceded by burning and immersion;
having cast fire into wind, wind into water, and water into the heart.
Having fixed the heart in a state of immobility, one should cast the sound into space;
then, with the mantra "oṃ hūṃ phaṭ," one should pierce the aperture at the crown of the head.
Then, one should place the living soul (jīva), together with the syllable *śabda*, in the ether (*ākāśa*),
by means of the seed-syllables of Vāyu, Agni, Yama, Śakra, and Varuṇa.

With these [syllables] placed in reverse order, together with the half-moon (ardhacandra) and the bindu, there is drying, burning, as well as covering, and finally the supreme consumption of nectar. 17.
One should perform the visualization for the sake of purification in the proper sequence;
thereafter, by means of the seed-syllable of the Goddess, one should [visualize] the atom in the form of Jāmbūnada gold.
Having reached that [point], one should divide it into two parts with the mantras "um," "hrīṃ," and "śrīṃ.
Above those parts, one should likewise place the world of the heart (hṛdloka), heaven (svarga), and space (kha).
Having completed [the foundation] with the remaining portion upon the waters of the netherworld (pātāla),
one should visualize there all the seven continents of the earth.
One should visualize those oceans within them as being the Golden Island (Svarṇadvīpa);
in its center is a jeweled couch situated within a pavilion of gems.
Always frequented by the flowing waters of the celestial Gaṅgā,
that auspicious place possesses a radiant red lotus upon its couch, ever graced by Śiva.
One should contemplate [the lotus] marked with the measure of gold, having the seven netherworlds as its stalk,
touching the realm of Brahmā, and having the golden mountain as its pericarp.
With a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon Mahāmāyā residing there, resembling a red lotus, with her hair loose and hanging down. (24)
Having mounted a moving golden chariot, resplendent with glittering earrings,
she wore a crown adorned with gold and jewels.
She was beautifully adorned with three eyes—white, black, and reddish—and her cheeks possessed a luster like that of the moon at twilight; her eyes were tremulous.
She had teeth like the seeds of a ripened pomegranate, beautiful eyebrows, and was radiant as a cow;
her teeth and garments were the color of the bandhūka flower, and her nose had the luster of the śirīṣa flower.
She had a neck like a conch shell, large eyes, and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
she was four-armed, naked, and possessed full, elevated breasts. (28)
With her upper right hand she holds a sword and a string of beads,
and with her two left hands she displays the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
She was delightful with her sunken abdomen, slender at the waist, and captivating; she possessed thighs like the coils of a serpent when bent, concealed ankles, and beautiful heels.
With her resolve fixed in the full-lotus posture, she shone while seated in the hero’s pose (nivīrāsana),
standing firmly as she properly leaned against a pillar of jewels with her body.
She repeatedly uttered the words, "What do you desire?",
while gazing at the well-vehicled lion standing before her.
She was radiant with all varieties of ornaments, such as pearl necklaces, golden and jeweled bracelets, and so forth, and her face was graced with a gentle smile.
Resembling ten million suns, endowed with all the primary marks, possessed of fresh youth, and beautiful in every limb. (34)
Having meditated upon Ambikā in this manner, one should first offer [the mantra] "namaḥ phaṭ" at one's own head, while contemplating, "She is indeed myself. (35)
Then one should perform the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) in due order,
using these mantras consisting of vowels and the syllables *aha*, *sṛ*, *mī*, *sū*, and *ma*, arranged in sequence.
Oṃ kṣauṃ—these [syllables], together with the praṇava, are red in color and captivating;
[this is] the mantra for encircling from the thumb to the little finger, phaṭ. (37)
First, one should perform the placement with the fingertips on both palms;
then, one should joyfully place [the mantras] upon the heart, head, crest, armor, and eyes. (38)
Then, one should [place] the root mantra (mūlamantra) sequentially on the face, the back, the belly, the two arms, the private parts, the two feet, the two shanks, and the hips. (39)
One should place eight syllables while likewise meditating upon the syllable *oṃ*. By these means, one whose body is exceedingly purified always deserves worship, and not otherwise;
for that [practice] effects the purification of the body, the concentration of the mind, and the expansion of the elements for men. (40)
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the Mahāmāyā-kalpa of the glorious Kālikā-purāṇa. || 53 ||
The fifty-fourth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: Then, having divided that mantra eight times over the argha vessel, one should mutter it.
With that [water], he should offer water, flowers, his own maṇḍala, and then the seat.
Thereafter, one should thoroughly purify all the articles of worship with the mantra "Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Hrauṃ," ensuring they are free from any loud or excessive noise.
Then one should worship the door-keeper and the seats of the Goddess.
Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, and Gaṇeśa are the door-keepers;
they are to be worshipped in order starting from the north, and the seats are to be worshipped in the center. (3)
O Bhairava, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Emā, which are well-known in all Tantras and ritual manuals.
One should worship the guardians of the ten directions, as well as Dharma, Adharma, and the others,
in the corners of the mandala starting from the southeast, situated in their respective side-regions.
The orbs of the sun, fire, moon, and the winds, as well as the lotus,
and likewise the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva— these constitute the yoga-pīṭha, the station of the Guru.
One should worship [the elements] beginning with the essence (sāra) and ending with the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), together with their primary and secondary limbs;
as well as the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍa), the golden egg (svarṇaḍimba), and the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
The seven islands together with the ocean, the Golden Island with its pavilion, the jewel-lotus with its couch, and likewise the jeweled pillar. || 8 ||
One must certainly worship Pañcānana in the center of the maṇḍala with the mantra "Rīṃ"; then, having bound the back of a tortoise to one's hands.
And one should meditate as before, having approached the supreme seat;
one should contemplate in the center of the heart the Golden Island, furnished with a couch. (10)
Then, as if seeing her before him, he should meditate on the Goddess with a one-pointed mind,
having brought her into his heart through mental offerings.
One should worship Śivā, who resides in the heart, with sixteen types [of offerings].
Then, by means of the seed-syllable of Vāyu and through the right nostril, [one should perform the purification].
Having drawn it out through the nose with the mantra "krīṃ," O Bhairava, one should place it in the center of the lotus; one must not separate that hand [from the disciple]. || 13 ||
O Bhairava, when the hand has been separated from that flower,
the Goddess is worshipped by the Gandharvas, yet the fruit is not obtained even by those who perform the worship.
Then one should perform the invocation with the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras:
"We know thee, Mahāmāyā; we meditate upon thee who art named Caṇḍikā. (15)
Having said that, one should then recite: "May He who impels our intellects [grant us wisdom]," followed by:
"O Goddess, this bathing water is for you; Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Namaḥ. (16)
Then one should offer bathing materials endowed with auspicious characteristics to the Goddess;
thereafter, with the root mantra, one should offer perfume, flowers, and a lamp.
One should offer incense and other such items, as well as sweetmeats, milk-rice, sugar, molasses, curd, milk, ghee, and various kinds of fruits. (18)
Red flowers, flower garlands, gold, silver, and the like, as well as excellent food offerings for the Goddess, a plow, sweetmeats, and white sugar.
And the fruits of the *śāṇḍilyaka*, the one called *tāmra*, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa*; as well as the fruit of the *harītakī* and the *nāgaraṅgaka*. || 20 ||
Substances dear to children, such as kaseruka, lotus stalks, and the like,
as well as coconut water, should be offered with diligence to the Goddess.
Red silk cloth should be offered, but never blue;
likewise, flowers dear to the Goddess, such as the Bakula and Keśara, [should be given]. (22)
Madhuka, white lotuses, and vajra-flowers; karavīra and kuruṇṭaka; arka flowers, śālmali, and very tender sprouts of dūrvā grass. (23)
Kuśa grass, mañjarikā, darbha, bandhūka, and lotus, as well as the leaf and flower of the mālūra, and the red leaves of the trisandhyā plant; || 24 ||
O Bhairava, these are dear to Ambikā:
jasmine flowers, bandhūka, bakula, mādhya, bilva leaves, and sandhyaka.
Among all flowers, milk-rice and sweetmeats are the best substances; for Śivā, a garland of bandhūka flowers or of bakula flowers is most excellent.
He who offers a thousand of the middle-sized karavīra flowers, having attained his desired wishes, rejoices in my world. || 27 ||
One should diligently offer to the Goddess an excellent unguent consisting of cooling sandalwood combined with kālīyaka. (28)
Camphor, saffron, the beard-grass, musk, and fragrant kālīyaka—among perfumes, these are most pleasing to the Goddess. (29)
Yakṣadhūpa, pratīvāha, piṇḍadhūpa along with golaka, aguru, and sindhuvāra—these incenses are considered pleasing. (30)
Among cosmetic ointments, vermilion is most pleasing to the Goddess;
likewise, fragrant rice-based food accompanied by honey and meat is dear to her. (31)
Cake, milk-rice, milk, and food are praised for the Goddess;
likewise, water with jewels and camphor, as well as Piṇḍītaka and Kumāraka.
Rocana and Puṣpaka are proclaimed as the bathing substances for the Goddess;
among lamps, a lamp fed with ghee is proclaimed as the most excellent.
One should offer three handfuls of beautiful flowers with the root mantra;
having offered all the ritual services (upacāras), one should worship these [deities] in the center.
Kāmeśvarī, Guptadurgā who dwells in the caves of the Vindhya mountains, Koṭeśvarī, the one named Dīrghikā, Prakaṭī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 35 ||
When [one worships] Ākāśagaṅgā, Kāmākhyā, Dikkaravāsinī, Mātaṅgī, Lalitā, Durgā, and likewise Bhairavī, the bestower of supernatural powers (siddhi). || 36 ||
Balapramathinī, Caṇḍī, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Grāṃ, Bhīmā, Śivā, Śāntā, Jayantī, and likewise Kālikā. || 37 ||
Maṅgalā, Bhadrakālī, Śivā, Dhātrī, Kapālinī, Svāhā, Svadhā, Aparṇā, and likewise Pañcapuṣkariṇī. || 38 ||
The intoxicant of all beings, the stimulator of the minds of all beings, the subduer of all beings, and the sixty-four Yoginīs. (39)
Having worshipped these in the center, one should worship the limbs with the mantra:
the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eyes, the arms, and the feet.
The worship of the primary limbs is performed with the first three syllables of the root mantra and so forth;
thereafter, one should increase each [syllable] during the worship of the multitude of limbs for the mantras.

One should worship Śailaputrī, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Skandamātā,

then, having directed [the rite] toward the Goddess and toward one's own desire.

"O Śrīgarva, O Vijaya, O Dharmapāla, homage be to you!
Having thus worshipped the sword with the mantras "Oṃ aṃ hrīṃ phaṭ," [one should proceed]. || 17 ||

Then, with the blood of those offerings, along with water, rock salt, and excellent fruits— || 18 ||
Having diligently perfumed [the offering] with honey and fragrant flowers, [one should say]:

This very [mantra] should be employed against Vetālas and Bhairavas by the virtuous;
thereafter, one should begin the recitation while established in meditation as before. || 22 ||
Taking a garland in his hand, he should meditate on Śivā in his mind;
having meditated upon the Guru at the crown of his head, [he should contemplate] how the colors and other attributes arise.
Having meditated upon the mantra white in color and golden in nature within the throat,

Thereafter, he should not speak of the Guru, the mantra, or himself;
then, having meditated upon the oneness of the Goddess with these, by way of the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
One should cause the single essential nature of reality to descend into each of the six cakras;
having meditated with effort upon Mahāmāyā within the six cakras for even a moment. (26)
One should suspend [the image] by means of its base alone, [representing] the sixteen primordial wheels;
she who resides within these sixteen primordial wheels brings bliss to the practitioner.
Meditating thus, the practitioner should begin the rite of recitation for the Goddess.
It is said that above the eyebrows lies the junction of the three channels. (28)
The region at its edge, located at the junction of the three paths, hexagonal and four finger-breadths in size, red in color, is called the *ājñācakra* by those who know yoga. (29)
In the throats of men, there is a coiling of three channels—suṣumnā, iḍā, and piṅgalā;
that forms a hexagon measuring six finger-breadths.
That is declared to be the six-chakras, white, situated in the middle of the throat;
furthermore, the three channels become one within the heart. (31)
That locus should consist of sixteen spokes and measure seven finger-breadths;
it is the first sixteen-spoked wheel taught by the knowers of yoga.
Because it is the primary heart of meditations, mantras, contemplation, and recitation, it is therefore called "Ādi" (the First).
At the beginning of the recitation (japa) and other rites, one should carefully sprinkle the rosary with water and worship it,

Oṃ, O rosary, O rosary, O great illusion, whose nature is all powers!
The fourfold aims of human life are entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. (35)
Having performed worship, one should then take up the garland with the right hand,

O Bhairava, taking each seed individually, one should recite [the mantra] with half [the number of repetitions];

The seed-mantra of the rosary should be recited, but one must not let the beads touch one another;

If one who is reciting the seed-syllable of the preceding deity should touch the seed-syllable of the subsequent deity with his thumb, that recitation of his becomes fruitless.
Holding the rosary near one's own heart with the right hand while meditating upon the Goddess, one should perform the recitation; one should not touch it with the left hand.
With crystal, indrākṣa, rudrākṣa, or those produced from the putranjīva tree;

A rosary made of *akṣamālā* beads should be fashioned, which is supremely pleasing to the Goddess;

Among all the seeds for rosaries, the rudrākṣa is both dear to me and not dear;

Elsewhere as well, one should recite the rosary, performing a mantra-recitation that is pleasing to the deity.

O you two of great fortune, I shall speak that which bestows all accomplishments;

Of that which is known as the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, and especially of the Vaiṣṇavī [Tantra]. || 1 ||

Thus, I myself am Mahādevī, possessing power in the form of the Goddess;

Oṃ, salutations to Mahāmāyā; Oṃ, salutations again and again to Vaiṣṇavī.

[the mantra] which Brahmā bears upon his head, Hari protects in his throat, and the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) holds within his heart.
May that primordial source, the seed within the lotus-like womb, which possesses every excellence, protect me. 49.

The first letters, together with the remaining groups of vowels joined with the consonants *ma*, *ya*, *va*, *la*, and *ra*— including those without vowels, as well as those with *anusvāra* and *visarga*— constitute the thousand and eight syllables known to Hari and Hara;
this Vaiṣṇava tantra-mantra dwells eternally within the bridge of the intestines.
May that supreme, unborn, and purifying one protect me within the region of the offered sky.
Likewise, there are eight limbs and eight Vasus here; likewise, the eight forms (mūrtis) are declared as the petals, and similarly, the eight Siddhis fashioned by Madhumati;
and the arts of love (ratikalās), numbering sixty-four, are the swift means for attaining the state of the eightfold body (aṣṭāṅga).
May the eight syllables not fail within me—that group which is yours, O Heart, of these [goddesses].
This excellent armor has been proclaimed as the means for accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth; this is the supreme secret, the accomplisher of all goals. || 52 ||
Whoever should hear this armor (kavaca) proclaimed by me even once,
he obtains all his desires and attains the state of Śiva in the hereafter.
Whoever recites this armor-armor (kavaca) proclaimed by me even once, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt about this. || 54 ||
In battles, one should conquer the enemy as a lion does elephants;
just as fire burns grass, so should one always burn the enemy.
Indeed, neither missiles nor weapons can penetrate his body;
no disease ever arises for him, nor does he experience suffering at any time.
The pills, collyrium, the Pātāla-ointment, and the foot-ointment—through these, all such powers as eradication and the rest become propitious and are accomplished. (57)
His movement shall be unimpeded by others, like that of the wind;
he is born long-lived, a consumer of all enjoyments, and wealthy. (58)
Having become self-restrained on the eighth day, and having worshipped Śivā according to the rules on the ninth day, one should meditate upon Śivā with the mind.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who places this armor upon his body:
he shall conquer disease, live for a hundred years, and always be handsome and virtuous.
He is born endowed with a flood of wealth and jewels and possessed of knowledge;
neither fire burns his body, nor do waters cause it to dissolve. (61)
The wind does not wither him, nor does the sun scorch him;
weapons do not cut him, and the sun does not cause him pain. (62)
No obstacle arises for him, nor does he experience any feverish distress; neither the vetālas, nor the piśācas, nor the rākṣasas, nor the leaders of the hosts [can harm him]. (63)
All the four classes of living beings come under his control,
who constantly recites with devotion this armor composed by Hari.
Thus, I am indeed Mahādeva, and Mahāmāyā is Mātṛkā;
Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa are eternally situated in his hand.
That wise man becomes a constant bestower of boons upon others through his wealth;
for him, the capacity for poetic composition and truthfulness of speech arise perpetually. (66)
He shall speak thousands of verses and likewise become one who retains what he has heard;
for in whosever house this armor (kavaca) of Bhairava remains written, [he attains these fruits].
For him, no misfortune ever arises, nor does any blemish occur;
all the planets are pleased with him, and kings come under his control. (68)
In that kingdom where there is one who knows the armor, there leaders are born;
O Setu-deva, seed of power, salutations to you for the destruction of the five delusions.
This second eight-syllable [mantra] is for Caitā through the power of Vāyu;
"Setur devo" is known as this six-syllable [mantra] for Vaiṣṇavī.
