But for him in whose mouth-tip these two always abide, the goddess Mahāmāyā indeed dwells forever within his body. (71)
The Praṇava is the bridge for mantras; that bridge is remembered as the Praṇava.
That which is not preceded by the Oṃ-syllable perishes, and likewise that which is not followed by it.
The *namaskāra* is a great mantra; it is called "the divine" by the gods.
This mantra belongs to the twice-born, as does [the word] *śūdra* in every ritual action. (73)
In ancient times, Prajāpati extracted the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* from the three Vedas and fashioned the *praṇava*.
That [syllable] should be udātta for the twice-born; it should be anudātta for kings;
and it should be pracita for those of noble birth—one should likewise recollect it even with the mind. (75)
That fourteenth vowel which remains, known as the letter *au*, together with the anusvāra and the moon, is called the bridge for the Śūdras. (76)
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant, even so the mantra of sacrificers leaks away in an instant if it is without a dam. (77)
Therefore, in all mantras, the twice-born of the four castes, having established a boundary on both sides, should commence the birth-rite (jātakarman). 78.
For Śūdras, there may be one initial boundary or two boundaries according to their wish;
however, the twice-born (dvijātis) are always declared to have two boundaries.
Aurva said:
"I have thus related to you this entire armor proclaimed by Tryambaka;
it is an impenetrable armor, the most excellent among the eight armors."
The ritual manual of the Mahāmāyā mantra, together with its armor and internal contents, joined with the six-syllable [mantra], is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. (81)
O tiger among kings, by reciting this constantly with devotion and chanting the Vaiṣṇava mantra, you shall attain all perfections.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Armor," in the Mahāmāyā-mantra-kalpa of the glorious Kālikā-purāṇa. || 56 ||
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard this dialogue with Bhairava, King Sagara indeed...
The Vetāla also questioned Bharga once more regarding Aurva. || 1 ||
Sagara said:
"O twice-born one, you have spoken of the mantra pertaining to the body and its limbs;
O best of the twice-born, let the limb-mantras of the Goddess be told to me. (2)
Likewise, all mantras and all places of worship in every respect, as well as the subsequent mantras and the various armor-mantras (kavacas) individually. || 3 ||
And [he told] the majesty of Kāmākhyā, together with its secrets and its mantras,
just as the Blessed Lord Mahādeva, the husband of Umā, had proclaimed it.
O Vetāla and Bhairava, explain that to me in full detail;
for as I listen to this great marvel, no satiety arises within me.
"Indeed, as you speak, my curiosity is great.
Aurva said:
"Listen, O tiger among kings, to how the Lord of Umā was [propitiated] by your two sons."
He spoke this great narrative; listen now as I relate it.
This is a supreme secret, most purifying, and a destroyer of sins.
It is known as a swift means of securing well-being for men, a rite for ensuring the birth of a male child in the womb;
it is auspicious, brings about prosperity, and bestows the fruits of the four goals of human existence.
To one who is deceitful, fickle-minded, an atheist, and of unsubdued self;
and to one who acts with false persistence toward the gods, the twice-born, and teachers. || 9 ||
It should not be told, nor should it be given, to one who is wicked, to one who is falsely accused, to one afflicted by lameness, blindness, or other diseases, nor to one devoid of faith.
Having spoken the ritual manual of the Mahāmāyā-mantra to those two, Vetāla and Bhairava, Umāpati spoke once again.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall proclaim the limb-mantra, which was declared in the supreme Tantra; know that very mantra as the first, which is applicable in all forms of worship. (12)
Having sipped water and attained purity, and having bathed well for the worship of the deity,
one should stand outside the sacrificial altar at a distance of four cubits, with a focused mind.
Standing at the doorway of your home, having bowed your head to the Guru,
you should salute your own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) with your mind.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated—whether on that very day or on another day—and which has not been dispelled by expiatory rites, one should indeed recall that sin with the mind. (15)
To dispel that evil, one should recite these two mantras:
"O Goddess, my mind has become ordinary and overcome by sin. (16)
"Extract that evil from my mind: HŪṂ PHAṬ! And salutations to you!
The sun, the moon, Yama, Time, and indeed the five great elements. (17)
These nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Then again, with "HŪM PHAṬ," [one should strike] to the sides, above, and below. (18)
Then, having gazed at oneself with an angry look, one should become well-disposed;
when this has been done first, the rite for the removal of sin is accomplished. (19)
Whatever sin may be most persistent remains far away;
once the worship has passed, it returns again to its own place.
Whatever sin may be most minute, it goes to destruction;
then, with the mantra "Oṃ Aḥ Phaṭ," one should enter the altar of worship.
For one who has abandoned all evil through worship, whatever is desired shall be attained in an instant;
having looked with the nārāca-mudrā, one should gaze upon the samayasattvas.
Flowers, food offerings, perfumes, and so forth—whatever defects in the flowers and other items have been overlooked by oneself, [one should purify them] with the mantras *hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. (23)

Whether it be the touch of the untouchable, or that which is acquired through unjust means, or likewise that which is defiled by the remains of an offering (nirmālya), or that upon which insects and the like have crawled; || 24 ||
All that [impurity] comes to destruction by the mere sight of the food offering (naivedya) and other items;
thereafter, one should touch the crest of the lamp with the mantra "ramiti."
By the mere touch of that lamp, it would become auspicious for him, even if it were a mass of raw flesh burning insects, worms, hair, and the like. (26)
The complete purification of fat, marrow, and bone, as well as their application in sacrifices and other rites—
whatever that may be in its unknown form— shall destroy all defects through mere contact.
The officiating priest, looking at the water contained within the jar, should touch it while reciting the Nārasiṃha mantra and using the Devatīrtha part of the hand, and then sprinkle it.
Then, holding [the vessel] with his left hand while it rests on his left side,
he should touch the water while consecrating the vessel with the *ādhāra-mantra*.

In this world, the mixing of sacrificial offerings, gifts, or forbidden drinks is considered a defilement; likewise, whatever other defect may arise regarding the recipient or the water through ignorance [is also a cause for concern]. (30)
In a reservoir of water, impurities caused by contact with a corpse or by bathing together are destroyed; indeed, these do not affect the water used for the worship of the gods.
The son of Prajāpati, ending with *ha* and *anta*, endowed with its own vowel, joined with the half-moon and the bindu—this is the Nārasiṃha mantra. (32)

The practitioner, for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, should know the foundational mantra (ādhāramantra) as consisting of the first letter of one's own name joined with the bindu and the half-moon. (33)
Then, having taken up his own seat with both hands while reciting the *ādhāra-mantra*,
and having quickly set it down, he should again touch it with his hand.
Then, one should enter that excellent seat with the self-mantra;
or, if there is any defect in the seat, such as being poorly crafted by a craftsman, [one should purify it].
The unknown [obstacle] goes to dissolution through the ritual seating accompanied by mantras;
first having invoked one's own syllable, conjoined with the essence of Soma. (36)
The practitioner should know his own mantra to be accompanied by the nasal bindu;
thereafter, he should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, conjoined with the nāda and bindu.
The wise practitioner should perform [this] upon his own body with the Mātṛkā-mantras,
regarding whatever is unknown in the ritual manuals concerning the practice of mantra recitation.
Whatever is defiled, or likewise touched by such blemishes as being separated from one's mother and so forth,
the Mātṛkā-mantras placed therein always destroy it indeed.
All consonants as well as Viṣṇu and the others who are the vowels—
all these are Mātṛkā-mantras, adorned with the moon and the bindu.

When all [the syllables] have been placed upon those venerable at the end of the ages, the Mātṛkās themselves, having been duly arranged, perform the filling of any deficiencies in the mantra and the ritual manual (kalpa).

That which has one measure is short; that which has two measures is called long; that which has three measures is to be known as protracted (pluta). These are the established durations of the phonemes.
For all the castes, the Mother Goddesses are the Mothers;
Śivadūtī and the others are their installations, residing within their respective bodies. (43)
They quickly fulfill those who are deficient in the four aims of life (caturvarga), they always grant protection, and they perform worship of the gods. (44)
This installation of the Mātṛkās, which bestows the four aims of life and grants the fruits of all desires, is the giver of contentment and nourishment. (45)
Whoever performs the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, even without the worship of the deities, from him the fourfold host of spirits is constantly afraid. (46)
Even the gods long to behold that one of great majesty;
he shall bring everything under his control and shall never suffer defeat. (47)
The practitioner should take a flower with the Viṣṇu-mantra using the tips of his fingers for the purpose of rubbing it during the rite of hand purification.
With the letter 'u' at its end, colored by the half-moon (bindu), joined with the void (visarga), and conjoined above with the end of Rudra (the letter 'm'), this mantra is considered Vaiṣṇava. (49)
Then, having grasped [the flower] with the *prāsāda* mantra using the tips of his fingers, the practitioner should perform the crushing of the flower with both hands.
One should smell it again with the Brahma-mantra using the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM);
its abandonment should be performed with the Prāsāda-mantra, especially toward the northeast.
When this is done, there shall be incomparable purification of the hands;
purification from the touch of leeches, hidden feet, and so forth, occurs through cleansing.
Whatever defilement of the hands arises from contact with foul odors or food remnants,
all that, being of an unknown nature, shall be destroyed through the proper ritual procedure.
The fingertips become pure by grasping flowers; however, both palms become thoroughly purified by massaging them. 54.
From the wiping [of the face], the back of the hand [is purified]; from the nose, the tip of the nose is supreme;
and the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) come together at the nose and the hand. 55.
Therefore, O Bhairava, these rites should be performed with effort;
they are joined by Vāsudeva, beginning with the letter *pra* and ending with the color *saṃhita*. (56)
Joined with the crest-bindu of Śambhu, it is called Prāsāda;
the Kāmabīja, however, is to be known as consisting of Vāsudeva, the moon, and the bindu. (57)
The consonant is both the first and the last; the former is preceded by the final labial;
thereafter come the two—the first and the last—followed by the consonant and the Praṇava.
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Brahman, which destroys all sins;
having first uttered the long Praṇava for the purification of the mouth. (59)
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva;
whatever be the form, ornaments, and vehicle of whichever deity [is being meditated upon].
One should contemplate that very [mantra] during its worship by means of inhalation (pūraka) and the other [breath-controls],
beginning with the mantra of the Vaiṣṇava-tantra which starts from the throat and so forth.
That seed-syllable of Vāsudeva, which is always like the full moon,
is first [conjoined] with the seed-syllable of the descent of the Gaṅgā and with the Dhenu-mudrā.
One should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) over the water placed in the arghya vessel;
[the mantra consists of] the guttural letter joined with the crescent moon, followed by the fifth vowel and the seed-syllable of Bala.
This is the mantra for the descent of the Gaṅgā, which destroys all sins;
Viṣṇu joined with two morae is declared to be the seed-syllable of strength.
When the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) has been performed, the water that is offered becomes nectar;
having become so, it proceeds for the pleasure of the deity during the worship of the gods.
Even the Gaṅgā herself comes toward the water in the vessel of worship;
one should perform the rite of "making nectar" (amṛtīkaraṇa) for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha.
The Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Ardhasvastika, and Paryaṅka postures are praised as the best seats for the worship of one's chosen deity. (67)
This is declared to be the foot-yantra, the most excellent of all mantras;
the wise one should first take it up with the seed-syllable (bīja) of Varāha. 68.
The fourth [vowel] following the seed-syllable of fire (ra), preceded by the letter 'mā' (ma) and others,
and accompanied by the sixth vowel (ū), is called the Vārāha seed-syllable.
Having purified the seed-syllable of Varāha within the two lines of the mantra,
one who beholds the desired deity does not perceive any fault in the lines.
Otherwise, it is not proper to see one's feet during worship of the gods;
through the [proper use of] the entrails, one obtains one's desired goals; therefore, one should be devoted to the mantra. 71.
The practitioner should perform the *pāṇikacchapikā* with the *kūrma-mantra*;
there, he should worship his own body with consecrated flowers.
By worshipping with that flower, one's own divinity arises.
The second is the Vaiṣṇava-tantra, the seed-syllable (bīja) conjoined with the bindu and the moon (indus).
The seed-syllable of the Tortoise (Kūrma-bīja) is proclaimed as that which rests upon the sixth vowel;
it is at the beginning of burning and bathing, and belongs to the tenth aperture.
The practitioner should perform the piercing with the mantra, namely the Praṇava;
he should then place it in the sky by means of the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva.
The seed-syllable accompanied by the vital breath (prāṇa) has been explained previously;
however, for those who are ignorant [of it], [the purification occurs] through the cleansing of the location of the maṇḍala. || 76 ||
There may be a variety of substances as well as combinations;
it has attained firmness through the masses of fat from Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The earth has always been pure in every respect during the worship of the gods;
even today, all the thirty deities do not touch the ground with their feet.
And they do not cast their own shadows upon the ground;
for the sake of liberation from that defect, one should write the King of Mantras upon the earth. (79)
The earth becomes pure either by sprinkling or even by inspection;
one should perform the inspection of the sacrificial ground with the seed-syllable of Dharma (Om). 80.

One who is self-controlled, endowed with strength, and possessed of the topknot and the bindu—this is declared to be the seed of Dharma, the means for accomplishing virtue, desire, and wealth. || 81 ||
Taking up [the vessel] and holding it, as well as arranging it for worship; filling it with water, and the depositing of fragrance and flowers. (82)
Next is the arrangement of the mandala, followed by the placement of the flower;
this is the procedure for the consecration as nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) and the presentation of the vessel, O man.
Āniruddha, having taken it up with the weapon-mantra, should perform the placement of the mandala in the vessel and join it with the tip of the seed-syllable of speech (vāgbīja). || 84 ||

The seed-syllable of Aniruddha consists of the primordial [syllable] followed by two dots (bindus). The weapon-mantra (astramantra) is proclaimed to be that which ends with *phaṭ* and is likewise preceded by Aniruddha. (85)
Śambhu, Ādyavala, Prānta, Ampūrṇā, and Sahitā—these follow one after another from the beginning; they end with the final syllable and are accompanied by the bindu.
The third is the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, which is both with parts (sakala) and called partless (niṣkala);
it is the fourth vowel, complete, joined with the Bindu and the Moon. 87.
The second seed-syllable, beginning with the first letter of the [first] group, is called Vāgbhava;
this is also known as Kāmarāja, and it is the means for accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha. (88)
The seed-syllable of the mind-born [Kāmadeva], conjoined with the Kuṇḍalinī power and united with Vāsudeva, is called the primordial Vāgbhava. (89)
This is known as the Sārasvata [mantra], which is remembered as the primordial *vāgbhava*;
each one is preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), while the great [mantra] of Tripurā consists of three such units.
The first and third [syllables] are beautifully adorned with the moon and the bindu;
this is the mantra of Madana, which bestows the fruit of the enjoyment of desire. || 91 ||
I shall describe that machine, resembling the sun, which is arranged in the form of a lotus; it is called Kuṇḍalī-śakti because of its non-difference from her. 92.
The officiating priest should perform the expulsion of the spirits with this mantra;
once this is done, the spirits inhabiting the site depart from the place during the worship of the deity.
While those beings remain there, the greedy ones constantly plunder the offering-maṇḍala, and the deities do not accept it.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the expulsion of living beings;
this mantra, accompanied by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), is prescribed for that purpose. || 95 ||
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
without causing harm to living beings, I perform this rite for vitality. (96)
Having removed the spirits from the sacrificial ground by means of this [mantra], the practitioner,
having then performed the binding of the directions, should drive them away from the quarters.
The mantra for the binding of the directions consists of the Viṣṇu-seed syllable ending with *phaṭ*;
by means of the hand, preceded by the *hoṭikā* gesture, one performs the encircling that constitutes the binding of the quarters.
Furthermore, by worshipping oneself, one gains the qualification for undertaking ritual actions;
and a worshipped seat becomes equivalent to the yogic throne (yogapīṭha). || 99 ||
The body, though by its very nature eternally pure and composed of the five elements, is joined with filth and stench, and is slippery with phlegm, feces, and urine. (100)
It is unsanctified by the flowing excretions of feces, urine, and saliva;
indeed, its five great elements have become like seeds.
But for the purification, in due order, of all those elements—wind, fire, earth, water, and space—which serve as the seeds attached to the body; || 102 ||
Drying, burning, the scattering of ashes, the raining of nectar, and flooding must be performed for the sake of purification through mere mental visualization. 103.
Through the contemplation and piercing of the egg, and by contemplating the deity within its center, one should practice the meditation upon one’s own chosen deity with one's whole being. (104)
Through the constant contemplation of "I am He," the nature of a deity arises; through the offering of flowers, the self's purification is perfectly accomplished. (105)
Whether it be myself as a god, or the food offerings, flowers, perfumes, and so forth, whatever serves as an implement for worship—it is for this purpose that the state of divinity arises here. (106)
For I am the support of the gods, the God who should unite the god with the God;
and through the creation of all the deities, purity also arises. || 107 ||
The purification of the mind and the individual soul (jīvātman) arises through breath control (prāṇāyāma);
whatever impurity resides within, that too becomes purified. (108)
If one should worship the deity in the house,
then one should perform the visualization of Him on all four sides in sequence by means of the solar seed-syllable (ādityabīja).
The final letter (ha), joined with the seed-syllable of fire (ra) and accompanied by the end (visarga);
likewise, the penultimate letter (sa) with its fourth vowel (au), followed by that same [final] letter in its entirety (sakala). || 110 ||
The seed-syllable of Āditya has been described as the destroyer of all diseases, the cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and the bestower of satisfaction. || 111 ||
Contact with impure birds, the dripping of bird droppings, the touch of mice, as well as contact with worms, insects, and the like; || 112 ||
Such things as these perish through the defilement of the home by worldly noise;
therefore, one should first perform meditation upon the seat of yoga.
Meditation alone enters the mandala as the seat of yoga;
when the seat of yoga is recollected, everything is equal, consisting of the seat of yoga. (114)
There exists no higher supreme seat than the Yoga-pīṭha, by meditation upon which the entire world—including the moving and the unmoving, as well as humanity—is pervaded. (115)
Who indeed would venture to describe the greatness of contemplating Him?
Behold how even mere contemplation destroys the sorrow of human existence! (116)
Because it is the support [of all], the Yoga-pīṭha bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
it resembles pure crystal, is quadrangular, and has four enclosures. 117.
The reins provided by the supporting power (ādhāra-śakti), which resemble the sun, are situated in the four corners beginning with the southeast, in due order. (118)
Dharma, knowledge, sovereignty, and dispassion are always present in succession;
these reside respectively in the directions starting from the east. (119)
Beyond that are non-dharma, ignorance, lack of sovereignty, and above that, lack of dispassion; these are established for the purpose of supporting [the subsequent qualities]. (120)
Above that is a mass of water, and within it the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is situated;
inside the cosmic egg is water, and upon that stands the Tortoise.
Upon the tortoise is Ananta, and upon him the earth is situated;
its stalk, joined to the body of Ananta, extends down into the realm of Pātāla.
In the center of the earth stands a lotus with the directions as its petals and the mountains as its filaments;
in its eight directions reside the guardians of the quarters, and heaven is situated in the middle.
In the pericarp is the world of Brahmā; below it are Maharloka and the others.
In the heaven are the luminaries and the gods, and within that [space] are the four Vedas.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities (guṇas) born of Prakṛti are eternally situated within the lotus, and likewise is the Supreme Reality (paraṃ tattvaṃ). || 125 ||
The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is situated there; its upper covering is above, and its lower covering is below; furthermore, it is located at the tips of the filaments (keśara).
Then, in sequence, the mandalas of the Sun, Fire, Moon, and Wind;
thereafter, the corpse-seat (śavāsana) upon the yoga-pīṭha, and beyond that, the comfortable seat (sukhāsana).
From this, one should contemplate the Ārādhyāsana and then the Vimalāsana;
in their midst, one should meditate upon the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving.
One should meditate upon oneself as present there during the worship, determined as the three portions consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
One should contemplate the mandala as the seat of yoga, and indeed as a lotus within a lotus;
one should also contemplate all four seats here, beginning with that of the corpse (śava). || 130 ||
Having meditated separately on the yoga-pīṭha as being one with the maṇḍala,
and having meditated on it again thereafter, one should then worship the seat.
Whatever water, food offerings, flowers, incense, and so forth are given to the Yoga-pīṭha through meditation, that presents itself to him spontaneously.
All the gods, along with the gandharvas, and the guhyakas of the moving and unmoving worlds, become meditated upon and honored when the yoga-pīṭha is worshipped. (133)
By meditating upon whom, even without the worship of one's chosen deity, one indeed obtains the fourfold aims of life, and contentment and nourishment arise. (134)
Immediately after the invocation, one should lower [the vessel] with both hands;
having placed the palms upward and slightly apart, one should lift them upward.
The worshipper, without bending, should perform [the rite] without interruption;
then he should descend from there by means of the seed-syllable of Heramba.
And by repeating [the name] for the sake of propitiating one's chosen deities, through the emission of the breath from the nose, the deity becomes situated in the sky. (137)
When the maṇḍala has been prepared in this manner, his stability arises.
The seed-syllable of the son of Hara (Gaṇeśa) is said to consist of the letter *svā* together with a pure bindu and a ray of light. (138)
It is the destruction of the seeds of obstacles and the means for accomplishing virtue, desire, and wealth;
likewise, there are perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. (139)
Whatever else is given— such as clothing, ornaments, and so forth—
one should recite their respective deity-mantras and perform sprinkling and worship over them.
Having cast [the offerings] away with the root mantra, one should present them by their individual names;
one should perform the sprinkling of them with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa.
Thus, with the root mantra, there is likewise the offering of the dismissal;
the seed-syllable of Varuṇa is said to be preceded by the letter *la* and followed by the moon (*i*) and the bindu (*m*). (142)
Beholding, worshiping, and likewise giving—these three are the distinct procedures for the rosary during the rite of recitation. (143)
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed;
first, the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati should be uttered, and immediately thereafter—
"O Mālā, grant me freedom from obstacles; may you be accepted"—with these words, the placement (nyāsa) of the rosary upon the head at the conclusion of the recitation is proclaimed. (145)
Taking a garland with both hands, one should likewise worship it with the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrī-bīja),
using the final and penultimate vowels along with the third letters of the first group of consonants.
Then, preceding each successive syllable with the seed-syllable Śrī, conjoined with the nasal drop (bindu) and the crescent moon (indu), the descent of the garland is performed upon the head. 147.
Having grasped that with both hands, one should indeed perform [the rite] with the Sārasvata [mantra];
it is the first of the Śrī-bījas, joined with the bindu and the half-moon.
This quartet is declared by the authors of the Purāṇas and the Vedas to be the seed-mantra (bīja) of Sarasvatī, indeed together with the root mantra.

One should perform circumambulation and prostration, which accomplish the goals of dharma and artha; having first looked at the ground and sprinkled it with the seed-syllable of earth (KṢIṂ), [one should proceed] from the east. || 150 ||
Touching the ground with his head, he should prostrate before his chosen deities;
[he should recite] the Bārāha-bīja, which is devoid of a final *visarga* and joined with a *bindu* and a crescent moon (*indu*). 151.
One should recognize the seed-syllable of the earth as that which bestows the fourfold aims of life;
then one should again sprinkle the mirror, the fan, the bell, and the chowrie.
O Bhairava, with the previously mentioned *naivedya-āloka-mantra*, one should [join] the initial syllables of these [names] with the bindu and the moon (the nasal). 153.
At the end of that [mantra], "namas to him" is said in the secret [tradition].
Then, one should perform the offering of these [substances] with the chosen mantra. (154)

O Bhairava, the binding of the mudrā should be performed with the second [syllable] of Vāgbhava, which is the Kāmabīja; the showing [of the mudrā] should be done with the root mantra (mūlamantra). 155.
One should perform the ritual release of the mudrā using the seed-syllable of Tārā; it is preceded by the letter *pra* and followed by the nasal bindu, endowed with the sixth vowel. (156)
The seed-syllable of Tārā is thus proclaimed as the means for accomplishing the goals of dharma, kāma, and artha;
because she bestows joy (muda), she is therefore celebrated as Mudrā. || 157 ||
When the mudrā has been displayed, the completion of the worship occurs; [the practitioner] herself becomes endowed with desire, liberation, likewise dharma, and wealth, along with joy. (158)
The deity, eager to depart, quickly grants [the boon] to the practitioner;
at the conclusion of the mudrās, one should utter these six great mantras. (159)
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is offered with mere devotion, and whatever food offering is presented—please accept that out of compassion. (160)
I do not know how to invoke you, nor do I know how to dismiss you;
I do not know the nature of worship—you alone are my refuge, O Supreme Goddess. (161)
Whether by deed, mind, or speech, there is no refuge for me other than you;
O Supreme Goddess, you are the protector of all beings who move within them. 162.
In whatever thousands of wombs I may enter, O Acyuta, may my devotion to you, the Acyuta, remain forever undeviating.
The Goddess is both the giver and the enjoyer of this entire world;
the Goddess is victorious everywhere, and she who is the Goddess is indeed I myself. 164.
Whatever may be corrupted by missing syllables or deficient in prosodic measures, may all that be forgiven, O Goddess; for whose mind is there no lapse? (165)
When these mantras are recited,
O Bhairava, the Goddess herself becomes gracious and will, before long, grant the fourfold aims of life.
In the northeast, one should prepare a mandala devoid of doors and lotuses, for the purpose of the dismissal [of the deities] and for the worship of the Nirmālyadhāriṇī. || 167 ||
Having worshipped with the *pādma* and other mantras, and having meditated upon the Goddess who wears the remains of the offering (*nirmālyadhāriṇī*),
one should cast that offering into it and dismiss her with the mantra.
Go, go to the supreme abode, your own station, O Supreme Goddess,
where even the gods beginning with Brahmā do not know that highest state.
Then, having released [the breath] with this mantra by means of the *pūraka* (inhalation) wind,
and meditating while reciting this mantra, one should bow and establish her within the heart.
"Stay, O Goddess, in the supreme abode, in your own place, O Supreme Sovereign, where all the gods beginning with Brahmā abide within my heart. (171)

Then, while mentally recollecting one's chosen deity with the seeds of Ekajaṭā, one should place the remains of the offering upon one's head; this is the means for accomplishing the goals of dharma, kāma, and artha.
Then, for the sake of prosperity, one should perform the ritual of the mandala;
with the tips of all the fingers joined together, one forms an eight-petaled lotus. (173)
O Bhairava, one should rub the mandala with the seed-syllable of the earth,
and then again with the root mantra or the all-subduing mantra.
One should also touch the forehead with the tip of the ring finger;
this concludes the end together with the completion mantra, followed thereafter by the seed-syllable of Tārā.

The seed-syllable of Smara, followed by the Visarga, and then again and again the supreme [syllable], becomes the seed-syllable of Ekajaṭā, which accomplishes the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha. (176)
Then, with the self conjoined with the seed-syllable of the Sun (bhāskara-bīja),
one should again offer the oblation to the Sun with the mantra for the sake of making it free from defects.
Salutations to Vivasvat, O Brahman, to the radiant one, to the splendor of Viṣṇu, to the pure creator of the world, to Savitṛ, the bestower of action. || 178 ||
Then, having joined his palms in reverence and recited the prescribed mantra,
he should maintain it without interruption through his words with a one-pointed mind.
May whatever flaw there may be in my sacrifice, whatever flaw in my austerity, and whatever flaw in my worship of me—
may all that become flawless through the grace of Bhāskara.
Then, one should again inspect all that has been offered—the flowers, the food offerings, the water vessels, and so forth—using the seed-syllable of the Goddess. || 181 ||
Wherever previously the placement of mantras was performed with either the hand or the eye, there the withdrawal [of those mantras] should be performed by means of this [rite]. || 182 ||

The fifth letter from the end [of the alphabet] joined with the sixth vowel of the seed-syllable of fire (Vahni-bīja), and likewise the penultimate letter preceded by the Vāgbhava syllable—this they declare to be the seed-syllable of Durgā. || 183 ||
On a sacrificial mound, in a blazing fire, in water, in the rays of the sun, in pure images, and on Śālagrāma stones; || 184 ||
Worship should be performed upon a Śiva-liṅga or a stone for the sake of prosperity;
with a one-pointed mind, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the maṇḍala everywhere.
By means of the seed-syllable of the Yoga-pīṭha, the practitioner [should perform the rite] upon sacrificial altars and other such sites for Vāsudeva, Rudra, Brahmā, and Mihira.
The wise one should practice this mode of conduct in all forms of worship.
Thus, he who worships Viṣṇu with these modes of conduct [attains the highest goal]. (187)
For him, Hari, Śiva, Mihiro (the Sun), or others such as Lambodara (Gaṇeśa) and so forth, will soon become the bestowers of the fourfold aims of life. 187.
By this rite of worship, all the gods become propitious;
especially so the Great Goddess Mahāmāyā, who consists of the entire universe.
One who constantly yearns for this practice in worship, and performs worship correctly in this manner, shall become a partaker of the fruit. (190)
Worship devoid of these [elements] yields very meager fruit, just as a man lacking his limbs is not a proper sacrificer. || 191 ||
Likewise, worship performed with deficient limbs does not partake of the full fruit.
This is the supreme secret; this is the supreme means of securing well-being.
Consisting of mantra and Veda, it is pure and the destroyer of all sins. (192)
Whoever causes this to be heard in the presence of Brahmins during śrāddha rites, sacrifices, or the worship of the gods,
shall obtain the full fruit of that action.
Even without performing worship, one enjoys that infinite [result]. || 193 ||
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the Uttara-tantra of the glorious Kālikā-purāṇa. || 57 ||
The fifty-eighth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Now, you two listen specifically to the Tantra of the Goddess."
And by means of which the Goddess, when propitiated, will soon become a bestower of boons. || 1 ||
Specifically from the Ūrva-tantra, as well as from the Uttara-tantra,
this was previously told to you both in its particular and general forms.
Furthermore, regarding the specific worship and acts of devotion toward the Goddess,
I shall again declare those remaining verses.
But he who, with a one-pointed mind, should perform devotion to Mahāmāyā—
this auspicious rite must be performed by him using the Aṅginī and Aṅga mantras.
Fruit, flowers, betel, food, drink, and whatever else there may be— one must never consume these without first offering them to Mahādevī.
Whether on a path, on a mountain peak, or even in an assembly hall, the practitioner,
having made his request in whatever manner possible, should prepare his own objective.
Upon seeing a vessel of wine, as well as women of red complexion, a lion, a corpse, a red lotus, and the encounter of a tiger and an elephant; || 7 ||
Then one should bow to the guru, the king, or Mahāmāyā;
and one should always engage in sexual union with a devoted wife during her fertile period.

Having meditated upon Caṇḍikā, one should then perform rites for prosperity, whether they be rites for pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika), as well as rites for desired goals and meritorious works (iṣṭāpūrta). || 9 ||
When he should perform [the rite], then, having bowed, he should conduct the procession of the Goddess;
when he beholds the triple symphony (tauryatrika) or even mere song alone.
And whatever one intends for one's own use— whether it be an ornament, a garment, or even sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains— that must first be offered to the Goddess.
One should apply oneself to one's own body and there place the mantra with the intellect;
whether in exertion or in ritual performance, in an assembly or in water or on land.
Wherever one may go, there one should always remember the Goddess;
whatever rite is an auxiliary to worship, that one should perform with its respective mantra.

O Bhairava, whatever ritual action constituting a limb of worship is performed devoid of mantra, that is fruitless; for whatever mantra is prescribed for a particular rite among the worship rituals, [that alone is effective].
One should perform each respective rite with the *naivedya-āloka-mantra*, and one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mandala for the Goddess with the chosen mantra. || 15 ||
At the conclusion of the worship, having smeared the mandala, one should apply a tilaka with it,
using the mantra that brings all under control and bestows dharma, kama, and artha.

Having cut the sacrificial offering for the *balidāna* rite, one should apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead with one's own blood drawn from the sword, using the mantra for subjugating all.
The fourth [letter] of whomsoever shall come under his control by means of fire, when it is joined with the sixth vowel and endowed with the *kalā* and the *bindu*. (18)
Then again, there is the letter ending in 'ka' situated near the end, followed by 'sa';
likewise, there is "dvirmohī" (dvirmohi), which consists of the fourth vowel 'a' joined with two vowels. || 19 ||

The syllable whose end is filled by the final [letter] of the third group, which is designated as the third vowel, as well as the fourth letter of the beginning [group], likewise [form the name]. (20)
The second was Svara, and likewise Kṣobhaśabda preceded him;
he too, along with Pura, was both a friend and an enemy to the Rākṣasa. (21)
A man who applies the *tilaka* in secret, even without performing formal worship, shall have his progeny unimpaired and shall be known as a king who has mastered all the scriptures. || 22 ||
By means of this mantra, everything shall constantly remain under his control—whether it be a king, a prince, women, or yakṣas and rākṣasas. (23)
All the four classes of living beings come under his control,
whether he is in a foreign land, on a road, in a difficult pass, when unable to reach his destination, or even in the water.
Whether bound in prison or even entered into the royal palace,
the wise man should perform the mental worship of Mahāmāyā there.
When fear has arisen, whether from being beset by lions and tigers or by the arrival of a hostile army, one should perform mental worship.
Having meditated with the mind upon the seat called Yoga within the heart,
one should perform the worship right there, in the center of the earth.
Having performed mentally the preparation of unguents, bathing, the act of cleaning the teeth, and indeed all other [preliminary rites], one should perform the worship. (28)
Just as worship with flowers and other offerings is prescribed in the external space, so too should all ritual observances be performed within the heart. (29)
On the eighth day, one should constantly be a sacrificer to the Goddess and always observe the vow;
likewise, on the ninth day, worship should be performed with one's own blood.
One should worship the Goddess as residing in a *liṅga*, and likewise in a book;
one should worship Mahāmāyā on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and also in sandals and images.
Furthermore, one should worship a trident or a sword, or even one situated in water;
the sword should be fifty finger-breadths long, and the trident should likewise have three points.
On a stone slab on a mountain peak, or likewise in a mountain cave, one should worship the Goddess daily, endowed with devotion and faith. (33)
In Vārāṇasī, worship always yields its full fruit;
however, it is said that in the presence of Puruṣottama, it is twice as great. (34)
It is said that in Dvārāvatī, in particular, it is twice as great;
in all sacred fields and holy places, worship is equal to that of Dvārāvatī.
In the Vindhya mountains it is said to be a hundredfold, and it is equal to that even in the Gaṅgā;
likewise in Āryāvarta, Madhyadeśa, and Brahmāvarta. (36)
Worship performed at Prayāga and likewise at Puṣkara yields fruit like that of the Vindhya mountains;
it is said to be four times more effective when performed in the waters of the Karatoyā river.
Therefore, O Bhairava, at Nandikuṇḍa the fruit is fourfold;
and it is declared that in the vicinity of Jalpiṣeśvara, it is four times greater than that.
In that regard, it is recorded as being twice as great as even that at Siddheśvarī-yoni;
and it is declared to be four times greater in the waters of the Lohitya river.
In Kāmarūpa, however, it is equal to that everywhere, both on water and on land;
just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all, so Lakṣmī is the most supreme of all.
The worship of the Goddess is likewise praised in Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods;
there exists no other field of the Goddess equal to Kāmarūpa. (41)
Elsewhere, the Goddess is rare; she is found in every house in Kāmarūpa, but she is said to be a hundred times more abundant on the summit of Nīlakūṭa.
Twice that [measure] is prescribed for an *eruka* Śiva-liṅga;
twice that again is prescribed for the *yoni*-shaped liṅgas of Śailaputrī and the others.
Then, it is said that [the merit] in the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is a hundredfold greater;
he who has performed the worship of Mahāmāyā even once in Kāmākhyā— || 44 ||
He obtains his desires in this world and the nature of Śiva in the next;
there is no other equal to him, and for him, no further duty remains.
Having attained his desired object in this world, he is born with a long life;
his movement shall be unimpeded by others, like that of the wind. (46)
He becomes invincible in battle or in philosophical debate.
By means of the Vaiṣṇavī-tantra mantra, having performed worship once within the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala, one obtains a hundredfold fruit. || 47 ||
The primordial form is Mahāmāyā, the yogic sleep that pervades the universe;
her Vaiṣṇava Tantra and mantra have indeed been explained previously. (48)
Those other forms mentioned, such as Śailaputrī and the rest, are merely divisions of her alone, having emerged from her very body. (49)
Just as rays constantly issue forth from the orb of the sun,
so do the goddesses Ugracaṇḍā and the others emerge from the body of Mahāmāyā.
I must describe to you their very forms as limbs;
indeed, the one Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) has assumed a state of diversity for the sake of her task.
Kāmākhyā, the Great Māyā, is proclaimed as the primordial form; yet that same Great Māyā is proclaimed under various names according to the sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 52 ||
Who indeed is like Viṣṇu? For he is eternal because of his constancy; and because he crushes (mardana) people, he is likewise known as Janārdana. || 53 ||
In that very same way, Mahāmāyā, united with Kāma on the mountain, is always called "Kāmākhyā" by gods and men alike. (54)
Just as a certain man may be called "Umbrella" because he holds an umbrella,
or "Bather" at the time of bathing, so too is she called by the name Kāmākhyā.
The body of Mahāmāyā was indeed present for the sake of desire;
it was smeared with red saffron that had been applied for the sake of passion. (56)
Having cast aside her sword at the time of desire, she herself takes up a garland;
but when she has abandoned desire, then she becomes a bearer of the sword.
At the time of desire, she rests upon a red lotus placed on a white corpse;
when desire has ceased, she stands upon a white corpse, having abandoned all longing.
Likewise, by moving here and there, she becomes a lioness who grants desires;
sometimes she is upon a white corpse, and sometimes upon a red lotus. (59)
Sometimes, assuming a form at will, she sports upon the back of a lion;
when she is seated upon a red lotus, then the lion moves before her.
When the Goddess has entered the state of a preta, she then gazes upon another;
when she becomes the bestower of boons in the form of Mahāmāyā.
At the time of worship, she is then seated upon a preta-lotus and a lion;
when one meditates on her upon a red lotus, one should then contemplate Hari before her.
When one meditates on Hari, one should contemplate the other two [deities] before oneself;
when all three have been meditated upon simultaneously, one should then contemplate the preta, the lotus, and Hari in succession.
When those [deities] who grant desires are present, one should indeed approach that goddess who grants desires;
likewise, one should meditate upon Śivā appropriately within each and every one of them.
Since she is the one, all-encompassing primordial nature (prakṛti) of the worlds, she, who consists of the universe, is upheld by the gods Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva. 65.
The great god Mahādeva is white, Brahmā is red, and Harir Hari is to be known as dark; these are the mounts of those of great splendor.
Since it was not appropriate for them to serve as mounts in their own forms,
those three assumed other forms and became mounts.
In whatever form the auspicious Mahāmāyā constantly delighted,
in that very form the three became seats.
Upon a lion is a red lotus; above that is Śiva, and above him is Mahāmāyā, bestowing the boons of granting wishes and fearlessness.
He who constantly worships Śivā while meditating upon her in this form has undoubtedly worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (70)
Thus, Mahāmāyā and she who is called Kāmā are always one in form; though distinguished by meditation and appearance, one should therefore worship her there.
Thus, O best of men, the specific tantras of Durgā have been told to you; now hear her limb-mantras (aṅgamantra). 72.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 58 ||
The Fifty-Ninth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall now specifically declare the ancillary mantras (aṅgamantra) of Caṇḍikā.
By those who have propitiated the Goddess, she becomes the bestower of the four aims of human life. || 1 ||
The final palatal [consonant] joined with the sixth vowel, the bindu, the moon, and fire;
likewise the penultimate vowel—these constitute the external Vāgbhava mantra. (2)
The seed-syllable of the eyes and that of Caṇḍikā—these three are proclaimed; they are to be placed respectively upon the left forehead and the right eye. (3)
This supreme secret mantra, known as the seed-syllable of Durgā, is always the ultimate cause for the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. || 4 ||
When the goddess, praised by the hosts of gods, had her body sustained by the splendors of the celestial dwellers within the hermitages of the sage Kātyāyana, [she became pregnant]. || 5 ||
Then, from the three eyes of the Goddess, the Root-form emerged— effulgent, the sustainer of the world, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Having assumed an excellent body through the splendors of all the gods,
she took up numerous weapons that had been given by the gods, each according to its portion.
The Goddess, praised by Brahmā and the other gods, slew the demon Mahiṣāsura along with his retinue, his followers, his ministers, his army, and his vehicles.
But when Mahiṣa was slain, the Goddess was then worshipped by the gods;
and by this very mantra, she attained renown in the world.
From that time forward, that image has been worshipped by all everywhere;
the original image remained well-concealed, while [the other] attained renown through its own form.
O Bhairava, listen to that form which, through the granting of boons by the gods and its employment by Brahmā and others, is worshipped by all. (11)
She was endowed with a mass of matted hair, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
she possessed three eyes, and her face resembled the moon within the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft. || 12 ||
She possesses the luster of molten gold, is well-proportioned, and has beautiful eyes;
she is endowed with fresh youth and adorned with every ornament.
She has beautiful teeth, sharp [fangs], and full, elevated breasts;
she stands in the *tribhaṅga* posture as the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She is endowed with ten arms, the touch of whose lotus-stalk-like hands is extensive;
a trident should be placed in her right [hand], and below it, a sword and a discus in succession.
A sharp arrow and likewise a spear were joined to his multitude of arms;
and above, a shield, a full bow, a noose, and a goad.
One should also place a bell and an axe in the lower left hand;
likewise, one should depict a headless buffalo beneath it. (17)
Likewise, he saw the Dānava, who had arisen from the severing of his head, holding a sword in his hand,
pierced in the heart by a trident, and adorned with entrails hanging out.
His limbs were stained crimson, his eyes flashed with red light,
he was encircled by a serpent-noose, and his face was contorted with a frown.
One should depict the lion of the Goddess as having its hair grasped by Durgā with her left hand, which holds a noose, and with blood vomiting from its mouth.
The goddess’s right foot is placed evenly upon the lion,
while her left foot is slightly raised, with the big toe resting upon the buffalo.
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Cāmuṇḍā, and likewise Caṇḍikā. || 22 ||
One should constantly meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa, and who is perpetually surrounded by these eight powers. (23)
The limb-mantra of this [goddess] is known as the Durgā-tantra;
listen with a one-pointed mind to this means for accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha. (24)
The wife of Vahni (Ra), the sixth vowel (Ū), the end of Ha (KṢa), the end of Pra (M), and Agni (Ra) itself;
preceded by Durgā (Dū), that is the mantra of Durgā beginning with Oṃ, as heard from the Śruti. || 25 ||
When the sun is situated in the sign of Capricorn, on that which is the fifth day of the bright fortnight,
one should duly worship Śivā with this mantra.
Furthermore, having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
one should perform abundant offerings of sacrificial oblations on the ninth day.
And at twilight, one should offer a bali-oblation smeared with the blood from the limbs of a goat;
when this is done, one is joined with auspiciousness and always rejoices.
Prospering with sons and grandsons, and with abundance of wealth and grain, no grief arises for him, nor does misfortune ever befall him;
he is born long-lived and endowed with all good fortune in this world. (29)
Whoever performs worship with flowers available at that time, including even *aśoka* blossoms, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, using this mantra: || 30 ||
For him, neither grief, nor disease, nor even misfortune arises,
provided he has fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
On the ninth day, [one should offer] food with sesame seeds, barley-gruel, and sweetmeats;
likewise, milk, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and flour-cakes.
One should worship with the blood and even the flesh of various animals;
then, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship with water mixed with sesame seeds.
With the mantra from the Durgātantra, three handfuls [of water] should be offered.
When this is done on the tenth day, whatever sin has been committed over ten lifetimes [is destroyed]. || 34 ||
Whatever is performed [on these days] goes to destruction, yet one is born with a long life.
This applies to the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and that of Śrāvaṇa.
O Bhairava, one should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite, which is supremely pleasing to the Goddess,
using the Durgātantra mantra and the Durgā seed-syllable (bīja).
O Bhairava,
one should perform the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) with the Vaiṣṇavī-tantra mantra and the seed-syllable (bīja) of Durgā;
specifically, having reached the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform the Pavitraka rite for the Goddess.
One should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa for all the deities in either Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa; it bestows the fruits of a full year.

The second lunar day is declared to be the auspicious date for the installation of the purifier (pavitrāropaṇa) for the Giver of Wealth; it is remembered as the most excellent among all dates for the Goddess Śrī.
The third belongs to Bhavabhāvinī, the fourth to her son;
the fifth is for Somarāja, and the sixth is said to belong to Guha.
The seventh is declared for Bhāskara, and likewise the eighth for Durgā;
the ninth is said to belong to the Mothers, and the tenth is considered for Vāsuki. (41)
The eleventh day belongs to the sages, the twelfth to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), the thirteenth to the bodiless one (Kāma), and the fourteenth is mine alone.
The full moon day (paurṇamāsī) is considered the auspicious date for Brahmā and the guardians of the quarters;
indeed, he who does not perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) to the gods [is at fault].
Keśava takes away the fruit of that person’s annual worship;
therefore, the supreme offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed with great effort. 44.
When this is performed, there is the attainment of great fruit, and that worship becomes fruitful;
[this is] by means of which sacred thread it should be done, as known by the wise. (45)
Listen to that authority, O Bhairava, from my words:
first is the thread of *darbha* grass, and after that, the lotus fiber.
Then there should be very auspicious linen, and after that cotton;
likewise, one should have sacred threads made of silk or other materials, but one should not have them made by anyone else.
Various purificatory rites must indeed be performed with diligence, adorned with fragrant perfumes and garlands as prescribed. 48.
A maiden, a devoted wife, or a widow of virtuous character may spin the thread; one of evil character must not spin it. (49)
That thread which has been pierced by a needle, burnt, or smeared with ashes and smoke must be carefully avoided in this purificatory rite.
One should carefully avoid that which has been used, that which has been gnawed by mice, that which is defiled by liquor, blood, and the like, as well as that which is soiled or dyed blue. (51)
One should prepare the purifier (pavitra) with threads, categorized as the smallest, the largest, and the medium;
that which is the smallest purifier consists of twenty-seven strands.
In the world of mortals, fame and renown increase one's happiness and good fortune;
this [work] consisting of fifty-four threads is declared to be the supreme medium [size].
This supreme among all tantras brings about divine enjoyments, is meritorious, and bestows both heaven and liberation; it should indeed be performed with one hundred and eight [threads].
Having given that to Mahādevī, one shall attain union with Śiva;
if one gives the most excellent pavitraka to Vāsudeva, [one attains the same].
Then the practitioner goes to the world of Hari; there is no doubt about this.
This is celebrated as the "Garland of One Thousand and Eight Jewels" (Ratnamālā). || 56 ||
This sacred thread (pavitra) of the Great Goddess bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
whoever offers this pavitra to the Great Goddess along with a garland of jewels— || 57 ||
Having remained in heaven for thousands of millions of aeons, one shall become auspicious;
this indeed is the sacred thread of Śaṅkara known as the Nāgahāra. 58.
Whoever offers me a beautiful thread consisting of one thousand and eight strands—for as many as that collection of threads may be—[he shall obtain such a reward]. (59)
For as many thousands of kalpas as there are flowers in the garland of eight thousand plus one offered to Hari, one rejoices in my world. || 60 ||
By the gift of its threads, one attains union with Viṣṇu;
that which is the smallest sacred thread (pavitra) should, however, reach down to the navel.
One should join it with twelve knots according to the measurement of one's own body; the middle part should be the measure of the thighs, and there one should apply the knots.
O Bhairava, its measurement is said to be twenty-four [finger-breadths], as well as that of one's own body; it is declared to be the supreme purifier, reaching down to the knees.
One should apply thirty-six knots according to one's own measure;
one hundred and eight knots should be made according to the proper rule.
Likewise, the one called Nāgahāra and others are prepared according to the prescribed rule;
furthermore, the knots are made with the sacred thread by which the purification is performed.
It should be made with a thread of a different color and endowed with the proper characteristics;
one should make seven knots on the ring finger using wraps.
One should prepare [the materials] with double the quantity for the middling [rite], and likewise with triple the quantity for the superior one;
having then consecrated the purifiers (pavitra) on the preceding day.
On the following day, one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the purifying thread;
there, the twice-born should carry out the mantranyāsa with the Durgā-bīja mantra.
O Bhairava, others may perform [the rite] with the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra;
however, the wise practitioner himself should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) upon every knot.
O Bhairava, in this practice, the recitation over the rosary is performed with the tip of the thumb;
one should place as many knots here as there are beads.
By means of those mantras, there should be the application of the limbs (aṅga) for him;
one should perform the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) using the Durgā-tantra mantra. || 71 ||
Having placed all the purificatory grass (pavitraka) into a single sacrificial vessel, and having deposited within it perfumes and other substances as well as most beautiful flowers; || 72 ||
Then, O Bhairava, one should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) with the tips of the fingers;
indeed, one should perform the tattvanyāsa using the root mantra of Viṣṇu.
This "idaṃ viṣṇu" mantra is indeed prescribed for the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) for a twice-born;
however, for Śūdras, the mantra used in the placement of mantras is the twelve-syllabled one.
The placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) is traditionally taught for me by means of the Prāsāda mantra;
by this [mantra] one should perform the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) and by this [mantra] one should effect the ritual gift (dāna).
Then, having smeared the purifiers with saffron, ushira, camphor, sandalwood, and other unguents, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
O Bhairava, a man who is self-restrained, having duly worshipped the Goddess in the mandala according to the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra or the Durgā-tantra mantra, [attains success].
One should place the purifying thread upon the head of the Goddess using the seed-syllable of Durgā;
for whichever deity is prescribed, the mandala should be made with that very same [seed-syllable].
Whichever mantra belongs to whichever [deity], and whatever its meditation, worship, and so forth—having diligently performed the worship with that very mantra, [one should proceed]. (79)
One should place the *pavitraka* upon his very head with the seed-syllable and the mantra;
[one who gives the *pavitraka* to me and the *pavitraka* to the gods... (80)
O Bhairava, you are the one who fulfills the purpose of all the gods:
Agni, Brahmā, Bhavānī, Gajavaktra, and Mahoraga. || 81 ||
Having worshipped Skanda, Bhānu, the group of Mothers, the guardians of the directions, and the nine planets— each of these individually in the jars according to the prescribed rite— 82.
With a concentrated mind, one should place a purifying ring (pavitra) on the head of each of these;
having prepared the *pañcagavya* sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and offered it to the Goddess, one should present three oblations (*āhuti*).
Having offered that very [oblation] to Viṣṇu and to Śambhu according to the prescribed rite,
[he should offer] one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, and likewise oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
The practitioner should offer one hundred and eight [oblations] to Mahādevī;
in this very same manner, the practitioner [should offer them] to Viṣṇu and the others as well. (85)
One should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha, with various kinds of food offerings, drinks, and sweets made of *vaṭa* flour and *modaka*. || 86 ||
With *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, coconuts, dates, and jackfruits, as well as with various fruits such as mangoes, pomegranates, *karkāru* cucumbers, and *drākṣā* grapes. || 87 ||
With all kinds of foods, both hard and soft, as well as fish, meats, and rice;
and with perfumes, flowers, incense, and most enchanting lamps. (88)
O Bhairava, the practitioner of Bhavānī should worship with garments and ornaments, as well as with troupes of actors and dancers, and with courtesans. 89.
Accompanied by dance and song, he should cause a vigil to be held at night;
he should also feed the Brāhmaṇas and his kinsmen together with the twice-born.
When the Pavitrāropaṇa ceremony has been performed, one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be presented:
gold, a cow, sesame seeds, clarified butter, a garment, or even vegetables.
Thereafter, the practitioner should recite this mantra while [worshipping] with garlands of gems and coral, mandārava flowers, and other such offerings.
"O Supreme Goddess, may this annual worship be yours;
then one should bid farewell to the Goddess with offerings and acts of devotion. (93)
When the offering of the purifiers has been performed by the Goddess according to the rule, the worship of the year shall become complete at the end of the year. (94)
For as long as a hundred million eons, a man shall dwell in the house of a goddess;
even there, his prosperity of happiness and good fortune shall be incomparable.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 59 ||
The Sixtieth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: One should perform the great festival of Durgā with the mantra of the Durgā-tantra.
On the Mahānavamī day in autumn, kings and others perform the offering of the bali sacrifice. || 1 ||
The lunar day which falls on the eighth of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina is called Mahāṣṭamī; it is supreme and brings great delight to the Goddess.
The ninth lunar day that follows it is known as Mahānavamī;
that lunar day is dear to Śiva and worthy of worship by all people.
O dear Bhairava, hear the distinction regarding the worship of these two:
a man, being self-restrained, having duly worshipped the Goddess in the mandala according to the rules— || 4 ||
O Bhairava, by means of the Vaiṣṇava tantras and mantras, as well as the Durgā-tantra,
the Goddess accepts worship according to the various forms [of her manifestation] for the sake of prosperity.
O child, when the sun is situated in Virgo, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should observe the Nandika vow;
subsisting on food obtained unasked, eating only at night, or eating only once a day, one should likewise overcome all calamities.
Bathing at dawn, having conquered the pairs of opposites, worshipping Śiva at the three times of day, engaged in recitation and fire-offerings, he should feed young maidens.
On the sixth lunar day, one should awaken [the deity] with bilva branches and the fruits of the goddess;
on the seventh, having brought that bilva branch, one should worship it thoroughly.
Furthermore, one should perform worship especially on the eighth day;
one should personally keep a vigil and offer a sacrificial oblation at the dead of night.
On the ninth day, one should duly perform an extensive offering of oblations;
one should meditate upon the ten-armed Goddess and worship her according to the Durgā-tantra.
On the tenth day, the best of practitioners should indeed perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana);
having performed that dismissal on that lunar day, he should observe the night-vow (nakta).
But when one worships the sixteen-armed Mahāmāyā, listen now to the specific procedure for that, using the mantra from the Durgā-tantra. (12)
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Kanyā,
one should take a single meal on the twelfth day and observe the nakta vow on the following day.
On the fourteenth day, having awakened Mahāmāyā according to the prescribed rite with the sounds of songs and musical instruments and the offering of various food oblations, || 14 ||
On the following day, the wise man should observe a fast even if it has not been requested;
in this very manner he should perform the vow until the ninth day arrives. (15)
Having worshipped [the deity] in Jyeṣṭhā, one should worship with Mūla;
having performed the worship in Uttarā, one should dismiss [the deity] at the end of Śravaṇā.
O Bhairava, listen also to this: when one worships the eighteen-armed Mahāmāyā with the mantra from the Durgā-tantra, [the procedure is as follows].
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kanyā, having worshipped during the day under the constellation Ārdrā,
one should awaken the Goddess with the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight, the untying of the Goddess’s hair is performed;
then, on the morning of the fifth day, one should bathe her with auspicious waters.
On the seventh day, there is the worship of the leaf-diagram (patrikā); on the eighth, there is likewise a fast;
on the ninth, there is worship, a vigil, and the offering of the bali sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
On the tenth day, however, there is the sending forth [of the image] accompanied by play, festivities, and auspicious rites;
on the tenth day, moreover, the great lustration ceremony (nīrājana) brings about an increase in strength.
O Bhairava, listen now to the special procedure for when one worships the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, the Great Māyā who pervades the universe. 22.
When the sun is situated in Virgo, the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight occurs;
on that night, she should be worshipped with extensive and magnificent offerings. (23)
On the ninth day, the offering of the bali-oblation must indeed be performed according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform the recitation of mantras (japa) and the fire-sacrifice (homa) there according to the injunctions for the sake of prosperity.
A man should worship the Great Goddess with the eightfold offering of flowers for the sake of obtaining Rāma’s grace and for the slaying of Rāvaṇa. (25)
In former times, the Great Goddess was awakened by Brahmā during the night;
thereafter, she abandoned her sleep on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
She went to the city of Laṅkā where Rāghava had formerly been;
having gone there, the Great Goddess then [confronted] those two, Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
The Mother, having herself become invisible, incited the battle between the Rākṣasas and the monkeys; she devoured their flesh and drank their blood.
She caused the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa to continue for seven days;
then, when the seventh night had passed, on the ninth day, [she slew] Rāvaṇa.
The Great Illusion, who pervades the universe, caused [him] to be slain by Rāma,
while the Goddess herself watched the play of their combat.
For seven nights she was thus highly honored by the gods;
and when the heroic Rāvaṇa had been slain, on the ninth day she was worshipped by all the deities.
The Grandfather of the worlds performed a special worship of Durgā;
then, on the tenth day, the Goddess was sent forth amidst nocturnal festivals.
Then Śakra also performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the divine army,
for the sake of peace among the celestial hosts and for the increase of the sovereignty of the gods.
And having observed the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa’s arrow, which causes fear,
[he saw] that which was situated in the northeast direction of Laṅkā on the third day.
When the great army of the gods was terrified during the conjunction with the Svāti constellation,
Indra, the lord of the gods, at the word of Hari, chose Śānti for the sake of pacification.
Then, on the tenth day, after listening [to the recitation] and having bid farewell to the auspicious Caṇḍikā,
Hari performed the bali-offering and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the sake of peace.
Having performed the lustration ceremony for his army there, Śakra, the lord of Śacī, approached Rāma, the descendant of Raghu,
and departed for heaven along with the gods.
Thus occurred in a former age, during the interval of Manu Svāyambhuva:
the ten-armed Goddess indeed manifested for the welfare of the gods.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga for the sake of the welfare of the worlds and of men,
it occurred just as it had happened in previous kalpas, and so it happens in every kalpa.
The Goddess herself indeed proceeds for the destruction of the Daityas;
in every kalpa, there shall be a Rāma and likewise a Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
In that very same way, battle arose and likewise the encounter with the gods;
thus occurred thousands of Rāmas against thousands of Rāvaṇas.
O Goddess, all beings that are destined to come into existence proceed in this manner;
all the gods worship her and also perform the lustration ceremony for Balarāma.
In that very same manner, all men should perform worship according to the prescribed rule;
the king, for the sake of increasing his strength, should perform the *balanīrājana* ceremony.
The procession should be carried out by women adorned with divine ornaments,
accompanied by dancing, singing, play, curiosity, and auspicious rites.
With modakas, flour-cakes, and various kinds of drinks, foods, and edibles;
likewise with pumpkins, coconuts, dates, and jackfruits. || 45 ||
With grapes, emblic myrobalans, and śāḍilyas, as well as with plīhas and karuṇas,
and with the roots of kaśeruka and kramuka, along with jambu, tinduka, and others.
With offerings of cow products, molasses, meats, wines, and honey, as well as with food-offerings dear to children, parched grain, unbroken rice, fruits, and so forth. || 47 ||
With stalks of sugarcane and sugar-candy, with *lavalī* fruits and oranges, with goats, buffaloes, rams, and heaps of his own blood; || 48 ||
One should worship the Mother of the World with various kinds of offerings such as birds and other sacrificial animals, using the mud of their flesh and blood. (49)
At night, having fashioned a doll of flour for Skanda and Viśākha,
one should worship them for the destruction of enemies and likewise for the pleasure of Durgā.
One should likewise perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and even meat;
furthermore, the eight auspicious Yoginīs, beginning with Ugracaṇḍā, should be worshipped.
The sixty-four Yoginīs, as well as the Koṭiyoginīs, and the nine Durgās should likewise be worshipped—the auspicious goddesses who are ever-present. (52)
Since those forms of the Goddess, beginning with Jayantī, consist of fragrant flowers, all the goddesses, as well as all the weapons and ornaments, are likewise composed of them. (53)
For the sake of prosperity, one should always worship the lion, the vehicle of Mahiṣāsuramardinī, together with all its limbs and minor members. 54.
In a former age, during the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga for mankind, the Great Goddess was constantly praised by all the gods.
For the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
she is Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the universe, and that which consists of the universe.
Endowed with sixteen arms, she is renowned as Bhadrakālī;
she dwells upon the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, possessing a vast body.
She has the luster of the color of an *atasī* flower, wears blazing golden earrings, and is adorned with a mass of matted hair, a crescent moon, and three crests. || 58 ||
Accompanied by a necklace of serpents and adorned with a golden chain, she likewise holds a trident, a discus, a sword, a conch, and an arrow. (59)
The goddess, whose teeth are ever radiant with smiles, constantly holds a spear, a thunderbolt, and a staff in her right arms.
She holds in her left hands a shield, a shield-skin, a bow, a noose, a goad, a bell, an axe, and a mace.
Seated upon a lion, with three eyes of red hue and blazing intensely,
the Supreme Goddess stands piercing the buffalo with her trident.
Having stepped upon her with her left foot, the Goddess, who is identical with the universe, stood there;
and seeing her, all the gods prostrated before the Supreme Goddess.
Seeing that Mahiṣāsura had been slain, they said nothing at all;
then the Supreme Goddess spoke to those gods, headed by Brahmā.
With faces blossoming with smiles and radiant with beaming countenances, go now, O hosts of gods, toward the interior of Jambudvīpa! 65.
Near the Himavat mountain is the excellent hermitage of Kātyāyana;
there alone will your goal be accomplished, without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, that great goddess vanished right there;
the gods also then went to the city of the sage Kātyāyana.
Having returned to the hermitage with their minds filled with wonder, they said,
"The Mahiṣa has been slain by the Goddess, for which purpose we had been sent."
This great goddess, the sustainer of the world and composed of the world, has been praised;
for what purpose did that goddess say she would go to the hermitage of Kātyāyanī? (69)
"What other desired task shall be ours?"—saying this, they all proceeded together with one another. (70)
Then, to the hermitage of the sage Kātyāyana situated near the Himavat mountain, Indra along with the world-protectors, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, [proceeded]. (71)
Eager to behold Durgā, they sat for a very long time, filled with joy;
then all the attendants of Rudra [reported] the actions of Mahiṣāsura.
Having arrived, they related the defeat of the world of the gods;
thereupon, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others were filled with great wrath.
They said, "Who else is there who is a great bull among the Dānavas, slain by the Goddess, yet who again brings about the total destruction of the world here? (74)
Thus, as they were becoming enraged, their splendors, in the form of powers, instantly issued forth separately from each of their bodies.
The goddess, whose body was sustained by his splendors, was indeed kindled and worshipped by Kātyāyana; therefore she is remembered as Kātyāyanī. (76)
Then, by that very mantra associated with the ten arms,
the Mother of the World, who is identical with the world, subsequently slew Mahiṣa.
When the Great Goddess was praised and awakened on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, she, who is identical with the universe, manifested herself.
On the beautiful seventh day of the bright fortnight, that goddess, the embodiment of the splendor of the gods, performed her rites; on the eighth day, she was adorned by them.
On the ninth day, having been worshipped with offerings, she slew Mahiṣāsura; on the tenth day, Śivā, having manifested, vanished again.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard this excellent account of the queen’s union, King Sagara,
still harboring doubts regarding her true nature, questioned Aurva once again.
Sagara said:
"If the Great Goddess slew Mahiṣāsura later, how was it that she previously took the form of Hadra-Kālī to [slay] Mahiṣāsura? (82)
For instance, all the gods beheld her being trampled by his foot and saw her heart pierced by a spear.
O best of sages, resolve this doubt now through your meditative concentration.
Aurva said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to how Bhadrakālī,
the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), manifested in ancient times together with Mahiṣa.
That very hero Mahiṣāsura, while asleep on the mountain at night,
beheld a terrible dream of a fearsome appearance.
Mahāmāyā Bhadrakālī, with her mouth wide open and appearing most terrifying, severed my head with a sword and drank its blood.
Then, at dawn, that Daitya Mahiṣāsura, filled with fear,
together with his followers, worshipped her for a very long time.
Then the Goddess was indeed propitiated by the asura Mahiṣa;
Bhadrakālī appeared, endowed with sixteen arms.
Then, having prostrated before Mahāmāyā, who is identical with the universe, the asura Mahiṣa, bowing his body and filled with devotion, spoke these words: (89)
Mahiṣa said:
"O Goddess, I have certainly seen in a dream that your heads, severed by the sword and dripping with blood, were released by you. (90)
"This must certainly be done by you; this has been known by me through valid means.
Grant me this one boon: let there be this drinking of my blood. (91)
"O Supreme Goddess, I am to be slain by you; there is no doubt about this.
Even for me, there is no sorrow in that matter—for who can transgress destiny? (92)
However, Śambhu was previously propitiated by my father for my sake, accompanied by you alone; it was from that [propitiation] that I was subsequently born. (93)
I too propitiated Śambhu and obtained such desired things as an excellent Asura kingdom for the duration of three Manvantaras.
I have eaten without thorns, and no remorse exists within me;
yet I have been cursed by the sage Kātyāyana for the sake of his disciple. (95)
A woman will bring about your destruction, of this there is no doubt;
[just as in the past] she destroyed the most excellent sage named Raudrāśva while he was engaged in ascetic penance. (96)
At that time, out of curiosity, I assumed the incomparable form of a celestial woman near the Himalayas and approached the disciple of the sage named Kātyāyana.
Deluded by me, the brahmin immediately abandoned his asceticism at that time;
for I was standing nearby, disguised as the sage Kātyāyanīputra.
Having then recognized her as an illusion, he was cursed by the fire of his wrath for the sake of his disciple:
"Since this disciple of mine has been deluded by you and fallen from his asceticism... (99)
"Since you have acted in the form of a woman, a woman shall slay you"—thus did the sage Kātyāyana himself previously curse me. (100)
The time for that curse has now arrived and is at hand;
I attained the status of Lord of the Gods and enjoyed the three worlds together.
