There is nothing here for me to grieve over, for whatever was desired by me has been obtained.
Therefore, I have indeed sought refuge in you; whatever remains for me to request, O Goddess Durgā, grant that. Again and again, salutations unto you! 102.
The Goddess said:
"O great Asura, choose whatever boon you desire;
I shall grant you the boon you seek, of this there is no doubt. (103)
Mahiṣa said:
"By your grace, I desire to partake in the sacrificial portion;
act in such a way that I may be honored in all sacrifices. (104)
"I shall not abandon service at your feet as long as the sun continues to move;
grant these two boons, if a boon is to be given to me. (105)
The Goddess said:
"Portions for the sacrifice have indeed been assigned separately to the gods;
there is no other portion remaining that I may now give to you. (106)
But, O Mahiṣāsura, when you have been slain by me in battle, you shall never abandon my feet; of this there is no doubt. (107)
"O Dānava, wherever my worship proceeds, there you are to be worshipped and meditated upon; for that very body of yours is present right there. (108)
Having heard her words at dawn, Mahiṣāsura,
having obtained the boon, was then delighted and his face became radiant.
O Ugracaṇḍā, O Bhadrakālī, O Durgā, O Goddess, salutations be unto you!
O Goddess, all forms whatsoever are your own manifestations, consisting of your very self.
O Supreme Goddess, by which of your forms am I to be worshipped in this sacrifice?
If you have shown me favor here, please explain that to me. (111)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahiṣāsura, you shall be worshipped in this world within those forms whose names have been proclaimed here by you. (112)
The form known as Ugracaṇḍā is indeed I myself as Bhadrakālī;
however, that form by which I shall slay you is celebrated as Durgā.
Always remaining at the feet of these forms, you shall be worthy of worship by men in heaven, as well as by the gods and the rākṣasas. (114)
In the first creation, you were formerly established by me in the form of Ugracaṇḍā;
but in the second creation, you were slain by me as Bhadrakālī. (115)
"Now, in the form of Durgā, I shall slay you along with your followers;
however, previously, I did not seize you by the soles of your feet."
Now that the boon requested by you has been granted, you must first accept the two previously desired things;
thereafter, you shall be accepted for the enjoyment of your sacrificial portion.
Aurva said:
Having spoken thus, that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) then revealed her body, known by the name Ugracaṇḍā, to the Asura Mahiṣa.
That form which is renowned as sixteen-armed Bhadrakālī likewise bears [the other two] with her remaining two arms.
In his lower right hand he holds a mace, and in his left hand a drinking vessel filled with wine;
upon his head he bears a garland of skulls and dwells in a cremation ground.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, fierce, mounted upon a lion, with blood-red eyes and a massive body, she is endowed with eighteen arms. (121)
Seeing Ugracaṇḍā and Bhadrakālī—the two forms of the Goddess—Mahiṣa immediately prostrated himself, overcome with wonder. (122)
Then, just as Mahiṣāsura had been struck down by being trampled underfoot,
in that very same manner the two goddesses seized him by the soles of his feet.
The buffalo was pierced in the heart by the spear, its head severed,
its hair grasped by the Goddess, and adorned with its entrails as it moved.
Seeing his own former body, which was large-bodied and blood-red, that asura was seized by fear; he then grieved and fell into a state of delusion.
Then, having steadied himself for a moment, that Dānava bowed down and spoke these words to the Goddess with a faltering voice: || 126 ||
Mahiṣa said:
"O Goddess, if you are pleased and the sacrificial portions have been assigned, then let it be so;
otherwise, this destruction shall certainly not be mine. (127)
"O Goddess, act in such a way that I shall not engage in a wondrous enmity with the gods, and that I may not undergo rebirth. (128)
The Goddess said: "I have been propitiated by you and a boon has been granted to you by me;
yet you are to be slain by me here—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (129)
And that which was requested by you, together with all the hosts of gods—that there may never be enmity between us—shall indeed come to pass. (130)
O Dānava, by the touch of the soles of my feet, your body shall not be shattered for the purpose of consuming sacrificial portions.
O great asura, all your vital breaths along with your individual souls shall remain for a long time solely through contact with the feet of Hara.
O Mahiṣāsura, for thirty-eight hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas, you shall have no further birth.
Having thus granted a boon to the asura Mahiṣa, the Goddess,
bowed to by him with his head, vanished right there.
O King, Mahiṣa, being once again deluded by her illusory power (māyā), returned to his own abode, assuming his former demonic nature as before.
Sagara said:
"Many Daityas were subdued by you through your power of illusion for the welfare of the world;
yet they were not slain, for you granted them auspicious boons."
"O best of the twice-born, explain to me correctly how this boon was chosen for this reason, and why it was granted to him."
Aurva said:
Mahādeva was propitiated by Rambha, the enemy of the gods;
after a long time, Śaṅkara became well-pleased with his ascetic penance.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, spoke directly to Rambha:
"I am gratified with you; O Rambha, choose a boon according to your desire. (138)
Thus addressed, Rambha replied to that moon-crested Lord:
"O Mahādeva, I am childless, if you have favor toward me. (139)
O Śaṅkara, may you become my son throughout three lifetimes—
invincible to all beings and a conqueror of the inhabitants of heaven.
"He shall be long-lived, renowned, and possessed of fortune, O Śaṅkara.
Thus addressed by the Daitya, the bull-bannered god replied:
"Let this which you desire be so; I shall become your son.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right there.
Rambha also went to his own abode with eyes blossoming with joy;
then, as he was traveling on the road, Rambha beheld a beautiful buffalo-cow.
Seeing that three-year-old cow, variegated in color, beautiful and in heat, Rambha was then deluded by desire for her. (144)
Then, taking her by both hands, he celebrated the festival of love;
as their amorous union proceeded, she was then [overwhelmed] by his splendor.
The queen then conceived a fetus, and from him Mahiṣāsura was born;
Giriśa, by means of his own portion, attained the state of being her son.
Then he grew by means of those missiles like the moon in the bright fortnight;
and the sage Kātyāyana cursed that Mahiṣāsura.
Having observed the misconduct for the sake of his disciples, he who acts to bestow grace upon his disciples recognized that Mahiṣāsura had been cursed by Kātyāyana.
Īśvara said:
"O Goddess who pervades the universe, this Mahiṣāsura has been cursed today by Kātyāyana, saying: 'She shall become the cause of the destruction of women.'"
"The word of the Sage will undoubtedly come to pass; there is no doubt.
O Goddess, you must perform my buffalo sacrifice within yourself. (150)
Hari, joined with yoga, must always be slain—both before and after;
he cannot bear you now in his form as Hari.
"In the past, Mahādeva formerly requested of the Goddess: 'This buffalo of mine shall become your carrier. (152)
By him, the Goddess seized Mahiṣāsura from Mahādeva;
through three births, the Lord Hara became the son of Raṃbhā.
In the three worlds, even Rambha became like a pillar (rambha);
that Asura performed such a most dreadful penance.
In that very manner, Śambhu was propitiated and granted a boon for the sake of a son;
likewise, he first approached his queen for sexual union. || 155 ||
In that [battle], the heroic Dānava Mahiṣāsura was likewise [slain];
and the venerable sage Kātyāyana lay down upon him in the same manner.
Thus, when this previous birth had passed away and he was in that subsequent birth as Mahiṣa, he worshipped the Goddess and then requested a boon.
Having obtained a boon in his third birth, he requested this boon for all future kalpas without exception: "May there be no further birth for me here. || 158 ||
Therefore, O King, this asura now stands at the soles of the Goddess’s feet; furthermore, his rebirth shall not occur until the end of the cosmic dissolution.
Thus, by the grace of the Goddess, that great Asura, born from a portion of Mahādeva, constantly attained supreme realization.
Thus, O King, I have told you how that Mahiṣāsura, having reached the sole of the Goddess's foot, rejoices even today. Listen now to what is at hand, O King; I shall speak, O best of monarchs. (161)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus has been told to you how King Sagara,
together with Aurva, held a conversation regarding the appointment of the queen as his chief consort.
Furthermore, listen, O best of sages, to that which was spoken once more to the high-souled Sagara—the supreme secret, more secret than the secret. (163)
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The sixty-first chapter.
Aurva said:
Just as the Blessed Lord spoke to the high-souled Bhairava...
O best of kings, listen likewise to what has been presented regarding the Vetāla. || 1 ||
The Blessed Lord said: That form which was Ugracaṇḍā, possessing eighteen arms,
appeared in ancient times on the ninth day of the dark fortnight when the sun had entered the sign of Virgo.
The Great Māyā appeared together with ten million yoginīs on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, at which a twelve-year sacrificial session was held.
Dakṣa began to perform the rite, and all the inhabitants of heaven were chosen;
however, I was not chosen by that high-souled Dakṣa.
Although she was a virtuous woman, she was not chosen as his wife because she was the daughter of that Kapālin; thereupon, filled with rage, that virtuous woman gave up her life.
Having abandoned her body, Satī then assumed the form of Caṇḍī;
thereafter, that twelve-year sacrifice also proceeded.
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight, during the month of Kanyā, he assumes the fierce form of Caṇḍamūrti,
together with Yoganidrā Mahāmāyā and ten million Yoginīs.
Then, abandoning her true form, she brought about the interruption of the sacrifice,
accompanied by all the attendants of Śaṅkara and by Śaṅkara himself.
That goddess herself brought that great sacrificial session of the high-souled one to an end;
then, when the goddess’s great wrath had subsided, the inhabitants of heaven [rejoiced].
The dwellers of heaven indeed performed an incomparable worship of the Goddess according to the previously mentioned method;
they offered her worship according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure.
Having performed [this], they attained supreme cessation for the sake of the destruction of suffering;
thus, others too should always perform the worship of the Goddess. (11)
He who, out of delusion or laziness, [fails to worship] Goddess Durgā during the great festival, in order to attain incomparable prosperity that bestows the four aims of human life— || 12 ||
O Bhairava, if one does not worship out of hypocrisy or even out of hatred,
the Blessed Lady, becoming enraged, truly destroys his desired objects.
And in the next world, having become possessed of the power of great illusion (mahāmāyā), one is reborn;
[this is achieved] on the eighth day with blood, great meats, and fragrant substances.
One should worship Śivā with offerings of many kinds, including oblations and foods,
as well as with vermilion, silk garments, and various types of ointments.
One who possesses sons should not observe a fast on the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī), even with various kinds of flowers and many sorts of fruits.
In that very manner, one who has purified his soul and observes the vow should worship the Goddess;
having worshipped her on the Mahāṣṭamī, he should likewise do so on the Navamī with sacrificial offerings.
One should conclude [the rite] on the tenth day with the Śāvara festivals during the Śravaṇa asterism;
this applies when the final quarter of Śravaṇa occurs during the daytime portion.
Then, on the tenth day, the wise man should cause the sending forth of the goddess to be performed by married women, maidens, courtesans, and likewise by dancers. (19)
With the sounds of conchs and trumpets, as well as mṛdaṅgas and paṭahas, with various kinds of banners and cloths, and with scattered parched grain and flowers. (20)
With the throwing of dust and mud, with the auspiciousness of playful curiosity, with the utterances of "bhaga" and "liṅga," and with songs concerning the bhaga and liṅga. || 21 ||
People may freely sport using words such as "vagina" and "phallus," provided that one who is not censured by others does not censure others. (22)
The enraged Goddess would bestow a most terrible curse upon him when the first quarter of the night falls during the asterism of Śravaṇa.
Then the rising of the Goddess occurs on the ninth day, but not during the daytime;
it happens at the final quarter of the night when the moon is in the asterism Śravaṇa.
Then, O child Bhairava, the rising of the Goddess occurs on the ninth day from the start of the day; the dismissal [of the deity] is performed with this very mantra.
Having placed [the deity] in water and then released it for the sake of prosperity, one should say:
"Arise, O Goddess Caṇḍeśī, having accepted this auspicious worship. (26)
Bestow auspiciousness upon me along with your eight powers;
go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Goddess Caṇḍikā!
O Goddess, may that which has been worshipped by me be fulfilled for me;
go to the current of the water, and remain in the house for prosperity.
Having immersed yourself in water and cast off the leaf-plate into water free from defects, you have been placed by me in the water for the sake of increasing the life and wealth of my son. (29)
With this mantra, one should install the Goddess in the water for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds and for the prosperity of all the worlds. (30)
Both Bhadrakālī and Ugracaṇḍā, as well as Mahāmāyā, should be worshipped with the Durgā-tantra mantra during the great festival.
The seed-syllable of the eyes (netrabīja) is proclaimed for the worship of all the Yoginīs, as well as for that of the Root Form (mūlamūrti).
O Bhairava, listen now to the mantra of Ugracaṇḍā separately:
the first two [syllables], the seed-syllable of the eye, and that which is between the end and the beginning of the mantra. (33)
The fierce tantra consists of fire (ra), the internal vowel (u), and the moon-bindu (m);
the second seed-syllable is said to be the "eye" (netra) repeated twice.
This mantra of Bhadrakālī is for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
it is when the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, the Great Māyā who consists of the universe, [is invoked]. (35)
The Vaiṣṇavī goddess is indeed worshipped; these are the eight Yoginīs mentioned in the Tantras.
O Bhairava, they were previously proclaimed as the daughters of Śaila in a former kalpa.
The eight [forms] beginning with Ugracaṇḍā are proclaimed in the Durgā-tantra;
one should worship Bhadrakālī with the mantra of Bhadrakālī. (37)
For the sake of increasing prosperity, one should worship these very eight Yoginīs:
Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī. (38)
One should worship Durgā, Śivā, Kṣamā, and Dhātrī on the eight petals;
for it is by means of the Yadogracaṇḍā-tantra that that Goddess is worshipped there. (39)
O Bhairava, the eight Yoginīs should be worshipped there, as well as others:
Kauśikī, Śivadūtī, Umā, and Haimavatīśvarī. (40)
Śākambharī, Durgā, Saptamī, and Mahodarī—O Bhairava, listen now to the Tantra of Umā, whose form is gentle. (41)
The Umā-mantra is traditionally remembered as beginning with *pādi*, ending with *phaṭ* or *namaḥ*, and consisting of either one or three syllables. (42)
Fair-complexioned and resembling gold, she is endowed with two arms,
and she always holds a blue lotus in her left hand.
One should contemplate her standing with her right hand placed upon the right shoulder of Bharga, holding a white chowrie.
Even in the absence of Śambhu, the devotee should meditate upon Rudrāṇī, who has two arms, whose limbs are fair as gold, and who holds a lotus and a chowrie. (45)
She always sits in the lotus posture upon a lotus placed on a tiger skin;
for her worship, eight Vetālabhairavas are prescribed.
The Yoginīs and the Nāyikās are also established separately:
Jayā, Vijayā, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Lalitā. (47)
Then Nārāyaṇī, Sāvitrī, Svadhā, Svāhā, and likewise Aṣṭamī;
formerly there were two Dānava brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Those two sons of Andhaka were great beings, possessed of massive bodies and great strength; they were like two elephants in rut. (49)
When that one named Andhaka, possessed of great strength, had been slain by me, those two,
along with their armies and mounts, took refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
Therefore, having performed severe penance, those two great asuras thoroughly gratified Brahmā; being well-pleased, he granted them a boon.
Having conquered the three worlds, those two, arrogant due to the boon of Brahmā,
made Śumbha the Indra and Niśumbhaka the Moon.
Śumbha himself brought the sacrificial portions for all the gods,
and Niśumbha attained the status of a guardian of the quarters.
Then all the hosts of gods, including Indra, went to the Himalaya mountain and,
near the descent of the Gaṅgā, offered hymns of praise to Mahāmāyā.
Then the goddess Anakeśī was praised by the hosts of all the immortals;
assuming the form of a Mātaṅga woman, she questioned the gods.
"O immortals, which beautiful woman is being praised by you here? For what purpose have you come to the hermitage of Mātaṅga? (56)
As that Mātaṅgī was speaking thus, a goddess emerged from her bodily sheath and said to me, "The gods are praising you. (57)
"Indeed, the two asuras Śumbha and Niśumbha are harassing all the gods;
therefore, for the sake of slaying them, I am being praised by all those gods. (58)
When the goddess had emerged from the body-casket of Mātaṅgī,
she who was black like crushed collyrium became fair-complexioned in an instant.
She, having taken refuge on the Himalaya mountains, became known as Kālikā;
the wise sages here call her Ugratārā.
Since Ambikā always protects her devotees even from terrible fear, her first seed-syllable and the triad [of syllables] have been declared. (61)
Because she is known as Ekajaṭā, she is therefore called Jaṭaikikā;
listen now, O Vetāla and Bhairava, to her proper method of meditation.
Just as a devotee, having meditated upon the Great Goddess—who has four arms, is dark-complexioned, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads—obtains his desired object. (63)
She holds a sword in her two right hands and a fly-whisk below them;
she likewise holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup in her left hands, respectively.
She bears a single matted lock upon her own head that seems to scrape the very heavens,
and she always wears a garland of severed heads both on her head and around her neck.
She bore a serpent necklace upon her chest, had blood-red eyes,
wore black garments, and was girt at the waist with a tiger skin.
Having placed the left foot upon the heart of the corpse and having set the right foot upon the back of the lion, he himself [should place] the corpse with its tongue lolling out.

Tārā, who laughs with a loud laugh, who is most terrible, and who is exceedingly fearsome due to her roar, should always be meditated upon before one by those possessed of devotion who desire happiness. (68)
I shall now fully describe these eight who are known as Yoginīs:
Mahākālī, Rudrāṇī, Ugrā, and likewise Bhīmā; || 69 ||
Ghorā, Bhrāmarī, Mahārātri as the seventh, and Bhairavī is declared the eighth; one should worship those Yoginīs. (70)
O Bhairava, she who emerged from the quiver of Kālikā’s body is renowned as Kauśikī; she is of beautiful form and captivating.
Emerging from the heart of the Goddess with the tip of her tongue was Caṇḍikā;
there exists no one equal to her in form or in beautiful appearance. (72)
In the three worlds, there shall be no one equal to her in beauty—
she who is Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, and who is considered the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti).
This goddess who is known as Kauśikī is her very nature as vital breath (prāṇa);
likewise, the seed-syllable of the eye is proclaimed to be her seed-mantra. (74)
O Bhairava, I shall now describe her entrails and her form:
[the letters] from *sa* to *ma*, together with the final labials (*da*, *dha*, *na*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*), preceded by the six groups of consonants and accompanied by the bindu. (75)
Touched by the sixth vowel and adorned with the bindu,
this Kauśikī mantra-tantra bestows all desired objects.
O Bhairava, I shall now fully describe that form of hers which brings delight to the world; listen with a one-pointed mind. (77)
With her hair bound in a *dhammilla* knot, she was as beautiful as the crescent moon facing downward; she bore a tilaka upon the parting of her hair, situated above it. (78)
Her cheeks were rubbed by her jeweled earrings, she was adorned with a crown,
and she stood joined together, filling her ears with two ear-ornaments of radiant light.
She is resplendent with necklaces of gold, gems, rubies, and serpents;
she is exceedingly beautiful, always adorned with fragrant, unfading flowers.
Wearing a garland around her neck and adorned with jeweled armlets,
she possesses lovely and auspicious arms that are soft, round, and as long as lotus stalks.
She shone forth, endowed with a bodice, possessing full and elevated breasts, a slender waist, yellow garments, and adorned by the appearance of the three folds [of skin]. || 82 ||
Holding a trident, a thunderbolt, an arrow, a sword, and likewise a spear in her right hands, the Goddess shone resplendent.
The Goddess holds in her left hands, in order from the top downwards, a mace, a bell, a bow, a shield, and likewise a conch shell. (84)
Standing upon a lion, Kauśikī wears a tiger skin and assumes an incomparable form that deludes both gods and asuras. (85)
Listen, my child, to those eight Yoginīs who are to be worshipped; when they are honored, they always bestow the four aims of human life upon men. (86)
Brahmāṇī is declared the first; thereafter Māheśvarī is considered [the second];
then Kaumārī, Vārāhī, and Vaiṣṇavī is likewise the fifth. || 87 ||
Likewise Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, and Śivadūtī as the eighth—these highly fortunate Yoginīs, who grant all desires, are to be worshipped. (88)
I shall proclaim the mantra of her who emerged from the forehead of the Goddess and is renowned as Kālī; listen, O Bhairava, for it grants all desires. (89)
The dental [letter] accompanied by the final [vowel], preceded by that [same letter], joined with the sixth vowel, the fire-bindu (ṛ), and the moon-bindu (ī), and likewise preceded by *sa*. (90)
This is declared to be the Kālī-mantra, which bestows dharma, kāma, and artha.
I shall now describe its form; listen, my child, with a one-pointed mind. (91)
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus and endowed with four arms,
she holds a khaṭvāṅga staff and a candrahāsa sword in her right hands.
Furthermore, in her left hands she holds a shield and a noose, positioned respectively above and below;
she wears a garland of severed heads and is clad in an excellent tiger skin.
She had emaciated limbs and long fangs; she was exceedingly tall and terrifying, with a flickering tongue and sunken, blood-red eyes, her roar being most fearsome.
Seated upon a headless trunk as her vehicle, with ears and mouths spread wide, this goddess named Tārā is also celebrated as Cāmuṇḍā. || 95 ||
If one desires to worship and meditate upon her, one should worship her eight Yoginīs:
Tripurā, Bhīṣaṇā, Caṇḍī, Kartrī, Hartrī, and Vidhāyinī. (96)
Karālā and Śūlinī—these eight are proclaimed. This goddess always bestows excessive desire and destroys dullness.
Indeed, there exists no other like her who grants desires;
this goddess emerged from the heart of Kauśikī as Hari was meditating. 98.
She who is surrounded by hundreds of gods is known as Śivadūtī;
I shall proclaim her mantra, which bestows dharma, kāma, and artha. (99)
Having heard which, the practitioner goes to the difficult-to-attain abode of Śiva, by worshipping that Great Goddess Śivadūtī, whose very nature is Śiva. (100)
Before long, a man obtains his desires and becomes all-conquering;
[this occurs] when the end is joined with the conclusion, preceded by ten [syllables], along with the *bindu* and the *indu*. 101.
The vowel [Sa], which has the penultimate dental [Ta] as its final part, is conjoined with the preceding final [Na].
That same [Sa] is preceded by a pair of dots (bindus) and has the penultimate fire [Ra] as its final part. 102.
Accompanied by the sixteenth digit (kalā) of the sixth vowel and joined with the first [consonant], this mantra of Śivadūtī bestows victory upon Śivadūtī. (103)
I shall describe her form; listen, O son who is honored as the foremost, for she has four arms, a massive body, and a luster like that of vermilion. (104)
He has red teeth, wears a garland of severed heads and a mass of matted locks adorned with a crescent moon, is beautified by serpent earrings and necklaces, and is radiant with his claws. (105)
Clad in a tiger skin, he holds a trident and a sword in his right hands,
and likewise carries a noose and a shield in his left, arranged from top to bottom.
With a broad face, thick lips, and a towering form that inspires fear,
he stands with his right foot placed upon a corpse.
One should meditate upon such a form of Śivadūtī for the sake of prosperity: her left foot placed upon the back of a jackal surrounded by hundreds of other jackals. 108.
By mere meditation upon her, a man shall obtain auspiciousness;
and by worshipping her, O Goddess, she grants all desires without delay. (109)
The practitioner who, upon hearing the cry of a female jackal—a messenger of Śiva that bestows auspiciousness—bows down with devotion, has all his desires held in the palm of his hand. (110)
When Mahādevī Mahāmāyā slew Raktabīja for the welfare of the worlds, then [these beings] issued forth from her body. (111)
Sāmbikā dispatched Śivā as a messenger to Śumbha;
therefore, she is celebrated by all the gods as Śivadūtī.
She is the bringer of security, the peaceful one, the mother of the Vedas, and the large-bellied one;
she is the formidable goddess who grants desires, whose mouth is the vulva, and who is garlanded with vulvas.
Bhagodarī, Bhagārohā, Bhagajihvā, and likewise Bhagā—these twelve Yoginīs are proclaimed for worship. (114)
These twelve Yoginīs are indeed always the messengers of Śiva;
wherever the Goddess herself wanders, she goes to that very place. || 115 ||
For the yoginīs are indeed the companions of others according to their respective arrangements;
however, in this case, the yoginīs of Caṇḍikā are proclaimed to be her companions. (116)
Thus, these mantras of Tvaṅgam have been told to you in brief;
now I shall speak to you only a portion of the Kalpa concerning the majesty of Kāmākhyā. 117.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the Śrī Kālikā Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Kāmākhyā. || 61 ||
The sixty-second chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"Since you have come to the great mountain with me for the sake of desire..."
The goddess Kāmākhyā is said to be dwelling in secret on Nīlakūṭa.
Because she bestows desire, is full of desire, is the object of desire, is beloved, grants the limbs of desire, and destroys the very nature of desire, she is therefore called Kāmākhyā. || 2 ||
Listen specifically to the majesty of this Kāmākhyā, who, in the form of Prakṛti, governs the entire universe. || 3 ||
When Viṣṇu, deluded by Mahāmāyā, fought against Madhu and Kaiṭabha for their destruction, she then deluded Hari.
But during the daily dissolution, when the one whose banner is Garuḍa has fallen asleep,
two Asuras named Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the wax of his ears.
Standing upon the back of the tortoise, the goddess became shattered by the waters;
Mahāmāyā, who is Yoganidrā, beheld her thus shattered.
To make that earth indeed more firm, the Goddess reflected upon a means: "How might the earth become solid? (7)
Now the earth has become soft with water like clarified butter;
how will it be capable of supporting living beings at the time of creation? (8)
Having reflected thus, that Māyā, whose form is the creation of the worlds,
approached Viṣṇu and reached him as he was fast asleep.
Having approached the Lord of the World, the Master of the Universe, as he slept,
she placed the tip of the little finger of her left hand upon his ear.
Having fixed her earthen vessel with the tip of her claw and drawn out the impurity of Śrāvaṇa,
that goddess Yoganidrā, the mother of the world, reduced it to powder.
From the powder of the wax from that ear, the asura named Madhu was born;
then, from the tip of the little finger of the right hand on the right side... [12]
The goddess placed it in her ear, and from that as well she extracted the impurity;
she then crushed that too with both hands.
From that there arose a great and powerful asura named Kaiṭabha;
and because he searched for *madhu* (honey) for the purpose of drinking, he was born [as such].
Then his great queen gave him the name Madhu, because he appeared like a worm when he was produced by the maker of the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā). || 15 ||
Then Mahāmāyā created for him a being named Kaiṭabha;
Mahāmāyā said, "Fight with Hari."
"By means of our faith alone, you two shall slay him here;
for whenever you both speak, saying, 'O Viṣṇu, bind him! (17)
"At that very moment he will slay you both, and not otherwise—even Hari himself.
Thus deluded by Mahāmāyā, the two of them then went to the body of Viṣṇu.
While wandering about, the two saw Brahmā arisen from the navel-lotus;
they said to that Creator, "We shall slay you here today."
Awaken Vaikuṇṭha if you wish to live;
then Brahmā [awakened] Mahāmāyā, the Yoganidrā, the mother of the world.
Then, out of fear, he propitiated her with many hymns of praise;
thus was that Goddess praised for a long time by Brahmā, the soul of the universe.
Being pleased, she quickly spoke to the agitated one according to the prescribed rite:
"For what purpose have I been praised? What shall I do for you? (22)
"Therefore, O illustrious one, speak; I shall do it for you today.
Then Mahāmāyā was addressed by that high-souled Creator (Dhātṛ).
Awaken the Lord of the World before he slays me;
delude the two invincible Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, the soul of the universe,
the goddess then awakened Vaikuṇṭha and deluded those two.
Then, having awakened, Kṛṣṇa beheld Brahmā looking filled with fear, as well as those two terrible Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Then Janārdana fought with those two asuras;
however, O heroes, he was unable to withstand the two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Even Ananta was not able to hold with the tip of his hood those great heroes— Vaikuṇṭha, Madhu, and Kaiṭabha— as they fought.
Then Brahmā fashioned that power of stability into the form of a stone,
half a yojana in width and half a yojana in length.
On that rock, O best of kings, Govinda fought with those two;
then that rock entered into the midst of the water.
When she had plunged into the water, Hari fought with her in hand-to-hand combat for five thousand years without interruption.
When Viṣṇu, the lord of the worlds, was indeed unable to slay them,
even Vidhātṛ then fell into deep anxiety out of fear of him.
Then, those two, arrogant with their own strength and repeatedly deluded by Mahāmāyā, the Mother of the World, spoke to that Viṣṇu once again.
"O Mādhava, we are pleased with your wrestling; choose a boon.
We shall grant you whatever you desire; we speak this truth, O sinless one. (34)
Having heard those words of theirs, Mādhava, the Lord of the worlds, said to them: "O you two of great strength, you are to be slain by me."
"Thus, grant me a boon, if there is one to be given.
Then the two said, "Destruction at your hands is not desirable for us now. (36)
"Kill us there where water is currently available.
Having heard those words of theirs, Mādhava, the Lord of the worlds, [acted].
He spoke thus quickly to Brahmā and to me with his own name:
"Having swiftly uprooted the stone of Brahma’s power, let it be held [in place] as before. (38)
Staying there, I shall slay those two most terrible and mighty ones;
then Brahmā and I indeed lifted up that rock.
In the center of that [city], on its eastern side, I indeed assumed the form of a mountain;
standing upright, I pierced a rock and entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
In the northeast there was Kūrma, and Parvata took up the rock;
likewise in the northwest was Ananta, and in the southwest was Sureśvarī. (41)
Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, assumes the form of a mountain;
and likewise, Viṣṇu is stationed in the southeast in his singular form.
Taking up the Brahmaśakti stone, the Blessed Supreme Lord [stood] in the center, while Brahmā, I myself, and another, Varāha, were likewise present. (43)
Then, at the rear of the boar's back, the Lord of the worlds stood,
supporting himself upon the rock that was the downward-turned power of Brahmā.
Having diligently placed his two heads upon her left thigh and hip,
he, who is the support of the world, exerted every effort.
Having assailed them with all his powers, he severed the necks of Madhu and Kaiṭabha one by one, except for the earth.
And as he advanced with steady gait, his power of Brahmā descended, even though it was being repeatedly supported with effort by the hosts of gods. (47)
Then, after those two had died, the Lord of the worlds extracted the power of Brahmā from their bodies and placed it within her with great effort.
When the earth had been lifted up, he made the ground very firm by smearing it with their fat, even though it had been saturated by the masses of water.
Because she was smeared with honey, that goddess Earth is even today called Medinī by gods, rākṣasas, and humans. (50)
Then, after a long time had passed since the creation of living beings, I took the daughter of Dakṣa as my excellent bride for the sake of a wife. (51)
Having received her from my father under an agreement, she became my beloved wife; [the agreement was]:
"If you should prove unfaithful, then I shall give up my life. (52)
Then, at the sacrifice, he chose all things mobile and immobile;
however, he did not choose me nor Satī, for she had already passed away at that time.
Then, overcome by delusion, I died;
in the morning, however, I was wandering here and there at that excellent seat.
Whichever parts of her fell down in succession from wherever they did so,
each of those places became most meritorious through the power of yogic sleep.
In that Kubjikā-pīṭha, the maṇḍala of Satī’s womb fell;
there, that goddess Mahāmāyā vanished.
While I, in the form of a mountain, was absorbed in yogic sleep,
that blue-colored mountain came into being when the circle of the womb fell away.
That mountain, exceedingly lofty, entered the depths of Pātāla;
indeed, due to her firm pressure, Druhiṇa held it within himself.
Formerly, that four-faced one assumed the form of a mountain in order to support the stone of Brahmā’s power;
with that mountain-form, he held me.
Brahmā, who had taken the form of a mountain, was upon me as I stood in the form of a mountain;
yet, overcome by the profound illusion (māyā) of the Creator, he sank downward.
When the earth had been lifted up, he made the ground very firm by smearing it with their fat, even though it had been saturated by the masses of water.
Because she was smeared with honey, that goddess Earth is even today called Medinī by gods, rākṣasas, and humans. (50)
Then, after a long time had passed since the creation of living beings,
I took the daughter of Dakṣa as my excellent bride for the sake of a wife.
She became my beloved wife after her father had made this agreement:
"If you should do anything displeasing, then I shall give up my life. (52)
Then, at that sacrifice, he chose all beings, both moving and unmoving;
however, he did not choose me nor Satī, for she had already died at that time.
Then, having succumbed to delusion and death,
I wandered here and there in the morning at that excellent sacred seat (pīṭha).
Whichever parts of her fell down from time to time,
each of those places became most meritorious through the power of yogic sleep.
In that Kubjikā-pīṭha, the maṇḍala of Satī’s womb fell;
there, the goddess Mahāmāyā vanished.
While I, in the form of a mountain, was absorbed in yogic sleep,
that blue-colored mountain came into being as the circle of the womb fell.
That mountain, exceedingly lofty, entered the depths of Pātāla;
indeed, due to her firm pressure, Druhiṇa held it within himself.
Formerly, that four-faced one assumed the form of a mountain in order to support the stone of Brahmā’s power;
with that mountain-form, he held me.
Brahmā, who had taken the form of a mountain, was upon me as I stood in the form of a mountain;
yet, overcome by the profound power of the Creator's illusion (māyā), he sank downward.
Then that boar, having become attached to me, and Mādhava, who was in the form of a mountain, proceeded to seize me, who was likewise in the form of a mountain. || 61 ||
He too went downward along with me; then, having traversed the goddess Earth who had taken the form of a mountain, he remained fixed in the ground, firmly embedded.
The three mountains were each a hundred yojanas in height;
yet when the Great Goddess stepped upon them, they all sank entirely downward.
Of those three, however, only one remains standing at a height of one krośa;
for that [one] is the single primordial nature (prakṛti) of all the worlds. || 64 ||
That mother of the worlds was supported by the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
there, the mountain of Brahmā to the east is called Śveta by the deities. (65)
Likewise, the mountain that assumes my form is called Nīla;
situated in the center, that sacred seat (pīṭha) is triangular and shaped like a mortar.
Constantly shining in the midst of Brahmā and Varāha,
that Varāha who has the form of a mountain is called Citra.
He stood at the rear of them all, longer than any of them;
he who was the tortoise in the northeast, mountain-like in form and of great luster. (68)
That mountain, which is of infinite forms and situated in the northwest, is renowned by the name Maṇikarṇa and is frequented by hosts of gods. (69)
This mountain known as Maṇiparvata is dear to Mādhava;
it is the mountain of Mahāmāyā, situated in the southwest.
That mountain, named Gandhamādana, is always dear to Śaṅkara;
for it was there, on the back of Varāha, that the two great asuras were finally cut down.
Hari went there and was remembered as Pāṇḍunātha;
he was situated in the middle of the eastern part of the Brahmaśakti stone.
But he who is mountain-like in form is called Bhasmacala;
thus, in this most meritorious seat known as the Kubjikā-pīṭha. (73)
On Mount Nīlakūṭa, the goddess was staying in secret with me;
there, Satyā’s vulva fell away and became shattered.
She attained the state of a stone on that mountain, and Kāmākhyā is established there;
by touching that stone, a mortal indeed attains immortality.
Immortal, established in that abode of Brahman, one shall attain liberation;
such is the majesty of that stone where Kāmeśvarī resides. (76)
It was a marvel that the iron in his private parts had turned to ash;
and she, too, became there daily an embodiment of the five forms.
For the sake of deluding all the worlds and for my own pleasure as well, Śivā has acted;
I, moreover, have quickly established myself in five parts by means of my five faces. (78)
Īśāna is situated in the eastern part, primarily associated with Kāmeśvarī;
Tatpuruṣa is in the northeast, and Aghora is in his proximity.
Then Sadyojāta is in the northwest, while Vāmadeva is joined with the Goddess;
O Bhairava, best of men, these are the five forms of the Goddess as well.
Listen, O Vetāla, for these secrets are always hidden even from the gods:
Kāmākhyā, Tripurā, and likewise the auspicious Kāmeśvarī. (81)
Then Śāradā, the great light, endowed with the qualities of assuming any form at will,
[manifested] upon me when I had attained the state of a linga within the yoni-mandala of stone.
All the gods assumed the state of stone and took on the form of mountains;
thus, I indeed sported with Kāmā in my own natural form.
Likewise, all the deities are concealed within the form of stone;
hidden in the form of stone, they are established upon every mountain.
And they always delight in their own true nature when united in seclusion;
here are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and all those guardians of the quarters. (85)
Other gods as well, who are always favorable toward me,
remained there then in order to worship the goddess Kāmākhyā, who can assume any form at will.
Sadāśiva is a blue mountain, triangular in shape and depressed in the center;
in its midst is a beautiful mandala endowed with thirty powers (śaktis).
There, from the Mind-born (Manobhava), there arose a creation of the Mind-born;
in that stone was a womb, beautiful in form like a stone, measuring one span in width and twenty-one finger-breadths in length. || 88 ||
She follows the path of the mountain of ashes, gradually becoming subtle and humble;
she is free from ego and illusion, the sustainer of the world, the primordial source, and eternal. (89)
Red as vermilion and saffron, the passionate woman, who grants all desires,
eternally sports in her fivefold form within that womb.
There, the eight eternal Yoginīs who are the primordial source—the ones previously mentioned beginning with Śailaputrī—are stationed on all sides of the Goddess. (91)
O Bhairava, listen now to the names of those sacred seats (pīṭhas) together:
Guptakāmā, Śrīkāmā, and another, Vindhyavāsinī. (92)
Koṭīśvarī resides in the forest, while Pādadurgā is another;
Dīrgheśvarī follows in sequence, and Bhuvaneśvarī is manifest. 93.
The eight goddesses, together with their respective yoginīs, are renowned by the names of the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
and all the holy fords (tīrthas) are present together here in the form of water, O Bhairava.
Situated there by the name Saubhāgyasaras, even though small, it bestows merit;
and on its bank, moreover, is Viṣṇu known by the name Kamala.
The youth named Kāmuka is situated near Kāmākhyā;
the two goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are established in attendance upon the Goddess.
Lakṣmī became known as Lalitā, while Sarasvatī became Mātaṅgī;
and Gaṇādhyakṣa was established on the eastern side of that mountain.
He was a perfected one (siddha), famous by name as the beloved son at the gate of the Goddess; he was a wish-fulfilling tree, a wish-fulfilling creeper, a tamarind tree, and an aparājitā plant. 98.
Having become thus, O beloved, he remained on that great mountain, supported by the Goddess;
for it is there that Hari resides as the Boar known as Pāṇḍunātha.
Having placed his two heads upon her hips, he slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
near that spot is the Brahmakuṇḍa, which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times.
O Bhairava, know that where Śiva is known as Īśāna, there is the one called Siddheśvara; it is the Siddhakuṇḍa in the form of a stone situated in the center.
Gradually becoming subtle and humble, she follows the mountain of ashes;
she is free from ego and illusion, the sustainer of the world, the primordial source, and eternal. (89)
Red as vermilion and saffron, the bestower of all desires,
that passionate woman eternally sports in her fivefold form within that womb.
There, the eight eternal Yoginīs who are the primordial source—the aforementioned Śailaputrī and the others—stand surrounding the Goddess on all sides. (91)
O Bhairava, listen now to the names of those seats together:
Guptakāmā, Śrīkāmā, and another, Vindhyavāsinī. (92)
Koṭīśvarī resides in the forest, while Pādadurgā is another;
Dīrgheshvarī follows in sequence, and Bhuvaneśvarī is manifest. 93.
The eight deities, together with their respective yoginīs, are renowned by the names of the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
and all the holy fords (tīrthas) are present together in one place in the form of water, O Bhairava.
Situated there by the name Saubhāgyasaras, even though small, it bestows merit;
and on its bank, moreover, is Viṣṇu known by the name Kamala.
The youth named Kāmuka is situated near Kāmākhyā;
the two goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are established in attendance upon the Goddess.
Lakṣmī became known as Lalitā, while Sarasvatī became Mātaṅgī;
Gaṇādhyakṣa was established on the eastern side of that mountain.
He was a perfected one (siddha), renowned by name as the beloved son at the gate of the Goddess;
he was like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī), a tamarind tree (tintiḍī), and the invincible (aparājitā). 98.
Having become thus, O beloved, he remained on that great mountain, supported by the Goddess;
there stands the Boar known as Pāṇḍunātha, who is yellowish-green in hue.
Having placed his two heads upon her hips, he slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
near that spot is the Brahmakuṇḍa, which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times.
O Bhairava, know that where Śiva is known as Īśāna, there is the one called Siddheśvara; it is the Siddhakuṇḍa in the form of a stone situated in the center.
Near that [place] is the field of Gayā and likewise Vārāṇasī;
having become a pool resembling a vulva-circle (yonimaṇḍala), it remains established there. 102.
Right there is the Amṛtakuṇḍa, filled with a multitude of nectar,
which was established by Indra together with the gods for my sake.
The head known as Vāmadeva is called Śrī Kāmeśvara;
nearby it is situated the highly meritorious Kāmakuṇḍa.
The sacred field known as Kedāra is situated between Siddha and Kāma;
it is fourteen vyāmas in length and is called Chāyāchatra.
Near that [place] is the daughter of the mountain named Guptakāmā;
she stands in the middle of Guptakuṇḍa, joined with the Kāmeśa rock.
Always known by the name Kāmākhyā, she is attached to the Kāmeśvara stone;
she is joined with the front part of the Yoni from the supreme path.
Between Kāmakāma and Ākhyā, Kālarātri is situated;
in the Dīrgha-pīṭha is he known by the name Dīrgheśvara, and at the boundary is Pracaṇḍikā.
At the edge of the Kāmākhyā stone slab resides the Yoginī named Kūṣmāṇḍī;
in the sacred seat (pīṭha) she is established in the form of the Yoni under the name Koṭīśvarī. || 109 ||
And that head called Aghora shall belong to Kāmā on the southern seat;
it is indeed proclaimed as Bhairava by those seeking the supreme truth.
Known by the name Bhairavī, Cāmuṇḍā dwells in close proximity to Bhairava;
she is the leader who grants the desires of her devotees and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa. || 111 ||
Between Kāma and Bhairava, the goddess herself is the celestial river;
may she always be for the welfare of all the world and for the pleasure of the Goddess. 112.
The head named Sadyojāta is at the seat of Āmrātakeśvara;
it is situated in the cave called Bhairava and is frequented by gods and sages.
Know that right there is the heroine named Durgā, whose form is the womb;
she is eternally renowned among the gods by the name Siddhakāmeśvarī. (114)

There stood well-established a tree with fresh leaves and beautiful shade—an Āmrātaka tree that was like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), accompanied by wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī). || 115 ||
On the sacred seat (pīṭha) known as Siddhagaṅgā, Gaṅgā herself has arisen near an āmrātaka tree for the sake of increasing my delight. (116)
That sacred field is named Puṣkara, while in the Pīṭha it is called Āmrātaka;
in the northeast, my head, known as Tatpuruṣa, is situated there.
O Bhairava, the seat known by the name Bhuvaneśvara is famous;
it is the cave of Bhuvaneśa, designated as Bhuvanānanda. (118)
Near that [place], however, the cow Surabhi is situated in the form of a stone;
she is renowned as Kāmadhenu, bestowing all desires upon the sacred seat. (119)
That form of mine as Śarabha, which was fierce in the middle region,
became known by the name Mahābhairava and was called Koṭiliṅga.
Established in five parts through my five forms,
I stand behind them, O Earth, as the one named Bhairava, due to my extreme proximity.
The goddess Mahāgaurī, who is a Yoginī possessing the form of a Siddha, dwells on the Brahma-mountain in the form of a stone, facing upwards. (122)
She was exceedingly endowed with beauty and was named Bhuvaneśvarī;
there Brahmā became attached to me while I was in the form of a mountain.
There stands the Kalpavallī tree, known by the name Aparājitā;
and not far away, in the eastern direction, is the Great Goddess Kāmadhenu.
The auspicious Caṇḍikā, who is Śrī Kāmākhyā in the form of the Yoni, is that Yoginī; know her to be established in the southeast, the bestower of all desires. 125.
The yoginī known as Caṇḍaghaṇṭā became Vindhyavāsinī at that sacred seat;
the yoginī Skandamātā became Vanavāsinī at that same seat. (126)
Known by the name of the Pīṭha as Kātyāyanī, she is called Pādadurgā;
that auspicious goddess is situated on the edge of the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila) in the southwest.
That Nandī, who was my own body, has assumed the form of stone;
he stands at the western gate as Hanumān, known by the name Pīṭha.
Aurva said:
Having heard these words of Śambhu of immeasurable splendor,
the Vetāla, filled with eagerness, questioned Bhairava.
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:

"O Father, O Śaṅkara, we have heard the sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭha) as well as the sequence for the worship of the Goddess; now we wish to hear [the teaching] regarding all five forms as well. (130)
The forms of the five deities and their mantras are present on all sides;
O Bull-bannered One, tell us there the mantras and the tantras.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Bhairava; I shall explain the Vetāla mantra and the tantra separately, as well as the form and the ritual procedure (kalpa) of the five forms of Kāmākhyā.
One who possesses desire should desire that which abides in desire, stands in the midst of desire, and is enveloped by the god of desire;
one should cause desire to be joined with desire within desire. || 133 ||
O Brahmin, the supreme, tranquil final consonant is said to be that;
one should first perform it in sequence, joined with that which consists of nectar.

Likewise, the seed-syllable of Śakra joined with Prajāpati and the [vowel] representing the beginning of the configuration, together with the half-moon, is declared to be the seed-syllable of Kāmākhyā. (135)
This is the bestower of Dharma, granting the goals of both desire and liberation;
this is the supreme secret, which is very difficult to find elsewhere. (136)
That best of men who, having uplifted his ear, listens from the mouth of the Guru, attains all desires and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (137)
May that which is the distilled essence of the Vedas, the necklace for the multitude of gods' throats,
the remover of all impurities, and the bringer of joy to the Consort of Śrī— [that glory] which shines with the splendor of its beautiful and noble logic— [illuminate us].
In this world, Śiva is everything; he is the destroyer of obstacles and the one who signifies the intended meaning through gestures. || 138 ||

Listen to the nature of the state of Śiva: it brings light to the eyes, it is beneficial to those in meditation, it abides in affection and noble conduct, it is established in the daily observance of divine truth; it is expanded into the supreme station and has worn away all misfortune.
The true form of Kāmadevī. || 139 ||
The mere sound of whose name, when heard, brings about great prosperity for those afflicted by suffering— he who is the sole abode of the path of ethics,
and whose power is like a serpent (kuṇḍalinī) in the counting of the hosts of gods— [to him I bow].
In this world, those whose hopes are destroyed should contemplate the supreme form.
Her ears are adorned with the sun and moon; she is the color of saffron-yellow;

she is variegated with jewels and gold; her ears are swaying; she has three eyes; her hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons; and she is distinguished by holding a rosary.
She is the Mistress of the Siddhas and the Lord of Desire, to whom the lords of gods and men bow down.
Seated upon a red lotus, resting on a crimson lotus throne, with a body as fresh as a new-born youth, her hair loose and adorned with a beautiful necklace;
she is enchanting, with a pair of broad and lofty breasts upon the heart of a corpse.
That Ārva Kāmeśvarī is a child, wearing uneven garments. 142.
Bestowing abundant wealth, with a smiling face and beautiful hair,
her nails and teeth like bees, slightly bent like the crescent moon,
she rests upon the stone of the mind-born god, languid with the *yonimudrā*.
Capable of descending, she is the one who has abandoned the abode of false promises. 143.
Thus, this [wisdom] is to be contemplated as having a radiance like lightning and fire;
it accomplishes the goals of Dharma and so forth for practitioners who desire their aims.
May the three [jewels] properly conceive of this noble goal that grants those aims.
O Vetāla, you are Bhairava, established in glory. || 144 ||
In that [mandala], the half-mandala which is indeed to be performed in the west should be made with sandalwood mixed with flowers;
the procedure for drawing it that was previously stated in the Devītantra is to be applied here first. || 145 ||
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Śrī Kālikā Purāṇa, within the Kāmākhyāpūjā Tantra. || 62 ||
The sixty-third chapter.
Īśvara said:
"I have previously declared the mantra of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra."
But the mandala, by way of practice, is that which is a synonym for the mandala. || 1 ||
In this manner, that [image] should first be prepared with flowers and sandalwood upon a stone slab;
likewise, one should apply the same procedure here for the consecration of bowls and other such objects.
Whatever ritual procedures have been prescribed for the Vaiṣṇava tantras and mantras,
all of those should be applied here, including the worship with the seat and other offerings.
O Bhairava, listen as I shall explain the specific distinction here that differs from those [other rites]:
first, one should offer arghya to the Sun with white mustard seeds.
After the offering of seats and worship was completed with flowers and sandalwood paste for the Great-Souled One and his retinue, all the deities mentioned in the Paṭha were invoked.
O Bhairava, having joined [the deities] by means of their seat-names in the center of the mandala, that distinct form of meditation is [to be performed] together with Vaiṣṇavī.
Everything else, however, is proclaimed in the *Mahāmāyāstava* [of Kāmā];
one should worship the sixty-four Yoginīs individually.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Guhā, Manobhavā, and the friend Mahotsāhā, as well as the guardians of the directions and the nine planets.
One should worship them according to their forms for the sake of attaining one's desired success;
first, however, one should worship Gaṇapati at the eastern gate.
One should worship Nandin and Hanumān at the western gate;
Bhṛṅgin is to be worshipped in the north, and Mahākāla in the south.
One should worship these gatekeepers of mine at the door of the Goddess;
indeed, during the rite of consecrating the vessel as nectar, one should perform it with the Kāmamudrā.
One should first perform the expulsion of obstructing spirits by means of three *tāla* gestures;
one should execute the *tāla* with the right hand against the left hand.
With the mantra "hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ," one should drive away the vetālas and other such beings;
the practitioner should perform everything as prescribed in the Uttara-tantra.
In this regard, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the nature already described;
first, the worshipper should bathe the Goddess with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
With honey, milk, clarified butter, curd, cow urine, and likewise with cow dung;
with water containing gems, with sugar, with jaggery, gems, and water containing *kuśa* grass. || 15 ||
With white mustard seeds, mung beans, sesame and milk, as well as barley, red sandalwood flowers, dūrvā grass, and together with yellow pigment (rocanā). || 16 ||
One should offer the arghya on the stone near the yoni with nine [mantras]:
first the seat (āsana), then the water for the feet (pādya), then the arghya, and after that the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for bathing, clothing, sandalwood paste and ornaments,
flowers, incense, a lamp, and thereafter collyrium for the eyes.
The food offering, the water for sipping, circumambulation, and prostration—these sixteen services are prescribed starting from the pedestal. (19)
One should invoke the Great Goddess with the Gāyatrī mantra joined with the Kāma-yoga;
know her alone, O Vetāla, as the secret deity Bhairava. (20)
O Kāmākhyā, come here to my presence as is fitting;
O beloved one, grant your presence here for the performance of worship.

This, however, is the Kāmagāyatrī; with this one should worship the Auspicious One.

Likewise, immediately after the invocation, there are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of Kāmākhyā,
as well as those of the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra and the ritual assignments (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs.

The vowels have been declared; by means of those vowels—accompanied by the half-moon (anusvāra) and the bindu (visarga), and joined simultaneously with the first two syllables of the root mantra—[the deities are to be worshipped]. || 26 ||
One should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) precisely in the order beginning with the little finger;
having performed both the placement of the limbs and the placement of the hands, the practitioner should thereafter proceed.
One should also place [the mantras] upon the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, mouth, belly, back, the two arms, the two hands, the two shanks, and the two feet.
One should worship the hand granting fearlessness and the boon, as well as the rosary and the sacred thread;
likewise, one should worship the Moon, the Sun, the head, and the digit of the moon.
There is a red lotus and a corpse, as well as Lohitya and Brahmaputraka;
there also is the Mind-born Stone (Manobhavā-śilā) situated within the corpse, established upon the Śakti.
The devotee should worship the sword at the side of the Goddess;
there, one should also worship the deities of the pedestal and the auspicious Kāmeśvarī.
One should worship Tripurā, the presiding deity of the pedestal, in the center;
and one should worship Śāradā, who possesses great vigor, in that very same central place.
Caṇḍeśvarī, the Great Goddess, who wears the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the Goddess,
is declared to be the Yonimudrā during the dismissal of Kāmākhyā.
As for this material substance— namely, vermilion, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron—
it is indeed this specific detail that I have prescribed for the performance of worship.
Having mastered all the ritual manuals (kalpas) pertaining to the domain of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, accompanied by these specific characteristics, one should worship Kāmākhyā.
Whoever worships Kāmākhyā according to this very procedure reaches the supreme goal within the secret cave of the mind-born god.
Brahmāṇī, Caṇḍikā, Raudrī, Gaurī, Indrāṇī, as well as Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Durgā, Narasiṃhī, and Kālikā. || 37 ||
Cāmuṇḍā, Śivadūtī, Vārāhī, and likewise Kauśikī;
Māheśvarī, Śāṅkarī, Jayantī, and Sarvamaṅgalā. || 38 ||
Kālī, Kapālinī, Medhā, Śivā, Śākambharī, as well as Bhīmā, Śāntā, Bhrāmarī, Rudrāṇī, and Ambikā. || 39 ||
Kṣamā, Dhātrī, as well as Svāhā, Svadhāparṇā, Mahodarī, Ghorarūpā, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, and Bhayaṅkarī. || 40 ||
Kṣemakarī, Ugracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍī, Mahāmohā, and Priyaṅkarī. || 41 ||
The goddess Kalavikariṇī, as well as Balapramathinī, the goddess Madanonmathinī, and Sarvabhūtadāmanī. (42)
Umā, Tārā, Mahānidrā, Vijayā, and Jayā, as well as the eight Yoginīs previously mentioned beginning with Śailaputrī, in their respective order. (43)

In this manner, a man endowed with devotion who worships the goddess Kāmākhyā, the bestower of boons, obtains all that is dear to him. (46)
The goddess who is Mahotsāhā is known as Mahāmāyā;

That very same maṇḍala belongs to him, as does the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa); that same worship in its various sequences, that same meditation, and those same deities. 48.
Thus has the Tantra been declared; there is nothing else whatsoever for the purpose of manifesting the mandala and so forth during the great festival of Mahāmāyā. 49.
As has been declared by him, one should worship that goddess of great energy within the mandala,
preceded by a ritual bath, with honey, clarified butter, and other such spirits.
Listen to the worship of Kāmākhyā, whose form is Tripura;
her root mantra was previously [revealed] in the Uttaratantra. (51)
For you two who desire [this], that has been duly set forth in sequence:
the Vāgbhava, the Kāmabīja, and the Ḍāmara—these three.
Accompanied by Kuṇḍalinī, it accomplishes all goals, including wealth and desire;
one should place three [offerings] before this, and the Great Goddess Durgā is to be meditated upon.
Thereafter, she became renowned as Tripurā, the Kāmākhyā who takes any form at will;
and the manner in which the bathing of that Kāmākhyā is proclaimed [is as follows].
The worshipper should perform the bathing with that very same root mantra.
Her mandala is a square with three lines, representing the triple city (Tripura).
The mantra, however, should be known as the syllable, and likewise form is threefold;
the Kuṇḍalinī energy is threefold for the creation of the three deities.
Because every triad is threefold, she is therefore remembered as Tripurā.
In the mandala, lines should be drawn from the north to the east.
Three lines should be drawn, and those very lines should be adorned with flowers and sandalwood; having performed the mantra in the northeast and then in the southwest, one should draw them.
Then, one should likewise draw a triangle within the interior of the maṇḍala, proceeding from the southwest to the northwest, and then again to the northeast. (59)
The line starting from the northeast is called Śakti;
that which goes from the southwest to the northwest, and then proceeds to the northeast [is likewise]. (60)
She is indeed proclaimed as Śambhu; one should pierce Śambhu with Śakti.
Having pierced the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa) with Śakti, one should then encircle him with the lotus.
Having meditated upon her as three-colored within an eight-petaled lotus, one should first worship her;
then, with three lines each, one should encircle both Śakti and Śambhu.
The sprinkling of the site, its thorough cleansing, as well as its scraping, and the removal of obstructing spirits through the application of weapon-mantras (astramantra). || 63 ||
Whatever has been declared in the Vaiṣṇava Tantras and Mantras, and likewise in the Uttara Tantra,
that which is common [to all] should first be performed by the male practitioner.
The sequence of worship, accompanied by the specific rites of Tripurā, is as follows:
this triangle is held to be the abode of the three gods. (65)
Likewise, Īśāna is in the northeast, the four-faced one (Brahmā) is in the southwest, and Brahmā is in the northwest;
thus they are proclaimed to be in the six corners.
The petal is said to be one city, and the filaments another city;
the remaining part is the triangle, and the triangle is remembered as the maṇḍala.
On the petals, the filaments, and also on the triangle, one should properly draw lines in three ways each, doing so again and again.
The northern gate should be in the shape of a bow;
the eastern gate is hexagonal, while the southern one is quadrangular.
The western [arch] should have the form of a gateway as in other maṇḍalas;
one should draw five arrows in the northeast and that bow in the southeast.
A book in the southwest and a rosary in the northwest;
having thus prepared the mandala and holding it with the left hand. (71)
Then one should worship the mandala with the mantra "Obeisance to the abode of speech. Having worshipped it, one should then worship the spirits with three stalks of reeds.
One should perform this with the root mantra and also with the previously mentioned mantras;
having performed the encircling three times by means of nine snaps of the fingers.
Then one should perform the sprinkling and the expulsion of the spirits;
furthermore, the reception of the vessel for the sake of the *arghya* offering is ninefold.
As before, the practitioner should perform burning and likewise flooding;
he should first perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Then one should perform the *yonimudrā* and touch the water in the vessel three times;
one should offer the *arghya* to Mārtaṇḍabhairava with *dūrvā* grass and consecrated mustard seeds.
One should offer red flowers and sandalwood to the assembly;
having formed the *pāṇikacchapikā* gesture, one should perform meditation with the *yonimudrā*.
O Vetālabhairava, at the beginning and in the middle,
one should sequentially prepare a mandala for the purpose of placing the vessel using the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
First, one should draw a hexagon for the purpose of establishing that mantra;
then, with the mantra "aiṃ āṃ klīm," one should pour water three times into the vessel.
One should likewise place incense and flowers in three ways, and again dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) in three ways;
then, one should assign [the mantras] "rāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ" in sequence to the thumb and the other fingers.

With the weapon-mantra "Oṃ Hraḥ," one should likewise perform the placement (nyāsa) three times each upon the back and the palm of the hands, and subsequently in the sequence beginning with the heart. 81.
Having joined the two hands together, one should separate the pairs of fingers beginning with the thumbs three by three, and then place the remaining parts [of the hand] accordingly.
Likewise, the ear-cavities, the Brahma-door, the hair-tuft, the pair of nostril-cavities, the pair of knees, and the two feet. (83)
One should perform the placement three times each with these six mantras, individually.
Then, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) by means of inhalations (pūraka) and retentions (stambhaka). 84.
One should also contemplate the goddess Tripurāmūrti during the exhalation;
having performed the burning and flooding, one should contemplate the primordial form.
Now listen, O Bhairava, as I describe how one should meditate upon that form in the heart in three ways:
resembling a mass of vermilion, with three eyes and four arms. (86)
Holding a flower-bow in his upper left hand and likewise a book in the lower one,
he holds five arrows in his upper right hand and a rosary in the lower one.
Having placed another corpse upon the backs of four corpses,
she stood with both feet evenly planted upon its back.
Her neck was bound by a mass of matted hair adorned with a half-moon;
she was naked, yet her beautiful waist, marked by the three folds of skin, was enchanting. (89)
Complete with every ornament, beautiful in all her limbs, auspicious,
flowing with a mass of wealth, and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Having first meditated upon her, one should contemplate oneself as threefold;
thereafter, one should [offer] a lotus flower with the *vāgbhava* mantra.
Then the practitioner should again place [the mantra] upon his own head and likewise perform the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa);
having recited the two mantras, beginning with the Vāgbhava, three times each.
One should sprinkle one's own head with the waters from those arghya vessels,
and likewise sprinkle the materials for the pūjā three times in the same manner.
Then, having meditated upon the seat of desire (kāmapīṭha), one should worship these in sequence:
Gaṇeśa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and likewise Gaṇanātha.
And one should worship Gaṇakrīḍa at the eastern gate and the others with the mantra;
the seed-syllable of Heramba is proclaimed as the mantra for these. || 95 ||
One should properly worship Vidyā, Śānti, Nivṛtti, and Pratiṣṭhā, as well as the door-keepers ending with Kalā, in due order starting from the east.
One should worship these *baṭukas*: the *siddhaputra*, the *jñānaputra*, likewise the *sahajaputraka*, and the remaining one, the *samayaputra*. 97.
But for each of the Baṭukas in the supreme enclosure, one should worship the goddess Śrī individually,
starting from the east, in due order, with the mantra "Śrīṃ."
Then, within the mandala, one should worship the maiden representing the Siddha, the Sahaja, the Jñāna, and the Samaya [kulas] in the corners beginning with the northeast. 99.
One should worship Yoraṭa, Ḍāmara, Lohajaṅgha,
Bhūtanātha, and Kṣetrapāla, beginning with Īśāna.
And in the center of the mandala, one should worship the five arrows:
namely, the melting, the drying, the binding, and likewise the bewildering. (101)
And one should perform the invocation with the central mantra itself;
thereafter, one should worship the three Yoginīs in the three corners.
Bhaga, Bhagajihvā, and Bhagāsyā—these three should be worshipped in sequence starting from the north; the other [deity] is to be worshipped in the center within the triangle.
Bhāgamālinī is in the first [wheel], Bhagodarī in the second, and the Yoginī Bhagarohā, who can assume any form at will, is in the third.
[He saw] Queen Anaṅgakusumā, likewise Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Anaṅgamadanāturā. || 105 ||
One should worship Anaṅgaveśā and Anaṅgamālinī, who are afflicted by passion,
in the middle of the filaments of the petals, and Madanāṅgakuśā as the eighth.
And the eight [goddesses] beginning with Śailaputrī, in the sequence of the worship of Tripurā, became the Yoginīs of Desire under these names, remaining unperturbed. (107)

Likewise, one should worship Durgā with the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], and then perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with the six mantras ending with the Netra-bīja; furthermore, these eight [limbs] are as follows: 108.
One should worship the Kṣetrapālas on the filaments and petals in the middle:
Hetuka, Vipuraghna, and likewise Agnijihva.
And [the lords] named Agnivetāla, Kāla, Karālaka,
Ekapāda, and Bhīmanātha, in the order starting from the north.
With these same eight mantras joined with the Kāmarāja [bīja],
one should worship these nine leaders, beginning with Asitāṅga, in their proper order.
In the four directions of the mandala, two each in the east and so forth in sequence; between the lotus and the mandala, one should worship the remaining single [deity]. || 112 ||
Asitāṅgī, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Bhayaṅkara,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Aṃhāra— these indeed are the nine.
A person should worship two leader goddesses each, starting from the northeast in successive order;
and one should worship two in the southeast, in the middle of the two lotus-maṇḍalas.
Brahmāṇī, Bhairavī, and likewise Māheśvarī;
Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, and similarly Nārasiṃhī as well. (115)
One should likewise worship Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā,
as well as the foundational powers (ādhāraśakti) and others, in the center of the mandala.
O Bhairava, one should worship all those [deities] mentioned in the Vaiṣṇava tantras and kalpas;
as for the five [faces] of Śiva previously mentioned, beginning with Sadyojāta and the others.
Those forms have attained the state of five corpses within the center of the lotus;
one should worship those five in the middle, as well as the red lotus and the corpse.
And there one should worship the Lion, known as the Support of the World, as well as Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī. (119)
One should worship Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svadhā, and Svāhā;

Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Aṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā—one should especially worship these in the center of the maṇḍala. || 121 ||
One should worship all the planets, beginning with Āditya, according to their forms and accompanied by their weapons, addressing each one individually in sequence on both sides.
O Bhairava, one should likewise [worship] all the guardians of the directions with the mantras of the dikpālas,
and all of them with the weapon-mantras (astramantras) of those [deities].
There, one should [meditate upon] the Lord Kāmeśvara, who has one face and four arms,
white with ashes, [worshipped] in the center of the heart with red flowers and saffron.
A trident and a Pināka bow are held in his two left hands,
and likewise a blue lotus and a citron fruit in his two right hands.
Having meditated upon her seated upon a white lotus, one should worship her in the center;
having meditated on Kāmākhyā according to her form, one should also worship Kāmākhyā. || 126 ||
There one should worship the goddess Kāmeśvarī, the supreme sovereign;
there also is Vetālabhairavī in the form that will be described.
One should worship the Lord Karāla, the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), who bears a knife and a skull-cup, whose lower lip is split by his fangs, and who is terrifying. 128.
The Tintiḍī tree and the Kalpavṛkṣa, both providing excellent shade and adorned with jewels;
the Trikūṭa mountain, which is black in color, and the Nīla mountain of great splendor. || 129 ||
Therein is a beautiful cave of the mind, five fathoms in length, endowed with a circle of jewels, red in color, and perfectly circular. || 130 ||
And there was the Aparājitā creeper, extending three fathoms in width,
constantly adorned with flowers of a deep red hue.
The boy named Kambala is golden-hued, seated upon an elephant, and has two arms;
he holds a staff in his right hand and a skull-cup in his left.
Bhairava and Pāṇḍunātha, who are four-armed and have red bulls as their vehicles, are to be worshipped at the front of the Goddess for the destruction of obstacles and calamities. (133)
Holding a mace, a lotus, a spear, and also a discus in his hands,
he who bears the form of Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the presence of the Goddess.
The cremation ground called Heruka is red in color and terrifying;
it is fierce, bearing a sword and a shield, and consuming human flesh. 135.
He is adorned with three garlands of severed heads from which blood flows,
and he stands upon a corpse whose teeth have fallen out after being consumed by fire.
One should worship, through mere contemplation, the Yoginī who possesses great energy, whose nature is that of Mahāmāyā, and who is adorned with weapons, vehicles, and ornaments. (137)
One should worship that city, Candravatī, which is located to the east of Mount Nīla, before the Goddess, according to its meditative visualization and its physical form. || 138 ||
It was two yojanas in width and half a yojana in length,
adorned with many lofty palaces, mansions, and dwellings.
It was expansive with palaces formed from floods of jewels, gems, and gold,
and it was covered by excellent pleasure-lakes filled with blossoming lotuses.
There, in front of the Goddess, one should worship the joined [liṅga] with mantras:
Lohitya, who has a body as fair as blood-red and is adorned with blue garments. (141)
Adorned with a garland of jewels and endowed with four arms,
he holds a book and a white lotus in his right hands.
On the left, there is the auspicious banner of the spear (śaktidhvaja) situated upon a porpoise;
one should worship these lords of the seats (pīṭheśvaras) in the center with these mantras.
One should worship the Lord Kāmeśvara with the Prāsāda mantra, and one should worship the auspicious Kāmeśvarī with the mantra of Kāmeśvarī. 144.
One should join the two penultimate letters with the power (*bala*) at the end of *madana*, and then sequentially with the *nāda* and *bindu*; this is the mantra for the *āyākaraṇa*.
That syllable which remains after the seed-syllable of Caṇḍikā’s eye is the mantra for the tamarind tree; this is what is proclaimed as the ritual procedure. 146.
The seed-syllable of the center of Ugrā is the mantra of Nīlaśaila;
it is the seed-syllable of Manobhava, joined with Mahādeva. (147)

Joined with the indicated moon (the letter *i*) and the drop (*bindu*), and conjoined with the letter *va* (vānta), this mantra is proclaimed as being within the cave of the mind-born one (Kāmadeva). || 148 ||
That seed-syllable which remains from the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra, being without a vowel, is joined below with the letter *va* (the last letter) and conjoined with the fourth vowel. 149.
That Aparājita mantra, conjoined with the lunar bindu, is the supreme seed-syllable of Viṣṇu in his form as Hayagrīva. (150)
The worship of Kambala, however, is proclaimed to have that same mantra;
it is used alone, or combined with the sixth vowel (Ū) along with the prefix *pra* and so forth. (151)
The seed-syllable of Hayagrīva, conjoined with the lunar drop (bindu), [is that of] Bhairava, Pāṇḍunātha, and he who has the form of Vanamālī. 152.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite with the Vārāha seed-syllable;
moreover, two others are joined with the anusvāra and visarga.
One should worship with the Mahābhairava mantra ending in Bhairava;
and one should worship Mahāmāyā of great vigor with the second eight-syllable mantra.
One should perform worship according to the Devītantra itself for the increase of prosperity;
the first syllable, moreover, is adorned with the letter *sa*, the moon (*ā*), and the nasal bindu.
The worship mantra of Candravatī, who is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament, has been proclaimed by her own name. 156.
The seed-syllable of Brahmā, which bestows prosperity upon King Lauhityanada, the son of Brahmā, is held to be my mantra, ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā). || 157 ||
One should likewise contemplate the second form as Tripura and the third in the same way; for the purpose of invoking the Goddess, one should do so with the yoni-mudrā.
Resembling the bandhūka flower, adorned with a mass of matted hair and the moon, she was complete with all auspicious marks and decorated with every ornament. (159)
She possesses the radiance of the rising sun, is well-seated upon lotus-thrones, adorned with strings of pearls and gems, and has full, elevated breasts. || 160 ||
She was graced by the charm of her graceful folds, delighted by the fragrance of wine, a delight to the eyes, pure white, and likewise the nourisher of the worlds. 161.
She has three eyes, is endowed with the yoni-mudrā, is possessed of a slight smile, is perfected in fresh youth, and has four arms holding a lotus stalk. (162)
In her left half she holds a book, and in her right, a rosary;
as the goddess, she grants fearlessness with her left [hand] and bestows boons with her right half. 163.
She bears a garland of heads from which flows a stream of blood, shining like the sun,
hanging down as far as her feet, and she stands having reached a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
One should meditate upon the second Tripurā, who stands within a grove of Kadamba trees, who brings delight through desire, who is auspicious, and who is beautiful and captivating in form. 165.
O Vetālabhairava, hear now of the third form, that of Tripurā:
she resembles the hibiscus flower, has disheveled hair, and possesses a beautiful face. (166)
