Having indeed visualized Sadāśiva laughing like a ghost, one should place [the goddess] within the heart of that deity, seated upon a half-lotus posture (ardhapadmāsana). || 167 ||
She wears around her neck a garland of severed heads interspersed with red lotuses, following her every step, and she possesses full and elevated breasts.

Likewise, she has four arms and is naked; in her right half, she holds a rosary and displays the gesture of granting boons, while below that, in her left, she likewise holds the world-illusion (jaganmāyā) and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
She holds a book below [her breast], has three eyes, and a smiling face;
she is distressed by the enjoyment of flowing blood, and likewise beautiful in all her limbs. (170)
The worshipper should meditate upon this third form;
the first form is that of Vāgbhava, and the second is Kāmarāja.
The Ḍāmara and the Mohana are proclaimed as the third;
each of these has three forms, which one seeking to accomplish one's purpose should first contemplate. (172)
With each of the three mantras, one should likewise worship [the deity] in the heart sixteen times with ritual offerings, just as one does externally.
Likewise, having brought the three mantras together in one place, the forms of the manas should be made into a single unity;
there, one should cause them to enter into the central form.
Having expelled her through the nostril and then again through the right one,
and having brought her down with both hands, one should invoke the Goddess three times.
Having recited the three Gāyatrīs, one should first bathe her;
furthermore, this mantra must be recited by the practitioners during the invocation.
"Come, O Goddess Śubhāvartā, to this sacrifice in my presence;
grant me a pure voice from the throat that shall never cease. (177)
Come, come, O Blessed Mother Tripurā, bestower of desires!
Accept this portion of the offering and manifest your presence here. (178)
"Let us know Nārāyaṇī, and let us meditate upon Āgmayā;
having spoken thus, may the Goddess then inspire us. (179)
We know you as Nārāyaṇī, and we meditate upon you as Caṇḍikā;
may she impel that [wisdom] for us, O Kubjī, at the conclusion of the portion. 180.
"May we know thee, Mahāmāyā; may we meditate upon thee, Sammohinī;
thereafter one should employ this [mantra]: 'O Caṇḍī, impel that [power]! (181)
These are proclaimed as the Gāyatrīs of the goddess Tripurā;
one should perform the ritual bathing for each of the three Tripuras with these three [verses].
One should first worship Śivā with the Vāgbhava mantra;
thereafter, one should indeed worship her with the Kāmarāja and also with the Ḍāmara.
Afterwards, one should worship her in a single location with three mantras;
then, indeed, one should offer the sixteen services (upacāras) with the mantra.
Having again worshipped the syllables of the limbs as proclaimed in the Kāmākhyā Tantra,
one should worship the limbs of the Goddess with those mantras used for the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
The remaining worship of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) is performed with the root mantra;
having worshipped each successive limb, one then offers [the oblation] to Tripurā.
One should worship the goddess Tripurā, who can assume any form at will, in nine ways;
one should worship these [deities] upon the four petals of the lotus starting from the north.
One should likewise worship Brahmā, Mādhava, Śambhu, and Bhāskara in those very directions starting from the northeast (aiśānī), following this sequence for the Goddess. 188.
First Jayantī, and afterwards Aparājitā in the northwest; Vijayā in the southwest, and likewise Jayā in the southeast. || 189 ||
In the triangle, at the end of the filaments, one should worship Kāma, Prīti, and likewise Rati, as well as the five arrows, the flower-bow, and the book.
One should properly worship Akṣamālā, Añcaśara, Ratnaparyaṅka, and Pretapadmaśiva right there. || 191 ||
O Bhairava, having worshipped the rosary made of crystal as before,
one should then take it and carefully cover it with an upper garment.
The practitioner should properly recite the Tripurā mantra as previously extracted;
having recited it, and having read the hymn of praise, he should prostrate himself again and again. (193)

One should offer an oblation (bali) to Tripurā; that [oblation] consists of the three types [of substances] according to their origin, combined with water and foam, along with sugar, honey, and rock salt.
O Bhairava, having sprinkled it with blood, one should offer it with the Kāmarāja mantra;
one should cut [the head] with the Vāgbhava mantra alone, and one should sport with the heads by means of the Ḍāmara mantras.
Wherever the practitioner offers an oblation during the worship of the deity,
he should take up that oblation prescribed in the ritual manual of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Then one should offer oblations to the Goddess according to this sequence of castes:
a Brāhmaṇa should offer cow’s milk, while one born of the royal caste (Kṣatriya) should offer clarified butter from a cow.
A Vaiśya should offer honey, while a Śūdra should offer flower-liquor and the like. Having smelled the flower, the wise man should then discard the remains (nirmālya) toward the northeast.
And her attendant goddess is Tripuracaṇḍikā, who wears the remains of offerings; having first released the Yoni-mudrā as well as the Padma-mudrā. (199)
One should display the half-seal and the triple seal individually;
then, one should take the floral remains (nirmālya) by means of that which is called Kāmarāja.
Thus, whoever worships the goddess Tripurā, who can assume any form at will, shall attain all desires and reach the world of the goddess. || 201 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the Śrī Kālikā Purāṇa, concerning the worship of Tripurā.
The sixty-fourth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Bhairava, listen; I shall describe to you the form of the Goddess as Kāmeśvarī.
By the mere thought of whom, the practitioner obtains his beloveds. || 1 ||
O Vetālabhairava, I shall first describe her Tantra, then the sphere of meditative contemplation, and thereafter the sequence of worship in due order.
Then Prajāpati, then Vahni, and after that Indrabīja, joined with the crescent moon on its crest and combined with the fourth vowel. || 3 ||
This seed-mantra of Kāmeśvara accomplishes all aims;
it is used for the sprinkling of the site, the drawing of the yantra, and so forth, as well as for the placement of the vessels and other such rites.

The best of practitioners should perform the expulsion of obstructing spirits and other rites as taught in the Vaiṣṇava Tantras, as well as those prescribed for the Yantra mentioned in the Uttara [Tantra]. || 5 ||
One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), as well as burning and flooding;
now hear, O Vetāla Bhairava, of her special maṇḍala.
The wise one should construct a six-cornered maṇḍala and contemplate it as red in color; having pierced Śambhu with his power, he should do so according to the Tripurā Tantra.
Then the wise practitioner should pierce the *śakti* with the *śambhu* in sequence;
having drawn a line from the northeast to the southwest, he should then place Kāmarūpa on the rightmost [line] and on the east.
One should draw the twelve secret symbols of the Goddess with her twelve hands in the corners of the maṇḍala, three in each of the cardinal directions.
The sequence for the mandala should be constructed with six lines each;
the rest is as declared in the Uttara-tantra and spoken in the Vaiṣṇava-tantra.
O Vetālabhairava, know the entire sequence of the maṇḍala:
"Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the maṇḍala"—herein lies the maṇḍala. (14)
Having first meditated upon the mandala as the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), one should worship it;
on a stone slab, one should draw the mandala, specifically the yoni-maṇḍala.
Afterwards, one should draw a triangle and encircle it with a lotus;
then, one should contemplate the enchanting form of the goddess Kāmeśvarī.
Resembling crushed collyrium, with dark and glossy hair, she has six faces, twelve arms, and eighteen eyes. (17)
On each of her six heads she wears a crest made of a crescent moon,
and upon her chest she bears a necklace fashioned from jewels, rubies, pearls, and other gems.
And she always wears [the image] around her neck, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a book, the Siddhasūtra, and likewise that five-arrowed [god].
She holds a sword, a spear, and a trident in her right hands,
as well as a rosary, a great lotus, a bow, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Holding a shield and the Pināka bow in her left hands,
she is white, red, yellow, green, and black.
The variegated [mandala] is arranged in sequence, first with its head toward the northeast, then to the east,
the south, the west, and likewise with its head toward the north.
And the middle one as well, O illustrious one; these are the heads in order according to their colors:
the face of Māheśvarī is white, and that of Kāmākhyā is said to be red. (23)
Tripurā is like the color of turmeric, and Śāradā is likewise green;
the face of Kāmeśvarī is black, while that of Caṇḍā is desired to be variegated.
The hair on each head is described as being tied in a *dhammilla* braid;
upon a lion sits a white corpse, and upon that is a red lotus.
Kāmeśvarī is stationed there, her face slightly smiling,
clothed in variegated silken garments and likewise wearing a tiger-skin mantle.
Thus one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
now the procedure for the worship of the Goddess on another seat (pīṭha) is described.
The specific procedure for the *pīṭha* must be stated, whereas for the general case, another method is intended:
one should join [the fingers] in pairs, following the sequence beginning with the thumb.
First, one should perform the finger-seal (aṅgulīyaka) using the six initial syllables of the root mantra, joined with the long vowels.
Then, with the right hand, one should likewise place the heart, head, armor, eyes, and weapons in sequence using the six mantras.
One should likewise perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the face, the pair of arms, the belly, the private parts, the pair of knees,
and the pair of feet, in sequence, with those six mantras.
Having recited the root mantra eight times over the water offered for the arghya,
one should provide the ritual implements with that water and, having sprinkled them, begin the sequence.
The teacher should worship the Goddess with the *pīṭha*, but never one who is not a teacher; for by the mere touch of his hand, the auspicious Goddess is not disturbed.
If one has come from another land to a sacred seat (pīṭha) in another land, then one should commence the worship according to the instruction of that local teacher. || 34 ||
If a person has arrived from elsewhere, other than from Kāmarūpa, one should worship him according to the instructions of that region and thereby obtain the fruit. || 35 ||

In whichever region a particular sacred seat (pīṭha) is located— such as Oḍra, Pāñcāla, and so forth— the deity in that seat should be worshipped by men according to the instruction of those born in that region.
O Bhairava, if one performs worship other than this, one shall not obtain the proper fruit; [it must be performed] with offerings complete with great magnificence.
Whatever sequence has not been explicitly stated here within the scope of the Vaiṣṇava Tantras,
as well as in the Uttara Tantra, should be adopted by the proficient practitioners.
First, one should worship the principle of desire (kāmatattva) at the eastern gate;
the principle of affection (prītitattva) at the southern [gate], and the principle of delight (ratitattva) at the western [gate]. (39)
One should worship these principles (tattvas) in order, ending with the principle of delusion (mohana-tattva) in the north;
O God, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the guardian of the door, in the northeast.
One should worship Agnivetāla in the southeast, Kāla in the southwest, and Nandin in the northwest; one should worship these in this sequence. (41)
He who knows the tetrad, the pentad, the hexad, the tetrad, the pentad, and the fourfold hexad is fit for the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
The first sacred seat (pīṭha) is named Oḍra; the second is Jālaśailaka;
the third is Pūrṇapīṭha; and the fourth is Kāmarūpa. || 43 ||
In the west, however, one should likewise worship Oḍrapīṭha, as well as Oḍreśvarī Śivā, Kātyāyanī, Jagannātha, and Oḍreśa. (44)
In the north, one should worship the excellent Jālaśailaka seat,
as well as the Great God Jāleśvara and Caṇḍī Jāleśvarī.
One should worship Dīrghikā and Ugracaṇḍā right there;
likewise, on the south [is] Pūrṇaśaila and the auspicious Pūrṇeśvarī. (46)
One should worship Pūrṇanātha, Mahānātha, Sarojā, and Caṇḍikā, as well as the goddess Damanī, Śāntā, and likewise Śivā.
Kāmarūpa is the great pīṭha, as well as the auspicious Kāmeśvarī;
likewise, Nīla is the best of mountains, and Kāmeśvara is the Lord. || 48 ||
O Bhairava, one should worship these in sequence at the eastern gate:
the Kṣetrapālas and the Gurus of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) beginning with Oḍra. (49)
One should worship the other gatekeepers and so forth in their respective places, especially while worshipping Kāmeśvarī of Kāmarūpa. (50)
O Vetāla Bhairava, listen to those situated on the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila):
the Lord is the god Kāmeśvara, and likewise the goddess is Kāmeśvarī. (51)
Karāla, the Kṣetrapālas, and likewise the tamarind tree;
on Trikūṭa, there is the Nīla mountain and also the cave Manobhavā.
The young ascetic named Kambala, and the creeper Aparājitā;
Bhairava and Pāṇḍunātha, and the cremation ground called Heruka. (53)
Yoginī and Mahotsāhā, as well as the city Candravatī, the Lauhitya—the king of rivers—and Prāntā, who dwells in the quarter of the world-elephants (Dikkaravāsinī). 54.
One named Jalpīśa in the northwest and one named Kedāra in the southwest—
one should worship these at the door as well as in the mandala of the Goddess.
The gatekeepers, the yoginīs, the baṭukas, and so forth, are likewise present in the supreme seat of Kāmarūpa, and similarly in Oḍra and the other [pīṭhas]. || 56 ||
In the center of the mandala, there are then [the rites of] liquefaction, drying, binding, and delusion, as well as that called attraction. (57)
One should worship these five arrows of Manobhava at the tips of the six corners, beginning with the north, as well as the group of six starting with Bhaga.
The wise practitioner should worship, in due order, that which is declared in the Tripurātantra mantras,
as well as Gaṇākrīḍa and the others, and likewise Vidyā, Kalā, and so forth.
The *baṭukas*, the sons of the *siddhas*, and so forth, as well as the *siddhas* and the young maidens (*kumārikās*)—this group of four times four is called the "tetrad" (*catuṣka*). || 60 ||
Kāma, Rati, and Prīti, as well as Anaṅgamekhalā and the others;
indeed, there are seven beginning with Tripuraghna, and nine beginning with Asitāṅga.
The goddesses beginning with Māheśvarī, together with the ten and five groups—
the second pentad— is proclaimed as bestowing the fruits of desire upon the sacred seat (pīṭha).
The primary power of support (ādhāra-śakti) and others are eternally established there,
as are the eight qualities beginning with dharma, as well as the guṇas beginning with sattva.
In one place are the planets and the guardians of the directions; another tetrad is prescribed for the goddesses, such as Ugracaṇḍā and the others, whom one should worship as the leaders. 64.
O Vetālabhairava, in the previously mentioned place, one should perform the invocation with the mantra or with devotion, as well as the presentation of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra). || 65 ||
Recitation (japa), the offering of oblations (balidāna), the worship of the limbs and weapons (aṅgāstrāṇāṃ prapūjana),
the mudrās, and the dismissal (visṛṣṭi)— this group of six is thus proclaimed.
The wise worshipper who knows these seven types is alone worthy to fully worship the sacred seats (pīṭhas) such as Oḍra and the rest. || 67 ||
He who performs the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjana) without knowing these correctly does not obtain the full fruit and is even born with a diminished lifespan. || 68 ||
O Bhairava, having first worshipped in these locations mentioned in the Tripurātantra-mantra, one should then worship the Supreme Goddess.
"O Kāmeśvarī, come here; O Īśvarī, be present before me.
Having thus meditated upon her with the mind and worshipped Kāmeśvarī within his heart, [he should proceed]. (70)
Then, having offered mental offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth, one should expel the breath through the right nostril and project that flower into the interior of the mandala.
One should invoke the Great Goddess, the Sovereign of the Lord of All Desires:
"O Kāmeśvarī, come here; be present before me. (72)
O Kāmeśvarī, we know you; we meditate upon you as Kāmākhyā.
May that Kubjī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), inspire us from beyond. 73.
Come, come, O Blessed Mother, you who bestow grace upon the worlds! O Mistress of Desire, you whose form is desire, O Beloved of Kāma, be gracious to me.
Then, having first offered water for the bath,
the worshipper should present the sixteen services (upacāras) while reciting the root mantra.
One should worship in the central portion, and thereafter perform the adoration of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga);
those mantras which were previously explained in the sequence for the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) [should be used]. || 76 ||
One should worship the limbs of the Goddess with those very same mantras;
one should worship these Yoginīs on the eight petals starting from the east.
In due order, for the sake of accomplishing desires, [one should worship] Kāmadāyikā, Guptakāmā, Śrīkāmā, and likewise Vindhyavāsinī. (78)
One should worship Koṭeśvarī, the Yoginī residing in the forest, Pādacaṇḍikā, Dīrgheśvarī, Prakaṭā, and Bhuvaneśī in their proper sequence. (79)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra syllables of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, which consist of eight syllables joined with the bindu and the crescent moon (indu). || 80 ||
Within the mantras, one should worship these six goddesses in the six corners, following the sequence starting from the northeast: Kāmākhyā and likewise Tripurā.
O Bhairava, Śāradā, Mahotsāhā, Prakaṭā Bhuvaneśvarī, and Siddhakāmeśvarī are also forms of the Goddess.

Having worshipped the Goddess again eight times with the "eight flowers" (aṣṭapuṣpikā), and having recited [the mantra], praised her, offered the bali-oblation, bowed down, and displayed the mudrās; || 83 ||
Having offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) to the goddess Siddhacaṇḍī and having bid her farewell from the mandala, one should establish the goddess within the *yonimaṇḍala*.
This Kāmeśvarī Tantra has been told to you both, O sons;
now listen, O Bhairava, to the great Tantra of Śāradā together with its mantras. 85.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of Tripurā," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The sixty-fifth chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
"In former times, during the autumn season, on the ninth day, she was awakened by the gods."
She is celebrated as Śāradā in the sacred seat (pīṭha) and among men in the world. || 1 ||
In that [tantra], however, the mantra known as the Seed of the Eye (netrabīja) has been previously explained;
likewise, the Durgā-tantra and its limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) have been mentioned before.
With those very two mantras, one should worship her who consists of the universe;
and [one should worship] the third, the unsurpassed seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) of Śāradā.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to that which bestows the fourfold aims of human life:
it is joined with the fourth vowel, has the letter preceding the penultimate as its final member, and is conjoined with fire (the letter *ra*). || 4 ||
Likewise, Kāmarāja, which has no end but is joined with the penultimate vowel, is ignited by Fire and endowed with all the drops and dots. || 5 ||
The seed-syllable ending with the word *hādi* (ha), together with the word for completion (*samāpti*), constitutes this fourth seed-syllable.
By means of these four syllables mentioned in the mantra, the six-syllabled [mantra] is declared.
This is proclaimed as the third mantra of Śāradā;
by worshipping [her] on the pedestal with this, one shall attain all accomplishments (siddhi). || 7 ||
Her form, seated upon a lion with ten arms, was previously described;
listen now properly, my two sons, to the sequence of her worship. (8)
One should construct a mandala with four gates there for the sake of prosperity;
the Mahāmāyā-maṇḍala and the maṇḍala of Śāradā.
Having performed the purification of the mantra-locations and so forth according to the ritual procedures of the Vaiṣṇava Tantras,
one should draw the maṇḍala upon the sacrificial grass using the seed-syllable of the eye (netrabīja).
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in the womb, one should place a triangle in the center;
this specific distinction has been declared again from the Vaiṣṇava maṇḍala.
The drawing of the mandala, as well as the expulsion of obstructing spirits, the ritual disposal of the vessel, and likewise the consecration as nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa). || 12 ||
The scattering of perfumes, flowers, and water; the worship of one's own seat; the threefold breath control (prāṇāyāma); and the purification of the elements and entry [into the maṇḍala]. (13)
Furthermore, burning and floating, as well as the "tortoise-like" hand gesture (pāṇikacchapikā), and the meditation on the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha)—these are declared in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra. (14)
In the same manner, one should perform the worship of the Goddess as prescribed in the Uttaratantra;
one should perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) over the water with the dhenu-mudrā.

O Bhairava, one should contemplate the form as having ten arms as previously described; the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement of the hands (karanyāsa) are performed according to the Durgātantra.
One should indeed perform [the assignment] with the nine-syllable mantra in the sequence beginning with the thumb,
and subsequently in the sequence beginning with the heart, as well as for the faces and so forth, as before.
The wise one should likewise mutter this same mantra eight times over the vessel of water;
then he should sprinkle his head with that water, as well as the flowers, scents, and other offerings.
In this manner, one should perform the sequence of worship there in the mandala of the Goddess;
having meditated upon the Sun in the form of Caṇḍikā on the eastern stone slab. (19)
The practitioner should offer the *arghya* to him with white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, and flowers,
using the *klīṃ* mantra and [the names of] the deities beginning with Ādhāraśakti.
The wise one should first worship Dharma and the others in the center as before, as well as Sattva and the rest, ending with the feet of the Guru, as taught in the previous tantra. (21)
One should worship Sumeru in the central lotus;
furthermore, one should worship the powers (śaktis) of the Goddess in the eastern part of the mandala.
One should especially worship all the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha), beginning with Nātha and Kāmeśvara and ending with Lauhitya, in the northern part of the maṇḍala.
Maṇikarṇa, Citraratha, and likewise Bhasmakūṭa;
Śveta, Nīla, Citra, Vārāha, and Gandhamādana.
One should worship these in the west: Maṇikūṭa and Nandana; then Jalpīśa, Kedāra, and the Goddess Dikkaravāsinī.
One should worship Dhātrī, Svadhā, Svāhā, Mānastokā, and Aparājitā, as well as the sixty-four Yoginīs, on the right side. (26)
The wise one should worship the planets and the ten guardians of the directions, starting from the east in the previously mentioned order, as well as Bhairava and Bhairavī, just as before.
Then, having again performed the *kacchapikā* meditation, the worshiper should meditate upon the Goddess residing in the heart with his mind, just as before. (28)
Having worshipped her, who resides in the heart, with mental offerings of fragrance, flowers, and so forth,
one should then draw her out through the right nostril into the mandala.
Having offered a flower to her named Kāmā, he should repeatedly invoke Śāradā: "Come, come, O Supreme Goddess; manifest your presence here! (30)
Accept this portion of worship; protect the sacrifice; let there be salutation unto you!
O Durgā, O Durgā, come here together with all your retinues.
Accept this portion of our worship; protect this sacrifice; homage be to you!
We know you as Nārāyaṇī; we meditate upon you as Caṇḍikā. (32)
In the remaining portion of the Gāyatrī, "tannaścaṇḍi pracodayāt" is used;
having performed the bath with this very mantra, one should indeed proceed according to the Durgā-tantra.
One should worship with the Netra-bīja, likewise with the Pīṭha-mantra in between,
and with the remaining three four-syllabled mantras.
Then, O Bhairava, one should offer the sixteen services, beginning with water for the feet, using the four-syllable mantra as previously described.
One should worship the limbs of the Goddess with the mantra from the Durgātantra:
with "Durge" [one worships] the heart, and again with "Durge" [one worships] the head.
The wise one should worship the crest, the armor, and the eye with five syllables each, and the feet and the soles of the feet with the remaining five syllables, in due order.
One should worship these on the eight petals starting from the east in the following order:
Jayantī on the eastern petal, and Maṅgalā in the southeast and so forth.
Kālī, Bhadrakālī, and likewise Kapālinī, Durgā, Śivā, and Kṣamā—these indeed by name in their respective order. (38)
In the center of Keśava, however, are these eight heroines;
by means of the mantra of the eye-seed, the six heroines are [placed] in the six [directions].
And for these [mantras], it is likewise [accompanied] by those six inserted in the intervals;
with "hrāṃ hrāṃ śrīṃ" at the end, and indeed with the first vowel at the beginning.
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Caṇḍikā. || 42 ||
Within the triangle, up to the edge of the filaments, one should worship Kāma, Prīti, and Rati, as well as the five arrows and the flower-bow, using the mantras of Kāma.
Having subsequently worshipped the Supreme Goddess with the eightfold offering of flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā),
[one should worship] the weapons, missiles, and vehicle held in the hands of the Goddess.
One should worship Pañcānana and Keśara in front of the Goddess, as well as the Goddess of the Seat (Pīṭhadevī) Śāradā and the presiding deity Kāmākhyā. || 45 ||
One should worship right in the center Mahādevī, known as Tripurā, the presiding deity of the sacred seat (pīṭha), Kāmeśvarī, who possesses great vitality. (46)
One should offer three handfuls of flowers with the four-syllable mantra;
having recited [the mantra], praised, offered the bali, prostrated, and performed the veiling (avaguṇṭhana), [one should proceed].

Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā* and offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) in the direction of the Wielder of the Trident (*Śūlin*), one should dismiss [the deity] with the words: "Salutation to Caṇḍeśvarī. || 48 ||
Then one should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun for the purpose of ensuring the rite's completion;
having placed the Goddess within one's heart, one should establish her upon the *yonimaṇḍala*.
In this manner, one should worship the goddess known as Kāmākhyā, the world-encompassing Yonimudrā, the great goddess named Śāradā, according to the rules of yoga.
Having fully attained all desires, one shall reach the world of Śiva;
provided that one worships the goddess Kāmarūpiṇī elsewhere only when a sacred seat (pīṭha) is absent.
Even at Nīlakūṭa, one should perform all of this in the same manner;
whether one worships the Goddess elsewhere, in water, or even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 52 ||
One may worship on a stone slab or similar surface, in fire, or upon a divine pedestal according to one's preference;
or one may worship or not worship at all, yet one must certainly worship upon a pedestal.
Thus, for one who [worships] Śivā, who bears five forms, with these five mantras—
either all together or with each one individually— she herself shall become the bestower of boons.
No obstacles arise for him, nor mental anxieties, nor likewise physical ailments;
there shall be no other equal to him in the abundance of wealth and grain. (55)
Whatever fruit arises for men from the gift of ten million cows, that same fruit a person obtains by worshipping Kāmākhyā. || 56 ||
Having rescued ten preceding and ten succeeding generations from sin, one shall attain my world simply by worshipping me once. || 57 ||
Having worshipped the Great Goddess Kāmākhyā twice in the yoni-maṇḍala, and having extracted a hundred bamboo shoots, one shall attain the world of the Goddess. 58.
The man who worships three times according to this rite, having ascended Mount Nīla to Kāmākhyā in the Yonimaṇḍala, [attains his desire]. || 59 ||
Having extracted a thousand lineages from the treasury of sin,
he shall obtain happiness, sovereignty, and long life in this world.
At the end of the body's life, having reached my abode, he shall become a lord of the Gaṇas;
on whichever eighth or ninth lunar day the practitioner [performs this], [he attains that state].
One should worship the boon-granting goddess Kāmākhyā, who possesses five forms, with the five mantras together with their ritual manuals (tantras), using separate mandalas for each.
Having meditated upon the five forms and indeed having recited the five mantras,
that person shall dwell in my world for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Having remained [in this state] through the grace of the Goddess, one shall attain supreme nirvāṇa;
or else, having obtained happiness and fame as well as all desired objects in this world. 64.
Having conquered his enemies like a lion among elephants, that righteous-souled one, endowed with long life, sons, grandsons, and prosperity, [reigned]. (65)
Having sported with young women with devotion like an immortal,
he shall eternally become a leader of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas;
having attained all his desires, he shall become equal to the king of the twice-born (Brahmā).
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 65 ||
The sixty-sixth chapter.
Aurva said:
Having heard this entire tantra, Vetāla and Bhairava—
With eyes wide open with joy, they both questioned Tryambaka.
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
"By your grace, we have heard the Tantra of Kāmākhyā along with its auxiliary limbs,
as well as the salutation, the mudrās, and likewise the offering of the bali."
In the same way, [explain] the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) and the sequence for worship from other sources;
O Lord of the World, explain all of this in detail.
As we listen to these grounds of joy, no satiety arises within us.
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of sons, I shall speak that which I have been asked by you both;
listen now with one-pointed minds, O tigers among men."
The triangle, the hexagon, the half-moon, the circumambulation, the staff,
the eight-limbed [prostration], and the fierce [prostration]— these are the sevenfold characteristics of bowing.
In the worship of Kāmākhyā, either the northeast or the north direction is recommended for the sacrificial ground and so forth; this applies to all forms [of the deity] in every respect.
As for the arrangement of the triangle and other figures, if one should worship facing the east,
then one should indicate the arrangement by proceeding from the west to the Śāmbhavī [line].
When the practitioner performs the worship of the deity facing north,
he should then go to the south or the northwest and take up his station there.
Having gone from the south to the western direction, and from there to the north-eastern (Śāmbhavī) direction;
then, having gone again to the south, the salutation is performed in the shape of a triangle.
The salutation known as the Triangle bestows pleasure upon Tripurā;
having gone from the south to the northwest, and then from the northwest to the northeast.
Having gone from there to the south, having abandoned her and entered the fire,
and having gone from the fire to the Rākṣasī, he thereafter went to the northern direction.
From the north, one should likewise move toward the southeast in the manner of two or three triangles;
this six-cornered salutation brings delight to both Śiva and Durgā. (12)
Having gone from the south toward the northwest, and having turned back from there toward the south, that which is performed as a salutation is proclaimed as the *ardhacandra* (half-moon). || 13 ||
Having performed a single circumambulation in a circular form,
the practitioner’s act of salutation is called "pradakṣiṇa" by the twice-born.
Having left one's own seat and place, one should thereafter offer salutations to Durgā; without performing a circumambulation, one should proceed by prostrating on the ground like a staff.
It is called *daṇḍa* by the gods, for it bestows joy upon the entire host of deities;
as before, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff with the heart. (16)
Then, by means of the chin, the mouth, the nose, the jaw, the aperture of the navel, and the two ears, there is a sequential touching of the ground. (17)
This is declared by the wise to be the eight-limbed prostration;
having performed three circumambulations in a circular manner, the practitioner [performs it]. (18)
Because the earth is touched through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) during prostration, it is called "Sugra" by the hosts of gods; this [mantra] grants satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
Just as the ocean is among rivers, as the Brāhmaṇa is among bipeds,
as the Gaṅgā is among streams, so is the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) among even the gods.
Among all forms of salutation, the fierce one (ugra) is likewise praised when performed with devotion using the three-cornered and other such salutations.
The devoted practitioner shall obtain the fourfold aims of life before long;
salutation is a great sacrifice that always bestows delight in every respect.
O Bhairava, for all the gods and others as well, that fierce salutation which is constantly pleasing to Hari [is the most excellent]. (23)
He who brings joy to Mahāmāyā is the supreme object of salutation;
the salutations mentioned therein have been stated—now you two listen to what follows.
The enumeration and the essential nature of the mudrās are given in their proper order:
the Dhenu, the Sampuṭa, the Prāñjali, the Bilva, and the Padma. (25)
The Nārāca, the Muṇḍa, the Daṇḍa, the Yoni, and likewise the Ardha;
the Andanī, the Mahāmudrā, and likewise the Mahāyoni. || 26 ||
Bhaga, Puṭaka, Niṣaṅga, Ardhacandraka, Aṅga, Dvimukha, Śaṅkhamudrā, and Muṣṭika. || 27 ||
The Vajra, the Randhra, the Ṣaḍyoni, the Vimala, the Ghaṭa, the lofty Śikhariṇī, the Puṇḍra, and then the Ardhapuṇḍraka. || 28 ||
Sammilani, Kuṇḍa, Cakra, and likewise Śūla;
Siṃhavaktra, Gomukha, and likewise Pronnāmonnamana. || 29 ||
The pure Pāśupata-imba, then Tyāga, Utsāriṇī, Prasāriṇī, the fierce Ugrā-mudrā, and the array of Kuṇḍalinī. || 30 ||
The three-faced [mudrā], the sword-creeper, union, division, then delusion, the arrow, the bow, and the quiver—these, O best of beings, are the mudrās. (31)
Of the one hundred and eight mudrās proclaimed by Brahmā,
these fifty-five should indeed be employed in worship.
As for the remaining fifty-three mudrās, they are prescribed for the *samayas*, as well as for the signaling used in bringing materials, dancing, and so forth. || 33 ||
In the contemplation, yoga, meditation, recitation, and dismissal of the deities, these first fifty-five mudrās have been proclaimed by Bhairava. (34)
O Bhairava, recitation performed without the mudrā, breath control, worship of the gods, yoga, and even meditation and the postures— all these are fruitless.
O you two sons, listen to the individual characteristic of each:
[it is formed] by the middle and tip of the right hand's index finger [touching] the left hand's index finger. (36)
One should join the left middle finger with the right forefinger, and likewise the right ring finger with the little finger of the left hand. (37)
The devotee should properly join the ring finger of the left hand with the little finger of the right hand by means of a clockwise rotation. 38.
The Dhenu-mudrā is fully described as that which grants satisfaction to all the gods:
having joined the two palms together with all the fingertips of both hands touching. (39)
Placing the two thumbs at the sides and joining them together is called the *sampuṭa* by the gods; this *sampuṭa* mudrā brings delight to all the deities. (40)
In meditation, reflection, yoga, and so forth, the *sampuṭa* mudrā is always praised; it consists of joining the two hands together with their palms turned downward and the fingers half-closed. (41)
The *puṭa* mudrā is proclaimed as having the shape of a hollowed vessel with the middle [fingers] empty;
it is formed by making the thumbs separate and joining the palms together in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*). || 42 ||
Joining the hands like a wood-apple fruit is proclaimed as the *bilva-mudrā*.
Having joined the two hands at the wrists, [the fingers] should be extended like a crane. (43)
Having likewise joined the thumbs and the little fingers, one should keep the three fingers of each hand separated from one another. (44)
The lotus mudrā is fully described as yielding the fruit of the four aims for men;
having joined the tip of the thumb with the index finger by means of an upward line. (45)
Likewise, by bending the other fingers and extending them, it becomes the Nārāca mudrā;
this "Beloved-Maker" mudrā should be offered for the pleasure of both me and Śivā.
O Vetāla and Bhairava, the Nārāca-mudrā is always for the sake of affection;
it is formed by making a fist with the left hand and placing the thumb inside.
Likewise, having diligently bent the right middle finger, one should then join the tip of the thumb with the middle and index fingers. (48)
The practitioner should join the right hand into the left fist;
this, which is displayed on the right side, is intended as the muṇḍamudrā.
This supreme ring, however, grants delight to Gaṇanātha;
it bestows satisfaction upon all the gods in all ritual acts.
Having properly bent the thumb, middle finger, and the others, and extending the index finger of the right hand, this is the Staff Mudrā (daṇḍamudrā).
Having joined all the fingers of both hands together,
one should wind them like a rope, starting from the little fingers of the two palms.
One should indeed place the tip of the left ring finger at the base of the [left] thumb, and likewise the tip of the left middle finger at the base of the right [thumb]. (53)
Having joined [the hands] after the *yojana* gesture, one should then rotate the fingers;
that center having the shape of a womb (*yoni*) is proclaimed as the *yonimudrā*.
O Bhairava, this Yonimudrā is pleasing to Kāmākhyā, to Durgā who possesses five forms, and it is dear to me and to Kāma. (55)
Having extended all the fingers joined together, one should join them with the tip of the thumb's joint and also with the tip of the little finger.
Thus, the half-yoni is proclaimed for the right hand;
however, the Great Yoni (mahāyoni) is said to be in the excellent Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
If one displays the *sampuṭa* or the *prāñjali* gesture upon the head,
this mudrā is known as the "Vandaniyā," which brings delight to Viṣṇu.
If that very [power] is attached to the ear, it is proclaimed as Mahāmudrā;
but when it is attached to the right limb, it is proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavī. || 59 ||
The Mahāyoni is indeed taught within the scope of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra;
it consists of the two bases [of the thumbs], the tips of the two thumbs, and the two little fingers.
Having joined the two hands and extended the fingers, one should join them again;
this is declared to be the Bhagamudrā, beloved by Lakṣmī, Vāṇī, and Śiva.
Having joined together the tips of all the fingers of the right hand in one place in front, this is known as the *puṭaka* gesture.
The wise one should join the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
he should bring their tips together in one place, while extending the middle finger and the index finger.
Having bent the two hands into a crouch, one should display them separately at the front;
this is the mudrā named Niḥsaṅga, belonging to Narasiṃha and Varāha.
By contracting the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger of the right hand,
while extending the index finger and the thumb, that [mudrā] which is performed— || 65 ||
That mudrā, called the Half-Moon, bestows pleasure upon the planets;
it is formed by raising the thumb of the right hand.
Having formed the middle finger and the thumb [together], one should likewise form the left fist with the thumb pointing upward; this is proclaimed as the limb-mudrā (aṅgamudrā).
By the successive removal of the little finger and the other fingers from this very same mudrā, eight mudrās are fully described; hear their names individually.
The Dvimukha, the Muṣṭi, the Vajra, and the Ābaddha; the Vimala, the Ghaṭa, the Tuṅga, and likewise the Puṇḍra. (69)
Nine rings for the nine forms of Viṣṇu, joined together with a half-ring, are thus described;
and likewise, nine [rings] for the heroines.
Having joined the backs of the two hands and likewise turned them evenly together,
one should again extend the pair of index fingers, joined on all sides.
When the two thumbs are likewise joined together, it is proclaimed as the conch mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā).
Having formed an añjali with the palms facing upward, one places the two thumbs between the two little fingers. (72)
Having placed the two hands at the base and joined them together, one should then display this mudrā; it is renowned as the Yoni, which grants satisfaction to the multitude of deities.
When the fist of the right hand has the thumb pointing upwards, that shall be the Śikhariṇī mudrā; it is beloved by Brahmā and the Sun.
Having joined the ring fingers and the little fingers together, and again with the wind [finger], one should perform the binding of the middle and index fingers like the *dhenu-mudrā*. (75)
Known as Sārdhadhenu, she increases the delight of the Moon;
it consists of all the tips of the fingers of the two hands placed together on one side. (76)
Having joined the two palms together and likewise having joined them below that,
the wise one should join the little finger, the ring finger,
and the thumb; he should bring their tips together in one place, while extending the middle and index fingers.
Having bent the two hands together, one should display them separately at the front;
this is the mudrā named Niḥsaṅga, belonging to Narasiṃha and Varāha.
By contracting the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger of the right hand, while extending the index finger and the thumb, that [mudrā] is performed. (65)
That mudrā, known as the Half-Moon, bestows pleasure upon the planets;
it is formed by raising the thumb of the right hand. (66)
Having formed the middle finger and its thumb [together], one should likewise place the left fist above;
with the thumb pointing upwards, one should thus form the limb-mudrā (aṅgamudrā), as it is proclaimed.
By the removal of the little finger and the others from this very same mudrā, eight mudrās are fully described; hear their names individually.
The Dvimukha, the Muṣṭi, the Vajra, and the Ābaddha; the Vimala, the Ghaṭa, the Tuṅga, and likewise the Puṇḍra. (69)
Nine rings for the nine forms of Viṣṇu, joined with half [a ring] each, are thus described in sequence; and likewise for the heroines. (70)
Having joined the backs of the two hands and likewise turned them evenly,
one should again extend the pair of index fingers, joined together on all sides.
When the two thumbs are likewise joined together, it is proclaimed as the Śaṅkha-mudrā.
Having formed the añjali with palms facing upward, one places the two thumbs between the two little fingers. (72)
Having placed the hands at the base and then joined them together, one should display this mudrā; it is renowned as the Yoni, which grants satisfaction to the hosts of deities.
When the fist of the right hand has the thumb pointing upwards, that shall be the Śikhariṇī mudrā; it is beloved by Brahmā and by the Sun.
Having joined the ring fingers and the little fingers together again with the wind [element], one should perform the binding of the middle and index fingers like the *dhenu-mudrā*. (75)
Known as the Sārdhadhenu, it increases the delight of the Moon;
it consists of all the tips of the fingers of both hands placed together on one side. (76)
Having joined the two palms together and having also joined them beneath that, one should join the tips with the tips; that is the *Sammīlanī* mudrā.
This [mudrā] increases the joy of the lords of sages who dwell on the earth;
it is formed by joining all the fingers of the right hand together. (78)
Having bent it down by a certain portion, one should make the base like that of a *kuṇḍa*;
this is declared to be the *kuṇḍa-mudrā*, beloved by the wise, the Goddess of Speech, and Śiva.
O Bhairava, having extended the fingers of the left hand, one should join the tips of the two thumbs at the middle of all the fingers.
Then, one should join the two thumbs facing each other and extend them;
this is declared to be the Cakra-mudrā, beloved by the Gurus, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (81)
Having bent the thumb and the middle finger of the right hand, one should then join the other three fingers at their tips.
The Śūla-mudrā is fully described as my favorite for seizing semen;
one should bend the hands together, with the group of fingers of the left hand [folded inward]. (83)
One should join the tips [of the fingers] in the middle of the palm of the right hand;
having placed the left hand underneath, this is known as the Siṃhamukhī mudrā.
This Bhagamudrā at the base of the ear is proclaimed as Gomukha; it is for the propitiation of Durgā and of the Discus-wielder, the Son of the Sun. (85)
This [mudrā] always bestows pleasure upon me, Viṣṇu, and Rāhu;
it is formed by turning both hands upward and joining them at the sides. (86)
Having extended the little finger and the others of the right hand in succession,
one should likewise extend each of the fingers of the left hand, starting with the little finger.
The eight mudrās have been fully described; hear them by name and in their proper order: Prollāsa, Unnamana, Bimba, and likewise Pāśupata. || 88 ||
Śuddhā, Tyāgā, Sāraṇī, and likewise Prasāraṇī;
those which perform the contraction of the fingers are Dakṣiṇā, and that indeed is Mudrikā. (89)
The Ugra-mudrā is declared by reversing one’s own hand;
these are proclaimed as the ten mudrās of Indra and the other world-protectors.
These increase the supreme delight of all the gods;
one should join the tip of the thumb with the tip of the forefinger.
One should show the fingers of the right hand, beginning with the middle finger, bent into a circular shape;
this bestows satisfaction upon the power Kuṇḍalinī.
Furthermore, for all the gods, this is a great means of producing satisfaction:
having joined the tips of the thumb, the index finger, and the middle finger together. (93)
Having contracted the middle and little fingers on the right hand, it is called the "Three-Faced" (trimukha) mudrā; it is always beloved by the Viśvedevas.
This [mudrā] is always dear to Keturatī and bestows satisfaction even upon the Mothers;
it is formed by joining the tips of the index finger and the thumb, while the other fingers [are extended]. || 95 ||
If one contracts three other [fingers], it is proclaimed as the Asivallī;
[this mudrā belongs] to the Pitṛs, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, and Viśvakarman. || 96 ||
That which always produces joy is proclaimed as the "Sword-creeper" (asivallī), because the two feet are joined at the soles and the two big toes are likewise joined. 97.
One should join [the hands] above at the navel, with the añjali likewise placed upon it;
this is declared to be the yogamudrā, which bestows the reality of the yogins. 98.
In the worship and meditation upon all the gods as well, the yoga-mudrā is declared to always bring about satisfaction and delight. (99)
The mudrā named Prāñjali is formed by joining the hands together with palms facing upward and downward;
having separated them, one should display the two hands extended upward and downward. 100.
This is declared to be the Bheda-mudrā, which is dear to me, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
it is formed by placing both thumbs into both hands.
One should first join the two little fingers together from behind;
then, one should join the other fingers, beginning with the index fingers, of both hands.
Having separated the tips of the fingers, one should show the little finger;
this mudrā is named Sammohana, beloved by Kāmadurgā. 103.
This is known as the enchanting and pleasing [mudrā] for all the gods here;
having bowed, one should likewise bend the middle and ring fingers of the left hand. (104)
Then, having joined the backs of those two [hands] together, one should subsequently join the tips of the thumbs;
thereafter, one should join the little fingers and the index fingers with their tips.
The Bāṇa-mudrā is fully described as that which grants satisfaction to all the gods;
it is formed by contracting all the fingers except the thumb and the index finger. 106.
Having extended the two hands, one should then join the tips of the thumbs;
likewise, one should join the tip of the index finger with the tip of the thumb. (107)
Even when extended according to one's capacity, it is proclaimed as the *dhenumudrā*;
one should join the tips of all the fingers at the *brāhma* tīrtha.
Having placed the tip of the thumb upon the back of the ring finger,
and having made [the hand] empty like a quiver, O Bhairava, [one should place it] within them.
The quiver-mudrā is proclaimed as that which increases the joy of all;
worship is established within the mudrās, and it consists of the contemplation of all things. 110.
The yogas are established in the mudrās; therefore, the mudrās are the bringers of joy, whenever they are employed in worship, in mental visualization, or in the practice of meditation.
In the beginning of a sacrifice or even during a hymn of praise, no manual labor with the hands is required;
at that time, one should perform the *iṣṭāpūrta* rite with both hands joined in the appropriate *mudrā*.
If one is capable in sacrificial rites and proficient in the ritual hand-gestures (mudrās),
then one should perform each respective rite only after forming the appropriate mudrā.
Divine ritual action is performed with hands released from mudrās;
since that [action] becomes fruitless once performed [in that manner], one should therefore be endowed with mudrās.
However, whichever mudrā has been prescribed for the dismissal of the deities, one should by no means employ that same mudrā at the beginning of the worship. || 115 ||
Having released the previously mentioned mudrā, the wise practitioner, endowed with mudrās, should perform all the rites beginning with worship during the increase of the ritual action. 116.
Therefore, mudrā is known as supreme; mudrā bestows merit.
Mudrā grants delight to the gods; for that reason, one should practice it with diligence. (117)
The Ardhayoni, Mahāyoni, Brāhmī,
and Vaiṣṇavī mudrās are always declared to be for the dismissal of Śiva and Tripura.
These mudrās are proclaimed for all the forms of Durgā:
the Yoni, the Sampuṭa, and likewise the Mahāyoni. (119)
Excluding those [already] mentioned by way of individual states, one should apply them elsewhere;
as for the other fifty-three mudrās that exist everywhere, [they are to be used] in the same manner.
When their positions are reversed, they become the *vāmā* mudrās, which grant supreme joy.
Thus, O Vetālabhairava, the mudrās have been described to you for worship, bestowing satisfaction upon those who are worshipped. Now listen to the sequence for the offering of the *bali*.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Mudrās," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The sixty-seventh chapter. The Blessed Lord said:
Now, the sequence for the offering of the bali-oblation, its nature, and so forth, beginning with blood—[is as follows].
O dear son, I shall tell you that which will truly bring you both complete delight.
The procedure for the offering of oblations (bali) to all deities, as taught in the ritual manual of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, is to be adopted by practitioners everywhere and at all times.
Birds, tortoises, crocodiles, fish, and nine kinds of deer;
the buffalo, the monitor lizard, cattle, the goat, the ruru deer, and the boar. (3)
The rhinoceros, the black antelope, the iguana, the śarabha, the lion, the tiger, and the man, as well as the blood from their own limbs. || 4 ||
The offerings to Caṇḍikā, Bhairava, and others have been fully described. Through these offerings liberation is accomplished; through these offerings heaven is attained. (5)
By means of the offering of a sacrifice, a king shall constantly conquer his enemies;
likewise, Śivā [shall be pleased] by the constant blood of fish and tortoises.
The Goddess obtains satisfaction for one month from the blood of wild animals, and for three months from the blood of men as well.
She grants auspiciousness and obtains satisfaction for eight months;
with the blood of lizards, she attains satisfaction for a year.
With the blood of the black antelope and the blood of the boar,
the Goddess constantly attains satisfaction for twelve years.
By means of the blood of goats and sheep, [the purification lasts] for twenty-five years;
and by means of the blood of buffaloes and rhinoceroses, it lasts for one hundred years.
Likewise, he attains supreme satisfaction through the blood of a tiger, as well as that of a lion, a śarabha, and even his own body-fluids. (11)
The goddess obtains satisfaction for a thousand years;
moreover, the pleasure she derives from the flesh and blood of someone is likewise [great]. (12)
The black antelope, the rhinoceros, as well as the rohita fish,
and the pair of vārdhīṇasa fish— the fruit of each of these is distinct.
With the flesh of the black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) and likewise with that of the rhinoceros (khaḍga),
Caṇḍikā attains complete satisfaction for a full hundred years.
O beloved of mine, by means of the flesh of the rohita fish and the vārdhrīṇasa crane,
one attains satisfaction for three hundred years.

One who has failed in his duties, whose senses are decayed, who is white-haired, aged, and lordless—such a person is called a *vārdhrīṇasa*; he is honored when offered oblations to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*).
The bird with a blue neck, a red head, black feet, and white wings—the vārdhrīṇasa—is dear to me and to Viṣṇu as well. (17)
A powerful man satisfies the goddess for a thousand years with a single offering given according to the rules; she attains satisfaction with a hundred thousand offerings from three such men.
Furthermore, by means of human flesh, Kāmākhyā Bhairavī, who bears my own form, attains satisfaction for three thousand years. (19)
Blood purified by mantras always becomes nectar;
Śivā likewise eats his head and his flesh as well. (20)
Therefore, during worship one should offer the head and blood of a *bali* animal;
likewise, a wise person should employ meats during feasts and fire-offerings (*homa*).
In certain rites of worship, the practitioner may indeed offer names and meat;
however, except for blood and the head, that [offering] becomes nectar.
The gourd, the sugarcane stalk, liquor, and spirituous extracts—
these are said to be equal to the sacrificial offering (bali), yet they are always equal to a goat for the purpose of satiation.
Cutting with a *candrahāsa* sword or a *kartrī* knife is considered the primary method; cutting with a sickle, a small sword, a saw, or a *śaṅkulā* is middling. (24)
The lowest type of adversary is described as being struck by razors, crescent-headed arrows, and spears;
other than these, a powerful foe must never be cut down with javelins, arrows, and the like.
O Queen, there is no offering of *bali* in that case; the giver shall meet with death.
He who cuts the animal with his hand—even if it has been consecrated (*prokṣita*)—is a practitioner (*sādhaka*). (26)
Otherwise, one incurs the unbearable sin of killing a Brahmin;
therefore, a wise man should not offer the *bali* oblation without first announcing it to Khaṇḍa.
Whatever mantras were previously taught for the invocation of the sword, those indeed, along with the powers of Mahāmāyā, should be employed there by the wise as prescribed. (28)
These mantras should be employed together with them for the consecration of swords and other weapons, for the worship of Śāradā and others, and especially for that of Kāmākhyā. (29)
Then "Dvikālī," then the word "Vajreśvarī" for the Goddess; thereafter, one should append "Lauhadaṇḍāyai namaḥ" at the end.
Having worshipped with this mantra and taken the sword in his hand,
he should consecrate that sword with the mantra of Kālarātri.
One should employ the center of the seed-syllable of the eye, repeating it twice;
thereafter, [the mantra] "Kālikālī" follows, and after that, "Karāloṣṭhī."
One should join the letters beginning with *ha* and ending with *nta* with the third vowel, which is indeed the eleventh; these two, conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*, one should subsequently apply.

Therefore, after the word *phetkāriṇī*, [one says] "devour, devour" (*khādaya khādaya*), then "all the wicked ones" (*sarvān duṣṭān*), and then twice "slay the buffalo" (*māraya māraya lulāyakam*). (34)
"Cut! Cut! with a sword; then indeed "kilikili";
then "cikiciki"; and then "drink! drink! || 35 ||
Then follows "rudhiram" and "cet," along with "sphaiṃ sphaiṃkiri kirī" and "kālikāyai namaḥ"; this is the mantra of Kālarātri.
When the sword has been consecrated with this mantra,
Kālarātrī herself becomes propitious therein for the destruction of enemies.
The mantras previously mentioned for Bali must always be kept secret by practitioners;
however, this mantra should be spoken for the sake of removing the sin of killing him.
"Beasts were created by the Self-born One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I shall cause you to be slain. Thus, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (39)
Then, with that sword, he should cut the sacrificial offering (bali), which is facing eastward, while dedicating it to the deity and according to his own desire.
Alternatively, while facing east himself, he should place that [linga] facing north;
he must certainly apply the previously mentioned substances, such as rock salt and so forth, to its face.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, brass, or even a leaf-cup;
or it may be made of clay, bell-metal, or sacrificial wood.
A vessel for the giving of blood should be prepared according to one's means;
it must not be made of iron, nor of bark, nor of bamboo, nor of leather, nor of lead. (43)
One should offer blood to the *bali* spirits upon the ground, or likewise with the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles;
it must not be given in a jar, nor on the bare earth, nor in a lowly vessel.
A supreme man desiring prosperity should offer blood;
however, human blood should always be offered in a vessel made of mahisha-horn or of metal.
The king should never give that [horse] upon a leaf or similar surface;
except for the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), he should never offer the horse as a sacrificial gift (bali).
Likewise, during the sacrifice to the guardians of the quarters (dikpāla-medha), the lord of men should give an elephant;
at that time, he should never offer either a horse or an elephant to the Goddess.
In the Hayākarṣa [rite], the lord of men should offer a chowrie, a sacrificial offering (bali), as well as a lion, a tiger, a man, and likewise blood from his own body. (48)
A Brāhmaṇa should never give liquor to Mahādevī;
by giving a lion, a tiger, or a human being, a Brāhmaṇa shall go to hell. (49)
In this case as well, he would have a short life, be deprived of happiness and good fortune, give his own body blood, and incur the sin of self-slaughter. (50)
By giving liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya or others should not offer a sacrificial oblation containing black antelope meat.
For if one gives a black antelope, the sin of killing a Brahmin occurs;
likewise, where the killing of a lion, a tiger, or a human is ordained [is forbidden]. || 52 ||
This sequence was prescribed by Brahmā for the offering of oblations and other rites;
having fashioned a tiger, a man, and a lion made of ghee, O Bhairava, [one should proceed].
Alternatively, one should cause [the victim] to be killed by means of a transformation of cakes or with barley flour, consecrated by that mantra known as Candahāsa.
But when there is an abundant offering of oblations, the practitioner should worship two or three of those placed in front, having made them the foremost, using the mantra for all of them. (55)
The general worship of the offerings has been described by me previously;
hear from me now, O Bhairava, that which constitutes the specific [worship].
One should offer a buffalo to the Goddess Bhairavī or to Bhairava;
with this very mantra, one should then worship that sacrificial offering (bali).
"Just as you hate me and just as you carry Caṇḍikā, so too, O buffalo, destroy my enemies and carry auspiciousness! (58)
O imperishable one who assumes an excellent form, you are indeed the vehicle of Yama;
grant long life, wealth, and fame—salutations be to you, O Kāsarā! (59)
When the ritual gift of the sword is performed according to the tantra and mantra,
one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the mantra beginning with "guhājātā."
O auspicious one, you are a sword in rites for the gods and the ancestors, resembling a sword yourself;
cut away all obstacles, O highly fortunate one born from the cave—salutations be to you!
This mantra is proclaimed for the gift of a black antelope:
"O black antelope, embodiment of Brahman, increaser of the splendor of Brahman! (62)
"O wise one, bestow upon me the wisdom consisting of the four Vedas and great fame.
Thus is this mantra proclaimed for the worship of Śarabha. (63)
O eight-footed one, born from the fallen portion of the moon;
O eight-formed one of mighty arms, known as Bhairava, salutations be unto you! 64.
Just as the boar was slain by you in the form of Bhairava, so too do you utterly destroy enemies and obstacles in the form of Śarabha. 65.
Just as you, Hari, carry Caṇḍikā in the form of Hara, so may you always bring me auspicious things and destroy my many obstacles. 66.
By that same truth through which you, as Hari in the form of a lion, slew Hiraṇyakaśipu—who was the very embodiment of the world's obstacles—while carrying him away; 67.
Thus, O sinless one, the sequence for the worship of the Lion has been declared by me;
now hear, O Bhairava, the procedure regarding human blood from one's own body.
If a mortal is given on a seat, one should offer the oblation in the cremation ground;
that which is called Heruka is indeed the cremation ground, as was previously explained. (69)
Know that sequence [of the cremation grounds] to be on the mountain at Kāmākhyā, beginning with Oḍra;
that cremation ground is my own form and is called Bhairava. (70)
In that regard, it will constitute one-third of the perfection of austerity;
however, in the preliminary limb known as Bhairava, there shall be the complete renunciation of the man.
One should place the head upon the right limb with a garland of skulls belonging to Bhairavī;
however, one should apply blood to the western limb in that which is called Heruka.
Having given [the offering] and worshipped the person, one should dismiss him according to the sequence of arrival;
one should not look at the sacrificial offering or the lamp for the offering at the sacred seats (pīṭhas) or the cremation grounds (śmaśānas).
Furthermore, wherever a great offering is given, there [the deity] is released;
elsewhere, having severed the head, the nectar is offered in another place.
The practitioner should employ [the disciple], but having dismissed him, he should not look back;
[he should employ] a man who has bathed, is radiant, and has restricted his food in the forenoon. (75)
Having deprived it of its enjoyment of meat and sexual union, and having smeared it with garlands and sandalwood paste,
one should place that [image] facing northward and [worship] the deities of the limbs upon its limbs.
One should worship that human being by name and as a deity;
one should worship Brahmā in the aperture of his crown (brahmarandhra) and the Earth on his nose. (77)
One should worship Ākāśa in the ears, Sarvatomukha on the tongue, the luminaries in the eyes, and Viṣṇu in the mouth. (78)
One should worship Candra on the forehead, Śakra on the right cheek,
Vahni on the left cheek, and Samavartin on the neck.
One should place Nirṛti at the tips of the hair, Pracetas between the eyebrows, Śvasana at the base of the nose, and Dhaneśvara on the shoulders.
Having worshipped the King of Serpents in the heart, one should recite this:
"O best of men, O highly fortunate one, O supreme one who embodies all the gods! (81)
Protect me, who have come to you for refuge, along with my sons, cattle, and kinsmen; protect me together with my kingdom, my ministers, and my fourfold army.
When death is certain, one should abandon even life;
for that immortality which is attained through great austerities, knowledge, and sacrifices—[that is what is gained]. (83)
Grant that to me, O illustrious one, and may you too attain prosperity;
[may there be no harm from] Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Vetālas and the like, or reptiles. (84)
Let neither kings nor other enemies slay me for your sake;
let them instead [slay me] with blood dripping from the stalk of your throat, mingled with their own limbs.
"May you swell with life as before, now that death is certain.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should worship with the ancient tantras. (86)
When this form of mine is worshipped, it becomes presided over by the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), as well as by all other deities beginning with Brahmā. || 87 ||
Even a man who has committed sin becomes free from sin;
for him, being thus purified, his blood quickly turns into nectar.
And the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, who consists of the world, was pleased;
he too, casting off his human body, died before long.
He shall become a lord of hosts and be highly honored even by me;
otherwise, he will be joined with sin and filled with impurities such as excrement, urine, and fat. (90)
Indeed, she who is known by the name Kāmākhyā does not accept that offering;
rather, she accepts it from the worship of other offerings, such as those consisting of buffaloes and the like.
The body attains purity, and the jackal indeed accepts the blood;
likewise, whatever is offered to other deities as well, [it becomes pure]. (92)
One should indeed give that which has been worshipped to a deity who has been honored;
[one should avoid giving] to one who is one-eyed, lame, excessively old, diseased, or suffering from oozing sores.

One who is impotent, or has missing limbs, or possesses the marks of an old man, or bears the signs of a low family; likewise one who is leperous, excessively short, or a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātakin). || 94 ||
A child under twelve years of age who is affected by birth-impurity (sūtaka), or one who has passed the age of one year but suffers from the death of a "great guru" (mahāguru). || 95 ||
In the rite of the funeral offerings (balikarman), one should avoid even those who have been honored—
whether they be animals, birds, or especially human beings.
One should not give a woman as an offering; by giving such offerings, one would attain hell.
Among the offerings made to a *saṅghāta*, women, cattle, and birds [are forbidden].
One should offer the bali-oblation, having set aside the human offering honored by the assembly;
one should not offer an animal as a bali to Śivā for less than three months.
One should certainly not offer a bird that is deficient in its three parts, nor an animal or a bird that is defective, such as being one-eyed or maimed. 99.
One should likewise offer a mortal being, as well as domestic animals and birds, to the Goddess—even those with severed tails or ears, and likewise those with broken teeth. (100)
One should never give an animal with broken horns or similar defects;
nor, O King, should one offer a Brāhmaṇa as a sacrificial victim, even if he were a Cāṇḍāla.
Likewise, one should give back to the king the son who was not surrendered to the twice-born gods,
even if he was won in battle from the enemy monarch.
One should not give away one's own son, nor a brother, nor a father who is not at variance with him, nor a husband’s younger brother, nor a sister’s son, nor a maternal uncle.
One should not give animals or birds that have not been mentioned, nor those that are unknown; however, if the prescribed items cannot be obtained, one may instead give a donkey or even a camel.
Upon obtaining others, one should not offer a tiger, a camel, or likewise a donkey;
rather, having honored a mortal, or even an animal or a bird, according to the prescribed rite.
Even that which has been severed, one should offer with a mantra, and indeed with a mantra alone;
one should properly offer the blood from the head of a mortal man to the Goddess.
One should offer a goat to the left, and present the buffalo in front;
one should offer a bird to the left, and the blood from the body in front.
One should offer the heads and blood of carnivorous animals and birds on the left side, and all those born in water on the right side.
One should first offer the meat of the black antelope, the tortoise, the rhinoceros, and the hare, as well as that of crocodiles and fish.
One should offer [the head] to the right of the lion and also to the right of the rhinoceros;
however, one must not offer the head or blood behind the body of Bali.
The food offering (naivedya) should be placed to the right, to the left, or in front, but never behind.
One should offer the lamp to the right, or in front, but not to the left.
The incense should likewise be offered to the left or in front, but never to the right;
one should present the perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the space directly before [the deity].
If [the ritual] is performed in the center of the mandala, as previously described for the left and right sides,
one should place the wine behind [the deity] and the other drink to the left.
Furthermore, where liquor is strictly prohibited,
a twice-born man should instead offer coconut water in a vessel of bronze or copper as a substitute for honey.
A twice-born man should never, even in times of distress, consume intoxicants,
with the exception of those made from flowers as previously mentioned, and especially avoiding the *gṛñjana* plant.
O King, a prince, a minister, a counselor, and those who are asleep and so forth, may offer a human sacrifice for the sake of prosperity and power. (116)
Having given a mortal man with the king's consent, one incurs sin;
however, during an eclipse or in battle, one may bestow a man according to one's desire.
No one at all, whether a king’s official or anyone else, shall ever on the day prior to the day of the offering present a human being as a sacrifice. (118)
Having placed the sword upon his head with the mantra "mā nastoke," with the Devīsūkta, and also with the verse "gandhadvārā," [he should worship].
Having applied fragrant substances and the like to that sword, one should consecrate it with them;
then, one should cause the fragrance and other offerings situated upon the sword to be placed upon its hilt.
With the mantra "Ambe Ambike" and that of Raudra-Bhairava,
when a mortal has been thus consecrated, the Goddess protects his sacrificial offering.
For him there are no diseases, nor dust from trampling, nor impurity; neither birth nor death occurring among his kinsmen shall defile him. (122)
Listen now to what is auspicious or inauspicious regarding the place where a man's severed head falls, as well as that concerning animals and other creatures. (123)

Likewise, a severed head in the northeast, a human corpse in the north, or one fallen in the rakshasa direction (northwest) should be declared as portending the loss of kingdom and destruction. || 124 ||
In the directions of the east, southeast, south, southwest, northwest, and north, respectively, there are prosperity, nourishment, fear, gain, the birth of a son, and likewise wealth. (125)
O Bhairava, one should point out the man with his head severed in due order;
likewise, the head of the buffalo is also [pointed out] starting from the north in sequence.
Listen now to what is indicated by a bird falling at the edge of the wind-quarter:
good fortune, loss, sovereignty, wealth, victory over enemies, or fear. (127)
O Bhairava, know that there will be the attainment of a kingdom and prosperity in due course for all sacrificial animals, such as goats and others, without exception. (128)
Thus one should know the results in sequence, excluding the aquatic and the oviparous;
however, for aquatic creatures and birds, there is danger in the southern and south-western [houses].

In other cases, however, one may give away prosperity; but when the head has been struck down and severed, there arises the sound of the teeth grinding against one another as the head is cut off. (130)
It causes disease for men, as well as for beasts, birds, crocodiles, and other creatures;
if a film (lotaka) arises in the eyes and flows down upon the head. 131.
If lac flows from the eyes on the head of a buffalo, one should predict the loss of a man's kingdom. (132)

When [the head] is severed, one should announce the death of the enemy king; furthermore, from the affliction of the heads of other sacrificial animals and the like, [one may predict their fate]. (133)
If one sees a corpse that has emerged from water, it brings supreme fear as well as disease;
however, if it is a headless man laughing, there will be the destruction of enemies.
There is an increase of prosperity and an increase of longevity for the giver at all times, without a doubt; whatever word he utters, that comes to pass without delay. (135)
From the sound "ūṃ," there shall be the loss of the kingdom; and from the discharge of phlegm from a wound, death occurs.
If he whose head is severed utters the names of the gods, [this is a sign of his imminent end]. (136)
Then, within six months, one should know that incomparable power will arise;
however, if at the time of taking blood, feces and urine should flow [instead], [the result is otherwise]. (137)
If the body of the donor should then be [drawn] downward or upward, death would occur;
or, from the drawing of the left foot, a great disease arises. (138)
At other times, auspiciousness arises through the drawing and moving [of the substances];
however, for the practitioner, it concerns the blood of a buffalo or a human. (139)
Having lifted [the offering] slightly from the ground with the thumb and ring finger,
one should deposit the supreme bali-oblation while reciting the Mahākauśika mantra.
To the deities such as Pūtanā and others in the south-western direction, starting from the east, there is a buffalo five years old and one twenty-five years old. (141)
A man should offer his strength to the Goddess; for his prosperity, he should offer his blood.
The three seed-syllables of the eyes, the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), Hantā, and Prajāpati [are the mantras]. || 142 ||

The seed-syllable of fire (ra) is likewise joined with the six vowels; that same [syllable] is further conjoined with these [vowels] and with the final letter of each of the initial classes of consonants. (143)
The sixth vowel, the crest-tuft, and the bindu, joined with the moon and followed by the end of the seed-syllable of Virmāṣikā—this is the consecration for Kauśikī. 144.
"This is the *bali* offering; *svāhā*"—this is the mantra remembered as belonging to Kauśikī.
Having consecrated the sword, the king should offer the *bali* to his enemies from the east. (145)
Then, having consecrated either a buffalo or a goat with the name of the enemy while reciting mantras,
one should bind its mouth three times with a thread using those same mantras.
Having severed his head, one should diligently offer it to the Goddess;
whenever there is an increase in the power of an enemy, that is the supreme time for the offering of the *bali*.
Then, for the destruction of that enemy, one should cut off the head of that animal and perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the life-force) of the enemy into it. 148.
When that [obstacle] is destroyed, the life-breaths of the enemy, joined with calamities, are destroyed;
first when it has a hostile form, O Caṇḍikā, and thereafter. (149)
"O enemy, you named so-and-so, go!"—this is repeated again;
thereafter, the mantra of the sword for the wife of Agni is proclaimed. (150)
He who hates is himself the enemy; destroy this one who has the form of a beast! O Great Plague, sphem sphem! devour, devour! 151.
With this mantra, one should place a flower upon the head of the victim;
then, one should offer that blood with the two-syllable [mantra].
If, on the Great Ninth day of autumn, an offering is made in this manner,
then one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with the meats arising from the eight limbs.
When the pure fire has been prepared with the Durgā-tantra mantra, by offering the bali-oblation in this manner, a mortal shall attain the destruction of his enemies. (154)
Blood from below the navel and blood from the back is for the sake of prosperity;
a practitioner should never offer blood from his own limbs [in these locations]. 155.
A human being [should not touch] the lips, the chin, nor the sense organs; likewise, [one should not touch] the area below the throat or above the navel, except for the hands on the arms. (156)
The practitioner should offer blood from the cheeks, the forehead, and the space between the eyebrows, but he should not cause excessive injury. 157.
From the tips of the ears, from the arms, from the necks and the belly,
from the throat upwards, and from the region of the heart in every direction— 158.
One should also offer blood from the flanks to Durgā;
however, one should not give blood from the ankles, nor from the collarbone, nor from the mouth.
Nor [is there any fault] from the bite of a disease-infested limb, nor from the killing of another, O Bhairava;
for one who has committed the act for that purpose, being full of faith and with an undisturbed mind, [there is no sin]. (160)
A man desiring success in sacred learning should offer blood upon a leaf of the lotus flower, or in a vessel made of gold, silver, bell-metal, iron, or even a ploughshare. || 161 ||
Having placed it [there], one should offer that blood to the Goddess preceded by the mantra;
as for the weapons such as the spade, the knife, the sword, the trident, and so forth—162.
By striking with the Bṛhadastra, one obtains a great fruit;
indeed, as long as the blood takes up the leaf of a lotus flower [from the wound], [the merit continues]. 163.
