The practitioner should never offer a red cloth that exceeds one-fourth of that measurement, nor should he ever perform the cutting of his own limbs.
Whoever should devotedly offer to the Goddess flesh produced from his own heart, the size of a masha bean, or even the size of a sesame or mung bean; || 165 ||
Within six months from that time, one shall obtain whatever desired object one wishes;
likewise, he who offers a lamp-wick upon his arms or even upon his shoulders [shall attain the same]. (166)
Even if a practitioner lacks a vessel of oil in his heart, yet offers it with devotion, listen to the fruit obtained from that gift of a lamp in a mere moment. (167)
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures at will in the house of a goddess,
and having remained there for three kalpas, he shall become a sovereign emperor.
He who, having taken with both hands the severed head of a buffalo along with its lamp before Śiva, remains standing for a day and night; || 169 ||
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures here with a long life and a purified body,
he shall go to my abode at the end of his enjoyments and become a lord of the Gaṇas.
Taking the head of a man in his right hand and holding a vessel of blood in his left, the practitioner remains awake at night.
A mortal who remains here for as long as a night indeed becomes a king;
upon my death, having reached my abode, he shall become a lord of the Gaṇas.
That man who, for even a moment, takes the blood from his head with both hands and meditates upon the Goddess while standing before her [attains success]. 173.
Having attained his desires here, he is honored in the world of the goddess, O Mahāmāyā, O Sovereign of the World, who grants all desires. || 174 ||
"I give my body and blood; be gracious and become a granter of boons.
Having spoken thus with the root mantra, preceded by a prostration, the wise one [should offer]. (175)
A man who gives his own bodily blood becomes like a perfected one (siddha);
for it is with truth that he says, "O Goddess, I give my own flesh for the sake of prosperity. (176)
"By that truth, grant me nirvāṇa; haṃ haṃ, homage, homage!
With this mantra, the wise one should offer his own flesh. (177)
Good fortune, the abundance of happiness, the supreme lamp, and splendor—may that flesh here illuminate me; *hnauṃ hnauṃ*, salutations, salutations! (178)
With this mantra, the wise one should offer a lamp on the night of Mahānavamī in autumn to Skanda and Viśākha. (179)
Having fashioned an enemy out of barley flour or even out of clay,
one should cut off its head and offer it as a sacrificial oblation (bali) while reciting the mantra over it.
Having consecrated the sword with this very mantra with great effort: "O red one! Kili-kili! O terrible one! O destroyer of the support of the terrible! (181)

The disciple of Brahmā’s disciple and the disciple of Ambikā’s disciple, [namely] such-and-such the best of enemies; the first [syllable] is the end-consonant (m) together with the visarga, and the other is that same [consonant] joined with the bindu. (182)
Having cut off the head, one should offer it as a bali-oblation after performing the rite with its mantra;
indeed, by this very mantra, conjoined with the bindu. || 183 ||
The mantra of Khaḍga for Skanda and Viśākha is said to consist of Brahmā (Oṃ), Agni (Ra), joined with the Moon of Yoga (U) and the Bindu (M), ending with Phaṭ, and used in offerings. || 184 ||
Having purified that artificial offering, which is the enemy, with red substances, and having applied a tilaka of red sandalwood upon his forehead; || 185 ||
Having dressed in red garlands and garments, and likewise wearing red clothing, one should tie a red thread around the neck and place a simulated dart at the navel. (186)
Having offered the northern head and shoulder, one should cut it with a sword;
then, one should offer that head consecrated with the Skanda-mantra.
Conjoined with the fourteenth vowel and the fire [letter], it should stand together with the letter *puraḥ* (ra);
each subsequent [syllable] shall likewise be preceded by [the same] and endowed with the moon-bindu (anusvāra). || 188 ||
This is the root mantra of Skanda; with it, one should offer a bali-oblation to him.
The third [syllable] is formed from the fourteenth vowel and the fire [letter], as before. (189)
This is declared to be the mantra of Viśākha; therefore, one should offer an oblation (bali) to him.
[The two attendants] Kuṭilākṣa and Kṛṣṇapiṅga are dark-brown in color and wear red limbs.
Likewise, they carry a trident and a sword in their two right hands, and a human skull and a small knife in their left hands. (191)
The two Gaṇeśas, acting as gatekeepers, were three-eyed, possessed of terrifying fangs, and wore garlands of human skulls upon their chests. 192.
One should always meditate with concentration on the two [deities] standing before the Goddess,
especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra.
O sons, one should gratify me, who am of a terrifying form, with wrinkled buffaloes, goats, honey, and meat; by that, I shall be pleased.
Regarding the offering of the *bali* to Caṇḍikā, one should sprinkle the head of the *bali* with water while reciting the root mantra, and then present it. || 195 ||
The practitioner should observe the slight breath moving in many ways, previously honored,
as well as the perfection of the body and the state of accomplishment.
Their chariot is a white phantom, resembling a seat of yoga;
within it, O Great Illusion, I meditate—salutations to you who bring about the realization of perfection. || 197 ||
If the head of one addressed by this [mantra] should tremble before long, then there will be success in that undertaking; however, failure results from the opposite.
Thus giving according to this aforementioned rule, the hero undoubtedly attains the fourfold aims of life through the offering of the bali alone.
Thus has the sequence and the form of the offering of the oblation been described;
now hear from me the chapter on blood and the ritual services. 200.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of the Sacrificial Victim," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 67 ||
The sixty-eighth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Bhairava, listen as I describe the sixteen modes of service."
For even another god is indeed pleased when one is properly satisfied with devotion.
First, one should provide a seat— either made of wood from the Pauṣṇa tree,
or made of cloth, leather, or silk— and place it to the north of the maṇḍala.
One should discard that lotus from the mandala at the very moment it is offered;
with words, flowers, and water, one should offer [another], for without a flower there would be a covering. || 3 ||
Outside that lotus, at the doors and other locations,

one should present the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the materials for bathing (snānīya), and the eye-ointment (netrarañjana).
One should offer honey-mixture (madhuparka), fragrance, and flowers upon a lotus;
and in the case of images, whatever is appropriate to be applied to the body should be offered to that very form.

One should offer suitable food offerings, meals, and so forth before [the deity]; as for the flower-seat that has been prescribed, if it is one containing a central cavity (garbhaka), [one should place it accordingly].
Then one should offer it upon a lotus and cast a vast quantity at the entrance;
[the offering] consisting of heaps of flowers arranged with flower-garlands and joined with *kuśa* grass threads and so forth.
O Bhairava, this smooth and auspicious seat, produced from sacrificial wood, brings exceeding joy to the Goddess, to me, and to you as well. 8.
One should employ a seat that is neither too high nor too wide;
one may also provide another excellent seat made of wood.
It should be free of thorns, mixed with milk, and devoid of heartwood; one must avoid those growing on a shrine or in a cremation ground, as well as the *vibhītaka* tree.
Bark, silk, and linen—these three are considered types of clothing;
and woolen blankets—this makes four kinds in total.
One should offer a seat fashioned from this for the sake of one's desired welfare;
[the skin] of a lion, a tiger, a hyena, a goat, or a buffalo.
Of elephants and horses, of the black antelope skin,
of the sṛmara deer, the rāma deer, and of the nine varieties of wild beasts.
It is heard that a seat made from the skins of all the gods bestows delight;
among garments, a woolen blanket is praised as a seat for the gratification of the gods.
An excellent seat made of wool, one made of leather, one made of wood from sandalwood, or a seat made of kusha grass—that is the unsurpassed seat. || 15 ||
For all the gods and for the sages of restrained self,
a seat and place similar to the yoga-pīṭha is prescribed.
By the gift of a seat, one obtains good fortune and liberation.
[The deer are: Śambara, Rohita, Rāma, Nyaṅku, Aṅkuśa, and Ruru. || 17 ||
The ena and the hariṇa—these are considered the nine kinds of deer;
O Bhairava, the hariṇa is also to be understood here as having many sub-varieties.
The ṛṣya, the rhinoceros, the ruru deer, the spotted deer, and the black antelope—these are proclaimed as suitable for offerings of meat and for gifts of skins. (19)
For all those belonging to the Taijasa class, a seat made of metal is said to be the best;
however, one should avoid iron, as well as bell-metal or lead.
One should offer a seat made of stone, or of crystal, or likewise of precious gems to the deities for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. (21)
In this very context, O Bhairava, hear also about the seat for practitioners;
seated upon which, while performing worship, one shall attain all perfections. || 22 ||
Fuel consisting of the four types—leather, cloth, and metallic—is always proclaimed as the seat for practitioners. (23)
For a practitioner, every seat is recommended for the rite of worship;
a practitioner should not sit on any seat according to his own whim during the rite of worship. (24)
A wise man should always make a seat of wood and other materials that is white;
a wooden seat is considered to be twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
One should make it sixteen finger-breadths in width and four or six finger-breadths in height; one should not make it taller than that.
One should avoid the aforementioned prohibited seats even during acts of worship.
The cloth should not be longer than two cubits nor wider than one and a half cubits.
One should not employ a height greater than four finger-breadths for the act of worship;
one may make it as large as desired for the sake of the eyesight, as previously stated, which bestows success.
One should make it six finger-breadths higher, but never taller;
for the worship of Mahāmāyā, [the seat] may be made of wool, leather, or stone. (29)
A praiseworthy seat has been prescribed for Kāmākhyā, and likewise for Tripurā; moreover, for Viṣṇu as well, a seat of kuśa grass is always recommended.
Wood that is very long, very high, and likewise very broad is said to be equal to earth; stone as well [is so] for all ritual acts.
One should arrange separate seats at each of the outer doors;
however, one should never use a leaf as a seat during worship.

One should not employ a seat produced from the limbs of a living being or made of bone—except for that of an elephant; among those derived from the tusks of an elephant, one may use it in rites pertaining to desire (kāmika).
One should take the skin previously mentioned, as well as that of the musk deer;
if one performs the worship of the deities in water, [these should be used]. (34)
There too, one should remain seated on a seat and never stand up;
in water, one should make a seat out of stone or even of kuśa grass.
One should not use any seat other than one made of wood or metal;
in the absence of a fixed place for the seat, the worshipper may remain seated upon the ground.
Having mentally prepared a seat, one should worship it in the water, provided that no place exists within the midst of the water to sit upon. (37)
Or else, remaining elsewhere at that time, one should perform the worship of the deity.
Thus, O son, has been explained this matter concerning the relationship between the object of worship and the worshiper. (38)
Now listen, O Vetāla Bhairava, to [the description of] the seat and the water for the feet (pādya).
Water intended for the feet is called pādya; it is simply water alone. (39)
One should cause [the guest] to be offered [water] with a vessel made of fire-gem (lapis lazuli) or even with a conch shell;
water for the feet is desired as the foundation for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Then one should offer the supreme seat from all sides with the root mantra,
using kusha grass, flowers, unbroken rice, white mustard seeds, and sandalwood paste.
One should offer the *arghya* with water and perfumes as they are obtained for the sake of success;
through the *arghya* one obtains desires, and through the *arghya* one obtains wealth. (42)
Through the offering of arghya, one indeed obtains sons, long life, happiness, and liberation;
however, a wise person should not offer arghya to the Sun with water from a conch shell.
Likewise, one should not offer arghya to Viṣṇu using a conch-shell vessel;
rather, one should provide water for sipping (ācamanīya) with auspicious, fragrant waters. || 44 ||
Whether with water scented with camphor, or perfumed with black aloe-wood smoke, or with any other fragrant substances that are free from foam, [one should bathe]. || 45 ||
One should cause that water—which is clear and free from froth—to be offered using either a vessel made of gold or a conch shell. (46)
That which is for the sipping of water by the gods is called *ācamana*;
one should offer that using pure water alone, not mixed with anything else. (47)
If available, it should be perfumed with fragrant substances and the like;
having bestowed longevity, strength, and the increase of fame, the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be offered.
The practitioner constantly obtains all desires as they arise, along with these five: curd, clarified butter, water, honey, and sugar. (49)
The madhuparka is said to be for the satisfaction of the multitude of all the gods;
it consists of a small amount of water from each, with equal portions of sugar, curd, and ghee.
One should employ honey as the most preeminent element among all [ingredients] in the *madhuparka* offering;
one should present it using a vessel made of bell-metal, gold, or silver.

This Madhuparka is prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma, Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices; for works of public utility (pūrta); for ritual acts (iṣṭa); and for worship; it grants satisfaction to the entire host of gods.
It is proclaimed as the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
this madhuparka bestows happiness, enjoyment, contentment, and nourishment. (53)
Then there is piṣṭātaka, musk, yellow pigment (rocanā),
saffron, jaggery, honey, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise the collection of all medicinal herbs.
White powder for cleansing, oil, sesame seeds with their oily essence,
and finally water— this is declared by those skilled in ritual manuals to be the bath-ingredients (snānīya).
One should offer water containing gold and jewels, perfumed with camphor and other fragrances, using vessels made of metal, bronze, or conch shells. (56)
It should be offered upon the mandala, the filaments, and the images of the Sun;
likewise upon the Śiva-linga, the sacrificial vessel (bhoga), the pedestal, and the body of the deity. (57)
One should smear the body of the image with fresh, unctuous, and pure ghee, or with red lead (sindūra), or with the paste of śrīcandana. || 58 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with a sword placed on a cloth or else in a mirror;
in this manner, one should especially offer the bathing water to Mahādevī.
Whether it be for Viṣṇu, Śiva, or others, wherever the worship may be performed,
the worshipper becomes long-lived through bathing and giving gifts.
By providing a proper bath, one shall partake in heaven until the end of the kalpa;
likewise, whatever is offered, such as water for the feet, fragrance, flowers, and so forth—|| 61 ||
Likewise, having performed all the ritual services with waters placed in the arghya vessels,
and having consecrated them through rites such as the *amṛtīkaraṇa*, one should bathe [the deity] with those waters.
One should offer [the water] to the chosen deities and then take it up oneself;
for that which is offered without those waters from the arghya vessels is not a true offering.
If anything is offered to one's chosen deities while the arghya has been rendered into nectar within the vessel [only] out of passion, greed, or negligence, all of that shall become fruitless. (64)
If water should flow out from the vessel, one should then make it nectar once more;
however, when only a small amount of water remains in the vessel, it has indeed been rendered nectar.
In that case, one should offer other water, for by that alone it becomes nectar.
If there are many flowers, or if there is an abundance of garlands, [the same applies].
Having sprinkled [the offerings] with water contained in the arghya vessels, one should release them;
however, that which is released with other waters—those waters other than those situated in the arghya vessels—is [ineffective]. 67.
The chosen deity does not accept what is offered even by hundreds of rituals if it is not placed in a consecrated arghya vessel prepared with the nine modes of reception.
All sacred bathing places and nectars abide everywhere;
therefore, one should perform the ritual services by sprinkling with the water remaining there.
One should not offer these by placing them in arghya vessels.
This has been declared to you, O Bhairava: the sixfold [offering] beginning with the seat (āsana).
I shall now speak of the ten [articles] beginning with the garment; listen for the increase of your higher knowledge. (70)
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 68 ||
The sixty-ninth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Cotton, wool, bark, and silk cloth are desired [as garments].
Having first worshipped that with mantras, one should offer it to the deity.
One that is ten days old, soiled, worn out, torn, or touched by the limbs [of another];
one belonging to another, bitten by a rat, pierced by a needle, or likewise kept [for a long time]. || 2 ||
Even a tiny fragment that has been washed away, yet is defiled by phlegm, urine, or other impurities,
[is unfit] for offering to the deities in rites pertaining to the gods or the ancestors.
One should avoid using it for one's own personal consumption, yet employ it in sacrifices and other such rites;
[it serves as] an upper garment, a shawl, a lower robe, and a garment of joy.
One should employ these five woven items for clothing:
linen cloth, silk, and likewise a sunshade.
Likewise, a caṇḍātaka garment should be seen; five sewn pieces are for the purpose of non-defilement.
One should employ sewn cloth on banners, flagstaffs, and the like.
And because that destruction occurs elsewhere, such as in the case of a veil and so forth,
a red silk garment is praised for the Great Goddess.
Likewise, one should offer yellow silk to Āsudeva;
one should give a red woolen blanket to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
One should offer a multicolored *aṃśu* to all the gods and goddesses; and one should give a cotton cloth, auspicious on all sides, to all of them indeed.
One should not give a garment that is exclusively red to Vāsudeva;
likewise, one should not offer one that is exclusively blue to Śiva.
Any garment dyed with indigo is to be avoided everywhere;
a wise person should avoid its use in rites for the gods as well as those for the ancestors.
O Bhairava, if a wise man should, out of negligence, offer to Viṣṇu that which is dyed with indigo,
his worship then becomes fruitless.
One should offer a garment that is multicolored and further dyed with indigo to Mahādevī; it should never be given to anyone else.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among bipeds and Vāsava is among the gods, so too, among all varieties of ornaments, clothing is said to be the most excellent. (14)
Through clothing, modesty is preserved; through clothing, one is not humiliated.
From clothing, success is attained in every respect, for it bestows the fourfold aims of human life.
O son, clothing has been described to you, which bestows all forms of pleasure;
it is an object of enjoyment and the finest of ornaments. Now hear from me about ornaments. (16)
The crown, the crest-jewel, the earrings, the forehead ornament, the palm-leaf fan, the necklace, the neck-ornament, and the finger-ring; (17)
The *prālambikā*, the jeweled thread (*ratnasūtra*), the *uttaṅgotarka*, the *mālikā*, the *pārśvadyota*, the *nakhadyota*, and likewise the *aṅgulīcchādaka*. || 18 ||
A tuft of hair is *jūṭālaka*; a crest-jewel on the head is *mūrdhatārā*;
a comb is *khalantikā*. An armlet is *aṅgada*; a bracelet is *bāhuvalaya*; and a head-ornament is *śikhābhūṣaṇa*. A gesture is *iṅgikā*. (19)
Then there are the rāga, daṇḍa, bandha, udbhāsana, abhipūra, mālikā, saptakī, śṛṅkhala, dantapatra, and karṇaka. || 20 ||
The thigh-string, the waist-knot, the clenched-fist ornament, the scattered hair ornament, the anklet, the swan-shaped ornament, the foot-ornament, and the small bell. 21.
These most beautiful ornaments are called the *sukhapaṭṭa*;
these forty are said to bestow happiness in both the world and the Veda. (22)
By the offering of ornaments, one accomplishes the four aims of human life;
having performed their worship, one should present them for the attainment of desired success. (23)
The wise one should worship them after pronouncing their respective deities,
or he should always offer golden [images] placed upon the head.
O Bhairava, the ornaments here consist of the crest-jewel and so forth;
from the neck-ornament up to the swan-shaped pendant, they may be made of gold or silver.
One should offer to the gods only that which is not produced from metal;
[this includes] vessels, implements, and so forth, even if they have been affected by calamities such as fire.
One should never give ornaments made of iron,
nor bells, fly-whisks, umbrellas, vessels, or other such ritual implements.
One should provide another ornament for that [image], because it is its accessory;
indeed, one should give everything made of copper, whatever ornaments and such there may be. (28)
Everywhere, copper is like gold; however, for the arghya vessel it is superior to that.
This applies also to the vessel for worship, the arghya vessel, the support vessel for the food offering (naivedya), and the vessel for the beverage (pānaka). || 29 ||
The copper [vessel] always brings delight and satisfaction to Viṣṇu;
the gods rejoice in copper, and the gods are ever established in copper. (30)
Copper brings joy to all; therefore, O Bhairava, a man should employ copper even for his own personal use, as it does for the gods.
On the upper part of the neck, silver shall never be worn as an ornament; nor [should one possess] a cloak, a drinking vessel, a water-pot, or even a house. (32)
Whatever else there may be, such as couches and the like, all that constitutes an accessory; likewise, whatever ornament might exist made of gold, excluding bronze.
In the absence of gold and silver, however, one should apply them to the lower part of the body;
whatever of these ornaments and such can be given by men [should be offered]. (34)
One should give each of those things as they are available, or indeed bestow everything if possible;
know that this ornament, which grants the four aims of life, bestows all happiness.
One should create this ornament according to one's ability for the sake of sacrifice, as it brings about contentment, nourishment, and joy;
indeed, this is declared to be the ornament that grants satisfaction to every deity. (36)
And listen well, my sons Vetāla and Bhairava, to the scent [of the enemy], whether he has been reduced to powder, rubbed, or even drawn out by burning. (37)
Whether produced by friction or originating from the limbs of living beings, fragrance is said to be of five kinds, bestowing delight upon the gods. (38)
Fragrant powder, fragrant leaves, and likewise powder of *sumana* flowers—whatever powders of leaves there may be that are endowed with excellent fragrance. (39)
These should be fragrant substances; this is known as the first type, "possessing fragrance. Sandalwood paste ground with powdered *meru* is [the second]. (40)
Furthermore, that for which incense such as aguru and other substances are offered, and whose fragrance is perceived even without being rubbed, is proclaimed as the second type. || 41 ||
Having burned devadāru, aguru, padmagandha, sāra, antacandana, and the woods of priya and others, the liquid produced by burning is collected. (42)
The third is proclaimed as the scent drawn from the *sadāha* tree;
likewise, there are the fragrances of *kara*, *vībilva*, and *tilaka*. (43)
That essence of the *prabhṛti* flowers which is extracted by pressing is the fragrance arising from crushing;
it is designated as *sammardaja* (the scent born of crushing). || 44 ||
The fragrance produced from musk, or indeed arising from its very pouch, is said to be born from the limbs of a living being; it bestows joy upon the inhabitants of heaven. (45)
Karpūragandhasāra and others reside in the powder and the rubbed [fragrance], while Candrabhāga and others are likewise associated with the liquid and the paste. (46)
Gandhasāra and arvarasa are employed for perfuming and other purposes; mṛganābhi (musk) becomes a powder when rubbed, even through its association with other substances. (47)
Thus, in every case, fragrance exists everywhere in five ways; through its various states, such as being ground and so forth, it becomes mutually a source of supreme delight. (48)
The detailed classification of fragrances, beginning with kālīyaka and others, has been declared;
all of them are instantly included within these five types alone. (49)
That sandalwood paste originating from the Malaya mountains which is esteemed for rites for the gods and the ancestors—its mud, its resin, or even its powder grants satisfaction to Viṣṇu. (50)
Among all varieties of fragrant substances, that which originates from Malaya is most praised; therefore, one should always offer sandalwood with every effort. 51.
O Bhairava, black agallochum mixed with camphor and sandalwood from the Malaya mountains is a fragrance that grants pleasure to the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī and to Kāmākhyā.
A fragrance made from equal parts of saffron, agallochum, musk, and camphor is praised as pleasing to Tripurā, as well as to Caṇḍī. (53)
Having first worshipped the fragrance with a dedication to the deity, the practitioner should always offer it to the chosen god; this bestows all accomplishments at all times.
Through fragrance one obtains desires; fragrance always bestows the Dharma.
Fragrance is the accomplisher of all goals; liberation is established in fragrance. || 55 ||
This incense has been described to you both, O sons Vetāla and Bhairava;
now listen to those flowers which are dear to the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī.
And with *bakula* trees, as well as *mandāra*, *kunda* flowers, and *kuruṇṭaka*;
with *karavīra* and *arka* flowers, and with *śālmali* and *aparājita* trees. || 57 ||
With *damanaka* and *sindhuvāra* flowers, as well as fragrant *kuruvaka*, with creepers of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and tender sprouts of *dūrvā* grass. (58)
One should worship the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Kāmākhyā and Tripurā, with clusters of Kuśa grass and beautiful Bilva leaves.
And there are other species of flowers that arise for the pleasure of Śiva;
hear of them as they are described by me, O Vetāla Bhairava. (60)
Mālatī, mallikā, jātī, yūthikā, and likewise mādhavī; pāṭalā, karavīra, javā, and likewise tarkārikā. || 61 ||
Kubjaka, tagara, karṇikāra, and then rocanā; campaka, ābhātaka, bāṇa, barbarā, and likewise mallikā. (62)
Aśoka, lodhra, tilaka, aṭarūṣa, śirīṣa, śamī flowers, droṇa, and the red varieties of padma, utpala, and bakula [are used]. (63)
At the three junctions of the day, Śvetāruṇa, Palāśa, and likewise Khadira; then Vanamālā, Sevantī, Kumuda, and Kadambaka.
The *cakra*, the *kokanada*, the *taṇḍila*, the *girikarṇikā*, the *nāgakeśara*, the *punnāga*, the *ketakī*, and likewise the *añjalikā*. (65)
The dohada, the bījapūra, the nameru, and the śāla;
likewise, the trapuṣī, the caṇḍabilva, and the fivefold jhiṇṭī. (66)
One should worship the boon-granting Śivā with the aforementioned flowers;
then, one should offer a leaf of Apāmārga and a leaf of Bhṛṅgāra.
After that, the *gandhinī* leaf; after that, the *valāhaka*; from that, the *khadira* leaf, and likewise the cluster of *vañjula* flowers. (68)
First the mango leaf, then the *baka* cluster, then the jambu leaf;
thereafter the leaf of the citron (*bījapūra*), and after that the *kuśa* grass leaf. (69)
Then the sprout of dūrvā grass is prescribed; after that, the leaf of śamī; then the leaf of āmalaka; and finally, the fresh leaf of āmala.
The bilva leaf is considered pleasing to the Goddess from all sides;
likewise are the kokanada flower, the lotus, the javā, and the bandhūka.
The leaf of the bilva tree is considered the best among all for granting satisfaction to Viṣṇu;
likewise, among all varieties of flowers, the red lotus is supreme here. (72)
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who, endowed with devotion, offers a garland of a thousand red lotuses to Mahādevī. (73)
Having remained in my city for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, that glorious one shall thereafter become a king upon the earth.
Among leaves, the bilva leaf is considered most pleasing to the Goddess;
a garland made of a thousand of them yields fruit as previously described. (75)
Moreover, what is the use of saying much here? This is stated in general:
with flowers already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, whether born in water or produced on land. (76)
One should worship Śivā with all available leaves, as well as with all groups of medicinal herbs and with all wild flowers and leaves.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess even with leaves in the absence of flowers;
and in the absence of leaves, one may worship with grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and the like.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, however, one should worship even with their fruits;
or with unbroken grains (akṣata) or even with water; and in the absence of those, with mustard seeds.
If even those are not obtained, one should perform mental devotion;
one may also worship with leaves from the edge of a sword and heaps of flowers.
One should worship with Tulasī flowers and leaves for the increase of prosperity;
in the rites of *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship with sesame seeds combined with Bilva leaves.
One should diligently offer oblations into the consecrated, kindled fire with unbroken grains or clarified butter, dedicated to Śiva, for the increase of one's desires.

The recitation that has been performed according to a specific number for the sake of accomplishing a desired object, and the worship which is prescribed to be performed at its conclusion by the twice-born; || 83 ||
That which is known as *puraścaraṇa* has been proclaimed by the best of the twice-born;
in that ancient account, it was previously described at length by those who spoke before. (84)
The practitioner should worship the goddess Kāmākhyā, who is indeed Vaiṣṇavī, with the prescribed rites;
here, he should offer the sixteen [upacāras] according to his ability.
One should not neglect the ritual services and the prescribed duties as they have been described;
having performed the complete worship according to the ritual manual, one should recite the mantra one hundred times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer oblations into the fire; at the conclusion of the oblation, however, one should present three bali-offerings.
Thereafter, one should bestow the three-fold caste [gift] and the triple symphony of music.
The wife, or the husband himself, or a brother, or a preceptor should prepare them;
or his own son, or even a disciple, may prepare all the offerings, such as the naivedya and so forth. (88)
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor:
gold, sesame seeds, and a cow; or, if unable to do so, at least a garment.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or on the ninth or the fourteenth, one who observes celibacy and has conquered his senses should perform the preliminary rite for the Great Goddess.
O Bhairava, having worshipped according to the detailed ritual prescribed in the Kalpa, one should receive [the teaching] from the mouth of the Guru on these lunar days.
Without having performed the complete worship, one should not take up the desired mantra;
nor should one perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), for by doing so, one comes to grief.
Furthermore, if it is possible, that daily worship should be performed in its entirety;
then, one should perform the worship as prescribed in the ritual manual with unwearied diligence.
O Bhairava, if one is unable to perform the worship of the Goddess in detail—
whether according to the ritual manual or that of another deity— the following procedure is prescribed for that occasion.
Having consecrated [the site] with cleansing and other rites, one should draw a mandala upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
then, having performed the disposal of the vessel, as well as the cremation and the floating [of the remains]. 95.
Then, for the purification of the twelve limbs, one should meditate upon the Self after consecrating it according to the nature of its constituent parts, from the thumb to the end of the weapon.
Having recited the mantra eight times over the *arghya* vessel, one should sprinkle the ritual offerings (*upacāras*),
employing the syllables of the root-mantra beginning with *Ādhāraśakti*.
Having meditated upon the deity residing in the heart and having projected [the deity] outward by means of the breath,
one should place [the deity] within the mandala and offer the ritual services according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped the six limbs as well as the deities of the eight petals, and having offered three handfuls of flowers, recited the mantra, praised [the deity], and prostrated; || 99 ||
Then, having displayed the mudrā in the fire, one should thereafter dismiss [the deity];
this very procedure is prescribed for all the gods alike. || 100 ||
If the worship prescribed according to the ritual manual cannot be performed, and likewise if one is unable to offer the ritual services, then one should offer these five.
One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings;
in their absence, one may use flowers and water, and if even those are unavailable, one should proceed with devotion alone.
Thus the abbreviated worship has been described, as well as the garments and other items;
now listen, O Bhairava, to the lamp for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
One conquers the worlds with a lamp; the lamp is remembered as being composed of splendor.
Since the lamp bestows the fourfold aims of life, one should therefore worship Śrī with lamps.
Whoever constantly worships the deity with flowers and lamps, by those very means the fourfold aim is attained; of this there is no doubt. (105)
Through flowers the gods are pleased; the gods are established in flowers;
and all things, both moving and unmoving, are always known to have the essence of flowers.
What is the use of saying much more? The mention of the flower is merely a hint; the Supreme Light resides within the flower and is propitiated by the flower alone. (107)
The flower is the means for accomplishing the three aims of life (trivarga) and bestows contentment, prosperity, nourishment, and liberation.
Brahmā resides at the root of the flower, while Keśava resides in its center.
Mahādeva resides at the tip of the flower, and all the gods are stationed upon the petals;
therefore, a person endowed with devotion should always worship the gods with flowers.
The mere utterance of the name arises for the welfare of all beings;
first is the ghee lamp, and after that, the one produced from sesame oil. (110)
Lamps made from the resin of mustard seeds, those originating from black mustard, those produced from curd, and those from food—these seven are proclaimed. (111)
It may be made from lotus fibers, or from the inner fibers of Darbha grass,
or likewise from hemp, from the bark of the Bādara tree, or from the fibers of a fruit-skin.
For the purposes of lighting lamps, wicks are always remembered as being of five kinds:
made of metal, wood, iron, clay, and coconut shell. (113)
Alternatively, a lamp-vessel made from grass or wood is praised;
and lamp-trees should be fashioned from metallic substances and the like, O Bhairava. (114)
A lamp should be offered upon trees, but never upon the ground;
for although the earth is all-enduring, it cannot endure these two things.
One should avoid striking the feet with the foot and likewise the heat from a lamp;
therefore, one should act in such a way that the earth does not indeed receive any heat.
O Bhairava, one should offer a lamp to Mahādevī and to others as well;
that man who offers a lamp while causing distress to the earth [is likewise blessed]. || 117 ||
He surely reaches the Tāmratāpa hell for a hundred years—[he who was] like a well-rounded wick with good oil, submerged in a worthy recipient, and beautiful to behold. || 118 ||
One should diligently offer a lamp at the very top of a tree that is well-elevated;
even if the heat of that lamp reaches [the deceased] from a distance of four finger-breadths, [they attain merit]. 119.
That is not known as a lamp; rather, it is heard of as the fire of the flood (oghavahni), which delights the eyes with its own radiance and is devoid of heat from afar.
A lamp with a beautiful wick, free from noise, smokeless, not too short, and with a flame that curls to the right, leads to the increase of prosperity. 121.
In a vessel placed upon a lamp-stand and filled with pure oil,
a beautiful and brightly shining lamp is lit using a wick that curls to the right.
O son, the lamp that provides satisfaction to all is declared to be the best; one devoid of a wick is proclaimed to be mediocre. (123)
One who is devoid of both the vessel and the oil is proclaimed as the lowest.
[The vessel] may be made of hemp, wood, or cloth, and it should be old or even soiled. (124)
The practitioner should not take what has already been used for the purpose of the wick;
he should always take only what is new for the sake of the constant increase of prosperity. 125.
One should not take cloth made from silk or wool for the purpose of making wicks;
nor should one mix fats such as ghee and the like with oil for use in a lamp.
Having prepared a mixed oil using fats, marrow, and bone-extracts— oils derived from the limbs of living beings— one shall go to the Tāmisra hell.
One should certainly not provide a lamp; having done so, one sinks into the mud.
Or else, one shall be cooked in a vessel made of bone, dwelling amidst the foul-smelling bones.
The wise, for the sake of increasing prosperity, should never offer a lamp in this manner;
they should take every care never to extinguish the lamp at any time. (129)
A person should not, out of ignorance or through greed and other such motives, take away a lamp that is constantly endowed with its proper characteristics and prepared for the sake of the gods. 130.
One who steals a lamp shall become blind, and one who extinguishes it shall become one-eyed;
[this applies even to] a piece of wood produced from a branch that serves as a substitute for a burning lamp.
Furthermore, in the absence of a lamp, one should offer a firebrand produced from a bilva fruit;
one should never, under any circumstances, cast away a burning ember for the purpose of lighting a lamp.
One should give that [lamp] for the sake of clarity, having set it aside from the formal ritual service.
Thus, O sons, the lamp has been described to you; now hear about the incense. (133)
The fragrance of burning wood—whether it be carefully prepared or otherwise—is exceedingly captivating and provides pleasant scent to the nostrils and eyes. (134)
Alternatively, that whose smoke, when ignited, produces no heat is to be known as incense (dhūpa), which bestows satisfaction upon the gods. || 135 ||
One should not perform the fumigation with those substances gathered together in one place;
by making a circular fire of husks, one shall not obtain that fruit.
Śrīcandana, sarala, śāla, as well as kṛṣṇāguru; udaya, suratha, skanda, and likewise raktavidruma. || 137 ||
Pītaśāla, Parimala, Virmadī, Kāśala, as well as Nameru, Devadāru, Bilvasāra, and Khādira. || 138 ||
Santāna, Pārijāta, and Haricandana-vallabha—these are proclaimed among trees as the incenses that grant delight to all. (139)
Arāla with its thread, śrīvāsa, paṭṭavāsaka, karpūra, śrīkara, parāga, and śrīharāmalaka. (140)
The powder of *sarvauṣadhī*, *ātī*, *varāha*, and *utkala*, as well as the powder of *jātī* buds and *kastūrikā* fragrance; || 141 ||
When the grinding has been completed, these incenses are declared and proclaimed:
yakṣadhūpa, vṛkṣadhūpa, śrīpiṣṭa, aguru, and jharjhara. || 142 ||
Pattrivāha, Piṇḍadhūpa, Sugola, and Kaṇṭha—these exudations resulting from mutual combinations are proclaimed as incenses (dhūpas). || 143 ||
With these smoky substances that leave a black trail, one should incense the deities;
for by the scents arising from such incense, living beings attain satisfaction through their sense of smell.
Resin, pollen, wood, and likewise fragrant substances, as well as artificial incense—these five are the supreme incenses that bring delight. (145)
One should never offer yakṣa-incense to Mādhava;
nor should one offer red coral to me, nor a beautiful chariot, nor likewise a female camel.
Yakṣadhūpa, putrivāha, piṇḍadhūpa, sugolaka, and black agallochum with camphor are known as the incenses dear to Mahāmāyā. (147)
Or one should worship the goddess Mahāmāyā with incense made from tree resin;
however, one should not employ incenses mixed with fat or marrow. (148)

Likewise, those belonging to others, as well as those that have been smelled, those afflicted by magical spells (kṛtyā), and flowers, incense, perfumes, and other such offerings—[these should be avoided]. || 149 ||
Having smelled [the incense] and offered it to the gods, a man may fall into hell;
one should not scatter incense upon the ground, nor on a seat, nor likewise into a water-jar.
Having placed it upon a support in whatever manner is appropriate, one should present it;
likewise, Raktavidruma, Śāla, Suratha, and Surala. (151)
Santānaka, nameru, combined with kālāguru, along with jātī, koṣa, and akṣa—this incense is dear to Kāmeśvarī. (152)
In the same way, this [lineage] belongs eternally to Tripurā and to the Mothers;
it belongs to all the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and to Rudra and the others, O sons.
This incense has been described to you both; now hear of that which delights the eyes, by which Kāmākhyā, Tripurā, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī are pleased. (154)
Sauvīra, yāmuna, tuttha, mayūragrīvaka, darvikā, and meghanīla—these are the six types of collyrium (añjana). || 155 ||
The *sravaddruma*, *sauvīra*, *yāmuna*, and *prastara* stones, as well as the *mayūragrīvaka* gem and the *meghanīla* which is fiery (*taijasa*), [are also mentioned]. 156.
Having ground these on a stone or a metallic vessel,
O son, one should offer them to all the gods and the goddesses as well.
That collyrium which is produced from copper and other metals through the application of ghee, oil, and the like, by means of the flame of a lamp, is proclaimed as *darvikā*.
But in the absence of all [these], one should offer that collyrium produced from burning to the goddesses:
Mahāmāyā, Jagaddhātrī, Kāmākhyā, and likewise Tripurā. (159)
Through these six ointments, they always attain great satisfaction;
however, a widow should not apply ointment for the sake of Mahāmāyā, even though it is supreme. (160)
The Goddess Vaiṣṇavī does not accept collyrium prepared by a widow; therefore, the practitioner should place that eye-collyrium in an earthen vessel. 161.
One does not obtain the fruit of worship with collyriums prepared in earthen vessels;
[proper] incense bestows the four aims of life, fulfills desires, and delights the eyes. (162)
Therefore, a person should devoutly offer these two to the gods.
Thus has the incense been described to you, as well as the collyrium for the eyes;
now listen again with a one-pointed mind to the food offering for the Great Goddess.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 69 ||
The Seventieth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Whatever substance is to be offered should be excellent and likewise purified.
Those five kinds of edible offerings and so forth are called *naivedya*. || 1 ||
Eatable food, soft food, food to be licked, food to be drunk, and fifthly, food to be sucked—
whenever he desires to worship, he should offer all of these as an oblation to the deity.
I shall tell you which among those is most dear to the Goddess; listen to it from me.
The Goddess is truly satisfied only by the offering of the five things beginning with food.
He does not accept anything according to the prescribed rules, nor is there anything given to him;
neither aregaru, nor wood-apple, nor grape, nor betel nut.
The Karaka, Varada, Kola, Kuṣmāṇḍa, and likewise Panasa;
Bakula, Madhūka, Rasāla, Āmrātaka, and Keśara. (5)
The *ākṣoḍa*, the *piṇḍakharjūra*, the *karuṇa*, the *śrīphala*, as well as the *audumbara*, the *punnāga*, the *mādhava*, and the *karkaṭī* fruit. (6)
The *jāmbava*, the *piṇḍakharjūra*, and the *bījapūra*—these are the three types of *jāmbava*.
The *harītakī*, the *āmalaka*, and the sixfold *nāgaraṅgaka*. (7)
Devaka, madhuka, śīta, paṭola, and that which grows from milk-trees;
the stalks of pāṭala and śāla, agnija, and the fruit of the kadalī—these [are used]. || 8 ||
The yellow flower of the *tinduka*, the *kāravinda*, the *karūṣaka*,
the *garbhāvarta*, and that flower which exudes milk, born of the bodiless god of love (*anaṅga*).
One should worship the Goddess with all kinds of fruits and flowers, including various fruits of water-lilies, lotuses, and wild plants.
Except for the śleṣmātaka, the bimba, the śailaka, and likewise the vaiṣṇavī,
among all varieties of fruits, this fruit is dear to the Goddess.
O Bhairava, the lāṅgala, the mātuluṅga, the karamarda, and the rasālaka—
such fruits should be offered to Kāmākhyā.
Likewise, one should properly offer to Tripurā and to the goddesses of the sacred seats (pīṭhadevīs) lotus rhizomes,
lotus stalks, lotus bulbs, and lotus fibers.
One should offer all such tubers as ginger, the golden tuber, the large bulb, and the bakulaka to the Goddess.
One should offer milk-rice, flour-cakes, barley-gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, sweetmeats, flattened grains, and other foods cooked in an oven.
One should offer to Mahādevī divine rice cooked with milk, mixed with clarified butter and sugar, as well as all kinds of side dishes.
Then, one should offer milk and other products from cows and buffaloes in their entirety, as well as the milk and other products of goats, sheep, and wild animals.
One should offer all kinds of honey and the like, as well as jaggery, parched grain, and sugar; likewise, one should present various foods, drinks, and meats.
One should offer to Mahādevī every side-dish, rich with fragrant scents and most enchanting, prepared from vegetables, meat, and other ingredients. || 19 ||
Having offered food, supreme rice-porridge, curd, clarified butter,
and sugar to Mahādevī, one shall then obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Having offered liquor mixed with sugar and combined with honey,
the king, after dwelling for a long time in the world of the Goddess, shall become [a ruler] upon the surface of the earth.
Having given a plough, a betel nut, a necklace, and a karamardaka fruit,
one attains incomparable charm and is honored in the world of the gods.
One should offer black gram, mung beans, lentils, sesame seeds, hemp, and likewise all grains such as barley, as appropriate. (23)
In whatever manner the food may be prepared and with whatever ingredients it may consist, having seasoned it with spices such as *veśavāra* and the like, one should offer it to Mahādevī.
Whether he be a great hero, a sage, a brahmin, or anyone else,
whatever food may be available, it should be prepared for his own sake in whatever manner is appropriate.
In that manner, filled with devotion, one should offer [the oblation] to Mahādevī; then, having consecrated the objects to be consecrated, one should become a consecrator according to the rite.
And according as she is to be refined, so should one give her various things;
for that which is joined with a foul odor, burnt, or unfit for consumption must be avoided.
Even if it has been mentioned, one should never give betel-leaf mixed with fragrance and scented with camphor and other ingredients to Mahādevī. (28)
One should offer prepared food made from crushed lotuses;
as for the wild animals and birds prescribed for the offerings of *bali*, [one should likewise offer them].
One should offer the flesh of those fish, prepared by mixing it with the flesh of rhinoceros, porpoise, and goat. (30)
Having offered once to Mahādevī a side-dish rich in flavor and fragrance, well-prepared and most enchanting, one shall become a sovereign emperor. (31)
By offering a fragrant side dish well-prepared in an iron vessel with radishes and the meat of a black antelope, one attains the world of the Goddess.
Having offered dates, cluster dates, and barley flour mixed with clarified butter to the forms of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By the gift of kṛśara-rice, incomparable good fortune shall arise;
by giving coconut water, one obtains the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice.
By offering rose-apples, *lavalī* fruits, *dhātrī* fruits, and *śrīphalas*, one obtains the fruit of the *Vahniṣṭoma* sacrifice and attains the world of the Goddess. || 35 ||
By offering grapes combined with sugar and accompanied by oranges to Mahādevī, one becomes possessed of fortune and beauty. (36)
By offering grain and flattened rice to the Goddess, one shall obtain prosperity;
likewise, by presenting stalks of sugarcane, lentil broth, and fresh butter. (37)
Having attained supreme good fortune, he is glorified in the world of the goddess;
and having offered sesame seeds mixed with fresh butter to the Goddess, [he attains the same].
Having obtained all desires in this world and having died, one shall attain liberation;
[offering] all food, excluding what is unfit to be eaten, accompanied by condiments. (39)
Then, having prepared it like food, one should offer it to Mahādevī;
[one should also offer] water from a coconut joined with water containing gems. (40)
One should offer to the Goddess a drink mixed with milk, clarified butter, and honey, combined with sugar and curd, served in a vessel made of precious metal.
Listen to the fruit of his merit with a mind inclined toward devotion:
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having dwelt in Devīpura, the steadfast one becomes a sovereign ruler on earth;
thereafter, he attains liberation (kaivalya) according to his desire.
Having offered kalāya and nivāra grains boiled and mixed with curd to Mahādevī, one shall surely obtain one's desired wish.
One should offer black pepper, long pepper, kola, cumin, and likewise tantubha, both during the consecration and in her presence, to Mahādevī.
Having offered a tamarind fruit combined with sugar while endowed with devotion, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and attains the world of the Goddess. || 46 ||
Rājamāṣa, masūra, pālaṅka, and potikā;
kālaśāka, kalāya, and the root of brāhmī. || 47 ||
Vāstūka, Kalambī, Kañcuka, Hilamocikā, Cakra, Vidrumapatra, and likewise Punarnavā— (48)
O Great Goddess, he who, endowed with devotion, should offer these vegetables, attains incomparable prosperity and is honored in my world. (49)
Through excellence in faith, inquiry, ritual preparation, devotion, materials, and zeal, there is an excellence of fruit; indeed, from what is inferior, one attains inferiority. (50)
One should never offer to the gods as food-oblations (naivedya) those things that are incompatible with the time of the mantra, nor those that have been designated for the Guru.
One should offer the food-oblation (naivedya), which is dear to me and dear to my beloved, upon a plate made of silver or gold, or even on one of copper, or else upon a lotus leaf.
One should take vessels made of bell-metal, or indeed of gold or copper,
for the purpose of consuming the offering or for the purpose of the *arghya* vessel.
A vessel made of sacrificial wood is also considered middling;
however, in the absence of all these, one made of clay is acceptable, provided it has been fashioned by one's own hand.
"O sons, this offering dear to Vaiṣṇavī has indeed been described to you both;
likewise for the goddess Kāmākhyā, and especially for Tripurā.
Now listen to you both regarding the rites of circumambulation and salutation. (55)
Thus ends the seventieth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 70 ||
The seventy-first chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: Again, having extended his right hand and bowing his head himself, he spoke.
Showing his right side, he was right-minded even in his thoughts.
One should circumambulate [the deity] once or thrice; thus the pleasure of the deities arises.
That [circumambulation] should be known as *pradakṣiṇa*, which grants satisfaction to the entire host of gods. (2)
He who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of the Goddess,
having attained all his desires, shall thereafter obtain liberation.
And he who, even with his mind alone, should offer a circumambulation to the Goddess with devotion, by that circumambulation shall not see the hells in the abode of Yama. || 4 ||
Salutation is known by those who know it to be threefold— physical, vocal, and mental— and is classified as superior, inferior, or middling.
Having extended his feet and hands, he fell prostrate like a staff upon the ground;
having knelt upon the earth, he touched the ground with his head.
That salutation which is performed with the body is the supreme;
it is done by touching the ground with both knees and touching the earth with the head. (7)

The salutation which is performed by placing the hands joined together at the head, however it may be done, without touching the knees or the head to the ground, is considered the middling physical prostration; that is called the lowest.
When a salutation is performed by one endowed with devotion, composed personally in both prose and verse, that is indeed the highest form of vocal homage.
When salutation is performed with either Puranic or Vedic mantras,
that is always the middle form of salutation, which is verbal.
O sons, that salutation which is always performed with human speech alone should be known as the lowest among verbal salutations.

Furthermore, mental salutation is said to be threefold—superior, inferior, and middling—according to whether the minds are directed toward the desirable, the undesirable, or that which is neither. (12)
And among the three kinds of salutation, the physical one is considered the highest;
the two [other] deities are always pleased by physical salutations. (13)
That very act of salutation which is known by names such as *daṇḍa* and so forth, is to be understood as *praṇāma*; it has been explained previously. (14)
Through the food offering (naivedya), everything is attained; the food offering becomes nectar.
Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa are all established within the food offerings. || 15 ||
This perpetual offering consists of all sacrifices; it grants satisfaction to all, bestows knowledge and the fulfillment of desires, is meritorious, and likewise comprises all objects of enjoyment.
Any man endowed with devotion who desires to offer a food-offering even mentally to Mahādevī shall become long-lived and happy. (17)
"Whoever, filled with such thoughts, shall always worship the goddess Mahāmāyā with devotion through various kinds of food offerings,
shall attain all desires and be glorified in my world. (18)
And he who, even with his mind alone, should devoutly perform a circumambulation of the Goddess,
shall not see the hells in the southern abode of Yama.
Gods, humans, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas—all these great-souled beings are gratified on every side by a salutation. (20)
The one of great intelligence obtains the fourfold aims through prostration;
for the sake of attaining all perfections everywhere, prostration alone is praised. (21)
Through dance one conquers the worlds; through dance even one's lifespan increases.
Through prostration, one attains long life and unbroken progeny. (22)
"Pay homage to Mahādevī and then perform circumambulation; offer food oblations abundantly"—he who speaks thus repeatedly, having attained his desires here in this world, rejoices in my realm. (23)
And that man who, possessed of great devotion, offers an oblation to Mahādevī with the intent to give it, shall also attain the world of the Goddess. (24)
Thus, these sixteen modes of service have been correctly described to you both;
what else is desired by you? I shall explain that as you ask.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sixteen Modes of Service," in the glorious *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
The seventy-second chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, and I shall tell you both the majesty of Kāmākhyā.
O Vetāla Bhairava, listen to that [teaching] together with its limbs and its secret.
Once, while Viṣṇu and his two devotees who were solely intent on Viṣṇu were traveling swiftly with Garuḍa,
he reached the goddess Kāmākhyā at Nīlasthāna.
Having reached that best of mountains and disregarding it, Keśava urged Garuḍa forward, saying, "Go, go! as they proceeded.
And the goddess Mahāmāyā, known as Kāmā, the mother of the worlds,
together with Garuḍa, paralyzed Kṛṣṇa between heaven and earth.
But he, utterly deluded by the illusion of Mahāmāyā, was unable either to go forth or to return; he remained as if bound. || 5 ||
Seeing that Garuḍa was unable to proceed, the one whose banner is Garuḍa became enraged and prepared to displace that best of mountains.
Then, having taken that mountain into his arms with both hands, Keśava, the Lord of the World, was not able to move it even slightly.
Desiring to shake that mountain, Kāmākhyā, intent on wrath,
bound Vaikuṇṭha with Garuḍa by means of the *siddhasūtra*.
Having bound him with the *siddhasūtra*, the Goddess cast him effortlessly from the tip of her grasper into the salt ocean; in an instant, he fell to the bottom.
Having reached that bottom of the ocean, he again employed his own illusory power (māyā) to restrain it,
and having stepped upon it, he seized him who was situated at the ocean floor.
With great effort, Hari did not wish to leap up; even as he exerted himself with great effort, he rose again [only] to submerge once more.
Kāmākhyā shall restrain its contraction and expansion;
that Goddess shall also restrain the arising of his knowledge.
Then, devoid of wisdom and lacking both strength and substance,
he remained for a long time submerged in the depths of the water like Garuḍa.
Searching for him, the Creator reached Hari, who was situated within the ocean, appearing as if he were an ordinary being reduced to fragments.
Having reached him along with Tārkṣya, the Creator, the Grandfather of the worlds,
took hold of him with both hands and desired to cause him to float up.
Even the Grandfather of the worlds was unable to float him up;
and the Goddess herself, having been bound by us, remained there in astonishment.
Then, after a long period of time, all those gods, led by Śakra, while searching [for him] within a region of waterless wilderness, met together. (17)
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, having approached those two,
made an effort to wash them away, but they were unable to do so.
Then all those gods, deeply deluded by that illusion, remained there just as Brahmā and Viṣṇu were situated. || 19 ||
Then, while searching for all those gods,
Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, [found] Mahādeva stationed on a ridge of the Himavat mountains.
Having approached the gods, he who is worshipped by the gods inquired after their welfare with great respect, having praised and bowed to them according to the prescribed rite.
The Guru said:
"O Mahādeva, abode of the universe and cause of the world's pacification, seeking Śakra and the other gods, I have come before you. (22)
Neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu were present in the abode of Brahmā, nor in heaven, nor anywhere else; indeed, they were not perceived at all, as they had been on other occasions.
O God, O deity of deities, please sever this doubt:
where do they abide, or why have they remained in such a state? (24)
O Lord, by your instruction I shall follow them all;
if you have compassion for me, please tell me their way of life.
Having heard those words of his, I spoke again concerning that matter,
describing all those deeds and how we were bound by illusion.
The Great Goddess Mahāmāyā, who consists of the universe, was disregarded by him;
therefore, bound by her māyā, Viṣṇu remains in the ocean.
Searching for that path, the thirty gods, led by Brahmā, were again bound by Māyā;
they remained in his vicinity, utterly restrained.
If you go here to search for them without me, you too will likewise be bound and will not be able to return. (29)
Therefore, I shall go there where the one whose banner is Garuḍa resides;
I will then liberate Brahmā, Indra, and the others from their concealment in due order.
Having spoken thus, Maheśvara, whose emblem is the bull, joined together with Garuḍa and went to that place where the hosts of gods were stationed.
Having gone there, Mahādeva addressed Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and questioned them all: "For what purpose have you gathered here? (32)
Devoid of coming and going, and like inert matter, bereft of consciousness—why did the gods become so? Let them explain that to me now.
Having heard those words of Mahādeva, Keśava then spoke this slowly to Bharga in the presence of Brahmā and the others.
The Blessed Lord said: "As I was traveling through the sky above the peak of Nīlakūṭa,
seated upon Garuḍa, I beheld the great mountain Nīla."
And when Garuda was prevented from seizing me by her hand,
there that great Māyā, named Kāmākhyā, who can assume any form at will, [intervened].
Yoganidrā herself, having assumed [her form], cast me into a lotus of the ocean;
then I, along with my vehicle, reached the bottom of that mass of water.
O destroyer of Andhaka, having fallen here, I have dwelt for a long time;
I have lived for a long time within these waters of the ocean.
"Even now, O Maheśvara, that Mahāmāyā does not dispel me;
for my sake, the gods beginning with Brahmā and Indra have arrived from all sides. (39)
They too have indeed been forcibly bound by the Great Goddess with the noose of Māyā;
therefore, please show us favor and lead us now to the abode of Śiva.
And we shall propitiate her by means of a proper bond and non-violence;
having heard those words of Hari, I too was filled with compassion. (41)
He himself spoke with supreme affection to Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding the most enchanting armor of the Goddess, which fulfills all desires.
"Having bound it to his body and immersed him, let them then go toward her;
for I have been bound by him here through his illusory power."
"Bṛhaspati was not bound here by association with me;
therefore, listen to my armor [of instruction] from me."
By which, leaping up from that bliss, we shall behold the Supreme Goddess.
Om; Bṛhaspati is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the Kāmākhyā-kavaca. 45.
The goddess Kāmeśvarī is his deity; the Anuṣṭubh is prescribed as his meter;
and its application is for the attainment of all perfections—let the deities hear this.
The goddess Kāmeśvarī is my head; Kāmākhyā is my two eyes; Sāradā is the pair of my ears; and Tripurā is likewise my mouth. (47)
May Mahāmāyā protect my throat, and may Kāmeśvarī protect my heart; may Kāmākhyā protect my belly, and may Śāradā protect me from the navel.
May Tripurā protect my two sides, and may Mahāmāyā protect my genitals; may Kāmeśvarī protect my anus, and may she who is called Kāmā protect my thighs. (49)
May Śāradā protect my knees; may Tripurā protect my shanks;
and may Mahāmāyā, the granter of desires, eternally protect the pair of my feet.
May Koṭeśvarī protect [my] hair; may Dīrghikā protect [my] nose;
may Bhairavī protect the collection of [my] teeth; and may Mātaṅgī protect [my] two arms.
May Lalitā protect my two arms; may Vanavāsinī protect my two hands;
may Vindhyavāsinī protect my fingers; and may Śrīkāmā protect the tips of my nails.
May Guptakā always protect me in all the pores of my skin;
may Bhuvaneśvarī protect me in the parts of the toes and the heels. (53)
May Setu protect me on the tongue; may Ka protect within the throat;
may La protect within the interior of the chest; and may Ha protect within the belly. (54)
May Sāmīndu protect me; may he who is praised within the intervals between the moon-drops protect me. May the letter *a* protect my skin, and may the letter *ra* always protect my bones.
May the letter *la* protect me constantly in all the channels, the letter *ī* in all the joints, the Moon in the sinews, and the Bindu in the marrow. (56)
In the eastern direction, in the southeast, in the south, in the southwest, likewise in the west, in the northwest, in the north, and in the abode of Hara [the northeast]. (57)
May the eight syllables beginning with 'a', belonging to Vaiṣṇavī and residing within the mantra, protect and remain forever for the sake of origination and growth. (58)
May the two "Setus" (bridges) always protect me above and below;
these are the nine syllables within the mantras belonging to the sphere of the Śāradā-mantra.

One should constantly contemplate me as the ninefold sound throughout the nose and other [senses]; and for the sake of warding off wind, bile, and phlegm, one should meditate on the three syllables of Tripurā.
May they protect me constantly from spirits and likewise from Piśācas;
may those two constant guardians of the bridge ward me off from flesh-eating demons.
Salutations to the Goddess Kāmeśvarī, the Great Māyā who consists of the universe;
she who, having eternally become Prakṛti, extends the state of being the primordial source of the world.
One should meditate upon Kāmākhyā in the southeast, who holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons in her hands; who carries the thread of the Siddhas in one hand;
who stands upon a white corpse; who is adorned with jewels and gold; whose complexion is yellow like saffron;
who is the foundation of knowledge and meditation and possesses supreme humility; and who is worshipped by Brahmā, Śakra, and the other gods.
I bow to her who resides in bliss for the sake of accomplishment, whose beloved object is the mantra ending with the bindu.

In the central portion of the center, she is perpetually bowed, possessing a series of expressions and gestures; she is the grace within the chamber of the world, endowed with all virtues, manifest in form yet uniquely humble.
She is the singular peace of both knowledge and ignorance, the bringer of tranquility through calming, the maker of well-being, and the one with the excellent face.
May the Sovereign Goddess, who holds the sacred *praṇava* in her excellent hand and who eternally protects us from falling, grant us our desires. 64.
If even this armor of Hara, residing upon the body, can indeed pacify the God of Death himself, then take it here and strive for liberation; this is the method, accompanied by the immortals.
The wise man who recites this armor-mantra (kavaca) of Kāmākhyā even once— the Great Goddess follows him constantly.
He has no fear of mental anguish or physical disease, nor fear of carnivorous beasts; likewise, he has no fear of fire, nor of waters, nor of enemies, nor of the king.
Long-lived and possessing great wealth, endowed with sons and grandsons,
he rejoices in the supreme abode for a hundred cycles while causing the Goddess’s temple to be restored.
In whatever manner a wise man may be bound in battle or elsewhere,
he shall be liberated at that very moment by the recollection of this armor.
Ishvara said:
Having thus heard the armor-mantra, Hari, Brahma, the gods,
and even Shakra each separately performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the armor upon their bodies.
But they, having laid aside their armor through the power of the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā),
leaped up from the waters of the ocean and quickly reached the earth.
Having reached the earth, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived at Nīlakūṭa in order to behold Kāmākhyā. || 72 ||
Having seen the goddess Kāmeśvarī, who is composed of the entire universe, Keśava himself,
recognizing her established power, spoke this to her.
You alone are the Goddess Prakṛti; you alone are the earth and the water.
You alone are the mother of the worlds, and you alone are composed of the world.
You are the creator of all worlds; you are the knowledge that bestows liberation. You are the Goddess whose nature is both supreme and non-supreme, as well as both gross and subtle.
Be gracious, O Great Goddess; when you, the auspicious one, are pleased, all the gods become gracious, O sinless one who bestows the four aims of life. 76.
Kāmākhyā, who is the personified form of Rati, [is the consort] of the high-souled Keśava;
Kāmākhyā, appearing in visible form, addressed Hari and spoke.
The Goddess said:
"O Keśava, together with Brahmā, all the gods, and likewise the Gaṇas, quickly perform your bath and drink [the water] today within the waters of my womb. (78)
Therefore, free from egoism and endowed with the prowess of others,
mount Garuḍa and go to the third heaven together with the Creator.
Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, Keśava, together with Edhas,
performed bathing and drinking in the waters of the Yonimaṇḍala.
Then the gods, having performed their ablutions, and Keśava, having likewise bathed,
departed joyfully toward the celestial realm with the consent of the Goddess.
As those hosts of gods were traveling together with Keśava and Brahmā, they then beheld that Kāmākhyā situated in the sky.
They beheld thousands of blue peaks situated there together with their sources, arranged in an upward and downward orientation.
Each of those gods, having ascended them one by one at that very moment,
bathed and performed ablutions as before, and thus attained incomparable joy.
Thus they departed, free from affliction, their minds untroubled by wonder,
praising and extolling the maṇḍala of the source known as Kāmākhya.
Then, having bowed to the preceptor of the gods and having praised me in turn,
they were dismissed by me and departed for heaven with eyes blossoming with joy.
O Bhairava, such is the majesty of the Goddess Kāmākhyā;
and such is the armor (kavaca) proclaimed, having attained the truth, O son. 87.
Having reached it, become happy by employing it as you desire;
what else shall I tell you regarding the majesty of Kāmākhyā?
Through union with that alchemical stone (yoni-śilā), iron and other metals attain the state of gold. || 88 ||
If a person bathes in the circle of the womb and drinks [the water] even once, he does not undergo rebirth here; he shall attain supreme nirvāṇa. || 89 ||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kāmākhyā-Kavaca," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The seventy-third chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Vetālabhairava, now hear the Mātṛkā-nyāsa."
By performing this very rite, even a human being indeed attains the state of a deity. || 1 ||
Speech is proclaimed as the goddess Brahmāṇī, the source of the Mātṛkās;
all their mantras, as well as the consonants and vowels, are likewise [her manifestations]. (2)
When joined with the lunar drop (candrabindu), they grant all desires;
as for the sages of the mother-mantras, Brahmā alone is proclaimed to be their [sage]. (3)
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī and the deity is Sarasvatī;
this [mantra] is for the primary purpose of purifying the body and accomplishing all desires and aims.
The application of the mantras is prescribed for the purpose of filling deficiencies;
the first group, beginning with 'ka', is traditionally held to be identical with the letter 'a'.
Having likewise uttered the form [of the mantra] externally with those syllables situated there joined with the lunar bindu,
one should likewise utter "namas" with both thumbs.
First, one should place the Mātṛkā-mantra upon both thumbs.
The other consonant groups, along with the vowels, or whichever others are used in the ritual of placement (nyāsa),
all of them should be joined with the moon (the vowel *a*) and the bindu (anusvāra) in every respect.
The short *i*-vowel is [joined] with the *ca*-group, and likewise with the long *ī*-vowel ending.
One should properly place [the mantra] on the two index fingers as before, ending with *svāhā*,
using the short *u*-vowel together with the eight consonant groups (*aṣṭavarga*) and ending with the long *ū*-vowel.
One should correctly place the *vaṣaṭ* ending in the pair of middle fingers;
likewise, the *tavarga* beginning with *e* and ending with *ai*, as well as *huṃ*. (10)
O Bhairava, one should certainly place there, upon the pair of ring fingers,
the entire group of consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *au*, without exception.

One should place [the mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ* on the little finger for the accomplishment of one's purpose, using the groups beginning with the letter *a* and the letter *ya*, up to the letter *kṣa*.
Up to the word "iti," one should place [the syllables] on the two wrists and the backs of the hands;
one should employ the *vaṣaṭ* syllable in the remaining portion during the assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
One should place [the mantras] in the six limbs, beginning with the heart, in sequence as before,
using the six corresponding groups of consonants starting with 'a' (the gutturals) and so forth, in their respective order.
Again, in the same manner, one should place the mantras upon the feet, knees, thighs, and private parts, as well as on the two sides and the bladder, sequentially with the syllables as before.
One should likewise perform the placement with six [syllables] upon the two arms, the two hands, the hips, the navel, the abdomen, and also the two breasts. 16.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) as before with the six groups [of mantras] on the mouth, the chin, the cheeks, the two ears, the forehead, the shoulders, and the armpits. || 17 ||

In the pores of the skin, at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), in the anus, in the pair of shanks, in the nails, and in the soles of the feet—one should perform [the rite] as previously described. (18)
Thus, that best of men who performs the Mātṛkā-nyāsa becomes purified and fit for all sacrifices and acts of worship. (19)
Indeed, there exists no mantra anywhere superior to this,
which is meritorious, grants all desires, and bestows the supreme fourfold aims of life.
Having meditated upon the Goddess of Speech (Sarasvatī) in his heart and upon all the letters as her forms,
he should drink the water three times with the Mātṛkā mantras in their proper sequence.
He becomes eloquent, wise, intelligent, and is born as an excellent poet;
first, the learned one should recite the vowels joined with the moon-bindu (anusvāra). || 22 ||
Then, one should recite all the consonants alone,
from 'a' to 'kṣa', in this manner using inhalations and breath-retentions.
Taking water in the palm of the hand and reciting the mantra as many times as there are syllables,
one should consecrate that water and first drink it by means of inhalations (pūraka).
The second [time] with retention (kumbhaka), and the third with exhalations (recaka);
thus, having drunk the water three times in this manner, the wise one— || 25 ||
Having drunk [the water] at the three junctions of the day, consecrated with the Mātṛkā-mantra, one shall become firm-limbed, wise, and endowed with sons and grandsons. (26)
Water attains the state of poetry, and likewise all desires are fulfilled for one who constantly performs [the rite] consecrated with the Mātṛkā-mantra.
O highly fortunate one, by means of the practices of inhalation, retention, and exhalation, he who drinks water shall attain all his desires and be enriched with sons and grandsons. (28)
Having become a great poet in the world, powerful and of truthful valor,
and having become beloved everywhere, he shall attain liberation in the end.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or even a wife,
one brings them under control without long delay by drinking the water consecrated with the *mātṛkā* mantra.
The sequence for the ritual of placement (nyāsa) has been declared; however, here specifically is the sequence of the groups (vargas).
Then, one should perform the drinking of water according to the sequence of the syllables.
Whatever mantras belong to the deities, the sages, or even the rākṣasas,
those mantras are eternally established within the mantras of Mātṛkā.
This Mātṛkā-mantra is said to consist of all mantras, likewise to consist of all Vedas, and to bestow the fourfold aims of human life. || 33 ||
Thus, O son, I have described to you the wonderful nyāsa of the Mātṛkās;
now listen, O Vetālabhairava, to the classification of the mudrās.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Mātṛkānyāsa," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 73 ||
The seventy-fourth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"That Yonimudrā which was previously described in the classification of mudrās,"
The Yonimudrā is of eight kinds; that which is first has thus been described.
O Bhairava, the second is the Khecarī Mudrā of Kāmākhyā;
know that to be a wondrous secret by which Caṇḍikā is pleased.
One should place the right ring finger upon the left index finger; one should likewise place the left ring finger upon the right index finger. (3)
One should likewise encircle those two with the index fingers, each preceding the other;
having placed the pair in the middle, one should position them on the upper part of the ring fingers.
From the joining of the tips of those [two fingers], and likewise with the little fingers,
one should place the thumbs at their roots, joined precisely by their tips.
This is your Khecarī-yoni; indeed, the Yonimudrā bestows all desires. If this very same [mudrā] is applied by joining the two little fingers downward, it is joined [as such].
This is known as the *Uhyayoni* [mudrā], which bestows satisfaction upon Kāmeśvarī;
it is formed by interlacing the two little fingers and the two ring fingers of the hands as before.
Then, having joined them at the lower part, in the middle, and likewise at the top—
if one joins their tips with one another, [it becomes a specific mudrā].
Having placed the middle finger in the middle [of the ring finger] and likewise the thumb at the tip, one should join them;
this is declared to be the Onistriśāṅkurī mudrā, which is Tripurā, always bestowing satisfaction.
