Likewise, one should encircle the two middle fingers as before,
and having placed the two ring fingers in front, one should place the two thumbs at the roots of those [two].
This mudrā is called Śāradī; it bestows satisfaction upon Śāradā.
It is declared to be the Mūlayoni within the scope of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Having joined the hands by placing the index and ring fingers in the middle and the little fingers in sequence, starting from the base of the little fingers; || 12 ||
Having inserted the tip of the thumb [into the mouth], it is proclaimed as the Great Yoni (mahāyoni).
Then, having encircled the two thumbs and joined the fingers of the hands together, [one forms the seal]. 13.
One should form two hands there with the tips [of the fingers] meeting while the middle is hollow;
this is the womb of the Yoginīs, which brings delight to the Yoginīs. (14)
These eight are declared to be the wombs dear to Kāmeśvarī;
through their various forms, they grant satisfaction even to other deities. (15)
Whether on a journey, in matters of war, in verbal debate, or in a quarrel,
he who remembers these eight wombs shall possess eternal victory.
These other [mantras] are declared for the rites of dismissal, worship, and recollection according to the distinction of their functions, as well as for the worship of Caṇḍikā. (17)
These wombs have been described in order for the sequential emission;
now hear from me the secret [teaching] regarding the left and right, and the purification of the mantra.
That which is performed by means of mantra, being the supreme mantra pertaining to the body, is called "the secret" (rahasya) by those skilled in mantras among all mantras. (19)
Within the petals of the hexagonal mandala of Kāmākhyā,
one should write the root mantra three times, positioned above each of the three junctions.
Furthermore, one should draw the threefold figures of Śakra, Hara, and likewise Madana together at the three lower joints upon the birch bark.
Taking up a thousand [beads] with his right hand,
and likewise taking up a garland, he should mutter [the mantra] while facing north.
The best of practitioners should wear this written yantra on their right arm or on the upper arm;
by doing so at the conclusion of the recitation, one shall become victorious over all. || 23 ||
Long-lived, bringing all things under his control, and possessing abundance of wealth and grain,
he who dies in the house of the Goddess goes forth with an intellect disciplined by the Yantra.
Then, having written [the mantra] upon birch-bark leaves with dissolved liquid lac within the eight petals surrounding the interior hexagon.
In the sequence starting from the north, one should place the eight syllables associated with the Vaiṣṇava Tantra in the middle portion, and as before, the Kāmarāja [Kaula] mantra.
One should draw three lines from the tip of the triangle of the seed-syllable of the eye;
having thus fashioned the yantra in three parts, one should hold it in the left hand. (27)
Taking the rosary in his right hand, he should mutter [the mantra] three thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, he should unweariedly perform meditation on the form of Vaiṣṇavī.
After performing a thousand breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), one should wear that supreme yantra written [therein] around the neck; by that means, one shall be victorious over all. || 29 ||
The prince shall become king, and another shall be his minister;
he shall be a learned man, a king among brahmins, or perhaps a poet and an eloquent speaker. (30)
From Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, or indeed from any other [source], no defeat ever occurs for one who possesses that knowledge. || 31 ||
Long-lived, strong, and wise, one shall attain liberation upon death;
having fashioned a complete mandala endowed with eight petals. || 32 ||
On the bark of a birch tree, one should draw a hexagon with the resin of the śrīphala fruit; then, within that [hexagon], one should draw [the syllables] upon its three eastern-pointed corners.
One should write the syllables of Tripurā, with the "eye-seed" (netrabīja) below; furthermore, on the eight petals, one should write those consonants associated with the Vaiṣṇava-tantra.
One should likewise inscribe the eight syllables upon all four doors, and with a one-pointed mind, [inscribe them] in the six corners according to the sequence starting from the northern corner. (35)
Having held that Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra in his right hand,
he should recite it ten thousand times with a restrained mind over the course of three days.
Having performed three thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), the wise man, filled with joy,
should hold [the breath] on his head at the time of twilight on the ninth lunar day.
He will live for a hundred years, subduing all, wise, and the best among the learned;
endowed with strength, heroism, wealth, and sovereignty, he shall indeed be a king. (38)
The wise man constantly beholds Mahāmāyā, Kāmākhyā, and Tripurā before his very eyes, as well as Mahocchvāsā and Śāradā. (39)
Whether they be lions, tigers, serpents, or any other predators, all of them, having encountered his body, undoubtedly perish; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Therefore, there exists no cause for victory in battle other than this [knowledge] derived from the treatises;
such a thing is not found in the three worlds. Hence, one should indeed construct the yantra.
Having first reached the temple of the Goddess, one shall thereafter attain liberation;
[these are] Mahāmāyā, she known as Śāradā, Kāmākhyā, and likewise Tripurā.
Likewise, for those mantras that possess great power,
one should further draw an eight-petaled maṇḍala in their midst.
Having first written down the previously mentioned collection of mantras equally as before,
one should write another pair at the location of the door and on the lips according to the syllables.
Having made that cloth into an upper garment using white silken cloths and the juices of the *vahniśikha* plant, one should perform the recitation of the mantra.
Having observed a fast and being purified, preceded by the placement of the *mātṛkās* (the alphabet),
he should indeed perform five thousand repetitions for each of the five groups [of consonants].
Having recited [the mantra] for five days,
one should perform at the conclusion thereof five thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) over those same five days.
First, one should perform the Kavaca-nyāsa of Kātyāyanī;
thereafter, with the Mātṛkā-mantras, preceded by the restraint of the breath (śvāsa).
One should drink the milk of a tawny cow three times while remaining awake during that night;
thus, one who performs this rite upon the body with a white garment [attains success]. (49)
He attains perfection here and goes to the world of the Goddess, he who wears an upper garment that has been consecrated with the mantra. (50)
O highly fortunate one, listen indeed to his power which is eternal:
weapons shall never enter his body at any time. (51)
Neither fire burns his body, nor do waters cause it to dissolve; nor do Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and other such malevolent beings [harm him]. (52)
Upon seeing that illustrious one, they indeed flee from fear;
and that best of practitioners may go everywhere unimpeded.
If a wise man, eloquent and indeed a king, should exert himself, he brings gods, monarchs, and other women under his control. (54)
Long-lived, highly fortunate, and possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain,
he becomes a poet endowed with wisdom and remains invincible to his enemies.
In whatever city he may dwell, there indeed no thunderbolt falls; neither mercury, nor the body, nor even weapons released by a firm hand can harm him. (56)
O Bhairava, they do not constantly slay this [person] everywhere;
O Bhairava, they are constantly offending him everywhere. 57.
Neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments shall ever arise for him;
that wise son of the Goddess, upon death, shall attain liberation. 58.
That devoted wife who maintains the household as a machine under the direction of her husband attains the sovereignty of her sons; she shall become a long-lived woman. (59)
Each one individually, combined together, and accompanied by the *āvardhana*,
these twenty mechanical devices have indeed been described by me here in sequence.
Having understood each of these individually, whoever should always place them in their heart, or having written all the yantras, should wear them around the neck; || 61 ||
By the power of this [act], he is born here on earth as a lord of the gods (devendra);
he instantly obtains all the fruits previously mentioned,
and he constantly beholds all three worlds, even though they are concealed from view.
Thus, having inscribed upon a white cloth the thousand [mantras] previously mentioned, together with all eight groups of yantras, upon one's own body—
By wearing it constantly, one shall indeed obtain everything. || 63 ||
He who has placed the syllables of the mantra first created by the Goddess within his heart should, at the time of battle, fix them upon his armor as his chosen abode.
And eight [are distinguished] by way of the external limbs. || 64 ||

One should draw the image of Hari on the throat, the ritual diagram (vidhi) on the chest, and Maheśvara accompanied by his son on the two breasts; likewise, one should draw Hara on the joints of the arms and Vaiṣṇavī.
And [he saw] Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī upon his two arms. || 65 ||
Having thus prepared this eight-limbed armor for his body, a man should meditate upon Śivā;
he should draw her as a tilaka-mark upon his forehead.
This is the supreme yantra consisting of all the syllables of the mantra.
Then, having placed his hand upon the eight sacred sites (tīrthas), he should mutter the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra eight times; thereafter, he may proceed to the battlefield.
That hero becomes my equal in battles;
just as blades of grass are consumed by fire, so too are the weapons of others rendered powerless before him.
Enemies flee from the wealthy man, and supplicants come for his riches;
from the foremost of lions, a tiger among men, he shall become heroic and powerful. (69)
O Bhairava, this secret of Kāmākhyā has been told;
now hear from me that of Tripurā among the principal tantras of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Of that [Vidyā], there are indeed thirteen million and twenty thousand mantras; among them, the first is known as Vāgbhava.
The second is called Kāmarāja, the third is Mohana,
and the fourth is proclaimed to be the Vāgbhava repeated.
The second is the seed-syllable of the eye (netrabīja), likewise the Vāgbhava syllable repeated twice;
that which is proclaimed as the first is [the fifth], consisting of four syllables.
The seed-syllable of the Eye is proclaimed as the first;
the second is the seed-syllable of Kāma, and likewise the third is Vāgbhava.
The mantra consisting of these three [syllables] is proclaimed as the sixth;
the seed-syllable of the eye (netrabīja) is the second, and by that, the [mantra] of Vāgbhava becomes the seventh.
Thus, that which begins with Vāgbhava is proclaimed as the eighth;
Vāgbhava and Kāmabīja are remembered as the ninth, [placed] upon the two eyes.
The first seed-syllable of desire is likewise [the first], and the tenth is the deluding one;
this eleventh is declared to be the Vāgbhava, beginning with the syllable Ḍāma.
The twelfth mantra has been proclaimed; now, for the remainder, listen with a one-pointed mind to this great Traipura mantra, that very splendor of Tripura. (78)
Its end is likewise its beginning, and fire [the letter Ra] is joined with the source of speech (Vāgbhava).
This is proclaimed as the first seed-syllable (bīja) of Tripurabhairavī. || 79 ||

The letter at the end of the first [syllable], the first letter of that [second syllable], and the vowel *śeṣa* (au) of the fire-syllable (*vahni*), joined with the fourth vowel, the bindu, and the moon (the nasal)—this is the second [mantra]. (80)
The "near-end" (upānta), its beginning (tadādi), the vowel remaining after the fire-syllable (vahniśeṣasvara), the conclusion (samāpti) joined with the bindu, and the third one joined [with it]. (81)
The man on earth who understands this truth is a jewel among men; he shall be superior to the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, or indeed equal to them.
These thirteen mantras have been declared as the most radiant among mantras;
they are proclaimed to be superior even to twenty thousand [others]. (83)
This is proclaimed as the first among twenty thousand [mantras];
O Bhairava, listen now to that mantra of Bālā Tripurā. 84.

The Vāgbhava [syllable] and the Kāmarāja [syllable], with the penultimate letter as the first [of the second part] and accompanied by the bindu, together with the completion of the remaining vowels—this is proclaimed as the mantra. (85)
This Tripurā Bālā has indeed been declared as "Middling" (Madhyā) previously;
the remaining one, this Tripurabhairavī, is declared to be "Radiant" (Tejasvinī).
The worship of Madhyā has been declared; now hear that of Bālā, as well as that of Tripurabhairavī, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments. 87.
Having pierced Śambhu with the Śakti, one should likewise pierce the Śakti;
for Śambhu, one should draw a six-cornered figure with filaments therein.
Just as it is in the door-mandala of the middle Tripurā, so too should it be made here; likewise, it should be drawn in the corners.
The rites for the removal of evil and the purification of the ground and other elements have been previously described in the Northern Tantra, as spoken at the seat (pīṭha) of Tripurā. 90.
In the worship of Kāmākhyā, the practitioner should perform everything that has been prescribed,
including the rites of burning and immersion, as well as the ritual handling of the vessel.
But everything else should be performed as before, just as in the worship of Kāmākhyā;
having performed the deposition of the body (dehanyāsa) here with the syllables of the mantra and its phonemes.
Then, with all the vowels as well as the consonants beginning with 'ka', one should contemplate the form [of the goddess], who has four arms, is red in color, and is adorned with red garments. (93)
In her right hands she holds a garland above and a supreme book below,
while with her two left hands she likewise bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
Resembling a thousand suns, three-eyed, and moving through the world,
she has a pair of full and lofty breasts and is seated upon a white corpse.
Her face is bright with a smile, and she is adorned with all ornaments;
on her head, chest, and waist, she wears three garlands of severed heads.
Threefold, adorned individually by those who have become threefold, with eyes rolling from intoxication and two lips red as blood. (97)
One should thus meditate upon the boon-granting goddess Tripurabhairavī;
for in the initial worship, she possesses the form of Bālā Tripurā.
The sequence has been stated regarding the yoga of the seats; now hear, O Bhairava, concerning the tantras and so forth.
She holds flower-arrows, a noose, and a flowery bow. (99)
And holding a noose while mounted upon a corpse, that young woman is known as Tripurā.
In the Manmatha-stotra, one should first recite the words "devīm vidmahe tripure. (100)
"Let us meditate upon you, Kāmeśvarī; may she, O Klinnā, impel that for us. This is the Tripura-gāyatrī, specifically for the purpose of invocation.

One should properly worship Bālā and the other Bhairavī with ritual bathing and other rites; whatever specific procedure exists for her regarding the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the subsequent rite [is now described]. 102.
Listen to all of that, along with the multitude of mantras, O Vetālabhairava:
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should contemplate the Supreme Guru. (103)
Then, one should worship one's own pure guru, and after that, Tripurabhairavī—four-armed, white in complexion, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a book. (104)
And she holds a rosary of beads in her left and right hands respectively,
seated upon an excellent throne inlaid with gold and jewels.
He wears a golden upper garment and golden earrings;
likewise, he should contemplate his own guru through meditation according to his [true] color. 106.
Having meditated upon Bhairavī, one should then rise and perform the friendly sipping of water (ācamana) as well as the cleansing of the teeth.
Then one should perform the morning bath, applying the Traipura sequence;
in all cases, whether for the mantras of the Goddess or even those of the Vedic tradition, [one should employ] Bhairavī.
One should constantly meditate upon Tripurā during the mantras of the deities in their proper sequence;
indeed, one should perform an immersion three times by means of the three seed-syllables (bījas) of Tripurā.
Among all the Bhairavas of the gods, one should always employ this [name] with its specific qualification; it must never be uttered without its qualification. 110.
Having recited the *Tripurabhairavī* mantra, "May the waters purify the earth," the Brahmin should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and likewise act according to the *Drupadā* verse.
One should always recite "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame" and "bhairavastu" during the rites of touching the clay. 112.
One should invoke the auspicious Bhairavī, who is Gāyatrī and the foremost of the Tripuras;
one should then present the water offering (arghya) to the Sun with the words, "To Mārtaṇḍabhairava."
The rays of light bear up that god Jātavedas, the Sun, so that everyone may behold him; one should utter the *Śeṣe Bhairava* [mantra]. 114.
One should employ [the mantra] at the beginning of the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites, saying: "May Brahmabhairava be satisfied.
At the invocation, one should personally address the ancestors as "the Bhairavas. (115)
"O Mother Bhairavī, may you be satisfied; O Father Bhairava, may you be satisfied.
One should also employ this [formula], preceded by "Tripurā," at the beginning of the libation (tarpaṇa). 116.
In rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Aśvamedha, wherever one may worship anyone,
there one should worship both the Goddess and Bhairava in the form of Bhairava.
Upon seeing a vessel of liquor, a woman dressed in red garments, or the head of a man, a twice-born man should meditate upon Bhairavī. (118)
Having seen young women who are exceedingly beautiful gathered together in one place, one should perform salutations and other rites for their pleasure, as [is done] for Tripurabhairavī. (119)
One should give with devotion while mentally contemplating Bhairavī, thinking:
"I accept Bhairavī; I am Bhairava, the receiver. (120)
In the sign of Virgo, the wise worshipper of Tripurā should meditate:
"Today I give the goddess Tripurabhairavī to Bhairava. (121)
Thus one should utter [the mantra] when giving away the daughter;
thereafter, the implements for her worship, the vessels, and so forth, are not for the worship of another.
The practitioner, a twice-born man, should never at any time consume fermented liquors and the like himself; however, he may have others offer wine to him once. 123.
Śūdras and others, however, should constantly offer the finest liquor;
in this manner, through the left-handed path (vāmamārga), one should worship Tripurabhairavī.
One should worship Bālā by means of both the left and right paths, as well as the goddess Śmaśānabhairavī and likewise Ugratārā. (125)
Ucchiṣṭabhairavī, Caṇḍī, and likewise Tripurabhairavī—these are to be worshipped with the left-hand mode (vāmamārga), without the right-hand manner. 126.
One should worship the sages, the gods, the ancestors, humans, and the hosts of elemental beings with the five sacrifices; thus one shall discharge one's debts. (127)
Performing worship according to the prescribed rules through ritual bathing and giving— that which is performed along with its secret essence is here called *dākṣiṇya*.
Because he is skillful (dakṣiṇa) toward all, beginning with the ancestors and the gods, and because the goddess Dakṣiṇā belongs to him, he is therefore called Dakṣiṇa. || 129 ||
Furthermore, she who, being worshipped by the gods and others from of old,
herself receives her portion of the sacrifice, is proclaimed as Āmā.
O son, even the worshipper there may always be a Vāmācārī;
he may or may not perform the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) when engaged in the worship of the Vāmā path.
For since the well takes a share of the worship intended for another,
whatever one worships with left-handed (vāmācāra) dispositions shall not serve as a clearing of that debt.
And for the ancestors, gods, humans, and others, it may sometimes arise;
having practiced the Tripurā-yoga, he becomes endowed with that yoga. (133)
If one becomes truly wise, then one shall attain liberation;
yet that liberation arises here only after a long time, again and again.
O Bhairava, one who is overcome by the sins arising from the non-clearance of debts may yet be endowed with happiness and sovereignty in this world, and be beloved everywhere. (135)
Shining with a body as beautiful as the god of love, he brought the king, along with his entire kingdom, under his control on all sides. (136)
He deluded all the women, and they were all overwhelmed by intoxication;
[he likewise deluded] lions, tigers, hyenas, and bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas. || 137 ||
Then, rising with the speed of the wind, he wanders about bringing [them] under his control—
whether it be the young goddess Tripurā, or the middle one, or even Bhairavī.
Whether one who worships with supreme devotion, or one whose form resembles that of Bāṇa, should worship Kāmeśvarī known as Kāmākhya according to their desire. || 139 ||
Whether through courtesy or through a contrary disposition, one shall attain success in every way;
[one should worship] Mahāmāyā, Śāradā, and likewise Śailaputrī. (140)
In whatever manner one may worship, it should be done solely out of courtesy; for he who worships Mahāmāyā without a state of courtesy [is deficient]. 141.
That sinner falls from the heavenly worlds and becomes afflicted by disease;
as for the other goddesses previously mentioned, such as Śivadūtī and the rest— || 142 ||
May they protect you both out of courtesy; indeed, they are to be honored by practitioners.
However, that worshipper who is a Vāmācārin is excluded from the others. || 143 ||
One should be a worshiper of all [these goddesses], for by that reason the right [hand] is supreme.
Now, O Bhairava, hear the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Tripurabhairavī. 144.
By the mere performance of this nyāsa, a man becomes like a god;
Dakṣiṇa is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra of the Bhairavī Tantra. 145.
The goddess Tripurabhairavī is declared to have the Paṅkti meter;
her application is proclaimed to be in the accomplishment of desire and wealth. || 146 ||
One should place the syllable *ha* at the navel, place the syllable *sa* at the bladder,
place the syllable *va* on the penis, and likewise place the syllable *e* at the anus.
Again, one should place the first [syllable] on the two thighs, the second on the pair of knees,
the third on the two shanks, and the fourth on the two feet.
One should install the threefold deity beginning from the navel down to the feet;
one should indeed install the first [syllable] of the second seed-syllable right here at the beginning. 149.
One should place the second on the left breast and the third on the right breast;
having placed the fourth on the abdomen, one should place the fifth on the two sides.
Having placed the sixth [syllable] at the navel, one should also place it three times and again three times;
then, one should place the first [syllable] upon the head of the third seed-syllable.
Having placed the second at the hairline, one should place the third on the face;
having placed the fourth on the heart, it should be such that each is threefold.
The first of the first [syllables] is on the right thumb; the second is on the index finger; the third is on the middle finger; and the fourth is on the ring finger. 153.
The first [mudrā] is on the little finger; the second on the left thumb;
the third on the left index finger; and the fourth on the body of the middle finger. 154.
One should place the fifth on the ring finger (anāmā) and the sixth on the remaining [finger].
Having thus performed the placement in three ways, one should then [place] the second seed-syllable.
Having formed pairs of fingers beginning with the thumbs on both hands,
the wise practitioner should sequentially place the third seed-syllables.
One should place all the seeds in a mass upon the two little fingers;
having placed the first on the palms, one should place the second on the backs of the hands.
Then, having given three claps of the hands, one should perform the encircling with the third [mudrā] at the ears, the chin, the cheeks, the mouth, the eyes, and likewise the nose. (158)
And on the two shoulders, the elbows, the abdomen, the head of the penis, the two feet, the two sides, the heart, and the pair of breasts. (159)
Furthermore, it should be placed again in the region of the throat according to the sequence of the mantra-syllables;
one should place [the mantra] on the *liṅga* with "Obeisance to Rati," preceded by the *vāgbhava* syllable.
One should then place [the mantra] "oṃ klīṃ prītyai namaḥ" at the heart;
thereafter, the third [syllable], "manobhavāya," should be placed between the eyebrows. || 161 ||
One should place the seed-syllable of Tripurā for the immediate attainment of divinity:
"Oṃ Īṃ, to the one whose form is Īśāna, and then indeed to Manobhava. (162)
Having thus recited up to the end of "namaḥ," one should again place Īśāna on the head;
and likewise, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face with the seed-syllable Makaradhvaja.
One should indeed place the terrible Kandarpa at the heart with the first seed-syllable;
or else, one should place Vāmadeva and Manmatha at the penis.
One should place Sadyojāta on the two feet and Kāmadeva; likewise, the syllable *o*, the syllable *ha*, and the letter *ra* joined together in one place. (165)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the directions beginning with Īśāna using these five mantras: the final vowel [ṃ] preceded by the vāgbhava [aiṃ], combined with the five short vowels. 166.
The faces have been described previously; one should then place them starting from the east, above one's own face, in the south and north, and finally in the west.
One should again place the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using the long vowels as the first syllables;
thereafter, one should assign the five arrows to the head and other parts.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ sauṃ; one should then place [the mantra] for melting upon the head.
Next, one should utter: "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the arrow of agitation at the feet. || 169 ||

Oṃ klīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ; having completed [the rite] with the half-moons at the end of the six syllables, one should place [the mantra] for subjugation on the mouth and for enchantment on the linga. || 170 ||
Likewise, one should sequentially place the *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) and the arrow upon the heart with mantras;
beginning with the *vāgbhava* [syllable] and ending with the letter *ka*, it is accompanied by the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
In this context, the remaining vowel *triḥ* (the letter *i*) joined with the half-moon (*candrārdha*) and the bindu constitutes [the fifth mantra].
With these five mantras, one should worship the eight Śaktis beginning with *krā*.
Furthermore, the knower of mantras should again place [the goddesses] in these eight locations:
Subhagā, Bhagā, and the third, the goddess Bhagarūpiṇī.
Then Bhagamālā is the fourth; after that, Anaṅgakusumā, then Anaṅgamekhalā, and likewise Anaṅgamadanā. || 174 ||
And likewise the goddess Aṣṭamī, slow with the intoxication of her amorous play—
one should meditate upon these according to their forms, just like Tripurabhairavī.
The eight Śaktis should be installed here upon the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the face, the ears, the neck, the heart, the navel, and the genitals.
On the head, the forehead, the pair of eyebrows, the ears, and the two eyes;
then on the two cheeks, the nose, the row of teeth, and likewise on the mouth. (177)
One should place the fourteen vowels upon these fourteen locations:
on the chin, then on the neck, on the region of the throat, and on the two sides. (178)
On the two breasts, the two armpits, the two elbows, and likewise on the hands;
on the two backs, the navel, the penis, and likewise on the two thighs. (179)

One should place the letters beginning with 'ka', each corresponding to a single mātrā, upon the two kneecaps, the two calves, the two buttocks, the roots of the feet, and the two big toes of the feet. (180)
On the girdle, at the region of the neck, from the portion of the arm ornaments, on the ring, on the garland, on the earring, and likewise on the hair-braid. (181)
Furthermore, the syllables beginning with 'ya' should be placed in the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) in sequence;
likewise, the three mantra-syllables should again be joined together.
Having arranged the mantras in reverse order, three times each upon the head,
[one should place] Amṛtā, Yoginī, and Viśvayoginī according to the sequence of the syllables.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the three seed-syllables on the head, the arms, and likewise the heart,
the wise knower of mantras should begin the worship as before.
One should worship the Goddess as before, excluding the deities of the seats; specifically, one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Suvabhagā and Krāntā. 185.
One should visualize [the goddesses] in the eight directions of the mandala, beginning with the east;
at the tip of the triangle, the three mothers, Amṛtā and the others, are to be worshipped. (186)
Then again, one should worship the eight ornaments in the center;
O Bhairava, [worship] my faces beginning with Īśāna, starting from the center. (187)
One should likewise worship there even those headed by Manobhava;
furthermore, the sequence for that worship is the same as that previously described.
That alone should be constantly accepted during the worship of Tripurā;
hear now, O Bhairavī, about this Goddess who wears the remains of offerings (nirmālya). 189.
Having performed the dismissal in the northern direction and discarded the floral remains (nirmālya),
one should worship that goddess Tripurabhairavī as the Trimūrti.

The practitioner should never recite fewer than thirty [times]. Furthermore, one should always offer flowers and other offerings using the three fingers— the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger— and should perform the rosary with a triple-strand cord.
Having mounted a leather seat, one should then place both feet behind it. || 192 ||
In a secluded place, the practitioner, with a one-pointed mind, should perform worship;
whatever flowers and other offerings or food oblations may be available, the wise practitioner should always present them using the left hand as the primary means. (193)
Tripurā is said to have three voids; if she is not worshipped correctly, [the result is as follows]. (194)
For indeed, a censured disease inevitably arises in the body;
likewise, sons, wives, servants, and others truly become dependent upon one. (195)
If she is worshipped otherwise, there will be a blow from a weapon for oneself and the loss of life, without a doubt; thus, she bestows three wounds.
O Vetālabhairava, this goddess Tripurā, as well as the others previously mentioned, constantly possesses these various modes in their entirety. (197)
All illusions belong to Bhairavī, who is the yogic sleep (yoganidrā) and the mother of the universe; through her many manifestations in the form of the phenomenal world, she herself sports. || 198 ||
Mahāmāyā is the primordial source; from her came Śāradā in ancient times, then Umā, the daughter of the Mountain; and after that, these [goddesses] who are dear to me. (199)
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, and the others, as well as Triśurā and the rest—of them too, I am always the one who assumes the form of Mahābhairava. (200)
The wise leader should dwell constantly with them at all times.
Previously, I have already proclaimed the mantra of my form as Bhairava. (201)
The form of Tripurā has been described in the rites of worship; this is remembered as the sequence: "We know Mahābhairava; we meditate upon Kālarudra. (202)
May that Bhairava, our desire, who is ever moistening, impel us.
This Gāyatrī of the form of Bhairava is established within me. (203)
Just as this body of Mahābhairava was assumed by me for the purpose of eating meat, wine, and the like according to my desire, so too [is it] in the enjoyment of sexual pleasure with women. (204)
But this [deity] is always to be worshipped with wine and other offerings due to his left-handed nature;
for even the body of Brahmā is "left-handed" (vāma) for the sake of consuming meat, wine, and so forth. (205)
He who is the propagator of the Cārvāka and other [heretical] doctrines was made known by the name Mahāmoha;
he is the form of Viṣṇu consisting of the Vāmā energy, called Narasiṃha. (206)
She, however, should always be worshipped by the wise with both right-hand and left-hand rituals;
likewise is the form of Bālagopāla, still enveloped in the fetal membrane.
Consuming liquor and meat, indulgent in enjoyments, and always lustful toward women—these are remembered as the many *vāmikā* forms of the goddess Caṇḍikā. (208)
The form of Lakṣmī known as Vāmikā is said to be Dahanabhairavī;
she is the one who brought about the burning of cities, villages, and houses by fire.
If Mahālakṣmī has not been worshipped, one should worship her at the threshold. || 209 ||
Vāgbhairavī is declared to be the form of Sarasvatī as Vāmikā. || 210 ||
Her mantra has been declared previously; she is remembered as being white in color.
Now, the form and meditation of the middle Tripurā are described here.
O Bhairava, the sequence of worship has been described in exactly the same way everywhere;
the form of the Sun is celebrated by the name Mārtaṇḍabhairava. (212)
Agnivetāla is said to belong to Gaṇeśa, as is the one named Vāmana;
these are especially to be worshipped with a humble (vāmya) disposition.

The first [syllable] is threefold as before; likewise, with the letters na, ma, ya, ra, la, va, and those ending in v (va), with double consonants (dvirepha) everywhere, it is formed in such and such a manner.
The remaining [consonants] are proclaimed to precede the anusvāra and visarga;
however, in the middle [of the line], they are pure [consonants] preceded by the anusvāra and visarga. (215)

Subsequently, that which occurs through the sequence of two or three, or indeed by means of a single syllable—whether individually or collectively, and joined with the letters beginning with *da*—[is the name]. (216)
Likewise, by means of the syllables of the first [deity] Tripurā joined together as a mantra, and similarly by the syllables of Tripurabhairavī joined as a mantra; || 217 ||
Having performed [the rite] three times with fourteen [syllables], one should scatter the three beginning with *ḍa*.
Having doubled the second [group], one should join it at the end and at the beginning of the remainder. (218)
There are twenty thousand [verses], and thirteen remain;
then the first of the first is proclaimed, and the third begins with the Vāgbhava syllable.
And thus, having understood this supreme quartet of mantras, a person who is devoted shall attain all desires. (220)
O Bhairava, he who recites this entire collection of mantras even once goes, upon death, directly to the city of the Goddess.
Having first performed the ritual placement according to his desire, the practitioner, for three days,
should contemplate with his mind the goddess Tripurabhairavī in her entirety.
Having obtained all desires, he who resembles the God of Love in his own form shall become a righteous king; as a Brahmin, he shall become a sovereign among the twice-born.
Indeed, one whose body has been afflicted by piśācas and other such spirits always becomes free from disease, long-lived, and strong. (224)
Thus has this sequence been proclaimed by me as Tripurabhairavī;
however, there are sixteen thousand [mantras] of the great goddess Vaiṣṇavī.
Listen again, O Bhairava, with a mind one-pointedly focused on Śiva, to the mantras:
namely, one thousand and eight, sixty-four, and three.
These mantras were proclaimed by the Great Goddess according to the distinctions of their forms;
they are doubled again by means of the anusvāra and visarga, and these are equal once more.

Furthermore, the knower of mantras should constantly extract [the syllables] from the conjunction of the *kādi* consonants, both upwards and downwards in their reversed order, by means of two and three [syllables]. 228.
Then, having performed eight [recitations] for each [of the syllables], combined both collectively and individually—
with the individual consonants as well as those with vowels, and including the anusvāras and visargas— 229.
Even by means of those [elements] alone, and likewise by their pairwise combinations therein,
there are thus up to one hundred and eight [varieties] through the occurrence of various conjunctions.
O Vetālabhairava, the mantras of the Goddess are known to be eleven thousand six hundred in number, according to the sequence.
Having understood those [mantras] of Vaiṣṇavī which have been declared by me in both collective and individual forms, a human being goes toward my very abode.
O Bhairava, he who recites sixteen thousand seed-syllables of the mantra just once on the eighth and ninth lunar days [attains success].
Meditating upon the form of Viṣṇu with a one-pointed mind, listen:
he shall become a king among men on earth, a highly joyful scholar, long-lived, an enjoyer of happiness, and preeminent in strength and vehicles. (234)
By reciting those very same [mantras] eightfold, one becomes a sovereign king;
upon death, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, and thereafter he shall attain liberation.
Thus, one who is free from faults through the multitude of all virtues,
a destroyer of impurities, and a possessor of excellent counsel for the increase of prosperity— such a person,
being a constant knower of everything regarding these two, becomes eternally so.
And he becomes one who has conquered his enemies, liberated from disease and sorrow. || 236 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter in the *Śrī-Kālikā-Purāṇa*, in the section on the threefold manifestation of Tripurabhairavī-Bālā;
[now] the seventy-fifth chapter:
The Blessed Lord said:
The practitioner should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) with twelve lakhs of mantra recitations without leaf-offerings, for the sake of attaining his desired object. || 1 ||
The *jātī* flower, the *bakula*, the *mālatī* flower,
as well as the *nandyāvarta*, the *pāṭala*, and thereafter the white lotus.
Clarified butter, cooked rice, milk-rice, curd, milk, as well as honey, and parched grain with camphor—these indeed are the fourteen [offerings]. (3)
The [mantras] of Tripurā are proclaimed to arise from the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
moreover, when twelve hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the practitioner [attains success].
One should offer all these substances into the blazing fire;
having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
The mantra-practitioner should offer four oblations of clarified butter mixed with camphor;
for nine hundred thousand repetitions, he should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) using these substances.
When eight, six, or all [mantras] have been recited, one should perform [the rite] everywhere;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure, hexagonal, and three finger-breadths larger [in width].
The measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for Tripurā, for Madhyā, and indeed always for Bālā,
as well as for Tripurabhairavī, has thus been proclaimed.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be quadrangular and measure two cubits;
for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of Vaiṣṇava worship, it is prescribed to be increased by eight finger-breadths.
The sacrificial pit for Kāmākhyā is triangular and one cubit in measure; likewise, for all these [deities] of the manifold world, it is according to their respective [forms].
O my son, one should duly consecrate the fire for the rite dedicated to Viṣṇu;
likewise, O my son, one should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices for Kāmākhyā.
First, one should offer fourteen oblations into the increased fire for Tripurabhairavī: four and then ten.
Thereafter, however, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) three hundred and eight times with the root mantra,
or nine hundred times with that same mantra.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer a bali-oblation with a Vaiṣṇava mantra;
therein, gems, camphor, and gold constitute the teacher's fee.
If [the prescribed materials] are not available, one should perform the preliminary rite for the Goddess with curd, flowers, clarified butter, and parched grain;
if they are available, one should offer oblations according to the ritual rules using the fourteen substances.
O Vetālabhairava, hear the secret of its yantra, by performing which the best of men obtains all his desires. (16)
Having constructed a hexagonal maṇḍala, one should write there the three-syllable mantra of Tripurabhairavī in three corners, and below that [mantra].
One should then write the three seed-syllables of the primordial Tripurā;
having written the three middle seed-syllables in the center of the pedestal-diagram (pīṭhayantra), [one should proceed].
Then, one should wrap it three times with all the letters of the alphabet;
having written it with lac juice, one should subsequently encase it with the three metals.
That should be worn constantly on the head; by that, one becomes victorious over all, always endowed with beauty, strength, eloquence, wealth, and jewels. (20)
He is born long-lived, an enjoyer of sensual pleasures, and possessed of good offspring;
having written a single seed-syllable in the middle, and another above and likewise below.
O Vetālabhairava, these six mantras of the sixfold [deities], beginning with the primordial Tripurā and likewise Bhairavī, are to be applied in their proper sequence.
Having inscribed it as before and then wrapped it once with the three metals,
[one should place it] on the left arm, the right arm, the heart, the throat, and likewise on the hand.
These [mantras] should be worn on the head in sequence; their respective fruits are the attainment of prosperity, good fortune, paralysis, subjugation, and enchantment. (24)
Furthermore, O Bhairava, there will undoubtedly be poetic skill everywhere regarding the Yantras, Mantras, and Tantras of the Tripura tradition.
He [attains] five or six thousand [verses] through the streams of mantras tripled;
having known that, the wise worshipper does not suffer in this world or the next.

That which is the preeminent Tripura, whose state is unshakable by floods of mantras and tantric spells; which is not to be given away even to Brahmins and others; which is the state free from fear; which bestows poetic inspiration;
which possesses the three aims of life and has three forms; and wherein all three gods reside in heaven—[that is this].
That flood of knowledge which is the fruit of all merit, known as the great Mahātripura, is well-established through those [streams]. || 27 ||
O Vetālabhairava, listen to the armor-mantra (kavaca) of Tripurā;
by knowing it correctly, the knower of mantras obtains the full fruit of worship. (28)
The ritual procedures (upacāras) that were previously described for worship are here proclaimed as the very same practice to be observed in daily worship (nityapūjana).
Neither I, nor Brahmā, nor Keśava, nor even Ananta with his many tongues, is ever capable of describing the greatness of this armor.
One does not encounter fear from flesh-eating beasts, nor even when overwhelmed by water;
by the mere recollection of this armor, one shall obtain all that is auspicious. (31)
Oṃ. Of this Tripurā-kavaca, Dakṣiṇa is said to be the seer (ṛṣi); the meter (chandas) is declared to be called Citrā, and the deity is the goddess Tripurabhairavī. 32.
O son, the application of the seeds of the one known as the primordial Tripurā is, in due order, for the accomplishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Previously, I have already proclaimed the names of the Vāgbhava and other [syllables], as well as the names of the seed-syllables (bījas) of Tripurabhairavī. (34)
Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and likewise Trailokyamohana. || 35 ||
May Vāgbhava protect my entire head; may Kāmarāja protect my fierce speech; may he protect all my desires fashioned by me; and may Īśvara always protect the entire aggregate of my senses.
Increasing the abundant splendor residing within the body, it is the cause of intelligence. || 36 ||
This yantra has indeed been declared by means of five syllables;
thereafter, my fierce and radiant mantra,
which consists of light and is eternally established in the Great One, may it spread within the heart in this tantra and produce excellent wisdom.
May Vāgbhava protect the foundation, and likewise may Kāmarāja protect the heart.
May the Enchanter of the Three Worlds protect [me] between the eyebrows and at the head. || 39 ||
May Bhairavī— the beloved one who knows the arts of the Vitata family,
the mother of all the worlds known as the burner of the city of Tripura—

This first one is Tripurā, while the middle one is the bestower of desires.

I am indeed always the illusion-less one, the great source, and the source of the universe;

One who is established in self, whose speech has ceased, and who is certain regarding defects, should utter the seed-syllable;

Just as one who is free from defects such as impurity is born, so too,

The placement (nyāsa) that has been taught must certainly not be abandoned; rather, one should perform it even more extensively.

Whether it be a Vaiṣṇava, a Raudra, or again a Mahābhāga mantra residing in the body during the worship of Mahāmāyā.

The mallikā, mālatī, kunda, vaka, droṇa, and white lotus; || 81 ||

she who is red in color and adorned with a garland of severed heads—91.

Likewise, the sixth mantra is for her in the description of the thirteen [deities].
O Bhairava, this [tradition] has been declared as always bringing about ease in the determination of the truth regarding the flood of poetic works and treatises. 93.
From this [seed-syllable], through its individual and combined forms and by means of the divisions such as *śukra* and *akta*,
there arise the sixty-four forms, or else the *vāgbhava* [syllable] from the *traipura*.
Mahāmāyā, the yogic sleep, the primordial source, the progenitor of the world;
she is the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, whose supreme nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance. (95)
O highly fortunate one, her very manifestations, beginning with Tripurā, have been introduced and described; for they are indeed eternally inherent within her own self.
Thus, O son, I have told you the captivating secret of the Great Goddess concerning the left and right [traditions]; now hear from me the accomplishment of the mantra.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Armor of Tripura," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
The seventy-sixth chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having first examined the purity of the mantra, one should receive the supreme mantra.
In that regard, the *siddha*, the *susiddha*, the *sādhya*, and the *śātrava*—mantra is said to be fourfold; know it by the distinction of its syllables. (2)
The eternal sequence of phonemes which was previously taught by me—
having first understood that, O Bhairava, listen now to my description of the *cakra* of the phonemes beginning with 'Mukha', known as the Vaiṣṇava Tantra. (3)
Those very syllables which constitute the root of the great mantra that was proclaimed should be augmented by others as well. || 4 ||
The letter *a*, the letter *ka*, likewise the letters *ca* and *ṭa*, the letters *ta* and *pa*, and the letter *ya* are proclaimed as the first members of the classes [of consonants]. (5)
A, Ā, I, Ī, U, Ū, Ṛ, Ṝ, Ḷ, and Ḹ—these are the short and long vowels;
likewise, Ai, O, Au, Visarga, Bindu, and so forth, as well as the Yājñika.
These vowels are proclaimed as being born within the sky (hvana);
the letters Kha, Ka, Ga, Gha, and Ṅa are proclaimed as the [first] class (varga). || 7 ||
The letter *ṭa* is traditionally taught as following the six letters beginning with *ya*, *ña*, *na*, *ka*, *ra*, and *ā*;
likewise, the letter *ḍa* follows the letter *u*, and it is also the very first letter of the word *bhairava*.
This third class, beginning with the labials, is proclaimed to end in the letter *ṇa*;
it consists of the letters *tha*, *da*, and the word *dharma* as its first member.
The fourth group is said to consist of the initial letters of the words *nava*, *eva*, and so forth; likewise, the initial letter of the word *phala* and the initial letter of the word *bahu*. (10)
The letter *bha* is said to be the fifth group, consisting of mind (*manas*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth;
likewise, there are the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. (11)
By these four groups, this sixth [chapter] is called Bhairava; the conjunction of the letters śa, ṣa, sa, ha, and the letter kṣa is known as Parivedaka.
O son, this seventh section on the remaining [groups], consisting of five [parts] through the combinations, unions, direct order, and reverse order, has been proclaimed.
O Bhairava, phonemes may occur at the beginning of a mantra-name or even in mere speech;
these phonemes bestow the four aims of life and likewise produce pleasure and pain.
Roga, Teja, Sampūjya, and Pūjakā are proclaimed [as the attendants];
and Ahaṃ, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Gāyatrī, and Brahmamātṛkā [are the deities]. || 15 ||
Furthermore, those who possess the nature of the lower Brahman bestow the bliss of the supreme Brahman;
one who is skilled in the lower Brahman attains the supreme Brahman. || 16 ||
Desiring to create, the Lord again brought forth the letters by his own will;
he emitted them from my mouth and indeed placed them in the mouth of Brahmā.
But I, O son, having established all the castes within the Bhairava Tantra, am increasing the path of knowledge which abounds in the letter 'A'. 18.
These letters which have been declared by me in the *Varṇaviniścaya* for the sake of discerning the purity of mantras— therefore, listen now to the *varṇacakra*.
First, one should place two lines representing the nature of Śakti and Śambhu;
in the middle of those, one should likewise place two lines representing the plane of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī.
Between those two lines, one should lay down two more lines equally spaced;
these are the lines for the spokes of that wheel, according to their number.
O Bhairava, four [vowels] should be placed in the midst of the vowels;
likewise, the distinct letters and the eight conjunctions (sandhis) have been proclaimed.
Its four rims are said to be located at the centers of its joints;
it is a wheel endowed with eight spokes and equipped with four rims.
The color-wheel (varṇacakra) is proclaimed as being joined with an outer enclosure,
according to the principle of the rising and setting of the zodiac signs beginning with Aries.
This very wheel shall be the cause of the increase of the glory of knowledge.
Having drawn this wheel upon level ground, facing north, || 25 ||
Facing east, being pure and bowing to his desired guru, he should write the letters;
he should write them in a clockwise direction upon that very [surface], following their proper sequence.
One should indeed write the letter *u* on the chest and also the letter *ra*;
however, among the vowels, one should avoid the long *a* and the letter *ī*.
Having written the collection of letters in a clockwise sequence, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', while omitting 'jha', 'ṭa', 'ña', and 'ṇa'. (28)
Taking the first letter of one's own name, one should perform the sequence of counting until the first letter of the mantra; therein, one should apply the [categories] beginning with "Siddha."
Success is achieved in the ninth, first, and fifth [houses]; the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) state is found in the sixth, second, and tenth;
and the "well-accomplished" (susiddha) is proclaimed to be in the third, seventh, and eleventh alone.
The *hātrava* is proclaimed to be in the twelfth, eighth, and fourth [notes];
through it, success is achieved by a perfected one (*siddha*) without delay, whereas that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) succeeds in time.
The enemy is destroyed step by step, and one who is well-perfected bestows accomplishment without delay;
this is the sequence of phonemes that has been declared for a mantra belonging to the southern tradition.
O Bhairava, listen here to the sequence regarding the mantras for the propitiation of Vāmī:
the pair ṛ and ḷ, as well as the letters ṅa, ña, ṇa, and na, are to be excluded from the range of phonemes.
There, the knower of mantras should write the syllables in the leftward sequence (vāmākrama) for Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, and the Praṇava of Grace (prasāda).
O Bhairava, for mantras of one or two syllables, as well as for all seed-syllables (bījas) intended for initiation, there is no need to consider [their] success or other such qualities.
One should not concern oneself with the *siddha* and other [categories]; rather, the ten [mantras] that are *vaśya* (subjugating) should be adopted.
Among them, the *susiddha*, which grants desires, should be accepted after considering the *sādhya* and *siddha* [categories]. (36)
The wise should not treat an enemy as one to be seized, for by being captured, he brings about calamity.
Whatever single-syllable mantra belongs to someone, that person is designated by its name. (37)
Combined with the moon and the bindu, that is called its seed-syllable (bīja). Likewise, Śakra is the letter *sa*, together with the half-moon and the bindu. (38)
That very [syllable] would be the seed of Śakra; one should apply it similarly elsewhere as well, in all cases of mantra-extractions, placed further and further forward. (39)
Even before this, another person stated the objection regarding the collection of Vaiṣṇava mantras consisting of sixteen thousand verses when it had not yet been mentioned. (40)
There, one beholds a wheel with sixteen spokes;
indeed, one beholds twenty thousand [spokes] of Tripurā.
In that place, a wheel with thirty-two spokes should always be drawn by the wise;
indeed, the accomplished one [should likewise draw] this great wheel with sixteen spokes and so forth. (42)
O son, one should perform [the rites] with additional lines within the purification of the mantra;
this, O son, has been described to you as the attainment of the mantra which grants all desired objects. (43)
He who correctly knows this, O son, shall be victorious and attain his desire; [he knows] the supreme secret through the various methods of application and so forth. (44)
I shall speak of that in brief; listen, O Vetāla Bhairava! The tooth of a winged cat is encased in its bark-like membrane. (45)
Having wrapped those three threads with the *nirmālya* of Viṣṇu using the Vaiṣṇavī mantra,
or having consecrated each one of them with its respective mantra, [one should wrap] the left thread.
Having taken up the first hundred mantras in his right hand,
he should then accumulate them on the eighth lunar day dedicated to Viṣṇu, with his senses restrained.
Therefore, the wise should hold the best of machines on the right arm;
from that, the twelve perfections will arise, provided the wearer does not neglect the *tritittilī*.
Victory in battles and debates, freedom from disease for the body, and constant subjugation of princes as well as kings. (49)
Bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas do not come within the range of our vision; yet, by meditating even once upon the subduer of women who are full of passion, they are brought under control. 50.

Placing his hand upon the head of the cat, he should recite the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra three hundred times and then establish it in his home.
O Bhairava, whatever woman, even one who is impure, should behold that cat,

even though the women in that household have died in childbirth, they will give birth to living sons.

And the fifth [category] consists of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) belonging to Caṇḍikā, who possesses five forms.
Having cooked the flesh of those three folds in a pot for three days,

One who has [these marks] on the forehead, the head, the throat, the two arms, the two hands, and likewise on the heart, is born radiant, a subduer of enemies, a poet, and eloquent. (60)
Having written the eight syllables of the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra in these locations, the wise knower of mantras [should place them]. (61)
On the eighth day, having become self-restrained, a man should first apply saffron, milk, the paste of sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, and excellent lac-dye on the ninth day.
Having placed his hand upon the Pratiṣṭhāna, the wise one should mutter the mantra eight times for each;
then, by the repetition of the mantras, he should subsequently worship Śivā.
Then, on that day, having offered three unadorned bracelets to the Goddess, he should begin the recitation of the mantra a thousand times according to its count.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having partaken of the sacrificial oblation, he should spend the night restrained;
O son, when this is performed once, his defeat in battle is certain.
May there never be [conflict] even once, nor [dispute] regarding doctrines according to the scriptures;
having acted thus only once, let it be so at the time of battle, however that may be.
A Kṣatriya should always draw this for victory in battles;
furthermore, this other eight-limbed battle is proclaimed as a secret. (67)
"By this very secret, you shall be victorious.
Thus we have told you everything that is auspicious, more secret than the secret. 68.
This mantra, which brings about happiness and prosperity and is accompanied by its yantras and tantras,
is that which all the gods constantly desire to hear, as they do nectar.
Thus has this been fully explained to you, O son Vetālabhairava;
having understood all this in its true essence, O son Bhairava, [you shall attain success]. 70.
Having attained all desires without exception, he shall eternally reach absolute liberation—
he who hears this being recited even once by the best of the gods.

endowed with long life and strength, he is always joyful and successful. He attains his desired object and reaches the abode of the Goddess. || 72 ||
Go to the sacred seat (pīṭha) called Nīlācala, located within Kāmarūpa. || 73 ||
Having bathed in the waters where the secret abode of Kāmākhyā resides—the place known as the Kubjikā-pīṭha—and where the Ākāśagaṅgā is located; 74.
"There, my sons, propitiate Mahāmāyā, who pervades the universe;
that goddess, being pleased, will soon become a granter of boons to us. (75)

Having spoken thus, he who was mounted upon a bull then abandoned his two sons, Vetāla and Bhairava, and vanished right there.
Then those two ascetics, having left Mount Nāṭaka, approached the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā. || 77 ||
But that sage, situated on the mountain of twilight, seeing those two sons of Hara approaching, honored them like his own disciples.
Then, following the instruction of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the two of them went to the great mountain Nīla, where Kāmākhyā resides.
Having gone there, the two high-souled ones took that goddess Mahāmāyā, who consists of the universe, who had been born within the sphere of the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Standing near the linga named Bhairava, which is of the nature of Śiva,
they bathed the excellent mandala upon the sacrificial ground with the celestial Gaṅgā.
Having performed the rites, those two tigers among men should mutter the supreme mantra;
having duly muttered that perfected eight-syllabled mantra according to the rules, they both [proceeded]. (82)
Likewise, for the Vetāla, there is that which is difficult to accomplish, numbering eight hundred thousand;
then, after three years, at the end of four hundred thousand [recitations].
With devotion, the two of them performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in three ways,
carrying out whatever was prescribed for worship in the Uttara-tantra and in the Kalpa-texts.
Having completed their third year, the two of them performed all of that, including the worship of Kāmākhyā, Tripura, and others as well. (85)
Then, having performed the pilgrimage to the sacred seats (pīṭhas) once according to the prescribed rites,
those two sons of Hara remained thus, with their armor fastened and the ritual placements (nyāsa) completed.
Then Mahāmāyā, who is identical with the universe, being deeply pleased, favored those two as they remained absorbed in meditation, chanting prayers, and performing sacrifices.
Then, having burst through [the earth], the Śiva-linga became manifest;
once it had emerged, the Śiva-linga became threefold.
Then the Vetāla Bhairava beheld that goddess, as well as the triad consisting of Bhairava, Bhairavī, and Heruka. 89.
Just as she was seen within the state of meditation, so too was she seen outside;
having beheld her, whose every limb was beautiful and whose breasts were full and elevated. (90)
She has hands granting boons and fearlessness, holds a perfected thread and a sword, resembles a red lotus, and is seated upon a white corpse. 91.
Then, closing both eyes, Vetāla and Bhairava said repeatedly: "Save us, save us, O Mahāmāyā! (92)
Then, having been nourished by the splendor of that Great Goddess, those two were touched by Vaiṣṇavī with the tip of her hand of boons.

Then, having become gods, the two of them praised Śivā, who is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) and identical with the universe, with hymns and prostrations. || 95 ||
The Vetāla and Bhairava said:
Victory, victory, O Goddess! O you whose lotus feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods; O source of prosperity for the universe; O Girijā, who takes delight in the sport of the moon-crested Lord!

O Goddess, who surpasses the splendor of the sun, the moon, and the Vahlika king with Your three eyes; O Pure One, born from the lotus, who causes the mass of red passion to dissolve through the devotion of the curved brow of Your central eye! 96.

O you whose beautiful countenance is like ten million skulls from the edge of the wheel of command, O peaceful one with the moon as your emblem! O you who possess the waves of yoga for the enjoyment of the body of manifold illusions!
In the movement of Padmavasu, one should begin from the beginning. || 97 ||
To the one intent on maintaining the auspicious *suṣumṇā*, the beloved of the birds dwelling within the central channel (*nāḍī*) that has been brought [under control],
whose universal form shines forth through the jewels held in his hands—
O you who abide in the great vehicle, the bearer of the six chakras! || 98 ||
To her whose beautiful, full, and lofty breasts, kissing the sixteen cakras from the base upward, embrace the serpent-king situated at the center of the earth;

who is endowed with four arms holding the matted hair, the excellent boon-granting gesture, the sword, and the lotus that has destroyed the mud of sins; To her who is joined with the root-jewel; [I bow].
For the sake of dispelling the fragmentation of the essential mercury bound by the yoga of the mantras and tantras of the *Jñānatālaka*,
[this work] is the jewel-necklace of the single supreme body of the reality of the Self.
O you who delight in the white spirits of the discernment of the aphorisms on liberation! 99.
For the sake of pacifying the sorrows of those separated from their lovers through the waves of passion arising from the union of all the essences of jewels,
and for the purpose of contemplating the state of being a servant to the dancing throngs of *yoginīs*—

O Lord whose body-cavity is embraced by the Lord of the Gods, whose hair is disheveled and whose face is delighted with the sport of boisterous laughter; O Master of the multitude of ornaments, foremost among which are necklaces and bracelets fastened and bound!
Give [it], O Goddess of pure intellect, who releases one from the bonds of grieving for the departed and destroys all evil! 100.
I bow to the auspicious Mahāmāyā, who embodies all vidyās, who is secret, who consists of mantra and yantra, and who is celebrated in both the world and the Veda. 101.

I bow to you, who consist of the higher and the lower, who are eternal, who abide uniquely as the support for that which is to be accomplished, who bestow the joy of desire, who are beloved, and who are composed of the entire universe.
O Goddess, who causes the world to flourish as one, you whose form is half-red by your power and who are supremely unmanifested beyond all conceptual proliferation—salutations be to you! 103.
I bow to the auspicious Acyutā, who is known as Kāmākhyā, Nityarūpā, Mahāmāyā, and Sarasvatī; she who is Lakṣmī dwelling upon the chest of Viṣṇu.
O Pārvatī, salutations to you, who consist of mantras and yantras, and who possess sixteen thousand tantras; may they be mine. (105)
Aurva said:
Thus praised by those two, Mahāmāyā, the mother of the world, spoke joyfully: "Choose a boon, you two."
Having seen Mahāmāyā directly before them, as she was previously the object of their meditation, those two sons of Bharga spoke these excellent words: || 107 ||
Vaitāla and Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, with this very body, we pray for eternal service to you and to Śaṅkara, as long as the sun and moon endure. (108)
O Illusion, who art composed of the universe, we shall not choose any other boon from you;
otherwise, by our devotion to you alone, we shall remain in a mountain cave.
Aurva said:
Having been addressed thus by those two, Mahāmāyā, who pervades the universe,
replied, "So be it," and she said "It shall be so" again and again.
Thus, having declared that supernatural power (ṛddhi) is the sustainer of the world, the auspicious goddess pressed her own two nipples and caused two streams of milk to flow forth.
Then, O great king, he caused the terrifying Vetāla to drink the milk that had issued forth; and as he drank it, the two of them also drank it at that time.
Having drunk that milk, they then attained eternal divinity;
they became free from old age and death, exceedingly radiant and auspicious.
Her milk was indeed nectar; having drunk it, those two became possessed of great strength. From that drinking of the ambrosia, Vaiṣṇavī then spoke to them.
O sons, may you both become lords of the hosts of the God of gods; and like Nandin, may you always remain as his constant gatekeepers.
Having spoken thus, Mahāmāyā, who consists of the universe, with the consent of Hara and accompanied by the host of Yoginīs, vanished on that very spot.
When she had vanished, the Vetāla and Bhairava then became joyful and supremely delighted, feeling that they had accomplished their purpose.
Then Hara, accompanied by the hosts of gods and his Pramathas,
arrived together with Vetāla and Bhairava, his two sons, in order to offer them the highest honor.
Having reached that mountain named Nīla, Mahādeva then revealed the entire sacred seat (pīṭha) according to its various locations.
Having seen Mahāmāyā directly before them as she was previously the object of their meditation, those two sons of Bharga spoke these excellent words: 107.
Vaitāla and Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, with this very body, we pray for eternal service to you and to Śaṅkara, as long as the sun and the moon endure. (108)
O Māyā, you who consist of the universe, let us not seek any other boon from you;
otherwise, we shall remain in a mountain cave solely through devotion to you.
Aurva said:
Having been addressed thus by those two, Mahāmāyā, who pervades the universe,
replied, "So be it," and said "It shall be so" again and again.
Thus, Siddhi, the sustainer of the world, was described; then, pressing her own two nipples, Śivā caused two streams of milk to flow forth.
Then, O great king, he caused the fierce Vetāla to drink the milk that had issued forth; and as he drank it, those two also drank it at that time.
Having drunk that milk, they then attained eternal divinity;
they became free from old age and death, exceedingly radiant, and auspicious.
Her milk was indeed nectar; having drunk it, those two became possessed of great strength. From that drinking of the ambrosia, Vaiṣṇavī then spoke to them.
O sons, may you both become the lords of the hosts of the God of gods, and may you always remain as his gatekeepers, like Nandin. 115.
Having spoken thus, Mahāmāyā, who pervades the universe, with the consent of Hara and accompanied by the host of Yoginīs, vanished on that very spot.
When she had vanished, the Vetāla and Bhairava then became joyful and supremely delighted, having accomplished their purpose.
Then Hara, accompanied by the hosts of gods and his Pramatha attendants,
arrived together with his two sons, Vetāla and Bhairava, in order to offer them the highest honor.
Having reached that mountain named Nīla, Mahādeva then revealed the entire sacred seat (pīṭha) according to its various locations.
Having shown him there the cave of Kāmākhyā, which is the source of the mind-born [god of love],
he then showed his own Cave of Desire (Kāmaguhā), his own parasol of shadow, and his own abode.
He also showed his own arrangement of the five forms,
as well as the entire seat of Kāmarūpa, which is composed of the deity.
The destroyer of Tripura showed them each one in succession:
first, the river named Karatoyā, which is the eternal Gaṅgā of Truth and is ever-auspicious.
[She is] composed of meritorious waters, pure, and flowing solely toward the southern ocean.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Siddhi by Vetāla and Bhairava," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. 76.
The seventy-seventh chapter.
Aurva said:
Then, to the northwest of Kāmarūpa, the Destroyer of Tripura [established his abode].
He revealed his own incomparable sign, known as Jalpīśa. || 1 ||
There, Nandin, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya) with his very same body. || 2 ||
There is the great Nandikuṇḍa, where in ancient times Nandin performed his ablutions;
having received boons, he drank the unsurpassed water there.
Having bathed and drunk there, that best of men, having accomplished his purpose,
goes to the abode of Hara and also to that of Nandin, who possesses great splendor.
Near her, not too far away,
stood the Great Goddess Siddheśvarī, who is the form of the womb, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and the essence of the universe.
Tryambaka revealed himself to the high-souled Bhairava,
where Nandin, by the command of the Moon-bearer, [encountered] Mahāmāyā.
Having worshipped with hymns of praise and prostrations, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
There, the Suvarṇamānasa is a captivating chief river.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon Nandin, that [lake] called Mānasa quickly became a lake;
it arrived even before Śambhu had begun his ascetic penance, by the command of Śambhu himself.
There is the auspicious river Jaṭodbhavā, which originates from the Himavat;
by bathing in it, a man obtains merit equal to that of the Gaṅgā.
In ancient times, at the time of Gaurī’s wedding, a water-consecration was performed by all the groups of mothers upon the matted locks of Bharga.
Because those ascetics (tāpasas) became [one] there, the river was thereafter named Jaṭodā.
Having bathed in it on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, a man who goes [to that place] shall attain liberation.
O best of men, one indeed attains a full lifespan and proceeds toward the abode of Śiva;
for that which was Gaṅgā during the Dvāpara age is the excellent river known as Triḥsrotas.
Originating from the Himalayas and emerging from the pure orb of the moon,
by bathing in her on the great full-moon day, one is not born again from a mother's womb.
Having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a man shall attain absolute liberation (kaivalya).
There is a river named Sitaprabhā, brought down by Mahādeva. 14.
That river, originating from the Himavat mountains, white in color, and flowing toward the ocean—on its tenth day of the bright fortnight, known as Daśaharā—[one should perform rites]. (15)
Having bathed at Viṣṇugṛha, a man indeed goes forth freed from sin;
there, previously situated to the east, was the river named Navatoyā.
For she purifies by constantly making herself ever-new;
therefore she is called Navatoyā, and she indeed originates from the Himavat. (17)
Having bathed in that [river] on the Mahāmāghī day, a man goes to the abode of the gods;
indeed, having bathed throughout the entire month of Māgha, he shall go to the house of Viṣṇu.
The lord of those rivers is indeed the river named Agada;
situated to the east of Pīṭha, it is meritorious and originates from the foot of Brahmā. || 19 ||
That [tirtha], originating from the Himavat and frequented by gods and gandharvas,
is such that by bathing and drinking there, a person shall go to the abode of Brahmā.

Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who performs ablutions in the great river named Agadā throughout the entire month of Kārttika; it is equal to that of one who has invested the sacred thread. || 21 ||
In this world, being free from disease and having attained supreme happiness,
he shall dwell in the abode of Brahmā and thereafter attain liberation.
Having bathed in the Nandikuṇḍa, a person should then offer food at night;
on the following day, he should go to the temple of Jalpīśa.
Having bathed there in the great river and having worshipped Jalpīśa,
one should spend that night restrained, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Then, when the following day has arrived, one should go to the auspicious Siddheśvarī;
one should worship her on the eighth lunar day and likewise observe a fast.
That goddess has four arms and full, elevated breasts; resembling a mass of vermilion, she holds a curved knife and a skull-bowl.
With her right and left hands she bestows fearlessness and the boon of grace;
her head is adorned with matted locks, and she stands upon a full-blown lotus. || 27 ||
The mantra for her is proclaimed to begin with the recitation of the five syllables;
the Kāmākhyā-tantra alone is declared to be the ritual manual (tantra) for her worship.
Having acted thus, the wise man is not born again in a womb;
even those Kṣatriyas who were previously terrified by the fear of Paraśurāma [the son of Jamadagni] [are liberated].

Having adopted the deceptive disguises of barbarians, they have gone for refuge to the Lord of Talkers; though they always speak the speech of barbarians, they are at all times speakers of the noble tongue.
Serving Jalpeśa, they protect that Hara;
they alone are his hosts, as enchanting as great kings. || 31 ||
Having thus satisfied them all, a person should worship Jalpīśa;
he has two arms, his hands bestow boons and fearlessness, and he resembles a kunda flower in color. (32)
One should worship the supreme deity with the mantra of Tatpuruṣa.
Thus is the merit-bestowing seat of the high-souled Jalpīśa;
knowing this, a man goes toward the supreme state of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 77 ||
The seventy-eighth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard this supreme dialogue between Śaṅkara and [the goddess],...
Of the great-souled Bhairava, accompanied by the Vetāla. || 1 ||
Furthermore, King Sagara, greatly delighted, questioned the high-minded sage Aurva once more with these excellent and truthful words.
Sagara said:
"O Blessed One, O best of sages, this which has been narrated is wonderful—
the configuration and the determination of the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa."
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, I wish to hear in detail the determination of the western, the middle, and the eastern regions. (4)
O tiger among sages, tell me all of that— how and in what manner Mahādeva and Ambikā are established therein— for I am eager to hear it.
Aurva said:
"O best of kings, the determination regarding the Vāyavya portion has been told;
now hear the determination concerning the western, northern, and middle regions of the mountain."
The river named Bahuroktā flows clockwise around Nanī and Karatoyā;
to the north lies Uttaraśrāvaṇī, and further east is Kāmarūpaka.
The cloud named Surasa is situated there, capable of assuming any form at will;
from it flows the river Bahurōkā, which bestows the merit of giving a bull.
Near the one named Surasa is the great bull, the Śivaliṅga;
there is the goddess Māheśvarī, whose form is the circle of the yoni.
Having bathed in the Bahurukā river and ascended the mountain of Surasā,
he worshipped Mahāvṛṣa and the Great Goddess Maheśvarī.
One who has shaken off evil and conquered the pairs of opposites is not born again in a womb;
he becomes four-armed, mounted upon a bull, and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident.
Resembling pure crystal, wearing matted locks, and possessing great virility—
his worship is proclaimed to be performed with the mantra of Aghora.
The essential nature of Kāmeśvarī is proclaimed to be that of Māheśvarī;
likewise, her worship bestows fruit in exactly the same manner.
There is the Vasiṣṭha-kuṇḍa, frequented by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
it was there that Vasiṣṭha stood when he was restrained by Naraka.
Before reaching the cloud named Nīla,
which was most excellent in its roar, he created there a pool for his own ablution, which is worshipped by hosts of gods.
Having bathed there, a person goes to the back of the celestial realm (nākapṛṣṭha) according to his desire.
To the east of Surasas is the mountain named Kṛttivāsas.
In ancient times, Kṛttivāsas himself dwelt there together with Satī;
having bathed in the river there called Candrikā, one would go to heaven. (17)
Having bathed in the Candrikā and worshipped Kṛttivāsas on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, a man shall become free from all blemish.
Having bathed in the moonlight during the full month of Bhādrapada, that best of men goes to see Bhūteśa, who is clothed in an elephant hide.
The excellent river named Candrikā always flows northward;
not far from Candrikā, in the eastern direction, is the river Phenilā.
And by name, that best of rivers was brought down as Śatānandā;
she is the daughter of Brahmā, Gaṅgā, who originates from the mountains.
Having bathed again at the time of Brahma’s awakening in the month of Phālguna at the Phenilā river, a man shall conquer hell and attain heaven. || 22 ||
Then, having first bathed in the river called Sitā, which flows northward,
one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā on the great full-moon day of Caitra.
Before that, at a distance of two yojanas, there was a river called Sumadanā, which King Janaka propitiated after worshipping Śiva, the bull-bannered god.
For the benefit of the one named Bhairava, [this teaching] was brought down from Sutīkṣṇa;
having ascended Mount Sutīkṣṇa and bathed in the waters of the Sumadana, [it was revealed].
Having worshipped Maheśvara on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one attains all desires and goes to the world of Śiva. || 26 ||
These rivers in Kāmarūpa flow northward from the southwest;
there, to the east of the sacred seat (pīṭha), is where Tripurā is worshipped.
