Thus has been told to you, O King, this supreme bestower of great merit, where Śambhu and Ambikā always reside to the southwest of Kāmarūpa. (28)
O Great King, listen now, O Lord of the Earth, as I describe in due order those very rivers which flow southward and originate from the Himavat. (29)
Above the Agada river flows the great river named Bhadrā;
by bathing in it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one shall go to heaven.
Prior to that, there is always the most meritorious river named Subhadrā;
having bathed in it on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, one shall go to heaven.
From that lake named Mānasa, however, the most sacred river called Mānasā descended,
brought down by Taṇabindu.
Having bathed in that [river] throughout the entire month of Vaiśākha, the best of men attains the world of Viṣṇu and thereafter shall obtain liberation.
Near the Himavat mountain is that radiant peak of great splendor,
upon which the Lord of Beings always dwells, assuming the form of Bhairava.
From that flows the auspicious river named Bhairavī, with its holy waters;
originating from Mānasa and other sources, it flows eastward like the Gaṅgā, bestowing rewards.
In which, having bathed during the spring season, one goes to heaven;
and in which, having fully worshipped Kāmākhyā, one may attain desired knowledge.
Having worshipped Mahāmāyā there, one obtains double the fruit.
Above that is the celestial Gaṅgā, the best of rivers known as Varṇāsā. (37)
Those excellent rivers beginning with Subhadrā and ending with Varṇasā, which originate from the Himavat, are eternally fruit-bestowing and comparable to the Mānasa lake. (38)
All those rivers originate from the Himavat and flow towards the north; however, the Madanā flows to the east, while [the others] are to the west of Brahmakṣetra.
It is the field of Ravi, where the divine Āditya is eternally stationed;
it is for the benefit of Bhairava, where all the lords of the universe reside.
In the great seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa, Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, and the others [reside];
likewise, at that time, the illustrious Sūrya is established on the mountain called Attva.
There is a river named Trisrotā situated in the eastern direction; behind it stands Kapotakaraṇa, where two pools are located. || 42 ||
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites at Kapotakuṇḍa and Karaṇakuṇḍaka,
and having ascended Tattvācala, one should worship the Sun.
A man goes to the abode of the Sun just once, [drinking] the nectar of the Kapota-rite produced from the rays of the Sun. (44)
"O Kapota, take away my sin which is known as being associated with impure water.
Having bathed at Kapotapuṣkara with this mantra, [one is purified]. (45)
Having performed the ritual ablution at Karaṇa, one should worship the Sun on the mountain of reality (tattva-śaila),
with the threefold seed-syllable of Brahman followed by the thousand-footed hymn at the end.
In the fourth [syllable], *raśmaye*, the wife of the god exerts herself;
this is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the limbs of Āditya, which grants the fulfillment of all desires.
The Sun-god (Bhāskara) is always seated upon a lotus, holds a lotus in his hand, possesses a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus, has seven horses and seven reins, and is two-armed. 48.
Its mandala is circular and endowed with eight petals;
likewise, there are six [mudrās] for the thumbs and fingertips, as well as for the heart and the other [limbs].
Accompanied by the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) at its conclusion and joined with the fire-syllable (vahni),
this mantra is prescribed for all ritual installations (nyāsa) and bestows all fruits.
One should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, mouth, belly, back, as well as on the two arms, the two hands, the two shanks, and the two feet.
And on the hips, one should place all the syllables of the mantra in sequence;
this is declared to be prescribed for worship, proclaimed as being to the north of Ramā.

The dismissal [of the deity] is likewise in the northeast; one should know that the powers (śaktis) of the petals are Vidyā and the others; Tattvacaṇḍa, who wears the remains of the offering (nirmālya), and Māṭhara and the others are on the two sides.
The seed-syllable of the *uttaratantra* was previously explained;
having worshipped within reality according to this procedure, the best of men [attains success]. (54)
Having obtained all desires without exception, he rejoices in this world;
happy at the end, he likewise shall go toward the abode of the Sun.
Not far from Bhāskara, on the auspicious southern peak,
there dwells an excellent Śaṅkara-liṅga.
Large-bodied monkeys always go about surrounding him,
and they stand encircling Śaṅkara, serving him.
Having bathed in the Trisrotā and beheld the Great-souled Mahādeva on Śubhācala, a man shall obtain his desired wish. (58)
Prior to that, there was the celestial river named Sukumālinī;
after that, another called Kṣīroda flowed toward the south.
O Great King, having bathed in those two [tirthas] which possess meritorious waters and flow with nectar, a person goes toward the abode of Śaṅkara.
To the east of that as well is another river called Līlā;
having bathed in that great river, one goes to the world of Śiva.
Prior to that, the auspicious Caṇḍī, known as the great river Caṇḍikā,
flows forth from the most enchanting mountain named Dhavala.
Two Śiva-liṅgas are situated there not very far away;
and Goloka and Śṛṅga are located at a distance of one krośa.
Having bathed at Caṇḍikā and ascended to Dhavaleśvara,
a man should gaze upon the southern ocean and inquire about the place known as Goloka.
Then, having descended again from the horned pedestal of the earth,
he worshipped Maheśvara according to the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha),
a human being shall attain all desires in this world and, at the end of the body, go to the state of Śiva.
All these rivers that have been mentioned flow toward the south;
therefore, in the northeastern quarter lies Mount Gandhamādana.
Where the very great Liṅga of Śiva called Bhṛṅga resides,
that best of mountains is reached at the western edge of the sacred field.
Having supported the goddess Brahmaśilā, she proceeds toward Sāvitra;
at the edge of Gandhamādana lies the pair of feet of Bhṛṅgeśa.
And there stands an intermediate pool with the waters of the Ganges flowing into it;
having bathed in that intermediate pool and having drunk its water, [one attains the fruit]. (70)
Then, having seen the two feet of Bhṛṅgeśa situated upon the stone and having worshipped Mahābhṛṅga, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
O Great Bull, unite these words of the Bull-bannered Lord, which have emerged from the feet of Śambhu and serve as the source for the vision of the intermediate space.
Having performed his bath within the water with this mantra,
he should then behold Bhṛṅgadeva, who dwells within the Kubjapīṭha.
Then, between Mount Maṇikūṭa and Mount Gandhamādana,
the Lauhitya flows forth, having been produced by Brahmā from fire.
To the south of Arṇāśā is the ocean named Lauhitya;
Maṇikūṭa is situated to the east, from which Hayagrīva, the Lord Hari, resides.
Having slain the demon Jvara in the form of Hayagrīva, Viṣṇu—now that Hayagrīva—remained there for the sake of sport. || 76 ||
Having thus destroyed the fever, Viṣṇu then made his residence there,
so that it might indeed be for the welfare of men, gods, asuras, and others.
Having destroyed the great demon Jvara with his body afflicted by fever, he, the physician,
proceeded for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds.
The lake that had arisen from the medicinal bath was named Ahāsa-saras by Hayagrīva himself, and it became one from which there is no rebirth.
Since one who is the best among men, having bathed there, is not born again,
that lake is celebrated by the name "Apunarbhava" (the state of no rebirth).
On Maṇikaṭācala, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Hayagrīva,
shines with an extent of one hundred vyāmas in width.
Therefore, to the east is Mount Bhadrakāma, which is triangular in shape;
there stands the Śiva-liṅga named Kālahaya.
Near that, to the south, is Apunarbhava-kuṇḍaka;
on the mountain at the shore of the Apunarbhū lake is Bhadrakāmade.
The stone there, renowned as Haravīthī, is of the nature of Brahman;
upon it dwells Mahādeva, the knower of yoga, intent on meditation.
Upon seeing which, a mortal practitioner of yoga attains liberation after death;
on that very stone resides Śaṅkara, known by the name Gokarṇa.
By him Gokarṇa, the friend of Andhaka, was slain in ancient times;
likewise, to the northeast of Gokarṇa is Kedāra, which is ultimately Śambhu himself.
Then [the mountain] equal to Andhaka was proclaimed as the sustainer of the enjoyment of Kamalākara;
where Śambhu Kedāra resides, that mountain is named Madana. (87)
In that very place, Kamala is proclaimed, he who bestows the great self-abode;
having bathed in the waters of non-rebirth and beheld the yogis Gokarṇa and Yoginī.
Having seen Kedāra and Kamala, liberation is attained upon the sight of Mādhava;
but having seen the god Mādhava, one should thereafter look toward Kāma.
Having beheld Kāma, one situated there should gaze upon the state beyond rebirth;
having thus performed the pilgrimage to the sacred seats (pīṭha) according to this sequential yoga.
Having rescued seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself as the fifteenth, that best of men leads them to the third heaven.
O Lord, you who arise from the abode of Viṣṇu and take away rebirth, remove my sin for the sake of attaining heaven, O great ocean of powerful associations! 92.
By this very mantra, the hero should bathe for the sake of non-rebirth;
the tantra of Hayagrīva has already been explained previously. (93)
Listen, O Great King, to what you should contemplate regarding his form:
[He is] white as camphor and the kunda flower, seated upon a white lotus. (94)
Four-armed and adorned with various ornaments such as earrings,
his two left hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In his other two hands, he holds a book and a white lotus;
his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and in some depictions, he has Garuḍa as his seat.
The entire sequence taught in the Uttaratantra should be adopted for the worship;
Viṣvaksena, however, is the bearer of the remains of the offering (nirmālya) during the dismissal of the horse-riders (Hayāri).
The one whose banner is Garuḍa remains forever concealed within the form of a stone, sporting with the Gandharvas and abiding for the welfare of the world. 98.
The accomplishment of the mantra of Hayagrīva is attained through two hundred thousand [recitations];
one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) while offering oblations of barley-meal, milk-rice, and clarified butter.
But by performing this preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) alone, O Indra among kings, one attains the fulfillment of one's desires here and shall reach the world of Viṣṇu. || 100 ||
With mantras, the twice-born worshipper should always worship the five forms of the five-faced one; in the east, he should worship Tatpuruṣa and the others, as well as Kāma and the rest.
Kāma is to be known as Tatpuruṣa, and he is proclaimed as Yogīśāna; Aghora, Gokarṇa, Kedāra, and Vāmadeva likewise. || 102 ||
One should worship Sadyojāta with those various mantras of Kamalā;
likewise Parvata, Kedāra, Śivagaṅgā, and Kālikā. (103)
To the east of Hayagrīva and to the west of Kedāra is the place called Chāyābhoga; likewise, there is the city Bhogavatī.
The man who goes from the place called Maṇikūṭa out of curiosity to [the shrine of] Punarbhava obtains the fruit of all pilgrimages to sacred fords. || 105 ||
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the fifteenth and eighth lunar days,
he who bathes in the waters that lead to non-rebirth and beholds Hari according to the prescribed rites,
shall uplift his entire lineage and attain union with Viṣṇu.
But he who constantly beholds Hari throughout the entire month of Jyeṣṭha attains absorption into Hari,
together with all his lineages.
This supreme, meritorious place called Maṇikūṭa has been described to you;
it is indeed superior to Vārāṇasī and is worshipped by Siddhas and Vidyādharas. 108.
The Brahmin who recites or hears this definitive account of Maṇikūṭa certainly obtains the fruit of all the Vedas; of this there is no doubt. (109)
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 78 ||
The seventy-ninth chapter.
Aurva said:
"O great king, prior to that was a mountain named Darpaṇa."
Where Kubera always dwells together with the guardians of wealth. || 1 ||
In its central part resides Rohita, who has the form of a red fish;
by his touch, iron and other metals instantly attain the state of gold.
Not very far from there flows the river named Darpaṇa,
which originates from the Himālaya mountains and is constantly similar to the Lauhitya in its fruits.
Once the son was born, Hari had him properly bathed with the waters of all the sacred fords by all the hosts of gods.
Because it shatters the pride of sin arising from bathing,
this [lake] was formerly named Darpaṇa by the hosts of gods.
Having bathed in that best of rivers, one should worship Kubera on the first lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika at Darpaṇācala.
Endowed with hundreds of prosperities here, he goes to the abode of Brahmā.
To the east of Darpaṇa is the mountain named Agnimālā.
Shaped like a serpent, seven hundred vyāmas in length and half that in width,
the fire resides there within the circle of fire at the upper portion.
On that beautiful stone slab, resembling a mass of vermilion,
a fire without fuel shines even today as it did eternally.
For the sake of Bhairava’s welfare, while he was engaged in the service of Kāmākhyā,
the Fire-god himself was already present there along with his attendants.
Having bathed in the waters of the Lauhitya and ascended the mountain named Agnimālā,
one who worships the Fire-god rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
To the east of the Agnimāla mountain is a pool named Vāruṇa;
on its bank stands an excellent mountain known by the name Kaṃsakara.
Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, dwells there eternally;
having properly worshipped Pracetas at that Kaṃsakara [shrine], [one attains his favor]. || 13 ||
Having bathed in the Vāruṇa pool, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa;
here, the first consonant is indeed joined with the fifth vowel. (14)
The seed-syllable of Kubera is said to be joined with the crest-lock of Śambhu;
it is the seventh [vowel] of the letter *pa*, conjoined with the bindu and the half-moon. (15)
It is known as the seed-syllable of fire; with it, one should worship the Fire-god.
The fifth letter of the group beginning with *ma*, conjoined with the lunar drop (*somabindu*), is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa.
One should constantly worship these deities with these mantras.
To the east of Varuṇācala is the mountain named Vāyukūṭa.
Divided into two parts and endowed with the mandala of the seed-syllable of wind (vāyu),
the moon is situated in the world of wind, from which the vital air (māruta) issues forth.
O King, having reached the upper and lower parts [of the body], it flows there constantly;
by worshipping the wind (vāyu) therein, one shall attain the world of Vāyu. || 19 ||
Formerly, the mountain to the east of Vāyugiri was known as Candrakūṭa;
it is triangular, resembling the moon, and above it is the lunar disc.
The first letter of the second group, adorned with a bindu, is declared to be the seed-syllable of the Moon; with that, one should worship the Moon.
Even today, on every new moon day, the Lord of Night still circumambulates that mountain, accompanied by ten celestial wanderers.
To the east of that very place is a lake named Somakuṇḍa;
by bathing and drinking there, a person attains absolute liberation.
When the Moon was descending from heaven to serve Kāmākhyā,
then masses of water issued forth from the collection of its rays.
With those waters, Vāsava himself fashioned a pool for Indra and Candra in the most meritorious spot, upon the Brahma-stone.
O Moon, arisen from the rays of the moon, great ocean of lunar nectar;
having encountered whatever state of being, O Moon, remove its impurity. (26)
"O Moon, source of nectar, you who bring delight, remove my impurity!"—having bathed in the waters of the moon with this mantra, [one attains the fruit]. (27)
That man who, having ascended Candrakūṭa, performs worship, obtains an uninterrupted and most beautiful lineage. (28)
Having pierced the lunar realm in the other world, one goes to the supreme state.
On the shore of Candrakūṭa, there is indeed a mountain named Nandana.
Indra dwells there, devoted to the service of Kāmākhyā;
having attained a fivefold state, Hari, the lord of all gods, constantly exists as a man in order to serve the Queen of the Thirty-three.
On the southern side of Mount Candrakūṭa is Girijanārdana;
to the south of that, at its lower part, is the lake named Aśvakrāntā. (a)
There is no holy place equal to it within the entire scope of the universe;
those who die here, whether in water or on land, go to the eternal Brahman. (b)
On Mount Janārdana, Viṣṇu, assuming the very form of a tortoise, remained there after piercing through a rock, served by gods and Gandharvas. ||c||
Having bathed in the water trodden by horses and having worshipped Janārdana, one uplifts ten million generations of one's lineage and becomes a Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) oneself. ||d||
Moreover, at every new moon, the moon performs a threefold circumambulation of Mount Candrakūṭa as well as Mount Nandana.
Having bathed in the waters of Candrakūṭa and then ascended to the Nandana grove. || 32 ||
Having propitiated Śakra, the Lord of the World, one shall obtain great fruit.
To the eastern part of Nandana, however, is the great mountain Bhasmakūṭa.
He who is himself the form of Bharga is eternally the supreme peace;
to the south of Bhasmakūṭa is the Goddess Pīyūṣadhāriṇī.
She was renowned by the name Urvaśī, who always brought delight to Śakra; she indeed became that which had been established by the gods in the past as inexhaustible food.
Then Urvaśī herself remained there, having taken [the form] of Kāmākhyā;
but Hara, in the form of a stone, remained standing, completely enveloping her.
And she, having made a small portion of that very heap of nectar,
constantly presents it within the circle of the source known as Kāmākhyā.
But Urvaśī, residing within the Sudhāśilā stone, dwells in the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa;
that pool, situated in the midst of the heap of Urvaśī’s ashes, is perpetually covered.
It is thirty-two bows wide and fifty bows long;
having bathed and drunk there, men shall attain liberation. || 39 ||
The Kāmākhyā-yoni always proceeds toward the northeastern direction;
indeed, the Yoginī Urvaśī enters into the Bhasmakūṭa.
Constantly nourished by nectar, the goddess rejoices;
filled with joy, the great goddess always delights in desire.
To the northeast of Bhasmakūṭa is the great mountain Maṇikūṭa;
there stands the Liṅga of Hara named Maṇikarṇa.
He who has the form of one just born is called Maṇikarṇa;
Sadāśiva is to be worshipped there with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Having bathed in the waters of Candratīrtha and beheld the Moon together with Indra,
and having seen Maṇikarṇeśvara, liberation is attained upon going to Bhasmācala.
The Moon (Śaśin) should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, adorned with gold, possessing ten horses,
holding a mace in his hand, having two arms, and granting boons.
He has a thousand eyes, a fair-complexioned body, and two arms; with his left hand he holds a vajra, a mace, and a goad, and with his right hand as well.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, with his quivers fastened and holding a bow tucked under his arm, he serves Maheśvarī.
The phoneme following the letter *va*, endowed with the lunar bindu, is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śakra; one should worship Śakra by means of it. (48)
The beautiful river named Sumaṅgalā, flowing from the Himavat mountain, always flows toward the east of Maṇikūṭa. (49)
He who, having ascended Maṇikūṭa, beholds that river,
shall attain the merit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā and go to the celestial realm.
To the east of Mount Maṇikūṭa is the Kulācala named Matsyadhvaja,
where Madana was once again consumed by the fire from the eye of Hara.
Having propitiated the bull-bannered Lord through austerity, he regained his body;
there, in the form of a fish, he remained equal to Kāmadeva.
Gazing all around at the earth from the plateau,
he saw there a river named Śāśvatī flowing toward the south.
On that mountain stands a lake named Kāmasaras;
having bathed according to the prescribed rites in the eternal waters and having drunk from the waters of Āmasaras, [one attains fulfillment].
Freed from sin and purified in soul, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
To the east of Gandhamādana is the mountain named Sukrānta. || 55 ||
At its edge is the Vāsava Kuṇḍa, where the food of Vāsava’s nectar is found;
standing there in the south in ancient times was Śakra, the lord of Śacī.
With his body exhausted, he drank the nectar within Kāmarūpa;
having bathed in the Vāsava pool, he then ascended Sukāntaka.
Having become beloved by Vāsava, one shall attain the world of Śakra.
To the east, however, is the mountain named Rakṣaḥkūṭa belonging to Sukānta.
There dwells constantly the god Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left, possessing a massive body. (59)
Adorned with a mass of matted hair, tall, resembling a black mountain, having two arms, dressed in black garments, and seated upon a donkey. || 60 ||

The seed-syllable of Nairṛtya is said to consist of the first letter [na] together with the final and penultimate letters [ṛ and u], along with the bindu and the moon (the anusvāra); therefore, one should worship him with that. || 61 ||
Having ascended the peak of Rakṣas, he who worships according to the prescribed rite Caṇḍikā, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas, [and] Nīti, the lord of the Rākṣasas— || 62 ||
O King, he never has any fear of Rākṣasas;
nor do the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Vetālas, and Gaṇanāyakas ever pose a threat to him. (63)
O King, seeing that man, Mādhava named Bhairava, who was previously a Rākṣasa in the eastern direction, was always terrified. (64)
Known as Pāṇḍunātha, he is established in the form of a stone;
one should constantly worship that Pāṇḍunātha with the eight-syllable mantra followed by the word "bhava. (65)
With that very [offering], one should worship the Lord Hari known as Pāṇḍunātha,
whose body is reddish-fair in complexion and who holds a mace and a lotus in his hands.
He has four arms, holding a discus and a spear in his two right hands; he is seated upon a red lotus and is radiant with a crown. (67)
[One should meditate on] the supreme Lord wearing pure earrings, with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest;
[one should worship Him] with the root-mantra of Hari: "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa. (68)
O King, one should worship in this manner for the attainment of the four aims of life.
To the north of Pāṇḍunātha is the lake named Brahmakūṭa. (69)
Formerly created by Brahmā for the bathing of the inhabitants of heaven,
it was one hundred vyāmas in length and half of that in width.
It is meritorious, removing all sins, and has come from the world of the gods;
it is produced from the water-pot and flows as the nectar of Brahmakuṇḍa.
"Take away all my sins and accomplish for me merit and heaven"—having bathed in the waters of that lake with this mantra, [he should offer oblations]. 72.
Having worshipped Pāṇḍunātha, one shall attain union with Viṣṇu;
and having bathed in the waters of Brahmakuṇḍa and worshipped the Lord of Umā (Śiva).
Having ascended Vāyukūṭa, a man shall surely attain liberation.
To the east of Pāṇḍunātha is the mountain Citrahara, which is Hari.
Where Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a boar, constantly delights—
that supreme abode of Kāmākhyā is known as Nīlakūṭa.
To the east of that dwells Brahmā, and furthermore, Brahmagiri;
it is situated on the ground-plate to the east of the mountain of Brahmā.
In this circle known as Kāmākhya, which possesses beautiful, deep, and auspicious whirlpools,
the Supreme Goddess delights in the form of Ugratārā.
Therein, she whose nature is auspicious should be worshipped in that very form;
her seed-syllable has been set forth previously in the [section on] the North. (78)
Listen, O best of men, to the form by which Śivā is always to be meditated upon:
she is dark-complexioned, pot-bellied, tall, with sparse teeth and red gums. (79)

She has four arms and a slender body; in her right hands she holds a knife and a skull-cup, while in her left hands she holds a sword and a blue lotus; furthermore, she has a single braid of hair upon her head. (80)
Placing her left foot upon the thigh of the corpse and resting her right foot upon the heart of the corpse, she let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
Adorned with a necklace of serpents and a garland of skulls, she is the supreme bestower of desires;
her mandala is triangular, and the syllable *huṃ* is its central seed-syllable.
O tiger among men, the names of the door-guardians and the yoginīs belonging to this tantra should be known as they have been declared in the Vāmyagocara.
Having bathed at Urvaśī according to the prescribed rites and likewise touched the Pāṇḍuśilā stone,
and having ascended Nīlakūṭa, one is not born again in a womb.
O destroyer of sins, O Urvaśī, when the wielder of the plow arrived at Vārāṇasī from the city of Purandara, he [purified it] with floods of water mixed with nectar; may that protect me. 85.
O Goddess who flows with nectar, who fulfills the flood of ambrosia;
O Urvaśī, my goddess, grant me today through your nectar that which is immortal.
O Goddess, beloved of Purandara, O eternal Ambhikā of Vārāṇasī, who are united with the Lohitya lake, remove my sin, O you who are under the control of Manu! 87.
Having bathed in the meritorious waters of the Urvaśī with these hymns of praise and mantras,
one is liberated from all sins and sports in the world of Viṣṇu.
Urvaśī is described as having two arms and wearing golden bracelets;
she holds a golden vessel for the pouring forth of nectar.
Clad in white garments, fair-complexioned, with full and elevated breasts, beautiful in every limb, pure, and adorned with all ornaments. (90)
The first syllable of her name is proclaimed as her mantra;
however, in the Umātantra, her mantra is proclaimed as follows: (91)
Gaṇeśa stands at the eastern gate of Mount Kāmākhyā,
and right there at the gateway stands the charming Agnivetāla.
The three—the form and the mantra—as previously described by Śambhu, I shall explain them to you; listen to me, O Great King. (93)
"Oṃ nama ulkāmukhāya"—this mantra, joined with the root seed-syllable and others, is proclaimed as that of Siddhagaṇeśa stationed at the gateway. (94)
I shall describe his form: he has the face of an elephant, three eyes, a protruding belly, four arms, and wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
Śūrpakarṇa, Bṛhadgaṇḍa, Ekadanta, and Pṛthūdara;
in his right hand he holds a staff, and likewise a lotus in the other.
A sweetmeat ball and an axe are proclaimed to be on his left;
he has a large body that seems to fill the sky, with thick shoulders, feet, and hands. 97.
Below that, it should be joined with intelligence and faulty intellect, together with mice;
and the entrails should be of the kind prescribed for the worship of Pañcavaktra.
That very tantra is to be accepted, which contains such injunctions and prohibitions;
[the deity] is two-armed, with a full face and red eyes, and is terrifying. (99)
A knife in the right hand and a vessel of blood in the left;
his face is terrifying with fangs, he is emaciated, and covered with visible veins.

Likewise, bearing long matted locks upon his head and accompanied by a terrible roar, he is the fourth [syllable] joined with the seed-syllable of fire (Ra) and adorned with the sixth vowel (Ū). || 101 ||
This Agnivetāla-bīja is the destroyer of fear everywhere;
one should worship Agnivetāla, the warder-off of fear in all places. (102)
For one who performs this worship, there shall be no fear again from spirits and the like.
O King, [I shall now describe] the sequence of the eight mantras of the Yoginīs.
The eight-syllable mantras of those headed by Śailaputrī, which are established in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, have indeed been previously declared. (104)
O tiger among men, the bodily mantra of Śailaputrī has already been explained; now, however, [I shall describe] the form of the Yoginīs in particular. (105)
O best of kings, these Yoginīs should be worshipped either with each individual seed-syllable, or according to the Durgā-tantra, or indeed with the seed-syllable of the eyes (the *netra-bīja*). 106.
One should worship Kātyāyanī, who is difficult to reach on foot, according to the Durgā-tantra;
that very form of worship was previously explained.
One should worship Kālarātri with the mantra of Kālarātri;
the form and mantra of Kālarātri have already been explained previously. (108)
One should worship the Mistress of the World with the mantras of the Mahāmāyā Tantra;
all these yoginīs bestow fruits just like Kāmākhyā. (109)
Where no specific distinction is mentioned regarding the form, the tantra, or the mode of worship, one should perform the worship there according to the Durgā-tantra and its mantra. (110)
O best of men, that most excellent of men who worships each Yoginī individually obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. 111.
The nature of the eastern [mountain] of Nīlaśaila has been explained;
it is to the east of the navel-mandala and to the south of Bhasmakūṭa. || 112 ||
To the east is a mountain named Karpaṭa, which bears the form of Yama;
there is a southern rock there, black and possessing a luster like that of blue collyrium.
On the plateau, O Indra among kings, one should worship Śamana, who is five fathoms in extent and who always holds a staff in his hand. (114)
He always holds in his hand the instrument for punishing living beings;
he is black in color, has two arms, and is radiant with a crown and diadem.
He always holds a sword and a dagger in his left hand;
he wears black garments, has thick feet, and protruding teeth. (116)
The practitioner should worship with supreme devotion the one who eternally grants fearlessness to horses and has a buffalo as his vehicle, using the seed-syllable of Yama.
The first letter of the penultimate group, joined with the bindu and the crescent moon (indus), is known as the seed-syllable of Yama; it bestows pleasure upon Yama.
Furthermore, whoever worships Śamana with this very mantra on the excellent mountain named Karpaṭa shall not meet an untimely death. || 119 ||
From the mountain named Karpaṭa in the east, there is one known as Citra,
which was situated at the edge of the eastern region in the south-eastern direction.
The Pīṭha is indeed the Brahmagrāva, and that mountain is called Prāka;
upon it, the nine planets dwell constantly according to their will.
Whoever worships them there shall never encounter misfortune;
for the form and the mantra of the Sun and the Moon have been explained. (122)
Now hear from me the mantra and the form of the other seven: he wears red garments, holds a trident, possesses a spear, and carries a mace. 123.
Maṅgala is considered to have four arms, a ram as his vehicle, and to be a bestower of boons;
he wears yellow garments, carries a trident, and is adorned with yellow garlands and unguents.
Buddha, golden-yellow in complexion and clad in yellow garments, stands upon a lion, holding a sword, a shield, and a mace in his hands; he bestows boons and is seated upon a golden couch. 125.
One should meditate upon the deity Tīrthaka as four-armed and omniscient, holding a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff in his left hands, while granting boons with the other.
Constantly praised by all the hosts of gods, it is enchanting;
it is clad in white garments, white in color, and situated upon the serpent Śaṅkha.
The preceptor of the Daityas always holds, in order from right to left, a noose, a garland, a book, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his four arms.
Resembling a sapphire, holding a trident, bestowing boons, and having a vulture as his vehicle;
bearing a bow and arrows, the son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be meditated upon in this manner. 129.
The seed-syllable of Kāmadeva is proclaimed as the mantra of Bhauma;
that which is the auspicious middle of the seed-syllable of Durgā’s eye is likewise [the mantra]. (130)
That mantra of the Son of the Moon (Budha) bestows the fruit of all desires;
it begins with the fifth vowel [Ū] followed by the syllable AṂ, and is joined with the four and six vowels [A, Ā, I, Ī, U, Ū, Ṛ, Ṝ, Ḷ, Ḹ, E, AI, O, AU]. (131)
This mantra of the Guru is proclaimed to end with the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa;
furthermore, the first two syllables are also joined with the bindu and the moon (the nasal dot). 132.
The letter *ma*, joined with the seventh vowel, is at the beginning and the end;
the first letter of the final class-consonant group is endowed with both the bindu and the nādabindu. (133)
The seed-syllable of Śukra, which grants the fulfillment of all desires, consists of the first letter of the final group [sa], joined with the lunar drop (bindu). (134)
Endowed with the vowel of the first mantra and joined with "tadeva" and so forth,
this is the mantra of Śanaiścara, which destroys all defects.
The mantra for all those planets is proclaimed to be either the first letter of their name joined with the *bindu* and the *candra*, or the name itself. 136.
In rites for pacification and enrichment, the wise and high-minded person desiring prosperity should always worship these planets with these mantras. (137)
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, likewise bearing a sword and shield,
seated upon a lion-throne, the wise Rāhu is described as being dark-complexioned.
Smoke-colored and large-eyed, having the form of a tail and four arms,
with sword, shield, mace, and arrow in his hands, Ketu has a corpse for his seat.
The penultimate letter, joined with the twelfth vowel, [is the first];
then the penultimate [letter] again, both joined with the fifth vowel and the moon-bindu (anusvāra). 140.
This mantra is used in direct order for Rāhu and in reverse order for Ketu;
alternatively, the first syllable of each may be joined with the mantra as before.
Having thus worshipped the nine planets on this excellent and variegated mountain,
one obtains one's desired objects and likewise attains supreme peace.
To the east of Citrakūṭa, however, is the excellent Kajjalācala; all the Vidyādharas and other divine beings reside upon this mountain. || 143 ||
Having ascended that mountain and bowed down to all the gods,
O best of men, they go to heaven and also attain incomparable prosperity in this world.
To the east of the Kajjalācala mountain is the auspicious Śubhaparvata,
where in ancient times Śakra, the lord of the gods, took delight together with Śacī.
To the east of that is the great goddess river Kapilagaṅgikā;
by bathing in it, a person obtains the fruit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā. || 146 ||
To the east of the abode of Kāmākhyā, and likewise in the southern direction,
there exists upon the earth the great Āvarta and the great Brahmabila.
O Lord of Men, from that [mountain] comes the beautiful river Sunadī, possessing a luster like white water, measuring twenty-five yojanas.
Since she issued from his opening, as the Ganges does, and since she bestows fruit just like that river, she is therefore celebrated by the gods as Kapilagaṅgikā.
Having bathed in the Kapilagaṅgā during all the Manvantaras,
a man first attains heaven and thereafter proceeds to the world of Brahmā.
Having crossed that river, on its eastern side, there is a river named Damanikā,
possessing very dark waters and likewise a subduer of sin.
Then there was another supreme river called Vṛddhā;
on the eastern side of that river, it bestows fruits just like the Gaṅgā.
By bathing throughout the entire month of Māgha, one shall attain liberation;
likewise, by [worshipping] with *damanikā*, one shall attain supreme *nirvāṇa*.
Then, to the east, there is that supreme river named Parādevī;
she is the great, divine Yamunā, who bestows fruits just like the Yamunā. || 154 ||
Arising from the Southern Mountain and flowing toward the Southern Ocean, one shall attain liberation by bathing in it during the month of Kārttika. || 155 ||
And right here, amidst these supreme, established, and destined enjoyments, resides the god Bhairava, the source of the enjoyment of the Resplendent One (Bharga). 156.
On the excellent mountain named Urjaya,
there exists a most terrifying middle region belonging to him who has the form of a Śarabha, situated within its fertile valley.
Having worshipped that very one known as Bhairava there with the mantras of the Five-Faced One, the wise person attains the state of the world of Śiva. || 158 ||
The worship of Kāmeśvara that was described in the *Nīlanirṇaya*—
having performed that worship on Durjaya, the best of mountains and the highest of immovable peaks— 159.
There lies the Bhairavagaṅgā and the lake indeed called Bhairava;
having bathed in those two, a person goes to the eternal world of Śiva. || 160 ||
To the east of the city named Durjaya is a supreme seat called Pura;
to its south is a great mountain known by the name Kṣobhaka.
On that mountain, upon the surface of a rock, resides the goddess Raktadevī,
known by the name Pañcapuṣkariṇī, who embodies the nature of the five wombs.
One should worship the five-faced one with various difficult-to-attain *yoni*s;
there, the daughter of the Himālaya mountain always remains in order to grant delight. (163)
On the eastern side of that mountain, however, there is a great river named Kāntā;
though it flows northward at first, it eventually enters the southern ocean.
The divine Kuṇḍa and Mahākuṇḍa are situated on the ground at the foot of the Acchela mountain;
having bathed there, one should worship that goddess. || 165 ||
O highly fortunate one, the man who bathes in the divine pool and worships the auspicious Pañcapuṣkaraṇī is certainly not born again in a womb.
There are five wombs and exactly five lotus-pools situated there;
because of that, she is considered to have five forms as the five lotus-pools.
Likewise, these Bakula flowers represent these five wombs;
they are the goddesses of the five lotus ponds, the Pracaṇḍās, who grant all desires. || 168 ||
Those [goddesses] should be worshipped by the best of practitioners according to the Tantra of Tripurā;
or else, one should worship Śivā with the Tantras and Mantras of Kāmeśvarī.
The mantra of this Bālā Tripurā has been proclaimed;
or else, the mantra of Kāmeśvarī is proclaimed for her worship. (170)
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, and Caṇḍā—these are proclaimed as the five Yoginīs with five faces. || 171 ||
And there, upon a stone, is the Śivaliṅga known as Heruka;
one should worship that leader situated to the southeast of the Goddess. (172)
Having worshipped with the mantra of Bhairava, one shall go to heaven;
the Goddess who wears the remains of the offering is celebrated as Caṇḍagaurī. 173.
O tiger among men, in ancient times this was spoken by Bharga regarding Kāntā;
having bathed in the water during the spring, O best of men, [one attains merit]. (174)
Having become possessed of beauty and virtue, he goes to the world of Śiva.
To the northeast of the great mountain called Kṣobhaka is the best of mountains. (175)
There, on the mountain named Tuṅgasandhyācala, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, formerly uttered a curse against the royal sage named Nimi. (176)
For Vasiṣṭha indeed became bodiless due to that curse, and Nimi likewise;
thereafter, by the instruction of Brahmā, [he was born] in a secluded place called Kāmarūpaka.
While he was performing penance on Mount Sandhyācala,
Viṣṇu then became manifest before that great sage by virtue of the granting of a boon from the god.
Having quickly brought down the nectars and fashioned a sacrificial pit on the slope of the mountain, he bathed there and drank; thus his body became restored and filled.
From that Amṛtakūṇḍa, the excellent river named Sandhyā has issued forth;
by bathing there, one becomes long-lived and free from disease. || 180 ||
Therefore, previously, the excellent river named Lalitā was brought down by Mahādeva from the southern ocean toward the east. || 181 ||
Any man who performs the Lalitā-bath on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha shall go to the abode of Śambhu.
On the eastern bank of the Lalitā is the mountain named Bhagavat;
there dwells the Lord Hari himself, Viṣṇu in the form of a liṅga.
Having bathed at Lalitā on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, he who, having mounted the Lord, should worship the Supreme Lord; || 184 ||
He goes to the abode of Viṣṇu with a radiant body;
these are all the rivers previously mentioned that flow toward the north. || 185 ||
In due course, those rivers equal to the Jāhnavī flow toward the southern ocean.
Having first beheld Kāmākhyā and bathed in the waters of Urvaśī, whoever performs a ritual bath in these [rivers] shall indeed attain liberation. || 186 ||
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 79 ||
The Eightieth Chapter.
Aurva said:
That eternal river which has been described as Matsyadhvajāsitā—
To its east, the river known as Dīpavatī is said to be situated. || 1 ||
And this river, born from the Himalayas, cuts through the darkness like a lamp; for that reason, it is known as Dīpavatī among gods and humans. (2)
To the east of Dīpavatī is a mountain named Śṛṅgāṭa;
there, a single liṅga of the god Bharga is established.
The river, however, is established as having three streams and flowing toward the southern ocean;
it flows constantly from the foot of the Śṛṅgāṭaka.
Doing what is pleasing to Bharga, she goes to the southern ocean;
that best of men who, having bathed in the waters of the Triḥsrotas, [performs this], || 5 ||
Having ascended the Śṛṅgāṭaka peak, one should worship the Liṅga Śaṅkara;
with a radiant body and a purified soul, he shall attain incomparable desires here on earth.
Afterwards, one goes to the abode of Bharga and from there attains liberation;
for in that place, Hara is always two-armed and has the bull as his vehicle.
He sports together with Umā through the mantras of Vāmadeva;
and one should worship the god Caṇḍikā with the tantras and the mantra of Umā.
To the east of that is a river named Vṛddhavedikā;
by bathing in it, a mortal obtains the fruit born of bathing at Dedikā.
Then there is the great river named Bhaṭṭārikā, which originates from the snowy mountains and is always joyfully worshipped by hosts of gods.
Whoever performs a ritual bath in it on all four Yugādi days goes to the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
On Mount Nāṭaka, however, there is a lake resembling Lake Mānasa,
where Hara always performs water-sports together with the Daughter of the Mountain.
O tiger among men, he constructs it adorned with golden lotuses;
behind it, there are three rivers flowing from the middle and the eastern parts.
Having descended, it flows directly toward the southern ocean;
on its western side, however, is a river known by the name Dikkarikā.
Because it was produced from the wounds inflicted by the elephants of the quarters (diggajas), it is called Dikkarikā;
that which flowed from the central part was brought down by Śaṅkara.
That river, which issued from the eastern side of that excellent mountain, is called Vṛddhagaṅgā; like Gaṅgā herself, she bestows rewards.
Renowned as Suvarṇaśrī, she was equal to the Gaṅgā in her fruitfulness;
she emerged from the body of Pārvatī while she was performing her ablutions in the lake.
These rivers carry the golden droplets that issued forth;
they were strewn with those droplets by Śambhu for the sake of sport upon his body.
Then those drops of sandalwood paste, adhering there from their original place,
flowed down from Umā’s body along with the water.
Then there is the river named Svarṇavahā, whose golden splendor is superior to all others;
having bathed in these during the month of Caitra, a mortal who is a bull among men—
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a person who remains at the temple of the goddess Ira for three periods of the day should, when the time is over, proceed to the temple of Brahmā.
Having first attained realization on earth,
one subsequently becomes a sovereign emperor on the bank of the waters of the aged Gaṅgā, the daughter of Brahmā.
The deity named Viśvanātha is endowed with the Śiva-liṅga;
the Great Goddess Viśvadevī has the form of the yoni-maṇḍala.
There the Lord, the Master of the World, fought with Hayagrīva;
having slain Hayagrīva, he then went to Maṇikūṭa which had arrived there in ancient times.
There, whoever should worship Durgā Śāradā with Tantras and mantras, and [worship] Garuḍadhvaja with the mantra and Tantra of Hayagrīva; || 25 ||
He who, having fasted on the twelfth day, worships Śaṅkara with supreme devotion according to the tantra and the mantra of Kāmeśvara; || 26 ||
Listen now to the fruit of his merit on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days:
having resided for thirty million kalpas in the abode of Śiva and in the home of Hari.
For that much time he remains there, and for that much time in the abode of Śiva;
thereafter, having reached the earth, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas.
To the east of Adyā, who possesses the splendor of gold, is the auspicious river named Kāmā;
and to the east of Kāmā is the river named Omāśanā.
To the east of Omāśanā is the river named Vṛṣodakā; further to the east is Kāmarūpa, the sacred seat (pīṭha), the progenitor of the worlds. (30)
The goddess Mahāmāyā, who pervades the world and dwells in the cardinal directions—these are the rivers that have been described, all of which flow toward the south. (31)
Having bathed and drunk from them, one shall attain the heavenly world;
at their end, the celestial river (Svarṇadī) always flows toward the quarter-dwelling goddess (Dikkaravāsinī).
Known in the world as Sitagaṅgā, she bestows the very fruits of the Gaṅgā;
that Goddess resides upon the sacred seat of the earth and dwells in the cardinal directions.
Floating within the water, she becomes visible to the gods;
having bathed in the waters of the white Gaṅgā, one beholds Śambhu, Hari, and Vidhi.
Having worshipped there the deity named Lalitakāntā, one is not born again in a womb;
for the Lord Śambhu himself resides there in the form of a Liṅga. || 35 ||
Viṣṇu, in the form of a stone and assuming the form of the Brahma-linga,
sports with the two-fold Śivā on the pedestal of Dikkaravāsinī.
One is proclaimed as Ugratārā, known by the name Tīkṣṇakāntā;
the other is named Lalitakāntā, who is the illustrious Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
O King, her form is eternally known as Tīkṣṇakāntā;
she who is Kṛṣṇā and Lambodarī is the auspicious Ekajaṭā.
One should constantly worship that goddess in that form;
her limb-mantras and her form have already been explained previously. (39)
A triangular mandala should be drawn for him, preceded by the mantra;
first the word "rekhā," then "tataḥ paścāt," and then the word "surekhā. (40)
Likewise, having attained the state, they remain therein;
therefore, this mantra of this mandala is proclaimed as belonging to Tīkṣṇā. || 41 ||
Nara, Tripura, Deva, Īśa, Vetāla, Durdhara, Anaśrama, and Antaka—these are proclaimed as the door-keepers. (42)
One should properly worship these in the eight directions of the maṇḍala;
first, having performed the invocation, one should then offer the vajra-flower.
Thereafter, at dawn, this mantra is proclaimed for them regarding the vessels,
the ritual implements, and so forth, as well as for the place and everything else.
Everything stated in the Uttaratantra should be understood in both forms as well:
Cāmuṇḍā, Karālā, Subhagā, Bhīṣaṇā, and Bhagā. (45)
And the Yoginīs are called Vikaṭā and so forth; these six belong to you alone. O Bhagavatī Ekajaṭā, we know [this] at the end of the word "vidmahe" (we know). || 46 ||
"O you with formidable fangs, we meditate upon that; may Tārā inspire us.
This is proclaimed as the *Tīkṣṇa-gāyatrī* of the Goddess of the Seat (*pīṭhadevī*). (47)
And her goddess is Vikaṭacaṇḍikā, who wears the remains of offerings (nirmālya);
her garland is said to be made of clay or even produced from rudrākṣa seeds.
This specific distinction regarding the worship of the Goddess has been proclaimed:
the performance of services such as the ritual offerings (upacāra), the presentation of oblations (balidāna), the recitation of mantras (japa), and so forth. (49)
But the rest should be understood as before, just as in the worship of Kāmākhyā;
O King, wine is recommended for the Ānandas, and a man for the offerings (bali).
Water, coconut, meat with condiments, and sugarcane products are proclaimed to be pleasing to those who are of a sharp temperament among the objects of taste. (51)
The goddess known as Lalitakāntā, Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, has two arms; she is fair-bodied, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness. (52)
Seated upon a red lotus throne, adorned with a crown blazing with jewels, wearing dyed silk garments, she has a smiling face and an auspicious countenance. (53)
Endowed with fresh youth, possessing beautiful limbs and graceful luster,
she [recited] that mantra spoken by Umā which formerly consisted of a single syllable.
One should know that this is her mantra; with it, one should worship the Goddess:
"We know you as Nārāyaṇī; we meditate upon you as Caṇḍikā. (55)
"Then, after 'tanno lalitakāntā,' [one says] 'pracodayāt.
This Lalita-gāyatrī is proclaimed for the propitiation of the Goddess. (56)
The day of Mars is proclaimed as dear to her,
as is the spring season, and the musical note is also the Pañcama.
On the eighth and the ninth [lunar days], worship should be performed for the sake of prosperity;
the goddess Lalitacaṇḍikā is her wearer of the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
Unbroken rice grains combined with dūrvā sprouts are supremely pleasing;
this specific detail regarding her worship has been proclaimed. (59)
In the worship of the Vaiṣṇava-tantra mantra, its inner essence (antra) should be grasped; the sequence of services and offerings prescribed for it has been established as before.
During the complete worship of the Great Goddess Mahāmāyā,
one should indeed offer the blood from one's own limbs for the sake of one's own welfare.
Whoever worships Maṅgalacaṇḍikā on a Tuesday—whether in paintings, in an image, or in a jar—with auspicious dūrvā sprouts and with *śiva* (water), [attains prosperity]. 62.
That practitioner, too, shall constantly obtain his desired object at will.
Thus has been described the sequence of worship for Dikkaravāsinī.
Having heard which, one who is devoted to listening does not incur any inauspiciousness;
Aruṇa is declared to be a Dikkara (the giver of the quarters), and likewise Śambhu is a Dikkara.
The Goddess dwells upon that [mountain], and for that reason she is known as Dikkaravāsinī;
indeed, there is no woman anywhere in the three worlds who is her equal in beauty. (65)
There is no other Lalitā; therefore, the goddess Lalitakāntikā was proclaimed by Śaṅkara in the past, and her method of worship should indeed be accepted.
Listen attentively, O King, to the procedure for the worship of Brahmā.
The seed-syllable of Brahmā has been declared of old; one should employ that mantra in every respect. (67)
By worshipping with that very [mantra], one shall attain supreme nirvāṇa;
and the ancillary mantra (aṅgamantra) of this [rite] is as it was spoken by Bharga.
O King, hear now the forms of Vetāla and Bhairava:
the third vowel (u) and the letter va, followed by fire (ra), conjoined with the remaining vowel (a). (69)
The Brahma-mantra is proclaimed as being conjoined with the lunar drop (candrabindu).
Whoever worships a Brāhmaṇa with this very mantra [attains the fruit]. || 70 ||
Having attained his desired object, he rejoices in the worlds of Brahmā;
[he becomes] Brahmā, bearing a water-pot, four-faced, and four-armed.
Sometimes he was mounted upon a red lotus;
at other times, his body was reddish-fair in complexion, tall, with lofty limbs and a towering stature.
He holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his left hand and a sacrificial ladle (sruk) in his right hand;
likewise, he holds a rosary (mālā) below the right hand and a sacrificial spoon (sruva) below the left.
The vessel for the *vājya* is on the left side; all the gods are stationed in front;
Sāvitrī stands on the left side, and Sarasvatī stands on the right. (74)
And all the sages should first perform this reflection:
[a mandala] that is four-cornered, with four gates, and endowed with eight petals.
The red maṇḍala, marked with four corners, [is prepared] with the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva);
all acts such as sweeping and whatever other ritual procedures there may be [are performed]. || 76 ||
Having seen those mentioned in the Uttaratantra, such as Aṅgikā and others at the Yoga-pīṭha,
one should likewise worship all [the goddesses], beginning with Ādhāraśakti.
On the eight petals, one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) of Adma.
We know the one seated upon the lotus; we meditate upon the one mounted upon the swan. (78)
After that, the words "tad no brahma pracodayāt" [should follow].
This is the Brahmagāyatrī; one should worship the ritual procedure with this. (79)
Sanatkumāra is said to be the bearer of his floral remains (nirmālya);
however, the ritual services are as before, with the exception of the collyrium. || 80 ||
A garment of red silk is supremely pleasing to Brahmā;
likewise, food consisting of rice with milk, ghee, and sesame seeds is excellent for the meal. || 81 ||
Sandalwood mixed with white and red [pigments] is thus prescribed;
one should worship Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu at the two sides and in front during the rite of empowerment (ūjana).
One should worship the sacrificial ladle (sruva) and other implements situated within the hand upon the mandala,
as well as Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, the swan, and likewise the lotus.
This specific distinction has been declared, as well as his prostration like a staff;
a rosary made from lotus seeds is prescribed for the rite of recitation.
O King, for the rite of worship, one should always accept the two lunar days when they are full;
and one should always offer an oblation of milk to Brahmā.
O King, this has been told to you just as it was spoken by Bharga,
who revealed the auspicious place called Kāmarūpa to his two sons.
In whatever place the practitioner performs the rite, having worshipped correctly upon the sacred seat (pīṭha), he shall attain supreme nirvāṇa. || 87 ||
The worship of Brahmā has been described; now hear the worship of Viṣṇu. The seed-mantra of Vāsudeva, however, has already been set forth. (88)
O King of kings, the limb-mantra is said to consist of twelve syllables:
first "Amo bhagavate," and then "Vāsudevāya" as the supreme [part]. (89)
This is proclaimed as the limb-mantra (aṅgamantra) of Vāsudeva;
its form as the limb of delight (ratyaṅga), however, is known by the name Dadhivāmana.
O best of men, hear the mantra spoken by Śambhu for him:
first, the word "Oṃ namo viṣṇave" is proclaimed. (91)

The word "pada" (foot) followed by "surapataye" (to the Lord of the Gods) in the dative case, ending with "mahābala" and concluding with "svāhā," is considered the Vaiṣṇava heart-mantra located near the heart. || 92 ||
But that man who knows the three entrails as the seed designated for each limb becomes the very body of the God; he is not born again.
The entire sequence taught in the *Uttaratantra* should be adopted for worship;
O King, now listen to the specific distinction regarding the three mantras. (94)
O King, first hear the form of the seed-mantra:
it is white, resembling the full moon, and situated atop the king of birds. (95)
Four-armed and wearing three yellow garments that envelop his body,
he holds a mace in his upper right hand and a full-blown lotus in the one below it.
In his upper left hand he holds an exceedingly fierce discus, and in the one below it, a conch;
his chest is always marked with the Śrīvatsa, and upon his heart is the radiant Kaustubha gem.
For he carries in his left armpit a quiver filled with arrows,
while in his right hand he holds the sword Nandaka, sheathed in its scabbard, along with a bow.
On his head was a brilliantly shining crown, on his ears a pair of earrings,
and around his neck rested a variegated forest garland that hung down as far as his knees.
One should meditate upon Hari, the bestower of boons, holding the goddess Śrī on his right side and bearing Sarasvatī on his left side. 100.
O King, the form of the seed-mantra has been told to you;
now hear from me the form of this twelve-syllable mantra. (101)
One should likewise [visualize him] as dark as the petal of a blue lotus and four-armed;
one should then employ a lotus held in the upper right hand and a mace.
One should meditate upon the God as the bestower of boons, holding an incomparable discus in his lower left hand and a conch in his upper [hand]; everything else is as described previously. (103)
O King, listen attentively to the meditation upon each limb of this eighteen-syllable mantra, which destroys the fear of poverty. (104)
One should visualize [the deity] as white in color, radiant like the full moon;
one should visualize in the left hand a jar filled with nectar.
To the right, a golden vessel containing curd-rice and sugar-candy;
and the God seated upon a lotus posture, situated within the orb of the moon. 106.
The god always wears white garments and is short in stature;
he is endowed with a slight smile, the lord of the three worlds, and Trivikrama.
One should meditate upon the God who grants boons and bestows the fruit of all desires, just as it was taught in the previous tantras regarding burning, immersion, and other rites. 108.
Likewise, the mantras are to be received, as well as those belonging to the Uttaratantra;
hear now its mandala procedure as spoken by Bharga.

In daily worship, [the altar] is prepared with lines and likewise with the five powders; in occasional worship, it should now be performed according to the distinction between difference and non-difference.
Eight cubits in measure, with four doors and resembling a lotus, it is charming, being joined at its four corners with four conch shells. || 111 ||
The gateway for the lords of the directions is likewise provided with weapons as instruments,
placed in the eight directions, together with an outer surrounding lotus.
O King, listen now to how the work is to be done with powders:
with white, yellow, red, dark, and green, in that order. (113)
One should construct the mandala with powders; otherwise, one should not perform it.
It may be four cubits, three cubits, two cubits, or even a single cubit in size.
One should construct the mandala everywhere as previously described or even larger;
for rites such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha, it is considered appropriate to be more than four cubits in size.

O King, because the ritual procedures do not deviate from the prescribed rules, in each and every instance, the sequence for drawing the weapons of the world-protectors and the lotuses is as previously described.
In the center, a perfectly circular lotus is to be made with white powders;
its pericarp is yellow in color, and likewise, the tips of its filaments are reddish.
One should fill the exterior of the lotus on all sides with red and yellow [colors].
[Then one should place] the vajra, the śakti, the iron staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, and the mace.
Furthermore, the tridents and weapons of the lords of the eight directions [are placed] in sequence:
Śambhu, Gaurī, Brahmā, Rāma, and likewise Kṛṣṇa. (119)
These five deities, being thus established, are to be constantly worshipped;
a fool should never effect a separation between Śambhu and Gaurī.
But if worship is performed during separation, it becomes fruitless for him;
however, that which is severed at the head, being a spirit, is indeed capable when worshipped.
In the ritual placement (nyāsa) of this mandala, one should avoid the defect of dust;
a mandala must be constructed everywhere for the worship of Vāsudeva.
In this very way, O best of kings, one [aspect] is fruitless while the other is otherwise;
for Balabhadra, Kāma, and Aniruddha arise from that.
Nārāyaṇa, as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are proclaimed as the sixth;
Narasiṃha and Varāha, along with Oginna—these eight are proclaimed. (124)

One should worship the white deities individually according to their forms and mantras on the eight petals starting from the east; however, one should worship Vāsudeva as the central leader in the middle of the pericarp.
Vimalā is proclaimed as the consort of that Vāsudeva;
now hear, O son of Pṛthā, of the yoginīs of Balabhadra and the others. 126.
The first is to be known as Utkarṣiṇī; thereafter Jñānā, then Kriyāparā; likewise Yogā, Prahvī, Aiśānī, and the eighth is Anugrāhī.
All are said to have four arms and to bear the conch, the discus, and the mace;
likewise, the Yogins and Balabhadra may optionally omit the ritual procedure (vidhi).
Here, however, the form previously described is Balarāma, who holds a plow and a pestle, as well as a club and a discus, and always has a mace resting at his side. (129)
Kāma, however, holds a flowery bow with his left hand;
he further holds a discus and a flower with his other hands.
He likewise holds a lotus at his side, and everything else is as before;
the discus and the conch are proclaimed to be on the right side of Varāha. 131.
Furthermore, for Nṛsiṃha, the discus and conch are on the right and left [hands] respectively;
likewise, for Viṣṇu, the conch and lotus are situated in the two right hands. (132)
O best of enemies, the conch and mace are held in the left hands of Nārāyaṇa,
while Aniruddha holds the mace in his lower right hand.
Likewise red, likewise yellow, resembling crushed collyrium, dark like the petal of a blue lotus, and possessing the luster of a red cloud. || 134 ||
O King, these yogins are said to be, in order of their complexion, dark as a bee, tawny, and golden-fair, [resembling] Vāsudeva. 135.
Whatever be the color and whatever be the meditation of each particular yogin, he should contemplate a Yoginī of that same appearance standing near him.
All the deities of the seat, headed by Ādhāraśakti, as well as all the planets and the guardians of the directions, [are to be worshipped] through meditation and likewise with mantras. (137)

O King, they are to be worshipped in their respective locations within the mandala according to the sequence; whatever the deity has conceived within his body, such as the lotus and so forth, [is to be worshipped there]. (138)
One should worship the wielder of weapons, as well as Vajra, Śakti, Garuḍa, and the others,
having attained the garland of phonemes according to the tradition of Śambhu through the yoga of sequence.
The mantras for Gadā and the others, according to the sequence of the first and second [sections], have been declared by Nārada as they appear in the portion taught in the Pañcarātra. (140)
The mantras for the discus, mace, and other [emblems] are to be employed everywhere in worship.
Garuḍa is like the sun in appearance, and the mace is made of black iron.
Sarasvatī is white in color, and Lakṣmī always has the luster of gold;
the discus, however, is proclaimed to resemble the midday sun. 142.
The conch is proclaimed to be like the full moon;
the Kaustubha is said to be reddish, while the Śrīvatsa has a reddish luster. (143)
The Kaustubha gem is to be known as slightly reddish; the garland is proclaimed to be multicolored;
all the arrows have the brilliance of lightning, and the bow has the luster of Indra’s rainbow. (144)
His garment is proclaimed to be the brilliance of gold dust;
two earrings, resembling the rising sun, adorn his ears.
A crown resembling the sun is proclaimed for his head.
Listen now, O King, to the ritual placement (nyāsa), by means of which one assumes the form of Viṣṇu. 146.
The practitioner should indeed always be one who bestows heaven and liberation;
first, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the twelve syllables. (147)
Then one should place the seed-syllable of Vāsudeva and likewise the seed-syllable of the Yogins,
using the great mantras consisting of eighteen syllables.
Then, with the six mantras beginning with the heart-mantra, and again in two ways,
one should perform a single worship by means of these four types of nyāsa.
First, the wise practitioner should place the first syllable of the twelve-syllable mantra on the right thumb,
and then the remaining seed-syllables in their proper sequence.
On the right hand, beginning with the little finger and ending with the left thumb,
one should subsequently place the remaining two syllables on the palms of both hands.
In the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the two shoulders, the two eyes, the navel, the back, the two arms, the two shanks, and the two feet, respectively. (152)
Then one should place the seed-syllables of the twelve-syllable mantra;
first, the principle of Vāsudeva is placed on the two thumbs. (153)
The yogi should place the eight seed-syllables on the two [hands], beginning with the index finger, and on the head, eyes, mouth, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and knees. (154)
O King, one should place the seed-syllables of Yoga and the mantras of the heart and other limbs, which were previously mentioned, upon the two feet of Vāsudeva.
Having placed those [mantras] at the base of the thumbs and on each pair of fingers of both the left and right hands, one should place the remainder on the palms.
One should again place those [syllables] in sequence from the heart to the weapon;
the wise one should place the first nine syllables of the eighteen-syllable mantra.
In the previously mentioned locations such as the head and eyes, which are the spheres of the nine seed-syllables,
one should place the remaining letters in a mixed manner upon the sides, the bladder, and the penis.
One should place [the hands] on the hips, the thighs, the shanks, and upon the toes;
whichever worship for whichever mantra is prescribed therein by the Tantras.
The mantra-practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of that tantra in that very [place];
or else, the wise one should perform the placement of all [mantras] in a single location. || 160 ||
Having purified his self and shaken off all impurities through the fourfold nyāsas performed,
the practitioner of mantra becomes Viṣṇu in person and shall obtain the full fruit of perfect worship.
Even without performing worship, he who performs the fourfold ritual placement (nyāsa) attains union with Viṣṇu, the supreme state; such a person is steadfast.
Then, having meditated upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), one should sequentially place Garuḍa, the discus, the conch, the mace, Lakṣmī, and likewise the lotus within these [positions]. || 163 ||
The wise knower of mantras should place [the deities] in order in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners, as well as in the south and the north. 164.
Having placed the forest garland, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem in the center of the lotus,
one should place the Śārṅga bow upon its right side.
One should place a pair of lutes on the left and a sword on the right;
having placed a shield on the left, one should then fashion Sarasvatī there.
And having performed all the worship, one should then display the mudrās—those such as the Puṭa and others which have been taught, as well as those belonging to Viṣṇu and the yogins. (167)
One should display the individual mudrās of the planets and the lords of the directions;
the remaining mantras were previously taught for the purpose of ensuring the rite is free from defects.
Having recited their respective mantras, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun;
Viṣvaksena, the bearer of Viṣṇu’s floral remains (*nirmālya*), is four-armed. (169)
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, bearing long beard and matted locks,
and being of a reddish-brown complexion, he stands upon a white lotus.
That which is joined with the third vowel-ending and with the moon-point (bindu) is proclaimed as his mantra; therefore, one should worship him with that. || 171 ||
The dismissal of Viṣṇu is likewise proclaimed to be in the northeast;
for others, such as Bala and the rest, one should perform the dismissal mentally.
Thus, whoever performs worship of Viṣṇu, Śambhu, or Brahmā anywhere on the pedestal of Dikkaravāsinī, he goes to the supreme state. || 173 ||
O best of kings, wherever there may be the worship of Viṣṇu,
right there this Tantra should indeed be accepted by wise Vaiṣṇavas.
In brief, one should worship Dadhivāmana right there;
however, in his worship, the worship of the limbs beginning with the heart (hṛdaya) must not be performed.
One should worship Vāsudeva either in brief or in detail, [offering] red silk cloth, as well as yellow and white. (176)
This garment is proclaimed to be a giver of joy to Vāsudeva;
among lamps, the ghee lamp is best, and among perfumes, that which originates from Malaya. (177)
Copper is considered pleasing when used for vessels for drinking, water-offerings, and food;
likewise, crowns, earrings, necklaces, and ornaments grant satisfaction to Viṣṇu. (178)
The conch shell in vessels for bathing and agallochum (aguru) among incenses are always proclaimed to be pleasing to Vāsudeva. (179)
The Kadamba, Kubjaka, Jātī, Mallikā, Mālatī, and the Paṅkaja—these flowers indeed grant pleasure to Viṣṇu. (180)
A person, a sacrificial mound, a place, a sacred ford, or even water—these are the objects;
the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and the Puruṣasūkta are the hymn of praise. (181)
A garland produced from Putrañjīva is praised for the worship of Viṣṇu;
the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is declared the [proper] date, and springtime is the most excellent season. || 182 ||
Among foods, śāli rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), barley gruel (yāvaka), milk-rice (pāyasa), ghee, and kṛśara are desired;
likewise, among drinks, milk is preferred. (183)
O best of kings, among leaves, the tulasī leaf, the bilva, and the āmalaka are those that bring pleasure to Hari. (184)
One should avoid all those things that belong to others;
thus, that best of men who would constantly worship Viṣṇu in this manner— || 185 ||
Having uplifted ten million lineages, he himself shall become Janārdana.
O King, this mantra of Vāsudeva has been recounted to you. (186)
Thus, Śambhu revealed the entire Kāmarūpa-pīṭha, including a concise determination of its nature. (187)
Accompanied by those two sons, he then went to Mount Kailāsa;
having arrived there, he established his two sons in their respective appropriate positions.
O best of kings, they became liberated from their curse and attained immortality—Śambhu, the Daughter of the Mountain, as well as Vetāla and Bhairava. (189)
Whoever listens to this great narrative with a one-pointed mind has no fear of curses, nor does he have diseases or mental anxieties. (190)
Endowed with sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty, beloved everywhere, and possessed of all auspicious things, he lives for a long time. (191)
That best of men who knows Kāmarūpa, the great pīṭha, becomes endowed with divine knowledge and shall attain supreme nirvāṇa. || 192 ||
He who performs the pilgrimage to all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) in Kāmarūpa, having reached all the seats, shall worship all the deities. || 193 ||
Having swiftly established ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first in divine knowledge, he shall attain liberation together with them all.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 80 ||
The eighty-first chapter.
Aurva said:
Having bathed and drunk [the water] at the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Kāmarūpa, one worships the deities.
And having worshipped it, many people in former times went to heaven. || 1 ||
Some attained nirvāṇa, while others reached the state of Śambhu;
Yama was unable to restrain them or lead them to his own abode.
O tiger among men, he became patient, though filled with trepidation for Śivā;
for the hosts of Śaṅkara obstructed the messenger of Yama as he was proceeding there.
Out of fear of that, the messengers of Yama do not go there, even when urged;
and having seen this, Śamana likewise desists from his own activity.
Having approached the Creator, he spoke these words:
"O Creator, having bathed and drunk here in this Kāmarūpa, a human being [attains his desire]. (5)
He attains the status of a gaṇa of Kāmākhyā, as well as the lordship of Śambhu’s gaṇas;
I have no authority there, nor am I capable of restraining them.
"Employ the policy appropriate for this situation, if it is fitting within your sphere of action.
Having heard those words of his, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted accordingly].
He went to the abode of Viṣṇu together with Samavartin; having approached him, he reported to Viṣṇu exactly what Yama had said.
The Lord of All Worlds accepted those words exactly as they were;
then, together with Brahmā and Yama, Viṣṇu approached Śambhu.
Honored by him and questioned, he spoke these words that had been uttered by Yama.
The Blessed Lord said:
By all the gods, by all the sacred fords (tīrthas), and likewise by all the holy fields (kṣetras), this Kāmarūpa is pervaded; there exists nothing superior to this.
Having reached this sacred seat (pīṭha), human beings attain divinity;
they achieve immortality and the status of a Gaṇa, for Yama has no power there.
Therefore, O Mahādeva, act such that Yama may be fit for his office there;
for where Yama has been cast out, no moral boundary is seen.
Aurva said:
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, he accepted that speech in his heart, together with Vidhi, for the sake of accomplishing what was to be achieved.
Having dismissed Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Yama, the one whose vehicle is the bull took all his own attendants and went to the interior of Kāmarūpa.
Then Śaṅkara spoke to the goddess Ugratārā and to Gaṇa:
"O Gaṇas, quickly drive away all these people from this place."
"O Ugratārā, Great Goddess, you too must quickly drive them away!
Then the Gaṇas from Kāmarūpa and the unconquered Goddess [also set forth].
They cleared the people away to prepare a seat for Hara;
while the world was being cleared, including the four castes and the twice-born, [the following occurred].
The brahmin sage Vasiṣṭha, having reached the mountain of twilight (the sunset peak), was provoked to anger;
yet even he was driven away by the goddess Ugratārā, who is all-powerful.
Held back by his attendants, he spoke, uttering a most terrible curse:
"Since I, a sage, was forcibly detained by you in order to drive me away... (19)
Therefore, together with your attendants, you must become worthy of worship through your state of being a Vāmī;
for those of dull intellect among the Gaṇas behave like barbarians. 20.
Therefore, may you indeed become Mlecchas in Kāmarūpa,
since even Mahādeva has exerted himself to drive me out.
May Śaṅkara, who wears bones and ashes, become dear to the Mlecchas— just as he was to that self-controlled sage rich in asceticism who had mastered the Vedas, yet appeared like a Mleccha.
But this place called Kāmarūpa, protected by Mlecchas and devoid of joy, Viṣṇu himself does not return to until this location [is restored]. 23.
May those scriptures that expound this be rare;
for rare indeed is the wise man who knows the Kāmarūpāgama.
"He himself shall obtain the full fruit when the time has arrived.
Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha vanished right there.
Those hosts became Mlecchas in Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods;
even the fierce Tārā became Vāmā, and Śambhu became devoted to the Mlecchas.
The scriptures were rare, and those that did exist were proponents of my [teachings]; they were devoid of Vedic mantras and excluded from the four castes. || 27 ||
Kāmarūpa, which was born in an instant and is governed by Yama,
became a fruit-bestowing sacred seat (pīṭha) even after Hari had arrived and been released from his curse.
Just as gods and humans would not remain properly upon that throne,
Brahmā devised a means for the protection of all the sacrificial pits.
Of both the Apunarbhava-kuṇḍa and the Soma-kuṇḍa,
as well as of the Brahma-kuṇḍa and the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa, and also of many rivers— (30)
For the protection of the rivers previously mentioned as well as those not yet mentioned,
he likewise established Brahman as the means for knowing the single fruit of everything.
By the wise son of Jamadagni, having produced his own son in the form of water within Amoghā, the wife of Śantanu, [he was restored].
He descended without agitation, flooding Kāmarūpaka;
that steadfast son of Brahmā continued flooding the multitude of sacrificial pits.
Having covered all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he made them hidden on earth;
only those men who know the Lauhitya alone truly know them to be there.
They certainly obtain the fruit of bathing in the Lauhitya, even if they do not know of other pools or sacred fords (tīrthas). || 35 ||
This concealment of the sacred fords (tīrtha) has come about due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha;
whoever knows that, as well as the excellence of those sacred fords, [is protected]. 36.
O best of men, he fully obtains that fruit of bathing after having bathed in all rivers and at all sacred fords everywhere;
then the Lauhitya, the son of Brahmā, flows toward the southern ocean. (37)
Thus, O King, the glorification of Kāmarūpa has been told to you;
whatever else pleases you, ask that, and I shall declare it to you. (38)
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 81 ||
The eighty-second chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard the words of Aurva, Sagara spoke again to that sage.
With his mind overflowing with joy, he questioned these best of the twice-born.
Sagara said:
How was the son of Brahmā, Lauhitya, [born] from Amoghā during the sacrifice?
And how did that lotus-seated one take delight in the wife of Śāntanu?
How was the son of Pārastraiṇeya born from his grandfather?
O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear all of that; please tell me.
Aurva said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, I shall relate a most magnificent narrative concerning the high-souled Lauhitya, the son of Brahmā. (4)
In Harivarṣa and Mahāvarṣa, there was a highly fortunate sage named Śāntanu by name; he was possessed of knowledge and devoted to austerity.
His wife was the highly fortunate and great chaste lady named Amoghā,
born in the hermitage of the sage Tṛṇabindu, the son of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Dwelling with her on Mount Kailāsa, which serves as a boundary mountain,
he stayed on the Gandhamādana range on the shore of the lake named Lohita.
Once, that ascetic, devoted to penance, went into a dense forest to gather flowers and many fruits within his range of vision.
At that moment, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds,
arrived at the place where Amoghā, the beloved of Śāntanu, was present.
Seeing that exceedingly beautiful young woman, who was like a daughter of the gods, he was quickly deluded by passion and his senses became corrupted. (10)
Having his senses aroused and desiring to seize that great virtuous lady,
Brahmā, afflicted by passion, then ran toward her from that place, facing her directly.
