Seeing the Creator running toward her, the great and virtuous Amogha cried out, "Not so! Not so! and hid herself within the leaf-hut.
Then the unfailing one, having become enraged, spoke thus to Dhātṛ:
having gone inside the leaf-hut, she blocked the door at that very moment. (13)
"I must not perform an improper act, one censured by the wives of sages.
If you carry me away by force after having violently overpowered me, I shall curse you. (14)
When Amoghā had spoken thus, O King, the seed of the sage Śāntanu, the creator, was discharged right there in the hermitage. (15)
When his semen was discharged, even Dhātṛ arose upon a swan-vehicle;
his soul overwhelmed with extreme shame, he quickly departed for his own hermitage.
When the Creator had departed, Śāntanu returned to his own hermitage;
having arrived, he then saw on the ground the disturbance caused by the tracks of the swans.
And that splendor, resembling a blazing fire, fell upon the earth;
it then questioned Amoghā, who was staying within her leaf-hut.
"What is this that is seen occurring here, O fortunate lady—this agitation of the birds' feet and what kind of splendor is this? (19)
Having heard those words of his, she, though indignant, spoke to Śāntanu, the best of sages, with a troubled and dejected face.
Someone with four faces, carrying a water-pot in his hand, arrived in a chariot yoked with swans and intensely entreated me for my daughter Rati. (21)
Therefore, having been threatened by me while I was hidden within my hut,
he withdrew his splendor, overcome by the fear of my curse.
O Śāntanu, if you are able, provide a remedy for this;
for no living being is capable of enduring such an assault.
Having heard her words and having thus resolved that Brahmā himself had arrived, he became intent on meditation and gave [the gift] with a cart. || 24 ||
Having understood through his divine knowledge that the task of the gods had arrived,
as well as his own descent to the sacred ford for the welfare of the worlds, the sage [acted].
Having understood the consequence and reflected upon it, he said this to his wife:
"By my command, drink this energy of Brahmā so that it may not be in vain."
For the welfare of the entire world and for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods' mission, Brahmā himself has come into your presence. (27)
Having entrusted to you his great task before departing for his own abode without having reached you, he said: "Therefore, you ought to carry out those words. (28)
Having heard those words of Śāntanu, that great virtuous woman was exceedingly ashamed; bowing down to her husband, she spoke to him as if consoling him.
I shall not bestow my splendor upon anyone else, nor shall you suffer any dejection of mind;
if it must certainly be done, drink it and then discharge it into me.
Then, having heard her words— which were both appropriate and true— Śāntanu himself drank that vital energy and deposited it within his wife.
Then, having received those splendors of Brahmā transferred by Śantanu,
the virtuous woman named Amoghā conceived a child for the welfare of the worlds.
When her time had arrived, a collection of water issued from her nose;
and in its midst was a son, dressed in blue garments and wearing a diadem.
Adorned with a garland of jewels, he is reddish-white in complexion like Brahmā;
he has four arms and likewise holds a lotus, a staff of knowledge, a banner, and a spear.
And Śāntanu, who brought peace to the world, was born with the head of a porpoise, his body covered by masses of water, and remaining in that state.
And he established them in the middle region between the four mountains;
Kailāsa was on the northern side, and Gandhamādana on the southern.
To the west is Mount Rārudhi, and to the east is the pair of Saṃvartakas;
in their midst, O son of Brahmā, is the Kuṇḍa of the mountains themselves.
Having done so, he grew constantly like the moon in autumn;
and having obtained that son who was situated in the midst of the waters, Druhiṇa [became joyful].
In due order, he performed his purificatory rites for the sake of bodily purification.
Then, after a long period of time had passed, the son of Brahmā [arrived].
It increased to five yojanas in the form of a mass of water;
in it, the gods drank and bathed as if in a second ocean.
In that place, which possessed delightful, pure, and white waters and was graced by divine hosts of Apsarases,
the powerful Rāma, son of Jamadagni, arrived at that moment.

At his father's command, he committed the terrible and improper murder of his mother; and for the sake of liberation from that sin, following the instruction of his own father, [he performed penance]. (42)
He went to the great pool named Brahma with the desire to bathe;
having bathed and drunk there, he removed the sin of matricide,
and having cleared a path with his axe, he caused him to descend into the earth.
Sagara said:
For what reason did Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, slay his own mother? And what was the name of his mother, and whose daughter was she? (44)
How was the sage’s son born, so cruel and possessed of great strength, that hero skilled in battle who crushed the royal warriors? (45)
Therefore, O best of sages, I desire to hear this in its true essence;
tell it to me, O illustrious one, even if it be a secret. (46)
Aurva said:
Listen attentively, O King, to the life-story of the son of Jamadagni; hear how he, being exceedingly cruel, slew his own mother.
The son of Brahmā was named Bhṛgu, and his son was Ṛcīka.
Seeking a wife, he once traveled across the earth and arrived at Kānyakubja in ancient times.
And he saw Gādhi, the son of Kuśika and born of the lineage of Jahnu, established in asceticism in the forest, O best of kings. (49)
Then, while that king was dwelling in the forest desiring a son,
a daughter was born to him and his wife, equal to a celestial maiden in her virtues.
Ṛcīka, the son of Bhṛgu, requested her as his wife;
"O great sage, my daughter is now worthy to be given by you. (51)
However, there is one family custom of mine regarding the collection of the bride-price:
to him who shall give a thousand dark-colored horses, radiant as the moon, my daughter shall be given. (52)
Ṛcīka said: "O King, I shall indeed give you a thousand such horses;
wait for a short time until I bring them."
"So be it," Gādhi said to the son of Bhṛgu;
he then went to Kānyakubja on the bank of the Gaṅgā to accomplish the horse-sacrifice.
There, having propitiated Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, the sage— the son of Bhṛgu—
then received from him a thousand horses.
O best of kings, because he obtained the horses there at that time,
that place became famous as Aśvatīrtha, which yields supreme and great fruit.
Having accepted a thousand horses that had arisen from the waters of the Gaṅgā and were duly presented by Pracetas, the sage then departed for Gādhi.
Taking those horses, Gādhi gave his daughter Satyavatī to Ṛcīka,
just as the ocean gave Lakṣmī to Keśava.
Having obtained the blameless Gādhi’s daughter as his wife,
Ṛcīka rejoiced and sported with her at his own hermitage according to his desire.
Having heard that his son had taken a wife, the wise Bhṛgu came to see his son and daughter-in-law;
and upon seeing his daughter-in-law, he rejoiced.
Having worshipped Bhṛgu, who was seated there and honored by the hosts of gods, according to the prescribed rule, the couple stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Then Bhṛgu, being well-pleased, said this to his own daughter-in-law:
"Choose a boon, O lady of excellent complexion; I shall grant you whatever you desire. (62)
"Whatever may be difficult to obtain or even impossible for you to acquire, from that [you shall gain] a son named Satyavān, who has mastered the Vedas through ascetic penance. (63)
And he requested from his mother an incomparable and excellent son;
having said, "So be it," he then became absorbed in meditation.
Having supported the entire universe with his mind, he laboriously exhaled;
from the wind of that exhalation, indeed, two vessels of sacrificial pap (caru) emerged.
Having given those two portions to her, Bhṛgu said this to her:
"O daughter-in-law Satyavatī, take these two portions of sacrificial porridge yourself. (66)
"Having bathed during every menstrual period, your mother and you, O daughter-in-law, shall perform the rite;
indeed, your mother shall embrace the Aśvattha tree for the sake of obtaining a male child."
Then she will eat this sacrificial oblation (caru) which is intensely red;
and you, having embraced a black udumbara tree, [will eat] the sacrificial oblation.
"You shall enjoy [the fruits], and your son shall be eternal.
Having spoken thus, Bhṛgu departed as he pleased, and she too was filled with joy.
Then, on the day of her ritual bath, that beautiful woman, accompanied by her mother, husband, and father, embraced an *aśvattha* tree and [offered] a reddish sacrificial oblation (*caru*).
Satyavatī took from her mother that white *caru* of *phalgu* grain;
but the sage Bhṛgu, possessing divine knowledge, realized that an exchange had occurred. (71)
Then, having arrived, she spoke these words to her daughter-in-law:
"O blessed lady, you have acted perversely in the matter of embracing the tree."
Likewise, regarding the consumption of meat, this shall happen to you:
your son will be a Brāhmaṇa who follows the conduct of a Kṣatriya. (73)
"A son shall be born to your mother who, though a Kṣatriya, will follow the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having spoken thus to Satyavatī, the virtuous lady, Bhṛgu then [departed]. (74)
He again propitiated him, saying, "May such a one be my grandson.
Having said, "So be it," Bhṛgu vanished right there.
Then, in due time, the daughter of Gādhi gave birth to a radiant son, Jamadagni;
and his mother [subsequently] gave birth to Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of asceticism.
Thereupon Jamadagni obtained the four Vedas without delay;
the science of archery (Dhanurveda) appeared of its own accord within that great soul.
Viśvāmitra also quickly obtained all the Vedas as well as the entire science of archery (Dhanurveda), and by the power of his asceticism, he became a Brahmin.
Blazing with splendor, the radiant Jamadagni, a great ascetic,
surpassed even the sun by means of his Vedic knowledge and penances, O sage.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 82 ||
The eighty-third chapter.
Aurva said:
Then, after some time had passed, Jamadagni, of great asceticism, [performed a sacrifice].
The daughter of the King of Vidarbha, won by his own effort.
He took Renuka, who was endowed with auspicious marks, as his wife;
from him she gave birth to four sons who were equal to the Vedas.
After him, the Lord Madhusūdana himself was born from her as Ruṣaṇvat, Suṣeṇa, Vasu, and likewise Viśvāvasu.
Requested by all the gods, beginning with Śakra, for the swift slaying of Kārtavīrya, he became their fifth incarnation, known by the name Rāma.
He was born together with an axe for the purpose of removing the world's burden;
he never forsakes that innate axe.
Due to the reversal of his own grandmother’s consumption of sacrificial porridge (caru),
this Brāhmaṇa Rāma became a performer of cruel deeds, adopting the conduct of a Kṣatriya.
Having mastered all the Vedas and the science of archery in its entirety,
he became an expert in Vedic knowledge and was constantly fulfilled in his purpose.
Once, his mother Reṇukā went to the waters of the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing,
and there she beheld a king named Citraratha.
He was with his wives of similar beauty, delighting in games upon the terrace; he was auspicious, well-clothed, youthful, and adorned with a beautiful garland.
Seeing the king in such a state, Reṇukā, her passion intensely aroused, longed for that radiant monarch.
As she was filled with longing, a moistening of her heart arose;
drenched by the water that had lost its consciousness, she went trembling back to her own hermitage.
Jamadagni perceived that Renuka had become thus deformed;
crying out "Fie! Fie! he reviled her from all sides.
Then that sage quickly spoke to all four sons, headed by Uṣaṇvan, addressing each one in turn.
"Cut down this Reṇukā, who is devoted to sin and unchaste!
But they did not act upon those words; they remained like the mute and the dull-witted.
Enraged, Jamadagni cursed them who were thus deprived of their senses;
and that king [Viśvāmitra] spoke to the sage, O tiger among kings, regarding Gādhi. || 15 ||
"O dull-witted ones, you who are greedy for cattle and wealth, become [as if] woven together from this day forward!
Then there arrived the last descendant of Jamadagni, possessed of exceeding prowess.
And his father said to that Rāma, "Cut off your most wicked mother," having seen his brothers likewise in such a state, devoid of knowledge.
The one of great splendor cut his mother with an axe because she had been cursed by his father;
seeing Renukā thus slain by Rāma, he became filled with rage.
Jamadagni, being pleased, spoke these words:
"I am gratified, my son; may it be well with you, for you have carried out my command. (19)
"Therefore, choose now the desired boons and objects of your longing.
Rāma, however, first chose the restoration of his mother to life.
The non-remembrance of her slaughter, the release of her brothers from the curse, the removal of the sin of matricide, and victory everywhere in battle—[these were granted]. (21)
O best of kings, Jamadagni, the great ascetic, granted him all those boons, including a lifespan lasting until the end of the kalpa, in due order.
Then Reṇukā became like a mother who had just awakened from sleep;
established in her innate nature, she did not even remember the killing.
At that very moment, Rāma indeed obtained victory in battle and long life;
then, his father spoke these words to him for the sake of expiating the murder of his mother.
"O son, the murder of one's mother does not depart by the granting of a boon;
therefore, go to Brahmakuṇḍa and bathe in its waters. (25)
Having bathed there, freed from sin, you shall return before long;
for the welfare of the world, my son, go quickly to Brahmakuṇḍa.
Having heard his words, Rāma, wielding his axe, then [performed] the slaying according to his father's instruction at Brahmakuṇḍa, where the water was that of a bull.
Having performed his bath there according to the prescribed rites and having washed his battle-axe,
he clearly beheld the murder of his mother as it emerged from his body.
Then, having gained full confidence, he reached that excellent sacred ford;
having cleared a path with his axe, he caused the son of Brahmā to flow.
Then, having issued from the Brahmakuṇḍa, that son of Brahmā fell into the lake called Lohita in the valley of Kailāsa.
Rising again on the shore of that very lake,
the mighty one brought the son of Brahmā toward the eastern direction with his axe.
Then, having pierced the mountain with its golden peaks even further beyond,
Hari brought him to that sacred seat (pīṭha) which is the interior of Kāmarūpa.
Vidhi himself gave him the name Lohitagaṅgaka;
because he was born from the Lohita lake, he thereafter became known as Lohita.
Having inundated the entire seat of Kāmarūpa with its waters and concealing all the holy fords, it flows toward the southern ocean.
Having already abandoned the divine Yamunā, that son of Brahmā travels twelve yojanas and falls again into the Lauhitya.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, that man who has his senses restrained,
remaining pure and with a disciplined mind throughout the entire month of Caitra— || 36 ||
He who bathes in the waters of the Lauhitya goes to the abode of Brahmā;
he who bathes in the waters of the Lauhitya shall attain absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Thus, O King, I have told you for what purpose the hero, the son of Jamadagni, formerly slew his mother, and why he was a performer of cruel deeds.
But he who hears this great narrative day after day becomes long-lived, joyful, and strong. (39)
Thus, O King, I have told you how the Daughter of the Mountain took half of Śambhu’s body, and how the two named Vetāla and Bhairava likewise [took their portions].
Or whose two sons were born and attained the status of Gaṇeśas?
O best of kings, tell me that; what else shall I say to you? (41)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Such was the conversation between Aurva and the high-souled Sagara concerning how half of Śambhu’s body was taken away by the Daughter of the Mountain.
O Brahmins, everything that was asked regarding the supreme Siddha known as Bhairava, as well as the definitive determination of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), has been told today. (43)
The origin of Bhṛṅgin and also of Mahākāla has indeed been told to you; what else, O best of the twice-born, do you wish to ask? 44.
Thus, having understood this entire collection of scriptures— which is purified by its tantras and mantras, which yields manifold fruits, which serves as a manual for the repose of the wise,
and which is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) solely intent upon the path of knowledge— [one attains liberation].
He who recites this tantra here will constantly leak [his vital essence]. || 45 ||
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 83 ||
The eighty-fourth chapter.
The sages said:
"The creation has been described by you, and our doubts have also been dispelled."
O illustrious one, O teacher, by your grace we have accomplished our purpose.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, we wish to hear this:
who else were Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla born as Vetāla and Bhairava?
O tiger among the twice-born, we have heard of Vetāla, Mahākāla, Bhairava, and likewise Bhṛṅgin; how is it that there are these four?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of the twice-born, when Mahākāla had gone to the earth and Bhṛṅgin was established among men, as were the two spirits known as Vetāla and Bhairava— 4.
When the Vetāla Bhairava had obtained his boon and joined him,
Hara made Andhaka, who was engaged in asceticism, as well as Bhṛṅgin, his attendants.
Andhaka, having previously opposed Hara, fell into calamity;
later, by propitiating Hara, that asura became his son.
Out of affection for Bhṛṅgin, Hara made that Bhṛṅgin his own through a sign;
out of affection for Mahākāla, Hara [accepted] Bāṇa, the son of Bali;
and he then made Mahākāla one whose arms had been severed by Viṣṇu.
Thus, O best of sages, those four were restrained by him in succession: Vetāla and Bhairava, and Bhṛṅgin and Mahākāla.
The sages said: "O Sage Aurva of great intellect, [please explain] that which was asked by Sagara regarding the policy by which a wife, a son, or even one's own self should be employed, O Teacher."
Those who abide by the political ethics of the virtuous, by the conduct of the good, and by the special rules proclaimed by the great-souled Aurva—[they shall not suffer]. (10)
Especially, O best of the twice-born, O ascetic rich in penance, we desire to hear them correctly; tell them to us, O illustrious one, O teacher of the world. (11)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Whatever specific details have been told by the high-souled Aurva, I shall declare all of that to you; listen, O best of sages.
Having heard this, King Sagara again questioned the great sage regarding the specific details of the ritual manuals for mantras and other matters, such as statesmanship (nīti).
Sagara said:
"Tell me of that policy by which a son, one's own self, and beloved ones are to be employed, along with their specific distinctions and the conduct of the virtuous."
Aurva said:
"Listen in due order, O Indra among kings, to the policy by which one is directed—whether it be oneself, a son, or a wife; hear from me the specific distinctions therein. (15)
One should first serve Brahmins who are advanced in knowledge, learning, and austerity, as well as those advanced in age, who are highly proficient and entirely free from malice.
And from them he should constantly hear the definitive conclusions of the Vedic scriptures;
whatever they say should be performed, and a wise king should act accordingly. (17)
The five sense-faculties are the five horses; the body is said to be the chariot.
The self is the charioteer, knowledge is the whip, and the mind is called the driver. (18)
One should make the horses well-tamed and bring the charioteer under one's own control;
likewise, the whip must always be firm, as must the steadiness of the body. (19)
Just as a rider mounting unbroken Sindh horses might, by following the will of the horses, set out upon a wrong path; || 20 ||
In that situation, even a driver who is himself powerless, by urging the horses according to his own will,
may lead even a heroic warrior who is mounted on a chariot to victory, provided he is under the control of another.
In the same way, a king should bring his senses under his own control when grasping sense objects, as well as his mind and firm wisdom. (22)
O best of kings, when knowledge is firm and the passions are subdued, the charioteer is self-controlled and capable of directing the tamed horses.
Therefore, having brought his own senses and mind under control, the king,
established upon the path of knowledge, should accomplish what is beneficial for himself.

One should eat as one desires, but should not give way to greed for liquor; one should look at what is to be looked at, and likewise, one should not look at what is not to be looked at according to one's own whim. (25)
That which is to be heard should be heard; one should not engage in further hearing beyond that.
For a wise person does not become subservient to mere scriptural learning in the absence of the true essence of the scriptures. (26)

In this way, having brought both the sense of smell and the skin under control by his will, the king should not enjoy them according to his own whims, nor should he pursue sensory objects with unrestrained passion. (27)
If a king were thus, then he would be one who has conquered his senses;
and the cause for conquering the senses is the service of the scriptures and the elders. (28)
A king who does not know the scriptures to be followed by the elders will fall under the power of his enemies;
therefore, a king should remain established in the scriptures and keep his senses conquered. (29)
Fortitude, confidence, enthusiasm, eloquence, discernment, dexterity, retentiveness, generosity, friendliness, and gratitude. || 30 ||
Firmness of command, truthfulness, purity, decisiveness of mind, knowledge of the intentions of others, and steadfastness in times of adversity constitute his conduct. (31)
The capacity to restrain the afflictions, worshiping the guru, the gods, and the twice-born, freedom from envy, and the absence of anger—the king should practice these virtues. (32)

One should constantly remain vigilant regarding the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, as well as virtue, wealth, and pleasure; and one should act upon them when the proper occasion arises.
Having understood the fourfold means— conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and punishment— one should employ those specific means at the appropriate time.
In the case of conciliation (sāman), however, a middling degree of distinction is proclaimed;
in the case of giving (dāna), conciliation is observed to be appropriate indeed. (35)
Indeed, in the matter of giving, punishment is proclaimed to be without wealth;
and in the matter of punishment, giving is likewise said to be inferior. (36)
Indeed, when conciliation is within range, punishment is considered the lowest of the low;
therefore, constant benevolence should be understood as superior to both sowing dissension and punishment for a king. (37)
Likewise, through chanting and giving, one comes into the range of goodness;
yet desire, anger, greed, joy, pride, and intoxication likewise remain. (38)
A king should destroy these excesses as he would his enemies;
he should employ them at the proper time, yet remain free from greed and pride. (39)
The brilliance of kings is indeed as intense as that of the sun;
one should completely abandon there that pride which is joined with disease and resides in the body and speech. (40)
Hunting, sexual indulgence, drinking, and the squandering of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and punishment—these seven one should avoid. (41)
One should absolutely abandon service toward women who belong to others and are devoid of passion;
one should properly establish one's residence with one's own virtuous wives. 42.
Wives have pleasure and offspring as their fruit; one should not abandon them entirely.
For the sake of accomplishing those two ends, women should be served, while avoiding excessive attachment. (43)
One should always avoid hunting, which is a source of heedlessness; likewise, one should not play with dice, which destroys attachment to virtuous deeds. (44)
One may occasionally perform what has been done by others, but one should not act on one's own initiative; for this is the seed of improper actions and the cause of abandoning one's duties. (45)
One should always avoid drinking [alcohol] during untimely intercourse, in the midst of a quarrel, or when honor has declined; for it destroys purity and auspiciousness. (46)
One should always avoid that which causes the loss of wealth and that which brings defilement upon oneself, even in the case of those accused as thieves, murderers, or assassins. (47)
The protector of the earth should always employ severity of punishment;
the best of kings should not exercise severity of punishment for any other reason. (48)
One should never, under any circumstances, utter harsh words;
truth must always be protected, for truth alone is the supreme refuge. (49)
O King, according to the occasion, one should practice both forbearance and brilliance;
likewise, there are the six measures: marching, encamping, seeking shelter, double-dealing, making peace, and waging war.
One should practice these six qualities and their eternal state; for he who does not know the measure [of these] in their proper place, in growth, and likewise in decline. (51)
He does not remain established in his kingdom if he lacks treasury, territory, and the power of punishment;
for each of these—treasury, territory, and punishment—must individually possess all three qualities. (52)
One should employ these according to the occasion, and then protect them;
one should exert one's influence over all three: the friend, the enemy, and the neutral. (53)
Kings should constantly apply their energy toward the desire for victory, the performance of dharma, the group of eight [royal measures], and the maintenance of the body's livelihood. (54)
One should apply everywhere an intellect born from the certainty of the mantra—toward the minister, the enemy, the kingdom, the sons, and the inner apartments. (55)
Agriculture, difficult terrain, commerce, the procurement of swords through taxes, the collection of levies from the army, and the capturing of elephants and horses. (56)

And the constant separation of people from the entrances of their dwellings in an empty place, as well as the binding of swift birds and the construction of bridges over lakes—this is the eighth [sign]. (57)
One should properly employ spies among these eight classes for the purpose of distinguishing between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done by those in charge of the eight departments.
The king should employ eight spies among the eight circles of states;
he should employ ten in the vulnerable points. Listen to them from me in due order. (59)
The sovereign, the ministers, the realm, the ally, the treasury, the army, and the fort as the seventh—these are to be known as the seven limbs of sovereignty, as spoken by the Guru. (60)
One should not apply the *urgamukta* among the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) nor within oneself;
therefore, these remaining five are the steps of movement (*cārapada*).
And regarding the determination of strength and weakness among those in the inner apartments, among sons, among the sun and so forth, in the kitchen, and even between a master and a female slave.
The king should employ spies among these eighteen [officials]; whatever he does not know openly, that he should ascertain through his spies. (63)
Having ascertained the remedy for that, one must certainly proceed through the breach;
according to their respective assignments, whosoever acts otherwise in any matter [should be dealt with]. 64.
Having learned this through his spies, the king should punish or dismiss [the offender];
meanwhile, the king, remaining in secret with his minister, should consult with his spies. (65)
At the time of dusk, one should inquire; at that very moment, one should carry it out.
[One should investigate] among one's own sons, in the inner apartments, and among those spies who are in the kitchen.
At midnight, he should question those appointed spies himself, O Minister;
indeed, the king should personally observe these scouts even without his minister.
Having examined others together with his minister, he should assign the reward.
A spy should not wear a uniform dress, nor should he be alone, nor should he be devoid of enthusiasm. (68)
He is not overly praised everywhere, neither too tall nor too short;
he never wanders about by day, nor is he diseased, nor is he lacking in intelligence. (69)
Neither lacking in wealth and power nor deprived of wife and sons, a spy should be employed by the king for the purpose of determining the truth and secrets [of the enemy]. (70)
Capable of assuming many disguises, accompanied by his wife and son, he was skilled in the languages and dialects of various regions and able to discern the intentions of others. (71)
The king should employ a spy who is firm in devotion, capable, and fearless;
likewise, he himself should supervise agriculture along with those who are equal to himself.
On trade routes, in difficult terrain, and so forth, he should appoint those who are capable;
in the inner apartments, he should appoint wise and elderly men who are equal to his father.
Those intent on the matter of intelligence should station eunuchs, fools, the elderly, or women at the door of the inner apartments; or else, wise elderly women should be stationed there.
A king should never sleep alone, nor should he eat alone;
he should not go alone to visit his queen for the sake of friendship.
The king, acting with constant benevolence, should appoint as ministers those who have been proven pure by the tests of integrity, and likewise his wives and sons. (76)
Because one approaches and is tested by means of the purification of each of the four aims— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— that is proclaimed as *upadhā* (an ordeal).
One should test one's wife and sons by means of the tests of wealth and desire;
however, one should test Brahmins by means of the tests of dharma, and ministers by all of them.
By these sacrifices and these gifts, one may become a king even in this very world;
therefore, you who desire sovereignty should practice righteousness in this manner. (79)
"By this very incantation, or indeed by means of sacrifices, this earthly king shall surely give up his life-breaths; you will become the king, of this there is no doubt. (80)
"Thus, the duty of a king, such as the horse sacrifice and other rites, the king himself does not perform; therefore, O best of beings, you must perform it. (81)
Having thus consulted with the ministers through secret counsel,
the king, having himself ascertained those matters unknown from others, should win over their minds by means of those [rewards].
If a minister should practice unrighteousness out of a desire for the kingdom, he would cause harm to the king and lead that righteousness to ruin. (83)
But one who performs malevolent magic (ābhicārika) excessively should be destroyed;
however, a king should banish a Brāhmaṇa who practices such magic.

This is to be known as the "test by heat" (gharmopadhā); by means of it, one should win over the ministers. One should likewise conduct such or another test in accordance with righteousness (dharmataḥ). || 85 ||
Having summoned the treasurers, he should deceive the royal ministers, as well as his sons and others who are incapable of maintaining the secrecy of counsel. (86)
"O best of men, this abundant treasury is at my disposal;
I shall bring it to you with your consent, if you will wait. (87)
From this wealth of yours, our livelihood shall be secured;
and as for you, what indeed will you not accomplish with your abundant treasuries? (88)
In this manner, by means of other methods involving the treasury, the best of kings should constantly examine all his sons, ministers, and others. || 89 ||
One who desires to act [as a king] should execute those who cause harm to the treasury and banish those who do so;
he should win over those with divided loyalties and indeed ensure the protection of the treasury.

And female slaves, female artisans, and elderly women who possess intelligence and fortitude—whichever women move both inside and outside [the palace] should be well-known to the ministers and other officials. (91)
Then the king, remaining in seclusion and unobserved by his wife and others,
should consecrate [the messenger] with mantras, consult with him, and dispatch him to the ministers.
Having understood your heart after approaching you, those women, devoted to discernment—led by the queen—the auspicious lady truly desires you. (93)
In this matter, I shall unite you with him if you have a desire for it;
O lady of excellent complexion, this minister, who is worthy of you, desires you.
"If you have faith, I am able to bring about that union"—
in this manner, and by various other such means and subsequent [arguments], [he spoke].
He should purify his wives, sons, daughters, daughters-in-law, and granddaughters, as well as his ministers, sons, grandsons, and other dependents.
One should execute those who have failed the test of integrity regarding sensual desires without hesitation;
however, women should be punished with fines, while Brāhmaṇas should be banished. 97.
A king should avoid a minister who is intent on the path to liberation, who is free from violence and slander, and whose sole essence is forbearance.

But one who is indifferent toward the path to liberation should not be punished even if he deserves punishment; since he possesses an equanimous mind toward all things, one should therefore avoid him. 99.
Thus the Sūtra and the various types of *upadhā* (tests) have been explained by Uśanas in his treatise; one should understand them from that work. (100)
A king should not constantly engage in conflict with others; rather, wars should be undertaken only when the acquisition of land, wealth, or allies has been firmly determined. 101.
The best of kings should always maintain faith in the seven constituent parts [of the state], and they should constantly and properly carry out the accumulation and protection of the treasury. 102.
The king, however, should appoint as ministers Brahmins who are experts in learning, disciplined, well-born, skilled in matters of dharma and worldly affairs, and upright. (103)
One should discuss the knowledge with them, but one should not go about with too many people;
the definitive determination of the mantra should be carried out with each one individually. (104)
Having ascended to a place where the mantra-hall is well-enclosed on all sides by all of these and other such designations, one should perform the consultation.
One should never, even for a moment, cause harm in the forest or in a secluded place to young ones, monkeys, bears, parrots, or mainas. (106)
One should avoid deformed persons in the mantra-house;
for the corruption that arises from the disclosure of mantras results in harm for kings. (107)
It is not possible to maintain order even by hundreds of skillful kings;
one should punish those deserving of punishment with punishments, but one must certainly not punish those who do not deserve punishment. 108.
A king who fails to punish those deserving of punishment, or punishes those who do not deserve it, incurs public reproach and shall incur the same guilt as a thief. (109)
The king should ensure that the fortress is made level with its ramparts, watchtowers, and gateways;
adorned with these, he should dwell in the fortress at a distance from the city.
A fortress is indeed the strength of kings, and a fortress is always praised;
for a single archer stationed within a fortress can fight against a hundred. || 111 ||
A hundred times ten thousand [times more secure] than that, a fort is recommended;
likewise, a water-fort, a land-fort, and a tree-fort. 112.

A king should construct a fortress—whether in the wilderness, on a difficult terrain, on a mountain, or in a region surrounded by enemies—in such a way that the fortress is situated within his own territory. || 113 ||
While constructing a fortress, one should build the city as triangular, bow-shaped, circular, or quadrangular; one should not construct a city otherwise.

A fortress shaped like a drum, however, constantly brings about the destruction of one's lineage, just as Laṅkā was once a fortress endowed with such strength for the kingdom of the Rākṣasas. || 115 ||
The city of Vali, named Śoṇita, is established with formidable fortresses;
since it has the shape of a fan, Manobhraṣṭa is the line of Śivas there. 116.
The good fortune of the king of Sālva and his five-cornered city,
as well as the sovereignty he holds in heaven, shall all fall away.
And that city of the Ikṣvāku kings called Ayodhyā, which was shaped like a bow, also became a bestower of victory from that [bow]. (118)
On the ground of the fortress, one should worship Durgā and the guardians of the directions at the gates;
having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, the king shall attain victory. || 119 ||
Therefore, a king should always construct a fortress for the constant increase of his victory; nor should he ever treat with contempt those Brāhmaṇas who have been insulted by anyone.
By disregarding Brahmins, a king shall become a partaker of suffering both in this world and after death;
he must not engage in opposition with them, nor should he withhold their rightful dues.
One should always worship those very persons at the times when duties are to be performed;
one should not engage in their censure, nor should one act with envy toward them. 122.
Thus the king was of great intelligence, endowed with the circle of reality (tattvamaṇḍala), possessed of splendor, having spies for his eyes, virtuous, and speaking very kindly. || 123 ||
Having attained great perfection both in this world and after death, he becomes a possessor of happiness and enjoyments;
with whatever qualities his own self is endowed, he should likewise endow his sons with those same qualities.
If the king acts with independence, he will constantly bring about his own destruction;
a son of a king who is independent certainly undergoes a transformation [of misconduct]. (125)
One should constantly employ those who are aged in matters that are changeless:
in eating, in sleeping, in traveling, and in the observation of men. 126.
The king should always separate his wives from their licentious conduct;
indeed, women must be kept perpetually under the control of the monarch. 127.
For such independent women always lead to one's downfall;
therefore, [win over] the prince and the queen by means of charming stratagems.
Having purified him, one should appoint him to the position of crown prince or to the inner apartments;
however, one should prohibit his independent authority regarding entry into the harem.
Regarding the wife of a king’s son and likewise regarding one who has gone abroad—this specific duty of kings has been declared by me in brief. (130)

O King, Uśanas [is the authority] regarding the distribution of virtues among sons, as is Bṛhaspati regarding those concerning wives; but for the treatises on statecraft, O Lord of the Earth, [one must look to] Bṛhaspati. (131)
He should also cause others to understand the specific distinctions between those two in the Tantras.
O highly fortunate lady, a king who thus applies these specific principles of royal policy never falters and enjoys ever-increasing prosperity.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of Kings," in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 84 ||
The eighty-fifth chapter.
Aurva said:
O Indra among kings, now listen specifically to [the rules] regarding good conduct.
Hear from me all those things which a king must necessarily perform. || 1 ||
The virtuous are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word "sat" (good/true) denotes them.
That which is their conduct is called "sadācāra" (righteous conduct). || 2 ||
One should adopt those established rules of right conduct as they are declared in the Āgamas, Purāṇas, and Saṃhitās, just like a householder.
One should worship the sages with the recitation of the Vedas, honor the gods with burnt offerings (homa),
satisfy the ancestors with śrāddha rites, and likewise gratify the spirits with sacrificial oblations (bali).
He should perform the application of ointments, bathing, cleaning the teeth, and applying collyrium with friendliness;
likewise, he should perform all the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception ceremony) just like a householder.
The king should employ Brahmins in all six types of duties;
likewise, he should appoint Kshatriyas and others to their respective stations.
The king shall impose a fine of one hundred [paṇas] upon him who, having abandoned his own duty, practices the duty of another; furthermore, he should subject that person to further punishment.
One should perform these rites specifically during annual ceremonies; O King, a ruler of the earth shall bring them under his control.
Listen now from me to those specific details.
In the autumn season, on the eighth day (Mahāṣṭamī), one should perform the complete worship of Durgā;
and on the tenth day, one should indeed perform the lustration ceremony (Nīrājana) for the increase of strength.
On the third lunar day of the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the Puṣyābhiṣeka;
having worshipped the goddess Śrī and performed ritual ablution, the king should conduct himself [accordingly].
O best of kings, for the increase of wealth and grain,
one should likewise perform the Śrīyajña sacrifice and the sacrifice to Viṣṇu on the Daśaharā day in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
On the twelfth day when the Sun is situated in Leo, one should perform the worship of Indra;
moreover, the king should especially perform sacrifices involving great expenditures for these [deities].
When these are performed, strength, sovereignty, and the treasury increase;
but when these sacrifices are not performed, there is famine as well as death.
All conscious beings are born from these; therefore, one should practice them with distinction.
This is the ritual procedure for the worship of Durgā on the Mahāṣṭamī day during the autumn season.
The worship was previously described by that very rite;
now listen, O best of kings, to the procedure for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
By performing which [rite] one obtains the worship of horses and even elephants;
this occurs on the third day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina when it is conjoined with the Svātī asterism.
In the northeast of his own city, he should take up an excellent site;
then, when the eighth day has arrived, he should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
The time for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) has already been told to you by me;
now hear from me the procedure alone, and you will have accomplished your purpose. || 18 ||
One should worship a single horse, a great being that is truly captivating, for seven days with perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings. (19)
Having worshipped [the deity] on the third day and thereafter, one should lead [the disciple] to the sacrificial mandala;
by observing his physical gestures, one should discern what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
If the horse flees, there will be the crushing of a foreign kingdom;
if the prince dies, it is when he sheds tears. (21)
If, while being led forth, the horse does not proceed,
or likewise makes a sound from its mouth, nose, or eyes, then there will be the death of the queen.
Whoever performs [this] facing the Kāṣṭhā direction shall conquer his enemies in that Kāṣṭhā;
having lifted his right foot, he shall become a horse before him. (23)
Then, O best of kings, if the monarch has conquered all his enemies,
he should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) on the morning of the tenth day.
And if that [lunar day] is not obtained, one should perform it on the twelfth of that same month;
or else on the fifteenth of Kārttika, O King, in its absence.
In the northeast of his own city, one should construct sixteen archways (toraṇas) measuring one cubit in height,
and there, indeed, one should make a broad archway ten cubits wide.
One should construct a mandala thirty-two cubits long and sixteen cubits wide for the sake of the sacrifice; one should designate an altar in the center. || 27 ||
To the north of the altar, one should construct an unsurpassed altar for the horse,
where the horse, having been placed, is to be worshipped by the family priests.
O King, one should further adorn it with banners featuring the marks of fish, conchs, and discs made from the branches of the Sarja, Udumbara, or Arjuna trees. (29)
The archway [should be adorned] with gold, jewels, and likewise various kinds of fruits;
and for the sake of success, there should be marking-nut (bhallātaka), rice, kuṣṭha, and rock salt.
One should tie it around the neck specifically for the sake of nourishment and pacification;
having drawn the Vaiṣṇava mandala, one should worship the guardians of the directions and the nine planets.
The priest, having mixed clarified butter, sesame seeds, and flowers, should worship the Viśvedevas, with Viṣṇu as their chief, by means of the mantra. (32)
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for seven days for Ravi, Varuṇa, Prajāpati, Puruhūta, and Viṣṇu.
For the sake of attaining the four aims of life, one should perform a fire-oblation every day for each [deity], either a thousand times or one hundred and eight times.
Furthermore, fuel-sticks made of *pālāśa*, *khādira*, *audumbara*, *kāśmarya*, and *aśvattha* wood should be offered by the priest. (35)
One should fashion eight pitchers according to one's desire— either of gold, silver, or even clay— and adorn them with fruits, mangoes, and cloths.
Into those very jars, one should cast saṃhaṇī,
haritāla, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu, and realgar.
Ñjanā, haridrā, white dantī, as well as bhallātaka, pūrṇakośa, sahadevī, and śatāvarī; || 38 ||
Vacā with nāgakesara flowers, somarājī well-protected, uttha, karavīra, and likewise a tulasī leaf. (39)
The domestic priest should place these in the midst of the jars,
along with golden lotuses, sacrificial wood, and likewise the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
O King, for one desiring peace,
this should be performed during the rite of lustration (nīrājana) for seven days, with worship and likewise with fire-offerings (havana).
Having worshipped those previously mentioned [deities], the king should perform the rite for seven days;
as long as he performs the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), so long shall the king dwell in his palace.
One who desires peace should not dwell on the sacrificial ground at night;
nor should the king mount that horse or elephant there. (43)
He should travel by some other vehicle for as long as seven days,
[providing] various kinds of foods, such as honey, milk-porridge, and barley-meal.
Or one should offer an oblation consisting of sweetmeats (modaka) and various food preparations for the aforementioned deities for as long as seven days; this is the best method.
On the seventh day, one should worship Rebhanta within the archway—
the mighty-armed son of the Sun, two-armed and resplendent in armor.
O Vāsava, with his hair tied up and wearing a blazing white garment, he held a whip in his left hand, while his right hand was likewise [raised]. (47)
Having placed the sword upon raw meat situated on white rock-salt,
he should likewise [place it] upon a statue or even in a jar while it is thus resonating.
One should worship within the archway according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the Sun;
having worshipped, one should likewise honor the Rebha, the elephant, and the horse.
Clad in unwashed garments, adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste,
he bore a sword inlaid with gold and was arrayed in various pieces of armor and other accoutrements.
It is proper, however, to lead the horse and the elephant guardians separately to the horse-altar previously constructed in the northeast of the sacrificial fire-pit.
When an elephant or a horse is being led forth, the king should diligently observe the previously mentioned omens and determine their resulting effects. || 52 ||
Standing upon a tiger skin to the north of the sacrificial fire-pit,
accompanied by one skilled in the science of elephants and one skilled in the science of horses, he gazed at the horse from Sindh.
Once the horse has been led there, the domestic priest, having consecrated it with propitiatory mantras, should quickly give it a fragrant ball of food.
If, upon smelling it, the horse should eat it, then all will be auspicious; otherwise, the result shall be the opposite.
Having repeatedly sprinkled with water from the jar the branches of the udumbara and mango trees along with kuśa grass, as well as the horses, elephants, the king, and the soldiers; 56.
The domestic priest should touch the chariots with mantras for pacification and nourishment, and then, together with the Brahmins, he should sprinkle the fourfold army.

Having performed the consecration in many ways with the mantras of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the planets (grahas), and likewise those of Viṣṇu, one should then offer a golden [image].
Then, having looked upon the king, the officiating priests,
the minister, the prince, as well as the counselors and the other soldiers, [he spoke].
Causing them all to tremble, that tiger among the twice-born should display his own fourfold army; having thus performed the rites of pacification and nourishment, he should proceed.
Having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of clay and having pierced its heart with a trident using incantations for malevolent rites, one should sever its head with a sword.
The preceptor, having consecrated the bit with mantras dedicated to Indra and the Prabhākaras, should himself place it again into the horse's mouth.
Having ascended with this mantra, the king,
accompanied by all his forces, should then proceed toward the northeastern direction.
Then all the sacrificial priests, family chaplains, and teachers should follow the king to observe other omens.
Accompanied by the tumultuous sounds of musical instruments and surrounded by parasols,
the king should proceed in the royal procession as if splitting the very earth.
Adorned with jewels, coral, pearls, gold, and gems,
the king then proceeded for the distance of one *krośa* by way of the eastern gate.
The king should enter his own city, and the domestic priest should proceed to the sacrifice;
having gone there, he should bestow sacrificial fees consisting of gold, cows, and likewise sesame seeds.
After giving [the offerings] to the twice-born, one should then give gifts according to one's ability;
having thus performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the king and his forces.
In this way, a king shall obtain stable prosperity both in this world and after death, O Saindhava horse, born from the nectar and arisen from the ocean! 69.
By that truth with which you carry Śakra, by that truth with which [you carry] Rebha, and by that truth with which [you carry] Bhāskara—by that truth, carry me here. (70)
"By that truth you carry [the king], carry me toward victory!
O King, one should perform the mounting of the horse with these two mantras. (71)
Then, having ascended first, he should cause [the image] to be suspended in the inner apartments (śuddhānta) of the queen;
thereafter, the queen [should honor] the king seated upon the couch.

One should worship him together with women using *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains, and white mustard seeds; this should be done on the third lunar day when the acquisition of land has been performed and the *nirājana* rite is concluded.
If birth-impurity (sūtaka) should occur there, it defiles only that place;
whether it be birth-impurity or death-impurity (mṛtaka), the king remains as he was.
One should perform the *balanīrājana* (the waving of lights for the army), especially with that [specific] measure;
for the king, there shall be immediate purification upon the inspection of legal proceedings.

"O King, this ritual of *nīrājana* has been described by me to you for use during consecration, sacrifice, and the subjugation of enemy kingdoms. Now, O Ruler of the Earth, listen to the procedure for the *puṣyasnāna*."
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 85 ||
The eighty-sixth chapter.
Aurva said:
Listen, O King, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the Puṣya-bath.
By means of which mere consciousness obstacles are constantly destroyed. || 1 ||
In the month of Pauṣa, when the moon is situated in the Puṣya asterism, the king should perform the Puṣya-bath;
it brings about good fortune and auspiciousness, and wards off famine and death.
If [the ritual] is obtained even during an inauspicious karaṇa such as Viṣṭi, or during Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, Vajra, Śūla, Harṣaṇa, and so forth; or during [such] a yoga— || 3 ||
If the third lunar day is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism and falls on a Sunday, Saturday, or Tuesday,
then that bath causes the destruction of all defects.
If planetary afflictions arise while the conscious beings are in their kingdoms,
then one should perform [the rite] under the Puṣya asterism, even if it occurs within another month.
This peace was formerly taught by Brahmā to his preceptor,
and by the Lord of the World for the sake of the peace of all the gods, beginning with Śakra.
In a place free from husks, hair, bones, anthills, insects, and the like, and devoid of gravel, worms, pumpkins, and heavily tilled ground; || 7 ||
In a forest devoid of thorns and free from *vibhītaka* trees, it was shunned by crows, owls, herons, ravens, vultures, and hawks.
In a place free from śigru and śleṣmātaka trees, as well as leeches and the like, and adorned in its own location by amr̥tā, aśoka, vakula, and other such trees; || 9 ||
On the pure bank of a lake crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks,
the king should take up an excellent spot for the ritual bath on the day of Puṣya.
Then, on the previous day, at the time of dusk, the king accompanied by his domestic priest should go to that place amidst the sounds of various musical instruments.
Standing in the northern direction of that place, the domestic priest [should worship] with fragrant sandalwood drinks scented with camphor and other ingredients.
With *gorocanā*, white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, fruits, and so forth, and with mantras beginning with "Gandhadvārām," all [the articles] were sprinkled. || 13 ||
Having consecrated that site, one should worship the deities there:
Gaṇeśa, Keśava, Śakra, Brahmā, and also Śaṅkara.
There, the king, together with his domestic priest, should worship the God accompanied by Umā, all the host of attendant deities, and the Mothers.
Having prepared auspicious jars and various collections of food offerings,
one should present milk-rice, sweet fruits, modakas, and barley-meal.
Having consecrated that place with *dūrvā* grass, white mustard seeds, and unbroken rice grains,
he should also expel the spirits from that location while uttering the mantra.
May those beings who dwell upon the earth depart;
without obstructing those who have been summoned, I perform the rite of bathing.
Then, joining his palms together, the king should invoke these deities worthy of worship for the Puṣya-consecration with this mantra: || 19 ||
"Let all the gods who desire this worship come here—indeed, all the guardians of the quarters and whoever else shares in a portion [of the offerings]. (20)
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should again recite this mantra:
"May the gods remain today, having taken possession of my place. (21)
Having received their own worship and granted peace to the king, the protectors [should depart];
then the king, together with his domestic priest, should pass that night.
The king, together with his domestic priest, should discern the auspicious and inauspicious nature of dreams;
having performed worship to the gods, the king should sleep at night in his proper place. (23)
The auspicious and inauspicious results of a dream should be understood according to the consensus of those skilled in [interpreting] dreams.
If an evil dream should occur, then [it is countered] by the Puṣya-abhiṣecana rite.
One should perform a fourfold *homa* after giving a hundred cows, as well as [gifts] of cattle,
horses, elephants, palaces, mountains, and trees.
Ascending [the throne] brings auspicious karma and causes the increase of royal glory;
likewise, the presentation of curd, divine objects, and gold to a Brāhmaṇa [yields great merit]. || 26 ||
A lute, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, fruit, flowers, an umbrella, ointment, the moon, a discus, a conch, a lotus, and likewise a friend; || 27 ||
Gains cause the destruction of the enemy who is like a mountain possessing a mine of jewels;
likewise, the sight of an eclipse and imprisonment with fetters [bring ruin]. (28)
The eating of meat, the overturning of a mountain, the growth of trees in the midst of water, and weeping for the deceased; || 29 ||
Approaching those who should not be approached, O well, and descending into the midst of mud;
likewise, [climbing] a mountain, crossing a river, and likewise leaping over streams. (30)
The death of his own son, the drinking of blood and wine, the eating of milk-rice (pāyasa), and likewise the mounting of a human being. (31)
O best of kings, these dreams bring about auspiciousness, happiness, good fortune, sovereignty, and likewise the destruction of enemies for a king. (32)
Mounting a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo brings about the destruction of one's kingdom;
likewise, dancing, singing, laughter, and recitation are inauspicious.
One who desires a woman who is red or black, dressed in red garments, adorned with red garlands, and anointed with red unguents, shall meet with death. (34)
There will be entry into the interior of a well as well as travel toward the southern direction;
there will be sinking into mud, bathing, and the destruction of wife and sons. (35)
He shall obtain gain even in a dream, as well as from kings;
having seized the umbilical cord of the fetus, the bird-like messenger departs. (36)
Having attained another kingdom, he shall obtain great prosperity;
it is twenty cubits long and sixteen cubits wide. || 37 ||
One should construct an excellent sacrificial mandala endowed with the proper characteristics;
then, on the following day in the forenoon, one should perform the worship of the Mothers.
One should likewise offer a stream of clarified butter (vasordhārā) clinging to the wall, as well as a Vṛddhi-śrāddha,
along with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, incense, camphor, and aromatic powders.
Having worshipped the site of the mandala, the wise one should write these two mantras upon it: "Hrauṃ, obeisance to Śambhu" and "Astrāya huṃ phaṭ."
One who knows the mantras and understands the mandala should first draw the mandala called Svastika with threads made of wool or silk.
Then one should draw a mandala measuring four cubits;
a lotus measuring one cubit is prescribed for the mandala.
The doors are one and a half cubits wide; it is radiant with pericarp and filaments, and is white, red, yellow, black, and green.
A king should likewise prepare a powder from rice flour, safflower, turmeric, and products derived from haridrā, as well as with collyriums, for the expansion of his mandala.
Having measured out a palm-span from the edge of the lotus toward the west, one should designate a hundred-petaled lotus in the middle of the western gate. || 45 ||
One who knows the divisions of the maṇḍala should, at the center of each door, separately fashion an eight-petaled lotus using colored powders.
Having fashioned the mandala with powders, one should then lay out the lines;
having laid out the first line, one should then worship the mandala.
Saying "Havanāya namaḥ," he should then separate his hand;
he should then hold the vessel of colored powder with his left hand supporting it. 48.
The wise practitioner, having placed the middle, ring, and thumb fingers on top as desired and turned the other fingers downward, should pour [the water]. (49)
A line should be drawn, variegated and colored with flowers;
it must be made straight by the skillful knower through the precision of the thumb-joint. (50)
One should never draw [a line] that is entangled, uneven, thick, broken, thin, crooked, or placed at the edge, nor one that is too short.
One should know that when [the lines] are joined together there is quarrel; when they are curved upwards, there is conflict.
When they are excessively thick, there will be disease; when they are mixed with distress, there is constant suffering.
One encounters fear from the side of enemies due to [the presence of] dots; there is no doubt.
If [the line] is thin, there will be loss of wealth; if it is broken, death is certain. (53)
Or there may be separation from his beloved wealth or children for him who, without knowing [the rules], should draw the mandala according to his own whim. (54)
One incurs all the defects that have been described above;
therefore, a wise person should draw lines with white mustard seeds and dūrvā grass.
The Vimala, Vijaya, Bhadra, Vimāna, Śubhada, Śiva, Vardhamāna, Deva, Śatākṣa, and Kāmadāyaka [palaces]. || 56 ||
Rucika and Svastika—these twelve are indeed the mandalas;
they should be applied by the wise according to the proper place and according to the specific sacrifice. || 57 ||
While the ocean was being churned by the hosts of gods for the sake of nectar,
she was fashioned by Viśvakarman for the purpose of holding that nectar.
Since they were fashioned by each of the gods having individually consumed a portion (kalā) of their power, they are therefore celebrated as "kalasas. || 59 ||
Nine pitchers alone have been declared; learn their names:
Gohya, Upagohya, Maruta, and another, Mayūkha. (60)
Manohā, Ācāryabhadra, Vijaya, Tanudūṣaka, Indriyaghna, and then Vijaya is proclaimed as the ninth. || 61 ||
O King, listen now to their other nine names in sequence, which are indeed always bestowers of peace. (62)
The first is declared to be Kṣitīndra; the second is Jalasambhava; then follow Pavana and Agni; and after that comes Yajamāna.
The sixth is proclaimed as Koṣasambhava;
Soma is said to be the seventh, and Āditya is likewise the eighth.
That vessel which is called the ninth, named Vijaya,
is said to have five faces and bears the very form of Mahādeva.
Just as the pot has five faces, so too does he himself have five faces;
he is properly situated in each direction according to his names, beginning with Vāmadeva.
At the edge of the lotus of the mandala, one should place a five-faced jar;
having placed the "Lord of the Earth" (Kṣitīndra) in the east, one places the "Born of Water" (Jalasambhava) in the west.
Having assigned Vāyu in the northwest, Agni born of fire in the southeast, the sacrificer in the southwest, and the source of the treasury in the northeast; || 68 ||
One should place the vessel of Soma to the north and the vessel of the Sun to the south;
having thus arranged the jars, one should contemplate these [deities] within them. (69)
Brahmā resides at the mouth of the jars, Śaṅkara is situated at the neck,
Viṣṇu is established at the base, and the hosts of Mothers are stationed in the middle.
All the world-protecting deities surround the ten directions;
within his belly reside the seven oceans and the seven continents.
All the constellations and planets, as well as the principal mountain ranges, all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and the four Vedas themselves. (72)
All these are contained within the jars; one should contemplate within them all the fibers, seeds, flowers, and fruits. (73)

The *bilva* fruit consists of all the [five] abodes (*dhāma*), namely diamond (*vajra*), pearl (*muktika*), lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), great lotus (*mahāpadma*), and rock crystal (*sphāṭika*), as well as the *nāgara* and *udumbara*. (74)
Bījapūraka, jambīra, kāśmīra, āmrātaka, and pomegranate; barley, śāli rice, nīvāra, wheat, and white mustard seeds. (75)
Saffron, agallochum, camphor, madana, as well as gorocanā, sandalwood, māṃsī, elā, and likewise kuṣṭha. || 76 ||
Asṛk-patra-cūrṇa, jala-niryāsaka-āmbuda, śaileya, badara, as well as the leaves and flowers of the jātī; || 77 ||
Black śāka, as well as pṛkkā, devīparṇaka,
vacā, dhātrī, mañjiṣṭhā, and turuṣka constitute the eight auspicious substances (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Dūrvā, mohanikā, bhadrā, śatamūlī, śatāvarī, arṇā, saralā, kṣudrā, sahadevī, and gajāhvayā— (79)
Pūrṇakoṣā, sitā, pīṭhā, guñjā, śirasikā, anala, vyāmaka, gajadanta, śatapuṣpa, and punarnavā. (80)
Having gathered these auspicious substances— the goddess Brāhmī, Śivā, Rudrā, and likewise Sarvasandhānikā— one should place them within the jars.
Having worshipped the ritual vessel, Śambhu, and Gadādhara according to their respective locations and in due order, one should worship Śambhu as the primary deity.
One should first worship Śambhu with the Prāsāda mantra and Śaṅkara with the Tantra mantra in the center, with various offerings of food and oblations.
One should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in their respective pitchers,
as well as in the pitchers of the planets that were previously placed outside.
One should worship the nine planets and the Mothers in the Mother-pitchers;
all the gods are to be worshipped in pitchers, with separate pitchers for each of them.

O King, those nine previously mentioned [deities] are traditionally considered the primary ones there, [to be honored] with various kinds of foods to chew, foods to eat, drinks, flowers, and fruits. (86)
With barley-gruel and milk-rice prepared as available,
the king should worship all the gods for the sake of the Puṣya-bath.
Then, having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the south of the mandala, [one should perform the rite] with milk-rice,
fuel-sticks, rice grains, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Likewise, with clarified butter alone, the king, accompanied by a pure priest, should satisfy all the gods through oblations for the sake of prosperity. 89.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should place a cloth, yellow pigment known as rocanā, and all types of ornaments upon the altar to the north of the mandala.
Increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) with each finger, up to a limit of twenty-six fingers,
it may be circular, square, lotus-shaped, or known as triangular.
One should worship Ratneśa in the center of the lotus along with Gomūṣṭika and Vināyaka, as well as the auspicious Umādevī, who possesses a beautiful form and the Śrīvṛkṣa.
A cloth measuring two cubits in length, one cubit in width, nine cubits in height, and ten finger-breadths [in thickness] should be prepared, adorned with all kinds of jewels and ornaments.
For the purpose of bathing, there should be a circular cloth (paṭṭa) measuring one and a half cubits and endowed with good qualities;
the bed should be four times that length, and the seat (pīṭhaka) should be the measure of a bow.
Adorned with gold and jewels, displaying the majestic bearing of an elephant or a lion,
it is called the "Lion" (siṃha) [seat], measuring one and a half [units] in width, or it may also be a staff-seat (daṇḍāsana).
One should have pillows made from tiger skins, leopard skins, or patterned cloths; or else, they may be made of other materials, stuffed with soft leather or cotton.
The bed should be long, wide, four cubits in length, and well-proportioned;
according to the science of the Guru, they desire it to be more than a span (vitasti) for a king.
One should fashion a square seat resembling a half-moon;
the pillows for the bed are distinguished by the different locations of their ears and other parts.
In this context, exactly sixteen items should be prepared, adorned with various colors:
a vehicle, a lion-throne, a ceremonial cloth, a bed, and so forth, including bedding and utensils. (99)
One should place that which is suitable for the new king to the north of the altar;
and to the west of those, upon an excellent seat inlaid with a multitude of gold and jewels.
On a couch constructed from a multitude of sacrificial wood, provided with a great covering and four surfaces draped in skins; || 101 ||
Having placed his feet upon a footstool adorned with jewels, the king likewise [placed] the wool of a bull, as well as those of a lion and a tiger [thereon]. (102)
Seated upon this throne in the paryaṅka posture, the king is adorned with various ornaments and richly endowed with jewels, [surrounded] by four [attendants] covered in skins.
Together with the Brahmins, he should bathe the king, who is endowed with happiness, having spread out a black woolen blanket and adorned him with new garments. (104)
One should bathe [the deity] with water from jars, bilva leaves, flowers, and the like, along with rice flour,
eight, sixteen, twenty, one hundred and eight, or even more times.
The number of jars is declared to increase progressively;
[they are consecrated] with mantras that grant victory and auspiciousness, which arise from blessings and belong to Śambhu.
Ghee is perceived as the splendor of the Vaiṣṇavas, the guardians of the quarters, the Gṛhamantras, and the Mātṛkās; ghee is the supreme remover of sin.
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; upon it the worlds are established.
Whether it be the oblation belonging to the intermediate space or the celestial realm, whatever portion has come to you at the appointed time.
May all that perish through contact with clarified butter;
then, having removed from his body both the blanket and the garment, [he should proceed]. (109)
O best of men, one should bathe the king with water-pots filled with flowers for the bath,
using these mantras which accomplish the purpose of the principle of the body (tanutattva).
May the celestial rishis consecrate you, as well as those who are the ancient perfected ones (siddhas)—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts. || 111 ||
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins who are the best of physicians;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, and Svāhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī. || 112 ||
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, as well as Diti, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū. (113)
May those who are called the wives of the gods and the mothers of the gods, as well as all the Siddhas and the hosts of Apsarases, consecrate you. (114)

The constellations, the auspicious moments (muhūrta), the fortnights, the junctions of day and night, the years, the twinklings of an eye (nimeṣa), the units of time such as kalā, kāṣṭhā, kṣaṇa, and lava. || 115 ||
May all the divisions of Time consecrate you, as well as the hosts of gods dwelling in celestial chariots, the Manus, and the oceans. (116)
The Saritas, the Mahānāgas, the Nāgas, and likewise the Kiṃpuruṣas;
the highly fortunate Vaikhānasas and those twice-born ones who move through the air.
The seven ṛṣis together with their wives occupy the fixed positions;
they are Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, and Aṅgiras. (118)
Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Dakṣa, Jaigīṣavya, and Abhinandana. || 119 ||
Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jāvāli, Kāśyapa, Durvāsas, Durvinīta, Kaṇva, and likewise Kātyāyana; || 120 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatamas, Śunaḥśepha, Vidūratha, Aurva, Saṃvartaka, Cyavana, Atri, and Parāśara; || 121 ||
Dvaipāyana, Yavakrīta, Devarāta along with his son—these and many others were devoted to the Vedic vows. || 122 ||
May those ascetics, together with their wives and disciples,
as well as the mountains, trees, rivers, and sacred groves, consecrate you.
Prajāpati, the earth, and cows—the mothers of the universe—as well as divine vehicles and all the worlds, both moving and unmoving; 124.
The fires, the ancestors, the stars, the clouds, the sky, the directions, and the waters—these and many other auspicious beings whose names are meritorious to recite. || 125 ||
"May they consecrate you with waters that destroy all portents," thus [he spoke] with these and other auspicious divine mantras.
With the *saura*, *nārāyaṇa*, and *raudra* mantras, as well as those originating from Brahmā and Śakra,
and with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," "sambhave," and "sure," [he should perform the rites].
With the mantra "mānastoke" and with "gandhadvārā," and with "sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye" and "śrīśca te," [the worship is performed] by those joined with the planets.
Having thus completed the bath and covered his body with woolen blankets,
he should put on a cotton garment while reciting the Sarvamangala mantra.
Having sipped water for purification, he should then worship the gods, his preceptor, and the Brahmins;
as well as the banner, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the bell, the horses, and the elephants.
Having recited the mantra, he should wear it and then proceed to the fire;
having gone there, the king should behold the splendor of the fire within the midst of the flames.
There, surrounded by astrologers, chamberlains, ministers, bards, and the citizens, he should observe the signs and the absence of signs through the drops.
Having performed the final propitiatory rite with tumultuous sounds of musical instruments and auspicious triple symphonies, he should then cause the twice-born to pronounce blessings.
Having performed the full rite according to the rules, and having given a sacrificial fee accompanied by gold,
as well as grains and garments, one should perform the ritual dismissal.
Then, with the remaining water, the family priest should sprinkle all the ministers and others,
as well as the fourfold army together with the kingdom.
Having done this, the king should thereafter remain self-restrained for three nights, abstaining from meat and sexual intercourse, and perform auspicious observances. (136)
If the third lunar day is found conjoined with the Puṣya asterism,
on that day the goddess Caṇḍikā was always worshipped by Śaṅkara.
One should delight the auspicious Caṇḍikā with the playthings of children, such as dolls and the like, as well as through the ritual of marriage. 138.
One should adorn all crossroads and the temples of the gods and goddesses with banners; by acting thus, one does not come to grief.
Having thus performed the sacrifice for peace as well as the consecration under the Puṣya asterism,
the king, together with his wives and men, [should proceed] accompanied by the fourfold army.
One who is united with the circle of sovereignty does not suffer in this world or the next;
there is no sacrifice greater than this, and no festival greater than this. (141)
There is no peace higher than this, and nothing more auspicious than this;
by this very procedure, the consecration of the king [is performed]. 142.
The royal priest should perform the consecration of the crown prince, provided that he first carries out the consecration of the king. (143)
By this very procedure, the king shall then become steadfast.
This sacrifice was ordained by Brahmā in ancient times for the sake of Śakra.
Having performed such a sacrifice, the king does not perish either in this world or in the next.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 86 ||
The eighty-seventh chapter.
Aurva said:
Now, therefore, O Indra among kings, hear about the rising of the Śaka and the festival of the banner.
Having performed which, a king never suffers defeat. || 1 ||
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) when the Sun is situated in Leo and the moon is in the Śravaṇa constellation,
a king should properly worship Viḍaujas for the complete pacification of all obstacles.
There was a king named Rājoparicara, and another named Vasu; by him this incomparable sacrifice was performed in ancient times. (3)
And during the rainy season, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas,
the priest, accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments and drums, [proceeds].
First, having consecrated a tree for the sake of Śakaketu, one should cause it to grow; this may be done by an astrologer or a gardener who has performed the auspicious rites and ceremonies.
One should avoid those trees that have grown in a garden, in a temple, in a cremation ground, or in the middle of a road, O Vāsavadhvaja.
One should abandon a tree that is entwined with many creepers, dried up, covered with many thorns, crooked, infested with vṛkṣādanī plants, or a tree completely shrouded by climbing vines.
One should carefully avoid a tree that is infested with birds' nests, possessed of many hollows, and ravaged by wind and fire.
A wise man should always avoid those trees known as "women" which are excessively short and excessively thin, at all times during the worship of Śakra.
Arjuna, aśvakarṇa, vaṭa, priyakośaka,
and audumbara— these five are indeed remembered as the best for the purpose of a banner.
Furthermore, other trees such as the Devadāru and Śāla, which are auspicious, should be accepted; those that are inauspicious should never be taken.
Then, having taken hold of a tree at night and touched it, one should recite this mantra:
"May there be well-being for those beings who dwell in trees; salutations be unto you. (12)
"Accepting this offering, let the banner of Vāsava be raised;
the king chooses you as his bride—may it be well with you, O best of mountains! (13)
"May this offering for the sake of the banner of the King of Gods be accepted.
Then, on the following day, having again cut eight finger-breadths from its base...
Likewise, having cut four finger-breadths from the tip, one should cast it into the water;
then, having brought it to the city gate, one should indeed construct the banner there.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should cause the banner to enter the altar;
a banner measuring twenty-two cubits is said to be of the lowest grade.
Thirty-two is greater than that, and forty-two as well;
more than that is declared to be fifty-two, which is likewise the highest.
O best of kings, five maidens made of *śāla* wood should be fashioned for Śakra;
all the others are the mothers of Śakra.
The Śakrakumārikās should be made according to the measurement of a ketu’s foot;
the Mātṛkās according to half that measure, and the Yantra likewise two cubits.
Having thus prepared the Kumārīs, the Mātṛkās, and the banner itself,
one should consecrate that sacrificial post on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight.
Then, having consecrated the sacrificial staff with mantras beginning with "Gandhadvārām," and having constructed the extensive Maṇḍala of Vāsava on the twelfth day; || 21 ||
Having worshipped Acyuta, one should thereafter worship Śakra;
one should fashion an image of Śakra made of gold or of clay.
In the absence of all [other materials], however, one made of clay produced from another metallic source—
having specially worshipped that in the center of the mandala— 23.
