Then, at an auspicious moment, the king should raise the banner, saying:
"O wielder of the thunderbolt, slayer of the enemies of the gods, many-eyed Purandara!
For the sake of the welfare of all worlds, please accept this worship. (24)
Come, come, O Lord of the immortals, wielder of the vajra, praised by all the hosts of gods and siddhas!
Having arisen at the first watch of the night, accept this worship; O Blessed One, homage to you! 25.
Thus, by means of the *uttaratantra* [teachings] such as burning, flooding, and so forth, and by means of this mantra and tantra, through various offerings and enjoyments, [one attains success]. (26)
One should worship for the increase of prosperity with faultless milk-rice, drinks, molasses, parched grains, and various kinds of foods both to be chewed and eaten. (27)
In the jar, however, one should worship the guardians of the ten directions and the planets,
as well as all the deities beginning with the Sādhya, and all the Mothers, in their proper order.
Then, at an auspicious moment, accompanied by the master craftsman who was skilled in knowledge,
he went to the site for the raising of the banner (ketu) to the west of the sacrificial altar.
The king should go together with Brahmins and family priests who bring great auspiciousness,
[carrying] the image along with its mother, bound by five ropes and fixed upon a mechanical frame.
It was joined by young maidens and by the banners of the world-protectors,
which were large, exceedingly beautiful, and well-filled with various articles.
It was joined with nets of small bells, clusters of large bells, and chowries, and was draped with cloths of various colors arranged according to their respective positions.
It was adorned with mirrors and various kinds of excellent garlands,
as well as many fragrant flowers and decorated with a necklace of jewels.
One should raise the great banner slowly and steadily with royal attendants, using four archways adorned with gathered garlands and cloths.
Having risen, one should lead that image— which has been worshipped within the mandala— to the base of the great banner (mahāketu), while meditating upon Śakra, the lord of the banner.
There, as before, one should worship Śacī and Mātali, as well as his son Jayanta, the thunderbolt, and Airāvata. (36)
Then he should also purify the planets, the guardians of the directions, and all the host-deities with offerings such as cakes, as well as oblations of milk-rice and other foods.
One should constantly perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the deities who have been worshipped;
at the conclusion of the oblation, one should offer a sacrificial gift (bali) to the high-souled Vāsava.
O best of men, one should offer oblations to the gods with sesame seeds, clarified butter, unbroken rice, flowers, and likewise dūrvā grass, each with its own respective mantra.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas;
in this manner, one should worship daily for seven nights, day after day. (40)
Accompanied by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
the king was celebrated everywhere at the sacrifices and in the worship of Śakra.
This mantra, "trātāram," is the supreme favorite of Vāsava;
having thus performed the initial ceremony for the awakening of Śakra during the daytime.
On the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, specifically during the final quarter of the night when the moon is in Bharaṇī, the king himself should dismiss Śakra.
If the king does not see [the deity] being dismissed while all the worlds are asleep, he shall meet death within six months. || 44 ||
Therefore, O tiger among kings, a king should not look at Śakra;
this is the mantra for dismissal uttered by those who know the ancient lore. (45)
O Purandara, O Śatakratu, together with the hosts of gods and asuras,
take this offering and go to the great banner of Indra.
When impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, or on a Tuesday or a Saturday,
or during portents such as an earthquake and the like, one should not dismiss Vāsava.
In the event of a portentous calamity or the appearance of a celestial disturbance, one should wait for seven nights;
having passed those days, and avoiding Saturday and Tuesday, one may perform the dismissal even under another lunar mansion.
But when the period of birth-impurity has arrived and that impurity has passed,
one should dismiss [the deity] on whichever day it may be, at the conclusion of the impurity.

Likewise, O tiger among kings, the king should protect the sacrificial banner (ketu) as long as birds do not alight upon it; for until its dismissal, O tiger among kings, the banner must remain protected.
One should lower it very slowly, just as it was raised at the beginning;
if it is done otherwise when the banner is broken, one shall meet with death.
O King, one should cast the Śakraketu, adorned with ornaments, into deep water at night while reciting this mantra.
"Stay, O Ketu, highly fortunate one, for a year in the water, you who are the destroyer of obstacles for the welfare of all the worlds. (53)
One should raise it amidst the sounds of musical instruments before all the world;
one should dismiss the banner in private—this is the specific distinction regarding its worship.
Thus, whoever performs this worship of the high-souled Vāsava shall enjoy the earth for a long time and attain the world of Vāsava. || 55 ||
In his kingdom there shall be no famine, nor shall there ever be mental afflictions or physical diseases; nor does untimely death occur among the people there. (56)
O King, there is no other beloved equal to him even for Śakra;
his worship is the worship of all, and Keśava and the others are present therein.

The worship of the banner of Śakra, which removes all impurities, destroys disease and famine, establishes all prosperity, and brings about every auspicious fortune, is performed by those dwelling in the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
One should worship [it] with many offerings every autumn for the increase of prosperity. || 58 ||
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 87 ||
The eighty-eighth chapter.
Aurva said:
O King, hear now of the sacrifice to Viṣṇu on the Jyeṣṭha-daśaharā day, and by what ritual procedure it is performed.
The king should always perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
Every year, the king should have an image of Hari made, whether it be fashioned from gold,
or from other precious substances, or even from wood or stone.
Having had it installed according to the rules by artisans using the proper measurements,
one should perform its formal consecration according to the ritual through Brahmins and family priests.

Having installed that [image] in a temple for the gods, or having one built with effort by himself, according to the previously mentioned procedure and with the seed-syllable (bīja) of Vāsudeva; || 4 ||
One should worship Vāsudeva with devotion using all ritual offerings.
At the conclusion of the worship, the twice-born man, standing in the middle of the sacrificial pit, [should perform the rite] in the consecrated fire.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva and performed the fire-oblation, the twice-born man should then offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter, which is dear to Hari.
With the king's permission, one should lead that image to the mandala;
having touched both cheeks of the image with the right hand.

O best of kings, one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) for the deity Hari within that [image]; indeed, once the installation of the vital breaths has been performed, [the deity becomes truly present].
The vital breaths of Viṣṇu will certainly enter that image of their own accord;
and once the vital breaths have entered it, its divinity will certainly be established.
As long as the consecration has not been performed, and in the case of images of living beings,
the state of being Viṣṇu does not exist in gold and other materials, just as it was before.
O King, the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) must also be performed for the images of other deities in order to achieve their divinity.
Gold remains gold, stone remains stone, and likewise wood remains wood;
everything else always retains its own essential nature, except for the locus of the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should perform the consecration of Hari with the seed-mantra of Vāsudeva, namely "tad viṣṇoḥ," as well as with the mantras of the limbs (aṅga) and the principal deity (aṅgin).
In the same manner, the knower of mantras, having placed his thumb upon the heart,
should perform the installation even in the heart while reciting these mantras.
"May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths flow forth! For the sake of counting [her] among the deities, svāhā!"—uttering this sacrificial formula (*yajus*). || 15 ||
One should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) everywhere in all images by means of the *aṅga-mantras*, the *aṅgin-mantras*, and Vedic mantras. (16)

In the worship of an image, the knower of mantras should first perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) within himself as well, for the sake of purifying the portion of the worship.
No wise person should perform the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) in this [image] except for the purpose of worshipping the image; having done so, one would meet with death. 18.
Having performed this sacrifice for Viṣṇu on the tenth day, that best of kings should then install the image on that very same full-moon day.
Thus, by performing a sacrifice to Hari on the Daśaharā day,
a king attains all his desires and becomes free from obstacles.
On the auspicious Pañcamī day, one should always worship the goddess Śrī with kunda flowers,
as well as Vāsava, who is seated upon the king of elephants, with the most excellent offerings.
The tantra of Lakṣmī and the great mantra previously declared for Vāsava are also to be employed here in the worship, as well as the mandala and other elements in their proper sequence.
When worship is performed in this manner, especially on the auspicious Pañcamī,
the king shall become endowed with prosperity and shall not suffer any loss of fortune.
O King, this specific excellence of right conduct has been told to you;
now hear the specific prohibitions by which one seeks prosperity.
Without having first worshipped Viṣṇu, Śiva, Agni, and Indra, and likewise without having given gifts, a king should never eat at any time. (25)
He should cause the Agnihotra sacrifice to be offered constantly by his domestic priests;
for by failing to perform the Agnihotra and yet eating, one would fall into hell. (26)
The king should never sleep in an unprotected house devoid of jewels and lamps; likewise, he should never lie down with a woman.
Having eaten food, a king should not eat the śrīphala fruit, nor the dhātrī fruit;
for these, as well as black gram, liquor, and clay, cause the loss of intelligence. (28)
The leaves falling from the nimba and āṭarūṣa trees are considered to increase the intellect;
therefore, a king should always avoid those things that cause the decline of the intellect in his food. (29)
The best of kings should eat every day that which causes the increase of intelligence;
however, a king should not mount his throne without having performed the ritual circumambulation.
He should not mount a vehicle, an elephant, or a horse without a low seat;
nor should a king ever travel alone, even in a desolate place.
One should never consume food that causes intoxication,
nor should one ever indulge in meat or sexual intercourse on the eighth lunar day.
O King, one whose father is living should not perform the Darśa-śrāddha, the Gayā-śrāddha, or the libation with sesame seeds; by performing them, he incurs sin.
A king should never consecrate sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others in the kingdom when a legitimate (*aurasa*) son exists, for the sake of the perpetual purification of the ancestors.
The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son—these sons are entitled to a share of the inheritance. (35)

The son born of a pregnant bride, the son received with a wife, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the slave—these six are the defilers of the lineage of sons. (36)
In the absence of all those mentioned previously, one should consecrate the descendant of a later generation.
However, one should not appoint a son born of a remarried woman, a self-given son, or a slave to the kingship.
Even sons such as Datta and others, though born from the seed of another, attain the status of true sons when they have been consecrated according to the rites of one's own lineage. (38)
O Lord of the Earth, a son who has been consecrated through his father’s lineage up until the end of the tonsure ceremony does not attain the status of a son from any other source. (39)

If the sacraments, beginning with the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), are performed according to one's own lineage, then those sons—such as the "given" son (datta) and others—are considered [legitimate]; otherwise, he is called a slave.
O King, after the fifth year has passed, having taken back the sons previously given away and others,
one should first perform the Putreṣṭi sacrifice for a five-year-old son.
One should bring back the son born of a remarried woman as soon as he is born;
indeed, having performed the Paunarbhava-ṣṭoma sacrifice for him immediately upon birth— || 42 ||
A man should perform all the purificatory rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
When the Paunarbhava-ṣṭoma sacrifice has been performed, the son is known as a Paunarbhava.
One should perform only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for one's father, not the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha or others;
a woman who has been purchased with prices is called a slave-woman (*dāsī*). (44)
The son born of her is known as a *dāsa-putra* (slave-born son);
he shall not share in the kingdom of the king, nor shall he perform the *śrāddha* rites for the Brahmins. (45)
He is the lowest among all sons; therefore, one should avoid him.
[One should study] the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Saṃhitās proclaimed by the sages. (46)
A king should not, at his own will, allow Śūdras to teach those [texts] prescribed for them;
in whose kingdom Śūdras always [teach] the Purāṇa as well as the Saṃhitā, [that kingdom perishes].
It is recited that such a Śūdra, whether out of delusion or through desire, shall have a short life, and the king, along with his lineage, shall be deprived of his kingdom. (48)
The evildoer who recites that which is prescribed for Śūdras, or whatever mantra has been extracted [from the Vedas], goes to hell together with his ancestors. (49)
Indeed, the Śūdras must always accept both of these from the words of the Brāhmaṇas;
for the king may appoint a Śūdra to oversee legal proceedings.
Having appointed him there, the king is cooked by him in Tāmisra;
furthermore, the people or even the king himself shall suffer a diminished lifespan.

A king should not appoint as his domestic priest one who is missing a limb, one who has no son, one who lacks supernormal knowledge, one whose senses are uncontrolled, nor one who is short of stature or afflicted by disease. (52)
A king should never seize the wealth of a miser;
likewise, he should not bestow even vast amounts of riches upon the twice-born. (53)
A king should never mount an elephant that is lustful or mad;
for by mounting such an animal, he suffers both in this world and the next.
A king should never perform an action that shortens his lifespan;
rather, he should always strive with all his wealth for the increase of his life. 55.
O best of kings, one should not apply collyrium or oil, nor consume betel leaf or food, on a cruel day (Tuesday), nor on the eighth or sixth lunar days.
The king himself should not look at an eclipse of the moon or the sun that is very slight or total, nor likewise at the sun when it is red.
Whatever portentous occurrence arises—whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric—the king should avoid looking at it with effort; having seen it, he should furthermore not eat for three days.
One should always wear the auspicious jewel together with dūrvā grass;
one should not show one's uncovered body to Brahmins. || 59 ||
One should not perform a sacrifice in water, nor eat meat on the sacred festival days (parvan);
one should not mount a donkey or a camel, nor even a left-handed pregnant woman.
Thus, a king who employs this method, increasing his fourfold army and constantly protecting himself, should always augment his own valor. (61)

One should constantly avoid food, drink, and beverages that cause the destruction of the vital seed (semen), as well as alkaline substances, leafy vegetables, and those that are excessively sour or excessively bitter. 62.
One should avoid water contained in vessels of bell-metal or silver, as well as water from a river that has been stagnant; such water increases urine, diminishes virility, and should be shunned.
Water kept in vessels made of copper, iron, gold, or lead, or in a fruit or a hide, increases semen; one should therefore consume it with diligence.
For one who abides in all the fundamental duties and in virtuous conduct,
having enjoyed various pleasures here in this world, he shall go to the supreme station of Indra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus did Aurva, the bull among sages, instruct Sagara in all the scriptures as well as the rules of right conduct and domestic rituals.
He recounted it many times to the high-souled Sagara;
there was nothing that had not been told to Sagara by Purūrava.
The policy of kings, the conduct of the virtuous, and whatever else originates from the scriptures— whatever is established in the Saṃhitās, the Purāṇas, and the collection of Āgamas.
Sagara heard all of this from the mouth of the wise Aurva;
however, O best of the twice-born, only a small portion of what was told to them has been extracted here.
Formerly, in private, I spoke of the science of statecraft and right conduct, which is in harmony with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
O best of the twice-born, constantly behold the secret of Viṣṇu; whatever has been proclaimed elsewhere that is contradictory or accompanied by doubt [should be disregarded]. (71)
O twice-born ones, the cutting away of doubts regarding those [topics] has been told to you.
The Purāṇa named Kālikā, which cuts away unspoken doubts, should be constantly practiced by a Brahmin; he shall obtain the fruit of the Vedas. (72)
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 88 ||
The eighty-ninth chapter.
The sages said:
"In brief, the conduct of the virtuous and the specific principles of statecraft [have been explained]."
I have heard from your words how Aurva spoke to Sagara.
Furthermore, in the Viṣṇudharmottara Tantra, abundance is found everywhere;
one should observe the proper conduct and behold those [teachings] through his grace.
Furthermore, there remains a doubt that you have not previously mentioned;
O best of Brahmins, resolve it, for we ask this because our curiosity is great.
"It is heard in both the Vedas and the world that there is no destination for one who has no son.
Long ago, Vetāla and Bhairava went to the mountain for the sake of ascetic penance."

O best of the twice-born, those two had not yet performed the marriage rite; nor have their sons been heard of—whether they were never born, or if born, whether they were many or few. I truly desire to hear about them and that supreme abode.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O virtuous ones, it is certain that there is no destination for one who is childless;
indeed, those who possess sons—whether their own sons or the sons of their brothers—have gone to heaven."
O Brahmins, those two wise ones, Vetāla and Bhairava, have fathered offspring;
I shall proclaim their lineages, so listen, O great sages! (7)
Having attained complete success, when Vetāla and Bhairava reached the temple of Hara on Kailāsa, they were filled with great joy.
Then, O brahmins, at the word of Hara, Nandin spoke these true words in private to the two of them, acting as an enlightener while speaking with consolation.
Nandi said:
"O sons of Śaṅkara, you two shall become childless until the birth of a son;
for one who has obtained a son, a favorable state is easily attained everywhere. (10)
One who is deprived of a son beholds a hell named Punnāma;
neither by ascetic penances nor by righteousness is he able to liberate himself from it.
From that alone—the birth of a son—liberation arises;
therefore, may you two produce a son among the divine beings.
Your immortality, however, arose from drinking the milk;
for it was because of Kātyāyanī that her sons became immortal and equal to herself. (13)
Therefore, by whatever means possible, having produced sons born from the wombs of gods,
you two shall before long become dear to Śiva and Śivā in their abode.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having heard these words of Nandin, their minds were pleased, and they both spoke to Nandin, saying, "We shall do exactly so."
Then, having constantly kept Nandin’s words in their hearts,
those two wandered here and there, making efforts for the sake of their son.
Then once, that Bhairava beheld Urvaśī, the most excellent of apsarases,
exceedingly beautiful upon a plateau of the Himavat mountain.
Then, becoming lustful, he begged her for the festival of sexual union;
and because of her profession as a courtesan, she was well-pleased and spoke to him as he desired.
Then Bhairava celebrated a festival of love with her;
as the goddess Urvaśī was delighted, he became supremely joyful through their amorous sports.
When Urvaśī was well-pleased, through the splendors of Bhairava,
a son was born instantly, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun.
But Urvaśī, having abandoned that son, went to her own abode;
afterwards, Bhairava took the child and went to his own place.
Having performed the purificatory rites for that son, Bhairava, filled with joy and accompanied by the lords of his hosts, gave him the name Uveśa.
Then, once he had reached maturity, they consecrated him, who possessed a splendor equal to Śakra and the Sun, in the sovereignty over the Vidyādharas.
That lord of the Vidyādharas, however, took as his wife the daughter of the Gandharva king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was exceedingly beautiful.
From her was born his son, the charming Ruru by name;
and from Ruru, Bāhu was born of Mainākī.
Bāhu had four sons: Tapana, Aṅgada, Īśvara, and Kumuda;
the youngest, however, was Manohara, born of Cārvatī. || 26 ||
To Kumada was born a son of great strength named Devasena;
that charming Devasena, having descended to the earth, [reigned]. || 27 ||
He repeatedly sought Keśinī, the daughter of Māndhātṛ Yauvanāśva, as his wife—she who possessed delicate limbs and was like an Apsaras. (28)
Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, also gave his own daughter Keśinī to Devasena out of a desire [to fulfill] the word of Śakra. (29)
Then, having married Keśinī, Devasena, together with her,
propitiated Hara, the auspicious Śiva, in Vārāṇasī, the city of Śambhu.
Hara was propitiated and, being pleased, granted him the boon he desired;
he too received from that Hara exactly the three boons he had wished for.
As long as the sun shall exist, so long shall his lineage endure;
and those of my own lineage shall likewise hold sovereignty in this very city.
"You shall always remain well-disposed toward my lineage.
Having thus received this boon, that highly virtuous Devasena [departed].
By the grace of Śaṅkara, he enjoyed that city for a long time;
then Devasena begot sons upon Keśinī.
Listen, you all, to these seven who have been proclaimed by name:
Sumanas, Vasudāna, Ṛtudhṛk, Yavana, and Kṛtī. (35)
Nīla and Vivekin—these indeed were all experts in every scripture;
they were all excellent sons of Devasena who continued his lineage. || 36 ||
Then, when the time had arrived, Devasena also, having entrusted the kingdom to his son along with his wife, departed for the abode of the Vidyādharas.
Thereupon, having installed Sutanu as their king, all his sons,
headed by Vasudāna, enjoyed supreme prosperity.

Three sons were born to him who were well-disposed, heroic, and possessed of great strength: Sumati, Virūpa, and Satya, all of whom had reached the further shore of the meaning of the scriptures. (39)
From Sumatī was born a daughter, and from Satya was born a son, Diṇḍima.
From Virūpa was born Gādhi, and from Gādhi was born a son, Mitra.
Kalpa was their king, and from Kalpa, Vijaya was born;
he, having conquered the entire earth and all the kings of great splendor.
With the permission of Śakra, he [Agni] made Khaṇḍava one hundred yojanas in extent;
for that which the powerful son of Pāṇḍu, Savyasācin, burnt brought supreme satisfaction to the high-souled Jvalana (Fire). || 42 ||
The sages said: "How did that Vijaya make the Khāṇḍava forest one hundred yojanas in extent?
We wish to hear that; tell it to us, O you whose wealth is asceticism. (43)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: In the Lunar dynasty there was a king of great strength and prowess, named Sudarśana, who was wise, handsome in form, and majestic. (44)
Not very far from the Himalayas, he indeed cleared away a great forest,
driving off lions and tigers, and in some places even the ascetics whose wealth is their penance.
There he built a beautiful city named Khaṇḍavī,
thirty yojanas in width and one hundred yojanas in length.
It was provided with high walls, equipped with watchtowers, water-channels, and arched gateways,
and was completely surrounded by very deep and exceedingly long moats.
It was unassailable by other heroes, crowded with various people,
and filled with long ponds, many groves, and throngs of celestial nymphs.
It was filled with gardens and also with excellent men; there, the people were constantly engaged in festivities, as if they were gods dwelling in heaven. (49)
Filled with joy and endowed with primordial enjoyments, they vied with one another;
that King Sudarśana, having dug and torn open the earth... (50)
He caused the divine Gaṅgā to flow through Kanakhala and Khāṇḍavī;
having flooded the middle of Akhāṇḍavī, he did so by means of the channels and paths excavated there.
Having followed crooked and winding paths, he proceeded toward the river Sītā;
he had conquered all the kings and brought back vast quantities of wealth.
The king brought people from other cities and established Khāṇḍavyā in the center, adorning it with numerous jewels. || 53 ||
The skillful Sudarśana, having repeatedly conquered the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas in battle, forcibly settled [the people] in Khaṇḍavī.
That king Sudarśana planted the celestial tree, the divine jewel, as well as the goddess and the medicinal herb in Khaṇḍavyā.
Viṣṇu indeed [spoke] to that King Sudarśana, who had committed many offenses against both the gods and men. (56)
He joined the heroic Vijaya, the lord of Vārāṇasī who was resplendent with victory,
to battle, having secured his assistance in that enmity.
Having gained an opening, Vijaya, possessed of great strength and prowess,
then launched a surprise attack upon King Sudarśana.
Sudarśana could not endure that assault by Vijaya;
he quickly turned his face toward the battle with his fourfold army. || 59 ||
Vijaya, having mounted his chariot and marshaled his fourfold army,
then quickly came face-to-face to fight Sudarśana.
Then there occurred a great battle between the high-souled Vijaya and King Sudarśana, like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
The valiant Rumaṇvat, mounting a golden chariot, advanced toward Vijaya at the head of Sudarśana’s armies.
Seven akṣauhiṇīs surrounded him on all sides;
with his weapons raised, he scattered that entire enemy army.
And Sañjaya, the commander of Vijaya’s army and conqueror of enemies,
seized Rumaṇvat along with his troops by means of an elephant division.
A great battle took place between those two heroic generals;
then Rumaṇvān showered Sañjaya with a rain of arrows.
Then, letting out a great roar upon seeing the elephant,
Keśarin pierced Sañjaya with twenty arrows, and Rumaṇvat likewise struck him.
With a razor-sharp arrow, he [Duryodhana] cut through the bow of that skillful-handed warrior;
he too, taking up another bow, then struck Sañjaya with three arrows.
He pierced him with arrows and, in that very instant, cut his bow with a broad-headed shaft;
he also destroyed eight hundred and five or six thousand elephants.
Saṃjaya swiftly struck down three thousand foot-soldiers and horses on all sides with his most terrible showers of arrows.
Then Rumaṇvat, taking up another bow and becoming exceedingly enraged,
struck off the head of that charioteer from his body with a broad-headed arrow.
With four arrows he sent his horses to the abode of Yama,
and he also pierced Śaṅkha with five arrows.
Saṃjaya also, taking up his mace with extreme speed,
instantly descended from the seat of his chariot and rushed toward Drumāṇvant.
Rumaṇvat, with swift hands,
covered the fleeing Sañjaya with a shower of arrows and held him back.
Having warded off that shower of arrows by the whirling of his mace, he fell upon Rumaṇvat like a lion upon a great elephant. (74)
Having reached that heavy mace and whirled it with great force, Sañjaya crushed him along with his chariot with a single blow. (75)
Struck by the mace, that great hero fell upon the earth like a blossoming śāla tree in the middle of a forest struck down by a thunderbolt.
Seeing Rumaṇvat fallen, King Sudarśana was overcome with grief and anger, like a fire enveloped in smoke. || 77 ||
Though his body was agitated, he blazed forth, intensely possessed by anger;
having mounted a chariot yoked with swift horses and covered in tiger-skin.
Mounting his chariot with its variegated golden parts, adorned with the lion-banner,
he took up his strung bow and stretched it again and again.
Accompanied by his army, the swift king rushed toward Sañjaya;
then, with his sharp weapons, he fiercely struck the vanguard of the host.
The king slaughtered that entire vanguard division of immense prowess, just as the lord of beasts slays deer. (81)
Like the sun dispelling the darkness, he struck down [the enemy] for two *krośas*;
having slain an entire *akṣauhiṇī*, the king then approached Saṃjaya.
He pierced him with sixty arrows and cut down his banner with one;
then Sañjaya, having pierced Sudarśana in the heart with twenty arrows, [struck again].
Then, with great dexterity, the powerful king struck him in the forehead with a single arrow;
having severed the monarch's bow with a razor-edged shaft, he [struck again]. (84)
Then Sañjaya pierced the charioteer with ten arrows;
thereupon King Sudarśana took up another bow. (85)
He rained down a fierce shower of arrows upon Sañjaya;
between the two of them there occurred a great battle that caused wonder even to the sages. (86)
With weapons and missiles that were exceedingly sharp, like those of Bali and Vāsava,
King Sudarśana then firmly struck his bow with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla).
He cut down his charioteer and struck him with sharpened arrows;
then Sanjaya, the slayer of enemy heroes, himself restrained the horses.
Taking up another bow and surrounding Sudarśana,
he pierced him with ten arrows and cut asunder his firm bow.
Taking up his bow, King Sudarśana sent Sañjaya’s four horses to the abode of Yama with his arrows.
He cut the bow from Sañjaya’s fist and pierced him with five arrows; deprived of his chariot and his horses slain, Sañjaya took up sword and shield.
Taking [it], he rushed forward in great anger toward the presence of the king;
then Sudarśana, with a razor-sharp arrow, [struck] his bow and sword.
Then, with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he cut it in two and likewise sliced through the shield;
thereafter, Sanjaya quickly approached that excellent chariot.
Sudarśana, however, felled Sūta with his two hands onto the ground;
as Sañjaya approached the chariot, Sudarśana [struck him].
Then he severed his head with a sword, and it fell to the earth;
that one of great strength then fell down near his chariot. 95.
Like a flowering śāla tree cut down by an axe in the forest, seeing Sañjaya fallen, Vijaya was overwhelmed with rage. (96)
Making the vault of the sky resound with the great blast of his conch shell,
he proceeded in a chariot variegated with gold and adorned with tiger skins.
Then, with his banner-bull raised half a yojana high,
he caused all the quarters to resound, surrounded by a multitude of chariots.
Discharging showers of arrows,
King Vijaya, the slayer of enemy heroes, approached and assailed that king Sudarśana.
Having pierced him in the heart with three arrows, he cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Sudarśana also [struck] Vijaya, who was roaring like an elephant.
Having pierced it with ten sharp arrows, he cut that bow asunder;
then, [he struck] him whose bow was broken in the region of the collarbone with three arrows.
Then, having pierced through him, Sudarśana let out a great roar;
taking up another bow, he [struck] with three heron-feathered arrows.
The hero Vijaya also pierced Sudarśana in the heart;
then, aiming at that king, he hurled a great, blazing spear.
He saw a Naga maiden filled with wrath, licking her lips as if insatiable,
holding a golden-staffed spear with an extremely sharp point, polished with oil and perfectly stainless.
Then Vijaya, having raised it up, hurled it toward the enemy;
that spear indeed entered the heart of Sudarśana.
Overwhelmed, he sat down on the floor of the chariot with his face cast downward;
and while King Sudaśana was thus fallen into a state of unconsciousness, [the battle continued].
O best of the twice-born, the king slew all those soldiers who stood before him as well as those at his side in a mere moment.
Ten thousand chariots, an equal number of elephants, and twenty-five thousand swift horses. || 108 ||
He destroyed two hundred thousand foot soldiers in a mere instant;
then, regaining his senses, he took up a firm bow.
Sudarśana showered Vijaya with a rain of arrows;
but Sudarśana, having warded off that rain of arrows with his own, [overwhelmed] Vijaya.
With a broad-headed arrow (bhallena), he instantly severed his strung bow;
then, with another broad-headed arrow, he struck off the charioteer's head from his body.
And he dispatched four horses of his toward death;
then, having thus deprived the king of his chariot, [he struck him] with ten heron-feathered arrows.
Sudarśana pierced him again in the heart and let out a roar;
with his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, he swiftly took up a mace.
Vijaya, desiring victory, rushed toward Sudarśana;
Sudarśana, showering a rain of arrows, [rushed toward] the great hero who was charging at him.
Just as a cloud pours rain upon a mountain during the rainy season,
Vijaya indeed covered that shower of arrows with his own shafts.
At that very moment, Vijaya approached him with his mace as he stood upon his chariot;
having reached that one of great prowess, Sudarśana, Vijaya then [attacked].
Striking him on the head with his mace, he felled him to the ground,
like a lofty mountain peak shattered by a thunderbolt.
Likewise, King Sudarśana, shattered by the mace, fell down;
when that hero had fallen, his soldiers fled with their armies. (118)
Fleeing from him in fear toward the cardinal and intermediate directions,
when his armies had been destroyed, Vijaya [entered] the city of Khāṇḍavī.
Having entered, he beheld there heaps like mountains,
as well as numerous collections of gold and jewels.
Having seen there the lakes filled with blossoming lotuses, resounding on all sides with the cries of swans and kāraṇḍava ducks; || 121 ||
He saw heaps of gold and jewels as vast as mountains,
and celestial trees in full bloom, adorned by wandering bees.
He saw vast, brilliant palaces resembling Mount Kailāsa, as well as elephants stationed in every house, in full bloom and rich with fragrance.
With eyes wide open, King Vijaya, the slayer of enemy heroes,
considered that city to be like Amarāvatī itself descended to the earth.
Approaching that king as he was departing for the city, the Lord of the Gods addressed him with words of victory, consoling him with gentle speech.
Indra said:
"O King, this was once a great forest, filled with hosts of gods, enchanting to Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and sages. (126)
Having driven away all the gods and others, he who delights in doing what is displeasing to me has destroyed this secret grove and exterminated those whose wealth is their asceticism.
"King Sudarśana forcibly turned the city of Khāṇḍavī into this very forest; therefore, O best of men, you must restore it once again. (128)
There I shall dwell in private with Takṣaka;
and by your grace, O King, this incomparable place of asceticism for sages shall also become the abode of Yakṣas and Kinnaras.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of Śakra,
Vijaya then spared that Khāṇḍava forest out of respect for Śakra.
"O people, let all of you go to your respective places as you desire; or, if there are those among you who wish to come to my kingdom again. (131)
"Let them go to Vārāṇasī, which is protected by me alone.
Having heard his words, some people [went] to their own abode. (132)
Some went to Vārāṇasī, which was protected by Vijaya;
then they [received] those heaps of wealth and jewels, each set apart individually.
Vijaya likewise blocked the city of Vārāṇasī with various kinds of jewels, gold, and base metals.
And that which was formerly brought by force from the Gandharvas and the gods—namely, the precious wood and so forth—having propitiated Vijaya, [one should use] that. 135.
And they, being greatly delighted, led Khaṇḍavya to his own abode,
which was thirty yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long.
Before long, Vijaya indeed turned that city into a forest;
there, with the consent of Śakra, Takṣaka dwelt together with his hosts.
He dwelt there for a very long time, and thereafter that forest became desolate;
there, the gods along with the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases sported.
And they hoped for victory that brings triumph in battles,
when the twenty-eighth yuga had arrived at the conclusion of the Dvāpara age.
The Fire-god, in the form of a brahmin, begged for alms from Jiṣṇu;
and when the son of Pāṇḍu had consented to give the alms, [the god spoke].
Assuming his own form, Vahni spoke these words to Jiṣṇu:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, I am Agni; [I have come] because of your excessive consumption of the portion intended for the ignorant. (141)
"I am afflicted by disease; therefore, destroy my illness now.
[Go to] the forest named Khāṇḍava, which contains birds, beasts, and rākṣasas."
O Śvetavāhana, if you are able to feed me,
then this disease of mine will indeed depart before long.
In former times, King Vijaya, having destroyed that city named Khāṇḍavī, established a forest there; therefore, it became known as the Khāṇḍava forest. || 144 ||
O Śvetavāhana, this forest was ordained by the gods for my sake;
however, due to opposition from Śakra, I do not venture to enjoy it myself.
Therefore, O illustrious one, protect me and employ me in that forest, so that by your grace I may be able to consume it all. (146)
Having heard those words of his, the mighty Savyasācin caused that entire forest, together with all its living beings, to be consumed by fire.
Protected by Vāsudeva, the son of Devakī, he,
devoted to the welfare of Agni, caused the Khāṇḍava forest to be consumed by fire.
Being well-pleased, Agni gave to that high-souled Arjuna the bow Gāṇḍīva, fashioned by the gods and belonging to Varuṇa. || 149 ||
Two divine, inexhaustible quivers, four horses rich in beauty, and the great monkey-banner presided over by Hanumān. || 150 ||
And the Fire-god gave a sharp, three-pointed sword to Savyasācin;
likewise, by the grace of Jiṣṇu, the Fire became free from disease. || 151 ||
With those arrows, with that bow, with that sword, with that banner, and even with that horse and chariot, Phalguna conquered his enemies. (152)
Thus, King Vijaya, born into the lineage of Bhairava and possessed of great majesty,
established the forest named Khāṇḍava.
Thirteen sons of great strength were born to Vijaya:
Dyutimat, Saumyadarśin, Bhūri, and Pradyumna; || 154 ||
Kratuṇḍa, Virūpākṣa, Vikrānta, and then Dhanañjaya; Praharṣa, Prabala, Ketu, and another, Uparicara. (155)
The king of these was the heroic Śeṣa Uparicara,
who in ancient times performed a hundred thousand sacrifices in the city of Vārāṇasī.
There has never been, nor will there ever be,
any highly fortunate king on earth who performed a hundred thousand sacrifices like the illustrious Uparicara.
This entire world is pervaded by these [beings] born from birth after birth;
what man on earth could possibly count them all in the course of time? (158)
Gradually, these three worlds have been pervaded by the lineage of Bhairava.
O brahmins, this progeny of Bhairava has thus been recounted to you. (159)
Having heard even a mere fragment of their story, a man is never born sonless;
indeed, whoever shall recite this meritorious life-story of Vijaya, [shall likewise obtain such fruit].
Victory shall always be his and never defeat, for he who listens to this supreme teaching with a one-pointed mind;
there shall never be a break in his lineage. (161)
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 89 ||
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of sages, listen now to the lineage of Vetāla.
Having heard which, one is instantly liberated from all sins. || 1 ||
And Dakṣa had a daughter known by the name Surabhi;
she was the highly fortunate mother of cows and the benefactress of all the worlds.
From her, a daughter was born of Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny;
she was named Rohiṇī, radiant and the granter of all desires to men.
From that sage Śunaḥśepa, who possessed great ascetic merit,
there was born a cow renowned as Kāmadhenu, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Resembling a white cloud, she has four feet in the form of the four Vedas;
with her four breasts, she brings forth dharma, artha, and kāma.
In the course of time, that virtuous woman, her body golden-hued,
attained a stainless and enchanting youth, like a wish-fulfilling cow.
As she was wandering on the summit of Mount Meru, beautiful in form and endowed with auspicious marks, that Vetāla saw her and, filled with desire, approached her.
Recognizing that Vetāla was lustful, Kāmadhenukā herself,
according to the custom of cattle, united with that son of the Moon.
The son of Śaṅkara experienced supreme delight in her,
and she too, being exceedingly joyful, attained the highest pleasure in him.
When their sexual union had proceeded, she then became pregnant;
and when the time arrived, Kāmadhenu gave birth to a great bull.
In a very short time, he became a truly great bull, endowed with a massive hump and possessed of beautiful horns. || 11 ||
With his pair of ears twitching and his long tail raised,
he appeared like a white cloud with its hump, two horns, and two ears.
O twice-born ones, he was seen by the gods as he moved like the White Mountain with its peaks;
the Vetāla gave him the name Śṛṅga.
That Śṛṅga, possessed of wisdom, propitiated the Lord;
and the Lord Hara, being pleased, granted him the desired boon.
Having assumed the form of a bull, he made that very [bull] his vehicle;
he was long-lived, powerful, and capable of supporting the earth. || 15 ||
He of great splendor, named Śṛṅga, became the banner of the Lord;
for he was considered as Śṛṅga by the high-souled Śaṅkara. (16)
Therefore, Maheśvara then proclaimed his fame as "Śṛṅgin";
and he, Śṛṅgin, [remained] while Mahādeva was occasionally absorbed in meditation.
Having gone to the house of Varuṇa, he fully enjoyed in amorous dalliance those daughters of Surabhi who were endowed with beauty and youth. (18)
O Brahmins, in the house of Varuṇa there are cows endowed with all auspicious marks; they dwell there eternally, and from them are born their offspring once again.
And many [beings] were born from their offspring and descendants;
this entire world is pervaded by them, and from them the sacrifice proceeds. (20)
The gods are satisfied by clarified butter; sacrifices are established upon clarified butter.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is dependent upon sacrifice. (21)
Clarified butter (ājya) depends upon the cow; therefore, everything resides in the cow.
O best of the twice-born, this entire universe likewise depends upon the cow.
And those cows are the lineage-descendants of Vetāla, always dear to him;
whoever should constantly hear this [account] of the high-souled Vetāla, [shall attain his favor]. || 23 ||
O best of Brahmins, his lineage shall flourish; he shall be happy and powerful, and neither his cattle nor his wealth shall ever perish.
Neither spirits, piśācas, nor other such beings ever behold him;
the Vetāla himself constantly provides protection for him. (25)
Thus, O Brahmins, I have related to you how Vetāla and Bhairava procreated sons; your doubts have been severed.
And how the goddess Kālikā deluded Śaṅkara, and how she was born so that half of Śambhu’s body was made her own—just as it happened. (27)
For him who himself utters, "Salutation to you, O Kālikā," liberation rests in his hand, and the three goals of life follow under his command.
Thus has been narrated to you this meritorious Purāṇa called Kālikā, consisting of mantras and yantras, pure, bestowing knowledge, and supremely granting all desires. (29)
Thus, O twice-born ones, this is the most secret thing in the world and likewise in the Vedas;
it is always to be coveted by the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and others.
And this supreme, immortal Purāṇa called Kālikā was studied from me by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha in the past. (31)
"All this was protected by him in Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods;
O great seers, that [protection] has now been fully described and made manifest. (32)
You too must never give this to anyone in the worlds,
nor reveal it to the deceitful, the fickle-minded, the atheist, or one who has not conquered their self.
This should never be given to one devoid of devotion and faith;
however, whoever should recite this Purāṇa named Kālikā even once— (34)
Having obtained all desires without exception, he shall attain immortality in the end—[he] in whose house this supreme Purāṇa is written. (34)
O twice-born ones, he for whom no obstacle ever arises remains forever steadfast—he who studies this supreme, secret tantra day after day. (36)
O best of the twice-born, all the Vedas have been studied by him here;
therefore, there is no other wise man who has accomplished his purpose superior to him. (37)
He becomes a happy cowherd in this world and is also born long-lived. || 38 ||
He who is the Lord of the world, who constantly sustains it,
who protects it, and who likewise brings it to an end at the conclusion—
[he knows] all this, whether it be delusion or non-delusion.
And salutation be to Him whose form is beyond description. || 39 ||
May that Lord Viṣṇu, the primordial Puruṣa whose manifold expansion resides in the hearts of yogis, who is the sovereign of the Purāṇas—he, the auspicious one, be gracious unto you. (40)
He who is the cause, the fierce one, the ancient, the eternal, the everlasting, the supreme Lord;
the creator of the Purāṇas, known through the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
I praise and bow to that which remains at the end of the Purāṇas. || 41 ||
Thus she who supports the entire world,
who deludes the Enemy of Madhu in her form as Ramā,
and who delights Hara in her form as Śivā— [she is the one].
May Māyā bestow upon you prosperity and auspicious things. || 42 ||
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter in the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa. || 90 ||
Thus ends the glorious Kālikā Purāṇa.
